I have played the game for a couple months but due to it being way too much fun I found myself spending too much time playing it which reflected on other aspects of my life.
However, I can really say that this game is probably the most underrated MMORPG out there. The incredible amount of activities you can pick from combined with the amazing art style (though this might be a matter of taste for some) are just the beginning of the depth that this game delivers. I've decided to list up all the things I've personally found to be standing out (listed in no particular order):

WildStar is an underappreciated game marred by an uncertain future. If you game to play rather than to invest, consider giving it an opportunity to impress you.
WildStar is beautiful. It's got varied and luscious landscapes. Its peculiar, exaggerated art style that is reminiscent of American cartoons like The Flintstones or The Jetsons, uplifted into three dimensions, and modernised with shading and wider color palettes. Its objects (characters) animate with satisfying articulation, and its particle effects tinkle, shimmer, glitter and wash confidently. My Cassian esper ambles with an adorable, upbeat gait. Its music spans the genres.
WildStar is expansive. Its got huge zones in which to quest and to explore. So much so that treating each quest hub as an all-you-can-take drive-thru can get exhausting after a few times.  It has a crafting system that provides milestones to let you progress through it selectively, and lets you build variants of things by applying secondary ingredients to your recipes.
WildStar combat is kinetic, and finely toes the line between being too simple and being too complex. For many abilities, explicit selection/targetting is optional. Harmful (and beneficial) effects are telegraphed by outlines projected in the world, making visual aiming and avoidance reasonable. Combat abilities are limited to sets of 8 player-chosen actions. Action sets may be swapped out of combat.
In WildStar's technical performance I found its weakest link. In most questing locations, framerate stays above 50 fps.  But, in capital cities, the game is unable to render their complexities without dipping below 30 fps at times. The game client supports user mods, and is in fact implemented as a multitude of official mods, many of which can be overriden by user-created replacements. Some of the official mods are buggy and/or CPU-intensive.  Some with features/panels may unexplicably stop working after a few hours of play, and require a /reloadui to bring back to working order.  I found the general Lua framework as flaky today as it was (and still is) in WoW. Mod writers stop playing, mods break, or become unstable, etc. An unsatisfactory, unpredictable experience. My system: Intel i7-6700K with dual GTX 980s in SLI.
Various conjectures circulate as to why WildStar has failed to keep the interest of players even during its post-P2P transition. I won't regurgitate them, but rather contribute the notion that slapstick science fiction is far from the ideal genre to cultivate long-term interest from a market that ostensibly prefers heroic escapism without pervasive and unrelenting caricatures. (I suspect, too, that what passes for humor in the game might be too literate and harmless by contemporary standards.) If you're willing to let that artistic choice slide, even for just a few hours per week, and for however long yet the game stays on, you might find the WildStar's enlightened mechanics, visual and musical splendor, and smorgasbord of stories and quests worth the time to experience.

Delver is a neat little rogue-like game that has a lot of potential.
PROS:
++ The 2d artstyle mixed with the first person perspective give it a fun look
+ Environments are pretty and neat
+ little notes along the way give bits of different stories to the history of the place
Neutral:
Randomized stat progression as you level up
No real tutorial/mechanics not explained
Still plenty of bugs (out of place textures, mobs floating into the ceiling but still able to hit you)
CONS:
- - Adds nothing new to the genre. Aside from the artstyle, it's the same as any other roguelike you can play
- A lot of useless items
- cannot sell items
- HEAVY on the random side. about 80/20 luck/skill ratio to getting through the game.
All in all it's a fun re-hash of rogue mechanics that is pretty and can keep you entertained for a bit. Has a lot of promise to be very fun, I just feel like it's missing something to make it really stand out.
Plays into fond memories of ultime underground

Well, what can I say - the game follows the events happening in Syria now, you are a dad who's trying to find his kid by going from one side of the map to the other, fighting/chatting/robbing/breaking in/picking up everything and everyone you think worthwhile, killing a boss in the end to go the next map. That's the whole game in a nustshell.
The game is fun at times and quite challenging - you can develop your attributes (mental, physical, agility, etc.) they will influence how likely you are to break into a house or to gather berries from a plant, you drag your trusty cart with you and it serves as your working bench, kitchen, in other words you use it to make new stuff from the resources you find.
Every new game is random so it has a very high replayability value. I can say that I really like that game at first, but I stopped playing it at stage 2 - too much fighting which isn't really interesting (fortunately you can hand it over to the PC), but still I'd prefer a bit more intellectual challenge.  It also makes you favor the "kill em all" approach as there's no way to ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t your way past the bosses.
The story itself is very shallow and generic - at least from the what I've seen so far - but then again, I'm spoilt by what they call "story-rich" games where game developers actually try to make you care and believe in the characters whose lives you supposedly control.
I'd give it a "meh", but it's worth it's salt and maybe I'm just being too hard on this one. A nice game, give it a try.

This passage taken from a discarded poem found in one of the cabins is actually a successful definition for the game itself. A sense of isolation, desperation and abandonment are the building blocks of
, a minimalistic psychological horror by David Szymanski. I've been meaning to play this for a long while, and finally managed to spare an undivided hour to complete it, which is a prerequisite of completion since there is no save game feature. The game is intended to be played in one sitting of an hour, and all there is to explore would fill that hour completely anyhow. The definition of my experience was an effectively uncanny environment mixed with a bit bleak story revelation.
The game starts in complete darkness, in a warehouse that resides on a shore line, and there is no one else besides us. We learn that
. We start walking, exploring the island and try to put things together through reminiscences of our character. By gameplay function, this is a walking simulation since there is nothing else to do rather than explore. So no monsters to jump at you if you are in expectancy of a "big bad wolf coming at you" scenario.
The island itself isn't that big; but the howling wind, the approaching darkness and constant clouds of dust establish an appropriately plain yet ominous setting. I wouldn't call graphics anything extraordinary - minimalistic even - but the choice and display in decoration combinations are in artistic value to set the mood. Added with a sorrowful soundtrack, there is no doubt that we exist in an ultimately forlorn geography without a clue to any happenstance and feel that isolation, that helplessness every second of our one hour gameplay.
On story purposes: aside being quite successful in atmosphere,
either fails to explain much, or intentionally leaves matters unspoken. In either case, anecdotal memories or vague dialogues exchanged by intended characters don't reveal much aside a single act of desperation that would either doom or salvage the former inhabitants. There is no explanation for the purpose of the island, or how people ended up being there in the first place. As it is, this game feels like a glorious demo which would promise for things to come. I heard that there could be some explanation for the background in David Szymanski's next game,
which I didn't play yet. If so, I strongly recommend playing two games back to back to track a complete story.
Do I recommend it? Yes, for observing a complete success on establishing an atmosphere with too little in graphics, but on narrative achievement, I must say that I've seen better. For your half a dollar, it is a good experience. I'll be keeping an eye for more David Szymanski games in the future.
Now that I've completed
, I'm positive that these two games should be played back to back. In unison, they form a beautiful story, the tale of a creation and its undoing. Buy them together, enjoy an age old story in some really radical context!

You wake up in the small side apartment on the second floor. The radio talks nonsense, there’s no food and all your neighbors are now scary pixelated monsters. It’s hard to tell if they have become zombies or some other♥♥♥♥♥♥has happened to them. The game isn’t heavy with going on the specifics of what is actually happening. This is an abstract story of a nameless protagonist, swallowing pills that change his dreams and exploring the building and its nearest surroundings.
Going outside is dangerous and challenging. Monsters can kill you easily; avoiding them is the preferred course of action. Ammunition is scarce. Rooms and corridors are dark. Batteries for the flashlight don’t last long. On top of that the character has to eat and sleep. And take those pills before having psychedelic dreams in which he talks with a man wearing a box for the hat.
A deconstructed version of classic survival horrors, Lone Survivor keeps only the most core features of them. 3D world is among them. This is a rare for 2D metroidvanias, most of them use a door for nothing more than a couple of completely separate rooms. Lone Survivor makes use of its scene. Corridors go around the floor, intersect with each other and make a dense maze that you have to study. Two sections of hiding in the shadows, turn to the left, then to the right, enter the gaping fleshy hole in the wall, find the new key, some canned fruit salad or even another survivor. So, no, you’re not really lone. But at least you’re survivor. You’ve got that gas can for the stove. There were a few very scary zombies in that dark corner where you’ve found this can, but you’ve managed to pass them unnoticed. Tonight you’ll eat some cooked ham. Who knows if you’ll be that lucky tomorrow?
Packing a lot of action on such relatively small map makes the game tense. The best compliment for a survival horror. The requirement of enough variety and challenge forces most metroidvanias with the flat world map to resort to some kind of red herring like gigantic elevators in Metroid. It’s a neat way of separating the parts of the world and still preserving the integrity of it. Extravagant ride on the carriage with undead horses in Bloodborne is essentially the same thing. Of course it’s more noticeable this way. You can now separate the “main” part of the world from this one. What you didn’t notice yet though is that “main” parts consists of such “separate” ones. Their connections are more believable. They could be one level from a technical standpoint, they could be separate ones — it doesn’t matter. You can still percept them as a whole. Lone Survivor is very careful with its level design. Architecture may make no sense when put in the actual 3D perspective, but the protagonist seems to be delusional anyway.
A small geographical anomaly is easy to overlook when you try to precisely target a zombie slowly coming at you. Perhaps, even easier than the supposedly unexpected subplot-which-was-the-actual-plot-you-fool. The game rather mimics the melancholic tone of Twin Peaks than its mystery; to the point that it manages to end anticlimactically. Those green, red and blue ending sequences are still better than their counterparts in Mass Effect 3, but they too are nowhere near the legitimately scary journey through post-apocalyptic nightmare that has preceded them.

Silent Hill has surely cast one of the longest shadows over the horror genre. Few major studios have attempted to capture its success with psychological horror (and not even Konami themselves can regain what they had), but indie developers are always ready to attempt their own thought-provoking thriller. Lone Survivor sticks about as close as you can to the Silent Hill legacy without calling down a lawsuit on itself, but the retro presentation and more immersive mechanics help make it a worthy game on its own.
You are cast as the last survivor of a mystery plague holed up in a decaying apartment complex. Uninterested in dying alone, you set out from your safe space to find someone, anyone, to share your company. Unfortunately, the whole place is overrun with gangly, fleshy abominations that would just love to eat your masked face. Owing to the retro 2D style this plays out more as an adventure game than even the restrained action of Silent Hill. Combat is something to be avoided if at all possible, taking alternate routes or skulking around with your flashlight off, or creating distractions with rotting meat. However, you can't get through the game without some fighting. Your weapon of choice is a handgun which you can fire straight, upwards, or downwards, and the enemies take some interesting locational damage. It's a good combat system supported by an intelligent balance of combat and sneaking.
Having your face eaten isn't your only concern, however. Your character gets hungry and tired as well, and you have to scavenge for supplies to keep yourself going. You'll find bags of chips and tins of beans along with more suspect foods, and as the game progresses you can combine foods for different effects and even do some rather involved cooking. Sleeping is necessary (and is also how you save your game), but coffee and pills can keep you running and have some additional interesting effects on gameplay. It's an interesting consideration to add because items are finite but you grow hungry and tired over real time, so you have to constantly be moving the story forward. After some early uncertainty I've come to really appreciate this mechanic, because it pushes you to forge ahead into the darker, more threatening areas in search of food. It adds a genuine sense of urgency that helps justify the terrible risks your character takes.
All of this is held together by a fantastically dark atmosphere, but one not without its holes. Most areas are VERY dark without your flashlight, but light attracts the creatures. The whole complex is rotting away, and there are far more sinister things taking the place apart as well. The sound direction is excellent, with uncomfortable cues for the monsters and some excellent atmospheric pieces while exploring. The writing is good, though I feel the atmosphere does take a bit of a hit when your character is speaking with certain... things. I think I know where the story is going with these elements I won't expand upon, but for now they feel a bit out of place. Additionally the low-res look doesn't always work in its favor, sometimes making things look a little too cartoonish or obscuring something that would otherwise appear horrifying.
These are just small nitpicks, though. Lone Survivor takes its inspiration from Silent Hill and runs with it, creating its own atmospheric experience that terrifies and intrigues. I knew I had played something solid when I finished an hour session around midnight, my wife asked me to check on the laundry in the basement, and the hairs on the back of my neck stood up. Yeah, I think I'll check it in the morning, thanks.

This was the game that introduced me to the 2D survival horror genre. And while the idea of a lone guy in an apocalyptic world with zombie-like-monsters is seen too many times already, I would like to point out that that is not the highlight of the game. The highlight of the game is the sanity of our character, and thereby your sanity. The things that happen in this game are illogical (even by psychological game standards), and it hints at the story outside of our character's head. You will find yourself questioning most of what happens in this game like:
Is there really an apocalypse?
Is the characters you stumble across people from our protagonist's life or just reflections of his own mind?
And what is up with that ending? (No matter what ending you get, this one counts).
To top that off I think that the art style is wonderful, the controls are nice and the soundtrack is plain up amazing.
I will say that your hunger and sleep meter could have been presented better than just the game spamming you with messages, but all in all I love this game. It is definitely one of my favorite survival horror games, if not my favorite.

There will be references to WoW, swtor and maybe few other games. However I dont claim this game to be "wow/x-killer" at all. Just comparisions.
IF you want to know about optimsation, skip to the end.
-I've played wildstar from the start. I was in beta and bought the game in first months. Raptr says -I've about 1000 hours on this game total.
-I've played bit less on F2P but I am familiar with all the changes to stuff it made.
-I played wow from vanilla to end of cata, then few months of pandaland till I quit. Between end of cata to end of pandaria (2 years or so) I tried everything to get back into that MMO-drive.
Swtor, tera, GW2, aion, allods - you name it.
Let me start by saying Wildstar is MMO I actually want to play. Usually I cant play MMO  games but so far only Wildstar and WoW has made me stick longer than 50 hours.
WS has the charm, it has the flow, it has the community, it has enough stuff to do for me.
Combat:
WS is "Healer, Tank, DPS"-mmo.
Tanks:
Warriors (2hand, plate, smashy)
Stalkers(rogue/thief, stealth, avoidance)
Engineers(medium-range "shotgun", pets, plate armor)
Healers:
Esper (Ghostly-"mage", builds combos, lot of target heals)
Spellslinger (pew pew 2pistols, aimed heals with dps/heal combo skills)
Medic (medium range, steady overtime-heals, pew pew)
DPS: All of them can be DPS!
Only casts that has to be targetted are some heals, even most heals have to be "aimed".
You dont choose target and press 1 - 2 - 3 to cast abilities. Also your "autoattack" is a build-up skill, not automatic white damage.
You have to "aim" at the target and infront you get telegraph that shows area that the spell will be affected. But unlike some MMOS, there are no awkward crosshairs that you have to aim or melee where effective area that is size of bean where being in wrong angle breaks your dps.
For melee this basically means all attacks are cleaves and for casters it means your pew pew will tends to hit in straight line. If you are melee you have less reaction time to dodge incoming enemy attacks and usually have to run further to avoid big booms. But have easier time to aoe-cleave mobs infront of you vs "straight line" positioning.
And most of the leveling is balanced around that. You tend to get 1-3 mobs at you. But unlike swtors "heroic combat" or WoWs "accidentally overgeared to OP" where mobs die in two seconds but are huge in packs, WS mobs give good challenge what you expect from leveling. Oh and there IS group-content while leveling from the start!
Combat is also more fast-paced. In cooldowns 60 seconds is a lot. Thats usually your class-trait. For warriors you get big and smashy, reset damaging spell's cooldowns and with infinite "rage" so you dont have to build any. For stalkers you get 3 stealths (dps, tank and "life-steal"(leveling/pvp)). Other CDs go from 2, 4 up to 11. Not more usually.
CC is usually broken either by waiting (usual MMO-fashion) or holding down either W, A, S or that D.
While QTEs are annoying in most games, it kinda adds whole new layer here. Break faster the faster you smash button. Skills *swoon*
One of the coolest things is having action-bar-sets. While you have lots of skills to choose from, you can only bind 8 of them. It makes most fights always different on how you play. Some need more mobility, some dont need interrupts at all, some need CC breaks. Every skill also has "point system" where you can talent the skills to do cool things. Like mobility having 2 charges, whirlwind pulling enemies to you so they have to walk more to get out, heals will heal more if you risk standing still whole cast etc. There is also PvP/Utility skill-tree.
Enemy side:
Typical MMO-fashion there are enemy autoattacks. These cannot be avoided unless you stun or CC the target or are DPS in dungeon. These hit for basic amount of damage, as expected.  You still get damaged but if you avoid/interrupt telegraphs you wont get MASSIVE DAMAGE.
Then there is telegraphs from enemies as well. Red (default color) means the enemies attacks will hurt, usually a lot.
Combat and teamwork:
Wildstar was done to appeal for hardcore-crowd. While this has massively changed since launch, some elements still remain on teamwork-side.
When I played WoW there was one thing that people just could not simply get right. Interrupting and positioning.
On Wildstar these 2 elements are important. Positioning is something you will have to start learning to git gud. Looking at reds, seeing where they go, where they spawn.
As for interrupts.. mobs have to be interrupt by almost whole team in order to avoid those red kabooms. Why? Because mobs have "interrupt armor". So you cant rely on one warrior or stalker to interrupt all attacks all the time. Enemies tend to have 2-3 (5-man content) or 20 (20-man content) armor's that you have to use your interrupts. All classes tend to get 2 interrupts, some 3. So interrupting and watching casts is also something people need to learn pretty fast. There is dungeon that teaches you this in painful way (dont interrupt at all = wipe).
"So just interrupt each cast and stunlock them?" - as usual to counter that, most enemies are interrupt- and cc-immune.
Housing:
Youd think F2P game with housing would have almost all the housing objects as microtransactions. But it doesnt. While costing lot of in-game money if focused, housing is done RIGHT. You can make it whatever you can imagine. I have mad max styled wasteland with sci-fi twist, my alt is building cyberpunk town, my friends have huge forests that look like you stepped into actual area of the game. Underwater, Mario party, Alice in wonderland, towns, bars, tea-temples, mazes, mini-games, hoverboard parks.. and thats just one part of it.
Rest:
Mounts - Loads
Pets - Loads!
RP - Works well because in player-housing! Its going and there are channels and addons for finding more. Want some private time? Put your house friends only and do .. whatever you do, cupcake. Or have open-for-all metal consert.
PvP - so and so, queue times are what you expect from MMO (30mins to hour :( ). If you are pvp-nut the game is cool but might not be for you at those wait times. Has few BGs and Arena mode. Ranked on both. NO ONE plays warplots (40v40 massive BG), even if its daily pvp quest. Its legend someone has step foot in it since beta.
PvE in short - Dailies (basic stuff), Expeditions (easy solo to 3man content), Adventures (Easy to medium-difficulty 5man story-dungeons), Dungeons (5-mans, medium to "haaard"),
2 raids (1 inc soon) (20man, very competitive to WoW's raiding),
World bosses (people ACTUALLY DO THEM. Well mostly due dailies but still), world events etc .. Need to help friend quest? WS has system where you can CHOOSE to get scaled to their level so you wont oneshot everything for them.
Addons:
What most MMOs besides WoW fails to provide, addons. Wildstar has pretty open API when it comes to devoloping addons. So there are loads of them. However pre-warning is needed here. Most addons are old. Like before-F2P-old. Sadly a lot of addon devs quit the game before F2P and that leaves the community to update the addons. Which in some cases it has done well. But for example most Auction house addons are still pre-F2P and that makes me, AH-nerd, sad.
You can also disable games UI elements yourself. Dont want that quest log and go HC? Disable it! Dont need social windows? POOF!
For new player I recommend addons such as:
TapThat (if QTE's are not your cup of tea. Does NOT remove stun QTEs), Chatlinks, KuronaBags, almost any questlog addon to replace bloated default one.
Optimisation:
The game runs kinda eeeh. Its CPU heavy game and in most systems you have to lower the settings a lot. AMD is still having trouble on the optimsation.
If you want to make the game run better: Disable WHO addon, Get ANYTHING that replaces default questlog, disable combat-log and turn spell effects low.

Quests. Dear god, quests. That is all this is, it seems. That one fact makes me want to cry. It feels like alot of love and care went into some parts of this. In the end the one thing that will over shadow all of it - is the quests.
The real issue I found was that there is no reason to get at all invested in them story wise, or for that matter - in any way. Quests in this game are like killing mobs is in any other game. You will pick up a quest, and chances are before you even get to the quest location you will have picked up 10 more and done 5 of them without even trying/knowing. This would be like in another game a quest telling you to go kill a mob, and you just happen to kill 10 others on the way there. There were times my quest log would have 57 missions and 32 of them were complete and I just needed to go back to where I got them to turn them in, but in the process of turning in a quest I would end up with 5 more on the way.
My other issue personnaly was detachment - the way the game flows everything felt detached from any level of character investment - In most games you would kill a generic mob and move on, that mob may have not had anything built into it, but it existed and was a seperate entity. In this game, every mob just feels like part of an ant hill and gives the same level of detatched investment as accidentally stepping on an ant on the way to the ant hill.
Beyond this the game feels pointless in the realm of character development. The skill trees are very lacking and by level 20 the future looks VERY bleak. I made the mistake of creating an engineer first - You will hold down button 1 from the start of the game to the end, not because it is the best attack, but because to do the other attacks you need to fill up your bar, which use of that attack does. The sound of that gun shooting is nightmare fuel after about an hour. To top that off, when you use a skill, you cant really be doing other actions, they all have cool down timers and attack timers and the way they collide makes skill variance seemingly pointless - especially when you have attacks with long attack times or that have to bechanneled.
That being said, I created a rogue (screw you, its a rogue - it cloaks and backstabs) and it seemed much more fun, focusing on being hidden and quick alpha strikes of crazy high damage. I enjoyed this much more than the engineer, but the other issues with the game are making it very hard to want to continue.

Magicite has a great concept and decent execution, however it is held back by bad game design choices which limit it's replaybility and fun.
The game is a rogue-lite and utilizes semi-randomly created  platform levels, the point of each level is to get to the end of the stage. There's 20 stages in each run and between each run there's a mini-hub town that serves as a resting point. Prior to each run you create a character by picking a race, items and pets once unlocked.
Each stage has 1 passive animal and about 2-3 enemy types, which gets quite repetitive very quickly.
My main issues with the game are:
- No save method in between runs, once you start you are locked in and games usually take me 45-55 minutes to complete. You have to commit to this game, as quitting halfway through will result in nothing.
- Characters, hats, and pets (each with their own distinct bonuses) are randomly unlocked (ie. 20% to unlock a new character once game is complete).  This forces multiple artificial playthroughs in the hopes of an unlock, and since you're playing with the same characters with limited choices on similar levels versus the same enemies, it's not fun
- Combat is quite bland, there's 4 or so weapon types (1 handed swords, two handed swords, staffs, and a bow) and any differences are purely cosmetic/stat wise. You choose 3 magic skills when leveling up and most of them are not fun or useful.
- The game handles healing in an odd way, forcing the player to eat food every couple of minutes for a 50% chance to heal 1 HP point or take a rare and hard to find healing potion (for 2 HP or 5 HP if you farm two potions). Most enemies will do about 4-8 damage per hit.
- There is basic item crafting, yet the crafting menu is atrocious and with a severely limited storage space you'll find yourself running out of room quite quickly
- The game has a weird love affair with random number generators- upon leveling you MAY or MAY NOT gain any stat points and again - not a fun game design choice.
Overall, the game is limited by it's love for RNG and poor game design choices. There's very little depth to the game and an artificial barrier of difficulty as you hope to get a lucky roll when leveling or unlocking new items. Nothing carries over between saves or playthroughs, aside from characters/hats/pets which may or may never unlock after multiple hours.
Would not recommend unless it was wicked on sale.

Legends of the Alliance is a free companion app to the board game Star Wars: Imperial Assault, a tactical strategy game set in the Star Wars universe. If you don't own that game, then this app is useless to you. If you do have it and are interested in playing it solo or co-op, there's really no reason not to try this.
In a nutshell, this app controls enemy behaviour. It will provide multiple options for each enemy to do in descending order of priority. It does it pretty well, all things considering. It's not going to be perfect and you're practically guaranteed to make mistakes, but it's still a fun time if you just go with it and can get past the QoL issues.
Pros:
+ Solo / co-operative play
+ Enemies are worth killing
+ No unforgiving time limits
+ Interesting missions
+ Item shop is more consistent and doesn't rotate after each mission
+ Rebalanced item costs, items now sell for the full purchase price
+ Character upgrades are unlocked sequentally after missions instead of requiring XP
+ Brand new campaign
+ Steam version isn't as horribly optimized as the phone version...
Cons:
- ... but it's still got some poor performance issues
- No undo button
- Very little compatibility with most of the Ally and Villain packs
- No support for the core or any of the expansion campaigns
- Only one campaign
- No AI skirmish mode
- Sometimes relies a little bit too much on the player to do things
- Seriously the game needs an undo button
- Tells you which tile numbers to take out but doesn't show you what they look like
- Often doesn't show certain parts of the map so you can't get it ready all at once
- Proper party composition can completely crush the enemy AI
* At the time of writing this review, this app is still an early build. Hopefully more compatibility / campaigns are added, but until then I'm counting these points as cons.

If you're more of fan of historical Paradox strategy games like Europa Universalis, Crusader Kings, or Hearts of Iron, I would highly recommend downloading an overhaul mod that sets the game in a sci-fi universe, like Star Wars, Star Trek, Mass Effect, et cetera. This makes the geopolitics at game start more dynamic and asymetrical, just like other Paradox games.
If, however, you're more of a space 4x fan and like games like Masters of Orion, Imperium Galactica, or Sword of the Stars, I'd recommend setting the number of civilizations in your galaxy to about 80% of the recommended value, because otherwise it ends up feeling like there is very little time or space to enjoy the explore phase of Stellaris.
Essentially, it feels to me like Stellaris is trying to be both types of games simultaneously, but falls short a little bit of the hype and its goals in its initial design. I guarentee though, that with the numerous inevitable expansions, it will undoubtedly improve tremendously.
Either way, it is an enjoyable game in its own right, even if it won't be able to fill the Masters of Orion shaped hole in our lives.

Alright for all those who are complaining the ships are too agile... Have you done any research? Flanking was possible in naval warfare, the issue was that on open ocean- where most naval battles happened- you would have at least 5 miles of sight at any given time, making it extremely difficult to flank- but most of the flanks happening in this game occur on the island maps where people can duck out of your los with the small numerous islands.
As for an actual review to this game each ship plays so differently that I dont think 1 blanket statement would cover it so:
Aircraft carriers- A sort of crappy rts rip copy. That is not to say it isnt fun, it has to be my favorite ship class as a matter of fact, why? Because I love the RTS genre of course- it is also equipped with the best AA equipment.
Submarines- I don't believe I am the right person to be writing this portion but whatever: the submarines in this game operate in a nice way- if I had to say honestly its either them or aircraft carriers that have the highest skill cap- the submarines have to pay attention to a handful of things when they play more so than other ships- depth, oxygen, where enemies were last seen, distance from enemies, speed/oxygen/distance, when best to surface- probably the most engaging submarine play I have ever used in a game before
Battleships- ah yes WW2 the age of the battleship (technically the dawn of the aircraft carrier but whatever) this is the ship I first planned to use and with much good luck, you aim your guns safely from behind a wall of friendlies while they/scout planes figure out enemy locations. Heavy Cruisers + Anything else I mightve missed- I haven't played these ships types, I fell in love with aircraft carriers and just stopped every other research tree

The Moon Sliver seems to be deeply tied to the The Music Machine -- including their story.  Now that I have played both (I actually started with The Music Machine), I can't help but make comparisons between the two.
In general, the horror in The Music Machine starts as visceral and later gives way to the more cosmic/intellectual; in The Moon Sliver, the progression is basically inverted.  For each game, the final type of horror in focus is also the type most effectively realized.
Compared to The Music Machine, The Moon Sliver's mechanics feel clunkier, its playtime much shorter,  its visuals less stylized (and, ultimately, less beautiful), and its setting alien yet largely unremarkable.  In short, The Moon Sliver is clearly an earlier, cruder effort.  At the same time, however, TMS's narrative somehow feels more natural and its gradual building of a sense of dread--leading to and through the excellent climax--more effective and better-paced than TMM's.

Play Length: One complete playthrough.
Positives: A great indie horror game, which takes a lot of influence from Silent Hill 2 and David Lynch.  Putting those influences through a retro filter creates a pretty unique and interesting horror experience.
Let's talk about the graphics.  The retro style can certainly work for a game like this, and I think it's a decent style.  It's heavy pixellated, even more so than most retro inspired games.  It's a bit of a peculiar look, but the abstraction works pretty well to create atmosphere.  The music is uncommonly good for an indie game... I would go as far as to say that this is the best soundtrack in any indie horror game, excepting maybe Corpse Party.  This is important, because a good soundtrack is vital to creating atmosphere, and Lone Survivor is much better at creating atmosphere than just about any other indie horror game.
The gameplay is very good for this style of game.  It has combat and stealth elements, both of which is very simple, while at the same time always presenting the player with choices.  A lot of the game is just exploration, monsters aren't all that common.  There's also some fun survival mechanics, as you have to collect food and manage your hunger and sleep levels.  There's a huge amount of food, all of which has different effects, and you can also cook meals if you can find cooking implements.  There's also drugs you can take, with various effects.  I like that these various systems add depth to this game without feeling out of place, or distracting from the atmosphere.
The story is very much in the mold of David Lynch / Silent Hill.  It works pretty well, and there's some pretty good set pieces and imagery.  You're never quite sure exactly what is going on, but you know enough to stay involved.
Negatives: While the graphical style is decent and works for the game, I think it could have been done better.  Sometimes the game's art can border on amateurish.  This is obscured by the heavily pixelated graphics, but I still noticed.  While I like the gameplay in general, one thing I felt that was a little lacking was the monster variety.  There could have easily been a greater variety of monsters, and it would have added more depth to exploration as well as keeping more surprises for the player.
About my rating system: I have two things I rate on.  The first is the overall score, and the second is soundtrack.  The reason why is because I feel like soundtrack is tremendously undervalued; to me, it's a tremendously important factor in whether I like a game.  For the score, I grade on a scale of 1-10, and I try to grade in such a way that each number has a meaning and each has equal importance.  The numbers have the following meanings:
0: Garbage, 1: Awful, 2: Poor, 3: Underwhelming, 4: Mediocre, 5: Decent, 6: Good, 7: Great, 8: Excellent, 9: Phenomenal, 10: Masterpiece
Lone Survivor's score:
Game Rating: 8 (Excellent)
Soundtrack Rating: 8 (Excellent)

Ah, Lone Survivor, a 2-D retro survival horror game that makes most of nowadays "horror" games feel ashamed. It's not the spookiest, but it's definitely tense as all hell.
First off, I'm gonna say, the difficulty of this game is truly remarkable, even on normal mode. Normal mode on other modern survival horror games basically holds your hand for the whole playthrough, with a puzzle now and then to hinder your progress, or they are rather linear. This game is hard. First, you get tired AND hungry at times. Second, food items might be common, but mostly ♥♥♥♥♥♥ ones. You can scavenge for food, cook it, collect water dripping from the ceiling with a bucket, stuff like that.
Third, and my favorite, what made games like the first Resident Evil true masterpieces:
Not enough ammo for every single enemy that you come across. So, you gotta play smart, hide from the monsters, distract them, use items, basically, you gotta think before you waste even a single bullet, because if you do, you are going to regret it later on.
I can describe this game for common folks with a single sentence. "It's like Silent Hill but 2D". That's what most of the ones that have played this game use to describe it. The story has something to do with the outbreak of a disease that turns people into some kind of faceless zombies that wander around all the time. You are locked inside of your apartment, and that's pretty much how you survived, but now you gotta find a way out of that dreaded building, having to face tons of enemies with just a few bullets, so to speak. The game's got multiple endings, so there is that, too.
This game might be short-ish compared to other stuff I've played before, but it's definitely worth it. It's nothing short of frustrating at times. The game starts nice and slow, but once you reach the basement, you can actually feel the difficulty spike going up your♥♥♥♥♥ Hard. No lube. I played wildstar since it was in beta, but not long on steam. Wildstar is probably the best MMO out there in many ways I'd like to go through the Good, the Bad, and the Unfortunate things about this game, because I want you to understand that  I think it's a shame the way it all turned out.
The Good
The combat is plain fun and challenging, the dungeon and raid content is superb, the pvp is robust, movement is crisp, I could go on. Those who played WoW in the burning crusade will remember karazhan, likely fondly, as the best entry level raid in any tier in WoW's history. Wildstar made a similar move with the first dungeon players encounter at level 15. See, wildstar's combat isn't trivial like all the other MMOs out there. There's a lot of skill involved, and it gets to be a bit more complicated than just "don't stand in the fire" and "interrupt the guy" -- The first dungeon acts as a brilliant introduction to the encounter mechanics one can expect in Wildstar, and lays out the roles of each player type properly.
At level 20, you move on to the first "real" dungeon. Again, anyone who's played WoW will understand here: This dungeon was the most challenging normal content I've ever seen in an MMO. The first dungeon you're dropped into in wildstar is on par with a Heroic Dungeon in WoW. Wildstar doesn't insult your intelligence or skill with mind numbingly simplistic dungeons and combat mechanics. It's a thrill to play, and I hope you get the chance to check it out.
The Bad
So what about wildstar is bad? Biggest thing: The interface. It still needs cleaning up after all this time. It's messy, and I really wish the game had been pushed back a bit just to clean it up. They seem to have neglected it after all this time, not to say the game has been neglected, mind you.
Also? The population size. You need a community for an MMO to function properly, and Wildstar's size has dwindled significantly. Maybe the world is burnt out on mmos, sure, but I think there's a bigger reason at play here.
The Unfortunate
Wildstar launched just before warlords of draenor, when a bunch of people got hyped to play WoW again. When people started feeling nostalgic for WoW and WoD launched, they jumped ship and quickly got burned out on WoW, never to return to wildstar. Had Wildstar waited for after WoD's launch, we might be seeing a more robust game right now. Another huge problem: subscription. Now, you'll notice the game is free to play now. That's because they abandoned the subscription model. In my opinion, they should have avoided subscription from the get-go.
These two things tied together hamstringed wildstar's capability to get its feet off the ground and become the thriving MMO it really deserves to be. Maybe it's not too late and it will come back to us, I hope so, but I can't hope too hard.
All in all, never have I seen a game so deserving of praise and recognition be so deprived of it. I hope you give it a try, and then maybe we'll see this game rise again.

WildStar. Where do I start? ABOUT HOW AWESOME THIS MMO REALLY IS. Yeah, it got some flak in the beginning, might have even lost some players, sure. Players. Do yourself a favor and check it out again. I played like a madman in the beginning and am now back into it. This is one of the best MMOs out there and let me tell you why.
- Free. To. Play. And NOT pay to win! Not by far! This will be one of the first games where you play and not feel restricted from the lack of going "signature." The signature bonus' are nice and can speed things up if you want that, but trust me, you could stay F2P the entire time and not even feel it.
- TONS to do and an enormous world to explore. Level solo the whole way, if you want. Keep playing through zones once you're maxed, if you want. There are 3 continents and a moon to explore with more quests than you'll ever see in a single game in your entire life. Oh and TONS of lore. Like, TONS.
- Dungeons, raids, world events, world bosses, adventures, expeditions... And most with a Veteran variety. Yup, lots right? Well, let me tell you something; this is one of the first MMOs where I felt I could jump on, get some end-game content in with some raid-status rewards and not feel like you were locked into it for 1+ hours. The world events and bosses alone give you tons to do and there's always groups going. Or you could just raid, there's those too.
- Dailies, daily zones, contracts, daily zones and daily zones. LOTS of dailies here. More than you'll know what to do with. A good thing. Arcterra will be one of your new homes. Contracts are something new and unique to WildStar. Look at them as daily bonus'.
- A STRONG player base. I've been playing straight for the last 3-4 weeks. It only seems to be getting busier and busier. So don't let anyone tell you this game is dead. Far from it. Even if it is lower population, the community is great. Find yourself a good guild and just play. This game isn't going anywhere for a long time. Don't let the Steam "people playing" numbers fool you. Steam can be kind of buggy with WildStar and most players seem to be playing on the original client, downloaded from the website.
- COOL microtransactions. The in-game store is neat and it has all kinds of stuff. There's kick♥♥♥♥♥rewards as you spend more and more currency in it too! So far, it's♥♥♥♥♥♥♥my wallet.
I could go on and on, but I think you get my point. It's free. So try it out, you won't regret it. See you on Nexus, cupcake.

Review:
Immersive gameplay,outrageously fantastic models/graphics/ambience, captivating sounds/music, and  rich with dynamic interaction and objective driven storylines. Plenty of time, and real estate to farm/grind if you wish get a little OP before moving ahead, but also complimentary of it's own chronological progression if you want to aggressively move through the game's main story. In terms of extras, the enchanting, blacksmithing, and training are all worthy addons that don't feel like an afterthought as they do in other games; and fishing is a nice little touch. Once you have "fished-out" all the currency (shadow tokens) it doesn't really serve a purpose, but that was ok for me. My only negative critique is that some of the champions aren't very useful. They feature fun abilities, great graphics, and have plenty of personality, but ultimately fall short in combat effectiveness. At the end of the day,  I've paid a lot more for a lot less because of hype etc. This is a GREAT game. NOTE: I suggest playing with a controller if you have one. Works fine with a keyboard, but it's just a bit clunky.

TL;DR : Cover based shooter, decent AI, its as hard as you want to make it, good customization, some scripted events, solid above average game, and play on Elite if you think its too easy. I think you'll get your money's worth ON SALE.
I bought this game on sale a year or two back and after considering buying it for a friend and seeing the reviews (recently) I was a little disheartened. So I won't disparage anyone's views, but here is my own personal take on playing the game through multiple times single player, coop with 2 others, and coop with one other.
The game is a solid shooter and I had no trouble using mouse and keyboard to take out enemies as needed. Gunplay is solid, and it feels nice. The weapon customization is pretty deep, nothing crazy, but it is there. I personally liked battle rifle setups as its an in-between of sniper/assault that let me kind of be an all round.
The cover system in this game is standard, and I heard complaints of the stealth being "Too good" as in near invisibility. Thing is, later in the campaign and on harder difficulties (my friends and I played on hardest difficulty) you will be glad you have it. A lucky shot from an enemy and you're down. One member K.I.A. (Which we heard a lot at first) and its back to checkpoint.
The A.I. being called alright is an understatement, 30k has saved our asses more than I'll admit he did, but at the same time they do get in the way when you trying to stealth/move. But thats why you can direct the AI "To a degree" to setup where you want them to cover/etc and if you aren't using everything available in the game to play it, then how can you complain when it doesn't function perfectly?
The game has a few scripted moments in slow motion that are supposed to make you feel cool, and the first time around if you manage to do them correctly, they are amazing. Some sections of the game also have instant failstates if the enemy is alerted, so the stealth take downs, careful planning of shots, and making sure enemies don't notice dead comrades is there in full and I enjoyed it.
There are a few sections of the game where my comrades pretty much could "Take heavy weapons" and bullet hose their way through semi-stealth missions that felt lacking to me. Also they railroaded you a bit into going certain ways, but I didn't expect "Open World Sandbox Recon" like the new one coming out. Also people are giving reviews based on games that came out after this did and the ideal of shooters might have shifted?
I had fun with this game, play a good bit of Mil sims and more casual shooters and arcadey shooters alike and this one is even fun to come back through for another 4-6 hour romp time to time.

Monumental Failure is certainly an interesting game, but is it good??
Honestly, it's hard to say, and it's going to depend entirely on whether or not you can find humour in a frustratingly obnoxious physics based building game, that isn't really even a building game to begin with. The extent of the building in this game starts and stops with you controlling a small group of people whose sole purpose is to push a block into place and lock it in before it somehow manages to flip itself over or knock your entire team off the scaffolding that you're working on, which happens way more often than you'd expect lol.
The gameplay mechanics and content are (in my opinion) quite shallow and for the asking price of $9.99, I personally would expect a little more than what the game currently has to offer. That said, Monumental Failure is still an enjoyable and fun experience that you can play on your own or with your friends if you have any (I don't), and, provided the developers continue to work on it and add more content in the coming months, could potentially evolve into something worthy of the current asking price.
TL:DR Monumental Failure is a fun, light-hearted game that currently lacks the amount of content I would personally expect from a $9.99 game. If however you have friends to play with and money is not an issue, you could always pick it up and give it a crack to see whether it's worth the asking price or not, for yourself. Even though I feel it's a bit pricey, I'm going to hold on to it and see what the developers do with it in the future.

When you first look at Monumental Failure you can tell that the game is not meant to be taken seriously. The basic premise of the game is that your helping to build some of the ancient monuments of the world. While you sometimes use practical methods to build the structures, most of the contraptions you use are not just strange but impractical. This wackiness is where Monumental Failure really succeeds.
Monumental Failure is really simple to play as you use the analog sticks (if using a controller) to move your characters and you use another button to lock the current piece in place. That is all there is for controls in the game. Usually the controls work pretty well. The problem is that the controls could use quite a bit of work for the challenges that require you to fly  helicopters, jetpacks and other contraptions that take your characters off the ground since the characters tend to have a mind of their own.
While Monumental Failure has both a single and multiplayer mode, I would probably advise against the single player mode. It is a decent single player game but the cooperative multiplayer is significantly better. Like most of these type of games it is just so much more satisfying trying to work with another player than playing the game by yourself.
The biggest complaint I had with the game is that there are only six monuments in the game. Each monument usually takes around ten minutes to complete. While they are fun enough to play multiple times, the lack of monuments does lead to the game becoming repetitive earlier than it should. Generally I would say the Monumental Failure is the type of game that you play for 30-60 minutes and then come back to another day.
If you like quirky cooperative games I think you will really enjoy Monumental Failure. If you don't generally like these type of games though, I don't think the game is going to be for you.

The time i've spent so far in the game, really haven't impressed me.
Most of you have probably already heard about the mixed reception for this game, and i can certainly say that i lean to the side of people who dislike this game.
The largest issue can be described with 1 word
Everything about it is just sort of annoying, the map layouts, the enemies, the floaty locations and the need to search for oxygen all the time.
One of the first enemies you'll encounter in this game are the Kragons, a sort of stone dragon which duplicates itself when it dies, you'll get tired of fighting those REALLY fast as they quickly go from being a few into a swarm, they are also very resistant to damage, much more than enemies at the start of any previous borderlands game.
And due to the maps being all floaty and the gravity being close to non-existant enemies (especially larger ones) will knock you off a ledge or into a pit and insta kill you VERY often.
I also dislike too that this game more or less bases it's story on telling how jack became the way he is in Borderlands 2, but that is done
badly, as its awefully forced, Its Gearbox way of saying: "Oh he was nice and caring before, but look. When he shoots this person he says
hinting at him starting to become the cold way he is in Borderlands 2"
I liked Jack in borderlands 2, and to convince me that such a well done character was transformed from nice guy to bad guy through the gap between this game and Borderlands 2 (which i assume is only about a year or two) Is EXTREMELY far fetched, and I don't like it.
To put it short, the game feels puzzled together, They had the new engine, they only re-modeled some things from Borderlands 2 added a few new gimmicks, but it feels like this wasn't the game that went through a testing stage of "Is it enjoyable to play"? Because i never felt that with this game. It felt slow and the new things they toss at you get old real fast, the lasers aren't very good. The zero gravity stuff was fun for a few minutes but then just became annoying and made the game feel much slower. And for a borderlands game where its much about grinding that's not a good sign when people don't even want to give it 1 playthrough.
I might flesh this out more when i feel like it, but after booting it up for a frustratingly annoying playthrough of it, i just gotta leave give my 5 cents about it.

As a huge fan of the first two games in the series, it is no surprise that I would recommend this outing as this is essentially more of the same - lots of bad guys, lots of guns and lots of bullets with plenty of innuendo and humour. As with each release however there are new classes to choose from to keep things fresh (and these are generally stronger and better constructed than the first two games, if anything) and the 'pre-sequel' storyline to play through (how Handsome Jack became so handsome). There is lots of content in terms of missions, secrets, Easter eggs, etc., so while this is perhaps unlikely to gather newcomers to the franchise, old hands will surely not be disappointed - particularly as this is appearing on sale with more regularity and deeper discount. Completionists will struggle bitterly with some of the challenges, it is safe to say. My only grumble is that the DLC remains overpriced. I suppose it is also worth adding that if you do not like Australia or Australians, you should steer clear...

One of the best street racing games ever made!
Build up your car, cruise around, race some folks, run from the cops, smash your brand new car, rinse and repeat. I have spent countless hours on this game as a kid and it's STILL one of the best games I've ever played. Don't get me wrong...the physics kinda suck and the game itself is buggy as hell. But it's still an amazing simulation of what street racing is. Being able to build up the entire motor, suspension and body. Tuning specific parts to change how the car behaves. This game taught me what tires couldn't fit on my car, what spring rates and timing was. Mixtures of Gearhead Garage and NFS:U.
Do yourself a favor and pick up this game. I promise that if you are into cars in the slightest (building them), then this game is definitely for you! Now that it's on Steam, and the Workshop is coming, I think Street Legal Racing could make an epic comeback. Join us and help bring back this gem!

Lone Survivor is the 2D, pixelated SIlent Hill, that just isn't. Sure, the monsters creep you out at first, mostly due to the noise they produce then the stickman figure they happen to look like. But they just tend to be more of an annoying blockade in the hallway than something you should fear.
This game also brings up some annoying mechanics like an invisible sleeping and eating meter. Cause God knows we need that much "realism" to a game so that people get so "immersed" in it! It's not at all an annoying and unnecesary mechanic, especially when the character ♥♥♥♥♥es and moans about it every 5 minutes.
This game also brings back the clunky aiming mechanics of the old Resident Evil. It kinda works for it since it's used in a 2D setting. Though you'll mostly want to avoid confrontation since the enemies  tend to be really bullet absorbent. Which is a plus considering it's a survival horror game.
As for the story...I'll be honest, I lost interest in this game after getting to the basement. And I really just did not care what was going on in the appartment. Who that lady in the cage was. If the monsters were actually people and the protagonist was just delusional this whole time. I just didn't give a damn.
Why didn't I give a damn. The narrative felt a bit lifeless. I didn't feel like I should actually care what was going on in this world. The fact that most of dialouge amounts to the damn hunger/sleeping meter prompts whenever the protag feels hungry and/or tired may have added to that.
Pros:
-It's, kind of an interesting take on a Horror game. (Though I wasn't impressed.)
-Some of the puzzles were actually kinda clever, like luring a monster to another room by placing meat near it.
-You can kinda mix and match items to make new ones, sorta. (From what I experienced, it was mostly to cook food.)
Cons:
-Hunger and Sleep meter...oh joy.
-Muddy pixel graphics (The filter made it seem nice, but it really just adds to it.)
-I didn't care for the story or mystery of the game.
(Which is a big con considering that's an important motivator to play these types of games.)
In short:
If you're interested in a 2D, sidescrolling horror game. Try something else.

Horror should be short. Not just because it's hard to maintain tension for long periods, but also because constant breaks in gameplay can disrupt the experience.
Moon Sliver is a prime example of this being pulled off exceptionally. It manages to insert the sadness of a character drama and the dread of a horror title into a condensed, one hour package. Setting and characters are established quickly and with a writing prowess which somehow pulls off being both descriptive and deep, yet minimalistic and straightforward. The writing is the star of the show, which is great since many horror games stumble over this portion. Furthermore, make no mistake that despite the game's length, it is undeniably scary and claustrophobic. In fact, it is likely because the game ended on such an abrupt - and sad - note that it will stay with me for quite some time.
5/5 stars.

A great game severely lacking in several departments.
What it needs to be a truly great game is:
1) A war system like Civ V
Paradox's war system that they seem to love (enforce demands, white peace (status quo ante bellum) and surrender) worked fine for CK2 and EU4, but on a galactic scale, the ultimate idea of war score and demands is dreadfully badly suited. For example, you could potentially end up steamrolling an entire empire just so you have a high enough warscore to take permanent control over one colony. For a 4X game, which is what Stellaris is trying to be, it needs so much more freedom with war. When you are ultimately decimating an enemy, you would expect the enemy getting more and more desperate in trying to end the war diplomatically, and, when the enemy does want to sue for peace, THAT'S when you should be allowed to propose your demands.
The current war system is like "Oh well, we'll destroy your space fleet and leave you a husk of an empire in battle but all I really want is to take that sweet♥♥♥♥♥frozen colony you have".
2) Expansion to win
Through my experience, all it takes to make a galaxy-beating empire is to just colonise as quickly and as much as possible. You can have each colonised planet making about 20 EC and 20 minerals per month for example, which is extremely useful when it takes ages trying to mine (and research) every non-habitable body for a comparitively negligible gain in resources or science, and is also very costly. And because more planets = more spaceports, the empire with the most worlds will ALWAYS be the most powerful. Therefore the most conceivable way of winning is just to eat the galaxy like Gabe Newell eats your wallet and pies, which doesn't really result in very fun gameplay.
3) Factions
Another thing that has worked in CK2 and would work in Stellaris if it had some tweaks. I was once playing as a fanatic militarist xenophobic kingdom, and wanted to keep it that way, but the Emporer (who I was playing as!) was leading a faction calling for more xenophobia and I had no option to close down my own faction that I never even wanted. Also, significant changes to an empire's ethos (like when I once had a pacifist faction trying to demilitarise my fanatic militarist empire), they should at least do so in rebellions instead of just crippling my empire's output. Like the civil unrest in Empire: Total War, any serious revolutionaries should take up arms, and further still, defeating them on the field of battle should eradicate any revolutionary fervour.

I was pretty excited for Stellaris when it was first released. I like EU IV, but I prefer starting games like this as one territory / planet / city and building up from there. I thought Stellaris would be excellent if it could take the best of EU IV and allow me to do this. Instead I found the game mechanically uninteresting. With the recent update that came out with Utopia I thought I'd give it another try.
The early game is OK, scouting for new planets to settle, building up the economy, etc. There is some balancing required of resources, which is good - keeping energy income in check with expansion, keeping influence income high enough to be able to hire leaders, issue an edict if need be, grab that new colony. For the most part developing the planets doesn't have difficult choices to make. It seems to work out fine to just put down the improvement that utilizes the resource on the tile. The one place a varied from this is the buildingd that generate unity. Due to energy or mineral constraints, it can be important to prioritize the order things are developed.
Like many space 4X games, the military aspect isn't very engaging either. Try scout out what types of weapons and defenses a potential enemy has, design your ships and throw them at the enemy. I wish someone would figure out to make the combat interesting in this type of game. I've enjoyed space combat that is more tactical, like in Master of Orion 1 & 2, but I haven't seen a more hands off appraoch be implemented in an interesting way.
Even diplomacy, the area the Paradox usually excels - feels watered down. For all the choices there weren't a lot that were that useful or interesting. I made some trade / research deals, but for the most part I was self sufficient. I do like the wargoals system that Paradox uses in their games. You can insult empires to♥♥♥♥♥♥them off. Try to keep people at peace. Diplomacy feels more fleshed out in a game like EU IV, and maybe one of the strongest features in that game, but in Stellaris it feels kinda watered down and not really as vital a system.
I had the same feelings about Cities: Skylines. A good city builder for those with some imagination or creativity, but not a great game from a strategy game perspective. I think Stellaris may be enjoyable for those who can use there excitement to fill in some details to make their story more interesting, but for a player like me who just focuses and the mechanics and trying to succeed - it falls flat.

For the price, it's honestly not worth it. The combat is very repetitive and boring due to the characters barely having any form of customisation to them in terms of giving the player the freedom to make the character what they want, and the game's pacing in terms of story is insanely SLOW - especially for the small size of the map, which is on rails by the way...
The gameplay requires barely any strategy, it's way too easy, and the game forces you to play the way it wants you to play. It's crazy linear, and that's bad in this day and age in my opinion for an RPG. The entire point of an RPG, is to give the player some form of freedom within a creative sandbox, and this game may aswell just have been a straight forward action game - the dev's should've stuck to making 'Darksiders'.
Another issue that's obviously there to help n00bz, is that you can only ever fight 3 enemies at once, and I honestly got fed up with it due to how easy I actually found the game. The slow pacing made it not possible for me to get a refund or else I would have my money back. It's like a weird mix of 'Darkest Dungeon' and 'Diablo' with random JRPG-style mechanics and elements thrown in there to claim that it's a JRPG when it's not - even FF13 was a more unique experience than this game... and that's REALLY saying something.
It's VERY grindy in terms of levelling and getting gear, and most of the gear for each character is practically the same so getting a new weapon etc. isn't anything to celebrate about, and the gear that you do get doesn't change a character's appearance, only the weapon does. The loot and crafting plays on the weird 'same but different' system that 'Darksiders II' and 'Borderlands' has, where you can pick up the exact same gear in terms of icon/model, but it has different statistics - I personally find this lazy, uncreative, and all that it is is an RNG-based stat system that isn't rewarding to a player at all. It's an old system that needs to be thrown out completely from RPG games because it's made the genre insanely stale. You won't find many unique weapons for each character like you would in a 'Final Fantasy' game, but if you like dungeon-based grindy games, then this one might be for you? It's definitely not for me.
The world map is another major issue - it's way too small... and it's on rails, yeah, an on-rails world map with barely any areas to explore. Games like 'Legend of Dragoon' did the whole 'on-rails world map' thing well because each area you went to was unique and different, whereas this game fails at this. The dev's obviously spent way too much time and money on aesthetics rather than creating any interesting content. The world map makes the game ridiculously linear due to how small it is and exploration is gimped for the most part because you're always on a straight path from which you're not allowed to leave so you never feel 'free' on the world map to do whatever you want to do. This is why RPG games like Skyrim etc. are still so revered amongst players. It's due to the freedom they offer to the player.
The game essentially forces you to continue with the story no matter what you do just to progress your characters, and the 'random encounters' aren't actually random at all, they're placed in front of you at all times so you know exactly what you're going to fight - even in dungeons. It's a shame that they decided on this, as the surprise of finding new and unique enemies is just thrown out of the window. Most of the enemies are just re-skinned versions of others enemies, which just shows that they ran out of ideas.
It has a turn-based system which is a carbon copy of the system that's in 'Final Fantasy X', where you can see who will go on what turn, so that's another 'GG EZ' mechanic for the people that don't want a challenge, but feels like 'Darkest Dungeon'. Essentially, this game has taken most of the challenge away due to the stupid design decisions that go against player freedom, and forces the player to play a certain way at all times. For that, I can't tell any RPG fan they need to play this, as there's no need.
The only reason people have given it amazing scores and reviews is because of the characters, art style, animations, and sound - the core gameplay and pacing is very bad. It's pretty much like the dev's didn't learn from 'Darksiders II' what-so-ever in terms of as to why people hated it. At it's core, it's a hand-holding simulator, and that honestly sucks. It's all style, and has barely any depth to it.
If you're like me, then you'll probably play it to see what all the fuss is about, and you more than likely won't ever complete it because of the negative reasons I stated above.
It's a 4/10 at best.

First impressions:
The art style is fantastic, and the game is very easy to pick up and start playing immediately. The audio (sound effects, music, etc.) is done very well and sounds great. Controls are responsive, and the game feels very well optimized (no lag in any areas). My favorite aspect of the game is definetly the animations. The death animations are extremely well done and make me smile every time I get a kill.
After ~4 hours gameplay:
Definitely one of the best rogue-like games I've played. The game just excels on so many levels. From my understanding, the goal of the game is to make it to the bottom level of the dungeon, retrieve an item, and make your way back topside to exit the dungeon. Each level has a set of stairs leading deeper into the dungeon, and each level down gets increasingly diffucult. The first few levels are easy; the real challenge starts to come around the ruins level - the farthest I have gotten in my playthroughs. This deep down, new obstacles start to appear that really display the depth of the game. Some of these include platforms that fall after being walked on, pillars that drop down to crush you, and others. There are also many more enemies tightly packed together compared to the early levels. The levels are randomly generated, with a mix of some prefab areas and it works well.
I would definitely recommend supporting the developers and picking up this game in early access. I came across the game completely by accident while prowling the creative section of twitch.tv, and the art developer (Joshua) is friendly and responsive. Well worth the cheap price.

Delver is one of the few dungeon crawlers that I love. This game has tons of potential to become an amazing dungeon crawler game and with the developer coming back after his first kid i'm hoping we can see more from the developer.
In broad terms the game revolves around you delving into a dungeon to retrieve the yithidian orb. Along the way you will pass through different levels/stages all being unique to each other such as sewers/temple etc. All of these levels have different mobs and level design so you wont feel that your facing the same thing over and over(although some of the enemies AI are similar). Also the loot from going into the dungeon is unique enough in its state, with different armor/weapons/ring each with different attributes. The game is like medium difficulty but can be difficult and put a fire under your♥♥♥♥♥at some points. Whenever you die you lose all your items and character progress, but along your playthrough you can collect gold, which can be used to buy items to help your future playthroughs. Combat is basic, with essentialy a charged attack for melee and wands, and shooting your bow and arrow. Although the combat is basic it's satisfying enough to enjoy and play the game over and over again, considering its RNG of level layout and armor. Whenever you level up you are able to choose from a pool of attributes, attack, speed, health etc. The attributes are really basic and some attributes are really underpowered, like defense or magic. The hit box for the enemies are kinda weird, but not annoying to where it becomes a major problem. Also I feel that for a dungeon crawler with getting loot and wanting the player to play again and again, I think it shouldnt make you lose all your items once you beat the game. Instead of losing your items it should let you keep your items, but ramp up the difficulty of mobs and mabye more levels. This would give the game more replay value and make the player feel more "rewarding" instead of just saying congrats you beat the game! and restart your character.
The mechanics for the game are basic but fun, it gives you the feel of an actual dungeon crawler, searching for loot and randomized levels. However, I feel the game lacks because it is very basic in some areas(i know its in early access). Only having a charged attack and simple character sheets leaves a lot of room for improvments and gear that can be more unique. The progress of the game has been very slow recently(and I know the developer just had a baby) but hopefully we can see some progress as I've seen the developer working on it on his twitch stream. Delver is one of those games that you come back to every once and awhile and feels new when you do come back to it, and I hope to see this game released in the future because I see potential for Delver becoming an amazing game.

Bat Stir-Fry
Ingredients:
2 tablespoons dark sesame oil, divided
2 garlic cloves, finely minced
2 pounds Short-nosed Fruit Bat breasts, skinless and boneless
1 head broccoli, stems removed
1 dozen mushrooms, sliced
3 carrots, peeled and julienned
1/4 pound green beans, diced
1 head bok choy, chopped
2 to 3 tablespoons teriyaki sauce
Heat 1 tablespoon oil in a saute pan over medium heat. Add garlic and stir. Place the bat in the pan and brown 4 minutes on each side. Remove from pan, slice into strips, set aside.
Heat remaining tablespoon of oil in a wok over high heat. Add the vegetables and teriyaki sauce. Stir-fry quickly until the vegetables begin to soften. Add the other bat strips, combine well and continue to cook for 2 to 3 minutes. Serve immediately.

Rating 8/10
Overview: First Person Action RPG
The Good:
+ 4 characters to choose from, each with 3 skill trees. The skill trees are more robust than previous games. The skills themselves are also more unique. Plenty of different character builds and options. Clap trap being one of the most unique characters to play as in the borderlands universe.
+ A good story that explains how the events unfolded leading up to Borderlands 2.
+ Two new gameplay mechanics. The first is the jump pad, this allows you to jump really high or traverse large distances. The second is the oxygen meter. Many environments have low gravity allowing you to jump really high and far which allows for faster traversal over the terrain as well as more interesting gun battles. Running out of oxygen is never a concern because there are so many ways to refill your oxygen.
+ Lots of good loot.
+ Plenty of graphical/audio/gameplay options, very well optimized
The Average:
The overall map design for most levels feel a bit too condensed. I was hoping for more open spaced levels where I could drive around but that never really materialized here.
Like every borderlands before it, side missions are not "optional". If you don't complete them you will be very under leveled for the main missions.  The side missions themselves are not the greatest either, many of them are not as creative as Borderlands 2.
Humor is very hit or miss.
The Bad:
-Multiplayer is near dead making it very difficult to get some achievements. The game is also a lot more fun when playing with more people.
Conclusion:
This game is really good yet never really gained the same attention or critical praise as its predecessors, partly because many people were 'borderlands fatigued' by the time this game came out and the fact it was made by a different studio gave the game the impression it was a quick cash grab. Other than the new characters and new features mentioned above this is almost exactly like its predecessor in almost every way. This isn't bad but those looking for a completely new experience will not find it here.  Is this game as good as Borderlands No, but this game can certainly stand on its own.
