I love this game. It's a F2P that's not P2W, which is a winner any day in my book.
The in-game music is lovely, classes feel like a fresh spin on classic archtypes, and are versatile enough to avoid that brickwall tanks and healers hit while leveling up in more standard MMOS.
The art style is absolutely beautiful. It reminds me of SWTOR and Ratchet and Clank, even possessing a crude personality very reminiscent of Ratchet and Clank. The game as a whole is very comparable to Borderlands.
Very little is locked out for non-premium members, and it's all "icing on the cake" type features.
Vanity items are wonderful, being comparable to WoW's trangmog system.
The ARPG combat style is a turn I see many new MMOS trying to take, mainly GW2. I enjoyed GW2, but it left something to be desired in the combat. Players just aren't fast or agile ennough for the action part of the combat to worrk. Wildstar fixes that. Being a ranged class able to circle strafe enemies and avoid half of their attacks in an MMO feels so satisfying.
Hoverboards. All I need to say about them is that one of the first two you can get is practically the hoverboard from Back to the Future 2. Glorious.
I highly recommend you give this game a chance or two. It just needs help in building up a more solid playerbase.

Time played on Steam is not accurate, I've played well over 1000 hours.
It is free (and incredibly fair to free players, more so than other f2p MMOs by far.) and it's fun. Try it. What do you have to lose?
Pros:
- Amazing fast-paced combat, emphasising on movement and reaction time. It's hectic in a really fun way. The telegraph system makes combat very intuitive. You'll know when and why you messed up in a fight.
- Double jump, dodge and sprint is part of every class and all are used in combat to really add an extra dimension.
- Real physics! It's unheard of in other MMOs. You properly gain momentum when going down a slope (did I mention hoverboards?). There are areas with reduced gravity and it feels right.
- Immersive lighting effects. They are not super advanced but they beat "painted directly on the texture" lighting in most MMOs. For example, there are areas where you have a helmet with a lamp on it to move around in the dark. The bundle of light points in the direction you are facing. This kind of tech does not exist in any MMO i've played and it can be really immersive. I wish they would use it more often though.
- The theme breaks away from the usual medieval fantasy MMOs that we've all been playing for years.
- The music is so good.
- Good story. It's easy to follow if you want it to be but there's additional lore all around to learn more if that's your thing.
- Free. The fairest cash shop model in any MMO I've seen and it doesn't constantly nag you to buy things. Most of the things you buy are cosmetic in nature anyway. You can earn a currency through just playing the game for free that will allow you to buy most of the items from the cash shop the same way you would with real money.
- Player housing is really good. I'm not interested in it but I've played around with it and you can do a lot of creative things with it.
Cons:
- There are bugs. Quite a lot of the bugs are UI related. Most of the time, a quick reload of the UI can fix it and there are certain addons that fix problems in the default UI altogether. Other in game bugs exist but fixes have been improving steadily.
- If you like story, it doesn't really start until lvl 30-35, but after that I really like it.
- The game does not perform nearly as well as it should. Some addons have been made that improve performance. But really, get to work, Carbine.
For maximum enjoyment:
- Join a guild! I can't stress this enough. Just because WoW thinks making content too accessible is a good thing, doesn't mean it is. Some group content is very hard to complete with strangers, due to text chat being too slow to communicate mid-combat. If you're used to the dungeon finder in other MMOs, this is harder. Guild groups make it incredibly fun and rewarding.
- Skip task quests while leveling. They're incredibly generic extra quests on top of the story/regional/world quests that usually don't give you enough of a reward. The exp is minimal and they are entirely optional.
- Ignore the doomsayers. People have been saying the game is dead for 2 years now. There aren't many players but there's enough.

Alrighty so, if you played this game for atleast more than 2 weeks (either 2.2.1mwm, mwmwle, 230le), I'm assuming you modded it and everything else, if so, you pretty much know what you're getting into, since you're probably informed about 2.3.1, if you're completely new and have no idea what you're getting into, well, it's a pretty simple game, you buy a wreck, repair a couple parts with whichever money you have leftover, and you go out racing and beating opponents, after beating a decent amount, you'll have some money, buy a better ride/upgrade your current ride and beat some other opponents, eventually you'll reach the top and get access to the race of champions, now in 2.3.1 you get even more events than the other versions, you're able to gain money through 'normal' (not 'illegal') race events, which is honestly pretty damn cool, that's the basic game loop.
No problem picking up my xbox 360 controller, if you're emulating a x360 controller with the most known programs you'll have no problem with that since I know it works on a PS3/ 5 bucks controller, as long as it's emulating a 360 one.
Physics aren't top notch, but honestly, that kinda makes it fun, from silly crashes, to rage inducing ones (losing a top notch engine can make you salty, expecially after all the tuning), Sounds are actually okay, if you use mods, expecially the V8 mod you won't regret playing with that throttle.
Graphics are okay, you can just use enb series to bump them up (and trust me this game looks above 2014 if you get proper settings for everything)
So far i've had no problems whatsoever with mods, everything has been compatible first try (But I haven't got over 60 car mods / a crapton of part mods), these are what make the game truly shine, high quality cars + wheels + tires + engines make building a car, and drifting it / taking screenshots of it worth it (Heck, I've got a screenshot on my profile check it out if you'd like), there's like a bazillion mods, more mods are made pretty damn often, like wheel packs(which are getting extremely high quality these days)
Honestly, If you know what you're doing you're not really going to crash alot, and even if you do, you won't lose progress, so far my only problem has been riding around in modded vehicles and the game randomly crashing.
If you're new to this, I only got one suggestion, if you're building a car from scratch,
or vice-versa, my most common crash is when i'm opening the wheels / tires pages, since i've got a fair amount of modded wheels and tires in, those take a while to load, and sometimes may crash, so I make sure I save whenever I'm about to go into running gear, sometimes modded cars / engines don't like loading so it's a good idea to also save inbetween that.
It's been my first 'serious' review, I'm pretty sure I shoulda covered more points, but I don't really feel like it.
If you want a good timewaster and you like cars hell yeah go for it, if you're not a car person, or if you demand top notch physics / whatever from a car game, then this game is probably not for you.

Ghost Recon: Future Soldier is a pretty average cover based co-op military special ops shooter.
I feel a little bit at a loss as to how to describe the game as its sort of generic. You play as a group special ops guys doing some secret mission stuff and being “future” soldiers you get a lot of tech stuff like magnetic vision and sensor grenades for making enemies appear on your HUD even behind cover. Camo that is incredibly useful for being stealthy. You also get a drone for marking enemies and an EMP to disable electronics.
The gunplay feels good. Its fun and enjoyable, you get to do a lot of cool slow motion breaches into hostage rooms. Its a blockbuster title; meaning lots of explosions and pretty looking environments. But more or less is a tad shallow in gameplay mechanics.
I noticed a lot of other reviews saying the mutliplayer is bugged. I did not try any of the co-op of the main campaign so I cannot speak to that aspect. But I did try the Guerrilla wave based mode and the regular objective based mulitplayer. I was able to connect and it worked just fine, it seemed again, very run of the mill.
The AI of your teammates in the campaign is okay, the only real complaint I have is they seem to really enjoy walking in between your gun and the people you are shooting. You can set up sync shots up to 4 people at a time. That also feels very satisfying. Coordinating 4 headshots at once indeed makes you feel like a proper special ops team. I imagine even more so playing with friends during the campaign.
The game does seem to be a console port; meaning limited graphical options and unfortunate poor optimization and having VERY deep frame drops that last about 2 to 3 seconds while the next area loads. But it never really gets in the way too much as there are never any enemies that need immediate attention after a load.

I am a huge Tom Clancy (games) fan, and Ghost Recon Future Soldier did not fail to deliver.

The various challenges added to the different missions will coerce you into adapting in order to try the missions in a different way, thus pulling you out of your comfort zone every now and then, which I find great. It really added to the replay value for me.

"From the Sun comes Life. From Life comes Death. From Death comes the Dust. From the Dust is born a new Sun. Such is will of Anaar, that which is all and none, the beginning and end, the Watcher of Creation and Chaos. In its unending dream may we find purpose. In its fearful shadow may we spread throughout the cosmos." -Excerpt from the Book of Ntuloak, Holy Text of the Anaari.
Okay, so there is my little contribution to the science fiction atmosphere of this surprisingly deep game. Stellaris is a Grand Strategy game. Unlike other strategy games involving squads of soldiers flung at the opposing team's base, Stellaris puts you in the shoes (figuratively speaking) of the ruler of species in cosmic space. From there, you will be in charge of growing your civilization throught the galaxy. Whether this is by scientific discovery, spiritual diplomacy, or militaristic conquest, the choice is yours for how you choose to rule the stars.
Stellaris has a rather steep learning curve. Expect to have several playthroughs before finally finding a government type that suits your tastes. I personally chose the egalitarian and xenophile approach (I am a nice person, can't help it). They might be digitized pixels, but I prefer to be on the good side of cosmic entities.
There is a considerable amount of resource management to Stellaris; do not expect the game to be fast-paced. A great deal of patience is required for a successful playthrough. The fascinating thing about Stellaris is that it is much like a black hole; by the time you realize you are being pulled in, it has already consumed you. The game offers a rich, storytelling experience in the same skein as Sunless Sea, where the story develops as a constantly evolving narrative. Your culture does not stagnate. The research options available, coupled with the anomalous events in space, can have drastic and sometimes dire consequences depending upon the choices you make.
Stellaris is a fascinating mixture of space sim, empire builder, resource management, and civics simulator.  If you are a fan of wandering through the stars and creating your own story amidst breathtaking beauty, it is definitely worth the purchase. See you in Space!

An impressive indie game. There's little in the way of gameplay, just movement and limited contextual interaction, yet it manages to engross by atmosphere alone. In fact, rarely has the term "atmospheric" applied to a game more strongly.
You explore a limited but engrossing environment and absorb backstory as you go. This backstory is presented only in the order in which you encounter it, yet is sufficiently cohesive that no one piece seems out of place, and this is partly because the backstory is so deliberately thin, or perhaps more accurately, so light of touch. It is used once again for the purpose of enhancing atmosphere, and this it does. Now, the actual "moon sliver" part is weaker, because at no point is it made entirely clear just what that even is, nor what the origins of its associated mythology may have been. Then again, this leaves it open to interpretation and imagination, which further serves to deepen the sense of mystery and general lack of groundedness that this game is so successful in engendering in the player. The overall effect of the game's combined elements is really quite striking, and feed well into its ending.
The only points to remember are these: 1) If you can't get into an area yet, then you just haven't found and read all of the available backstory material, and 2) take advantage of the power outlets to recharge your flashlight [it only takes one zap]. Experience and enjoy.

The Binding of Isaac is a great game to spend a few minutes or even hours playing.
The game is about a boy who's mom is overly religious When God asks her to lock her son away and take all his things away, even clothes, she is more than happy to do as instructed. God then says Isaac is still "corrupted" and tells Mom to kill Isaac, which she goes to do without a second thought. Isaac, in  desperation searches his room for a way out and finds a trap door under a rug which he flings open and jumps in just as Mom lunges into Isacc's room with a knife.
In the basement is where the game takes place. Isaac has to fight through countless monsters with only his tears. The goal is to get out of the basement but that is where all of the monsters come in making Isaac's world a living hell, by cornering him and killing him.
The game is procedurally generated, permadeath and is really quite fun and challenging. There are plenty of items to enhance  Isaac's powers. One can make a deal with the Devil or meet Krampus himself.

The Binding of Isaac is a great game, even though it was released a few years ago. The story is interesting, the look of the game itself reminds me of the good 'ol gaming days, when graphics weren't the focus of the game, the substance was. Many items and combinations are able to be created every time you play, and there are even challenges to play through to see how good of a player you are. It's a truly amazing game, which you shouldn't judge by how  it may look at first.

Expectations were high for another Drakengard/Nier installment and it performed well beyond.
The story is solid while throwing in great immersion with the environments and manipulating your emotions with the music. The music alone is a masterpiece. If it had an OST DLC I'd get it in a heartbeat.
The close combat maneuvers/hacking maybe a bit repetitive but it's offset by the great amount of variation in the enemies you fight, aside from the fact that you're fighting in a bullet hell.
The characters are unique. And when I say unique, I don't mean it in a shallow way of being different from each other. Each character has their own set of traits that make them relatable or understandable as a person. You can see the effort and creativity put in to them.
It's a rare gem in an era where games are often sold incomplete, massively toxic online or riddled with microtransactions. Not this one. Buy it, play it, and take some time off in this melancholic world because you deserve it.

As a hardcore Borderlands fan, you'll be disappointed for sure but as a regular FPSRPG game, you will not be disappointed. Some good points that the game has and does better than Borderlands 1 & 2 is that the characters are more fun to play as and combat is more interesting as you have the ability to do double jumps and butt slams. For each character, you can come up with many different builds and that really helps up the replayability. Another good touch that the game has is that the character you play as actually responds to what the NPCs have to say.
However, as much as I like this game, there are still some glaring issues with the game that I would like to point out. One of the issues is that some of the missions just drag out for too long. This makes it very tedious for the player to go through and also makes it very repetitive. Speaking of repetitiveness, this game can get boring at times in my opinion. While I do believe that there is a good amount of replayability withtin the game, this game does not have as much replayability as Borderlands 2 as it suffers from the lack of end game content. In Borderlands 2, after you finish the campaign, you are able to farm these raid bosses for loot. In Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel, however, there is only one raid boss to farm and that raid boss is the same as the final boss but just a more beefed-up version.
Overall, I do recommend this game as it is a lot of fun and you are sure to sink in tens and probably even hundreds of hours into the game.

Don't judge a book by its cover. That's this game in a nutshell. When I first saw this game I thought “Oh a Chinese rip off of World of Warships that has subs.” I decided to take a look just to see how it compared to WoWs and well here I am 14 hours in already...
Now as someone who has put a good amount of time in for both games (over 100 hours in WoWs) I decided that to put these two games side by side to see if it really is a Copy/Paste game. So with that said lets take a look
First the similarities
Both games are based of naval engagements in WW2 that a given
Both games have HP systems
Both games are F2P
Both games have community's that have Kancolle fans in Kongo class BBs screaming KONGOU-DEUS BURNING LOVE. At the start of a match not that there's anything wrong with that.
etc
Now the fun part the differences. Here I will put major differences  for both games
First WoWs

Graphics: Now it isn't like comparing a potato to a nuclear reactor but WoWs has graphics that are true to the current gen of gaming and SO is more like in 2010-12ish  so WoWs wins that one
Optimization: WoWs takes this one by a mile. Currently in SO if a fleet of 8+ ships are close to you and are packed together (like at the start of a game) the FPS will fall to below 30 unless you have NASA's CPU on your rig.
UI: WoWs takes this one as (Targeting is a different story though) SO's UI is a bit of a mess unlike WoWs that is so simple a 7 year old could understand it, SO's UI has f^#ktons of info in your face at once and can take time to get your head around.
Physics: Neither game gets them right but WoWs system is much more real then SO's as in SO a fully loaded battleship takes about 7 seconds to stop and reverse which causes a physics induced rage on people like me. (and also because my torps missed and my ship is now at the bottom of the ocean.)
Now for SO
Subs: This is the main thing people stay behind when talking about this game saying “IT HAS SUBS” Now are the subs balanced? They are, that was something I did not expect from this game is how well the subs are integrated into the game with the limited O2 system from the Battle-stations series.  So that a + for SO.
Balance: On the subject of balance this game beats WoWs by a long mile. Unlike in WoWs where a destroyer player of equal equipment tier can take down a battleship in a gunnery battle via HE shells. This game makes it very clear. Unless you have A) Numbers or B) Battleship covering fire or C) enemy BB is a very low HP, don't try to take on a enemy BB in a destroyer/cruiser in a gunnery duel you will most likely die in one volley of the BB's mains as in this game a 14 inch gun is a 14 inch gun and that 14 inch gun vs your destroyer is a nuclear warhead vs firecracker in terms of armor and firepower, But you always have those torps...
Skill play: Unlike in WoWs you have to actually try and aim your torpedos before you fire them. Gun play also requires a bit of skill as this game has taken WoT's aiming circles for SPGs and implanted them into the game, as shown in the game you must not be turning for the aiming circle to zero in this in turn stops people in destroyers from zig zag sniping you from 2kms away...
And lastly
Night battles: A very fun game mode that those who are not past tier 4 can play this gamemode changes the way you play for any ship class BIG TIME as you and the enemy will not be able to see each other in the darkness till you are both in each others faces. Thankfully the game has flares and spotlights to put light on certain areas just be careful when you fire a flare or turn on spotlights the enemy could see and you could end up like IJN Kirishima at the end of The battle of Guadalcanal.
Verdit.
Both games have their ups and downs
If you want a game that runs smoothly and easy have fun in and understand then play WoWs
If you want a game that has a bit a skill curve to it and has subs and night battles then play SO
These are both great games and both deserve a chance to be played so before screaming its a rip off play SO a hour or two before praising/demoting it.
And that's my two cents on this, Now if you will me excuse I have to watch as my torps miss a break-dancing Kongo class battleship while chat is being filled with “BURNING LOVE” as my ship sinks.

To preface this - I have been playing World of Warships since the Closed Alpha test, which while insanely fun and enjoyable experience - slowly turned to garbage as development advanced, and Wargaming continued dipping their filthy, vodka-coated hands into the WoWS pie. WoWS slowly became an unbalanced, overly-simplistic, insanely unenjoyable and mundane experience wherein Wargaming plays the usual role of being 100% incompetent at development, community skills (this includes listening to the playerbase more than literally never.), and balance. Now, I do not want to say I hate WoWS - but after playing this game, I find it increasingly more hard to root about for reasons to play WoWS more often than one or two matches.
To also give you perspective, I am an AVID Aircraft Carrier fan. I love my Japanese CV's, and was heartbroken to find that they were implemented in WoWS in such a laughably bad way. (Better torpedo bombers and more active wings simultaneously at the cost of less planes per wing, and useless fighters.) While this was acceptable for a short while, it increasingly grew more and more unbearable; patch after patch, faulty rebalance after faulty rebalance - and Japanese Carriers no longer had a purpose, with inferior fighters and torpedoes that have virtually no chance to cause flooding (easily neutering the warship), and coupled with new meta that arose wherein USN CV's use their numeric superiority of fighters to shoot down all opposition and then proverbially squat atop the enemy carrier and♥♥♥♥♥♥on the captain's head - I lost all remaining faith in Wargaming and had decided to quit playing WoWS to find new horizons.
After Navyfield 2 failed in such an awful matter, I really needed to find a new game to play that was a naval combat MMO - and I was insanely lucky when my friend just so happened to link this game as a joke. A Chinese knockoff of World of Warships that is supposedly better than WoWS. After beating a dead horse and nagging at my friend about how ♥♥♥♥♥♥ WoWS is, I realized the futility of this and waited for Steel Ocean to be released. While the release slipped my mind at first, I recalled the game, downloaded it, and much to my shock and awe - played an infinitely better naval combat than World of Warships.
To begin - let us list the negatives, of which this game has surprisingly few.
Absolutely heinous graphical performance. Both in literal performance and graphical appeal. The game runs poorly on my computer despite the game looking like it was made in 2008. (AMD HD Radeon 6970 Sapphire Dual-X)
The community understandibly, yet bafflingly seems completely braindead. Frequent teamkills, no idea as to what to do, useless Battleships not moving an inch from spawn, Carriers suiciding off into the enemy team. (Hopefully a meta begins to float around to shine light on what to do.)
Map sizes either seem small, or Destroyers awfully fast. Granted, this might be an error entirely on my fault - but I can't help but feel like a few maps are far too easy to traverse for DD's and ends in a Battleship's untimely death. (Either that or superior captaining, I'll just leave that up to the playerbase.)
Mediocre UI elements. Such as a lack of grouping carrier-based aircraft together, clunky tabs, and awkward management of the tech tree.
Cringey voices for pilots, crew, captain, et cetera. An option for national crews would be amazing. (Japanese voiceovers for the IJN, German for the KM, accented English for the RN, et cetera.)
Much more advanced and intense gameplay. Requiring you to micromanage aircraft significantly more (this includes assaulting with dive bombers and torpedoes; requiring you to manually set the path of assault and correcting it to compensate for movement, potential turning, and to avoid AA density. As well as the removal of EZ-mode aim assist, and a lot of UI elements that made WoWS far too simple to play. (Lead indicators, shell impact time estimates, auto torpedo and bomb drop, et cetera.)
CUSTOM AIRCRAFT CARRIER LOADOUTS. This is the biggest point for me. This, this right here makes Carriers so much more damn fun. No ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ gimmicks, no "assymetrical balance", no preset loadouts - the ability to customize and tailor your aircraft carrier to fit your needs and wants. I love this so much.
CONTROLLABLE SECONDARIES, ANTI-AIRCRAFT GUNS, AND DUAL-PURPOSE GUNS. This is the second biggest point for me. In WoWS, your faulty, ♥♥♥♥♥♥, AI-and-RNG driven AA and secondaries would consistently fire misses until you were either sunk or barely managed to survive. AA in WoWS is completely useless at lower tiers, and makes the grind much more unbearable and the playerbase's opinion of Aircraft Carriers inherently low. In this game, being sunk by aircraft means you had nobody to blame but yourself. Always remember to check the skies if you're in a battleship as you're destined to be targeted by carriers. Also, with the aid of secondary guns - you're more than capable of defending yourself in an aircraft carrier against Destroyers or surfaced Submarines. Also, this enables you to lay down more fire, more efficiently in Battleships and suppliment your high reload time on your main battery with rapid, low-damage, yet surpressive fire.
BATTLESHIPS ARE USEFUL. I cannot emphasize this point enough, as a scorned lover of Battleships in WoWS; this is another huge point for me. Battleships are fun and useful in the right hands. I am early in the game for BB's (Proto Kongo), but it is just so damn enjoyable I don't even notice a grind to the Kongo 1931. I am extremely excited to see what course this game takes with battleships, and I cannot wait to see more choices in the Battleship lines.
Destroyers now have a role outside of being torpedo-♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, however this role is still retained. Destroyers can now hunt submarines utilizing depth charges. However, due to the lack of CL and CA on most teams - they are left to submarine hunt without much support outside of that, also considering they remain spotted as long as the Submarine is within radio distance of their allies - the DD has to swiftly shoot out their short-ranged depth charges, or utilize torpedoes. Either way, DD's finally have a role outside of being tedious.
Submarines. While this isn't much of a plus or negative to me, they're in the game - and whatdoyaknow; they're actually well-balanced and seem to be enjoyable. I cannot offer much input on this other than more ship and role diversity, but submarines are in the game and they're pretty okay.
Spotting system in this game, after getting acquainted with something that doesn't work like garbage and has a clear and understandable function - is actually pretty good. Your ship must maintain a clear line-of-sight on the enemy vessel(s), or must be within radio range of allies that have spotted the enemy warship. While spotting distance is fairly low, this positively influences combat and keeps games from being long, drawn-out, and mundane.
Steel Ocean may seem like a WoWS ripoff, but it is not. Drawing elements from multiple games, World of Warships, World of Tanks, the Battlestations series, Navyfield, et cetera. It is a moderately unique game and is worth at least an 8/10 for gameplay, mechanics, balance, and content. I hope the developers of Steel Ocean keep surprising new players with a fresh take on the newish Naval Combat MMO genre.

Stellaris is the one time Paradox decided to move away from history, and move into deep space, where history isn't really established beyond what little exploration humanity has already achieved. You still play a role as a starting empire growing to become, essentially, the center of the universe, but it's a bit different than usual. For one thing, people tend to wage war just because they feel like it, as diplomacy amounts to how much someone likes or hates you, and if they want to be your friend, or shove a doomstack down your throat. The ship designer was pretty much made because the game is more than just doomstacks. Not having a well equipped fleet will mean just having massive numbers can still end up with most of them in a trash heap. On top of that, going overboard on something like point defense and anti-shield weaponry, means someone who relies on lasers and raw armor is probably going to eat you alive.
Personally, I enjoy it. I love space, I love space ships, and I love fleet battles. This game has fleet battles with space ships. IN SPACE! The ship designer is a nice way to make every encounter feel different, though the ships automate all the combat in standard Paradox fashion, at the very least this is the most detailed they've been of actually watching the fight go down. Instead of swordsmen swinging their swords at each other in a way that implies they're hoping their enemy will be too scared to approach and give up, both fleets will begin their approach and engage at will. When they engage depends on weapon range, so sometimes you can take damage before you even get a shot off. It's still a 2-D map, but there's actual 3-D models within it. Plus I guess with everything mostly depending on how well you equipped your ships, it's a nice spectacle to watch when you're not worried about giving your army commands, even if it does take you out of the game.
So even if the diplomacy is a bit weaker, the game is still fun to grow into a massive empire with a death fleet that eats planets for breakfast, and their fleets for lunch. Though the fact Fallen Empires can make Titans, a class you can't make like the filthy cheaters they are, still annoys me.

However, the AI is absolute - and I mean COMPLETE -♥♥♥♥♥♥ It might do attacking well against you and your systems, but outside of that it is entirely braindead. A ~200 year campaign as a martial empire, at one point the largest blob on the block, and the strongest outside of the Fallen Empires.
It is at this single point that the
appear to make my day pretty bad. They appear a few systems away from my borders in the heart of the only local empire near my size and strength. I figure things might get bad and the Fox Empire will need some help.

The entire 3/4 of my Empire, the Fox Empire, and several smaller empires around us are obliterated by wave upon wave of 60-90k death stacks. At this point I have a single 50k stack and thats pushing the limits of my naval capacity. I fight/lose a protracted genocide of my people and my xeno slaves as they creep ever closer to my homeworld.
At this point I'm thinking 'Clearly this is either ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t or some Deus Ex Machina will save me during this, right?'
Some Fallen Empire answers my prayers and Awakens to fight off the horde sprawling across the galaxy. They have a call-to-arms for an 'alliance' to oppose the horde unified. I immediately jump on board, praying for safety. The caveat? I have to ban slavery across my empire. At this point I'm desperate and accept - significantly cutting in to my already depleted resources - and await for the help that does not come.
After calling for a unified alliance and attack against the monsters, the Awakened Empire proceeds to do nothing but war against some two-bit empire in the opposite direction for decades because they're mean or something.
I'm one of only two empires that joins the alliance.
The Awakened Empire sits with their MULTIPLE 100-200k death stack fleets that could EASILY beat the Unbidden sitting at their planets.
My newly slaveless economy is in shambles as I fight delaying actions with an ever weakening fleet as I desperately try to reinforce with every mineral I have, Redesign the fleet to take on the
, research ANY technology that might even the playing field - including taking an Ascension perk that increased my damage against them by 50%.
But nope, too little too late. My fleet was gone. Shambles. The Unbidden take the last of my core worlds as my last two colonies hastily set up next to the Awakened Empire's border get ready to be consumed.
Any other empire could have pitched in and fought the obviously more important enemy. Instead they warred amongst themselves as the only thing standing between them and oblivion was consumed from the inside out.

Few games can successfully straddle the line between fun and frustrating as all hell. Usually, when games attempt this, they end up either really fun or really frustrating, usually the latter. Binding of Isaac, like Super Meatboy before it, is successful at this feat. While I wanted to review Rebirth, the more balanced remake, my computer lags with that game for some reason (and only that game), so I'll be reviewing the old version instead.
Binding of Issac is an addicting, frustrating, fun as all hell roguelike game based around Isaac, a young boy who loves drawing, and his mother, who watches Christian broadcasts all day. One day, she hears a voice in her head, presumed to be God, telling her to take all of Isaac's things, including his clothing. Still not satisfied, the voice speaks to her again, and she locks him in his room, away from the evil of the outside world. One last time, his mother hears the voice, and she grabs a butcher knife from the kitchen. Isaac, seeing it all from a crack in his door, starts panicking and finds a trapdoor under the rug, jumping in just as his mother opens the door.
The gameplay largely consists of crying at your enemies until they die (I'm not kidding, tears are your weapon), and trying not to lose all your hearts. On every floor, you'll find various items that will help you on your quest, as well as soul hearts, pills, tarot cards, and other assorted items. Occasionally, you'll be able to make deals with the devil, who offers you really OP items in exchange for permanent loss of heart containers. Every time you beat the game, you unlock more levels to go through, offering nearly a dozen instances of beating the game before you see all possible endings. Many of the endings are Isaac finding some sort of silly gag item, but the first and final endings are the most interesting in terms of symbolism and what the game is really about, but I won't spoil it for anyone.
Long story short, Binding of Isaac is simply a must-have for anyone with a Steam account, ranking up there with Portal and Half-Life. If I had to, I'd give this game a really high rating, perhaps a 98/100, losing a couple points for the game occasionally being imbalanced if you get the right combo of items.

This game is absolute madness. The setting is unoriginal and generic, the characters cartoonish and ugly, and the gameplay over-the-top and messed up beyond belief. Combine that all together, and you get a love you either can't stand, or love beyond belief. And I went with the latter.
Loadout is fun. That's all it really is, fun. There's no stress you might get from other FPS/TPS games like CoD or Borderlands, mostly because of the fact you can't take this game seriously. The creators did everything they can to deliver a game that'll make you lose or die with a smile on your face, without feeling the frustration from similar games. Of course, this doesn't apply to everyone, but you get the general point here.
The weapon customization is awesome. Instead of choosing stock guns from different categories, you can design it in any way you want, from snipers to mini-guns to healing rocket launchers and whatnot. Even though some combinations might be considered "OP", it's all about the way you use it, or the way you dodge it. I have to agree the balance tends to tilt a teeny bit from time to time, but you can find that in a lot of similar games. The main point is, you can be as creative as you want with them,
The game modes currently available are Blitz (Control Points), Jackhammer (Capture the Flag), Death Snatch (Kill Confirmed), Extraction and Annihilation. The first three are what they are: Blitz is a simple "capture the control point" mode, where you need to stand on a point long enough to capture it, and 6 captures will decide the game. Jackhammer is basically Capture the Flag with a hammer instead of the flag that allows you to smack your enemies in one shot. Death Snatch is that CoD game mode with Blutonium (ore) instead of dog tags, and the most fun if you just like killing people. Extraction involves collecting the beforementioned ore enough times to win, and Annihilation is pretty much a combination of the first 3 mentioned game modes, also known as the "Competitive" mode.
Of course, the game isn't perfect. The outfits are awfully expensive (but look epic), the server still bugs out from time to time, and the party system might still throw your friends into the enemy team, even if there's enough space in the lobby. But then again, the game's still fresh, so they're expected issues.
In overall, this is currently one of the best F2P shooters out there. It's easy to pick up and play, a lot of fun to play with friends, and just insane in overall. If you're more of a serious gamer, it's best to stay away from this (although giving it a try won't hurt). If you're a casual(ish) gamer, give it a shot. And if you're a flying grapefruit like me, you'll absolutely love this game. Even if it's just to see yourself walking around with a giant hole in your body, or with just a brain and eyes, Loadout is fun for every game who likes to have a laugh every now and then while shooting off someone's head or arm. It's mindless fun with rather mindless characters.

Battle Chasers will take in most RPG players with its great steampunk styling and beautifully rendered graphics and animation work. There is little not to like about the great Diablo/Torchlight style. Dungeons are randomized using individual stylesets that the game chooses from and places accordingly -- so even though its random, players can enjoy the incredible level of work and detail that went into designing each level.
It is worth noting here that the game is not 100% complete yet, so there is likely still a lot of work to be done, but I will delve a bit into my issues with the game as far as gameplay.
The first thing to note is that this game is SLOW. Walking around the instanced dungeons, or even the world map itself feels like its moving at a snails pace. It may be that I am simply used to faster paced gameplay but, having read the reviews, a lot of players are stating the same thing. The game would do well to speed up map movements, as some of the dungeons can be quite long as it is, and the slow walking speed is a constant source of aggravation.
Likewise, the game pace is slow in terms of leveling, with the party leveling up once per dungeon instance which can take as long as an hour to complete. However, the leveling speed is intentional by design -- Battle Chasers is a highly linear environment. No matter how much you grind, you'll find that your level will always closely match that of the opponents you're facing in the storyline. The game is designed to penalize players attempting to overlevel by dramatically decreasing the amount of experience earned for enemies that are a lower level than you. This is dissapointing, as you never really feel as though you're progressing or becoming more powerful during gameplay, as there is no incentive to fight enemies lower level than your own.
Adding insult to injury, all character weapons and equipment in the game are heavily gated with level requirements. Essentially this translates into very restricted gameplay -- not only can you rarely outlevel your opponents, but even if you find that ultra rare weapon, it will either be specifically for your character level (meaning its not overpowered) or you won't be able to equip it until much later in the game....basically when it won't be as cool a find.
When it comes to equipment in general, there are a few ways you can obtain it. You can purchase it from vendors, find it in battles or in chests, or craft it yourself. The crafting system in the game is not something I've really dived into, owing to its complexity. As far as I know from my admittedly limited time playing the game, you may only craft items at specific workbenches that you'll find in dungeon crawls. Unfortunately I think this really plays against any crafting system. Dungeons are for looting and leveling, not for crafting equipment, and this gameplay mechanic seems very out of place.
More importantly, I felt that crafting in the game was entirely too complicated and ultimately a waste of time. In order to craft equipment, you must first purchase the various crafting books to teach you recipes. The crafting books themselves cost several hundred gold a piece, whereas the equipment that you'd be crafting is readily available for purchase at the vendors for just a few hundred more. Crafting is also gated behind the leveling system, meaning you won't be able to craft high level items until your character level matches (though even if you could, you still wouldnt be able to equip them)
Possibly the worst aspect of the game is that even though its obvious the developers spent a lot of time regulating leveling and equipment to maintain game balance, there were still a lot of instances where it felt very off. I could be going through a dungeon decimating all enemies in my path without even using skills, only to die unmercifully to the end stage boss. Part of the reason for this is due to the games heavy reliance on DOT mechanics, which can add up to several hundred damage per turn. This wouldn't be so bad if your characters could inflict a similar level of DoT damage on enemies, but it is actually paltry in comparison. Likewise, its difficult to tell how much damage your character will take from any of the many DoT effects, making it hard to properly prepare for in battle.
The game is good, but needs some work to really shine, especially in the gating and crafting areas.

"My name is....
Doesn't really matter, I suppose.
Used to know how long I've been here
Now I've got no idea."
great psicological adventure that dares the player to fight their most intricate fears and question its reality, As you embody the nameless survivor you must face the harsh world that's left behind after a catastrophic-Apocaliptic-esque infection.
While this game uses very common horror concepts like a dystopic world ravaged by an unknown infection and zombie-like enemies it still manages to avoid the "More of the same media" Gap by throwing a really fragile (Both Physically and Psicologically) protagonist to the mix, the same character clearly suffers from a severe case of depression (given all the horrors he has faced alone) and manages to transmit that feeling to the player, The post-apocalyptic world is indeed a nightmare, Not a bullet-frenzy zombie killing spree that some other media has led us to believe so many times before.
With intricate dialogue that usually includes personification of inanimate objects and self-loathing and some hallucinations the player gets to know the background story, It would seem unexistan given that it's not directly narrated but on the contrary, it's there, waiting for you to figure it out by yourself.
As you progress through the story you will notice that the survivor will often hallucinate talking with a variety of characters, often passes-out and even finds himself unable to remember doing some things (like writing on his diary). as you struggle to find food, water and enough sleep while you evade the nightmarish creatures the horrors take it's toll on the survivor's mind making the setting all the more depresing.
speaking about combat and scavenging, both dynamics are present and are a core feature of the game, you have to eat to stay alive, and not just "Eat anything". Eating rotten meat and rats will allow you to stay alive, but also have a higher negative impact on the character's sanity than taking the time to find and cook the ingredients for a propper meal (even when that meal canned beans).
sleep is also necesary to keep you sane, and getting too much or not enough will affect your final sanity.
The combat is Reminiscent of the golden days of resident evil, only in 2D. and while it lacks the weapon variety of the former it compensates by giving you the chance to clear the whole game without firing a single bullet, Using your wits and stealth to traverse the infected-filled streets.
While the creatures in the world are few in variation the character stays human and vulnerable the whole game, Making the first enemy as deadly as the last one. nonetheless the game also pushes some interesting variations to keep your♥♥♥♥♥♥scared and some giant scary monsters to keep things interesting.
My final rating: 9/10
Brilliantly executed.

Lone Survivor is a 2D sidescrolling, pixel-based survival horror game that reminded me a lot of Silent Hill 2. Much like James Sutherland, Lone Survivor's protagonist searches an apartment complex that's overrun with zombies while a noise layer obscures vision. Also, much like Silent Hill 2, the threat may possibly be more psychological in origin than real.
The game has multiple endings, and if you play it like you would an action game - shooting everything in sight while not caring much about the actual "survival" elements, you'll likely end up with one of the "bad" endings. This left a sour impression on my first play because of the character's constant nagging for food and sleep, and the ending I got seemed nonsensical.
But if you play the game more how it's meant to be played, the hero bothers you less, and you could put yourself on a path to one of the better endings, which reveals more what the story is really about. You'll probably also pay more attention to the clues here and there and get a better sense of everything on a replay. So, those extra endings are really worth going for, though it probably won't hurt to look at a FAQ to be sure you'll get them. I ended up coming to appreciate the game much more as a result, and it certainly doesn't hurt that the soundtrack is excellent, too.
And one of the things you can do is adopt a kitty! Bonus points just for that!
Rating: 3.5/5

Suicide seems to be the only concept that makes sense of this abstract electronic product.  Now I do not have any particular stance on suicide from a moral POV.  From a neo-evolutionary/emotional selection pressure POV I do, but that is beyond the scope of this review.  So I guess I will end it with suicide.  When the POV of your life is reduced to something equivalent to this bleek islandscape with acidic water and skeleton trees + you have a belief that there was a super natural being who was supposed to protect you - it looks like this super natural being has abandoned you = suicide.  Due to the nature of how intellectual pursuits reveal knowledge in this never-ending unfolding of layers like a constant interative adventure, I find it difficult to believe that an individual caught up in learning could ever consider suicide for the sole fact that there is still so much left to know.  But the same author of this game explored in a prior game called fingerbones that very subject - how a father who, due to being "enlightened" from intellectual pursuit, thought the only way for himself to become free was to experience an end of the world type of apacalytic event.  It is clear that there is much to be understood about the collective human mind once it has experienced the beauty of knowledge - how on one side a world of curious scientists are born who strive for the improvement of mankind and the other a world of curious scientists come forth who only wish for mankind's demise.
That last part gave me a chill up my spine

Understand, that while many games have an easy mode and a useful tutorial, this one doesn't have either to learn by. You can't set up an ai team. A friend who took it upon himself to help me think about buying Stellaris did his best to help me out and I can only say thanks and have kind words to say about him. My observations are that Stellaris is just a artsy pretty version of "who has the most ships wins." There's no real strategy to this when the research is so randomized and the resources always skewed against you. I and opposing race had 2.4k miliary power fleets. My ships did twice as much damage as his, he just had more of them. I designed my ships with more armor more shields etc. than stock, and yet, he won with half his ships to spare.

And whose bright idea was it that is a build control mechanism? Same old same old ploy of the hallowed ground versus corrupted ground called "creep" of Warcraft III fame (similar to Starcraft where things have to be around the pylons or zerg building on their corrupted soil, and no one else can build on their corrupted ground).
Sure I appreciate a lot of what's in the game for apperances sake and the music, the creativity that went into all of that, but by not providing an easy mode to help build confidence through playing the game is denying the game a large part of the audience that's attracted to this type of game, people like me who get frustrated and may even write it off as we would rather not have high blood pressure conditioning.
Another game to mention is Pax Imperia you'd budget for espionage and could advisors or assassinate them, steal technology from their science officer, see their production and finances through their financial officer, etc., and Pax Imperia Eminent Domain you'd be able to literally take over a planet by causing a rebellion. Imagine EU:IV, in space (and somewhat more combat and narrative oriented).
I like to think that it improved on the existing mechanics of EU:IV. The concepts are pretty much the same, but instead of managing provinces inside your country, you manage planets and systems on your empire.
Unlike the previous titles, this time, you get to:
+ Design ships
+ Manage army composition
+ Opress minorities by setting "their rights" as you see fit
+ Be a ruthless xenophobic empire? A Federation of species? A peacekeeping force? etc...
+ Terraform planets
+ Lose everything to another much stronger empire that started a war because it just "Can't even!"
The UI has been improved and it's a lot more friendly than ckII ou EU:IV, but you still have to manage vast amounts of little things, through many different menu screens.
And, as expected, the game receives constant support and new content, either through free or paid DLC (which i dont mind as long as its not bloat). Stellaris is the one time Paradox decided to move away from history, and move into deep space, where history isn't really established beyond what little exploration humanity has already achieved. You still play a role as a starting empire growing to become, essentially, the center of the universe, but it's a bit different than usual. For one thing, people tend to wage war just because they feel like it, as diplomacy amounts to how much someone likes or hates you, and if they want to be your friend, or shove a doomstack down your throat. The ship designer was pretty much made because the game is more than just doomstacks. Not having a well equipped fleet will mean just having massive numbers can still end up with most of them in a trash heap. On top of that, going overboard on something like point defense and anti-shield weaponry, means someone who relies on lasers and raw armor is probably going to eat you alive.
Personally, I enjoy it. I love space, I love space ships, and I love fleet battles. This game has fleet battles with space ships. IN SPACE! The ship designer is a nice way to make every encounter feel different, though the ships automate all the combat in standard Paradox fashion, at the very least this is the most detailed they've been of actually watching the fight go down. Instead of swordsmen swinging their swords at each other in a way that implies they're hoping their enemy will be too scared to approach and give up, both fleets will begin their approach and engage at will. When they engage depends on weapon range, so sometimes you can take damage before you even get a shot off. It's still a 2-D map, but there's actual 3-D models within it. Plus I guess with everything mostly depending on how well you equipped your ships, it's a nice spectacle to watch when you're not worried about giving your army commands, even if it does take you out of the game.
So even if the diplomacy is a bit weaker, the game is still fun to grow into a massive empire with a death fleet that eats planets for breakfast, and their fleets for lunch. Though the fact Fallen Empires can make Titans, a class you can't make like the filthy cheaters they are, still annoys me.

Nier:Automata was my first Yoko Taro game. I gotta say, it was an amazing experience...
It had: One of the most interesting universes and stories I`ve ever seen, the best sound track I`ve heard in a video game and AMAZING gameplay.
Nier Automata`s combat system is absolutely perfect, it takes some time to master, but once you do, you feel so powerful! (That`s Platinum games`s combat for you, it`s very similar to Bayonetta)
Story: Nier Automata is a roller coaster of emotions, questions and answers. The more you play, the more questions start popping up on your head, the game has a confusing story at first. Throughout the playthrough it does answer everything though. (That is, if you take your time reading through the collected arquives, if you don`t, you`ll miss a few cool details that clarify a some past events and tells you why the world became how it is in Automata). The characters are full of personality... And the game managed to develop the relation between 2B and 9S in a great way.
The game`s story is put in a way that the first two endings are only the part 1 of the story, while the 3 last endings are part 2 (and the part where the game REALLY gets insane). - Don`t get me wrong though, endings A and B are pretty good too.
NOTE: YOU DO NOT NEED TO PLAY THE PREVIOUS NIER OR THE DRAKENGARD SERIES TO UNDERSTAND AUTOMATA (Though the previous games do have a LOT of details about the world inside Automata and why it has developed into what it is). - Still, you can get most of that through the arquives.
Soundtrack:  B-E-S-T    T-H-I-N-G    E-V-E-R
Characters: Overall great, the main and side characters all have their moments, and show a lot of personality and development.
2B: The ``perfect soldier``. Throughout the first playthrough, 2B is shown to be the coldest of characters, pretending to only care about the mission. Later, she develops into a kindhearted and caring character, and shows her true colors.
9S: The emotional one. 9S is the humor part of the game, and he does a pretty good job at it. He is a pretty nice guy, and I pitty him (for reasons).
A2: A2 is a thing of her own, due to her past (won`t say anything else)
Gameplay: Platinum Games. (I`m just gonna say that)
Cons: Performance is lacking, I was able to play the game just fine at arround 45-60 FPS, however, at 1600x900p and with everything except for texture filter at low. The game also presents performance issues on the PS4.
(Nothing game breaking though, the game still looked pretty good with my settings, and if you have a better machine, you`ll be able to pump up the graphics just fine)
I guess there are no more cons.
Veredict: 9/10 due to a few performance issues - The rest was perfect in my opinion though. (I`d say, if you got a monster machine and can play this game at 60 fps all the time, it`s a 10/10)

The turnbased combat is very reminiscent to Final Fantasy games while introducing it's own unique mechanics such as  "Overcharge"
Overcharge is basically temporary mana a character is given whenever they do regular actions in combat. It's a mechanic that encourages activity over inactivity, the first I've seen in a turnbased game and probably one of my favorites.
Exploration in Battle Chasers: NW shares similarities with
(for its level designs) and
(for the dungeon layout & enemy encounters). Also, the layout of the dungeons changes whenever you revisit them, this gives a non linear grinding/farming experience.
The main plot is not that spectacular, but the rest of the writing itself is excellent in my opinion, the characters outside of the main cutscenes are endearing and the bits of lore found all across the world are all the more intriguing. But behind the dark undertones, what I enjoy most are the subtle jokes the writers slip in from time to time...
One time when I was fishing, the game told me I caught a fish that legends say could talk, but since I hooked it out of the water, it died and I can never test the theory anymore.
The 2D and 3D aesthetics of this game blends together so well.
The UI, the animations, the 3D models and environments, every visual aspect of the game shares the same artistic motif, it's very consistent and enjoyable to look at for hours and hours of gameplay.
And with Joe Madureira himself behind the creative direction is just icing on the cake.
I'm a bit biased on this one cuz I'm a real sucker for comic book artstyles, specially for Joe Mad's art. If you are too, you would probably enjoy the visuals as much I did.
----------------------------------- SUMMARY -----------------------------------
VISUALS: Epic.
COMBAT: Final Fantasy w/ It's own unique mechanics.
DUNGEON CRAWLING: Torchlight + Kingdom Hearts: Chain of Memories
NARRATIVE: Meh Story, Endearing Characters, Great Lore, Funny but can be dark at times.
BUGS/GLITCHES: No game breaking ones

A very short first person perspective story-driven, psychological horror, exploration game. It has an intriguing story and a very interesting narrative style expressed through the concept of implied horror. It is best played in one sitting on a weekend night while it is storming outside. Go in without expectations, and enjoy the hour or two of playtime that you would get out of it.
Even though it is short, try to play it slowly. It can be finished in less than an hour if you ignore the exploration and narrative parts of the game. Try to immerse yourself and understand the story that is being told. You'd be surprised at some of the implications made throughout your playtime, and its ending. Also, don't forget to make your surrounding atmosphere fit the one in the game. Play with good headphones on, if possible, turn off the lights, and try to remove all nearby distractions.
Disclaimer: I know the developer of the game.

NOTE: Please buy the 'Wrath of the Lamb' DLC if you're going to get this. It will make TBoI a million times better, and will allow you to update the game to get the Hard Mode.
With randomly generated dungeons for every playthrough and a top down dungeon crawling experience in the same vein of the original Zelda trilogy, The Binding of Isaac is a roguelike game that can be picked up for less than a dollar and provides hours and hours of fun on end.
Following Isaac, a young boy who is trying to defeat his murderous mother after almost getting killed by her, TBoI has hundreds of items, ranging from the cutest of fashion accessories to the most grotesque parasites and diseases. With a randomisation system that makes no two playthroughs the same, TBoI is an adventure, a big step forward in the world of indie gaming, and ultimately, you'll have a hell of a time playing it.
My criticisms with the game are that it's impossible to predict what items you're going to get, and while this adds to the mystery, this also means you can become obscenely OP or obscenely UP and it can become frustrating having to play through with what could be called a dead weight on your leg, which combined with the VERY steep learning curve, makes for a frustrating time with some playthroughs.
Nonetheless, with a game that you can pick up for less than one dollar, where can you go wrong? I highly reccommend TBoI, and if you like it, go pick up the remake, The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth!

After more than 700 hours I think it's finally time to review this game, since I think I have played a good amount to give my unbiased oppinino on The Binding of Isaac.
First and foremost: Yes, I have played Rebirth. I think it was around my 500 hour mark when Rebirth was released and I was hyped like everyone else but my interest for Rebirth died down really fast and I continued playing Classic Isaac (for a more detailed review on why I prefer Classic Isaac over Rebirth, feel free to check my Review for Rebirth.)
However, I absolutely love this game. I would even go so far and say that it's the absolute best game I have ever played and I started playing games when I had a SNES, so calling a game that was made in flash my favorite game of all time is a huge accomplishment.
The skill cap in this game is something that is insanely good, games where you can feel that you get progressively better are very rare to come across, but the more you play it, the more you learn what which items do how you can get the most out of every single floor and of course dodging, the more you play it, the better you get at it.
The cool thing is, that even after 700 hours you might not find any more secrets or anything like that, but the game never feels repetitive, since every run has a different layout of floors, the items you find are different, the bosses you find are different and the drops you find, as well.
Also what this game has over Rebirth, in my opinion, is the limited amount of Items.
Sure, there are people who say that at some point u just get specific items and just restart a run to the point where you get an item that is useful, so you limit yourself to a certain amount of items. But that's all up to oneself. You can either restart all time until you get your desired item, but you can also start off with a really bad item and get god-tier items along the way. The way how you play a run with a bad item and how you eventually make it work is all up to your skill at the long run.
What I was trying to say is, there are less items in Classic Isaac than in Rebirth, so ultimately you have more control and it is more likely that you get an item that you actually like. As I said, some might see that as a negative, since you limit yourself to certain items, but if I play 20+ runs and only get 1 run where I get 1 item that I like, that's no fun to me.
All in all The Binding of Isaac is my favorite game of all time, I would even say the benchmark for all Rogue-like games.
(Eternal Edition) As far as the eternal edition go (which is an update for Isaac that was released a couple of days ago) I totally enjoy this update. It adds a Hard Mode to the gae, so for people who have played this game for 700+ hours and don't wanna switch over to Rebirth, this is a great addition, because the name "Hard Mode" is exactly what it says.
There are "eternal forms" of regular mobs and bosses who are way tougher to beat. They have more hit points and different attacks. Another thing that they fixed, which they also added for the regular version, is the time you freeze whenever you pick up an item, trinket, pill, tarot- or playing card. The frame in which you freeze and can't move has been reduced which makes it easier for you to dodge enemies.
Once the bugs have been ironed out (there is currently a bug where you can't get out of a room when you fight the eternal form of "Loki" this update will be even more awesome than it already is.
As I said, if you love Rogue-likes, chances are that you already have this game, but if not, you should definitely give this game a try.

Review based on version 1.5 with all DLC.
IN SHORT:
It's fascinating, addictive, enormous. Might work better as a turn-based strategy (akin to Civilization).
PROS:
- Creative, unique stories and events. Lots of them.
- Absolutely thriving modding community that elevates the game by leaps and bounds with its extreme high-quality content. Developers should be very, very, very thankful.
- Surprisingly great ambiance loops (turn off the music).
- Empire creator is absolutely fantastic (with mods even better)
- Mind-boggling scale on largest maps.
- Meaningful complexity (things don't feel redundant).
- "Just one more technology..." syndrome (they're fascinating).
- More "hard" s-f than space-opera (great for me) [wormhole stations can't be built within sol-system grav-well; a most satisfying detail!]
- Variety, variety, variety.
- Randomizing systems do their job. No playthrough is alike (with exceptions in cons, below).
- The overall quality of the simulation of what running an interstellar civilization that's in contact with other intelligencies is actually pretty convincing.
CONS:
- Wars are a nuisance (but I'm a pacifist).
- Normal aggressivenes setting for AI makes them literal warmongers (at least for me).
- Diplomacy is lacking substance, but mechanics are sound and appropriately complex already.
- Mid-to-late game crisis scenarios are a particular nuisance. Spawning of utterly undefeatable super-dimensional invaders in the middle of your territory are normal (I have them turned off - yes, you can turn them off, but then I feel like I'm missing out on content).
- Some ship and station design feel very generic and uninspired.
- Things tend to happen too fast and all at once, especially when at war (turn-based gameplay would help here).
- I don't know if it's just me, but Stagnant Empires, Advanced Starts and Awakened Empiers tend to spawn too often right next to my doorstep. On normal aggressiveness settings, that means You're dead in approximately 6-8 hours from session start.
- It's just so ♥♥♥♥ing addictive!

Steel Ocean is fun as hell and it's got a lot of... depth. Follows the War Thunder/World of Tanks etc. model , however there is one huge thing that sets it apart from the crowd: variety.
Yes, the biggest thing I love about this game is that it has a huge amount of gameplay variety compared to some of these other games.
-Destroyers (my favorite) are fast, agile, and are deadly at close range with depth charges to destroy submarines and torpedoes to take out carriers and battleships. Now, eventually the subs get smart and realize that if they surface they can avoid your depth charges and are almost too small to hit with your main guns. BUT what they don't seem to have caught on to yet, is that you can actually ram any ship smaller than you and it typically results in an instant kill, so if an enemy sub surfaces to try to escape the depth charges just smash into them.
-Cruisers are essentially larger destroyers- more health, and bigger guns. They are maneuverable enough to dodge torpedoes and are quite effective against Destroyers. Light Cruisers have depth charges, making them alright against subs, and Heavy Cruisers have main batteries making them able to punch through the armor of Battleships at long range.
-Battleships are the big guns, able to deal ridiculous amounts of damage at very long range. They are good at destroying pretty much any ship except Submarines and Destroyers which are small enough to practically ignore their volleys. Their major drawback is that they require Carriers, Destroyers, or Submarines to scout for them so that they can stay back and deal damage without getting into torpedo range.
-Submarines are the stealth hunters. They can submerge under water and become immune to most attacks, at the cost of speed and limited oxygen supply. Going just below the surface allows them to fire (and be struck by) torpedoes while avoiding cannon fire, and diving deeper makes them safe from everything except depth charges. Because they are slow while underwater and vulnerable to depth charges, they are very vulnerable to Destroyers, but extremely strong against Battleships and Carriers which basically cannot hurt them.
-Carriers are the odd ones out that don't really fall into the Rocks Paper Scissors circle. They can send scout planes all over the map, making them excellent for recon, and can harass ships with dive bombers, destroy enemy planes with fighters, and even take out subs with torpedo bombers. However, planes can be shot down fairly easy if the victim is paying attention, so they are most effective at taking out ships already engaged in combat.
What ends up happening in most matches is, the Battleships and Carriers sit back, while the Destroyers, Subs, and Cruisers usually charge in. Carriers are ironically the first to the front lines with their planes. Because Battleships are the most powerful in terms of dealing damage, the trick is to scout out the position of the enemy Battleships so that your Battleships can destroy the enemy's while yours stay hidden. Alternatively, if your Submarines can sneak past the enemy Destroyers, they can easily destroy their Battleships and Carriers as well.
Or if you like to yolo it up like me, you can just play a Destroyer and charge straight at the enemy Battleship. If you're still in one piece by the time you get close, you're going to be getting a lot of kills.
This variety makes every ship play totally differently, you really feel like you are important to your team as everyone has their own role to play. It's free and worth your time.

To everyone reading this, dont base this off World of Warships. Its as far away from World of Warships as you can get (And Tone isnt an effin premium like those money vampires in St. Petersburg...). So here's 10 reasons SO is better than WoWS.
1) Most of the ships arent paper designs.
While you have things like the Illinois-class, Kongo Prototype, Nagato Prototype, and the H-classes, they only represent a small amount of ships (I can probably count them on the 15 fingers on each hand of an Agent Orange baby), the significant majority of the ships there are realistic, and some have specific years to designate how old/outdated their technology is compared to their modernized versions (Like for instance, Furutaka (1921) won't have the same statistics as the Furutaka in World of Warships, which has multiple hulls depicting multiple years modernizations took place (Or in WoWS Paper ship terms, different designs)), and most ships are balanced by what they possessed in terms of firepower, speed, and overall difficulty to wield (For instance, Pensacola is Tier 5 whereas Cleveland is Tier 8 in SO, meanwhile in World of Warships, because Pensacosta is apparently a better upgrade, Cleveland is Tier 6 and Pensacola is Tier 7).
2) Graphics
Im gonna cut right to the chase, the graphics in this arent the best...and they arent really Triple-A game worthy, but then again, look at WoWS graphics...they arent exactly Crysis 3-level graphics...
3) Speed of the matches
This one is a fun one. SO feels much quicker to get to the enemy, leaving less time to plan and read your favorite Bible Book while your R key does the rest like in WoWS. In SO, you get to the middle of the map much quicker (Possibly due to the small map size?), and it doesnt give you much time to♥♥♥♥♥♥around getting lost like in WoWS.
4) Submarines
I haven't played them yet, but they look interesting to say the least. From what Ive seen (And not PhlyDaily, if I could find a blade that's edgier than him, Id be the luckiest man on Earth), the Oxygen forces you to make choices that will affect your chances of survival by being forced to the surface every couple of moments to replenish oxygen, and a single torpedo hitting you will probably sink you. With the inclusion of the...oh wait Ill mention that next, with the next function, it pretty much balances the Sub out in terms of no Sneeki Breeki Iv Damke for you!
5) Torpedo safe-zone
Who knew that including a safe-zone from torpedos can help balance a game! I BET THOSE GUYS AT WARGAMING NEVER THOUGHT ABOUT THAT...
6) Battleships
Battleships seem to be actually worth the EXP in this game, whereas Heavy Cruisers always dominate WoWS to no end. BBs now have the ability to absolutely destwoy enemy ships with a single salvo, ranging from other BBs to HCs to LCs to CVs, and everything inbetween. For once I can actually go to enjoy Based Nagato /o_o/
7) Gold is...much more expensive...
While WG is pretty greedy, this game is even more greedy, in terms of the amount of gold you can buy...though to be fair, the 311 USD deal (Nice try goyims) is much better than WG if they tried a 1 dollar = 250 gold conversion (77758 (Rounded up) from WG compared to 155,500 (Plus 155,500 for your first purchase) by SO) for 311 USD.
8) LOTS of ships
SO has many historical ships that actually served in the Pacific and Atlantic Theatres, including most of the ships from BS:P (Which would be the closest match in terms of amount of historical ships), and they dont try to add names to ships THAT NEVER HAD NAMES,
9) Gun reload times.
My Tenryuu in WoWS had a 5 second reload time on its 14cm guns. In SO is 12 seconds. Which do you think is the most realistic. Take your pick. Choose your poison. Whichever suits your fancy. SO is more realistic. Whatever floats your boat. Or sinks it.
10) There's a tutorial that allows you to get into the game.
In WoWS, you dont really get any introduction, and you're essentially told "Go out there and shoot at things." This would be fine if they told you what exactly you're supposed to do and expect from the weapons you have at your disposal. SO's got you covered.

I was looking for a game to pass the time, until the release of No Man’s Sky. Stumbled upon this and decided to give it a try, as used to dabble in World of Warcraft many years ago.

The cut-scene videos in some instance runs, and the ability to hand quests in without having to travel all the way back to where you first picked it up, is a nice touch.
These types of games are very linear, and there will be times where you’re grinding, but the developers have done their best to give abit of variety. Best example of this will be the challenge quests, and also the explorer quests (if you choose to go down this route).
I’ll probably get bored of it eventually, but so far I’m having a blast. If you’ve played World of Warcraft and want to try it again, but can’t / won’t pay for it, this is an excellent choice.
Overall a very good game.

Feel smart while you are playing a dumb game simulator.
This isn't a tactical or a stealth game. It APPEARS to be however. It wants to look professional, detailed, using a lot digital interface effects that float in 3D, but when you actually PLAY the game you'll feel something is wrong. And here is why.
This game, like many these days, does not offer challange. Does not offer depth. It's a generalized experience that exists only to serve the player, not to challange him/her. You are walking around in practically godmode, being invisible, spreading the glorious headshots, and in case anything goes wrong you have an "oh sh.....t!" button that is supposed to be "tactical command", but basicly a button to instantly kill any enemy at any time, anywhere, saying your squad members shoot them. Who are also following you under the gentle cloak of godmode invisibility. Of course the maps are very limited to guide you towards scripted wins and perfectly ideal situations, just you can feel smart you killed 3 guys at once because you marked 2 for death, and shot one yourself.
There are no tactics, there is no tension, no andenaline, no actual smart play, even if the game tries so hard to create the illusion of these for the player while all it really does it bows down before you, so you can W+M1 through it. Or actually W+F here with the "tactical command" that is God Strikes You Down instant death. Of course while your teammates continually compliment you for it and you get all kinds of "HyperSuperDuperUber skilled player you are!" stuff.
Verdict? It's not only boring, but boring for all the wrong reasons. I couldn't get myself to luanch this game a second time. I feel so served, so unchallanged, so bored of walking as god among mere mortals, that it is actually deeply discouraging to even play. Because I don't play, I do zombie mode, while the game fails so hard to create this feeling of professionalism, challange and pro play, that isn't even there at all, but also fails at faking it, because it pushes too hard to the point where the obvious just starts to hurt.
