(I bought the mobile port before buying the game on steam, there will be an explaination that reason below)
When I first saw this on mobile I believed that the game wasn't interesting because of the lack of detail with the posted in-game images (as in, 8-bit pixel sprites instead of the 16-bit characters you see now), however during the small and random "Rogue-like" phase of mine, I bought it anyways.
And man was I surprised.
(Looks and Sounds)
The game takes on a similar look to Minecraft in a way with it's 16-bit pixel isometric textures, minimal HUD, and virtually astethic delvering music. My experiecne with this is that it's really disorenting on with the FOV and the textures, however over time I got used to them.
Yes, it's pixel barf, but you'll get used to it eventually, think of it like a harder version of Minecraft.
The music, enemy sounds, and sound effects are all in line with the theme, playstyle and overall idea of the game. each section within the dungeon changes music to the needs of the dungeon's style, and it gets darker and darker as you go. The Enemy sounds are just right, you know that they're there when you get into their line of sight, and that's because they make an annoying sound.
From the splashing water, boilling lava and the annoying bat flutter sounds in the distance, the air within the game matches the "delvering" style of the game.
(besides those bad ones of course)
In my personal opinion, Rogue-like games are the best because you have to master the game in different parts (ex: enemy playstyles, testing unknown potions, etc). Even though I might not master Delver's gameplay (as I have yet to complete ANY rogue-like game) the sense of perma-death and the randomly generated dungeons give the sense of a renewed exploration.
You will die a lot in this game, mostly because of something you did wrong.
===================/=====================
At the end of the day, this game is linear, but it exceeds my expectations of what a rogue-like should be. It's hard, it's complicated and the gameplay is great. I would recommend both the Mobile AND the PC ports of this game because it gives different, but similar gamestyles.
And I only found out that there was a PC version because Vinny from Vinesauce actually livestreamed the game on PC. He said it was good and unique, so that kept my hopes up and bought the game on Steam. I honestly didn't know that Delver was first on PC before Mobile, but it's a small world out there.
===================/=====================
On another note however, from my personal experiences in the game I never really ran into any bugs or glitches of sorts, maybe if I tried I would.
A wise gamer once applied the term "Slow and steady wins the race." to games when they are being produced. And I guess he was right in a way.
tl;dr (You really should read the full review!)
Delver is a good game, maybe not worth as much as it's sold for simply due to low level of content but the gameplay is solid enough to balance this out. Give it a try.

Peggle might look like a kid’s game but the game is more complex then what it appears on the surface and a great game to just relax to and play on the side. As you play through the game you begin realize there is more to it than just hitting red pegs and completing the level. There’s strategy, timing and angles involved for those who do the Challenge levels which I'll get into in a bit. Combo's are a huge part of this and can result in massive scores and free balls by going for pink pegs (Score boost), green pegs (your peggle masters ability) and hitting enough pegs to build up your combo meter.
There are 50 Adventure mode levels split between 10 different peggle masters and 5 master levels at the end.
The Adventure mode is designed to teach you the different "Peggle Masters" aka characters and their abilities.
Different characters abilities are better for curtain scenarios depending on what your strategy is.
There are 75 Challenge mode levels which require you to complete the specific level in a particular way, the further you progress through the challenge levels the harder they get. Towards the last 15 or so they become very hard and only the best/luckiest players have a chance at beating them. Some examples of levels I had a very hard time beating and got a little lucky when I did beat them were "Complete a level starting with only 1 ball", beat a master AI score over 3 levels, score 750k over 3 levels etc. Ones that I tried and just couldn't do are like "Score 1 mil over 3 levels, "score 750k in a single level" and "beat 10 levels in a row".... yeah no thanks. In total I beat 70/75 challenges which is good enough for me.

Project codename: "STELLARIS"
Project type: Artifact research
Project starting year&location: Galactic Year 3464, Sol System, Sol III
Preliminary analysis shows this was an effective entertainment device used by the civilization of Sol III, albeit primitive enough to be compatible with pre-quantum computers and electrochemical displays (or, indeed, even cathode ray tubes, a technology so ancient the science team has all but forgot about its existance by now!).
It appears to be a simulation of sorts, of how a fresh star empire would contend with the new frontiers of diplomacy, economy, warfare and scientific progress once FTL technology is achieved and made economically feasible. Note: Some claim that it might have been a training simulator for the first leaders of the human species once they achieved spaceflight, but that claim is heavily disputed by the fact that the artifact predates the human FTL capacity by at least 70 standard galactic years and the species was far from capable of forming a global government at that point.
The first thing that amazed the science team was the sheer variety of simulated governance forms, from completely democratic to completely totalitarian, from scientifice oriented, to spiritually oriented, peaceful to utterly aggressive and the list goes on. At this point we note that no member of the science team ever had any doubt in the fact that a directorate of the state's most brilliant minds is objectively the best way to govern, but there is useful data to be found in simulating and analyzing less efficient and more primitive government forms with focuses on lesser pursuits, be it pure physical dominance or economic control.
The simulation has quite a wide array of settings to be played on, from a large galaxy all but devoid of civilized life, to one completely cramped with budding empires struggling for influence and territory, with modifiable aggressivenes of the simulated "players". Additional parameters may be set to modify the behavior of the simulation at later points in time, when the empires establish themselves, by adding tougher challenges into the mix and sending the player a clear signal that there are things far greater, far more awesome, and far more dangerous than they could have ever imagined lurking in the galaxy.
Most features of the simulations have been built upon and improved as time went by, signifying that this was a rather long-term project, compared to many that stopped receiving support quickly after being made publicly available. While this of course must have incurred additional costs throughout the project's lifetime, there has been clear appreciation of the continued development.
The simulation itself plays on a large two-dimensional map with rather streamlined graphic details, probably in order to reduce the amount of aesthetic distractions that could easily cause the player to stop paying attention to the relevant information on their display screen. Fleet combat also seems to be an abstraction of background calculations rather than a faithful simulation of what the spaceships engaged in battle would be expected to be doing - and there is no way to issue tactical orders to the simulated fleets directly past selecting their AI core design. An impressive array of weaponary is available, though - tachyon lances, why don't we think big like that more often?
Technological advancement is a bit obscure, however, since rather than having a clearly marked flowchart of scientific progression, the simulation instead gives the player a handful of separate available research options, and only some base rules are set so that a more advanced technology can't appear before what would logically be its precursor. Still, the research is not as structured as one would expect, and sometimes the player's advancement would be hampered by sheer bad luck. Luckily our directorate knows better than leave science decisions to the whims of lesser minds.
Diplomacy simulations have been changing a lot through the project's lifetime, and, as in reality, most of the time they felt as if there's still something missing, as if the players were still very limited in the scale of their diplomatic actions - for example, at the point of writing of this report there is still no option to mark certain technologies as strategically vital and excluded from research agreements.
The political simulation has been changed several times along the course of the project's lifetime as well, constantly adding new features such as delegating political rules to the species level and allowing the players to interact more precisely with the simulated society they were in charge of and could manipulate different social groups though granting (or limiting) their liberties, social, and economic status.
The economic simulation is both streamlined and complex, with clearly defined "energy credits" that serve as currency, "minerals" that serve as physical resources and production, "food" that is, well...food; but on the other hand the more abstract ones are "influence" that is supposed to represent the political clout an empire holds at any point in time and "unity" which effectively allows empires to better themselves from within. And then there's the scientific resources that are grouped into "physics", "social" and "engineering" resources, and the science team shall not comment on what they feel about making it all sound that simple. Still, juggling all of those could have been a challenge.
While the visual aspect of the simulation is, as mentioned, quite minimalistic and rudimentary, the audio aspect is quite well developed, with a clearly expertly composed musical track to keep the players entertained and interested. Unfortunately, we have found no indication of who this "Mercedes Romero" person was, but apparently someone important since they got a whole track dedicated to them. Note: Part of the science team maintains that was an inside joke by the project's creators.
In conclusion, as primitive as this artifact is, it seemed to have served its purpose well enough despite its flaws. In fact, even some of the science team seem to have taken a more than only academic interest in the thing, and had to have their access to the artifact limited to only a few hours per day, with supervision of a senior scientist. In fact, one of the team members proposed that this artifact is partly at fault for the human civilization not existing anymore, because it caused them to stop reproducing because they got too hooked on it. A ridiculous claim, to be sure, but it needs to be researched, if only to refute it.
Science mission leader signing off to take another look at the artifact, poke at it some more and see what data comes out if played with some more.
My interest is merely academic. Really.

There are a few gamemodes varying from your traditional team deathmatch to a new take on a capture the flag mode where you have to capture a giant electric hammer that you can use to crush your enemies into nothing but blood and powder. While playing this game, you quickly realise that each trigger pull heralds a fountain of blood and viscera erupting onto your screen. Many a player can be seen limping off with chunks of their knees missing while others may be nothing more than a walking pair of legs. The gore, while cartoony, is quite vivid and is alone enough to warrant trying this game.

I've played Wildstar for about a year now, and it's still one of the best games I've played. It's got just about everything you could ask from a MMORPG, and a whole lot more. Memorable characters, exotic places, and even more to make the experience more amazing.
There's a boatload of things you can create and customize, each with your own little flare. The character customization is spot on, and gives you a good understanding of what your class and path will allow you to do, even before you take your first steps on the planet Nexus. And even after you get settled in, you'll find that you can make just about anything- from your outfit to your own housing lot- specialized to fit your liking.
Wildstar is just filled with lore, making it a great game to spend time on trying to figure out what's going on behind the calm atmosphere of Nexus. And with 2 sides to choose from, it just opens up mystery and excitement if you're into stuff like that. And no matter what class and path you pick, you'll still be following the story, although the Scientist path really allows you to see the core of what's going on. Every mission brings up questions, and there's great load of collectables and 'Datacubes' that allow you to take a peek into the story even more.
The planet Nexus is just filled with amazing and awesome places to explore. Snowy wastelands, lush jungles, even abandoned space stations! Each with its own quests and chances for loot, while assuming you are the appropriate level, of course, as most areas are sectioned by your character's level. Both PVE and PVP zones have secrets waiting to be discovered, and the Explorer path can help you reach and discover secret places that only you can find. Even if that's not your style, Nexus is still pretty huge, and you'll often be caught looking in awe at the beautiful- or terrifying- landscape.
Wildstar's combat system and PVP matches are extremely fun and challenging. Even if you don't want to wait for a lobby, there are certain areas on Nexus that are PVP friendly, but you can turn this off if you want to. Back to the bloodshed, though, there's various dungeons and types of PVP matches you can queue in for. PVP matches can include a CTF type mode where you scramble around with your team to capture and defend masks, the ever so original 2v2, 3v3, or 5v5 arena mode, and you can even make a huge party and set up a War Plot, then participate in a whopping 40v40 PVP match. Meanwhile, PVE can still satisfy your thirst for blood with interesting enemies and challenging bosses to keep you on your toes. Each class gives you different ways to be effective on your enemies, making teamwork sometimes very essential.
All in all, I recommend Wildstar. The community isn't very toxic, there's fun events and challenges, but I HIGHLY recommend that you get a friend or two to play this with you, since the experience is even better with friends. I hope you enjoy Wildstar as much as I did.

Let me start by saying up until this game I thought I was seriously done with MMOs. I was completely burned out. I have been playing MMOs since Ultima Online - EQ, EQ2, Meridian 59, Vanguard, WoW (of course), Rift, Tera, LoTR, DDO and on and on. So when this went F2P and on steam I was curious as it looked very nice.
First, I had never heard of it which is sad because if this game had some decent marketing when it launched it would probably garner a much deeper fan base. That said, it is still fairly well populated.
Second, it is a beautiful game. Graphics are top notch and run flawlessly. I cannot say how it was at launch but today it is a very polished game.
As with most MMOs everyone compares them to WoW as that is the elephant in the room and this is no different. Mainly because of the cartoony feel. However, all resemblances to WoW end there. The combat is so much better than most MMOs. It is directional and very skill based. You are limited to 8 skills, 1 gadget and 1 buff/heal slot. It is very much a sci-fi theme (reminds me of Firefly in some things) and does not seem to take itself too seriously. It is actually a lot of fun to play. Dungeons are very challenging and Veteran (read heroic) versions are even more so. I have only participated in some world boss raids but those are very hectic and lots of fun. They remind me of WoW BC and Litch King raids or Veeshan's Peak raids in EQ2. They are very technical and tactical. Well thought out and scripted with very little RNG that I can see at this point.
Endgame seems well thought out and I do not feel like I am grinding the same things over and over. I would compare it to BC dailies that ranged over several zones. These are over even more areas and I am hard pressed to complete even half of the available daily quests in any given day. This may change but so far I am pleasantly surprised. Crafting is a bit meh, but unless you really get into crafting I would guess this might be most people's reaction to it.
Downside - there are some bugs and broken crafting trees and (imo) lack of support from NCSoft to put sufficient resources into fixing them. If the game starts pulling in sufficient revenue they may put more resources into the game. Time will tell. Queue system for dungeons, while not exactly broken, is not really useable. Basically, no one uses it so you can sit there for literally hours and never get in a group. With cross faction chat now a thing your best bet is to find a group through chat. If enough people start using it this might fix itself - again time will tell.
In-Game MT shop - No pay to win here, mostly cosmetics, mounts, pets, account unlocks and xp, rep buff pots. I normally don't care about cosmetics that much but some of these are just downright cool looking. There are special keys to buy to unlock bonus chests at the end of dungeons/expeditions and such. You don't have to buy these and they are relatively cheap, but these chests do tend to have some good gear in them so they are encouraging you to get them. The gear in the chests are not game breaking, they are on the level of what you get in the dungeon anyway so it's just a bonus chest so to speak.
All in all it's a very good game and I hope it succeeds and stays around for awhile.  8/10

Peggle Deluxe is a casual game that takes fun to new levels, its objective is simple, but its execution can be frustrating. With 10 different characters, all with rewarding power ups makes this game a jem among dirt. Completing this game is an amazing sight, but the fun doesn't end there, once you complete the game you unlock Dual and Challenge mode.

Peggle might look like a kid’s game but the game is more complex then what it appears on the surface and a great game to just relax to and play on the side. As you play through the game you begin realize there is more to it than just hitting red pegs and completing the level. There’s strategy, timing and angles involved for those who do the Challenge levels which I'll get into in a bit. Combo's are a huge part of this and can result in massive scores and free balls by going for pink pegs (Score boost), green pegs (your peggle masters ability) and hitting enough pegs to build up your combo meter.
There are 50 Adventure mode levels split between 10 different peggle masters and 5 master levels at the end.
The Adventure mode is designed to teach you the different "Peggle Masters" aka characters and their abilities.
Different characters abilities are better for curtain scenarios depending on what your strategy is.
There are 75 Challenge mode levels which require you to complete the specific level in a particular way, the further you progress through the challenge levels the harder they get. Towards the last 15 or so they become very hard and only the best/luckiest players have a chance at beating them. Some examples of levels I had a very hard time beating and got a little lucky when I did beat them were "Complete a level starting with only 1 ball", beat a master AI score over 3 levels, score 750k over 3 levels etc. Ones that I tried and just couldn't do are like "Score 1 mil over 3 levels, "score 750k in a single level" and "beat 10 levels in a row".... yeah no thanks. In total I beat 70/75 challenges which is good enough for me.

As the description mentions, Magicite is heavy on Rogue-like elements such as permadeath and random stage generation. This game has outstanding music to ease the repeatedly flailing of one of, as of this review, 15 custom-trait characters through up to 20 stages per playthrough
. Twenty stages may seem like a short game map, but this is easily made up for by the extreme difficulty and highly rewarding gameplay, as well as multiplayer (I don't know specific server sizes, but my knowledge is that local multiplayer is capped at 4 total players).
Magicite does have some potentially less desirable features though; the game has somewhat limited replayability after completion, especially after all 46 unlockables have been found, and the enemy-filled stages are generated in sections instead of completely random platform placement. To whomever it may apply, there is also yet to be controller support.
|Note: Below section is all based on the version out at the time of review, more may be added along game development|
Also note that all 15 unlockable character 'races' have unique starting traits, any of the races can wear any of the 24 unlockable 'hats', and be followed by one of 8 unlockable special 'Companions' (only one hat and companion at a time); so long as the player has met the requirements for acquiring each unlockable item and is lucky enough on percentile-based chances where they occur. Additional stat improvement can also be made in-game via crafting and wearing specialised armors, or wielding specific items.

The Moon Sliver is a game that delves deep into themes like loneliness, lack of purpose, solitary life, living after a pseudo-apocalypse and even religion and belief. Before playing it though, you must keep in mind that it is a game that relies entirely on its story and atmosphere.
Pros:
+incredibly authentic atmosphere
+brilliant story
+original setting and ideas
+combines elements of atmospheric, horror and even fantasy
Cons:
-graphics isn't that great, but then again, it's as good as you could expect from such a small indie project
-gameplay elements range from poor to inexistent, but it definitely makes up through its story
-you require two keys to progress which are found in the same house, but which might be easy to miss and, if you do, the game really gets annoying.
-a bit short
Overall, I would give it a 9/10. I definitely recommend it, especially given its low price. It's a great piece of indie gaming!

Review based on version 1.5 with all DLC.
IN SHORT:
It's fascinating, addictive, enormous. Might work better as a turn-based strategy (akin to Civilization).
PROS:
- Creative, unique stories and events. Lots of them.
- Absolutely thriving modding community that elevates the game by leaps and bounds with its extreme high-quality content. Developers should be very, very, very thankful.
- Surprisingly great ambiance loops (turn off the music).
- Empire creator is absolutely fantastic (with mods even better)
- Mind-boggling scale on largest maps.
- Meaningful complexity (things don't feel redundant).
- "Just one more technology..." syndrome (they're fascinating).
- More "hard" s-f than space-opera (great for me) [wormhole stations can't be built within sol-system grav-well; a most satisfying detail!]
- Variety, variety, variety.
- Randomizing systems do their job. No playthrough is alike (with exceptions in cons, below).
- The overall quality of the simulation of what running an interstellar civilization that's in contact with other intelligencies is actually pretty convincing.
CONS:
- Wars are a nuisance (but I'm a pacifist).
- Normal aggressivenes setting for AI makes them literal warmongers (at least for me).
- Diplomacy is lacking substance, but mechanics are sound and appropriately complex already.
- Mid-to-late game crisis scenarios are a particular nuisance. Spawning of utterly undefeatable super-dimensional invaders in the middle of your territory are normal (I have them turned off - yes, you can turn them off, but then I feel like I'm missing out on content).
- Some ship and station design feel very generic and uninspired.
- Things tend to happen too fast and all at once, especially when at war (turn-based gameplay would help here).
- I don't know if it's just me, but Stagnant Empires, Advanced Starts and Awakened Empiers tend to spawn too often right next to my doorstep. On normal aggressiveness settings, that means You're dead in approximately 6-8 hours from session start.
- It's just so ♥♥♥♥ing addictive!

Let me just preface this by saying that you should stop wasting time reading this review and instead start playing this absolute multiplayer masterpiece.
Let me start by saying HALLELULAH, A free to play shooter which actually has an excellent business model, i.e most purchases are cosmetic, and the only ones that can give actual advatanges are limited to buyable weapon slots, Loadout slots and double XP/Blutes (The games currency). This is an extremely fair system as neither of this results in a Pay to win situation.
Now onto the actual game itself… Loadout takes pride in its insane amount of weapon customization. M4 with holo sight?? , Meh… Fireball lobbing cannon with a shotgun barrel firing bouncing projectiles guidable by a laser designator while firing full auto??? Check! This game puts most games to shame when it comes to customization. In addition, the initial unlocks available are actually quite useful and provide a leveled playing field for all levels, which is simply not the case in most shooters these days.
The actual gameplay screams ‘PC GAME PC GAME’… The controls are hyper responsive, there is 0 mouse lag, infact I didn’t even care that it was a third person shooter due to the greased lightning like response from the game. In this aspect, this game reminds me of shooters of old such as Wolfenstein Enemy territory, where bulky or bloated movement was never an issue. In addition to this, your character is capable of rolling by simply double tapping the movement keys, UT Style. This can also be used by pressing CTRL + any movement key. The jumping height is also high and if you time it correctly you could reach areas which are normally unreachable by conventional means. You could also do some wall running on certain levels. The main game modes available are Capture the Hammer,  A spin on the classic capture the flag, the twist being that the ‘Hammer’ could be used to reduce your enemies to a fine blood strewn mist, and will also YIELD MORE POINTS if you perform kills. There is also Blitz, which is a capture the point game mode, nothing special but really fun. Extraction is quite interesting as it requires collecting ‘Blutonium’scattered across the level, however only a randomly selected collector can collect it. The last gamemode is DeathSnatch, which is basically Kill Confirmed from the COD Games, but unlike the that game, this will involve bubonic plagues of projectiles lobbed at each other and fast movement. Oh did I mention, NO REGEN HEALTH FOR ONCE!!!!!
The game’s graphics are quite pleasing to the eye as it has a unique cartoonish aesthetic, which I find quite different from games such as Borderlands or TF2, especially the extreme blood and gore. Speaking of which, I would say that 25% of the fun probably lies in the ridiculously over the top death animations. You can blow off legs and watch your enemy or yourself yell in a cartoony fashion as a torrential downpour of cartoony blood pours forth, you can get completely burned, electrocuted, bashed or otherwise throughoutsplattered…. Well you get the idea.  The game is also extremely crude, immature, and stereotypical, or in layman terms FREAKING AWESOME. You will have a good laugh at the ridiculous characters that people come up with as well as the over the top ‘emotes’. The character models are also suitably hilarious as well as bad♥♥♥♥♥ One thing I noticed in particular was how well the characters hair and bandana were animated, it feels very fluid in a cartoony way. Another feature I found noteworthy was that projectiles will deform metal, quite a nice touch.
Overall Loadout needs no introduction,
It is undoubtedly the best Free to play Shooter out there  which sometimes get undeserving scores such as 5.8’s or 6.3’s. This is a game that I feel would get better the more you play it, as you unlock even more insane gear as well as simply getting better at the game. My only Real complaints about the game are the fact that there are only 4 game modes and about 6 maps in total. But I am sure that developer Edge of Reality will rectify this in the future as well as (hopefully) more weapon parts, characters, MOARRR LOADOUT.
Score:
Gameplay: 10/10, Fast, Fluid and hyper responsive, if you miss the days of old school arena shooters, look no further.
Feel, Atmosphere and Aesthetic: 9/10 The game is rich in colour and has a wonderfully crafted feel to it. IT simply oozes premium. It is also hilarious!
Replayability: 9/10: Despite not having a lot of maps or gametypes, the ludicrous weapon crafting as well as meaty gameplay will satisfy me for hundreds of hours, as I’m sure other people will do so as well.
Business Model: 10/10: Important in any Free to play game.I dare you to find a better business model.
Sound Design: 8/10: The characters, ambiet sounds and impact sounds are quite meaty however some of the weapons (especially shotguns) do not have the punchy sound assets I would have expected.
Overall: 9.1/10: An exemplary shooter which doesn’t take itself seriously at all. Only a lack of maps and gametypes prevent this from scoring higher. This is what a PC shooter should feel like, as well as how F2P should be done. Actually IT stretches beyond that, shooters should abandon the concept of trying to be Edgy Gritty and realistic while only managing to create a pseudo reality with jam covering your face when you get shot by a laser SMG. Loadout is a Gem of a game that no shooter fan should overlook, if you do then you just  do not like to have fun.
Kudos to Edge Of Reality, cannot wait to see what you guys come up with Next.

One of the very best games ever made. Some of the old, great games perhaps do not age very well, but a few are timeless simply because of their quality. No frills, no gimmicks, no set pieces, no cover systems or achievements - just gameplay and game design in it's purest, most endearing form. Medieval II is one of these games.
The game, in typical Total War fashion, involves economy, politics and army management with the ultimate aim of meeting  certain victory conditions, which will vary for each faction. A world map acts as the main user interface of the campaign, but the majority of gameplay will happen in the series' trademark - the battles.
In my opinion, this is the greatest game in the Total War franchise. Rome I had more varied unit rosters and was truly groundbreaking for it's time, but Medieval II is just Total War perfection. Hitting the "sweet spot" for complexity, political obstacles and size of the campaign map, the game has, whether by design or accident, remained the most (obssessively!) playable Total War to date. The difficulty levels of the campaign feel "just right", whether you are new and play on easy or normal, or want more of a challenge and pick legendary. This was the first Total War game I played, and increasing the difficulty felt organic and like a real progression.
Everything just comes together in a way which will be evident if you have played any other Total War titles, but regardless of that fact, the campaign is the best experience Total War has to offer. Battles are at their best in the series, with a level of strategic depth which keeps a dedicated online battling community alive to this day, but with an accessibility and satisfaction which makes you
. Winning a campaign, defending a castle against the odds and winning online battles are some of the most rewarding feelings I've ever felt in games.
The battles here are Total War at it's best. Every unit has a purpose and a counter, and winning a battle feels truly tactical. Unit speeds feel perfect, and units engaging each other feels crisp, unlike the floaty cluster effect seen in later games in the series. Losing a battle will always be down to a tactical error which will have you wanting to learn and coming back for more. If they managed to break your infantry lines with a clever charge strategy, you will feel like you were outsmarted. There are no gimmicks.
The atmopshere of the game is good - the medieval setting and campaign map match the visuals and the soundtrack well. Despite being an old, outdated game, there is a certain charm to the graphics, which makes it stand the test of time as opposed to Rome I, which has poor visuals to the point where it intrudes on the gameplay. Very few games have charming visuals which can stand the test of time, and this is one of them. To illustrate what I mean, others might include the Pokemon series and the Jedi Knight series. Whilst not the strongest point of the game, it does not, however, detract from the gameplay, which is the important part.
The only one gripe I can think of is that the armored knights and cavalry might be too cliché and similar for some. A conquistador in full plate armor and an English Knight in full plate armor look similar, with only the heraldry and colours making them identifiable. Personally, however, I never minded this, but it is one issue people have when discussing why Rome I might be better - Rome I had very varied and visually distinct units.
An extremely engrossing game, one of the best of all time, I can't hesitate to recommend this. While not as groundbreaking for it's time as Rome I, which is the darling of the series, this is the better, more refined and perfected title.

This is still one of my favorite games ever. Is it sometimes reminiscent of Silent Hill? Absolutely. Does it feel like a clone? Not in the slightest. Does asking rhetorical questions make me feel like a phony? You betcha.
Those looking to get the game for action-packed fights, or even more than one weapon, are going to be disappointed. The game is more about exploration and, in later playthroughs, taking care of yourself.
The game sort of draws you in initially by seeming like your typical survival horror game, only pixelated and with really cool atmosphere. While it still does have really cool atmosphere, it becomes obvious very quickly that the story of this game is about more than just a zombie outbreak or whatever. In lots of ways, you could argue that all of that side of the game is just metaphorical anyway. While I wouldn't be able to confidently explain all aspects of the story, I can see some pretty touching themes about coping with loss, as well as free will vs. fate: Do you have the courage to keep moving on after loss, or will you just stagnate? Will you take your future into your own hands, or will you give in to what you believe is your "true" nature?
The choices you make affect the ending of the game, and if you're anything like most people who have spent their lives being conditioned by videogames, you will get a pretty bad ending on your first try, which is in part due to the fact that killing enemies counts against your mental score. The idea of NOT killing living things in a survival horror game is going to feel very foreign, and sometimes, you're going to need to really work your brain to figure ways around conflict. It's really neat trying to find the "good" way to handle enemies rather than taking a gun to them, which the game clearly implicates as being the easy way out. It wants you to show some of the most powerful traits that human beings possess: resilience and compassion.
In more direct terms of things, the game's just fun to look at, play, and listen to. Most of the time any item you pick up is going to be something unique. There are so many food items, and it's fun to try them out and see how the main character likes them. There's even some stuff with cooking later on, or other things you can do with the food. Sprites are all really well done. Music (or atmospheric sound) is always spot on. The game also keeps tossing in new twists or things to do and it never really gets old, despite never giving you more than one kind of gun (WHOA!).
I guess that's about it. Some say the main character is kind of whiny, but I don't think those people really fully appreciate the kind of situation this guy is in, or for how long he's been in it. It's a cool game with a cool story and if you've gone through some kind of painful loss, there are definitely things that you could relate to in it. The creator, Jasper Byrne, is also a super cool guy who has even responded to emails I've sent him. Mr. Byrne, if for some reason you read this, hello, and I have bought three versions of this game. I'd love to see more like it.

I absolutely loved this game. It has so much going for it, and I would love to see more from the creators! I've played through twice, and keep thinking about when I should play it again. I would really suggest giving this game a chance, perhaps your eyes are in for a little adjustment, but it is SO.WORTH.IT. Great music, characters, and awesome story to enjoy with the lights off, and volume up high. 9/10 hands down!

I really wanted to enjoy this game, but sadly, I just wasn't having fun playing it.  The game is more "survival" than "horror" as I wound up trying to keep myself alive rather than soaking in the atmosphere and as a result, made me just stop playing the game.
Atmosphere: 4/10
While the atmosphere does give off an eerie feeling at times and give off the feeling that everything is dead, I wasn't really scared or even creeped and I didn't feel very threatened.  You can tell when standard monsters are around only because they create what sounds like radio static, you can easily outrun them, and they won't follow you to another screen.
Story: 2/10
The story was not very interesting and sometimes hard to follow.  The basic plot is that you are believed to be the last man alive but leaves his appartment to try and find if there are any other survivors.  It's a good setup, but the pacing is so slow that it doesn't seem in any rush to progress past the "escape the apartment" portion which takes a long time to actually do and has the character go through multiple halucinations and black-outs instead of moving forward.  Taking bule or green pills before sleeping will put you in a dream state where two different characters bring up psychological topics to ask you.  As much as I like this idea though, it distracts from the main story and just took me out of the game.
Graphics: 6/10
I have to be honest and i don't mean to offend anyone, but the characters in this game look pretty ugly.  I am not expecting them to look like something out of a AAA title so I do cut it some slack, but they still look unappealing.  The monsters look basic and the "walkers" as I will call them do not look very threatening.  The graphics' saving grace is the backgrounds as they do look dead and abandoned giving the game a sense of dread.
Gameplay: 3/10
Surviving is a challenge itself as you WILL be dying more times than you can count.  When encountering monsters, you are mostly given items such as rotten meat or flares that will only distract enemies and the only thing you have to kill them with and defend yourself is a shoddy pistol with VERY scarce ammo.  More often than not, you will wind up running out of ammo as monsters take quite a few hits to kill and the later monsters take even more hits to kill, so you will be constantly backtracking looking for blue pills or ammo you hope you had missed; and you'll be lucky if you can find them.  This could have easily been fixed if a better gun was available or at the very least a melee weapon, but the protagonist says he would rather keep his weak pistol.  If you want the player to stick with one gun, don't throw in something that will make us want something different.
There is a hunger mechanic that seems to just be there and didn't really affect my survival.  The game just seemed to nag me when I got hungry or got sleepy to make me eat some food I had found or go back to my room and sleep to the point where it felt more like a chore.
Replay Value: 2/10
I honestly, can't see myself replaying this game anytime soon.  There is not a lot of things I understood even looking back at them and it will just be the same repetitive gameplay that gets boring after a while.
Final Verdict: This game has potential and so do the developers.  I honestly want to see them go far an make some very enjoyable games.  This particular game, however, was a bit of a disappointment; if you are looking for a game that will scare you and keep you invested, you might want to look elsewhere.
Final Score: 17/50
3.4/10 - Cannot Recommend

Let me start by saying up until this game I thought I was seriously done with MMOs. I was completely burned out. I have been playing MMOs since Ultima Online - EQ, EQ2, Meridian 59, Vanguard, WoW (of course), Rift, Tera, LoTR, DDO and on and on. So when this went F2P and on steam I was curious as it looked very nice.
First, I had never heard of it which is sad because if this game had some decent marketing when it launched it would probably garner a much deeper fan base. That said, it is still fairly well populated.
Second, it is a beautiful game. Graphics are top notch and run flawlessly. I cannot say how it was at launch but today it is a very polished game.
As with most MMOs everyone compares them to WoW as that is the elephant in the room and this is no different. Mainly because of the cartoony feel. However, all resemblances to WoW end there. The combat is so much better than most MMOs. It is directional and very skill based. You are limited to 8 skills, 1 gadget and 1 buff/heal slot. It is very much a sci-fi theme (reminds me of Firefly in some things) and does not seem to take itself too seriously. It is actually a lot of fun to play. Dungeons are very challenging and Veteran (read heroic) versions are even more so. I have only participated in some world boss raids but those are very hectic and lots of fun. They remind me of WoW BC and Litch King raids or Veeshan's Peak raids in EQ2. They are very technical and tactical. Well thought out and scripted with very little RNG that I can see at this point.
Endgame seems well thought out and I do not feel like I am grinding the same things over and over. I would compare it to BC dailies that ranged over several zones. These are over even more areas and I am hard pressed to complete even half of the available daily quests in any given day. This may change but so far I am pleasantly surprised. Crafting is a bit meh, but unless you really get into crafting I would guess this might be most people's reaction to it.
Downside - there are some bugs and broken crafting trees and (imo) lack of support from NCSoft to put sufficient resources into fixing them. If the game starts pulling in sufficient revenue they may put more resources into the game. Time will tell. Queue system for dungeons, while not exactly broken, is not really useable. Basically, no one uses it so you can sit there for literally hours and never get in a group. With cross faction chat now a thing your best bet is to find a group through chat. If enough people start using it this might fix itself - again time will tell.
In-Game MT shop - No pay to win here, mostly cosmetics, mounts, pets, account unlocks and xp, rep buff pots. I normally don't care about cosmetics that much but some of these are just downright cool looking. There are special keys to buy to unlock bonus chests at the end of dungeons/expeditions and such. You don't have to buy these and they are relatively cheap, but these chests do tend to have some good gear in them so they are encouraging you to get them. The gear in the chests are not game breaking, they are on the level of what you get in the dungeon anyway so it's just a bonus chest so to speak.
All in all it's a very good game and I hope it succeeds and stays around for awhile.  8/10

You HAVE TO spam the skill keys almost ALL the time in combat situations and while that might make it seem like it is more "actiony" than most other games it is a dead stopper for people with arthritis or any problems with their hands or wrists in general. Sorry to the team behind the game but until there is a way to play without the CONSTANT key spamming then I will have to give it the thumbs down.

The main plot is pretty bad.
From the other hand, there is a lot of good storytelling hidden in it. Destroyed villages and cultures, some suggested relationships between characters, various routes.
Still, though, it's too basic as far as the writing goes. Good humans, evil goblins (they are evil = they torture people), great war between nations, the main hero with amnesia. There are some role-playing choices, but not too many. In most of the cases you can either accept a quest or refuse it (what gives you no value whatsoever), threaten someone to give you more money (which almost never works) and basically you can only choose between being an annoying a s s hole or a good guy.
When you get actual choices, it get's quite interesting. But generally speaking, I don't think you should play Eschalon: Book I for its writing.
As far as the gameplay goes, it has A LOT of walking and some cool strategic fights with strong RNG elements. The basics are very strong, but there are some details that provide issues or don't work well with each other. Some abilities are overall useless, while others are very significant. Most of the strategic value seems to be addressed toward melee characters - I played as a ranger and while I used a bow, there were a lot of enemies that were very punishing (even exploding) when they were dying next to you. Some of this depth vanishes when you can keep a large distance.
Magic in this game is great. Various spells are focused on utility and even a fighter should play around with some basics spells during its adventures. It has some The Elder Scrolls vibe, but I found myself needing to use spells in this game much more. Also, you never reach the point of becoming hilariously overpowered  aside of the very end of the game, where it gets rewarding and satisfying.
At the same time, the character creation was quite pleasant. You can screw yourself in many ways if you don't know which skills are strong and which aren't, but it's nothing like the oldest TES games where you were spending half an hour reading everything. The only problem is the "roll your stats" elements. I hope the sequels avoided it.
It's a 5/10 game. 6/10 if you like RPGs, 7/10 if you like open world RPGs, 8/10 if you absolutely don't care about bad story. I'm definitely going to play the first sequel next.

So, I don't have a lot of logged hours on this game on Steam, but I bought it on DRM-free CD a decade or so ago and beat the crap out of it at the time, and have since replayed most of it as one of the few offline games my garbage laptop can support. If you like turn-based, story-heavy RPG's that also support indie game development by small companies, this one's worth the price. The game does have some limitations, but it's D&D/Diablo-esque (if Diablo were turn based), where you can pick your stat upgrades, talents, etc. There really are a lot of ways that the game can be "broken," and borderline cheat your way through once you learn how the mechanics work, and it's easy to make mistakes during character development that make the game harder. You can also save-scum your way through, both to get drops, and to basically loot every thing ever. It's easy to miss out on great loot by making wrong conversation choices. In any case, it's generally fun, it's expansive, and there are a lot of ways to play it, so I do recommend. It does hold up to the test of time.

Everyone who plays it knows about the more strongl feeling materialists and how they doubt a lot of the more dramatic and 'otherworldly' endgame material, but that annyonce is a symptom of not being able to change cultural traits more easily. It of course should cost resources and cause some dissent to make these changes, like anything else major you do here, plus perhaps a 10-30 year period for adjustment depending on ethos. However, the AI being stupid sometimes is pretty typical of games of this genre, so I list it as a minor issue because I'm conviced many people aren't bothered by it. I am, but not enough for me have my experience ruined by it.
The second problem is much more sutble, but much more major. The game is not quite immersive enough, depsite being immese, tacically well thought out and generally intelligently designed. This is a huge shame, because the one thing that could possibly make the game experience go from 'good' to 'great' is for me to feel more like I'm really commanding a space civlization.
I should also complain about the new background, but I fixed it with a mod, so I won't, and it was never a huge deal anyway.
As for the AI issue with sectors, it never really effected me because I tend to sector planets soon after I get them and have the basic buildings up, or not at all, so this AI issue did not impact my experience any. I still hope they fix it eventually for those who find this bothersome, nonetheless.
Other than these issues, the game is the one that sets the bar for how the 4x science fiction game aught to be. Not the specifics, which contain such odd and implausable-in-real-life things as giant aliens, exotic resources and vestigal civilizations that can still kick your butt.Thost things would not fit in most other 4x games very well. But the overall picture is one of the beauty of elegant real time strategy design, supported by the firm hardness of the bottom-line question of all speculative fiction: Why? Here, in this game, you can be the answer to many of those questions due to creating your own coherent history of a spacefaring civilization. Your actions can spell triumph or ruin, make friends or enemies, you can uplift a low-tech civilization or conquer your neighbors. This freedom of tactical choice makes this the first game I've played where I feel like a leader, and not the only normal employee at a large company full of eccentrics.
The designs of the alien portraits, while limited in number, are all quite good, actually in the ballpark of what I want the species I play to look like, which is much more than I can say for most 4x portrait designs. The special research lines and anomalies are all quite interesting, enough I can persue them in game after game without boredom. I LOVE the precursor civilizations in particular, all with their own lesson for your civilization and you to learn, even though most met a rather sad end. The really strange lifeforms you sometimes find in space are also pretty cool, though some you migh have to fight.
I will now end this review so I do not give away too many spoilers. Overall, this is the first game in YEARS that is a RTS I give a 8.5/10. If only someone would fix the few things that reduce flexibility and find some way to increase immersion a bit further,it would be perfect.
I have not played this game with the Utopia expansion yet, so take this review with that small grain of salt.

I fully recommend this game. It's fun, fast-past and humorous with and an abundance of weapon customisation options. There are no unfair pay to win advantages, and getting all your favourite gear and making your perfect guns won't take long.
The game play is addictive and always moving. Weapons are crazy and ridiculous and learning to use the dive ability well will help you survive much longer. Teams are restricted to 4v4 for somewhat 'controlled chaos'. The colour scheme is bright and vibrant, unlike games such as Call of Duty. The graphics are unrealistic and 'cartoonish', but it still looks great. If you have ever played the game Team Fortress 2, this will feel quite familiar.
There are many different game modes to chose from:
JACKHAMMER: Similar to capture the flag, except the hammer is a 1hit kill AOE melee weapon with 5 uses, and each kill increases your teams score when you capture the hammer.
BLITZ: Where a random control point is activated on the map and the team who reaches the target capture amount first wins
DEATH SNATCH: Killing an enemy will drop a small 'test tube' like thing of blutonium, capturing that will increase your team score. you can capture a deceased ally's blutonium to stop it being stolen
EXTRACTION: blutonium is scattered across the map and the person who is still alive the longest is chosen to be the collector. Pick up the blutonium and throw it in the collection machines to score points for your team, or throw it at enemies to deal big damage in emergencies.
The game uses two currencies to purchase in game items with; Blutonium and Spacebux.

Blutonium will be awarded when you play a match and you will be awarded extra on how well you did. There are also daily prizes that award you Blutonium which can be very nice when want you come back and play this every day. Blutonium is used for buying new gun parts or equipment. Using a gun part on gun while playing will cause it to gradually level up. you can upgrade it using blutonium once it has completely levelled up to give it bonus stats.
Spacebux is a purchase only currency, that can be used for buying cosmetics items, which there are plenty of options for. You could become a guerrilla warfare personnel, a mafia member, maybe someone who just got out of bed in his tightie whities, or a mixture of all 3. It can also be used to purchase more weapon slots in your inventory, but you find yourself needing it that much.
Now we come to the trump card: weapon customisation. This is probably one of the games most important features. you create your perfect weapon best suited to you. You can customise so many things, from the type of barrel, to the sights of the gun, and even the stock. Some combinations won't work so well, for example: using a bolt action magazine with a Gatling barrel. But getting the right weapons to destroy everyone else feels so great, and that is what I like most about the game.

Flawless animations, fast paced gameplay, great weapon customization and hilarious death-animations.
But the best thing about this game is that it's not a single trace of pay-to-win like most other free-to-play's.
Blutes, which is the currency used for unlocking weapon parts, can't be bought, and is earned at a fairly quick rate. Blute boosts can be paid for via microtransactions, but apart from that there's no way of unlocking weapon parts except from playing.
The game has four main types of weapons. Bullet, pulse, launcher & beam. Once you've selected your weapon type, you can customize it by changing out the barrel, the trigger, what kind of damage it deals and how the projectile behaves, and more.
Say you want a high damage laser that zaps enemies. Attach a sniper barrel and get the "Tesla" damage type and watch electricity arch between enemies. How about a laser-guided rocket launcher that sends missiles crawling along the floor? go ahead and make it. Want to shoot healing cannonballs at your friends? there's nothing stopping you. The customization in this game will always keep the game fun. The things that can be customized are: stock, barrel, trigger, magazine, sights, damage type, & projectile.
Loadout has many fun maps and good gamemodes to go along with it.
- Death Snatch is very similar to "Kill Confirmed" from the CoD series. Kill your enemies, and steal their blutonium.
- Jackhammer is the game's Capture the Flag-equivalent, but with a twist: the flag is a mighty hammer that will smash your enemies in one hit, adding additional points when you capture it.
- Blitz is the conquest gamemode of the game. A new point is revealed on the map, and the teams rush to it's location to capture it. Once it is captured, a new point is revealed another place.
- Extraction is a gamemode unique to Loadout. Each team has a collector, whose job is to run around and collect blutonium for the team. The other teammates has to either protect the collector, or harass the enemy collector.

So I decided to start as France because I LOVE heavy cavalry and I doubt anyone has done it so far.
I started my campaign by absorbing the nearby rebel settlements into my empire.  The first battle goes poorly, I just barely win and only from capturing the center of the town, I am beginning to doubt if  France was the right choice.  The second battle, however, goes very well.  I use proper cavalry tactics and completely descimate the rebel settlement, adding it to my glorious French empire.  After that I begin dominating the map, settlement after settlement, battle after battle.  Finally, My empire is the largest, the strongest, the richest, the most advanced, and the most populated in the world.  I have also allied with the British, the Polish, and the Holy Roman Empire, with dreams of conquering the British Isles.
I am soon given that chance when I recruit a mercinary fleet of ships.  I get Military access from the foolish British and set my armies in key strategic locations.  The next turn, I execute order 66.  The British are taken off guard and I kill all but two of their generals, king included.  I then turn my eyes to their last territory, where their peasant king's son awaits.  My king's army marches forth to this English coward, and just when we have our siege equipment ready and our swords drawn, the other British general attacks us from the west.  Nevertheless, we have the advantage and as my my ballistas are aimed for their gate, my horses crush their western army, and my troops storm their city and kill their king, but at a cost, my king is bravely killed as well.  This soon turned out to be good news, because we had apparently been excommunicated from the church just prior and were finally let in at news that my "heathen" king had been killed.
Just as I make preperations to incorporate these accursed Islands into my empire I am betrayed.  As it turned out, HRE actually hated my Polish allies and decided to attack me as well.  I am enraged to see their sorry yellow and black hides besiege my forces in Metz.  I quickly show these traitors whose boss and wipe out their troops.  But then, their leader, alone, attacks some of my forces near Metz.  I am surprised he beat me with few casualties as he charged DIRECTLY INTO MY LINE OF SPEARS!  He then retreated directly into the stygnian depths of Germany where I could not reach him. No matter, revenge can wait till he's watched his country burn.  I begin hitting him, hard, and end up splitting their empire in half.  Unfortunately, In my viscious assault I am, again, excommunicated from the church.  Thankfully the pope dies and I am reconciled, and to top that, the new one is polish so HRE is then excommunicated.  Sadly the pope calls a crusade on Cairo, and if I don't send my leader, I'll be excommunicated.  So, I do what I must, and before too long, have a crusading army worthy of many gasps.
The crusade goes poorly, and that's putting it mildly.  I end up, for no reason, having my men continuously desert to "find another party that will be more on track to the destination".  So I end up wasting thousands of florins on disloyal mercinaries who constantly desert me.  By the time I make it to Cairo, the crusade is over and I am lacking in any reasonable army.  So I start back to paris.  On the way there I reach Constantinople and notice it is lacking in any good military, and just can't resist taking it from the Byzantines.  Back in Europe I have finally taken over the British Isles and was attacked by Spain, who happened to be allied with the HRE.  Now I am in a war on three fronts and have the number one military in the entire world.  And one more thing.  Word has reached me that the mongols have risen so now I seem doomed.
Nevertheless, I manage to take two spanish cities and most of Byzantium.  After that, all that happens are pointless bloody battles that leave thousands dead in their wake.  Finally, gunpowder is made, and France is pushed into a new golden age.  I conquer the Spaniards and the Moors, I take all of Germany and execute their king, and I destroy the rest of the Byzantines.  It seems france will never be beaten.  Then, just as I attack Jerusalem (my victory region), The Mongols attack me and a hopeless battle is fought.  I lose the battle and swore vengeance on the Mongols.
I start World War 1 with all of Europe facing against the mongols.  And after years of costly battles, me and my allies make it to their main capital city which, ironically, is Cairo.  We barely win the battle.  For years the world is at peace.  Then, the Timurids attack, and it all goes awry.  They take over the Papal states, and much of eastern Europe (including Byzantium).  My troops are barely able to defend what is left of France, and I do not know if any other European nations survived.  The Pope betrays me and takes Cairo to start a new eastern catholic civilization.
END RESULT:
-Europe and Asia are controlled by only three major nations (France, Timurids, and Papal States), all of which are constantly at each others throats.
-America is where the capital of France lies, and is slowly being taken from the Aztecs.
-There are unconfirmed rumors that Milan survived and currently owns part of south-east Asia.
-I hope for luck and divine intervention as the Timurids are slowly closing in on the America's.
-The world is plagued with inquisitors and pagans, all whom corrupt the lands and murder people.
-No one's faith is seen as "satisfying" from the Pope's perspective, and crusades/jihads are constantly being called on me.
Fin

Europe stands as the heart of monarchy, since the fall of Rome and the establishment of the Kingdoms. The Church determines the fate of all and cries for war upon the Islamic Kingdoms to the east. The year is 1066 and the Duke of Normandy; William (the Conqueor) has been given consent from the Pope to invade England and overthrow the Anglo-Saxon Kingdom. After the victory at Hastings, the Kingdom of England has been born and a new chapter in Medieval Europe has begun. With the Islamic push stopped at the Frankish victory of Tours, the Christian faith now demands retaliation and cries for Muslim blood. With the age of the Crusades now beginning, the world will now watch the world become divided by two religions and the age of Chivarly, Faith, and Conquest has become the objective for any ruler who possess such power and nobility. Despite the church having united Europe to the power of the Pope, rivalries continue to plague Europe with war. Lords use the peasantry as fodder in order to gain both wealth and reputation to become the most powerful ruler Europe shall ever have. Chivarly, Faith, Wealth, Total War...
This is by far my most favorite Total War game ever, with improved graphics, gameplay, animations, and new weaponry   when compared with Rome: Total War. Watching Knights clash in shiny armor make every soldier a spectacle on the battlefield, watch as massive armies butcher each other leaving literally mountains of dead. This game has captured the brutality and chaotic atomsphere of medieval combat, especially with the aftermath of a battle as you are left speechless at the sight of a sea of dead stretching all over the battlefield. Remember Braveheart? That first battle scene at Stirling Bridge? That is pretty much what you would witness with each battle, as the game captures a more realistic and brutal spectacle compared with the First Rome Total War. Defineitly a must-buy, especially with the Kingdoms DLC, so worth it. Stretching from the wars of independence that ravaged England, to the Crusades in the Holy Land, to the wars between the Christians and the remnants of the religion of Paganism in the Baltic region, to the jungles of Central America as the New World has been discovered. This game plus the Kingdoms DLC is worth every cent and shall always remain as my favorite Total War game.

You find maps around the game with some places or rooms marked, which is helpful, but getting to the places and finding other necessary rooms or items is just random on your first playthrough. The world isn't that large, in the long run, but it is not easy to simply explore everything.
The game really is a survival game. You have to make sure that your character eats healthy food, to both restore health as well as simply feed yourself and prevent death. You have to make sure you sleep regularly, which is bad if your character is starving, and getting back to your room is very difficult in some scenarios. You are very limited in what you can acquire, in terms of ammo and food, and it is relatively difficult to get around enemies your first run-through, as most do not have hiding spots near them.
To be honest, this game actually scared me, and I did not expect that. The sound effects are really good, despite how simple they are, like the monster scream. I also enjoyed the pieces of music here and there throughout the game, especially the beginning/ending song. As far as graphics, again, simple, but effective. My only complaint in the aspect ratio and not really having a different resolution. At the beginning, text was taking up nearly 1/3 of my screen and I had to move back to read it. After adjusting, the whole game screen only took up like 1/4 of its available space. I understand not wanting to have some crazily detailed game (in some senses), but there could have been a better way of doing that. Either way, the graphics were mostly fine, though too fuzzy in many places.
The monsters creeped me out and I often ran away as expected, and I died quite a few times. In most horror games, after I lose a few times, the monsters wear off on me. Not here. I was still creeped out by the end, mostly because the game doesn't let you get any real "safety." You have to make it through chunks of the world before getting back to your apartment, and there's no other way than to push on through. That gives the game a good atmosphere, as does the exploration and lack of direction. Lack of direction is not always a good thing, but it is fine in this game, as the world is not "too big" to explore.
Story-wise, there really isn't much on your first playthrough, very likely. I made many guesses about what was going on, but by the end, I still don't know, though I have more information. I got the "bad" ending of the game. There are multiple endings, and it seems intentional that you need to play the game multiple times to get other endings. Many actions in the game influence your ending, and some things (like avoiding killing enemies) are really hard to do on the first playthrough because of your limitations.
Despite not getting a fulfilling ending (although that's not really that rare anymore), I was still happy by the game's end. If I get into the mood again, I will try another playthrough and work harder for a better ending. One of the reasons I don't really want to do so now is because the game will play the same. I will have more items and know where to go, but nothing will really change other than some of my actions and getting a slightly different ending.
I already did all of the side quests, such as visiting The Director all the time, helping Hank, and adopting the cat (which was actually a lot more enjoyable and fun than I expected). I loved the cat. Oh, and I loved the fact that Lone Survivor has a mentality system. Little cheesy actions help your character keep collected, such as talking to a plush toy, playing a handheld game system, adopting the cat, reading comics, etc. They're small things, but in such a simple game, everything comes together in a nice form.
But at the same time, that is pretty much why I don't want to play again right away. I looked into the actions that influence your ending, and I pretty much did the majority of "good" actions to influence towards the positive ending. The only thing that mainly influenced my ending then, was that I had to kill a lot of the enemies because they were unavoidable and you do not get items like flares until late in the game. So basically, I would have to replay the game, changing nothing but using extra flares instead of firing my gun. If I hadn't done the side quests and other things, then I would replay immediately.
All in all, everything was put together very well, besides the graphical sizing. I think that this game surprised me a lot, and will probably surprise others who don't know what to expect of it. I suggest playing the game, to delve into its little (rather creepy) world. Fight through, but enjoy, the atmosphere. Try to put the story together. I will return to it again, once I feel like it, and if you play it, you should return later as well.

It's a great game.  I'm not sure about the comparisons to SH2, but I suppose that they are similar in that they are both well executed psychological horror games with an emphasis on metaphor and story-telling.  I feel like there should be more games that fit that description (SH2 came out in what, 2001?); maybe that's why I don't like the comparison rather than it being inaccurate.
In any case, while it is certainly inspired by SH2, it stands on its own with fascinating mechanic design, great sound design, and  well-implemented mystery.  The mechanics are designed specifically to help tell the story.  There are thematic/narrative reasons that there are several options to dealing with obstacles, and there's a very good reason why some are harder to use than others.  Oh, and the sleeping, eating, and pills mechanics--Genius.
It has great replay value because replaying the game is part of the story.  In most cases, you are SUPPOSED to play this game more than once. (What does the Blue Man say?  "You'll have to do better than that!" or something like that)
This is one of those games that I finished, frowned, thought about it for a few minutes, then went to the forums to find out what other people thought of the game and what it meant.  It is very thought provoking.  There aren't many games that I finish and want to have a real discussion about.  They should teach this in schools, seriously.  There isn't really a big reveal that explains to the player what exactly is happening.  There are clues scattered all over the place in a couple of short cut-scenes, odd NPC conversations, the environment, You's overall behavior, You's attitude toward certain objects/people, and in playing the game over again that lead to the answers.
I haven't worked up the courage to play through it again yet, but I plan on it.  Very tense game.
I guess I didn't like everything about it.  For whatever reason, I found the combat walked (and occasionally stumbled across) a fine line between tense/desperate and frustrating.  I got stuck a few times by getting killed by the same mobs over and over.  However, I was playing on hard (why? Because no reason), so this might be an anomaly.  Also, I'm normally not a huge fan of pixel art-style games, but it didn't distract me or decrease the effectiveness of the game.
Overall, I hope to see more great games from this developer.

Despite being fairly short, this is one game that horror fans shouldn't miss.
As the lone survivor (teehee) of some unknown apocalyptic disaster or outbreak, you must struggle to survive on your own with your life and sanity intact.
The game focuses very much on psychological horror.  It opts for a very tense and oppressive atmosphere rather than jump scares and over the top horror cliches.
It can be argued that horror is one of the most difficult genres to break into.  Fear is a subjective response and what frightens one person may not frighten another.  While there wasn't anything that made me reach for a new pair of pants, I was certainly on the edge of my seat the entire time.
In my opinion, the best horror games are those that make you incredibly tense and afraid of the unkown.  They make your body cry out for you to quit, they make you hesitant to press on, while at the same time making you crave more.  This game did it for me, and I hope it will for you as well.
In conclusion, Lone Survivor is a great horror game.  It's certainly not without it's flaws (which I haven't covered here, because they truly are minor), but will certainly not disappoint.

Nier:Automata was my first Yoko Taro game. I gotta say, it was an amazing experience...
It had: One of the most interesting universes and stories I`ve ever seen, the best sound track I`ve heard in a video game and AMAZING gameplay.
Nier Automata`s combat system is absolutely perfect, it takes some time to master, but once you do, you feel so powerful! (That`s Platinum games`s combat for you, it`s very similar to Bayonetta)
Story: Nier Automata is a roller coaster of emotions, questions and answers. The more you play, the more questions start popping up on your head, the game has a confusing story at first. Throughout the playthrough it does answer everything though. (That is, if you take your time reading through the collected arquives, if you don`t, you`ll miss a few cool details that clarify a some past events and tells you why the world became how it is in Automata). The characters are full of personality... And the game managed to develop the relation between 2B and 9S in a great way.
The game`s story is put in a way that the first two endings are only the part 1 of the story, while the 3 last endings are part 2 (and the part where the game REALLY gets insane). - Don`t get me wrong though, endings A and B are pretty good too.
NOTE: YOU DO NOT NEED TO PLAY THE PREVIOUS NIER OR THE DRAKENGARD SERIES TO UNDERSTAND AUTOMATA (Though the previous games do have a LOT of details about the world inside Automata and why it has developed into what it is). - Still, you can get most of that through the arquives.
Soundtrack:  B-E-S-T    T-H-I-N-G    E-V-E-R
Characters: Overall great, the main and side characters all have their moments, and show a lot of personality and development.
2B: The ``perfect soldier``. Throughout the first playthrough, 2B is shown to be the coldest of characters, pretending to only care about the mission. Later, she develops into a kindhearted and caring character, and shows her true colors.
9S: The emotional one. 9S is the humor part of the game, and he does a pretty good job at it. He is a pretty nice guy, and I pitty him (for reasons).
A2: A2 is a thing of her own, due to her past (won`t say anything else)
Gameplay: Platinum Games. (I`m just gonna say that)
Cons: Performance is lacking, I was able to play the game just fine at arround 45-60 FPS, however, at 1600x900p and with everything except for texture filter at low. The game also presents performance issues on the PS4.
(Nothing game breaking though, the game still looked pretty good with my settings, and if you have a better machine, you`ll be able to pump up the graphics just fine)
I guess there are no more cons.
Veredict: 9/10 due to a few performance issues - The rest was perfect in my opinion though. (I`d say, if you got a monster machine and can play this game at 60 fps all the time, it`s a 10/10)

**This review is based solely on my experience from MyCareer**
TL;DR: The MyCareer experience is a solid 10/10.
When you start your MyCareer for the very first time, you quickly realize, this "ain't no Spike Lee joint", but that's probably the best part of the story during your first season of your career. Without spoiling too much I can reveal that you're given two friends in the NBA (Justice and Denver) who will accompany you on your journey. These two are by far the best thing 2K have come up with as they are extremely well thoughtout characters, and the actor behind Justice, Michael B Jordan if I'm not mistaken, known from TV does an extremely good job at portraying your best friend. Put in contrast to 2k16, where Vic was supposed to be your best friend, the characters in 2k17 are actually likeable.
Besides that, the story is well ridden and you get more "off court time" as you attend practices and endorsements/meetups, the latter being rabbitholes, but for "roleplaying" it's still nice. You get to actually play in college this year, although it is only for four or five games. Personally I would've loved to have played more in college, although I know other players hated the college experience. In the future I hope we get a chance to pick our starting conditions. i.e., do we want to play the college experience or 2k15's version where you are undrafted, and that way get a chance to pick who you play for (to some degree)
Now to the actual gameplay.
The gameplay this year feels much smoother than previous games. Your teammates are actually smart and will make plays and are more likely to shoot if they are open (no more 2k15 hugging of the ball when they are completely open). Defense play seems much smoother and thusly easier and the greatest change is the AI's better understanding of pick'n'roll plays, where you can with fewer button hits and thusly much faster tell them to screen for you and go to the basket for your easy assist.
Final Judgement:
If you're thinking about getting this game primarily for the MyCareer experience I can only strongly suggest that you do, as I rate this year's MyCareer a solid 10/10. You really feel part of the team, although the people who make you feel this way aren't on the actual team. The friendship you build are well written and the cutscenes make you want more.
**A few bugs have happened for me though primarily the "no cutscenes bug" where you will go your first 10-13 games without getting cutscenes with Justice. **
