I have been holding off writing this review because the game could be so good and I was hoping it would change.
This is a hex-based wargame in the SotS universe and that's exciting stuff. (I just realized that will sound like a joke to non-wargame fans, but it's true).
Based on the screenshots you would think was a cool, deep, fun game. The information in the encyclopedia in game is a nice touch.
Try to play the game though and you'll find a confusing, fiddly mess. There are far too many phases and lots of fiddly things you have to keep doing. The user interface is really bad both in usability and in showing you what's going on. A lot of this is because of the developers making the bad decision to have a "unified user interface" on mobile and PC, which means no tooltips, only one button used and no scrolling when you get your mouse to the edge of the screen. This cripples the PC UI and the developers flat-out refuse to change it to make the PC version easier to use.
The tutorial has been through a few changes but still remains awful at teaching you the game. This is both due to the content of the tutorial and the way it is presented, which makes it hard to tie together the UI with what the flash-card like windows are telling you.
I bought the game at the start of the Early Access on Steam and I was disappointed to find out that the game was not as finished as I thought it would be. From the store page it seemed like the only thing missing were some campaign missions, and the ironing out of the last few bugs:
"With this Early Access release, Ground Pounders is feature complete, and the main differences between now and final release - besides a few last minute cards and units - is there is only 1 campaign (instead of 2) and 5 scenarios (instead of ten)."
It turned out that early adopters really were unpaid beta testers and only by assiduously playing when it wasn't fun and giving feedback could we turn the game into the good game it had the potential to be. I mean, it wasn't just bug fixing, there were actually changes to how the game worked, and there was really the feeling that the game hadn't been tested at all before putting it on steam.
I did this for a short while but then I just couldn't be bothered any more- it was just not fun. I decided to put the game down until they finished it and see how it was. As of today the game is still in Early Access but is 66% off on a certain online game store. Because the Steam store page went out of its way to point out that we were saving money by buying into the Early Access game at the start vs. buying when it launched I felt a bit betrayed by this; I also took it as a sign that the studio may be in some sort of trouble. The game was planned to be released in March according to the Steam store page and it's almost June now with no release so maybe that's why.
Anyway, I suppose if you do get a deep discount on this or even get it in a bundle (there have been a lot of Early Access games in bundles recently) then it may turn out to be the game you expect, but at the moment it's unlikely that it is.

A great game for its price; I highly recommend it. It's definitely short (average playthrough is about an hour or so) and a few of its design choices are a little lacking (the text can be a little hard to read at some points and too obstructive at others).
However! It does a
job of creating a really, really great atmosphere of tension and foreboding. The plot is also interesting, and tells you a great deal in a short amount of time while leaving you wanting more, making guesses to fill in the blanks. The absolute key to psychological horror is only giving you glimpses of what you should fear, and leaving you to fill in the rest. The Moon Sliver does this very, very well, and creates a wonderfully claustrophobic, lonely atmosphere where you always worry you're never truly alone.
It's an interesting story that's very entertaining to explore, and gets really tense as it goes on. It is short, and could be improved in a few technical aspects, but, overall, it is definitely worth the price. Set aside an hour or so and give this a run-through. You might very well love it, and it's hardly expensive enough to be much of a risk.
Oh, and, as a side-note: Contrary to the implication it gives at one point early on, the game is
timing you or anything. Feel free to take your time and explore, when you're reasonably safe. The time progresses as the story does, not in real-time.
...I
hate real-timed games so I felt the need to mention that.

Overwatch exists at an intersection between design and artistry, a crossroad at which pure tactile joy meets refined, intelligent design to create a rare spark of magic. As a 6v6 multiplayer, objective-based shooter, it finds accessibility not by lowering the skill ceiling, but by broadening the definition of skill. The person with deadshot aim is no more valuable than the person with the decision-making ability to know when a well-timed ability will turn an engagement, or the person with the map-sense to find the optimal locations to place sentry turrets. While it didn't exactly drown me in options, maps, and modes, it’s blessed with a multitude of tactical layers, and none of them ever came between me and my enjoyment of its intense, swirling teamfights, and thrilling overtime comebacks.
Overwatch does a great many things well, but above all else, its success is built on the backs of its many excellent characters. It’s fitting that the main menu is dominated by one of them at all times; their diverse appearances, origins, and personalities are all laid bare with every pose they strike. Reinhardt’s rocket hammer lands on his shoulder with a meaty clank that invokes a broadsword resting against a medieval knight’s plate armor, and Tracer’s jovial smile is just briefly interrupted by a rebellious bang that slides across her face, tempting her to blow it back into place before re-addressing the camera and blinking all over the place. There’s an intelligent gorilla scientist, a lithe, blue-skinned assassin, and a cybernetic, zen-practicing healer too. It speaks volumes that the one character that adheres to well-worn shooter tropes feels like the odd man out here. They’re all so different that you’d imagine them looking silly standing next to one another, but through careful, subtle visual cues baked into their equipment and attire, they manage to appear as if they share a common world, even if they all hail from different corners of it.
This diversity continues to bear out when you pick a hero and hit the battlefield with them. Though the 21 characters (all of whom are unlocked from the start) are roughly grouped into one of four “roles,” no two feel alike. The robotic, transforming Bastion and the anarchic, explosive-tossing Junkrat are both technically Defenders, but they couldn’t play any more differently from one another. The former looks for a cozy spot overlooking a key choke point and transforms into a minigun turret to run point defense; the latter plays an area-denial game by lobbing timed grenades over long distances, which then sit on the ground blinking angrily, as if to say “go somewhere else” to encroaching enemies before exploding. This strong sense of differentiation is important because it keeps team composition strategies from devolving into simple formulas. No, two Tanks, two Supports, and two Attackers is not the magic solution for a winning team. You have to look much deeper – and when you do, the true beauty of Overwatch’s gameplay shines through.
One of the surprising keys to surfacing these nuances is its refusal to offer up crutches to lean on. With very few arguable exceptions, no character is focused solely around one catch-all gun or skill to the extent that you can find success by using it alone. Tracer’s dual machine-pistols have a high rate of fire but poor accuracy, a short clip, and middling damage if you aren’t scoring headshots. Genji’s shurikens are highly damaging and boast unerring accuracy, but their slow rate of fire and long travel time can make hitting a small moving target difficult. Almost every primary weapon fits this mold: they’re useful, and in the right situation quite powerful, but never versatile enough to be a security blanket to constantly cling to. Not only do these little details help differentiate characters, they pushed me to explore their other abilities in search of success. And once I started looking more closely, I couldn’t stop discovering new things. Revisiting Junkrat’s toolset, he doesn’t have a single standard, reliable gun to just directly engage an enemy in front of him. Sure, he could skip grenades along the ground, leading his target as best he can, but even if you were good enough to reliably win one-on-one firefights this way, you wouldn’t be realizing his full potential.At face value his other two skills – Steel Trap and Concussion Mine – seem straightforward. One immobilizes enemies that wander into it, the other blows them sky-high when triggered. In practice though, they can be so much more. Steel Trap can be an escape tool, allowing you to disengage from fights with faster enemies trying to get in your face. Its positional alert upon being triggered allows it to double as an early warning system too, letting you know that someone on the other team is attempting to flank your defenses and holding them there long enough for you to respond. Or, plant a Concussion Mine on top of a Steel Trap and just detonate it when you see it triggered while you’re off somewhere else peppering the objective with grenades. You can even use Concussion Mine as a regular old grenade by tossing it at a group of enemies and detonating it manually as it gets there. Perhaps most amusingly, you can detonate it under yourself to rocket-jump up to otherwise-inaccessible areas. Just two abilities on one character opens up all those possibilities, and as you might imagine, once you get 12 characters scrapping over objectives, using their abilities to help and hurt one another, further layers of tactical nuance begin to unfurl.
For example: On her own, Pharah can be a major headache by hurling herself high into the air and hovering there while raining rocket-propelled death down on opposing teams from angles that render both cover and positioning moot. But with Mercy the winged medic tending to her, Pharah becomes a whole different kind of problem. Mercy’s Guardian Angel ability allows her to swoop toward any ally in range, even ones up in the sky. Combined with her ability to slow her descent with her wings, she's the only character that can follow Pharah wherever she goes. So you end up with a dynamic duo flying all over the place – the one shoving rockets down people's throats while the other switches between healing her up and buffing her already substantial damage output as needed.
Overwatch is rich with synergies like this: Reinhardt and Lucio, Zarya and Reaper, Torbjorn and Symmetra…there's no shortage of opportunities for keen, coordinated play, and when you reach a point where you feel comfortable switching your character on the fly in the middle of a match to capitalize on weak enemy team composition, you feel like a tactical genius.
You could spend many hours playing Overwatch before getting to that point by properly wrapping your brain around all the little intricacies it has tucked away behind its approachable veneer, but you certainly don't need to just to have a good time with it. Just trying out different characters, popping off their abilities, and moving through their world feels almost indescribably right, and it's all because of tiny, almost imperceptible details. The lid on Junkrat's grenade launcher flaps and clanks about with his every move, Lucio's movement has just the slightest touch of inertia, so you actually feel like you're skating when you play him. Zenyatta's reload animation might be my favorite.
Therefore Overwatch is an incredible achievement in multiplayer shooter design. It bobs and weaves almost perfectly between being the quick-fix adrenaline hit you might want after a long day of work, and the thoughtful, strategic multiplayer experience that becomes the center of evening-long binges with friends. It might not have the most exhaustive list of maps and modes, but it provides nearly endless opportunities for exhilarating, coordinated play, and when you’re the one at the center of it, it feels like nothing else.

Usually I'm not the kind of guy who writes negative reviews, especially not after only 50 hours of gameplay.
But this time, enough is enough.
I've started multiple games now and never got further than 50-75 ingame years before I simply got crushed by the A.I. with not a single chance to stand my ground.
In my last game I didn't even make it beyond the 25 years mark before the A.I. decided to simply wipe me out with no chance of defending just because I wanted to focus on developing my empire first instead of pushing the flottila limit to the maximum just to make sure that the A.I. is not going to screw me over after 5 minutes.
It seems to me that you are literally forced to handle 3 things at the same time: Your economy, your research and your military. And if you fall behind in any of these 3 aspects you can forget to win the game. You just can't expand your empire step by step in all serenity and peace, you have to rush the 3 things mentioned (especially the military!) above and that just sucks. And (at least to me) it seems you can't rush all 3 things simultaneously, you simply lack the resources for it.
Not to forget that you can't improve relations to a neighbour without bribing them with credits or minerals. I just mean seriously, I have to stone them to death with desperately needed credits or minerals to keep them from killing me for maybe 10 more years?!
But on this point I'm ready to get corrected, but so far I didn't find an "improve relationship" button in the diplomacy menu.
I mean, I'm not the master genius strategist to begin with, but I'm surely not a complete idiot in regard of strategy games, I dare to say that after almost 300 hours of Europa Universalis IV and almost 250 hours of Civilization 5 I know how to play such games.
But Stellaris, forget it.
I feel really sad that I "have to" write a negative review about this game, I really hoped for a "good" and beginner friendly strategy game in space,something like Europa Universalis IV or Civilization in Space, but I just got very disappointed.

Medieval II: Total War throws you into the Middle Ages.You can choose from a good number of states like the Holy Roman Empire,Byzantine Empire,France,England,Scotland and so on.The game has Single Player,Multiplayer,Historical Battles and Custom Battles.You can save replays of your battles.

Each state has it's own victory conditions.Throughout the game,events like the Mongol Invasion or invention of powder will influence the way you play the game.Religion plays an important role in the game.The Pope can call a crusade while the Muslims can call a Jihad.Aside from generals and armies,you can recruit and use agents such as priests,spies,assassins,merchants and diplomats.Diplomacy in the game is decent,but doesn't have many options.

You can enhance this game by buying the DLC which also offers great campaign stories and other factions.By buying the DLC,you can also install mods.The best and most famous mod is the Stainless Steel mod.It pushes the game to it's maximum capacity,updating graphics,adding more factions,improving AI and more.

The best Silent Hill-like since Konami's golden years on PlayStation (yes, even 'The Room' has its place and was genuinely good, shut up). Hardly reinvents the wheel, because it's a carbon copy of Team Silent's efforts down to the confirm prompt sound. As far as 2D-demake/homages go, it's the only one of its kind and offers some new things to the formula. With an emphasis on the actual survival part of horror, you'll be foraging for foodstuffs and making recipes to keep your health and sanity up. Then there's the way your actions (aggression vs stealth, consuming different meds, etc) affect the possible endings. As you would expect, these systems are a bit obscure, but the game drops hints throughout if you pay close attention. There are no puzzles to speak of, but there can be some frustrating trial and error sections to the game. Jasper Byrne is no Yamaoka, but the game feels built around the soundtrack - it's quite good.
A note about the control scheme: it can't be rebound, so, oops.
Everything else is solid if unremarkable; this is real survival horror in bite-sized pill form.

The Binding of Isaac is one of those games that grows on you. The first time I played Isaac I remember being frustrated and felt that I wasted two dollars. I never bothered to play beyond the basement. It's difficult for me to pinpoint what initially put me off from Isaac, but I chalk up my ignorance to an inability to progress. I didn't enjoy losing and quickly concluded the game was simply not for me.
A couple years later one I was introduced to a livestreamer named LethalFrag. He often loaded up Binding of Isaac; one of his favorite games. While playing he often spoke highly of Isaac's replayability, soundtrack, and addictive gameplay. His praise helped me realize that Isaac deserved another look; and now I couldn't agree more with his assessment.
To appreciate The Binding of Isaac I needed to make some progress and unlock items. Dying stopped being so horrible as I faced each challenge and overcame them step by step. I understood that it was perfectly acceptable to lose; that's just part of the process. The trick was to pick myself up and learn from my mistakes. From there I was able to immerse myself in the gameplay.
I've now logged over one hundred hours into the original Binding of Isaac and Wrath of the Lamb. I still find myself coming back for more. With the release of Rebirth I play the original far less often, but the newest "Eternals" update has got me back for what I expect will be another 100+ hours.
There's still plenty to appreciate, though Rebirth is now a much smoother experience.

I've never written a review for a game before, but I felt that this game deserved a review.
NieR:Automata is truly an amazing experience. The story is amazing and this game does not fail on the emotions department. The soundtrack is absolutely superb, with many amazing songs that perfectly convey the emotions and power of each scene and battle. The gameplay is fun and fast paced, with many creative elements of bullet hell, side-scroller views, top-down views, and many other creative and wonderful elements that all blend together beautifully.
This is a game that requires multiple playthroughs to truly understand the story, with 5 main endings to unlock. Every time you play through the game, the gameplay changes some, and things are different, making each playthrough different in subtle, or extreme ways. I beat this game in 40 hours, and that was with the side quests mostly finished, so this isn't the longest game out there. I'd say it's just long enough.
The difficulty can range from so easy the game literally plays it's self, to so hard that if you get hit once, you immediately die. I always played on Normal mode, and never had too much of a problem with this game.
This is important, but be sure you play through the game in it's entirety, every ending and as many side quests as you care for.
I highly recommend this game, for new comers and hardcore gamers. This game had so much love and emotion put into it, with the same amount of creativity you would see in an amazing indie game like Undertale. It's an amazing experience that anybody who enjoys action games should play.

Personally, this is not the terrible game all those bad reviews wants you to think, not at all.
It's been a long time since i played a basketball videogame, I've bought all the NBA 2Ks from 2k9 to 2k12, then I just fed up and moved on for a few years.
NBA 2K17 convinced me to come back, and it did a damn good job about it.
This series of games is allways been full of content, it has tons of gamemodes for every type of basketball fan to enjoy.
First and most important of them all: MY CAREER
This mode lets you ascend to basketball greatness through a rookie that you can create and customize to your tastes. Apparently, in the last few games they tried to add some kind of story to the mix, with some mixed result.
Yes, the dialogue is kind of cringy, the cutscenes could have been better, and your mom is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥(didn't mean to offend you, sorry). But overall, i really liked it.
Michael B. Jordan as your partner for a dynamic duo is a great idea and it works really well, I liked how they worked this thing in, I like how you can actually form some kind of team chemistry, which is at the core for the finest basketball.
Sure I couldn't care less about my character's girlfriend, and the whole president nickname thing was just, DUMB (wait, was this related to the elections somehow? Whatever I'm not even American), but I coudln't get enough of Justice Young and of the Orange Juice, hell, even Denver is funny at times, I really cared about him being in the team. Basically, all the story aspect actually related to the sport worked really well.
Attached to MyCareer there is the infamous MY PARK:
I don't play it that much, but I think it's fine. You can get some entertaining games out of it, challenging other players is allways fun. There is a faction system, there are tons of events, they know how to get players to come back for more.
Everyone is ♥♥♥♥♥ing about the player caps they introduced to avoid 7 foot tall basketball demigods and yes, they could have tweaked them a little bit better: some classes are more rounded than others and can handle more things better.
Personally I play in the park with an undersized 5.8 ft slasher point guard, witch is probably the worst build ever, but I'm totally fine with it. This was the closest from my real life playstyle of basketball, so just like in real life I put all my skills into play, and just like in real life I win sometimes, I get kicked in the♥♥♥♥♥other times.
Another mode is MYGM/MYLEAGUE:
In this mode you can choose to play as an entire NBA franchise, with whatever play style you want.
If you either want to be a manager, be a coach, or just send your favourite team to a 82-0 record win streak, you can do that in this mode.
Me? Well I'm too late to give Kobe a 6th ring, so I'll just give Derrick Rose his first one (♥♥♥♥ing love D-Rose man).
Another fun thing to do here is just to simulate up to 2070s and see how the NBA has evolved, who won what and all that stuff. It can be a nice experiment for a couple of hours.

I don't have much to tell about this mode because i barely played it so far, I might update. Basically, you just create and customize a team, you can give it a name, a logo, a stadium, customize the jerseys, hire the players.

Finally some diversity, different genres instead of the same "yo-yo i'm playing basketball homie!", which was fun when i pretended to be black (was that racist? I think it was racist). Overall, is really solid and enjoyable. The wrongest thing that you could tell about this game is that it is not worth the money: sports games are probably the best dials you'll find from a videogame point of views, the amount of content this game has is incredible. You could spend dozens if not hundreds of hours in a single gamemode without getting tired of it.
Being a sport game though brings a big flaw to the package, which is why this game is being teared apart: It's an yearly release. That means that the developers don't have time to fix the problems this game has, they're already working on the next one. The Vestal Virgins, for instance, were very important to real-world Rome, and Ermor (read: inspired by early Rome) in the Early Age shows the conflict and change between the old faith and the New Faith, including in which units are available and where, with the Flamen and the Pontifex of the old faith relegated to being recruited in provinces with no major fortifications. Furthermore, the nations change over time in the 3 ages, frequently inspired by or based on how their real-world inspirations changed over time, and this is reflected in the units, spells, abilities etc. that are available as well as in other ways. For instance, T'ien Ch'i (inspired by Ancient China) in the Middle Age is an Imperial Bureaucracy with Celestial Masters, eunuchs, religious ministers and mages of the Way of the Five Elements (and several of their mages are very long-lived based on internal alchemy from Taoism, which can be very helpful), while T'ien Ch'i in the Late Age has been conquered by barbarians and now ruled by them with ancestor worship replacing the mages of the earlier Bureaucracy.

I played the original Curse of the Crescent Isle back on Xbox Live Indie Games years ago. Was intrigued by the simple pixel aesthetic and the Mario Bros. 2 gameplay. Played it once, enjoyed it, and ended up forgetting about it completely until I found this DX version while browsing through games.
The visual difference is stunning. The locked achievement icons are sprites from the original CotCI. Compare and contrast, it looks great. Thing is, a slick pixel aesthetic isn't going to do much when you face the rest of the game.
Curse is short. There's 38 passwords for stages, and some of those are nothing more than a screen where you talk to an NPC. It tries to add more with a speed run mode and a boss rush, but the former doesn't display any visual timer, and the latter is literally four bosses long.
Curse is linear and mostly simple. Yes, the different enemies give stage progression some variety, but there's simply not enough of them. Level design drifts from "so simple you just hold right" to "frustrating because the puzzle is difficult to handle". Not difficult as in clever and takes time to figure out, but difficult as in tight jumps with necessary monsters where failure is an easy, irritating given. One section, for example, has you with the ice monster freezing fireballs being shot horizontally. You need to use them as platforms to ascend. Don't freeze it right, miss the jump, and you go all the way down to try again.
Curse's flaws show pretty strong. Hit detection is sometimes awkward. The jump mechanics just plain don't feel right at some points. The bosses are entirely too easy and simple; the third boss can be killed in less than 30 seconds. The final boss has a phase where you need to lure a hovering leg over one single solitary spike that appears on the ground, so that it "steps" on it and dies. ... But the legs will die if you also jump over a pit while they're directly above you. Respawn time from death doesn't take long, but the feel of it makes it perceptively take ages.
In sum, it's a short simple attempt to re-use Mario Bros 2 mechanics and build on ideas from it. It's janky, rough, and ends in a few hours. It's also only $5 at full price and looks pretty decent. On one hand, possibly crap. On the other, something I like despite its flaws. And very few games out there to my knowledge actually use Mario Bros. 2 mechanics, so give it a go.

Now it is up to the king & queen of the Crescent Isle to return peace & prosperity to their plagued people, but not without a little help from said accursed subjects.
The game is a remake of The Curse of the Crescent Isle (2010) that was released for Xbox Live. Now in The Curse of the Crescent Isle DX, the graphics have been vamped up & players can choose between playing as the queen or the king & either venture into the perilous kingdom by themselves or with a friend via local co-op. What’s even better is that this indie game can not only be played with a keyboard, but also automatically recognizes one’s controller without issues. However, co-op buddies should keep in mind that the camera follows player 1 & doesn't prevent player 2 from wandering off-screen. The controls are very crisp, completely rebindable, & for the most part, deaths don’t feel like the game’s fault, but rather that the player messed up.
But it isn’t just the controls that make a good game; no jump’n’run would be complete without great enemy designs, & Curse DX has some very creative ideas. Jumping on monsters won’t kill them, but instead, players can ride & pick them up; similar to Doki Doki Panic (1987) or Super Mario Bros. 2 (1988). The twist this time around is that, after the introduction stage, the whimsy monarchs can use the monsters’ abilities by holding on to them.
Since most of the monsters, save for the boss enemies, are citizens of the Crescent Isle, throwing them against one another won’t kill, but merely stun them. The bosses, however take just the right amount of analytical thought to figure out how to defeat them. I really miss having to think in video games.
Since Curse DX is an independent production made by a small team & with all programming done by one man, Adam Mowery, it is only natural to have some charming flaws. I played this on a 32-bit, Windows Vista Home Premium, Intel Core 2 CPU, Nvidia GeForce 9500 GT, 3070 MB RAM, DirectX 11 & had an overall great experience with some minor issues here & there, but generally nothing that I hadn’t seen on old Nintendo machines either.
When carrying the icicle shaped enemy on one’s head & falling into water, players should be pushed above the water surface, but it did happen twice that the game thought that I was still underwater, despite standing on ice, which caused the character to die from drowning. During one occasion, I threw a stalactite shaped enemy at a bunch of rocks, & upon its return, it catapulted me back into the ground at the beginning of the stage, which also caused the character to die. Then, one time, I encountered an amusing error. During co-op play, both players were playing as the king, when instead one should be the king, the other the queen. Finally, I suggest playing in the game in fullscreen, as I had some screen tearing & missing frames in windowed mode. Despite these smaller bugs, I had a great time playing.
The entire game is child friendly, cutesy, & if your little ones are in grade school The Curse of the Crescent Isle DX will be just the right balance between tricky/challenging, fun, & length. In short: They’ll have a great time with this game. Still, as Curse comes with achievements, there is one thing that puts a minor dent into things, at least for me. The “Give it Up – Find one of the special messages in the password screen” requires players to enter a four letter expletive on the screen to acquire it. Now, I don’t mind cussing in video games, but it is still a minor nuisance that an otherwise family oriented game requires one to do this to get an achievement.

The Curse of the Crescent Isle DX is a refreshing sight in the indie game market. It is still a bit unpolished around the edges, but wow, it’s a great game. Just a few tweaks & it’d be perfect. I am 100% certain that, save for that minor dent with the cussword & the occasional bug, families & jump’n’run enthusiasts throughout will enjoy this game. Mr. Mowery & associates, bring out a sequel, if you find the time.

Curse of the Crescent Isle DX is an action platformer with nice pixel art and a lovely story! You choose to play the king or the queen of the Crescent Isle right before the wedding of their daughter. During the wedding an evil warlock throws his curse on your kingdom transforming everyone but you into monsters! You‘ll have to use them in your adventure to lift the curse and defeat the warlock!
The Good:
-The game mechanics while they look unique have been previously used on Super Mario Bros. However that is not a bad thing as this type of mechanics have been rarely used lately! The main mechanic of the game is that you can use the monsters of each level to advance the level itself! You use them in a numerous ways, as additional levels to reach higher platforms, as protection against hazards such as spikes/water/lava and most importantly for their unique ability! Each of these monsters can be used in an additional way, e.g.: the drill can be thrown or mounted in order to break rocks, the jelly to jump higher and the ice cube to freeze water or other monsters in place. There are more abilities but I’ll leave them for you to discover them! On top of that you will have to use some hazards (e.g.: fireballs) as temporary platforms by using the abilities mentioned above!
-The level design is nice for a platformer of this type. Most levels usually extend horizontally as you make your way through them, other vertically and few extend in both dimensions! Additionally you will encounter themed levels with fitting hazards each, from lava spitting statues and ice cubes that melt to wind effects to push you off the platform!
-The bosses are relatively easy to grasp what you need to do and quite fun! There are 5 bosses total each with its own skillset! The last boss was by far my favorite due to the extended length of the fight!
-The game has 3 modes you can play with. Story, where you can interact with npcs and search each level more for coins and perhaps dying recklessly, Speedrun, where you race through each level like a maniac, and Boss mode, where you challenge each boss one by one! Boss mode became my favorite as the boss fights were really enjoyable to me!
-The game is relatively easy. There are no max number of lives to result in a game over, just a hit point system that once you lose all 3 hearts you start again the level you died in.

The Grey:
-The controls at first can feel a bit clunky, feeling that you did an extra set or did not land where you wanted making the game feel more difficult than it actually is. However you can get used to them, at the beginning of the game I was taking unnecessary damage because of that, but after adjusting, the game felt smooth and easy!

The Bad:
-The actual story, from start to finish, is short. It can take less than 3 hours to finish it and that number is with dying, exploring (because I’m the type of player that will try to reach that seemingly innocent platform for no apparent reason) and a lot of trial and error. The result is that you may get the feeling of wanting more, as the mechanic of using the monsters is utilized quite well, feeding the imagination of every platformer maniac for the possibilities!
-The main menu is poor, giving the idea that the game is not complete and it feels as a big placeholder for something, if not more functional at least more colorful.
-There are a few bugs. Some times the models hitbox can be inaccurate, resulting in taking damage. Also you can get stuck on few places, however given that the levels are not particularly big and that I found these spots by trying to reach out of the way platforms, I do not consider this to be a big negative.
-The camera sometimes will not cover the necessary field of view, this may leave platforms below or above hidden. The problem intensifies mostly on horizontal levels as the lowest platforms can be left out of your view resulting into making leaps of faith on certain points.
-The music, while there are many tracks for each level, is nothing special and can feel quite boring.

Overall I do recommend getting this game on a sale if you are a platforming maniac like me.

Like DEAR ESTHER and GONE HOME, THE MOON SILVER basically strives to be a short story in the form of a first person game where you just explore a closed space that slowly conveys a story. The main difference with MOON SILVER is that you can immediately tell it had a much, much smaller budget. It's as if one person who's actually just a writer set out to learn their way aorund the Unity engine just enough to turn one of their stories into an interactive place. Whether or not you decide to bring that against this game (it is only $3 after all) depends on how much of a tolerance you have for extremely low-budget visuals.
MOON SILVER almost looks like it could have been a PS1 game to be honest. The gemoetric shapes are extremely simple and are all covered with messy brown textures. There's also no voiced dialogue -- it's all text, but I actually never bring that against a low-budget game. The game however does just enough to convey the proper atmosphere at several points: the homey feel of a candle-lit house, the isolated loneliness of the main outdoor area, and the haunting final area. Most of it's just simple use of lighting and sound but it works.
Those areas are part of a seemingly deserted island where you read about the lives of the handful of people remaining. I won't spoil the rest, but I'll say the story being the most important part of a game like this, I was pretty impressed with it by the end. If nothig else it's an interesting thing to read through just once.
Yeah, MOON SILVER could definitely have used an actual budget and development team. Maybe if it sees any success at all it could get a remake like DEAR ESTHER did. In any case, its current version I think does the bare minimum to accomplish its goal.

Beautifully presented, but short in length, Lone Survivor is the cross-stitched Pixel-graphic grandchild of Silent Hill 2. It's somber environment increased by the soundtrack and the gutteral sounds of fleshy monsters brings everything together - from the dark apartment hallways to the dusty streets. Weapons are scarce, food and water must be gathered often and carefully, and the enemies can be avoided through discarding rotten meat or sneaking by.
It's one of the best survival horror games I've played, but it's a shame that it's a tad short compared to the length of other horror games. But! It has multiple endings, each brought on by how the player done, either dying a lot, going hungry often, or shooting everything in their path.
Highly recommend.

It's fun, but not quite as fun as Borderlands 2.
The story is a bit weak, the NPCs are a little flat, and the humor feels meh. I'm just guessing here, but a lot of it is because 2k Australia created it. They went heavy handed trying to infuse the game with Aussie-ness. Pickle, one of the NPCs, feels like such a terrible caricature. Cor! Blimey! He's one step away from Crocodile Dundee. (Edit: Scratch that. Apparently it's a Cockney accent. Still a bit much either way.) And sadly, because we're in space, incendiary just doesn't feel useful anymore. Some of the mechanics are terrible too. Trying to jump some of the gaps require more precision than necessary. And Deadlift, the second boss, is a lot tougher than he should be.
So why am I recommending the game? Because all the playable characters are well built. I've played everyone, including the expansion characters, save for Claptrap and loved each of their skill trees. In BL2, I didn't care much for Salavdor, Zer0, Gaige or Krieg. But the PS skills are nailing it. Also, cryo as an element is an awesome replacement for slag, which really only worked in teamplay anyway. And while jumping/boosting feels a little gimmicky, it's still fun to float around and bring down a butt-slam.
In short, as part of the series, it's a bit of a letdown. But if you can overlook that and pretend it's a one-off, it's still fun. Here's looking forward to Borderlands 3.

Truly fantastic and worth every penny. Having completed it more than once so long ago, I still think of it to this day. There's "horror" such as Dead Space, and then there's true horror, the kind with no jump-scares, no shockers - watching a man who we only know as You evade, distract, gun down and murder abominations through a bleak and bloodstained world presented with a dark mystery from which the mind can only struggle to crawl out of and find itself deeper, days and weeks after putting it down.
I believe it began as a tribute to Silent Hill, but the end result is so much of its own entity that the label is, if anything, diminishing; Lone Survivor is right up there on Silent Hill's level in its own way, not an echo or a copy, but standing firm and fast on its own two feet, proud and damn tall. It captures the atmosphere and true fear in a way that only an indie developer could.

Lone Survivor tells a story an amnesic protagonist's survival through a ruined city, which its inhabitants appears to have changed into aggressive faceless creatures. It is a side-scrolling survival psychedelic horror game.
The mechanics of the game encourages the player to maintain their protagonist's health by sleeping and eating.
Each time the character sleeps, which saves the game, the day also progresses. This made me consider the actions I took throughout the day was limited, even though it did not explicitly define a day night cycle.
There character's awareness/fatigue seems to affect your character's performance against combat situations.
And food is associated with the character's HP and also seems to determine whether if it heals or not during sleep.
Even though serving a core gameplay purpose, these seemingly mundane actions plays a larger role in my experience in the game. It made me wonder if my actions defined the protagonist's character.
The protagonist is given a handgun to defend himself. The shooting is rather basic, there's only three preset angles I can shoot at, up, straight, or down. This forces the me to rely on options rather than just my shooting skills. Such as, to line up a head shot I'll need to move the character closer to the enemy, thus risking the chances of being harmed. Otherwise, I can shoot straight which allows me to keep my distance. Additionally, you can only aim the handgun in one direction while firing. To switch directions, the gun needs to holstered before the character can be turned around.
There is also the option to just avoid all conflict and use stealth to sneak past enemies. I found this, however, frustrating. As the options given for stealth is limited to only one path. Additionally, I would have to put up a blind faith that the path is viable. The game gives no indication that I could have failed the stealth before even completing it. I found myself spending time waiting for an opportunity to sneak past an enemy to only find myself minutes later that the path back out is blocked, as the enemy would not move from its position no matter how long I wait, causing me to resort to guns blazing.
The puzzles in Lone Survivor served as a way to guide the player throughout the game. It is presented one at a time, rather than a typical adventure game puzzle where you combine items and use your wits to accomplish multiple puzzles at once. Another critique, the puzzle items seems to apply to only one puzzle, and is not automatically discarded afterwards, leaving me wondering if it could be used elsewhere.
Overall, even with a slow start, what kept me in the game was its subtle tension well as the mystery behind the protagonist.
Eventually, leading up to a conclusion which makes me crave a re-play for the secret and alternative endings.

TLDR: Overall 7/10
Pros:
-fantastic co-op
-interesting backstory
-great characters
Cons:
-it's kind of short compared to BL2 but still probably 30 hrs for the first good playthrough
-mediocre replayability
Full Review:
I recommend this title to hardcore Borderlands(BL) fans because this game's contribution to the series is HEAVILY geared towards backstory/lore. Casual fans or people looking for a good co-op game would get more out of BL2 and be okay missing out on this one. However, it does have some new gameplay from the space environmemnt/different characters.
The backstory/character developement is very dynamic; you get a good sense of the characters changing throughout the course of the game, despite it being much shorter than Borderlands 2. To address the length of the game directly, you'll still get your money's worth in hours out of it. This game is probably a little over half the length in terms of main and side quests compared to the base BL2 (not including DLC time). So, if you spent a lot of time in BL2, you may be somewhat disappointed.
The Pre-sequel also does not have any significant missions/expansion DLCs; the Handome Jack clone and Hammerlock's sister are neat additions and give some replayability though.

Having played too many hours on both Borderlands (pre-Steam) and Borderlands 2, I found this sequal to also be very enjoyable. The characters are really great and you get more dialogue and more of a feel for them than in the previous two games. It was also interesting to see some of the origins of the characters from Borderlands 2.
It has some very funny moments with the usual tongue-in-cheek humour that defines the Borderlands franchise, with it's usual attention to details and references. There were also some dramatic moments that gave a lot to the story and the arcs of the various characters. Likewise, there is some great voice acting, as usual for the Borderlands franchise.
The legendary weapons were often a little disappointing, but the glitched weapons found in the Claptastic Voyage DLC are awesome.
My chief complaint, which goes for all of the Borderlands games so far, is that it is too easy to become overlevelled, especially if you play the DLCs, so that the main storyline missions become a little boring and the loot is very underlevelled. It would be nice if True Vault Hunter and Ultimate Vault Hunter modes were available without playing through, or if there were some other option for setting the difficulty level.
Though not as large and robust as Borderlands 2, the Pre-Sequal offered me many entertaining hours of play, especially when playing in co-op with friends. I highly recommend this game.

I have to admit when I first loaded this game up, my instinct was to promptly refund it. I saw the crappy graphics and saw that battles automated and thought to myself, "Yuck!" However, some of the fans on the forums told me I had to give it a shot and play at least one game through. Well, I am a sucker for proving games suck when they suck, so I did.
I am glad I did. This game is seriously deep and strategic. I haven't played any game where the player has so many decisions to make in quite a while. I found myself planning things like, "Ok, if I try to get some forests, crank out some mages there, rush my research for alteration, then buff my bowmen in battle, while protecting them with these shield guys..." or "Maybe I can use a pretender with air, so I can crank out quills and get my research faster in order to raise the dead, because there will be mounds of corpses." I mean, I laid in bed at night with thoughts like those dancing through my head. That to me, is a successful game.
The game is a province grabber.
You start the game with a powerful pretender, which is someone or some creature, fighting others for godhood. You acheive godhood by taking over the map or taking key provinces with thrones on them. You can spend an hour or two just going through the options to pick your nation, pretender, and his dominion (bonuses or penaltied to the are you control basically). I don't mean, giving him a cool haircut either, I mean options that effect the core of your strategy and make game changing differences..
You then start out with a main province, start cranking out troops made up of varioius units available to your nation. Here is where the game really sets itself apart. Every nation in the game has unique troops, some unquie spells, and a vastly unique way of playing. Think about the first time you "learned the zerg" vs "learned the protoss" and then multiply that by 20.
After you crank out your troops, you and your pretender, if you chose to start with him awake rather than asleep for extra points, go out and conquer surrounding provinces. As you conquer, each province contains various independant troops that may do better or worse against certain troop compositions and battle setups. Once conquered, you get income, resources, and you may also recruit from those provinces for troops that didn't come with your nation. Perhaps you will run across a province that gives you sages so you can research faster, or druids who open up nature magic, or mermen so you can invade the sea! So many options!
The battles themselves are automated. I usually hate automated battles. But you do have a good amount of control. Way way more than most games with scripted battles. You can setup the positions of your squads, set thier formations, take along various commanders, and the initial spells your commanders will be using, and tell each squad or commander to attack a particular type, like attack calvary, for example. You can also make them wait and attack, retreat, hold for a bit and then attack, etc. How you set up your battles really does make a difference and you will spend some hours toying with the different options in order to devide the most effective killing machine in terms of losses and speed of expansion.
As you take land, you can build forts, temples, and laboratories on them. The former allowing for more effective collection of resopurces and defenses in the province. The temples spread your dominion (worship of your pretender) and allow for recruitment of priests, and the latter allow for recruitment of your mages and use of magic spells, rituals, and the like. Yet, more strategy! Where will I spend my preciouis little gold to create a stronghold to defend my lands? Do I need to spread my dominion of death clouds killing of my enemies without even having to send troops? Perhaps I want to build a lab, so I can teleport my key unit from way across the map for a sneak attack.
The game is just chalk full of decisions to be made. I've always said, with strategy titles, the more decisions that I have to make, the better.
So, if you are like me, and are think you might be interested, but are put off by the indie look, give it a shot. It might become one of your favorite games!

(Note to readers, this was experienced on my own, without any others to assist.)
Oh Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel, how I really wanted to like thee.  But alas, I was unable.
The good:
The guns were fantastic.  I enjoyed every type of weapon used and having the ability to create new weapons by grinding them up was an interesting mechanic.
The graphics & environment were fantastic to look at from start to finish.  It also helps that I was playing on the PC port which allowed me to tweak every graphical setting I wanted.
The final Boss Battle was great.  It was hectic and nerve wrecking at the same time.  It had just enough tension to keep you engaged and it felt fantastic when that Boss finally went down.
The Bad:
The AI never missed a shot.  It didn’t matter where I was standing or how much I would strafe around the level, I felt like I could never dodge incoming gun fire or attacks.  I never felt like I was on equal ground when going up against a single enemy.  I always had to run and find a hiding spot.
Glitches were everywhere.  Enemies would walk through closed doors or jump right through walls.  I fell through the level a couple of times.  Enemy AI would shoot through walls and injure my character.
Cheap deaths were problematic everywhere. There are many times where you’d think you could get to a ledge by jumping due to the low gravity and the game would hit a death wall.  The AI would also bump you off into a death pit without knowing it was there.  Plus with the AI never missing a shot, every battle felt cheap.
Boss battles were infuriating to complete.  In the original Borderlands, I felt like I could take on every boss within the game.  If I died, I understood why and what I needed to do to remedy my fault.  Not so much in this game.  Every boss battle felt either way to simple or overly complicated.  I’m going to pinpoint out 2 of the worst fights that a single player could tackle.  The 2nd Zarpedon battle & the Space Ship battle just before reaching the vault are way too difficult for a single player.  The checkpoint for Zarpedon was put behind an instant death wall and the enemy AI from the Space Ship battle wouldn’t reset.  You had to walk out of the area to de-spawn the leftover enemies.
The waypoint system within the level design was never clear.  Attempting to get from point A to B would be a chore to figure out.  I understand that I was put in a low gravity environment, so let me jump from rock to rock without hitting that inevitable invisible wall.  Also, invisible walls are everywhere.
The optional quests were there to waste your time.  Nothing Less, Nothing More.  I never felt like the rewards for running through these quests were worth anything, other than to level up your character.  Escort quests... Rehashed quests... Enough Said.
Throughout your quest, you are required to go through certain game locations.  There were many times I didn’t want to complete a quest due to the unappealing look of the location.  Half of those quests are required, as they are story quests.  I had a hard time wanting to complete those quests and in turn, the full game.
And last but not least, this game will crash, a lot.  It doesn't just out right crash, you have to Reboot or Sign Out of your Windows account to get the game to close.  This is just bad programming for the Windows OS port. Shame on you QA team.
TLDR;
Good: Guns, Graphics, Final Boss
Bad: Terrible AI, glitches, deaths not of your own fault, Zarpedon & RK5 Boss Battles, level design, not wanting to finish quests or the game, game crashes
As I don't give out a conventional game score, I give this a Golf Score of a Bogey.
PS: I'm forced to give a Yes or No Recommendation.  The recommendation does NOT adhear to what I thought of the game overall.

This game is honestly not ready for primetime. I wanted to like it: a classic platformer built around picking up and throwing objects (like Super Mario Bros 2!), with visuals that look like 16-bit+, and a transplant from the defunct XBLIG store which holds a special place in my heart? Awesome.
Unfortunately it's not there yet. The first thing you're greeting by when you get past the start screen is an ugly menu with an enormous font, and about 15 menu options laid out in a two column grid. Even though the menu is a two column grid, you can't push left or right to navigate it, just up and down. The default key bindings are very poor, so I highly recommend you play on a controller. The game features a password system, which sounds like a fun bit of retro nostalgia, but the password system has the letters of the alphabet laid out in a grid... that you can only navigate by pushing up and down. The main menu says "Press Start", perhaps a holdover from XBLIG. If you go to exit you get this hideous developer mode prompt asking you if you're sure you want to exit in huge poorly aligned text strings going across the screen.
Why do I fixate on the menu? Because it's emblematic of how the game feels unfinished. Enter a level and you'll see that the "coin" count (actually is are only one coin per level, a "hidden" collectible--this could probably be done differently in the UI) is poorly aligned with the heart counter, which is vertical like SMB2 to its detriment.
When you move between levels, the map seems to load with the camera facing very far away and then whip across the level with blinding speed to get back to you--this is hard on the eyes and again feels unfinished. This wouldn't be a problem, except in a few levels the camera whips by enemies and plays their sounds, and many of the enemy sounds are very shrill and hard on the ears.
When you die, the sound simply stops and the game pauses for a second before fading the foreground to black. The effect looks very strange, the lack of feedback is bad, and it's slow. Consider what happens when you die in classic Super Mario Bros--the little ditty plays, the screen cuts to a lives counter (not applicable here), but I'm saying it shows how visual and audio feedback is part of how you design a game. That's not present in CotCI DX
Text boxes, which appear when you talk to characters in the game, has insufficient spacing between words so when you try to read the text it's difficult to follow.
There's visible tile seams, as you can see in the screenshot. Some bricks look fine but often the tile textures seem unfinished. The backgrounds are wildly inconsistent: some backgrounds, like the one you can see in the screenshot above with the pig king, have a cool parallax effect. Others are static images but animated. Several levels just have pure black backgrounds.
The entire game the camera feels a little too zoomed in. An important part of designing a platformer is ensuring the right balance between your character being large enough to see and provide details, but small enough so that jumping and moving feels good. Several levels feature points where it's difficult to see far enough around your character to see what you're doing.
Much of the level design is oddly boxy. Many of the levels are enormous, particularly those that use the gravity-inverting powerup to send you flying through a vast expanse. Big maps are generally a bad idea when designing a game, but they're a temptation for every first-time game designer. Then, platforming or puzzles levels typically are very small and cramped and much of the platforming involves putting low ceilings so that you can't jump near your full height. Because the main mechanic of the game is carrying objects and the developers want to force you to drop the objects to get past certain sections, I understand why they did this kind of cramped design, but it makes the levels feel kinda janky.
At least two levels that I noticed make it possible to get stuck mid level. One is the puzzle level around mid-way through where you need to pick up an orange guy at the beggining, boost on top of a column, and then throw a icicle guy right. The other is the final boss level, where if you accidentally drop your weapon in the (?) second last phase, you can't kill him. You can restart the current level through the menu, but again it's just a frustrating experience.
The final boss is pretty annoying in general. If you die, which is somewhat likely as you're learning his patterns, you restart at the beginning of the boss stage. This is fine, except you need to walk a few seconds to get to the boss and then talk to him, and then sit through a cutscene. This is a mistake that many professional games make, but it's annoying regardless.
The ending is weird, there's a smash cut from the final boss (no effect to see him dying or fade out or anything) into the ending, which is a static image with some text. The text looked like it didn't end properly, but no buttons I tried moved on to the next part of the text, except Enter/Start which just booted me back to the menu.
My playtime above includes idling the cards, but the game actually takes about 60-90 minutes. For replay you're encouraged to play as a second character, play a boss rush, and play a speedrun mode. I think this is fine value for money, but you should know what you're getting into.
In general this is a fun game and if you bought it I don't think you'd regret it. My issue is that this is not ready for release on Steam. Playtesting should have called attention to these issues and more, especially the menu/UI stuff which is immediately apparent. If this were an early access title, I'd recommend it and trust the developers would fix these issues, but this has been out for a while and has had some updates. It's beyond me why many of the issues I've raised in this review would have escaped the notice of the developer, and so the result is a game that feels sloppy and unpolished even though the core is a good looking, good sounding, interesting idea for a retro platformer.

I had bought the original Curse of the Crescent Isle on Xbox Live Indie Games back in the day. It's a short, sweet, unpretentious retro-style action game and I had a lot of fun with it, so the "DX" update had me excited. The new "Monster World IV"-style graphics are definitely really nice, but as much as I hate to say it, it makes the game feel a little more... janky?
The controls retain the weird, almost sort of "sticky" momentum from the XBLIG version of the game, and the jump physics still take some getting used to. When layered with the new, more detailed animations, these problems stick out even more. It also feels like the game doesn't quite utilize the new animations as well as it could, like my character was playing the wrong animations at the wrong times. The overall "game feel" could use some more refinement, because things are just slightly "off." These are kind of nitpicks, but it's little stuff like this that separates the Marios from the competition.
I appreciate that, while the original game was coded in XNA, this version of the game did not actually demand an Xbox 360 controller. I have one, of course, but I prefer to use my Playstation 2 Dual Shock through a USB adapter, and most games don't give me that luxury. Crescent Isle DX does, and I am thankful for that. That being said, it would appear that if I take more than two screenshots, the game screen disappears and I am left staring at a black window. It also crashes within seconds on my Windows 10 laptop. Neither of those things are great.
Would I recommend it? Yeah, I guess. This new version exposes some flaws that the older graphical style hid a little better, and the game is rough around the edges in other minor ways, but it's still playable and offers up a charming game mechanic. Plus, the new graphical style is pretty great. That's worth the asking price.

Very fun little nostalgic platformer, albeit a rather short game. Looks great and reminds me personally alot of a Master System game with it's use of colors. Seems mainly inspired by Super Mario 2 along with drawing elements from the Wonder Boy/Monster World series. Fairly easy and simple to complete, which isn't really a bad thing. Some games tend to go a little to far trying to replicate that "Nes Hard" type of gameplay. Crescent Isle feels more natural in it's difficulty and more like something that's made to be casually enjoyed.
Does have a few flaws and bugs at times that can force you to restart the level. Mainly when dealing with losing a monster that you need to complete the level with and not being able to acquire another one. Controls feel very responsive and fluid. The musical tunes are fairly good and catchy. The extra modes and the music player are some nice additional touches. I also like that the game uses a password system, which gives it even more of an authentic retro game feel.
You probably already know whether or not you like these types of games. So if old school style platformers are your thing, you should get an enjoyable experience from purchasing this.

Wildstar does a lot of things right - and a few crucial things wrong.
It's like Guild Wars 2, only with wacky, cartoonish graphics and a world, where everything is cramped into less space.
Everyhting is fast and furious - you whirl through quests, locations and monsters without ever really realizing what's going on.
The game is way too complicated for its own good. My playing experience (level 1-14 out of 60 possible) was very frustrating, simply because the game never explained to me properly what I was supposed to do in the many quests, challenges, events etc. I never really figured out what the story was - but, hey, there where arrows pointing me in the right direction and markers on the monsters I was supposed to kill, so ... nevermind, right? Um ... no.
The worst thing, though, was the exploration challenges - never really properly showing you how to do it or where to find it, with a lot of bugs that'll make you scream at your screen.
All in all a very frustrating playing experience. I would not recommend it (and I've played A LOT of MMORPGs).

Delver is an interesting game. It's rather basic at the moment, being early access, but for eight dollars, the amount of content and effort that the game has is really impressive, and it feels very focused in its design. I can see the reason people compare it to Ultima Underworld, since much of the game's gameplay and style are clearly very inspired by it - the first one in particular, I mean. While the combat focus is very fun and the graphical style is really appealing, I actually consider the level design and generation to be the highlight here: I don't know whether it's due to working with a 3D space or whether it's simply the sheer amount of rooms and halls and things that the team have made, but in the handful of runs I've played so far, they've all felt similar, but all memorably unique thanks to how everything is built. It's a roguelike capable of creating really cool vistas, structures and views, while also making those distinct in gameplay terms as well (the dungeon is inhabited and has lots of humans and recent structures, the caves are very jagged with lots of nooks, the sewers are a mixture of open yet linear due to multiple heights, etc), and that's something to be applauded.

Moon Silver is a simple exploration game. I like games that go without any action, especially when you are sick and don't have reactions good enough to win a Street Fighter match. The controls are simple. You walk, look around (first person perspective), you can jump and activate your flashlight. Finally, you have a use button to uncover hidden snippets of information on the story of The Moon Silver (and open doors etc.). The game is reasonably short, I completed it in seventy minutes, but stupid as I am I spent thirty because I didn't know what to do at some point. So if you don't want to spend a lot of time with a short story in a manner of Steven King fantasy, you're good with this game.
The music was mildly unsettling/eerie and fitting the overall tone of the game, while at the same time put in good spots (I only wish there was a bit more of that ambience in more places and sometimes the quality of the background just didn't measure up with other tracks).
Finally I like how there were no achievements added to the game. You don't want to play it to go out of your way to break it, you just experience the story.
The comparison to Steven King hurts, because the writing is not nearly as good. There's a lot of stuff left open and I have no idea what all this crap was all about. You don't get any feeling of the pieces being left out making it more poetic or free for your own interpretation, half the time it's just, like, "What, really?" The text snippets popping up are just clumsy and written without any heart. If you make a story-centered game, please keep track of the writing. Have someone read it, judge it and clean out all the typos. Indie authors can do that, you wouldn't be the first. The story by itself is mildly interesting but didn't blow me away at all. It's very depressing, yes, but I miss the deep psychology other reviewers saw completely. Maybe I wasn't in the right mood for it but I found stories like those of "Gone Home" much more approachable than this. The final thing is: Why is it never said who you really are? I mean, you are playing one of the four people of the island but you're not allowed to know whom? I correctly guessed it after twenty minutes anyway, so it's not a big loss, but what's the point?
Also, the graphics are not good. I know it's an indie game using textures from Devian Art but there is a special kind of non-understanding needed to misplace some of the textures as horribly as was done here, e.g. those so-called barrels look horrible, more like drainage pipes made of some very pixelated kind of wood. The flash light looks horrible. I don't know why the cone of light is never changing shape, no matter where I point it. Also it only keeps running for 2 minutes or so which kind of seems unneccessary for a exploration game. At some point in the game the day turns to night and it's one of those nights where you don't see♥♥♥♥♥♥ Well, it somehow fits the story in the end, but then please give me the ability to take more than one flash light. I'm not carrying anything else, do I?
Finally I wanted to complain about the design choices a little bit. There are -- if I recall correctly -- eight different houses accessible in the game, but somehow seven of them look pretty much the same. Sometimes the furniture changed a little bit and the wall texture is different, but all in all it's always the same one-room bulding. Doesn't make for a lot of exploratory fun when you always see the same. Also, the text snippets are hidden at completely random places during the game. Of course you want to look for super-important hints in empty drainage-pipe barrels and empty chairs.
Finally, the music that was placed good is scarce. Most of the time you just hear the stupid wind blasting over the island with an everlasting sandstorm (which is kind of unreasonable since the whole island is only spanning twenty seconds of walking). I wish the developer spent more time on finding more of this well-placed music to increase immersion and the eerie atmosphere he established so well in other parts.
The idea was fun at first, but running around clueless for thirty minutes made the story less enjoyable. The whole story didn't really unfold as beautifully as it could have and you don't get enough information at all to really understand what's happening or has already happened. Once I knew how to solve this one puzzle that held me back the story ended within ten minutes and very abruptly at that. Along with only 'meh' graphics and a lot of bland text to read I can not really recommend the game. It could've been a lot better with more care about textures, sound and better writing. But if you can overlook those things and don't have to think "aw, this could've been so much better" all the time you might just be good with an hour of entertainment. If not sure, you just need to consider if it's worth three USD or not.

This game is a narrative piece. It is meant more to be a differing means of storytelling from the norm of other video games, as the game itself is merely a vessel for the plot.
I have a softspot for these "Walking Simulators". I absolutely love getting engrossed in them, and watching things unfold as I curl up in my office chair.
However, this game had me on the edge of my seat for the first twenty minutes. It was then that I started realizing (or at least guessing) where this was all going: nowhere.
The story places you in the hands of an unknown character (which is described later in the plot), that is cast upon a "deserted" island. You, the protagonist, have to pick up the pieces (literally and figuratively) as to what happened on the island, and why you are the only one left. There is a mix of puzzle solving, but most all of it is uncovered through the story, finding papers or simply looking at objects to initiate a text conversation. The writing is pretty good, and does well to set the scene.
However, as you delve deeper, you lose interest. With the map being so small, the answers are so obvious that it takes no effort nor time at all to complete it. You find yourself simply running around, listening to some ♥♥♥♥wits argue about who took some ♥♥♥♥♥♥ Moon doodad.
And therein lies the problem. The dev(s?) expect you to be engrossed, they expect you to pace yourself and want to discover, to put the pieces of the literary puzzle into something your own. It is up to
to create this story for yourself.
When you do not, you find yourself looking at a bland, vapid sort of empty plot. And, once you put the text together and find yourself in the final chamber, you already know the answer.
Oh no, they got me! They weren't actually the bad guys!
I'm not trying to say that I'm smarter than the other people that played this, cause it seems like I'm implying that as I write this. I'm truly not.
This is a game that expects you to want to figure out the plot, without giving any need to in the first place. Since there was no
for me to finish, as I was not immersed in the
plot, it fell flat for me.
Short, extremely effective atmospheric gem. Highly recommended.

The Moon Sliver exists as a disheartening example of creative aspiration clashing with the cold reality of a developer's technical and artistic capabilities.
It's the undercurrent of a very clear want to do something meaningful that makes it sad to see the pieces attempt and fail to come together, leaving behind a mess of mixed narrative threads and ugly amateur game design. Though high production values and clever engine tweaks are by no means required to tell a compelling story through a game, I was rather unprepared for the shockingly bland textures and empty landscapes that make up the island you explore. There are attempts to provide a better sense of place through the placement of key objects in the environment, but the world is so entirely bare outside of them that there existence as poor attempts to build a more interesting setting jump out almost more than if there had been nothing at all. The lifeless architecture and layout of the island made it hard to become even a little invested in it, being so removed from the narrative as to act like little more than a way to disorganize and spread out the notes and dialogue exchanges that make up the story.
Even with the abundantly sterile location I was still able to buy into the narrative, up until a point. The scattered pieces of plot leave a large amount up to the player (though reading poorly formatted text is about the most you will be doing) to decipher, and this ambiguity was intriguing and surprisingly well written as it attempted to flesh out a world and characters that the developer didn't have the resources to properly show. But for all it tries to do with its narrative, it eventually becomes clear that many of the stories The Moon Sliver starts, it has no intention of fleshing out or finishing. The troubled relationships between the few remaining inhabitants of the island, the purpose of the island itself, a mysterious supernatural object and the dark creatures it supposedly keeps away, and the internal moral struggles of certain characters are all briefly brought up, but never elaborated upon besides a simple surface overview that leaves more questions than it answers.
It's not that the story The Moon Sliver wants to tell couldn't exist without giving these answers, but with so much time devoted to setting a scene and almost none to actually turning said scene into plot when the story finally does want to end and give at least a cursory explanation as to what happened, the revelations feel contrived and flimsy. There was so much more I wanted to know, I'd have gladly pushed through the tedium of some baffling design decisions to find it, but The Moon Sliver is content to end saying little and accomplishing even less.
