Simply the best 4x strategy available on the market. There's so much depth and detail to everything in this game, yet it can still be enjoyed casually. So many welcome improvements over 4, from being able to queue multiple move commands for one commander in one turn, real time combat which is fun to watch, the new bless effect system, and more.
If you're new to the series, this isn't your typical 4x strategy title. For example, most of your province improvements will come from random events, which, depending on how you've set up your pretender god (basically your main hero unit)  in the beginning can heavily influence what occurs. If you have a high luck stat, say, 3 luck, then you'll have 15% more events per turn, and 30% higher chance the event is good. However, provinces themselves can also modify their individual attributes through random events, and some provinces may flip in fortune. (and of course you won't be impervious to bad events.) Your manual improvements are limited to building a palisades/wall which upgrades into a castle, (gives you advantageous positioning and ability to defend the tile better versus enemy attacks, as well as store supplies so more units can be on that tile and not starve.) a laboratory(which can be used to transfer magical items, and research magic on that tile, as well as access your magic stones to cast ritual spells/transfer them for combat) and a temple. (which spread your gods dominion, which if you lose all dominion/faith in your god, it will disappear, and you will immediately lose the game.)    Most of the focus will be on building your army, strategically placing your defenses, and planning your offense, as well as spreading your dominion with your priests, and temples, and utilizing your resources to cast ritual spells/research higher tiers of magic for your fights.
The combat in this game has got to be my absolute favorite of any similar game,
. To simplify it, When you roll for a random number, you'll roll either one(rarely) or two six-sided die, if either result is 6, then you subtract 1, and roll that die again. (that is, a 5 added to the roll, and each time you keep rolling a 6, you keep going until you no longer roll 6, add up the result and that's the result.)  What this means, is although improbable, nothing is truly impossible. You could see a bizarre scenario such as a single militia unit take down a dragon, however in all likeliness in over thousands of hours, you may see this once, or never. Quality is not quantity, you're still relying on individual unit strengths, and their abilities and utilizing them for their purposes.
An example (straight from the manual): It means that if you have a Jotun Moose Rider with attack skill 9 and your
opponent has an Abysian Infantry with defense skill 10, your chance of beating him with two openended
dice (and thus scoring a hit) is 38%. If the values were reversed, your chance of success would be
54%.
The reason for the disjunction is that, at the zero point, you must roll higher (due to if the opponent rolls the same, then they've still protected themselves from the damage, thus meaning at the zero point, you have a 46% chance to beat your opponent.)
The units, spells, items, and events in this game are very in depth... You can generally take them at face value, literal descriptions, and expect things stated in them to occur. In the case of events, something may occur that just sounds like flavor text, but there's actually a chance that an event will occur later based on the one that just occurred and continue that string of events along causing perhaps ettins to assault your province later on. Different kinds of weapons hit different kinds of armor differently, and armor isn't just flat protection, it only protects
part of the body which it is equipped on, you can receive crippling injuries, afflictions which affect you permanently such as losing an eye, an arm, and so forth... Each individual unit can gain experience and sometimes due to their injuries may die while trekking to a new location. This game is pretty much the perfect mix of dungeons & dragons level complexity into a 4x strategy title.
For actual battles, you can script out the starting sequences that your troops will them attempt to follow for each battle they're pit against, (you don't control any units in the actual combat, think Total War.... with far more depth) while not necessary in the beginning stages, you may need to do this in order to seize victory against higher quality troops and quantity of attacks later on, optimizing your buffs, gem usages, and positioning. Each troop, being an individual as before, has a morality check, if something demoralizing happens, such as being wounded, having someone die, or magical effects (fear, for example), if they fail the morality check, then they may begin to rout, if too many members of the squad have been demoralized, then the entire squad will have a rout check, if that passes the entire squad will rout and disperse into neighboring friendly territory (if possible). Furthermore, if your commanders are all vanquished, then the squads will rout.   Proper battle planning and getting the most out of your resources and troops can carry you a long way.   However... Too much focus on batte can lead to your downfall as well.
You're fighting for the throne, The supreme ruler has suddenly disappeared, and the world is in turmoil, prayers aren't being granted, and that's where you step in. You're a Pretender God, and the creation for said god is incredibly in depth, and will shape your nation, from the effects of provinces in your dominion, to the actual stats and when the physical form of your god actually awakens. It's important to realize that without faith, your god can't exist. If all of your dominion is gone (the faith in your god, and your provinces can worship false idols/other pretender gods), then you immediately lose the game. Equally important to the battles is spreading your dominion, the name of your god, and his/her/it's deeds far and wide, as well as claiming the Thrones of Ascension. In order to do so, your god or prophet must be on that tile to claim it . Thrones will often be heavily guarded by either a large number of units, or a small number of very powerful units capable of wiping entire armies out by themselves... often a single unit with incredible power. By claiming a throne, its abilities can aid you, and/or cause a global enchantment to occur.
The ways of victory are either to: Claim all the thrones of ascension, Spread your dominion so that every province worships your god, wipe out every other god, or... Have the most thrones claimed when the cataclysm ends. If there are any thrones left, (in that event, the horrors called by the cataclysm will win the game.)
All of this, and I haven't really gotten into any of the deeper details, as others have pointed out, there's an insurmountable amount of content and depth this game has to offer... Mercenaries for example, can be hired on any tile you own in your province, providing you're the highest bidder of said mercenary during that month. They'll be in your service for 3 months after, before returning to being able to be purchased to the highest bidder, and like everything else in the game... The mercenaries have depth as well, Each mercenary unit is an actual unit, that can lose members of its squad, and need to recruit more, accrue permanent afflictions, and even die. If a mercenary unit is wiped out, it can't be bought. I've run out of space to write, so I'll leave you with this: This is a must play title if you like strategy games. The soundtrack is awesome as well, and I implore you to give it a chance. There's so much depth that I can't go into detail here because of the word count, and others probably explain it better anyways. Check it out, You won't regret it.

Peggle is a casual puzzle video game developed by Sukhbir Sidhu and Brian Rothstein of PopCap Games. Initially released for Microsoft Windows and Mac OS X systems in 2007, it has since had versions released for Xbox Live Arcade, PlayStation Network, the Nintendo DS (with the help of Q Entertainment), Windows Mobile, iOS, Zeebo and Android; the game has also been ported as a Java application, and an extended minigame incorporated into the massively multiplayer online game World of Warcraft. A sequel was released in September 2008, titled Peggle Nights.
Inspired by pachinko and bagatelle, each level of Peggle challenges the player to shoot a limited supply of balls at a field of colored pegs to clear out specifically marked pegs while attempting to achieve a high score through skilled shot planning. Special powers associated with a number of cartoon "Peggle Masters" can be activated to aid the player in this task. Peggle initially sold slowly but was boosted by the inclusion of a specially designed demonstration in Valve's The Orange Box, and has since enjoyed over 50 million downloads from the Internet. Both its release on Xbox Live Arcade and the iPhone OS have enjoyed similar success. PopCap, now a subsidiary of Electronic Arts, have announced a Peggle 2 at the E3 2013 convention.

If you have ever found yourself going through the whole Silent Hill or Fatal Frame walkthrough on Youtube to get the story because you can't tolerate jump scare or can't invest time to play it yourself, then this game is for you.
If you have ever found yourself digging the internet to search for background story and theories about Silent HIll, then this game is absolutely for you.
The game might be difficult at first and the player might cluelessly fumble a lot. But once you figure out how the system works, then it's quite easy to finish to the point that it turns into a routine. The game is all about survival. Your food is limited. Your weapon is limited. Your time and energy is limited. You have to think economically and plan ahead. And you have to take Lone Survivor's mental health into account too. You can choose whether you will sneak your way around or blast your way through with your gun, or whether you will trade your health for more energy to run. But whatever you choose, you will face the consequence.
The storyline is quite linear and short; you can finish this game in about 3-4 hours. But there's multiple endings which allow you to explore the story deeper. And personally I consider the beauty of this game is at its story: it doesn't actually tell you, even at the ending scene, what had happened and leaves the conclusion open to your speculation. This unfinished story gives incentive to play the game again and see it from the new perspective. Some dialogues and visual cues will make more sense after you finish your first run and form a theory in your head.
Another beauty of Lone survivor is the sound and music. This game should be play with headphone. The sound alone can make you feel creepy. The game will ask you to immerse yourself in by turning off the light and putting on your headphone. Just do it.
In short, I highly recommend Lone Survivor for those who is looking for a good survival horror, and those who loves to solve the puzzle behind the story.

I've seen The Moon Sliver compared to Dear Esther, and while it's not quite in that company, for reasons we'll get to later, it's not a bad explanation of what the game is. An interactive narrative, a stroll-em-up, a walking simulator, whatever, the point is that it's atmospheric and tells a more than competent story.
The Moon Sliver takes a novel approach to its story telling. You enter the world not knowing anything about what's going on, but it soon becomes apparent that you're on a small, doomed island and the population have disappeared. As you explore the handful of abandoned buildings you'll discover paraphernalia that you can click on, filling part of the screen with text. As you move around the room the text will fade being replaced with new text you've discovered. The story is deliberately vague, but by walking around the room in the right way you can at least piece together the order it's supposed to be read in.
Apart from one, arguably 2 puzzles, the only other gameplay mechanic is your torch, which has the battery life of a Game Gear. You have to keep charging it at one of the outlets otherwise it will flicker and die. You need the torch to see where you're going, and yes, the repeated need to charge it does its job of adding tension, but it feels a little cheap.
Graphics don't make a game, or they shouldn't, but there's no denying they can help. The Moon Sliver isn't an expensive game, it wasn't made by a big team, so that it isn't jaw dropping is both understandable and forgivable, but it is to its detriment. The game looks desolate, as it's supposed to, but not always in a good way. Buildings look simplistic, the barren plains a little too barren, and interiors are almost completely empty. There’s little in the way of texture work, the same features are repeated, and environmental effects are limited. Dear Esther worked largely because it looked cold, empty and uninhabited, the evocative moments punched harder because they looked so picturesque. It may be unfair to compare to two, but Dear Esther is indicative of where The Moon Sliver doesn’t work, it doesn’t convince you of its world, it doesn’t take you there.
Still though it does tell a good story, and despite all the odds it The Moon Sliver does get tense. The uncertainty and the change of environment, it works, and it’s all set up by the narrative. The music doesn’t quite flow as smoothly as it should, you can hear the moment it clicks back to the start, but it’s tonally perfect, foreboding. The Moon Sliver is worth your time, and it’s cheap enough that it’s probably worth the gamble if you fancy a narrative experience. You do get the feeling that if the developer (David Szymanski) took another stab at this in another couple of years (or his previous game, the surprising and dark Fingerbones) they’d see a huge improvement, but what’s there is still a game that stayed in my thoughts for a few days

I got into this game right away.  It seemed pretty cool at the start.
I had dreams of playing through with all 4 characters.  Then buying two DLC to get two more.  I have played way too many hours of Borderlands 1 & 2 that I was confident I was making the right choice to play this one.
Now, I'm not so sure.   It just seems that there are a lot more opportunities to die in this one.   I don't mean getting killed by the opponents...that's "OK".  It's getting killed because you fell or jumped wrong that bothers me.   It really sucks the fun out of it.
Pros:
- It's Borderlands!  IF you have played the others, you know how to play this.
- They introduced the oxygen limit.  Not a biggy, but it does give you some extra incentive to move through an area.
Cons:
- They have made this a 3D platform game.   There are too many timed missions (side missions, thank goodness)  But, other missions require timing jumps and such.   Fail and die.  Yes, there are LOTS of them in the OTHER games, but at least you don't die if you fail.
- Timing is WAY too critical.  The first time I got the Stingray I thought it would be great to jump.   But, it's almost worse than the moon buggy.  I died countless times trying to jump a gap to get to Dave.
- Navigation is poor.  I thought it was very neat when I got to Concordia and they displayed some waypoints to show you how to get to the roof;  later in the giant spaceship you end up going "off the map" to get to where you need to.   And you have to repeat the process several times.  Sometimes it was not clear that you had to go north to go south!
- Voices on the characters were VERY hard to understand.   I turned the music way low so I could hear the characters, but finally had to turn on the subtitles to figure out what they were saying.
- I ended up dying a LOT.  Probably about 100 times more than I did in the other Borderlands.  It's way too easy to jump a bit too far and plummet to your death - especially INSIDE the spaceship.
- I spend too much time going to the web trying to figure out how to get to the next part of a mission.  I should be playing, instead.
- They kept the same "Badass" rep from Borderlands 2.  Sure, you can turn it off, but then it's off for ALL of your characters.  I really like the way Borderlands 1 did it;  the more you used a particular weapon type the better THAT character got with that type of weapon.  Made a lot more sense.
Still, after getting through some of the ridiculous jumping and timing missions (YES, they ARE optional missions for the most part) I have enjoyed playing the game again.   Sort of a half-hearted recommendation, I guess.   But, I'm too much of a diehard fan to let dying bother me.
Now, after playing even more, it's just not as fun as the first 2.   Changing my mind again as I just want it to end.   The others I wanted to keep going!

So I'll be honest.  I've played a few walking exploration games, and they mostly seem to have one thing in common that I can't stand:  slow walking speeds.  Playing Dear Esther, I felt like I was trudging along in concrete shoes, thinking, "Yes, your landscape is fabulously beautiful, it's very atmospheric, but if I have to stare at one more lovingly hancrafted path for the next hour on the way to the next bit of plot, I may scream."  Basically, I usually feel the slow walking speeds are an artifcial way of drawing out the plot to make us feel like the playtime justifies the price, when the truth is...I honestly don't care how long or short one of these games turns out to be.  I LIKE plot.  I also enjoy short stories as much as ten-book epics.  As long as the story is good, I'm happy to pay for it.
The Moon Sliver, thank goodness, doesn't suffer from this problem.  You're not zipping along at mach speed, but "trudging" hasn't replaced "level grinding," either.  The landscape is stark, but that fits perfectly with the plot as you uncover it.  The story itself is fairly minimalist, but it's easy to piece together, and you're able to extrapolate large swaths of background from the hints it gives you.  Yes, it's short--I completed it in an hour, which is what the dev tells you to set aside time for--but looking at the screenshots on the community page, I see I still managed to miss things.  And it's nicely creepy without relying on gore or an endless string of jump-scares.
Overall, if you're looking for a good, interactive short story that won't leave you feeling like you're at the mercy of a narcissistic modeler...I totally recommend The Moon Sliver.

Atmospheric horror is one of my favourite genres in games. There is just something exciting about being scared without knowing exactly what it is that's scaring you. This game does a fantastic job of that, especially towards the end. Gameplay is simple - you move around, you have a flashlight, and you can interact with certain objects to try to piece together the story behind this strange island. It reminds me a lot of realMyst in that sense. The music and sound effects also add to the environment and build up the suspense well.
All that said, there are a few issues that I have with this game. Firstly, the puzzles are not difficult (which is okay in some contexts, but in a game where the only challenge is solving puzzles, there should at least be some challenge involved). Secondly, there are several misspellings throughout the game (again, this is something that I can normally overlook, but in a game where the only storyline comes from on-screen text pop-ups, it detracts from the overall experience). Lastly - and I'm going to attempt to avoid spoilers here, but it may be wise to skip this point if you've not yet played the game - it would be nice if the text pop-ups only popped up once after they've been triggered,
.
Overall, I highly enjoyed this game, even though it only took about 40 minutes to complete. Despite its length, it manages to create a dense, tense environment for the player, and the ending was very satisfying - gave me chills! I would recommend this game, and give it an 8.5/10.

By far this is one of the best Total War games to date.
What is Total War? Total War is a game where you pick a kingdom to dominate the world with. On the campaign map you will move your agents, and armies, and build upgrades to cities. When two armies meet you will go into a battlefield with thousands of soldiers fighting each other at the same time in an RTS battle.
This game is severely tactics based, so if you aren't good at micromanaging you are going to have a tough time. People with better strategies can win battles that were severely in the opponents favor.
As the game progresses you build your own story. You might raise a huge army to go destroy your enemies in a fit of rage for them killing your favorite general. Or ally with the kingdoms around you and double-team your enemies.
The general's in the game are a part of your royal family. As time progresses, your family will expand and each of these new children will grow up and become generals that you can have govern a town or be at the head of an army.
In the game there are also smaller things that add on to the game such as Crusades, Jihads, the discovery of gunpowder, the discovery of the americas, the mongols, and so on. Those things make the world feel fleshed out and make it feel alive.
Along with diplomacy is The Pope. Now, the pope sort of plays favorites, if you are friends with the papal states and another catholic kingdom declares war on you, the pope may excommunicate them from the catholic church, allowing a crusade to be called against them. When the crusade is called against them, all of Christendom will declare war on said faction and march their armies against them.
Now on to the pros and cons of the game
PROS:
- A large amount of factions with their own culture, units. advisors, and strengths
- Detailed Diplomacy
- Rebellions
- Large Strategic battles
- Jihads
- Catholic church and the pope
- Crusades and world events
- Long Campaign
- Family Trees
- Upgrading Cities
- Personal Stories
- Active modding community
- Multiplayer
- Not many bugs or crashes
CONS:
- Old game, poor graphics
- Animations are wierd sometimes
- Broken tutorial
- Co-op campaigns are done poorly
Overall this game gets a 10/10, Legendary
If you have never played a Total War game before, start with either Medieval 2 or Shogun 2

Update: While the developers decided to stay silent with the crashing issues, AMD has since rolled out a fix, and the crashing issues have been resolved *on my end*. That is to say, while my issues are gone, I'm aware that other people are still experiencing issues. That said, the fact the fix came at all, and that a lot more people are able to play this game now, indicates that I have a lessened reason not to recommend this game now. So I'd say it's worth picking up. You still might run into issues, but I've read about various potential fixes around the web, and I'm sure on AMD's end there will be more concrete fixes should the need arise.
Note: If you do pick it up, do yourself a favor and get the FAR mod; it's a vast improvement over the default game.
Original review: I can't in good conscience recommend this game in its current state. I really, really want to give it a positive review, but I simply can't. When I purchased this game, I had an Nvidia card (1050ti), and it ran like a dream. I was easily getting 80-100 frames and had absolutely no issues. The parts of the game I got through were nothing short of fantastic, and were this story to stop there, this would be 100% a strong recommendation from me. However, I upgraded my graphics card mid-playthrough to an AMD model, and I have been unable to make any progress since then. I'm plagued with crashes and freezes, and there's no fix in sight. During the limited time I'm allowed to play, I also noticed I now am limited to 60 fps. This isn't a huge concern, but it seems weird to have that limitation imposed only after switching cards. The developer says they're aware of the issues the game has, but as of this review, there has been no patch or patch announcement. However, there is a DLC announcement. This shows the company's priorities, and it does not look good at all. It genuinely pains me to leave an overall negative review for this game because I can tell that I would otherwise enjoy every moment of it. But it's pretty clear that a lot of fixes need to roll out in order for this game to be in a playable state, so for now, I say pass on this game until there's confirmation from the developer that the game-breaking problems will be addressed.

Europa Universalis in space meets Total War in Space. Solid game with a great future.
Ambitious but certainly bare bones at launch. I still pumped 200+ hours into it at release despite it lacking some of the depth of Europa Universalis games by Paradox. It will grow immensely with time as Paradox is dogged in expanding their games after release for the better part of a decade in most cases. Many patches are free DLC that add content and new mechanics.
DLC expansions are likely to follow the Paradoxian model of four major expansions a year for at least six years. Each expansion having a free patch/update with it that is also basically a DLC as well. Not to mention several smaller DLC in-between major expansions that will add depth and fluff to the game throughout that six year time span.
All of the DLC, unlike a lot of other companies who merely go for add-on dlc campaigns that do nothing for the grand/main campaign, these expansions and minor DLC will all expand the base game into ultimately the best space strategy game ever made. Albeit at a hefty price for some.
Stellaris like anything on the Clausewitz engine is extremely moddable. And not just with the sheer of amount of mods you can download easily from other players on Steam that add great breadth to the game. You can also easily tweak just about anything you do not like in the game yourself without a lot of scripting or modding knowledge by digging around in the game files with notepad and change whatever irritates you.
Though I highly recommend notepad++ (free program) to do the above with more precision. Also reading a few tutorials on modding the game would not hurt and there are plenty online.
This aspect of the game is really what sets Stellaris apart from most other space games. Total conversion mods have already seen this game turned into a Star Trek game and a Star Wars game as just two examples, both still actively being developed.
The amount of things you can add and change in the game with some basic scripting knowledge is almost limitless. Even if Paradox stopped making new content for the game players can and will easily match DLC-grade mods for this game in new and improved content as time rolls on. No other space game has that.

Magicite is a fun little game provided you play it with other friends. There's nothing wrong with it if you go solo, it just raises the difficulty and lowers the hilarious fun factor. As advertised it’s a rogue-like with short, procedurally generated levels that includes a good bit of risk-reward gameplay. The game loses several points in my book however for its crafting system and control scheme.
The craft system is content to let players stumble about, guessing at what they need to do to make something until they get fed up and go to the wiki for recipes. Even something as simple as Terraria's crafting system, giving you a list on the side of everything you can make with what is in your inventory would go a long way. Any game that all but requires external resources to play is docked a point.
The controls are fine and responsive but out of place. A and D move you left and right, W interacts with things but Q and E are short dashes. Its basically imposable to press both D and E to do a right dash while continuing to move (and it’s a twitchy game so if you aren’t still moving after a dash its not often useful) therefore dashes only get used in non combat situations like avoiding static environmental damage. Also, your leveling abilities are tied to Z X C V by default which makes it equally impossible to press the Z triple jump ability while moving left. Controller support would have made the game much easier to play.
Despite all that, we still had a blast. You will die a lot learning the game but if you have a buddy with you, they can revive you when you do, drastically extending the lifetime of each play through.
7/10 Certainly recommended at <$10

Every iteration of dominions has added subtle but significant improvements, and dominions 5 is no exception.
The changes to the battle system make it so that it's significantly harder to get cheesy tactics to work.  This also has the side effect of making the AI a little more competitive.  A single shielded infantry won't draw all arrow fire, and units guarding commanders can't manipulate control of the battle as easily.  Cavalry units seem pretty useful again.  The map movement changes are a little confusing to understand at times, but seems like it will make raiding more fun and effective, and no longer restricted to flying units.  I also think the changes to commander recruitment makes a lot of sense;  it's no longer quite as clear that forts should do nothing but infinitely produce mages.  The new blessing setup opens up a whole host of new strategic options.  Couple that with all the nations and units available, there's a ridiculous amount of replayability in this game.
No other fantasy 4x comes close to touching this game, especially for multiplayer.  I will concede that the in-game multiplayer support is comparatively minimal.  However, the PBEM server solves this issue thanks to the tremendous effort of llamabeast. I also want to recognize Lars for the wonderful work on the mod inspector utility.

Similar to other games I play, the difficulty gets increasingly more and more difficult as your team progresses through the challenges. In this case, the game becomes overly complicated and overly frustrating. Peggle is a casual puzzle video game developed by Sukhbir Sidhu and Brian Rothstein of PopCap Games. Initially released for Microsoft Windows and Mac OS X systems in 2007, it has since had versions released for Xbox Live Arcade, PlayStation Network, the Nintendo DS (with the help of Q Entertainment), Windows Mobile, iOS, Zeebo and Android; the game has also been ported as a Java application, and an extended minigame incorporated into the massively multiplayer online game World of Warcraft. A sequel was released in September 2008, titled Peggle Nights.
Inspired by pachinko and bagatelle, each level of Peggle challenges the player to shoot a limited supply of balls at a field of colored pegs to clear out specifically marked pegs while attempting to achieve a high score through skilled shot planning. Special powers associated with a number of cartoon "Peggle Masters" can be activated to aid the player in this task. Peggle initially sold slowly but was boosted by the inclusion of a specially designed demonstration in Valve's The Orange Box, and has since enjoyed over 50 million downloads from the Internet. Both its release on Xbox Live Arcade and the iPhone OS have enjoyed similar success. PopCap, now a subsidiary of Electronic Arts, have announced a Peggle 2 at the E3 2013 convention.

Peggle is an epic pinball game that manages to be both vastly amusing and immensely frustrating.
The point of the game is to eliminate the orange pegs to clear the stage and move onto the next. Blue pegs become collateral damage (or annoying obstacles) in this quest while green pegs release the special powers of your chosen "teacher."
With a new map loading every time you reload (or fail and must retry) the level, there's endless possibilities for replay. However, that also means that some maps may be easier or more difficult than others, depending on the placement of the orange, blue, and green pegs. In some cases, this meant for me that I had to replay the same level several times to gain a map where I could beat the stage.
The game also comes with several other ways to play besides the 55 level adventure mode: Quick Level, Duel, and Challenge, that are fairly self-explanatory. Quick Level allows you to select any level you've already beaten and unlocked in the adventure mode, with your choice of any of the teachers and superpowers that you've already unlocked. Duel allows you to challenge someone else (friend or an AI) to a level and compete scores, and challenge gives you access to 75 new "challenge" levels beyond the adventure mode.
There aren't any achievements to unlock, however, leaving you to compete solely against yourself to see how many points you can get per level/stage (unless you utilize the duel mode).  The music isn't particularly exciting, but it's also not entirely distracting, either.
Overall, for $4.99, it's not a bad way to kill some time and I don't regret playing (or buying) it.

Where do I start? This game is extremely frustrating to get the hang of. Unless you are a god, you probably can't beat it the first time you play. It took me 42 attempts to beat all six floors and Mom for the first time.

The Binding of Isaac is not, and I repeat, NOT, a bad game. As much as it is frustrating, it is really addictive. I thoroughly recommend this to fans of dungeon-styled and bullet hell games. Despite Isaac's innocent look (which he kinda is...look at those big crying eyes!), the style of enemies, rooms and pickups can be incredibly morbid and disturbing. The cries of Mulligans and the appearance of Hives are incredibly distressing, adding to the games overall atmosphere. Nonetheless this really adds charm to the game as a whole. Bear in mind this is coming from the creators of Super Meat Boy, so expect some blood along the way. But what's fun is you never know what to expect. All of the dungeon floor layouts are randomly generated everytime you start a game and aside from Mom being the last boss in the Depths, you never know what boss you will get upon entering its room. There are set bosses for every floor type and the game will randomly select one of these for you to battle. There is a sense of mystery about this game, mainly regarding the bosses, items you can find and what each pill does in every run.
Now stop reading this and go buy The Binding of Isaac!!

NOTE: This is based on SINGLE-PLAYER ONLY, I did NOT play Co-op or MP, which apparently has some problems.
Ghost Recon: Future Soldier (GRFS for short from now on) is a continuation of the "Ghost Recon" super special operations that existed long before COD Ghosts came along. There are no "waves" of baddies coming at you, no cinematic mow-downs, no angst-driven baddie that always got away. Instead, you are the the elite of the elite (cliche, I know), a special cadre of "operators", augmented with the best technology available, from CrossCom that lets you easily coordinate fire among your teammates, sync shoot that lets you designate targets for simultaneous extermination, optical camo that makes you nearly invisible... if you don't move very fast, sensor ball that picks up baddies in the area... X-ray viewer mode that picks up metal in ANY condition, even blinding sandstorm, as well as aerial and ground drones. And at the finale, you'll get access to Warhound... a mobile fire support platform that has missiles and mortars you can call in. Imagine the stealth kills you can do with the active camo... if you don't want to shoot them in the head.
Obviously there's always bazillion bad guys between you and your objective. And with suppressed weapons taking them out quietly is always an option... or you can go loud and just go guns blazing, but make use of cover or your teammates may not save you in time. At other times you can shoot through enemies cover, and that really makes you feel powerful.
The weapons can all be customized and there are a lot of changes possible, muzzle can be changed to different flash supressor or sound supressors. Sights can be changed from iron sight to red dot scope to 4x tactical scope and more. Magazine can be single, extended, double, or even loaded with armor piercing ammo. And so on. Every weapon is customizable, with parts that you can unlock through playing and accomplishing missions and challenges (i.e. make X kills with weapon Y, or such).
There are multiple levels of difficulty and let's just say, this game REALLY punishes you for tactical mistakes, i.e. exposing yourself when you shouldn't, picking the wrong targets, fail to flank, and so on. Though at easy levels you'll have a chance to recover, albeit unlock things much slower as well.
The graphics are very nice for a shooter, everything looks proper as they are. Jungle looks like jungle, village looks like village, and desert looks like desert. And you get to enjoy watching the operators move, crawl, lean against cover, and so on wit the third-person view, with seamless first-person if you go to scope mode.
The game is an Ubisoft product so Uplay must be installed and game activated through Uplay, but it's not overly tedious. However, it's rather annoying to have to deal with TWO platforms instead of just one.
All in all, as a shooter this game really makes you appreciate what a futuristic soldier will be like, without getting into power armor, exoskeleton, and jump gear of the further future. We have the tech to make this now... or at least in a few years, and we'll need them to solve problems developing around the world.
And yes, I am recommending this game. But remember, I only care about the single player game. And it works fine.

I just LOVE retro games, even though I didn't exist in the 80's or even the 90's. And you don't see tweens who would rather play Centipede than Call of Duty enough these days. (Maybe only where I live.) Anyways, the simplistic fun of those games just tugs at my heartstring. Everything from Coleco-vision to the Nintendo 64 I love. (And I don't think E.T. for the Atari 2600 is that bad either.) Well, I shouldn't say EVERY GAME or EVERY SYSTEM. (shudders at the thought of the Philips CD-i) But, I bet you get the picture. I was looking in the Google Play store on my tablet, searching "What other users installed" for Minecraft Pocket Edition. I scrolled WAY down until my eyes caught the glimpse of a simple 8-bit figure wearing a green shirt and holding a stick. I decided to check it out. Now what I DON'T like is a classic game ripoff. But I can't find a game in the back of my head that is almost exactly the same as the game Delver. So, I decided to buy it, hoping my money didn't go to waste. The description of the game is definatly true to its word, and I enjoyed it. Sure, there were a couple bugs in the game, and the controls were kind of awkward, I really love the graphics, the concept and, overall, the entire game. A while after that, I got Steam. When I discovered Delver was also on Steam, I couldn't be more excited. The controls were MUCH better than the version I had on my tablet. I just couldn't wait for the next updates.
I've read some of the negative reviews on Steam, some of them complain that there is little story to this game. I could care less about a story than those guys. I would rather just play the game and explore a dangerous dungeon in which I would probably die a horrible death in order to get a useless item because "what the heck," than sit through endless cutscenes or do a lot of reading. The leveling up system is both very simplistic, but very effective and game-changing at the same time. The music is AWESOME! I could listen to the game's tracks all day. Getting to the Orb, the music is somewhat calm but suspensful and adventurous at the same time. When you go back to the surface, though, the music immediatly switches to all out frightening and suspensful, raising your stress meter. The abundant variety of weapons, armor, wands and the ability to hold something on your left hand is remarkable and you can't help but to be very stingy about the items you have in your inventory. You never know what the potions would do in each game, and which ones to drink or not. But as long as you know which potion is which in the earliest floors, The relevently small inventory space show that there is not a lot to spare and you need to be very conservative, in which I like. The easier reach to the Orb will make you feel that this game is to easy and you become cocky. But once you get the Orb, you realize that Delver's adventure is not yet over. You still need to escape to the surface. That's when all heck breaks lose. Enemies start to respawn, not to metion those annoying skeleton mages whose magic cooldown seems like a half a second. The difficulty gets much harder than ever before, and you have a very long way to go before you get to the top. The entire thrill and the adventure of the game captures my heart.
There are not many things for me to wish anymore about this game. Although, a few things doesn't mean anything at all, despite how amazing I believe this game is. Every once in a blue moon, the rest of the dungeon becomes impossible to progress and continue, which is very dissapointing the moment you discover it. On your journey to the Yithidian Orb, I noticed that enemies don't respawn. I would like the developers to add respawning to the first half of the game to make it a little harder, but not too hard though. When you get to the boss, I would like the boss fight to be nessecary to get the Orb. Plus, the boss fight is insignificant and easy. All you need wolf down an arcane and iron skin potion and you practically won the fight. I've also noticed a pattern that some of the rooms are exactly the same in other runs, and that more variety of rooms and maps should be added. Bigger and more floors would be nice, too. Other than that, I have no other complaints.
I can't wait when Delver is going to be off Beta stage. I hope more people will come and play this wonderful game. Delver team, don't stop on improving the game. Please know that this game has HUGE potential and that there are fans, eager to play the game.

A very interesting blend of dungeon crawl and roguelike, this game has held my attention since I first purchased it.  It's a good addition to your library.  It's simple enough to start playing when you have limited time or attention, but robust enough that you don't feel like you're playing an indie throwaway.  Its randomized levels provide replay value and the ability to stockpile gold between runs allows for you to splurge on a run to give yourself a head start.  Also, the developer is very active.  It's obvious Delver is a labor of love.
Some tips, for new players:
1. Your HP refills when you level up, so stockpile your food in early levels.
2. If you inventory is getting full, leave a treasure trove of food and wands at the ladder down to the next floor.
3. Heavier armor slows you down, but not as much as you might think.
4. When leveling, I prioritize Health > Attack > Speed.  I've never put points into the stats that buff wands or archery.
5. Zombies and caterpillars (but not spiders, as of when I wrote this) will poison you with their attacks.

This game is obviously inspired by Silent Hill 2. But its unique in that while it will gross you out or scare you, it will make you question certain things. The reality of the game or your reality. It will make you wonder where those monsters come from, or what they actually are. Do you actually die when they get to you, or do you just retreat to your safe haven? Who are these people you see in your dreams?
You'll only *think* you know what really is at the end. In my case, I didn't do so well, but I thought you were supposed to shoot the ''zombie'' things. You actually aren't! At least... if you want the good ending...
So if you're curious about this little psychological horror title, give it a shot. You can tell the maker put a lot of thought into these pixels. It won't be scary like Outlast or Amnesia, but it WILL suck you in. And while its fairly creepy, you'll wonder if its not all just in his head. If you think I'm making this up, just read the official description.
Oh... and choices. This game is full of choices. They seem pretty much irrelevant at first, but... they'll have consequences. Good or bad, they'll influence the outcome at the end. And this game isn't long, but that's ok.

For so many years I have been looking for a game that I could immerse myself in. Something that would actually get me excited to play it when coming home from work. I've tried countless titles but in the end I would always lose the motivation to even bother playing or completing them. Finally the search is at an end.
I never played any other games from this series, but it looked really interesting to me for some weird reason. It wasn't the same type of garbage that has proliferated over the years. My cardinal rule is to never preorder games, no matter how good they might look in the trailers or advertisements. I broke that rule for this game though and I'm glad it turned out even better than I had imagined it would.
The story earns a solid 10 out of 10. I never thought I'd get so invested into the game's characters and lore but I couldn't even help myself from exploring side quests that before I would have waved off as tedious. This game has marevelous little details that I have never seen in a modern game. Everything is so well thought out. Not once did I think that something wasn't necessary. Everything felt like it was in the right place.
The gameplay is also a solid 10 out of 10. It feels so fluid! Combat is just so enjoyable in this game. There is a large variety of weapons and weapon types, and upgrades to make them more powerful. You're like a robotic acrobat that can destroy large swathes of machine lifeforms as if it were some sort of marvelous performance. I never got frustrated with any of the game's mechanics. Even the one that most people seem to be complaining about, but one that I'd rather not spoil for new players. It was a little janky at first to get used to, but it becomes a powerful and interesting tool. Combat aside everything else is just perfect in this game.
Now performance seems to be the largest issue when it comes to this game, judging from other reviews. I didn't suffer from any of those personally so that will not affect my review. It ran smooth from start to finish and I'm not gaming on a very powerful computer either.
Overall this game has given me a breath of fresh air from the stagnation and lack of creativity in games nowadays. I genuinely wanted to play it, and I truly enjoyed it. It's the best game I have ever played in my lifetime.
To Yoko Taro and all of the developers of this fantastic game: Thank you. Thank you so much. You made someone who had given up all hope of finding a good game feel happy again. <3

Update: While the developers decided to stay silent with the crashing issues, AMD has since rolled out a fix, and the crashing issues have been resolved *on my end*. That is to say, while my issues are gone, I'm aware that other people are still experiencing issues. That said, the fact the fix came at all, and that a lot more people are able to play this game now, indicates that I have a lessened reason not to recommend this game now. So I'd say it's worth picking up. You still might run into issues, but I've read about various potential fixes around the web, and I'm sure on AMD's end there will be more concrete fixes should the need arise.
Note: If you do pick it up, do yourself a favor and get the FAR mod; it's a vast improvement over the default game.
Original review: I can't in good conscience recommend this game in its current state. I really, really want to give it a positive review, but I simply can't. When I purchased this game, I had an Nvidia card (1050ti), and it ran like a dream. I was easily getting 80-100 frames and had absolutely no issues. The parts of the game I got through were nothing short of fantastic, and were this story to stop there, this would be 100% a strong recommendation from me. However, I upgraded my graphics card mid-playthrough to an AMD model, and I have been unable to make any progress since then. I'm plagued with crashes and freezes, and there's no fix in sight. During the limited time I'm allowed to play, I also noticed I now am limited to 60 fps. This isn't a huge concern, but it seems weird to have that limitation imposed only after switching cards. The developer says they're aware of the issues the game has, but as of this review, there has been no patch or patch announcement. However, there is a DLC announcement. This shows the company's priorities, and it does not look good at all. It genuinely pains me to leave an overall negative review for this game because I can tell that I would otherwise enjoy every moment of it. But it's pretty clear that a lot of fixes need to roll out in order for this game to be in a playable state, so for now, I say pass on this game until there's confirmation from the developer that the game-breaking problems will be addressed.

Fifteen hours in, I realize that I’m playing Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel as a flying Ghostbuster Captain America. My character class, Gladiator, grips a round shield in her left hand when her class ability is triggered, absorbing or reflecting damage before hurling the shield like a boomerang-frisbee. In my right hand is my favorite weapon, Miss Moxxi’s Vibra-Pulse, a laser gun that spits a wavy line of volts like Egon’s proton pack. And the shock damage it deals cascades like Diablo’s chain lightning spell, arcing between enemies in reach. As I’m electrocuting and shield-tossing, I’m floating through the air, kept aloft by the low gravity of Elpis, the Pre-Sequel’s lunar landscape.
Borderlands is best when its irreverence is reflected in its combat, when it’s layering the insanity of its characters atop weird weapons and enemies. Near-weightlessness is a terrific tweak to that formula; launching rockets at vulgar mutants and mechs its more playful when you (and your co-op teammates) are lilting softly through the air. I bounded my way through most of the game; tapping the jump button while airborne spends a single mid-air boost from your Oz kit (a new item that takes the place of relics), and hitting Ctrl sinks your character straight down to the surface.
The Oz kit is also what keeps you breathing while you’re out in the vacuum of space. I was worried that oxygen would turn out to be an annoying fuel gauge in The Pre-Sequel, but refills are plentiful and having to manage your air counter in the middle of a shootout discourages you from cowering behind cover. Oxygen also comes into play a little bit on offense: headshots knock out some enemies’ breathing masks, and some grenades sap oxygen. You’ll hear a new line or two when you shoot the air out of Borderlands’ bad guys, but basically it amounts to being another form of elemental damage.
The changes to movement bring novelty and a weird gracefulness to Borderlands’ combat. But otherwise, The Pre-Sequel feels like a super-sized mound of Borderlands 2 DLC. While the new setting, classes, and weapon types reinvigorate things a bit, The Pre-Sequel doesn’t deviate much from the feel and format of Borderlands 2. It’s fun, but it’s also exceptionally familiar.
I finished The Pre-Sequel wanting a greater variety of missions, especially missions that made creative use of the new movement mechanics, of which there are nearly none. Almost every story and side mission I completed followed the same structure: go to a location, press the use key on a computer console or character, and shoot some enemies along the way. Even quests that are thematically different, like delivering flowers to suitors for Nurse Nina (the stand-in for Dr. Zed), or exploring ice caves to place a mining drill, or retrieving a scientist’s lost teddy bear, feel like equivalent errands punctuated by similar firefights. My least favorite were missions where I had to scour a room for a hidden Echo device, about as fun as searching someone else’s room for a missing wallet. The Pre-Sequel would’ve benefited from a large-scale combat sequence or something like an escort-sniping mission.
The problem with mechanically simple missions is that their fun relies entirely on funny dialogue and interesting firefights, both of which are inconsistent throughout The Pre-Sequel. Combat is occasionally great—one of the first bosses pounces and floats between a bunch of indoor platforms, some of which are electrified. Chasing him without shocking yourself and fending off his airborne minions was frantic and tough.
The Pre-Sequel ends on a high point too. The last chapter mercilessly throws a variety of jumping, somersaulting, flying, cloaked, ranged, and melee aliens and soldiers at you alongside enemies that, similar to the Goliaths in BL2, enter a cocoon state and level up if you don’t kill them quickly enough. It’s a terrifically exhausting sequence that demands careful spending of abilities and the mid-air dash maneuver to dodge and reposition yourself for reloads. Most of the skirmishes at the end of the game had me cycling through all four of my weapons, throwing multiple grenades at a time and narrowly making it out alive. I wish more of The Pre-Sequel had put me in this kind of pure chaos that the last section of the game did.
New guns help mitigate these threats. Cryo weapons freeze enemies into solid blocks when their elemental effect triggers—I liked sniping jetpacking bandits into ice cubes to make them plummet back to earth. Better are the new lasers: wrangling a wavy line of energy in mid-air is like trying to spray someone with a firehose after leaping off a trampoline.
But broadly, that’s the extent of what’s new in The Pre-Sequel; there aren’t many other new weapon types or attributes to fill out the armory further. Having spent a hundred-plus hours with the series, everything else feels exceptionally templated. Enemies pour out of spawning points that are helpfully beside explosive barrels and sets of ammunition containers. I was starved for a mission that wasn’t a fetch quest, and though pieces of Elpis are gorgeous, the orbiting space station that you spend about half of the game on is a set of familiar, futuristic city interiors lined with unpopulated facades. Elpis is meant to be the Australia of Borderlands, and it’s a decent frontier, but the game as a whole feels underpopulated. There aren’t many NPCs that you can have meaningful reactions with.
I love the way that 2K Australia pokes some reverent fun at its homeland, though. The best dialogue in the game comes from the inappropriately cheerful citizens of Elpis, who casually shrug off the moon’s many dangers and drop exaggerated Australian slang. New characters—and cameos from old ones like Roland and Sir Hammerlock—miss more than they hit. Jack has some charming one-liners, but as The Pre-Sequel is primarily his backstory, he spends most of the game being kind and helpful—character development that came off as more off-putting than interesting to me.
Loot-wise, a new station, The Grinder, gives you something to do with unwanted rare guns. Three weapons of the same rarity can be loaded in and destroyed to spit out a weapon of higher rarity. When operating the machine, you can optionally spend moonstone, the resource used to upgrade ammo capacity, to create a “luneshine” weapon, which adds a bonus attribute. It’s a good addition to the game: I found myself using The Grinder a lot, and it spat out weapons that stuck with me for a few hours.
The Pre-Sequel is a happy to be Just Another Borderlands Game. I enjoyed it for that, but I also finished it thinking my time would’ve been better spent on one of the more original games that’ve released this year. I love seeing Borderlands embrace the FPS trend of unconventional movement. Apart from the low-gravity leaping, though, The Pre-Sequel doesn’t do much to freshen what we’ve been playing since 2012.

I cannot stress enough how much I love Stellaris. I've gotten about 7 hours of game play for every dollar I've put into the game. For someone that used to play Spore back in the day, this game is everything that Space Stage should've been. And for someone who's played plenty of 4X games, I think this one is my favorite. From colonization to empire and ship design to managing species, Stellaris really has a lot to offer. And with so many possibilities for empire builds and galaxy generation, you'll never have the same game twice.
Now, Stellaris isn't perfect; there's a steep learning curve, and issues with combat and war score have plagued the game from the beginning. There was a point after 1.6 was released when empires wouldn't declare war on each other and the AI would nonsensically and continuously terraform inhabited worlds. But the developers are generally quick to respond to issues and regularly introduce new content into the game. And there are plenty of mods in the workshop that add to the game experience if you get bored with the vanilla game.
Overall, Stellaris is extremely well done and I highly recommend it to anyone that loves space and 4X games.

The best games are those that are simple, and hex cells manages this while still presenting plenty of challenge. The format is similar to the classic Minesweeper, but no guessing is required and as you advance additional markings come into play as well as the simple 'this many surrounding cells'. I did have to search online to clarify the rules at one point as it was unclear whether the '-x-' marking meant they cannot touch each other at all or simply that they aren't all in a block, and I was easily able to find clarification on the forums (it's the latter). It is a short game, I consider myself very good at these sorts of puzzles and although steam says I took 1.8 hours I know some of that was time I left the game open while doing other things, I'd estimate the actual time to be 1.5 hours at most, but I think the average player would get more out of this game.
The only flaw is that there are no procedurally generated puzzles however this is included in one of the sequels and at the low price of the game that seems fair. The interface is simplistic in a very good way and the game feels very well polished for the low price. Time to start the second level pack! (Hexcells Plus)

Hexcells is the first entry of a trio of puzzle games by Matthew Brown, a game all about using logic and nothing else to solve a collection of puzzles. I'm not always one for puzzle games but did I enjoy this one? This is what I think of Hexcells.
Yes. Yes, I enjoyed playing this game very much. For such a simple concept it really is engaging, and playing this set of puzzles through after so long playing the random puzzles on Hexcells Infinite showcased exactly how much better and faster I've gotten at solving these than when I last played some years ago. I don't play a lot of puzzle style games but this series is definitely a favourite of mine. It's just so relaxing.
The whole point of the game is running through a series of levels that increasingly get harder as you go on. The objective is simple; colour in certain hexes and delete others in a Minesweeper-esque fashion but without the guesswork...most of the time. Fans will lecture you that logic is all that is required but even now I occasionally had to take a leap of faith on a couple harder levels. I guess I just suck. I'm ok with that.
As you move through the game it throws more rules at you as the puzzles get bigger. You start with hexes with a number in them that indicate how many hexes surround it. That turns into outside numbers noting the number in a certain column, as well as numbers in brackets indicating hexes are chained together or are separate in the same row or around a certain hex. It is great progression, and with such wonderful hand-crafted levels, it is a joy to play through.
It's a short game though. It could have done with more levels, and you can say this of any of this series, apart from Hexcells Infinite with its random generator providing endless levels. I think it's intended to be a short and sweet type of experience but I thought it worth mentioning. Also, as I said, a couple of times I had to guess but that might just mean I'm not smart enough. Take that as you will.
Overall, this is the start of a great series. I wasn't overly smitten with SquareCells and have yet to try CrossCells and I was eager to try Hexcells again after finding I preferred this style to SquareCells. It certainly didn't disappoint. Although short, It was a great time even if you are used to Infinite's random levels. Well worth a purchase simply to run through the excellent levels. Get the whole series in the Logic Puzzle Pack bundle, should be pretty cheap and if you are in to a chilled, relaxing experience this is the series for you.

Yes, Peggle came out 7 years ago. And I played the demo (years ago), and it never really appealed to me. But since I picked it up in the recent Humble Bundle weekly sale featuring PopCap Games, and since people have been talking about the upcoming release of Peggle 2, I thought I've give this old favorite another try…

I suppose the most interesting personal observation I made while playing this was that I noticed how annoyed I always felt upon hitting the final orange peg and the ball starts bouncing around wildly while the "Ode to Joy" fanfare plays—something that I've heard many people report enjoying. So it's hard for me to understand how some people seem so excited by the reported new feature in the upcoming Peggle 2, which each "Peggle Master" will have their own, unique fanfare…

The Moon Sliver was the best $3 dollars I have spent. But I wish I didn't have to spend $3.
The story was simple and light, fitting perfectly in the small span of playtime forone round, without being too much to understand. Each character was explained quickly, given their own personallity, without spending too much time on this.
The atmosphere that this game created was pretty immsersive, and managed to outdo what many AAA developers attempt, using 12 times less resources.
I was especially impressed with how the developer managed to do so much with so little. While not quite as grabbing as many other similar games, The Moon Sliver managed to really get me into things in a matter of thirty minutes, while all the developer had was Unity. For this, I had to give this game a thumbs up.
However, going back to what I said at the start, I wish I didn't have to pay $3 dollars for this game. With it only taking me about 30-45 minutes to finish the game, the experience was over, and I was 3 bucks in the hole. Not that the game felt rushed or unfinished (it does an amazing job of starting this up, then wrapping them up). Its just that, unless you are crazy into this game, and want to play it again, or take a very long time to examine every piece of evidence you can, you might be upset by your loss of money.
That said, this game definantly was really fun, and mostly made up for its short playtime with alot of content and atmosphere. So I say, if you have the money, and like this time of game (more about narrative or the story), absolutely go for it.

Wildstar is really, really good fun.
Here's a short review with a few details.
It's not an in-depth review, because that'd take time away from playing Wildstar.
I've made 2 characters (limit on Free Account) so far, 1 from each Faction in the game, so i could try & get a broad spread of the storyline's & lore.
My favorite so far is my Engineer, DPS or Tank character (depends on your Gear stat's) that also has Bot's scuttling around shooting or shielding.
Wildstar is a mmorpg & uses a lot of the same mechanics (i think that's the right word? EDIT?) as WoW, but there are a few cool difference's other than Sci-Fi vs. Fantasy.
The combat is Skill-Bar based like in most mmo's, except in Wildstar every skill has what they call a telegraph, which is like an Area of Attack highlight. You need to move your character a lot. You move to make sure your telegraph is on your enemy so the attack hit's, & you need to move out of enemy telegraphs to avoid damage from their attacks.
The same applies to healing. You need to make sure that your telegraph for your healing skills is covering the player-characters you are trying to heal.
You can't just Tab target & press a skill hot-key & expect the skill to hit the target. You need to move your character, so that the telegraph is within range of the target.
As far as Free-2-Play vs. Pay-2-Win goes, from what i can tell the in-game store only has items that are either cosmetic, fancy skin's of items you can earn in-game, or Boost's that allow faster Leveling, Crafting, etc.
It seems to me that most of the Store items can be bought with the in-game currency (but i could be wrong) instead of real $'s, although you may have to grind for quite a while to be able to afford some of the fancier stuff.
Also, you get a gift everyday that you log-in. I got a Spacefaring Dagun (Wolf with a Astronaut Helmet) Pet on Day10, & the item giveaway callender isn't re-set if you miss a day like in a lot of other mmo's.
I stated playing this a few days after it came out on Steam, & since then i've missed 2 days due to commitments in-real-life. Considering it's a FREE game u may as well give it a try. I think the DL was 14GB's for those watching bandwith.
Like i said at the start, really, really good fun.

In short, NBA2k17 is excellent from a gameplay standpoint. Pick a team and play with your friends and it's incredibly fun, as are most of the 2k games. Play on your own against the AI and it's incredibly fun. Play MyCareer and it's again just fun.
But there are a few issues. I mostly play MyCareer and MyLeague. There aren't really any specific issues to MyLeague that aren't also in MyCareer, so I'll only talk about the latter.
The biggest issue are the archetypes. I have no issue being limited in creating my player, after all it should still be realistic. That said what 2k did here isn't limiting, it's crippling. While the playing itself is fun, you won't create a superstar, like you did earlier in the series. You might be one, depending on how good you are at the game, but you could just choose a random role player and play just as good. If you only play myCareer it might not be apparent, but I have a higher rating than Patrick McCaw for example, but McCaw is clearly the better player, and it's not even close. I read that 2K is apparently tricking with their ratings in MyCareer, which to me seems to be the case.
I understand that they want to make their competitive scene more interesting, but I think this is the wrong way.
Another big problem is time. While it seems like they actually were able to cut loading times of games, the games feel a lot slower. What once was skippable pretty much immediately (timeouts and such) now takes forever. And while I appreciate the new style of the interviews, after the 10th time I just want to pick my answer and move on. Why do I have to watch myself walk out of the arena after every single game? Why do I have to watch myself walk at all outside of a game situation. I actually like the time managment and practice and all that, but just load. I don't want to wait ten seconds to walk out of my gym just so the game can THEN start to load.
I probably forgot some things already. I can only stress that despite all of this the game is really fun. But if 2K were to improve some of these issues the game could be amazing. Right now it isn't, and that's so disappointing. At least it looks like 2K got back on track again after the abysmall 2k16.

A massive step backward from 2k16 which was already a shaky game. Do Not play against the A.I. though, stick to pvp as it is much more balanced.
The game is designed to be challenging but it reaches a certain point (especially in MyCareer) when the game has to make you worse in order to keep up. Which is complete and utter ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. There were countless times where players I was defending literally glitched through me and made shots. I created a guy that had his shooting stats maxed out, I spent hours perfecting the timing on his shot. Yet, even if I played a game where all I took was wide-open shots, I would probably end up shooting 30-40% which is nonsense. The only time I felt my player shot a decent percentage we end up blowing out teams by 60 pts. so I turn the difficulty up hoping to balance it out. Wrong. My teammates who all have significantly lower shooting attributes shoot around 50-60% (with heavily contested shots) yet I can't make more than 2-3 shots in a row even if all of them were wide open.
The hit detection is absolute garbage. I've had some of my shots blocked only to look at the replay and see the guy who blocked me not even touch the ball. I watch as the ball just kinda glitchs through my hand as though the game was like: "Oh, hey you're about to make an easy layup? LOL I don't think so idiot!"
Trying to get good at this game while playing the A.I. is like trying to make free-throws in real life while an evil leprachaun makes fun of you and punches you in the♥♥♥♥♥♥everytime you're about to make one. It's beyond infuriating. Either the A.I. is really easy to handle or it just makes you look like you should've never played video games in the first place. There is no challenging in between where it's not infuriating but I still have to work for it. The worst part about the difficulty scaling is that once you reach a certain rating with your player you feel the need to bump up the difficulty a little, otherwise it gets too easy and the game isn't fun. So as your player gets better attribute ratings you bump the difficulty up a little so that you can still play well but also have to keep working for it. However, it reaches a point where it gets so difficult that you may as well just sit back and simulate the games (unless your some kind of nba 2k17 god) it reaches a point where the game is working so hard to beat you that it is nearly impossible to play well, regardless of your rating. I may end up with 26 pts. when it's all said and done, which is good, but I'll probably end up shooting 20% just to get there.
Shot timing is very finnicky, especailly on harder difficulties. Sometimes the shot meter even starts before you've caught the ball and you're stuck with a late release. Wouldn't it make more sense for the shot meter to start when, oh I don't know, you start shooting the actual ball!!!! I can't remember the number of times I wanted to shoot immediately off a pass  by holding down shoot only to see the shot meter is already past the threshold for a make before I even release the ball. It's completely counter-intuitive and frustrating. The best option is to wait until you've caught the ball and wait for a moment so that the pass catch animation can finish before you shoot. The only problem is it takes waaaaaay too long, so by the time you can actually make a shot, you sort of can't because the A.I. moves nearly perfect on defense (especially beyond pro difficulty). So, by the time you've gotten open, caught the ball, and are now ready to shoot, you have a defender in your face who will make you miss the shot anyway. Yet you can also watch your teammates make the same shots with no problem at all, as the A.I. gets a near perfect release just about every shot.
These seem like such minor problems that should have been fixed through beta testing, but, I would be surprised if they beta tested it at all. For now, I don't recommend this game until they figure out a way to fix all the shoddy mechanics. Stay away from MyCareer, as fun as it is in the beginning it quickly becomes infuriating. Play with teams in online pvp or manage a team in MyGM/Franchise and leave it at that. It's pretty much all the game is good for at the moment.

I have been playing the series for close to 15 years now, and it only keeps getting better.
Dominions is pretty much the Dwarf Fortress of 4x games. It is an extremely nuanced and detailed simulation that will require literal years to just sample what it has to offer, much less master it all. On the other hand, just as with Dwarf Fortress you can easily play it on a rather casual level if that is your preference. Unlike Dwarf Fortress, it is a game that shines in multiplayer, though single-player games are absolutely possible.
Most of the turn-based gameplay takes place either on the overhead strategic map, or studying (if not just enjoying) the animated battle replays. While the player has no direct control over troops during combat (something that actually adds to the gameplay in my opinion), the troops will attempt to follow pre-set orders issued prior to the engagement. This is an extremely crucial part of Dominions as a series, as building appropriate battle scripts can easily take longer than any other part of the game. For a lot of the fights this will not be necessary, and you can simply rely on basic orders, but taking on more dangerous armies will greatly benefit from customized orders.
There is an entire elaborate magic system in place (both to research, utilize during combat or for strategic benefits, and use for artifact creation), as well as a fully customizable character equipment system for your commanders. While you cannot equip general troops separately, there is a large collection of spells modifying things with individual to army-wide effects.
Frankly, the game is so complex that it would take days simply to describe all the potential it carries. The amount of customization assures that for a long time each game can be played completely different way.
$40 might seem like a lot, but the amount of content included easily matches games like Crusader Kings 2 or Europa Universalis IV with all the DLC Paradox sold separately, which really does make it a bargain. On top of that, you are getting Illwinter's outstanding post-release support (Dominions 4, a game released in 2013, still received a major update a few months back).
If you enjoy grand strategy games and never tried the Dominions series, you are missing out on one, if not the, best titles ever released, and certainly the most detailed one.

He started his campaign (that eventually carried his force across the empire, over the Silver Mountains to the dark lands beyond) with a legion of imperial cavalry and foot. Step by bloody step, Bas Tardo's Brigade carved a bloody swathe across the land in the name of their living god.
After each of his countless battles, he replenished his losses with foreign infantry, barbarian outriders, ogres, hill giants, deserter janissaries, conquered beastmen, crystal wizrds, witch doctors, undead thralls, griffons, fire lizards, and mercenaries of all kinds. He lost an eye and gained a limp. He contracted jungle rot and battle tremors; he went slightly mad; and in the end, after fording the Black River for a strike into a kingdom of heathens, he was afflicted by a wasting plague that would lay him low.
His army fought a series of desperate pitched battles near the enemy capital, culminating in a siege of the foreign king's fortess. After his loyal captains carried him forth (he had grown too weak to walk in his black plate armor) and seated him on his dread charger Skelgrenn, he led the charge that broke the enemy lines and won the day--and cemented his name in the annals of imperial military legend.
That night, Lord Bas Tardo died peacefully in his slumber, attended by a couple of camp hookers. RIP.

Though it's driven by logic, what I want to highlight is just how dreamily relaxing and casual this game can be.  You think, point, and click (left/right), and that's all.  I play to unwind at the end of the day; on a big TV, it's easily played lying on the couch (at a proper angle), and you may eventually be lulled to sleep.  The only downside to this approach is that the white screens are bright and need to be muted with a color-temperature app; SquareCells, one of the follow-ups, is not quite so good on the puzzle side but has the considerable advantage of a dark mode.
OK, in a bit more detail.  As you must know, this game is a series of well-crafted puzzles in a simple ruleset inspired by Minesweeper, where you get more information as you make correct deductions.  Much like Sudoku, it is an inherently incremental sort of puzzle game where you fill in the blanks by a series of inferences based on a few simple insights.  The challenge is in patiently looking around the board for the next opportunity.
On the one hand, I regard this type of puzzle as 'busywork'.  It doesn't really ask for creative insights or unusual maneuvers like some of my favorite puzzlers (Stephen's Sausage Roll, Snakebird, Cosmic Express).  On the other hand, it is satisfying and relaxing, and there is real artistry in the designs here and in the two sequels (which grow a bit more challenging).
