I'll start out by saying that while I AM giving this game a recommendation, I most certainly am NOT recommending it to anyone for the full retail price of two dollars and ninety-nine cents.  Even those of us who don't expect ten hours of gameplay per dollar we spend should probably wait for a sale, 'cause it's DANG SHORT.  I'm also not going to recommend it to anyone who doesn't enjoy READING, nor anyone who expects anything vaguely resembling ACTION.  Still here?  Okay, let's examine it a little closer then...

Despite being one of those people who very much believes in the notion of "experimental storytelling" in video games, I must say this one's pushing its luck a little.  A short story format may well have served the tale being told here better than a "game"; which, even by my own broad definition, this only BARELY qualifies as.  Gone Home, on the other hand, NEEDED to be a game, and would have made an appallingly♥♥♥♥♥♥"read" in and of itself...so why was this so?
Well, simply put, it was a game where you had to explore a defined area, discover clues as to what had happened there, and gradually piece the story together.  The Moon Sliver operates on much the same principle, EXCEPT...the area you explore is much, much smaller, and the vast majority of the "clues" are given not so much as real-time items which you can find and interpret the meaning of as you see fit, but rather as literary passages which represent memories of, I assume, the character you are playing.  In that sense, perhaps, it's also quite a bit like Dear Esther, but again...even THAT game was longer and arguably more substantial in the information which it ultimately delivers.

Which isn't to say that The Moon Sliver doesn't create an atmosphere, or is completely lacking in game "mechanics".  Quite to the contrary, it actually has one "mechanic" which was so prominent as to be almost obtrusive and annoying at times...which is to say, that while trying to keep one's flashlight fully charged was an essential part of the SUSPENSE of a game like Outlast, it's mostly just an irritation in this game. Especially when your primary light source starts flickering in the middle of a climactic, night-time wind-storm, amidst which you have to find your way to a specific location with ♥♥♥♥-all visibility.
In my opinion, the game would have been plenty atmospheric enough with a fully-functional flashlight throughout...but then again, after all the flak which the second Amnesia caught on account of its severely stripped-down "mechanics", one can't really blame designers for playing it safe and throwing one or two (however unnecessary) "gameplay" elements in there, especially at this juncture in time.

The Moon Sliver definitely tells an interesting story - though one which, I imagine, will only "blow the mind" of people who haven't read a great many horror and/or science-fiction short stories - and it tells its tale well enough, within the confines of how it chooses to do so.  It's only the chosen medium and the price-tag which I'm really querying, not the talent involved.  I definitely look forward to future games from the chap who made this, I just hope that he'll get more ambitious and more realistic about market values from here on in.  Imagine how many more people would give this a shot - and with a little luck, be pleasantly surprised! - if it were being given away for free or for something as negligible as, say, zero dollars and ninety-nine cents.
Wait for a sale, and enter with an open mind, and you just may get that small but pleasant surprise after all, in spite of all the reservations I've just expressed.  A very nice "demo", but I'm still reluctant to qualify it as a fully-fledged product/game.

A couple of years ago if I'd played The Moon Sliver I'd have praised the non-linear narrative and clever repurposing of the video game medium.  Now, I can't help but compare it to those who went before, and, in the context of the exceptional
, it's hard not to see The Moon Sliver as Dear Esther Lite.  It is shorter, it has less polished graphics, it has text overlays but no narration, and it has a story which, while it is definitely interesting, lacks the many layers of its predecessor.
Is it worth playing?  Certainly, especially at this price - for a couple of dollars you get what is by design a mysterious vignette that takes about an hour to play through, and also get to show your support for storytelling of this kind.
However if you go into it expecting the next great walk-'em-up you will find the lack of polish confronting and distracting.  The piece is certainly competent, but it is not exceptional.  The ambient sounds and music are apt, but fairly generic.  The story is told in location-triggered text overlays which sometimes overlap each other, making them hard to read.  The mechanic of the torch running out of battery and needing to be recharged periodically would work in a horror game like Slender, but in this context, where there is mood, definitely, but no danger, the torch recharging is a distraction from your progression, causing you to have to backtrack several times, which can break your immersion when this causes previous set text displays to reappear, this time in reverse.  Little details like this detract only very little from the story, but you will certainly notice them.  The Moon Sliver feels like someone's Game Design final project rather than a commercial release, although understand I mean that less as a criticism and more as a recognition that the game is endearing.  It's not overlong, it manages to avoid being very pretentious, it does what it sets out to do, and what it sets out to do is take an hour of your time and make you wonder what happened on this island.
Beyond the flashlight there are two aspects of the game I found a little weak.  One is that there is a hatch at one point, behind which is a lot of story, but which can only be opened by guessing the door code.  Unless I missed something
at no point do you learn the code, it is purely guesswork.  It's not hard to guess, but it feels odd to go to the effort of placing a keypad only to not give the player any way to know the key, and then place important story behind it.  The second is that in order to progress you need to 'wait until night', and even wandering around enjoying the atmosphere and the art, I had finished exploring every nook of the island long before night fell, and had to idle my game for about twenty minutes waiting for the next part.  This isn't great for immersion.
Why am I spending so long detailing minor gripes like this in a game that is both very short and which I have recommended?  Because if you know about these little things before you play, the story and the atmosphere of the game are such that you may still really enjoy your brief time on the island.  It is only if you expect a long, polished narrative experience that you might be disappointed.
For what it is - a short, intriguing, rudimentary, mysterious story-game - The Moon Sliver is charming and engaging, and deserves support.

Delver is a fantastic game of procedural dungeon crawling, satisfiying real time combat, and exploration. Delver contains smooth RPG-like combat, where by charging your attack makes it more likely to hit your target (guarenteeing a hit when fully charged); a mysterious setting of an anchient tower holding one of the greatest treasures known; and oogles of replay value.
Even though the game is currently in Early Access Beta, it feels well polished, and expertly crafted. Every update adds in more generation to every level in the game, and there are very few if any bugs to be found. The game has a very fair-unfair bipolar, in the early levels, the enemies are relatively easy to dispatch, but if they land a hit, it can take a sizable amount of health away; and towards the end, your going to run out of health a LOT.Delver is a relatively short game; you trek through 10 levels per playthrough of ever increasing difficulty, fight and defeat (as far as I am aware) a single boss, and make an excruciatingly hard, and harrowing journey back up to the surface from whence you came.
The final level is the MOST unfair and difficult level in the game, and is probably the one and only constant level throughout your journey, as it appears unchanged through each playthrough. It introduces several enemy types not seen before on any level, and ALL of them hit really, really hard. I have never successfully managed to beat the final boss, and have only made it to him twice.
All in all, it is very challenging, and you will die a LOT, but it never feels like you couldn't stop it from happening. Delver is an incredibly fun, semi-addicting, dungeon crawl with danger lurking around every corner, and an unfair boss level.

This game is the best Total War game in existence. This is by far my favourite. Not only are the vanilla and expansion campaigns a lot of fun, but the almost infinite fantastic mods adds the replayability of this game a thousand fold.
Pros
- Campaign experience is awesome. Lots of depth. Plenty to do. Complex enough that its not difficult to learn, but not easy to master either. It's so easy to get immersed into your kingdom and care about your subjucts. History is your oyster. You become what you want. You can be a benevolent king who's people adore, or a bloodthirsty tyrant that rules with an iron fist, a bumbling general that doesn't inspire his men at all, or the greatest commander alive who even peasants will fight to their death on his command.
- More campaign stuff. Cities are realistic in that people actually live there and can be murdered upon sacking the city or plague occurs. The buildings you construct will be present on the battle map. Manpower limitations and recruitment pools disable players from spamming 1 unit type. You have to fill your ranks with a variety of units or wait a very long time for your perfect army. Crusades and Jihads are heaps of fun.
- Battle pacing is perfect. The units don't kill each other in a matter of seconds with a bunch of fancy kill animations. They slug it out and get bloody. Everything depends on tactics. You don't just win because you bring lots of elite units. You have to outsmart your opponent or else your quality units won't count for much.
- Sieges. No Total War game has more epic sieges than this. Sending four thousand men to assault a citadel garrisoned by half that number will take you a long time to win and push your tactical skills to the limit. 3 layers of walls require you to constantly think about reserving your artillery or your rams. If you run out of ammo or your rams break or theres nobody left to pick up a ladder with 1 wall ring left to go - well you're screwed and you have to retreat. It's awesome. If you are forced to retreat and come back the next turn and they haven't repaired the walls it's all damaged in the exact same way you left it.
- The sound track is the best out of any Total War game
- MODS. Third age, Westeros, Call of Warhammer, Stainless Steel. Just to name a few.
Cons
- The AI is pretty stupid and passive. If you're new to the game you might have some difficulty at first but once you understand the AI thought pattern its very easy to outsmart even on the hardest difficulty.
- The game is full of exploits and bugs that were never patched out.
Overall I give this game 93/100. Which is pretty good considering I gave Warhammer 80/100. I'll still be playing Medieval 2 long after everyone forgets about Warhammer in a year or so.

Stellaris is your typical Paradox grand strategy game which is set in space. The early-game is fantastic and it gives me great pleasure to explore the universe and its anomalies, making first contact and react to events. Once I reach mid-game, the game grinds to a painful halt. Many of the features and functions of this game are undeveloped and sometimes not very well thought through, but, knowing Paradox, this is something they will work on with future DLCs. All in all, this is a good game with greater potential waiting to be unlocked.

I am not a picky gamer, If a game is fun, enjoyable and unique I will most likely enjoy it. What I hate seeing are games that do the same thing over and over again with very little in variation. That being said, I REALLY enjoyed stellaris and I regret having not bought it sooner. Whether you are new to 4X style strategy games or if youre a veteran Stellaris will really up the quality of what you get. So many of these types of games will constantly bombard you with new systems that make no sense or the same systems but put into weird designs. Stellaris takes an extremely complex and intricate system of menus, resources, commands, units, planets, bases, command, etc, etc, and blends them all together into an extremely user friendly and easy to learn UI. No fancy words that are specific to the game, nothing that isnt relatively self explanatory, You spend maybe an hour or two hours learning the ropes and then you play! Even during those learning moments, it isnt set up in a way thats boring. If you love strategy or 4X games this is a good buy. I for one very rarely buy into strategy games and I played 5 minutes of a friends copy, immediately stopped and bought the game myself.

Stellaris - There's something! I posted a boo-boo.
Since I boo-booed my original review (an accidental cut & paste – see my comment below), I will change my recommendation accordingly.
I am enjoying this game tremendously. Although this account only shows about 3hrs at the time of review, I have about 35Hrs on my Sons account.
Stellaris has multiple layers of interest running simultaneously. Here’s an interim review to keep you slightly informed.
SETUP
=====
Here’s the thing. Stellaris has this AMAZING pre-start setup sequence, in where you choose nearly every aspect of the gameplay except what color underwear you’re going to dirty the first time you get into combat. It seriously is that great. What you can’t change isn’t in the game anyway 😉
GRAPHICS
========
The graphics are exceptional for this style of game, with the combat (if you zoom in) providing an interesting play element. But the planetary objects. WOW! The team really need a well-deserved pat on the back, just for that! My encounter with every heavenly body makes me wish I was aboard those little spaceships, looking at the main viewer. To feel the gravitational pull and the heave of the deck under my feet at every Hyper Jump.
Come on NASA and EU Space, get your♥♥♥♥♥♥♥together…lol.
SOUND
======
Let me start of by saying the Music in this game is awesome. It plays dynamically along with the gameplay but it doesn’t change until AFTER something happens. Brilliant! This aspect seems to evade most Dev’s. DON’T let the Music give the Gameplay away.
The Sounds are crisp although unoriginal in the whole since there are only so many ways you can make lasers and missiles sound. There ARE a few surprises amongst the dead leaves for you to discover, and discover them you will. The option screens and the Advisors are well flushed out with FULL vocals. I couldn’t find a way to NOT display the Advisors words on-screen, but I’m sure it’s there.
========== GAMEPLAY ==========
EXPLORATION
============
I love this side of the game. There’s no telling what you’ll find over the spatial horizon. New planetary systems, Black Holes, Debris Fields…Pirates! Damn them, the fiends. I really enjoy the process of scanning each planetary body to discover what’s there. Just as I imagine it may be like.
FLEET ACTION
===========
There does seem to be a problem with ship movement with larger fleets though. Perhaps if the elements could pass under and over each other (clip fix) this would allow the fleets to organize in a more streamlined and Naval like fashion, rather than the chook feed they look like currently.
There’s no Fleet strategy to play here, it’s all about the numbers. If your side has more (and better equipped) chances are you’ll win. That’s all there is to it. Which means you need to Research!
RESEARCH
========,
Ahhhh. The backbone of all 4x4, Space Conquest style games. Some games – like the King of 4x4’s ‘Master of Orion’, invented the whole ‘Research to Advance’ challenge in games, and like all its predecessors, Stellaris too has a large – very large – R & D element. Unlike the latest MoO though, there’s no ‘Research one, get two Free’ initially apparent. I like that.
The time it takes to research each field seems balanced, with Three head researchers doing the hard yards to ensure your Empire gets its biggest bang for its buck! However, the descriptions prior to research seems sparse, with the effect of each showing very basic info. Instead of needing to Wiki every item, a more comprehensive Science and Engineering (at least on the numbers side of things) would be welcome, so you have a better idea on what to research next.
Working out the balance of your Tech isn’t up to par during Combat is a poor way to discover you made the wrong choice when it came to buying those new Torpedos.
Overall, at this stage, I can recommend this game for purchase AND play!
A more up to date review shortly. Cheers!

Magicite is a Rogue-like, Survival RPG in which your goal is to get as strong as you can in order to fight the end game boss. Simple, right? There is more to it than this!
On your way to the end boss, you will encounter a wide variety of monsters throughout the 10 biomes (including boss) that you can slay and loot. Some monsters drop incredibly rare items, some drop vital resources for your survival. Defeating monsters will reward you with experience which you can use to level up your desired stat and select your class skills. The game also features mining, wood cutting, plant gathering, you name it! On top of that, the game uses a complex crafting system where you have to combine 2 items together to create your desired object (eg. wood plank + wood plank = wooden blade. stick + stick = axe handle. axe handle + wooden blade = wooden axe). The possibilities are endless!
At the start of the game you will be asked to choose your hero. You can pick between 15 different races! Each one have their pros and cons. The more achievements you complete, the more classes you will unlock. That itself will keep you entertained for a good 10 hours! Once you have selected your character you can pick your companion and a hat, both will benefit you in their own way. Your unique character gets randomly generated stats and skills and whatever is generated will influence your play style. Once that is done, you have begun your adventure!
That aside, lets talk about the game's graphics. Each biome has a different setting and each have their own unique climate. The dark and eerie environment of certain biomes give you shivers. The pixel styled art, along with the interesting use of colour, really does amaze me. It's just beautiful. This itself has persuaded me to purchase this game. The art style really does suit Magicite. The dev really knew what he wanted!
To sum it up, this pixelated styled, Rogue-like game is definately one which will be loved for a long time. Each adventure is different in their own ways. You are guaranteed to play this game for some time! I would give this game a 9/10!

I think dom5 is definitely worth the money, it feels much better polished than Dom4 and also better balanced ...which is a pretty big achievement from the devs considering this game is only out for some days now.
As usal, the devs will do a lot patches for years and you can expect a ton of mods from the community to further increase playing experience as well as quite a bunch of new and  beautiful maps.
Here is my pros and cons compared to Dom4 :
Pros:
General and pre game :
- The Music is great, usually i turn off the music right from the start in most games I did play over the years, but not  in Dom5
- The game is much better optimzed for higher resolutions so that I dont get pain in the eye playing it , like I did in Dom3 and Dom4 playing on widescreen.
- Random maps get much better results and are generated really fast even when doing huge maps
- starting choices are much better, pretenders are pretty good balanced even without mods and the scales you can choose are also slightly tweaked to make all choices pretty good and viable.
- I really like that you can now choose what bless effects you want for sacred units, also some nations get bonis for some blesses. This isnt very well balanced at this point though( look at cons later on)
- The screens are much more polished and its much easier to get important informations already at pretender design, e.g. about unit roster of the nation
- You get more options for the game: Hall of Fame can now consist of up to 20 names, global enchantments can be upped to 9 at once,etc.
I would recommend to set resources at least to 200% and supplies to the maximum (300%) if you want to play vs better AI. This results in the AI recruiting more and better troops in its forts.It does make the game also slightly easier for you but the good thing is: There are also recruitment and commander points that do limit unit availability on top of money/rescources/holy points.
In game:
- There are many more things visible on the global map, most changes are good some are not( look at cons, especially I have a hard time seeing temples now)
- Commander and recruiting points are really nice. Most mages cost 2-4 points and starting region usally has 3 commander points, you can churn out 1 high level mage every 1,5 tunrs...or choose to make 3 assassins at once
- Forts start at lowest level and can be upgraded which gives additional commander points, more income and there seems to be a special fort defense now on top of province defense, which also gets better with upgrading.
- Research is much less complicated and less micro management, while still being equally deep and requiring planning , great change
- AI seems to be better in vanilla dom 5 compared to vanilla dom 4. Most armies I did encounter so far ,consisted of more national troops
- Battles are played out a lot faster, since attacker and defender hit at once and not after one another.
This makes battles a lot less real life time comsuming to watch , which to me was one of the biggest drawbacks in all old dom games. Since I like huge maps and usually play at hardest difficulty possible and mods that make it even harder, it took a ton of time to watch battles in all my SP and MP games. This time is roughly cut in half i would say.
- Battles seem to be more bloody because of this change, too. This did result in some balance problems though( see cons). But overall I do like it, since even a good player will lose more units per battle, which in turn makes the AI slightly harder to beat. No more finetuning starting position of units/commanders pre battle in order to get the first hit.Good change.
- multi turn movement for commanders can be activated pre game. A simple but great change. You dont have to "babysit" all your commanders now, since they automatically follow the movement path to destination every turn.
- The fatigue system has been slightly reworked. I still hate this system in general but it has less impact now on the game, making units with high armor(and thus high fatigue) a bit  better now. They still are handicapped because of slow movement though and it is my impression that movement in battles now is more important than before.
- + many more changes that are good
Cons:
- game only comes with 2 or 3 premade maps. Sure , random maps are much better now but still...this isnt enough.
Where are all the classic dom 2-4 maps that came with vanilla release?
Sure, the community is very active and therefore we will have enough maps very soon...but not every player of Dom 5 will visit the forum/dom sites to download them.
- Blessing choices are great but not very well balanced at this point. Also there seem to be some bugs:

Undying also seems to work for non undead sacreds and only costs 1 bless point...this is extremely powerful since you can take it several times at pretender generation.
You only need 4 bless points to get to +3 magic resistance...this is also extremely powerful.
All in all this is still a great change, at least once patches and mods are out.
- the new global map has its drawbacks:
1. I have a hard time seeing temples
2. I loved the candles displaying the dominion strength, they seem to have disappeared, instead you get your provinces highlighted in yellow that have your dominion. So far so good, but you have now to click on the province to see the actual dominions strength AND on some maps that use a green/yellow color pattern for most provinces,e.g. cradle,  you simply cant see the yellow highlighted province very easy.
3. Cold provinces will be colored differently and behave differently...looks good on paper, but this vastly improves all nations liking cold climate and vastly hampers hot climate nations imo. I
This is a pretty big balance issue I have right atm.
- while battles result in more casualties now, which is good, assassins are right now a ton weaker.
I played LA Abysia in my test games and loved to conquer neutral provinces with Assassins, killing the commanders and then just sending one commander of my own to conquer the province.
This Strategy was balanced before imo, since I had to invest quite some time and money in order to make that strat work...and here and there my assassins would be killed,too. Since both combatants hit and once now, most assassins either die alone or manage to die but poison the enemy commander so that he dies ,too. Very rarely Ive seen my blessed assassins to kill neutral province commanders and survive. This makes ist necessary to also give them items right from the start, which isnt cost effective anymore.
- last but not least: If you compare Dom 5 with Dom 4 latest patch, there are only a select few new nations( if at all).
Sure, I expect to see quite a some new nations patched in for free over the next years, but still...
Also , all nations basically use the same unit roster as in Dom 4.
All in all I can easily recommend this game to every Domx player and to every player that likes 4 x games like this.
The game is tough to master though and very time consuming but if offers unlimited replayabilty and very, very active MP community . MP games are where this game really shines. BUT I can also recommend this game for players that only be play SP. The dominions series is one of my most favorite one of all time, right after Master of Magic but slightly  ahead of games like HoMM,Age of Wonders,etc..
I would give Dom 5 9/10 rating because I firmly believe most problems will be solved soon.

I've been a Dominions fan since Dominions 3.  This series is like Master of Magic on steroids with no diplomacy.  It's awesome.  It's also worth noting that this game is actually pretty easy to understand after a while because its systems are incredibly consistent throughout the game design.  Therefore its learning curve is not that bad at all.  So don't be intimidated.
However, each sequel is more of an incremental improvement on its predecessor than a complete redesign.  Dom5 is the best Dominions experience out there, but it isn't dramatically different than Dominions 4.  It has some welcome new features, great new music, and slightly better graphics, but the underlying game mechanics are the same.  It's not like going from Civilization 4 to Civilization 5, for instance.
Therefore, I recommend the following:
-If you like Fantasy 4x games, definitely buy this game.
-If you like 4x games in general, strongly consider this game if Fantasy doesn't turn you off.
-If you own Dominions 3 only, definitely get this game.  It's a huge upgrade compared to 3.
-If you own Dominions 4, consider waiting for Dominions 6 if you're on a budget.

Oh I loved this game. The only bad thing I can say is that it's maybe too short to my linking. Took me about 2 hours to finish all levels on perfect. If you're buying this game please do as others say and grab the complete pack (which includes infinite). You won't regret it, trust me.
The game itself is kind of a crossover between minesweeper and picross (from a logical perspective, naturally). If you've played any or both of them, you'll quickly find yourself using the learned skills and mindset you already got when playing them. The complexity though, doesn't come from the fact that the mechanics of either are difficult by themselves, but rather from their wonderful combination. Though I must admit that from the minesweeper perspective, a hexagonal grid makes things a little too simple, considering that each cell can only have 6 neighbors (instead of 8) and that the board isn't filled evenly (sometimes neigbor cells are void). But again, it's the added twists that hit the sweetspot on the difficulty level.
If you're a hardcore minesweeper player, do yourself a favor: Before launching the game go to the other tab and swap the mouse buttons. Also, marking cells that shouldn't be marked counts as a mistake, so avoid marking compulsively. Your long earned habits can sometimes get in the way (as it happened to me). Thank me later.
PD: If somebody else says that minesweeper is random, take that comment with a grain of salt. Minesweeper IS deterministic at its core. It's the game imlpementations that create puzzles where hints are not enough to completely determine the locations of mines, leading you to the situation where you have to guess and risk losing the round. If only implementations were a bit more wiser than simply dropping mines at random and then filling the surrounding squares with hints...

Stellaris is a 4X game with a heavy emphasis on exploration: it manages to instill the wonder of exploring the "final frontier" in its early game with different types of alien species, random events, a vast tech-tree with a research system that changes the flow of every game, as well as semi-randomly generated alien species in every new game. However, all of this doesn't stop the game from stagnating as time goes on as you get boxed in by the AI unwilling to wage war or interact with you in a meaningful way, serving mostly as a hindrance as you try to explore the rest of the galaxy.
The updates, DLC, and mod support have alleviated this problem somewhat at the time this review was written, but I fear Stellaris might follow the route of other Paradox strategy titles where improvements will be locked behind paid DLC.
Great game for those looking to explore the wonders of the galaxy, perhaps not so much for those looking to wage galactic war and/or to create an interstellar empire.

All in all, this is a good game with greater potential waiting to be unlocked.

I am not a picky gamer, If a game is fun, enjoyable and unique I will most likely enjoy it. What I hate seeing are games that do the same thing over and over again with very little in variation. That being said, I REALLY enjoyed stellaris and I regret having not bought it sooner. Whether you are new to 4X style strategy games or if youre a veteran Stellaris will really up the quality of what you get. So many of these types of games will constantly bombard you with new systems that make no sense or the same systems but put into weird designs. Stellaris takes an extremely complex and intricate system of menus, resources, commands, units, planets, bases, command, etc, etc, and blends them all together into an extremely user friendly and easy to learn UI. No fancy words that are specific to the game, nothing that isnt relatively self explanatory, You spend maybe an hour or two hours learning the ropes and then you play! Even during those learning moments, it isnt set up in a way thats boring. If you love strategy or 4X games this is a good buy. I for one very rarely buy into strategy games and I played 5 minutes of a friends copy, immediately stopped and bought the game myself.

SETUP
=====
Here’s the thing. Stellaris has this AMAZING pre-start setup sequence, in where you choose nearly every aspect of the gameplay except what color underwear you’re going to dirty the first time you get into combat. It seriously is that great. What you can’t change isn’t in the game anyway 😉
GRAPHICS
========
The graphics are exceptional for this style of game, with the combat (if you zoom in) providing an interesting play element. But the planetary objects. WOW! The team really need a well-deserved pat on the back, just for that! My encounter with every heavenly body makes me wish I was aboard those little spaceships, looking at the main viewer. To feel the gravitational pull and the heave of the deck under my feet at every Hyper Jump.
Come on NASA and EU Space, get your♥♥♥♥♥♥♥together…lol.
SOUND
======
Let me start of by saying the Music in this game is awesome. It plays dynamically along with the gameplay but it doesn’t change until AFTER something happens. Brilliant! This aspect seems to evade most Dev’s. DON’T let the Music give the Gameplay away.
The Sounds are crisp although unoriginal in the whole since there are only so many ways you can make lasers and missiles sound. There ARE a few surprises amongst the dead leaves for you to discover, and discover them you will. The option screens and the Advisors are well flushed out with FULL vocals. I couldn’t find a way to NOT display the Advisors words on-screen, but I’m sure it’s there.
========== GAMEPLAY ==========
EXPLORATION
============
I love this side of the game. There’s no telling what you’ll find over the spatial horizon. New planetary systems, Black Holes, Debris Fields…Pirates! Damn them, the fiends. I really enjoy the process of scanning each planetary body to discover what’s there. Just as I imagine it may be like.
FLEET ACTION
===========
There does seem to be a problem with ship movement with larger fleets though. Perhaps if the elements could pass under and over each other (clip fix) this would allow the fleets to organize in a more streamlined and Naval like fashion, rather than the chook feed they look like currently.
There’s no Fleet strategy to play here, it’s all about the numbers. If your side has more (and better equipped) chances are you’ll win. That’s all there is to it. Which means you need to Research!
RESEARCH
========,
Ahhhh. The backbone of all 4x4, Space Conquest style games. Some games – like the King of 4x4’s ‘Master of Orion’, invented the whole ‘Research to Advance’ challenge in games, and like all its predecessors, Stellaris too has a large – very large – R & D element. Unlike the latest MoO though, there’s no ‘Research one, get two Free’ initially apparent. I like that.
The time it takes to research each field seems balanced, with Three head researchers doing the hard yards to ensure your Empire gets its biggest bang for its buck! However, the descriptions prior to research seems sparse, with the effect of each showing very basic info. Instead of needing to Wiki every item, a more comprehensive Science and Engineering (at least on the numbers side of things) would be welcome, so you have a better idea on what to research next.
Working out the balance of your Tech isn’t up to par during Combat is a poor way to discover you made the wrong choice when it came to buying those new Torpedos.
Overall, at this stage, I can recommend this game for purchase AND play!
A more up to date review shortly. Cheers!

A great, roguelike game, for the strategically minded. It brings along classic 2d platformer indie elements like permadeath, MLG lewts, and challenging hp system(no regeneration for you, drink a potion m9), crafting, etc. To be honest, unlike other games, its hard to explain- besides calling it a crafting, survival, roguelike, permadeath and unlock-stuff-by-doing-different-tasks sort of game.
However, with it, it lacks one thing.....
No save system.
This is where the rage comes in
Magicite is a particulary fun game, with its classic rpg-roguelike-crafting feel, but you can only play one session untill you restart, which pisses me off because then I can't restart on my epic loot adventures when something on my schedule seems to pop up, or when my friend has to go  we have to restart from the beginning. Sure, its a permadeath game, but that doesn't mean sometimes I want to hop back on in order to get my character with loot I spent hours getting. Also, I don't feel like they're not going to update the game anymore, so, no chance at getting a save system.
Overall, Magicite is a fun, roguelike fantasy rpg game with crafting that puts you into an underground enviornment where you have to survive, kill monsters, and get to the end. There's permadeath, and in order to unlock new things you must do different tasks and then die. On the dark side, no save system ties it to 2-3 hour long play sessions, where if you don't finish the game when you quit it can feel kind of abandoning, not allowing you to get back the loot you spent hours trying to get.

When I played 2K16 I remember thinking "Well, this is just minor tweaks over 2K15". 2K17 on the other hand is a massive improvement over last years game. Graphically its a decent step up. Gameplay wise, theres a huge improvement.
This year feels more realistic than ever before. I was really impressed with teammate AI. They still do dumb stuff, but they react in really realistic and helpful ways. Like cutting to the basket when youre backing someone down. They tend to move in ways that you can create offense in very fluid and dynamic ways. Its beatiful to watch and very rewarding once you learn how to execute plays and create within the offense. I can make gameplay complaints. Like how it feels impossible to get an offensive rebound even when you have your opponent boxed out. But its all minor complaints and no sports game is perfect. The fact of the matter is that 2K17 is the best basketball game to date.
Not just in terms of gameplay but variety as well. I bought 2K17 with full intentions of MyCareer being the mode I spent my time with. Ive yet to even touch it. So far Ive spent all my time with MyTeam which is rediculously addictive. Just within that mode alone theres so much variety of stuff that you can do. The fact that Ive played this game for 69 hours so far and I still havent even played MyCareer, MyGm (which Ive always loved in this series) or PRO-AM, speaks to the unrivaled variety and value this game offers.
It even runs great. I didnt buy the game at launch so I dont know how that went. But right now the game is running great and its never once crashed on me. Ive only played a few online matches in MyTeam so far but they were lag free. How the game ran online was a big worry for me, but its been great so far.
I was originally going to try everything before I wrote a review, but I see now thats going to be hundreds of gameplay hours from now. Take it from someone who has been playing 2K since the original game on the Dreamcast. Back when Iverson was the only player you needed or wanted on the cover every year. If you love basketball, you want this game.

Dominions 5 is a fantasy 4x turn-based strategy game where you control one of the pretender gods, you pick a faction and fight other pretender gods for the throne of ascension. By default you won the game once you have defeated all other pretender gods.
Now let's review the game.
Most of the people here said that Dominion 5 is a complex game but for me it's a simple game why? Because of it's high level management. You don't move your every soldier in the battlefield instead they move on their own, your role here is to issue a strategy in pre-battle. Will your cavalery target the rearmost unit? Will your infantry attack the closest unit or large enemy monster? it's all up to you in the strategic screen.
You can see your provinces in the strategic map, the resources, income, recruitment point (which I still don't understand how it's work) and the units you can hire. There are some unique unit in certain provinces like lizarmen, shamblers, mermen, jaguar warriors, etc. You can recruit them but to move unit you have hired to another province, you'll need a commander. Units can only move from province to province by the lead of a commander, once your commander dies your unit will disperse, you'll lose your units. You might regain some unit if you are lucky.
There's a dominion mechanic, it's like spreading your religion. You'll be given a prohet that you picked yourself. This prophet will spread religion of your pretender god not only a prophet a priest can also do the same but it is not as powerful as a prophet. Spreading your religion is important because it expand your dominion, if you have no dominions left you lose the game.
It's just that, simple isn't it?... no need to think tactical, just give high level command and let your unit go crazy. But, it by no means a CASUL game. If you are careless, you'll got rekt and you'll realize it's too late to fix that. Like me, I was focused on building my military but neglected my religion spreading, I got huge military on every province and every nation feared me but my dominions keep decreasing and in the end it's gone completely, I got domkilled.
The music is nice at first but it's repeating. I think it only has one track. I advise to turn off the music and just open youtube and search for epic music, it'll do beter, trust me.
Certainly, dominion games has a minimalist art, 3D for environment and 2-frame 2D sprites for units and characters. For me the art is okay, I can relate to it, I can imagine it. It'll grow on you eventually.
I'll give this game a 8/10, great game.

Want to start the Galactic Federation and bring the galaxy into a new era of peace and prosperity? Play this game.
Want to bend all other species to your will under your grand galactic plan? Play this game.
Want to clear the galaxy of all of the Xeno filth that plagues the galaxy, leaving only your pure, clean race? (If you get the Utopia DLC you can have your race eat the other species of the galaxy) Play this game.
Want all of your hard work of Empire building to be undone by the sudden invasion of energy beings from another dimension? Play this game.
Want to start the next robot uprising? Play this game.
In all seriousness though, this is a great addition to the 4X strategy genre of games. There are multiple different racial builds to suit many playstyles such as the unstoppable tide of the endless swarms of babymakers colonizing every habitable planet within sight, or the hyper xenophobic militaristic people who will not rest until the galaxy is free from the plague that is foreigners (BUILD THAT WALL), or the diplomatic alienlovers who want to bring the galaxy into a peaceful cooperation, but happened to spawn neighboring that before mentioned hyper xenophobic empire and so end up in an endless cycle of war that allows you to swoop in mop up both empires relatively easily, or the enslaving militarists who really love aliens, but you know, greater good and all that so they are going to have to mine for the rest of eternity.
Things the game does well:
1) War Goals: before you declare (or shortly after war is declared on you) you pick what goals you are after in the war. These goals each have a percentage called its war score. this war score builds up over the course of the war, either negatively or positively based on how well you are doing in the war. During peace negotiation you can then demand anything that you had previously declared as a war goal. if you manage to get your warscore to 100%, then you can force an unconditional surrender which gives you everything you declared as a war goal. This system allows you to invite other empires at the start of the war and allocate some war spoils to them as a reward for their participation in the war. It also prevents such wars in other 4X games that end with a complete conquest of another empire quickly.
2) Ability to customize your own empire. Don't like any of the default empires? Make your own. I did and I conquered the Galaxy under the rule of High Empress Vasserian a bring a new order and prosperity to the Galaxy.
3) Late game events to spice things up. There is a chance to trigger a crisis event later in the game that can add new tech and change borders if left unchecked for a while.
4) Giant Lasers.
5) Space Hitler.
6) The total number of empires is never static. It can always change either increasing or decreasing. You can liberate planets of an empire through war and create a new empire of those planets with your government type, so you can basically gain a toady if you're close enough to them. In addition there are a number pre-Space Travel planets strewn about the galaxy that will develop over time and some may enter the galactic stage or some may October 23, 2077 themselves into a nuclear wasteland.
7) You can grant new settlers 40 acres and a robot to help work the mines.
8) Mods. You can mod this game to be Star Wars, or mod it to be Mass Effect, or Star Trek. You can mod it to change some features or rebalance some features, like I did not like the number of genetic modification points you can get in the default, so I added a mod to let me get more through research.
9) The AI reacts to things you do and how you interact with them. If you are buddy-buddy with an empire, help them out with research, help them in war when they ask, they'll be cool toward you. If your empire constantly conquers planets neighboring you or enslaves conquered aliens, certain empires may see you either negatively or they won't really care. If another empire starts getting very large and very powerful, they may start to build up alliances to try and combat or at least deter them or you.
10) Random anomalies and events, some good, some bad. Some super helpful, some super destructive.
11) Can reverse engineer enemy tech if you can destroy their ships. You can even skip some prerequisite techs to get it.
The game has many weaknesses though:
1) There are sometimes long periods of time where not much really happens.
2) Losing an entire fleet that you can't quickly replace basically means that empire has lost the entire game.
3) Federations are super weak and not worth the effort it takes to create one outside of multiplayer where everyone is on the page.
4) There comes a point when technological development essentially ceases.
5) AI is not good at responding to the late game crises. Often they will send a myriad of vastly underpowered fleets when they require a single large fleet to deal with the threat effectively.
6) Only 3 victory types: Conquest, Domination, and Federation and they are super tedious to complete.
7) Can not join a war in progress, you have to declare a new war with new war goals that you have no idea if they overlap with the other war's goals. You can not look at another war to see what either side is trying to get out of it.
8) No espionage. Closest thing you can do is send a ship into enemy territory (assuming their borders are not closed to you) and literally looking to see what their ships have. In order to see how you compare technologically, you have to do some roundabout ways. An espionage system would really help this game.
9) No trade routes between empires. Trade system is a joke and not really worth it. Most strategic resources are moderately helpful and sometimes are completely worthless.
10) Ground combat is woefully underdeveloped. You only really need like 1 single army to take control of a planet that you've been orbiting.
TL:DR - It's a really good 4x space strategy game with a lot of interesting takes that also happens to have some fixable flaws.

Very enjoyable clicker game. Simple premise: you click to make money. Upgrade your stores and add managers to make money while you play other games. It is certainly one of the best free games on steam, and it adds a nice spin to the clicker market, with other clicker games (such as tap tap infinity or time clickers) being much less entertaining compared to AdVenture Capitalist in my opinion.

Adventure Capitalist is a game that shouldn't work. It shouldn't be fun, or entertaining.
However despite what the 1,000+ negative reviews (as compared to the 18,000+ postivive ones) say, it does work. But why, oh why, does it?
It's not the gameplay. There hardly is any. You start of clicking a button a few times, basically "running" a lemonade stand. That earns you money, which you use to buy more stands for more profit. Eventually you hire someone to squeeze the lemons for you. This continues on through paper routes, shrimp boats, and up to banks and oil companies. For each and every one, you hire managers, let them earn you money, come back and buy more.
Oh, and there are also upgrades, which allow you earn even more money. And for some reason angels come down from heaven to invest in your stuff, but only if you toss away all your money and follow Jesus. Then they join you and raise your profit margins, so you can go and buy more stuff.
Oh, and you can sacrifice angels to Satan for even more upgrades. Yes, really.
That's pretty much it for the gameplay. It's simple, but somehow effective. There are no graphics to speak of, just a window with menus and bars. The music consists of one track that plays endlessly. Really there is so little here it would be impossible to charge for it.
Yet, as a free game, it works. As a rule, gamers like really big numbers. Hell you could even look at this as a learning exercise. I've never even heard of denominations in this game. Decillion? Duodecillion? Trevingillion? What the ♥♥♥♥ are those?!
You'll come back, and watch the money pile up and the numbers get bigger and bigger and bigger. Eventually brancing out to the Moon and to the newly available Mars, to do the exact same thing with different investments and different soundtracks.
There really is no point to the game other then watching your pile of fake money grow and grow and grow.
Oh yes, one more thing. There is microtransactions. Yes, really. You can spend real money to make your pile of fake money grow faster, buying multipliers, advancing time to get your money now, and allowing you to get the angels to join you without giving up all your wealth.
Yes, I have spent money on this. I also have it on my Android phone. And yes I spent money on it for my phone as well.
My god, my god, why have you forsaken me?

Reviewing games based on "potential" is unfathomably silly. Any game has the "potential" to be great. E.T.: The Extraterrestrial would be perfectly fine for a 2600 adventure game if entering and exiting pits wasn't so clunky. Pacman on the 2600 would be great if the play control was tightened and the playfield was redesigned to be more like the arcade. If Color a Dinosaur offered slightly more coloring options, and perhaps a way to print out one's creation, it would be a great little game for preschoolers. If Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 5 had patched out the many, many glitches, it would be great! If <X> changed the things about itself that make it a crappy game, it would be great!
Initia: Elemental Arena might have potential. I say "might" because the game doesn't even feature AI bots to allow someone to experience the basic "flow" of the game. But hey, capture-the-flag can be fun, and the moba influence here seems like it could lead to interesting diversity and techniques.
But in essence, this game is almost nothing. It's a handful of empty maps you can run around in. The maps look to be standard Unreal engine fare, neither excessively great nor astoundingly terrible within the confines of Unreal engine maps. Maybe they're balanced. Maybe they're not. The attacks may be very visceral and satisfying, or may be just as frustrating as the most finicky worst of first-person melee attacks have ever been. The gameplay may be great, may be slow, may be too quick and spammy-random - who knows!
A multiplayer-only game requires SOMETHING to get a playerbase established - a well-known developer, a publisher with deep enough pockets to fund a large advertising campaign, an industry contact who can get a game featured in a highly-watched esports event, even just being highly hyped within a specific community - League of Legends style. But a game does require SOMETHING to get it to the point where there's 50 or so people playing it at any given moment. At THAT point, you can sit back and try to let grassroots word-of-mouth turn a game into the next cascading avalanche of self-propelled hype.
This game, on the other hand, not only lacks any of those perks, but then has the chutzpah to charge $20 for the experience. It's hard enough convincing buddies to download and install a free-to-play game, let alone one of those $5'ish indie titles. But convincing seven other people to pay $20 each to play a game which may or may not turn out to be fun? Good luck, gamer.
At the time of this review, 20 people have given this game a positive recommendation.
At the time of this review, the most players this game has ever had online at one time - according to
- is 4.
The bare minimum amount of players required for this game's matchmaking system to start a game is 8.
I'll let that speak for itself.
It's entirely possible that this game will end up becoming the next TF2, the next DOTA, the next Big Game™. But as of June 11th, 2016, it isn't.
If you want to spend twenty dollars right now on the gamble that at some point in the future, this game may deliver twenty dollars worth of entertainment, then you're incredibly stupid and probably either can't read this review, have already downvoted this review, or have already left a nasty comment saying that this game isn't Color a Dinosaur, there aren't even dinosaurs in it, how could I be so dumb?
For the rest of those reading this review, you'd have more fun taking that twenty dollars and spending it on booze, drugs, good food, crappy food, Netflix, Amazon, Youtube Red (lmao), Redbox (ahahahahahaha), games that you can actually play, lottery scratch-offs, or really just setting it on fire for a badass Instagram selfie.

There is a
that this game is overly complex or hard to get into.
Fear not, with a few guide videos on the controls and game concepts (text and video guides are included), you will be able to play fairly well.  Start off with training wheels, then get going consuming the world in the bloody reign of a necromancer or claim the realms of the land with lovecraftian horrors.  I had known of Dom 4 for ages, but was never willing to take the plunge.  It only took a game or two to understand the core mechanics.
The sheer ammount of content is astounding, and the numbers are not like the Borderlands "500 bazillion guns," most spells, units, blessings, etc. are tremendously different and can have entire strategies developed around them.  I have played as a celestial empire ruled by a shapeshifting astral dragon and a kingdom of norsemen ruled by a race of dwindling elves.  It is the immense quantity of well developed, interesting nations and innumerable viable gods for them that guarantees there is always something new to try.  The nations are based on amalgams of dozens of cultures from throughout history as well as literature and some things that are just downright strange.  Point is there is something, or probably many things, for everyone.
The game is based on a turn based overworld, with variable regions (the random map generator works great and can be tailored to your desired game) and a pseudo-realtime battle replay.  The overworld relies on resource management, the claiming of territory, building construction, exploration, and of course, spreading your dominion.  These concepts are very familiar, just with their own unique flavor.  The combat is all pre-planned, so there is no tactics or direct control.  At first I thought this was offputting, but the forethought and creativity of planning an army and giving it orders, all in advance turns out to be just as fun.  And, if you don't really care, you can just read the results.  Definitely a better autobattle system than Total War.  Like Dwarf Fortress, every unit is fully simulated.  You can watch your units who where lit ablaze, diseased, entangled or crippled limp behind the rest of your army.  Will you care about every archer?  No, but the attention to detail and quality of the simulation is astounding.  Due to the remarkable variety, the interactions of different units can be downright hillarious.
I know that Dom 4 had a great modding scene as well, including many total conversions.  The game is very mod friendly and allows unbelievably creative maps and units.  The game has a very modular nature, making the possibilites for mods endless and relatively easy to develop.  I look forward to what the community will cook up.  That said, there are a few issues regarding balance and mechanics, but I am not enough of an expert to explain.  It is fun, and if it is too easy, ramp up the difficulty or knock down some of the map generation figures.  No game is perfect, and not on release.  There are also a few UI quirks that don't really make sense or are a bit irritating to use, but none are gamebreaking.
I would highly reccomend this game to anyone who has a bit of an imagination or loves grand strategy/god games.

Want to start the Galactic Federation and bring the galaxy into a new era of peace and prosperity? Play this game.
Want to bend all other species to your will under your grand galactic plan? Play this game.
Want to clear the galaxy of all of the Xeno filth that plagues the galaxy, leaving only your pure, clean race? (If you get the Utopia DLC you can have your race eat the other species of the galaxy) Play this game.
Want all of your hard work of Empire building to be undone by the sudden invasion of energy beings from another dimension? Play this game.
Want to start the next robot uprising? Play this game.
In all seriousness though, this is a great addition to the 4X strategy genre of games. There are multiple different racial builds to suit many playstyles such as the unstoppable tide of the endless swarms of babymakers colonizing every habitable planet within sight, or the hyper xenophobic militaristic people who will not rest until the galaxy is free from the plague that is foreigners (BUILD THAT WALL), or the diplomatic alienlovers who want to bring the galaxy into a peaceful cooperation, but happened to spawn neighboring that before mentioned hyper xenophobic empire and so end up in an endless cycle of war that allows you to swoop in mop up both empires relatively easily, or the enslaving militarists who really love aliens, but you know, greater good and all that so they are going to have to mine for the rest of eternity.
Things the game does well:
1) War Goals: before you declare (or shortly after war is declared on you) you pick what goals you are after in the war. These goals each have a percentage called its war score. this war score builds up over the course of the war, either negatively or positively based on how well you are doing in the war. During peace negotiation you can then demand anything that you had previously declared as a war goal. if you manage to get your warscore to 100%, then you can force an unconditional surrender which gives you everything you declared as a war goal. This system allows you to invite other empires at the start of the war and allocate some war spoils to them as a reward for their participation in the war. It also prevents such wars in other 4X games that end with a complete conquest of another empire quickly.
2) Ability to customize your own empire. Don't like any of the default empires? Make your own. I did and I conquered the Galaxy under the rule of High Empress Vasserian a bring a new order and prosperity to the Galaxy.
3) Late game events to spice things up. There is a chance to trigger a crisis event later in the game that can add new tech and change borders if left unchecked for a while.
4) Giant Lasers.
5) Space Hitler.
6) The total number of empires is never static. It can always change either increasing or decreasing. You can liberate planets of an empire through war and create a new empire of those planets with your government type, so you can basically gain a toady if you're close enough to them. In addition there are a number pre-Space Travel planets strewn about the galaxy that will develop over time and some may enter the galactic stage or some may October 23, 2077 themselves into a nuclear wasteland.
7) You can grant new settlers 40 acres and a robot to help work the mines.
8) Mods. You can mod this game to be Star Wars, or mod it to be Mass Effect, or Star Trek. You can mod it to change some features or rebalance some features, like I did not like the number of genetic modification points you can get in the default, so I added a mod to let me get more through research.
9) The AI reacts to things you do and how you interact with them. If you are buddy-buddy with an empire, help them out with research, help them in war when they ask, they'll be cool toward you. If your empire constantly conquers planets neighboring you or enslaves conquered aliens, certain empires may see you either negatively or they won't really care. If another empire starts getting very large and very powerful, they may start to build up alliances to try and combat or at least deter them or you.
10) Random anomalies and events, some good, some bad. Some super helpful, some super destructive.
11) Can reverse engineer enemy tech if you can destroy their ships. You can even skip some prerequisite techs to get it.
The game has many weaknesses though:
1) There are sometimes long periods of time where not much really happens.
2) Losing an entire fleet that you can't quickly replace basically means that empire has lost the entire game.
3) Federations are super weak and not worth the effort it takes to create one outside of multiplayer where everyone is on the page.
4) There comes a point when technological development essentially ceases.
5) AI is not good at responding to the late game crises. Often they will send a myriad of vastly underpowered fleets when they require a single large fleet to deal with the threat effectively.
6) Only 3 victory types: Conquest, Domination, and Federation and they are super tedious to complete.
7) Can not join a war in progress, you have to declare a new war with new war goals that you have no idea if they overlap with the other war's goals. You can not look at another war to see what either side is trying to get out of it.
8) No espionage. Closest thing you can do is send a ship into enemy territory (assuming their borders are not closed to you) and literally looking to see what their ships have. In order to see how you compare technologically, you have to do some roundabout ways. An espionage system would really help this game.
9) No trade routes between empires. Trade system is a joke and not really worth it. Most strategic resources are moderately helpful and sometimes are completely worthless.
10) Ground combat is woefully underdeveloped. You only really need like 1 single army to take control of a planet that you've been orbiting.
TL:DR - It's a really good 4x space strategy game with a lot of interesting takes that also happens to have some fixable flaws.

I have chosen to recommend this game, but I wouldn't say that it's for everyone.
Firstly, it's short. So short that it took me about 35 minutes to complete with only a couple of parts missed out (optional info that tells you more in relation to the story). This doesn't mean it's terrible however. No game should be judged primarily on its length, but understandably this will put people off paying for it.
Secondly, it's not a sandbox, nor does it have levels, skilltrees, gun mods or anything like that. It's in an incredibly similar style to the mod/indie game 'Dear Esther'. I enjoyed Dear Esther very much, which is why I grabbed a copy of this in the first place, but if you're not a fan of just walking, looking and listening then it might not be the game for you.
The game is creepy, at least in my opinion. Not in a spine-chilling, survival horror kind of way, but more in a "What happened here?!" kind of way. You're a resident of a deserted island that consists of nothing more than a short mountain, a small abandoned settlement and some underground tunnels. As you analyse objects and enter certain areas, you'll learn about the various ex-members of the island's community via a series of text boxes. I like a game that forces you to read rather than listen, so this wasn't a bad thing for me, however I did start to tire of the boxes fading in and out in transparency every time I moved further or nearer to the objects that generated them.
Graphically, I can't quite call it beautiful, but it has a weird sort of prettiness to it. The visuals ever so slightly remind me of the point and click puzzle classic, Myst, in that it's relatively bleak yet still colourful in it's own right. The textures and shadows aren't what you'd describe as impressive, but again have their own style of charm, and are more than enough that's necessary for this particular game, should you choose to describe it as that.
The sound effects are a little bit dull, but the droning, atmospheric, ambient soundtrack that bobs in and out of the story's progression sounds great. It's very well fitting for this type of story, puts you on edge from time to time, and adds a thin, but satisfactory level of tension and fear.
The ending (don't worry, there are no spoilers) didn't quite wow me, but it was very nicely done and was a fitting end to what turned out to be a chilling, mysterious tale.
I enjoyed The Moon Silver all in all and would recommend it to those that love to explore desolate, post-apocalyptic like environments. Those of you that enjoy a nice mystery would enjoy it also, as it takes a little bit of thinking here and there to figure out the order of events. I would, however, NOT recommend it to those that prefer to have a lot of options, weapons, inventory screens etc. This is a fairly simple game designed purely to tell a story. 7/10.

I've been known to like some so-called "Walking Simulators" but the best ones show, rather than tell. The Moon Sliver doesn't just dump narration on you to make up for how little the world communicates to you through what you can see -- it dumps it in a messy way, plopping big blocks of text on screen in whatever order you happen to come across the prompts. Are you looking at two text-prompt hotspots at once? Enjoy your big overlapping blocks of now unreadable text.
And somehow, despite getting your HUD bombed with pages and pages of narration, you're probably still not going to have any idea what's going on or why you should have sympathy for these characters. For all the words it uses to tell you the story, it ends up telling very little.

Very enjoyable clicker game. Simple premise: you click to make money. Upgrade your stores and add managers to make money while you play other games. It is certainly one of the best free games on steam, and it adds a nice spin to the clicker market, with other clicker games (such as tap tap infinity or time clickers) being much less entertaining compared to AdVenture Capitalist in my opinion.

Adventure Capitalist is a game that shouldn't work. It shouldn't be fun, or entertaining.
However despite what the 1,000+ negative reviews (as compared to the 18,000+ postivive ones) say, it does work. But why, oh why, does it?
It's not the gameplay. There hardly is any. You start of clicking a button a few times, basically "running" a lemonade stand. That earns you money, which you use to buy more stands for more profit. Eventually you hire someone to squeeze the lemons for you. This continues on through paper routes, shrimp boats, and up to banks and oil companies. For each and every one, you hire managers, let them earn you money, come back and buy more.
Oh, and there are also upgrades, which allow you earn even more money. And for some reason angels come down from heaven to invest in your stuff, but only if you toss away all your money and follow Jesus. Then they join you and raise your profit margins, so you can go and buy more stuff.
Oh, and you can sacrifice angels to Satan for even more upgrades. Yes, really.
That's pretty much it for the gameplay. It's simple, but somehow effective. There are no graphics to speak of, just a window with menus and bars. The music consists of one track that plays endlessly. Really there is so little here it would be impossible to charge for it.
Yet, as a free game, it works. As a rule, gamers like really big numbers. Hell you could even look at this as a learning exercise. I've never even heard of denominations in this game. Decillion? Duodecillion? Trevingillion? What the ♥♥♥♥ are those?!
You'll come back, and watch the money pile up and the numbers get bigger and bigger and bigger. Eventually brancing out to the Moon and to the newly available Mars, to do the exact same thing with different investments and different soundtracks.
There really is no point to the game other then watching your pile of fake money grow and grow and grow.
Oh yes, one more thing. There is microtransactions. Yes, really. You can spend real money to make your pile of fake money grow faster, buying multipliers, advancing time to get your money now, and allowing you to get the angels to join you without giving up all your wealth.
Yes, I have spent money on this. I also have it on my Android phone. And yes I spent money on it for my phone as well.
My god, my god, why have you forsaken me?

Another great entry to the Borderlands series.  However, for the most part it just can't help but fall short of Borderlands 2.  While it is a fantastic game, it has some pretty major shortcomings.
-The story is stellar, best yet in the series.  Although it doesn't have as many interesting characters as Borderlands 2.  The humor is also on point as usual.
- Borderlands 2's area design is much friendlier to single player or multiplayer game play where PreSequel is mostly just big open areas that only work for multiplayer.. making a single player run rather boring.  In BL2 single player was arguably better than multiplayer.  BL2 was clearly designed with both modes in mind... PreSequel disregarded it entirely.  I hope this isn't the start of a new trend for the series.
- The actual shooting engagments are fun, but because of the moon atmosphere gimmick, it feels like Borderlands in slow motion, it gets old pretty fast.
- Graphically it's definitely the best looking game in the series, although it COULD have been a much bigger leap if they hadn't re-purposed so many BL2 assets.
- The thing that fails this game the most for me is the lack of variety.  The entire game looks basically exactly the same.  It's all blue, on the moon, slow, floaty, and neon.  Borderlands 2 took place over a vast array of wildly interesting and beautifully designed locals.  PreSequel feels like just one of those areas taken and expanded into an entire game.  And that to me is the games biggest problem... the gimmicks the game play are based on should have been explored in a DLC.. not stretched into a full game.
However, while it's clear that the Aus team isn't as talented as the regular team, the game is still a great Borderlands game.  I'm just more excited about Borderlands 3 than I have ever been because this game wasn't as fantastic as I was hoping for.

This game has incredible opportunities for growth. Very reminiscent of having a huge variety of spells and combinations like in early Elder Scrolls games like Morrowind or Oblivion. However, it's not without flaws, as it is still in Early Access. I'll go into a more detailed description below, but for brevity's sake:
TLDR:
Pros:
- Combines many different aspects of element manipulation reminiscent of incredible games (Teleportation - Dishonored, Speedy magic attacks - Elder Scrolls, Invisibility/Stealth water powers)
-Dedicated team of developers that are working hard to grow fan base (giveaways, promoting) and improve the game
-The competitive modes are objective based and seem like fun!
-Simple interface, and very beautiful soundtrack
Cons:
-Lack of players (probably won't find a match)
-Higher level graphics require a decent computer and video card
-Lack of tutorials or control guides
-No single player mode (you can play against yourself in what would be competitive multiplayer, but no bots)
Expanded:
This game has a very unique concept. As someone who's main experiences with online multiplayer have been console Halo and CoD (I was young, please forgive me), it was startling to see such variety in choice for character abilities. And it's only scratched the surface! Floating as a ball of light to navigate treacherous floating islands, teleporting between locations, activating invisibility on command, creating tornadoes... and that's only scratching the surface.
In order to get the game to play decently on my bootcamped Mac, I had to turn the graphics to low. Even still, it was glitching and making it near unplayable. However, I turned on V-Sync and the game proceeded to run much better! Keep this in mind.
At the moment, it's biggest flaw lies in it's lack of users. If there were even a handful of players on, this game could be great! But as it is, it's very difficult to find a match. I'm hoping to join one of the planned games later in the week, so we'll see how that goes!
You also need to be willing to learn the controls solo, in a map all to yourself. They're mainly self explanatory, but there are a few tricks worth experimenting to find (double tapping space leads to a neat jump/sprint that took a while for me to learn).
There's also a limited number of maps (2), and only 2 multiplayer modes I could see.
However, despite the above, I have extreme confidence in the development team and their ability to turn this into a polished product. I've watched them try to increase the user base through giveaways on steamgifts, and working to publicize the game.
Even with the limited elements in the element shop, combinations can produce magnificent results! It makes you feel like a truly nifty wizard (no Harry Dresden, but close) by combining new abilities to flutter your way around the map. I flew across islands as an invulnerable ball of light, then was able to drop and immediately go invisible and sneak around! If my imaginary enemy were there, they'd be trembling in fear.

This game is amazing so far still needs a larger player base but if you can get a group of your friends to join you then you are in for a ton of fun.
I think it needs a more detailed tutorial for inexperienced players but that won't stop them from enjoying, you can see for yourself.

Hexcells is a rarity of a puzzle game: A perfectly logical game with relatively simple rules that manages to explore the space of its idea without getting stale. The first puzzles in the game are easy; by the end, there's some decidedly non-trivial reasoning going into every click. But every move can be made perfectly logically - not a single guess is required, no matter how maddeningly it may feel like a puzzle has no information left to share.
It and its two sequels are the games I judge other logic-puzzle games by. Some live up, many don't, but I haven't found one that surpasses it yet.

Disclaimer- Ihave like 11 hours of play on *this* Steam Install, but Ive been all over Automation since before the migration to Steam; I was one of the first to buy into Early Access. Ima also a huge gearhead, so I may have a slight bias for or against certain aspects.
To preface, I think I need to say that I absolutely love this game. I can sit down, crack open a beer, and just fiddle with the engine creator for hours. I greatly enjoy tweaking, editing, and massaging power and reliability out of a plucky little Inline 6 or small V8 (anyone can get 1000HP out of a Biturbo V12). The car design is a bit clunky still, but the elements are all there; I like that I can choose between different eras and the design tools are just robust enough to make me feel like I can create something of my own without taking 28 hours and using 400 context menus. With some refinement, this is gonna be truly spectacular.
Now, that being said, I do have one complaint; the creators are biased towards modern cars. That is, there is a blanket disadvantage to relaibility and usability to older vehicles and engines, regardless of the application. There is also total lack of pre-war designs and engine availabilty. The oldest I can go is 1948, and they make my big displacement inline 6 motors fail because they think old is bad and unrelaible.
To clarify, Im not some old fogey who thinks modern cars arent as good as old ones; cars in general are the best theyve ever been from a technical standpoint and I know that. However, not including vintage bodies and hampering the performance of older engines on priniciple is simply a grave miscalculation.  Some of the most beautiful, opluent, sporty , crazy vehicles ever produced came from the 1920s and 1930s. Bucciali, Packard, LeSalle, Bugatti, Rolls Royce, W.O. Bentley, Hispano-Suiza, Isotta Fraschini, and the almighty Duesenberg are just a few examples. The Bugatti Aerolithe still stands as a marvel of luxury and engineering due to its riveted, hand made, all-magnesium body and bespoke interior. The Chassis on a Duesenberg could sit for decades and not rust through because they were so overbuilt.
Specifically, however, the thing that drove me to this complaint was the previously mentioned bias against engines; basically, according to the devs, Old=Bad, and New=Good. This is generally the case, except that instead of creating a baseline level of functionality and then giving improvements based on modernailty, they chose to make modern designs good and penailze older ones. Fred and August Duesenberg created a 420CID Inline 8 with dual overhead cams in 1928 that made 265HP naturally aspirated, and 320HP with a supercharger! These motors had gobs and gobs of torque, driving the nearly-3-ton Duesies to go over 100mph. Ettore Bugatti put a massive 12.7L Inline 8 in the famous Type 41 Royale that was so torqe-y and reliable it would later be put in locomotive train applications. There were absolutely bulletproof (albeit simple) and genuinely powerful engine designs that deserve recognition, and its a glaring oversight that these were not only barely included, but then also hampered by the game.
Just my two cents.
Overall though, I love it and I cant wait to see what it becomes.
