A really good futuristic/fantasy tactical third person shooter that can be played passively or aggresively.  I say it's futuristic/fantasy as there's a good deal of tech that you get access to in this game that maybe in the future could exsist.  Though that tech does add a lot to the fun you can have with the game, whether it's the UAV, active camo or the walker thing you get,  All the tech ties in nicely to playing the playstyle you want, using that tech to either run and gun through or to take out enemies one by one or in small groups.
The tactical portion of the game is really good as well.  Again using the tech and your squad you can tackle various challenges throughout the game.  Your teammates also don't suck and routinely help out with objectives/revives/kills.  There's a good deal of cover to move between and ways to move around the map that add to the tactical fun.  One of the most satisfying parts of the tactical portion for me was using active camo and UAV to set my team mates up for multikills.  The game played a lot slower that way, but it felt right clearing areas out without alerting the enemy and watching all 4 enemies falling over.
The levels were all really well done as well and again allowed for multiple ways to clear out objectives.  The layout of the map as well as enemy placement would allow you to sneak through or find a way to dispatch of all the enemies before clearing that part of the map.  There is also a good diversity of maps and enviroments to fight through, some jungle/desert/tundra(snow)/urban made each map feel some what unique.
Story felt bland and kind of unresolved.  There wasn't much in the story that really makes you want to come back for it, or even pay that much attention to it in first place.
The guns are nice and there is a good deal of customization that you can make each weapon unique to how you want to play.  You are given a recommended set of guns before the mission starts but you are able to change them if you so choose which is nice.
Game is old, so don't expect much from the multiplayer if anything.
Few minor annoyances though during my single player playthrough.  You use the shift button to move between cover, however for me, every now and then the shift button would bring up the Steam overlay without pushing the tab button along with it, no idea why it happened.  As moving between cover can be tricky there was a few times where I'd select something, either not go to the one I wanted, or not return to cover after I finished moving.  Also there are parts in the game where it's recommended to go stealthy and when you move over cover it breaks your active camo which can alert enemies.

This is weird fiction in the form of a "walking simulator" video game. There is a supernatural story here, and a powerful one - but the details are left to your interpretation. This game is short (and rightly so for this type of work). But it rewards exploration. I don't know what the minimal set of steps required to finish the game are, but you shouldn't worry about them. Wander the island, and events will progress at their own pace. As you revisit old locations, parts of the story which you had read before will make more sense, or suddenly tie into information found elsewhere.
The art is minimal but evocative. It actually reminded me of older 3d games, where the shapes you see on screen act as suggestions to your imagination, rather than attempts at photorealism. I've come away from The Moon Sliver feeling like I know the island on which it's set like a real place. The developer gets extra credits for evidently having done most of it on a  shoestring. The taste and care in the assets used is a triumph in itself.
Downsides? The developer felt the need to to include two very silly game-y elements.
The first is a torch with batteries that run out after a couple of minutes and have to be recharged. I'm not sure if this adds to the atmosphere of the darker sections, but it certainly adds to the mood-breaking annoyance. I sense that the developer felt the silliness of this mechanic, because the game is littered with recharging points, and recharging is an instant operation.
The second is two instances of a very simple lock puzzle, which feel like vestiges of a previous design when maybe this game was more puzzle-oriented. I will improve your experience of the game by telling you now that there is no technique for these, you just have to guess - but there's so few options that it's the work of seconds to do so.
Neither of these impair  a brilliant short narrative experience. Score out of ten: yes do play it.

The non-linear story telling is what makes this game shine, and if that's what you're looking for, drop a couple of bucks and enjoy this enigmatic gem.

I did originally write a very, very long winded review about how incredible this game is, but when I read it over I discovered I was not only a horrible reviewer but also a horrible debater. So instead, I will sum up my experience with the game.
-The story and it's implications gave me shivers and chills both for a good solid 20 minutes. Not because it was terrifying (it isn't a horror game), but because it was that powerful.
-The graphics are Gamecube worthy, but the story, sounds, music, etc. overshadow that.
-You have a flashlight in the game. It isn't a huge part of anything, really, but if you use it you have to recharge it at electrical outlets. This wasn't a problem for me as I really only used it to see where walls were so I didn't run into anything. Might be a downside for some people, as it isn't completely necessary.
-The soundtrack is incredible, and it's timed perfectly. Not just the music, in fact, but everything. Nothing is out of place in this game.
-For the best atmosphere, turn your gamma down (if you don't know what that is and your monitor isn't blinding you right now don't worry about it), only use your flashlight when you need to (but don't stress over it), and pay attention to the story. But you should be doing that anyway; it's a story game.
-If you don't like story games or narratives or things that go bump in the night, this game isn't for you.
-Written as a story, it reads like something [guy who wrote The Road] and Issac Asimov could've worked on together.
Overall, it's definitely one of the best games I've ever played. Given, it's a pretty long list, but it's up there in the top 50 or 25.

My issue with the game, and the reason why it's getting a negative review are as follows.
1. Awful PC support
2k just doesn't care about PC nearly as much as consoles, as PC is the black sheep and the consoles are where most of the cash cows are. They have their whales on PC im sure too, but console is where a
of their whales are. Whales are people who buy obscene amounts of VC, which leads into my second and most important point. But first, there just isn't the support console receives on PC. Broken Vsync, a 60hz refresh rate, blatant port of certain menu features that are extremely weird to navigate on PC.
2. VC has become the central focus of 2k, and thats unacceptable.
We've gotten to a point in the gaming industry where DLC is extremely prevalant, and generally accepted. This is a mistake in my opinion, but i won't go on a tirade about the industry. 2k pushes microtransactions on you CONSTANTLY. It was bad enough last year, but its only gotten worse. The amount of grinding necessary to get VC incentivizes microtransactions through the irrtation and slow nature of progression. This was clearly intentional. To get into the practice screen, you have to go through at least 4 loading screens, so by the time you get there your ready to rip your hair out because you've done this 20 times. This leads to people spending hundreds of dollars to upgrade their player, which is ridiculous in my opinion. A lot of people use the justification "well lots of games use grinding, it adds play time." There is NO way in hell it should take more than 40 hours of playing without microtransactions to max out your player. Everywhere you turn in 2k games there is ads for vc, begging you to buy more. Its not enough that we spend 60 dollars on a video game, no. You also need to have a continuous stream of income dumped into the game to be competitive unless you'd like to spend half the year grinding away in extremely boring modes. Having everything center around VC is a blatant and digusting cash grab that i hope stops, but i know it wont.
Ultimately, if your looking for gameplay only, i suppose its an ok investment. Honestly spending 60 dollars just to play a few hours of pickup games makes me feel like an idiot, and unless you REALLY, REALLY love the other modes in NBA, id just steer clear of this. Although I have not written a review in a while, I can still vividly recall my month-long indie game spree, beginning with Devolver Digital’s Hotline Miami and culminating in Superflat Games’ Lone Survivor, which I will be reviewing today. Lone Survivor bills itself as a post-apocalyptic survival horror game in which the player controls an unnamed protagonist who spends his days exploring the dark hallways of his apartment complex in search of companionship amidst a “zombie” apocalypse. What distinguishes Lone Survivor from other survival horror games is twofold: everything is rendered in 2D, an aesthetic choice not typically associated with the horror genre, and it was all made by one man, Jasper Byrne. So is immersion still possible in such unconventional circumstances? Read on to find out!
The moment you launch Lone Survivor, you can easily see the amount of care Byrne has put into his game. Each pixel is carefully placed and every nuance, from the character animations to the background scenery, is extremely detailed. While some may argue that the pixelated composition of the game’s monsters and objects makes visual cues all the more confusing, I personally found the art style helpful in simultaneously maintaining an aura of mystery and urging the player’s own imagination to take hold. Equally as impressive is the game’s soundtrack which features not only your eerie but generic horror music, but also soothing guitar riffs which supplement the more lighthearted segments of the game.
In addition to its survival horror roots, Lone Survivor also prides itself in being a psychological thriller—and with good reason. The plot is all sorts of crazy, and to even mention any particular event in detail would be a potential spoiler. Unfortunately, this also makes the ending a bit easier to guess as all the nonsensical happenings can only suggest so much. Maybe there is a twist waiting at the end of the journey. Maybe there isn’t. Maybe the twist is that there is no twist! Lone Survivor’s narrative, or at least its method of storytelling, isn’t its strongest quality. However, that is not to say that its world lacks depth. Byrne did a fantastic job with the writing. None of the dialogue I came by struck me as cringe-inducing. Quite the opposite: every word uttered by the protagonist effectively fleshes out his character and conveys his feelings of hopelessness.
But what really matters, beneath the aesthetics and story, is the gameplay and it is with this that I have my biggest gripe. I wouldn’t go as far as claiming that the mechanics behind Lone Survivor are bad, but I found them rather frustrating. There are some stealth elements present such as hiding behind curtains to avoid monsters, but there is no sense of danger once concealed and it all boils down to waiting for the creature to pass by. At some point in the game, the protagonist will acquire a firearm but the aiming mechanism hinders its usefulness. Shots can only be fired at 45 degree angles, making it difficult hit foes at their weak points until they are too close for comfort. What I did grow fond of were the survival aspect of the game, which encourages resource management and exploration, and its side quests, which help further flesh out the post-apocalyptic world our protagonist finds himself in.
Lone Survivor is a decent indie title that can be had for a dollar or two plus change during any video game sale. For the three plus hours of entertainment to be had, this is far from a bad deal. If the idea of a psychological thriller told with unconventional visuals appeals to you, there is no reason you shouldn’t make the purchase. But I suppose if you stand adamantly against pixelated graphics, the survival horror genre, or supporting stellar developers, then there really is no convincing you, is there?
Grade: 3/5

One of the best RTS games ever made.
The Paper-Rock-Scissors-Gameplay works flawlessly, for example, it's very costly to send your cavallery against the enemy spearmen, but the spearmen take heavy losses from archers (if not in proximity) and the archers can't really hurt armored units like knights.
The Turn-Based gameplay between skirmishes is a bit dusted by the oldschool complexity style; but you can automate most of it.
The peak of the gameplay are of course defense of and attacking a castle. Therein, however, also lies the biggest flaw of the game: The AI.
I've won battles against an overwhelming amount of enemies, just by standing on the walls and waiting for the enemy chilling in the arrow fire to perish - nope, they didn't move a finger even though they stood right infront of their ladders which they had built up to seize the walls.
It's just astounding how much the AI can ♥♥♥♥ up - for example, all units tend to jam gates and on the strategymap, the AI keeps declaring war and declaring peace every 5 or so turns.
It is to mention that you only have specific (historic) empires to play, which differ mainly on their starting position (duh), leading in significant disadvantages for some to join crusades (playing as England, an entire army deserted while being on a ship (however that works lol), because it took them too long to reach Jerusalem).
However, I've played many RTS games set in the medieval (fantasy) setting, none of which had such thrilling (and hard) combat. Every battle is a new challenge, and that makes this game great.
I haven't played any more recent Total War Games though, so maybe you'll be better off with some better graphics (they tend to tire your eyes quite quickly).
TL;DR: I can warmly recommend this game to anyone that likes medieval RTS games and seeks a challenge. Don't expect the AI to be too much of a genius, though.

Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel is Borderlands in space and the best Borderlands so far.
The first Borderlands introduced us a lovely shoot 'n' loot game with a rich world full of tales and wicked characters. One of the most tiring things while also being part of its charm was actually the part of Pandora that we saw. The surroundings. Sand, sand and more sand combined with fifty shades of brown. Me and my co-op partner felt like drowning in sand and dust after the playthrough. After all this Borderlands 2 rose like a phoenix and showed us Pandora in a completely different light with green pastures and maps that weren't only taken from Mad Max! With a story that for the first time felt like a proper story and more lunatic fellows and guns and loot and more everything, it made the first part look shameful.
Most of the aspects from the old parts are here in The Pre-Sequel, just better or at least at the same level of quality. In the story we see our beloved villain Handsome Jack's path from a wannabe hero into the horrible monster of Borderlands 2. The gameplay is the same old good Borderlands that you have gotten used to with some space twists like weaker gravity and the often absence of areas with oxygen. Jumping in space is seriously fun and also convenient, so it's pretty hard to get used to gravity again. Anyway, I'd like to praise the story. Who crazy plays Borderlands for their stories? I do, especially from now on. The jokes are as funny as ever if you find the Borderlands humor endearing and the plot is interesting to follow while exploding heads just like in the second part. The feature that I experienced as compelling was the fact that your Vault Hunters finally join the discussions and are more engaged in the story instead of just some random catchlines. This adds a good amount of replay value for those who are not only interested in different skill trees but also in interacting characters. I felt like really being part of the story and not just a mute shell doing quests. Something that seems so minor was a huge change in my eyes. Why wasn't it always done like this? It's a good start and even more dialogue from the Vault Hunters is what I absolutely desire.
Remember the complaining about dust? I love space. There's a lot of space in this game. The areas aren't boring though and shouldn't make you want to never see space again, but at the same time the game maps aren't from as large scale as in Borderlands 2. For a guy like me who sees dreams of Mass Effect, I can't say I mind too much.
The Pre-Sequel doesn't reinvent the wheel, it attaches rockets to the wheel and sends it out of Pandora. And the wheel speaks now. That's enough for me, but for the next game it's only reasonable to demand bigger differences. The series is going into a great direction and I expect wonderful things from Borderlands 3. Meanwhile, enjoy the fresh air of Elpis!

A pure shoot-and-loot game. Even though this review is mostly for Borderlands 1, it applies to all three, so I copied it to all three. Since the games have been out for quite a while, there are convenient bundles with two or all three of them etc., make sure you check them out before purchasing.
At first, I didn't get "it" and thought that the game sucks. I thought it was just a generic shooter (and once again with failed FOV - *sigh*) with gimmicky cartoon shader, very generic loot containers, guns with somewhat randomized values, and the super obvious fetch quest cliché.
But then, a year later, I tried again - and I got "it". It's a well done generic shooter (whose FOV can be edited in a file) with an interesting fun-depressing otherworldly feel, cartoon shader, reliably balanced generic loot containers, a surprisingly powerful procedural weapons system, and simple quests that make you deal with all these things in various places and that give you some story background. What makes all this work is the whole that emerges from it. It's like acid music of the 1990s. The Roland TB-303 alone sounds boring, but if you use it right and let it play together with other stuff, it's a very powerful driver, and music history might remember you for
.
I ended up buying and playing through BL1, BL2, BL The Pre-Sequel (which came out after 1&2 but whose story plays between 1&2), and almost all DLC. No regrets. It was not a perfect experience, but there's a reason I bought and played
games, and the story didn't contribute much to this reason. It's just the mix of all the gameplay ingredients and - excuse me - the mindlessness of it. A simple but sufficiently deep shoot&loot trip that goes on for tens of hours. (According to
, roughly: BL1 20-60, BL2 30-80, BLps: 20-40)
The quests become available over time, and you can choose freely which of the ones you soaked up into your quest management screen you tackle at which time. There's an indicator expressing how hard they will be for your current character level.
I thought the procedural weapons approach would probably be stupid, that it would be e.g. just a bit more power or range. But no! There are many changing variables, even the weapon designs (and visual effects) change, fitting the weapon's character. Hunting / comparing for the best weapon and learning about where you'll probably find those and where rather not turns into a passion.
Too bad the inventory interface is not half as good as it should be. Well, at least you can mark weapons as garbage so that you can bulk-sell them once back at a vendor or machine, and you can even do a buyback for the identical price. But what
thought it would be a good idea to have the inventory interface move around incessantly? And you need to realize: You'll spend
with this interface, because comparing your guns is a core element of the game.
Then there's the fact that the game will just forget where you have already killed people - they'll just be back on your next visit and loot containers will be refilled, you don't even have to die or reload/restart the game for this. This has upsides, of course, which would be why they decided for this, e.g. now you can keep grinding, and you can enjoy your new toys and your leveled-up character against old foes. It's rather important for balancing that you can't just wipe the world clean. But even though hypothetically, people would repopulate fortresses in reality, you will have to make yourself blind to the feeling that all you're doing is in vain, your actions leave almost no lasting consequence in the world. Just like in real life, right? Except in real life, you don't constantly whip the lands with powerful guns.
What also sucks (but again makes sense, of course) is that you lose a lot of money whenever you die. There will be deaths, though, that are just unnecessary or unfair, or you might even get caught in a loop of dying, which maximizes frustration. This happened to me when I fought Wilhelm and didn't realize that I could just travel away via the obvious terminal. Why didn't I realize? I was mostly blinded by the fact that the arena is a place you can only reach by dropping in from a height that you can't jump, so you can't get out again. This clear message and the fact that I was still relatively new to Borderlands made me blind to the fact that there was an electronic exit right there.
You can't save your game. At least it's not a classic campaign shooter quicksave that bakes every relevant world state detail into a nice file. Instead, you have your character profile which will change as you progress (e.g. incl. money loss from deaths; hint: If you Alt+F4 while you're still dying, nothing is lost.), and it's rather one of those "general player state" and "checkpoint" saves. On the one hand, this very character of savegame is a good thing: Checkpoints have the clear upside of getting you more involved and making the reality more real because you can't beat it into obedience by saving/loading at your leisure. The downside is: The game completely forgets everything but you. While fortresses have been repopulated when you revisit them even without loading, there are a few aspects of the world that stick - until you exit to main menu or out of the game and then continue playing, that is. It all couldn't revolve
just around you.
And there are the quite hard boss fights. Personally, I don't like boss fights, so ignore this paragraph as an actual negative, but I just find them stressful, and what others might misinterpret to be a sense of achievement in me is really just the relief that I managed to overcome this obstacle between me and more of the satisfying gameplay I want to enjoy. You know, like 1990s Eurobeat "music" (That I never liked.) where the painful hectic rap was the desert you had to endure before reaching the next fountain, making the refrain ever so slightly better than it actually was. The game does not have a whole lot of boss fights, but I had to throw everything into them and was often very frustrated when I didn't manage, because dying cost me a bunch of cash, and I had to start the fight completely from scratch.
But Borderlands is fun. A well done shoot&loot world to forget yourself in.

When I saw the 70% sale and the numerous positve reviews on the store page, I immediately took the opportunity to try out the new "walking simulator" game.  Turns out it was error on Valve's part as the game wasn't inteded to be that cheap.  Suffice to say, after finishing the game at half an hour (30 minutes short from the expected time), I could definitely say this discounted price value is exactly its worth.
As someone who considers Gone Home as 2013 GOTY, I am definitely in tune with the so-called interactive novels (aka: walking simulators) but this is a game that relies too much on interpretation that the novelty of the interactive aspect is diminished.  The game has an unnecessary gameplay cue such as recharging your flashlight which ends up adding tedium to the already lacking of a sprint button; to which certain moments in the game would have you backtracking if you ever miss some parts.
There is but 2 puzzles (1 with guesswork) in the game and it does certainly disrupts the flow of the narrative especially if you were given the free ability to explore how you wish.  However, the game's short nature justifies the entire experience as you are left wondering what "The Moon Sliver" is and its intended purpose.  Anymore would be already in spoiler territory so I leave it to you to make what you have.
Clearly, this is game with an interesting storyline but to charge for it is asking for too much.  I can only recommend this when the price goes back to the 70% range again.

If you haven't played Gone Home, then you should try this game anyway. You'll either love or hate it, and for only $2, it's not a ridiculous bet to take.  I've sold Steam trading cards for more.
Ultimately, "The Moon Sliver" is a short, short story in game form, and although it's rather rough and cheaply made, it's still a beautiful piece of art.

The Moon Sliver is an ambitious horror/exploration game that benifits greatly from the risks it takes. It is very short, and with such a modest asking price it is not a very big investment of time or money. But boy does it pay off.  I beat the game in well under an hour, but I haven't stopped thinking about it since. The horror in this game is not the kind that says "boo" and you chuckle about it later. It crawls over you like a rising tide, and your desire to know more about the narrative is challenged by your growing sense of dread. Luckily for me, my desire to complete the game won, and I was very moved by a narrative that is simple, but is told in such a powerful way, and actually leaves you with questions that the game doesn't answer for you. Obviously I love this game, but if your the kind of person who says that narrative/exploration games are not really games due to their lack of gameplay, you'll for sure have the same problem with this game. If that doesn't bug you, do yourself a favor and buy this game, it is truly excellent, and look how cheap it is!

Very good but not quite great, "Ghost Recon: Future Soldier" is an enjoyable title with a few quirks.
On the positive side, there don't seem to be any "throwaway" game mechanics. Success depends on being able to understand the various, easy-to-basically-grasp techniques available to you, and how to put them all together to deal with different situations. Cover-to-cover movement and shooting are, of course, critical, but you also need to be able to use your gear and team intelligently. In particular, the sync-shot mechanic is key, and manages to stay fresh through the game by way of not being overused. Also, the ability to customize your weapons to fit your style is very welcome. There's just enough customization depth to be interesting without it all becoming overwhelming.
The downside to the game is that it's just a touch too linear and constrained for this kind of gameplay. It would have been brilliant to be given a list of objectives, plopped into a huge map, and given free reign to figure out your mission. Instead, you mostly get herded into restricted spaces so that you can be presented with a series of highly defined tactical puzzles. The viable solutions to these tactical puzzles seem to be pretty small in number, especially when an enemy alert will fail the mission. You either do things in the one right way...or you try again.
One thing that stood out to me particularly as feeling a bit odd was the "body discovered" mechanic. There were several spots throughout the game where I simply could not figure out how the enemy had located a dead comrade. The ability to spot a body seems to be driven less by intelligent AI and more by fixed, programmatic factors that aren't necessarily easy to suss out. I could swear that there was more than one occasion where a body was discovered by a soldier who was looking in the opposite direction, and through concrete. (Another thing that hurts suspension of disbelief is the apparent ability for an enemy grunt to see a body...and then immediately devine the exact location of everyone on your team. It feels bizarre.)
Ultimately, GR:FS is a little overscripted for being a stealth tactics game - but it's still quite enjoyable.

SIMPLY. AMAZING. GAME.
Iv been on a MMO hunt for the last 4 years. Must have dug through everything out there. Played WoW since vanilla, and RS before that. For as long as I can remember, I have been looking for that first MMO feeling again, you know, that one where you click random things in shock and awe, run around like a lost potato for hours and have the best time of your life.
This is my first review for any game. Ever. But Wildstar deserves it.
I am only level 15 so I have yet to see everything that Wildstar has to offer, but even that has been more than any other game has offered me in a long time.
Display - Flawless beautiful. Huge open world, so many unique areas with unique monsters. Countless amount of times I wonder what the designer genius behind this must have smoked to obtain such creativity.
Content - Tons on top of tons. The amount of quests is insane. Couple that with settler type missions, resource grinding, world events ( which there seems to be tons of but I have not jumped into yet). Dont ever say you dont have something to do.
Combat - Uses a telegraph type system ( I believe thats the name). Extremely engaging. Each monster has its own unique attack pattern that always manages to intrigue me. Just make sure to remember your 5 D's of dodgeball: Dodge, Duck, Dip, Dive, and most importantly Dodge.
Professions and Skills - Takes a little getting use to, but the amount of depth is fantastic. Looking at all the skill trees, I may have to take a vacation day or 2 to just get use to that.
PVE - Granted I have only done one dungeon, it is very on par with vanilla dungeons from WoW. Skill is required, they are not easy, but so much fun. Yes, Wildstar dungeons and raiding is the best I have seen thus far, Amazing.
UI - Also takes a little getting use to. The Quest tracker is holy amazing. Pressing N allows you to open up content interface allowing you to look through and choose content in a fantastic, organized fashion. Add the quest navigator. It is just amazing, pure and simple.
Community - Nicest people I have ever met in an MMO, Higher levels actually offer help, guidance to lower levels. The loyalty they have for this game is just beautiful.
Perhaps the only issues that could use improvement is PVP ques, and some extra players.
The amount of F2P content you get is just insane, frankly, its just amazing. No MMO comes close, i have looked and I have found.
And lastly...you get to play as an evil hamster with pistols. EVIL HAMSTERS WITH PISTOLS! crazy,

No review can do this game justice, but I have an obligation to fulfill to the gaming world.
Nier automata is not your average Devil May Cry, Onimusha, Bayonetta, Shadow of Mordor, etc. They are all fine and fun, but this game is the only one that breaks away from all of these.
You don't just get fun when you play, you get emotions and immersion. You get inside the world in your mind before you even realized it and when it does, it hits you hard. How does the game achieve this?
The game manage to create a beautiful experience for the player due to its believable world, excellent story and amazing music arsenal that fits every moment of the game. It also manages to surprise the player of various twist and turns and gameplay mechanics that are not found in other games; all these without breaking the action-rpg element of the game.
Nier automata is not a perfect game, its graphics and combat are good enough and it has enough annoying things. However, all these are easily forgiven. It is the by far the easiest of quirks to let go and enjoy the game, simply because these are parts that make the game what it is and we are aware of that. It is very hard for me to convey this message to you and you will only understand once you have finished this game as well.
In summary, A more traditional review will look like this:
+ Amazing Story, theme and execution
+ Amazing music, on point for every aspect of the game
+ Amazing gameplay
- Minor Quirks, which arguably is negated as they maybe essential to the game.

I can't stop playing this game. This is a prime example of how small indie titles can stand up to the best AAA releases of the day in terms of audience retention -the devs have got the difficulty right at the point where you can't help but try for one more solid run.
Gameplay:
The Binding of Isaac is an indie rogue-like dungeon RPG, with heavy focus on repeated runs and variety. When you start, expect to die quite a bit while getting used to the various enemy types and item mechanics, but you'll quickly start to make progress, just that little bit further. This is where the game truly shines. The game is hard, there's no doubt, but remains enticing and that glimmer of hope for success never fades. I found myself dying and restarting for hours and hours, even within a small title like this. Controls are nicely responsive, a standard WASD affair that never feels sluggish, and projectiles can be launched with either the mouse or the directional keys.
The basic goal is to descend lower and lower into 'the basement'. Each floor contains at least one upgrade and a boss. Defeating the boss spawns a trapdoor which will allow Isaac to progress further on his journey.
There is a huge range of items to collect on the way, which can complement one another, often to spectacular effect. Upgrade items will grant Isaac a new ability or powerup, with a humorous cosmetic change to boot. Others may influence the rate of pickup spawns, or result in a permanent damage boost, for example. There is an allure to collect every item at least once and find new combinations to ensure victory.
Graphics:
Nicely retro-styled, but not in a cheesy way. The art style is simple yet polished, massively important for a venture of this kind, something that I feel was actually lost somewhat in the sequel, 'The Binding Of Isaac: Rebirth'. Enemies (particularly the bosses) are varied yet memorable, and don't feel generic in the slightest. The general theme of 'macabre/bodily fluids' is very amusing, and extremely enjoyable in a dark kind of way.
Sound:
Sound is rather limited, and perhaps the only area where this game falls down. The few musical passages that are present are suitably atmospheric, but do become repetitive rather quickly.
Should I buy?
Absolutely. Even if you're not a fan of the genre, as I myself am not, this game manages to be incredibly satisfying without being too deep. You can pick up and play for five minutes as easily as sitting there for an hour. The only case to avoid it is if you've already purchased 'Rebirth', as you've essentially experienced everything the series has to offer.

Survival horror and psychological horror are two overused buzzwords that a lot of games errorneously use shamelessly to sell themselves to dopey suckers for the genre like myself.  Once in a blue moon, however, someone comes along and surprises the hell out of you with a gem like this.
First things first, if you've played the original Silent Hill games, you'll notice that the game feels very familiar.  The ambient noise, wispy fog, derelict scenery, and ironically upbeat-yet-sobering title and ending music all feel like they were ripped straight from the good old Silent Hill stylings, but it's done impressively enough in the 16-bit-esque graphical style to make you forgive it.
Having only completed my first playthrough, I have to admit, this game's story left me with a LOT more questions than answers.  I just know I'm going to be pondering this game obsessively for days, and there will be many more playthroughs.  This, of course, should sum up how I feel about this game.  It's kinda short (I finished this playthrough in just over 3 hours, though I understand it can take significantly longer than that depending on your choices), but for a retro-styled game it actually does a superb job of creating a depressing and haunting atmosphere.  There weren't really any moments that I felt truly frightened, but the game is just disturbing enough to make me inch forward on my chair, staring wide-eyed at the screen.
As I understand it, the game watches your every move and decision, modifying the story and what you experience accordingly.  The story actually makes you start questioning fairly early on whether or not the protagonist has all his marbles.  After reading the game's analysis of my decisions at the end of this first playthrough, I've deduced that the game must have labelled me as either batshit crazy or possessing a single-digit IQ, and either way, along with the aggravatingly vague conclusion I got, it's succeeded in making me want to play through again and again to try and piece together just what the ♥♥♥♥ I just saw.
Finally, this game actually comes the closest to true "survival horror" that I've ever experienced.  You have to keep yourself fed, get enough sleep, and generally avoid doing anything colossally stupid (I failed), much like you yourself would do in real life.  Some food you find will be spoiled and actually do more harm than good, and other foods may be edible as you find them, but have much greater benefits if you cook them first, which may required other ingredients (like water).  Supplies like food and ammo are scarce, forcing you to ration carefully.  Best of all, neglecting your physical and mental well being will gradually cause you to slip even further into madness.  I've never seen a game so effectively instill in me the feeling of hopelessness that is sure to come with living in a post-apocalyptic nightmare world, not knowing if any other human beings still live.
If you prefer to turn your brain off while playing video games (nothing wrong with that), like your stories spoon-fed with everything neatly packaged for you, or are a rabid FPS player, this game isn't for you.  If you want something that will make you think and keep you guessing about exactly what it is you're seeing, then give this game a shot.

The Moon Sliver is an indie title in the story/exploration genre. While sometimes called "walking simulators," there is more interaction in this than something like Dear Esther.  Priced appropriately for its approximately 1 hour run time (55 minutes in my case), it's a moody, intriguing experience and a decent recommendation for players who are inclined to like this sort of game and have their expectations in check.
Over the course of the game, players explore a desolate island, encountering story snippets that help piece together what has happened. While the island is small, players can go where they please, though certain things must be discovered, and a few minor puzzles solved, before they can progress.
The writing was interesting, and struck a good balance between giving the player snippets of dialogue that allow them to piece together what's happened, but not so little that nothing makes sense. I thought the quality of the writing was professional and evocative. It also avoided being too wordy, being economical with words and then getting out of the way to let the player's imagination do the rest.
While the island's graphics are unimpressive to behold at first, the transition to night makes great use of sound and atmospheric effects.  The audio in the chapel and the tunnels was excellent and moody. Overall, the game's atmosphere won me over for the most part, despite the poor visual quality.  Ironically, it's at night, or in the lightless interior segments, where the visuals shine.
The Moon Sliver is recommended for those looking to spend a few bucks for an hour spent discovering the interesting fiction crafted by the designer.
Edit: To do my little part for games critique (and comply with the new Steam subscriber agreement), I should disclose that the key for this game was given to me by the developer.  Did this affect my judgement?  Perhaps, though looking back I think maintain that it was a pleasant little game that wasn't very long, nor was it asking for very much money. Still, if I had not been given the key, I probably would have never discovered the game.

It merely told me to come back at night, so I waited. And waited. It took me a few minutes to realize that the time only changes after emerging from another area. Even when I was told it was nighttime, the door did not open. I ended up climbing a mountain, then jumping off the side. I got stuck between an invisible wall and a slope that couldn't be scaled.
I also could not understand the fact that the flashlight had to be charged in an outlet, nor why the houses did not have electricity (yet there was an electrical outlet on top of a mountain).
This is a simple Unity game intended to take about an hour. There is no save system. The textures repeat in an obvious manner. The music goes audibly silent (no white noise; sounds as if there's a *pop* between loops) before restarting. I tried to understand the developer's way of thinking, but it was very difficult. Unfortunately, The Moon Sliver is not for me.

We tamed the Morvarc'h, fierce sea-horses gallopping over the sea and able to change shape into nightmarish fire-breathing mares. As the priests casts the blessings of our God, a creature composed of the shifting sea herself, the lances of our riders shimmer with holy power and zeal. None can catch our blessed cavalry as it dances around the bulk of our enemy's defense to strike at their leadership while our sorceresses rain down fire, thunder and rain on those poor fools daring to oppose us.
Then, I am human, master of the secret isle of Avalon. Our armies are guided by mysterious witches capable of the forest magic. We summon allies from these forests, for our priests are weak even though our hearts are strong. None can match our skills with the longbow or the cunning of our witches. Their mastery over nature provides us with food, so we can field and supply much larger armies than those of our neighbors.
Now I am a lizard king, long mummified and honoured by my people. Stout warriors of C'tis, some of them. But mostly a rabble of low morale. They break easily, scattering to the neighboring realms. It is for the dead we summon to hold the lines while the sauromancers prepare spells to drain the souls of our enemies, and reanimate them on the spot.
Dominions 5 is about choice and strategy. With countless nations to play, each one very different from the other, and countless tactics for each of these, it's a game with immense replay value.
Players of the series will recognize most nations, and most units. However, the Bless effects have been completely reworked. The random map generator is a piece of art to the point I'll be using it to generate world maps for my tabletop sessions. The nations have been slightly rebalanced. Research has been simplified, and the UI has been made even clearer.
Like every Dominions release before it, it's easily the best of the series. Highly recommended for newcomers willing to get a real strategy game, and for those of us who are playing since Dominions 1.

I tried playing myplayer but they have made these terrible cut scenes that you CANNOT skip until your completed one iteration of myplayer. The thing I live for in NBA 2k is playing against other people online, full court, NBA teams, I'm not interested in that mycourt stuff.  Playing online is terrible - the input lag is awful.  The players move around like they are skating on ice.  7 footers repeatedly miss uncontested 2 foot shots.  Instead of 7 footers simply laying the ball in or dunking they take fade away jumpers from 3 feet.  There are these repeated stupid canned animations for the ball rolling around the rim or bouncing up over the backboard to go out of bounds - it can happen upwards of 10-20 times in a 20 minute game.  They have made the defensive adjustments menu confusing.  Charges and over the back calls happen way too often.  I can't tell you how many times I will grab a defensive rebound and due to the input lag my player will then whip a full court shot. I'm upset there is no way to request a rematch after playing someone online.  There is no way to send a friend request after playing someone online. First off, if you are fan of Kuroko no Basket stop reading this review and buy the game immediately.
Otherwise:
Pros:
> Great Gameplay - Even more fluid than past iterations, with more animations and potential plays making more more organic looking basketball.
> Lots of Teams - In addition to the 30 current NBA teams, 2k17 also offers a selection of european sides and some of the greatest teams of years past such as the '95-'96 Chicago Bulls and the 2000-'01 Philadelphia 76ers. This gives the roster some much appreciated depth allowing you to assemble dream teams of the best players of all time.
> Custom Rosters - 2k offer 2 initial rosters to use: the official 2k roster (up-to-date NBA roster) and an injury free roster. But where 2k17 really shines is in its offering of community created custom rosters, such as an All Star roster (the greatest lineup for of all time for each team), a roster where Kobe isn't retired and a Kuroko no Basket roster (Where the 76ers have the generation of miracles and kagami).
> Blacktop - Play streetball ranging from 1v1 to 5v5, half-court or full-court. A nice addition which varies the gameplay a little as it feels and plays like the real thing putting emphasis on dribble moves and attacking the paint rather than the perimeter.
> MyGM - Exactly what you would hope for from a GM mode in a sports game, nothing to seperate it from the pack but equally nothing really wrong with it either.
> MyTeam - Whilst not my prefered mode this mode is akin to Fifa's Ultimate Team and allows you to build your dream NBA sides by collecting player cards, but as to expect from any mode of this nature it is full of necessary consumables and requires you spend money on packs to get a half-decent side. But as far as an Ultimate Team-esque mode goes, MyTeam does just fine.
> Soundtrack: A combination of hip-hop and trap music which suites the action of the game well and is varied enough as to not become stale.
Cons:
> MyCareer - MyCareer fails to deliver, with nothing but long un-skippable cutscenes and grindy and monotonous gameplay to entice you into buying VC via microtransactions. Don't even consider heading online to MyPark or the ProAM without a fully maxed out MyPlayer as you will just be stomped by those who have either played the game for hours upon hours or paid real money in return for stats. This is a greedy move on 2k's part and has ruined a mode which otherwise had the potential to be truly special. This  pay-to-win RPG model works fine in a free-to-play game like Freestyle2: Street Basketball- but in a fully priced AAA release is frankly disgusting and puts a real downer on the whole experience.
> Player Base - The PC player base for 2k17 is small to begin with and is highly concentrated in the MyPark and ProAM modes, so if you wish to play MyTeam or exhibition matches online buy the game on console.
In Conclusion:
If what you are looking for is a fun basketball game to play offline exhibition matches and MyGM then this is a definite buy.
However if you are looking for a fufilling career mode or to play online then I recommend that you look elsewhere as this game is pay to win and you will struggle to find a game in the online modes.
TL;DR If you want to play offline then definitely buy this, if you want to play online then I recommend that you give this one a miss.

I found this game quite early in its development, when all you could do was make inline 4 engines. I was looking for a modernized and improved version of an old game called Detroit. That it wasn't back then, but the features they promised seemed like it would become exactly what I was looking for, eventually. After trying the game (what little there was available at the time) and reading the developers' plans for future, I got a feeling that what they were promising might actually come true.
It has taken longer than I thought it would in 2012, but a lot of those promises have come true and the game gets regular updates that bring it closer and closer to what I imagined it should become. It does look like we're actually getting that modern & better Detroit. The lite campaign already feels much better than Detroit's business simulation, even if it's still missing stuff like advertising.The car and engine building is versatile and I can replicate real life cars very close to the real life ones or make something completely my own that will still look and behave realistically and the technical details of the design will matter much more than in Detroit's very simplified and boring system.
The move to the Unreal engine has made the game look really nice. I have made many wallpapers for my desktop with the photo mode. I also find it not super difficult to mod in your own bodies or fixtures like grilles, wings or headlights and such. I made a few fixture mods that received positive feedback and that's something from a guy who's never made mods to a game before.
There's also a fun community on the official forums and discord. We share our designs and talk about cars and all kinds of stuff. The developers actively communicate with the players also. They listen to player feedback and seem to be constantly hard at work. Occasionally some modded bodies and fixtures even get added to the vanilla game because the devs keep an eye on what people like to see in the game.
If you've ever imagined what kind of cars you would make if you had your own car company, get this game. It's not feature complete yet, but what's already there is fun to play with and I have total confidence in the developers. It's only really missing a more fleshed out campaign and more body & engine options, all of which are coming soon.

It really sucks being into cars and also being into video games. In terms of realism, there aren't a lot of choices compared to shooting games, RPGs, soccer manager sims and the like. If you like sim racing, you have to deal with no single game having the right to have every brand of car in their game. If a game has the brands of cars you want to simulate racing with, it likely won't have all of the customization options you want. If the game has the customization options that you want, it won't have game modes that you want to play. If you like designing cars, you have to play something from years ago, or text based, until Automation.
This game is like a shining beacon of light in the darkness for people who are very much interested in engine and car design, but lack the money and/or knowlege to do it in real life. If you don't know what you're doing, the game has some very good tutorials to teach you how engines work. Once you do know what you're doing it becomes very enjoyable. I've spent hours making crazy engine/car combos; Tiny V12s in a compact body, I4s with insane turbochargers, with the ability to adjust almost every conceivable detail at my disposal it takes a while to get bored. There are also Challenges where you must create a car for a specific task, or for a specific demographic and time period. These can be relatively simple, or very difficult depending on the... difficulty. The best to me is campaign mode, this is where the "tycoon game" part of the title comes in. The culmination of all the skills you developed while learning to build engines and cars gets thrown into an environment where you must also consider demographics, time period and economy. Although currently only available on the old engine; they are working on the campaign for the UE4 version, and I'm looking forward to it.
You do have to be into cars to like this game, otherwise you will probably get lost in the details and leave a bad review because there is a high learning curve. The engine design is currently more in depth than car body design, if you don't care much for engine specs you might find this dry.

For anyone craving the pacing and puzzles of the beginning of the Silent Hill series will be happy with this 2D retro survivor horror game that adds in a bit of David Lynch throughout the weird story.

2D Silent Hill is an apt descriptor here: Its map system, monster design, sound cues and lighting are all meant to evoke that particular classic, and with a less than a quarter of the pixels and none of the polygons, it succeeds. But it's also got an adolescent bent to it, and as with Silent Hill 2, its fear comes from the psychological underpinnings of its protagonist.
Extraordinarily tense and beautiful to look at, Lone Survivor is at times alternately terrifying, puzzling and touching, and above all else it's fun. It's a game that's fun to play, fun to talk about, fun to figure out.
You won't always know what's going on, even after the credits roll, but you get the idea that the creator and characters do. You get a sense of complete world, much of it outside the frame. So I call it a success. Play this.

The game appears to have a "correct" path to its exploration that will reveal the plot in a linear fashion, but it's not essential to follow that path. If you can take the information presented and arrange it properly, the story still flushes out nicely.
I was hard pressed to slam on the shift button every time I felt like a long hallway was in need of a sprint button. The lack of sprinting made the game drag out a bit longer than was absolutely necessary. For a game that boasts in the beginning of taking an hour long, it certainly holds to it because you'll spend half of that time staring at every single book on the wall just to read another paragraph of text and the other half walking down hallways, unsure of whether or not you should turn your flashlight off.
Despite this, the game played well. Ever since the game dipped into its horror side, I felt chilled and uneasy the entire time. The progression from day to night was flawless, although getting to the final area in flashlight-repressing darkness was a challenge from the Chapel. I'm thankful the game is only worth about $2 or so because if I paid any more I'd be complaining that there wasn't enough content to be worth the price. As it stands, The Moon Sliver has a very interesting story that could be expanded upon in a sequel (or prequel, because
). The game is worth the price tag but not the time spent to complete it. There's a lot of character development to characters that you don't get to meet, but that might be on purpose because,
The ending explains why you've been mucking about on a deserted island well enough, but I get the sense that the final moments were the entire point of the game and everything prior to it was just narrative filler.
For a $2 game, I'd give it a good 5/5 stars. For a game you actually want to invest more than an hour in, I'd give it 2/5 stars.

This is a story driven game.  Think Gone Home & Dear Esther.  For what it is, he's done a great job at driving the story and making the characters come alive. You're by yourself trying to figure out what happened to these characters as there are remnants of recent activity on the island. The moon silver is less of a game and more a playthrough short story.
It masterfully utilizes the videogame format as a story telling medium and is a master class in what can be achieved with limited graphics.
I don't want to spoil the story so I shall instead describe the expirence, I was almost like living though one of H.P lovecraft's works.  I was affected emotionally in a way I have not been by mainstream videogames or films in recent memory. The process of learning more about this world as the story progresses and the identity of the person you are playing as fit was incredibly well done.
Look, if you're into mindlessly running around and shooting things then this isnt for you, go play COD or TF2 if you're 6.
But if you want a demonstration as to how videogames can be the highest form of storytelling, I strongly suggest you get this immediately.
I cannot overstate how impressed I am with this work.

Well, this game pleasantly surprised me.
In all honesty I purchased the game purely as it was tagged as a Psycological Horror, yet there were no screenshots to "prove" it. I'm a huge fan of "don't ask me about the game, just play it" and love the unexpected. If you are likeminded, its definately worth picking up The Moon Sliver.
The graphics aren't incredible and the controls are very simple, but that all adds to the charm, and to a certain extent, the creeepiness of the game. The Moon Sliver is saying more through less as its the lack of entities that make it such a chilling piece of work. I'm unsure as to whether this is as a result of a lack of time or resources from the author, or whether this was intended to be so, but either way it works terrifically well.
As you can see, it took me roughly an hour to complete the game. I have more to say about playing The Moon Sliver after 60 minutes, than I do about some horror games that I have invested 10 hours into. If you appreciate story, atmosphere and more subtle horror then you'll get your monies worth out of this short and sweet experience.

Well, here is my review for the game so far. The dev is a great writer, and is able to give you a sense of fear phycologically which is an art in itself; however, considering this game was made by unity in the most barebones way possilbe is dissapointing. I am currently developing a walking simulator type game and thought to give this game a try. Figuring it uses the engine I am using, and is in this type of genre. Here are the pros and cons.
Pros:
1. Great Writing.
2. Wonderful music, though I wish there was a little more variation
3. The feeling that it was tyring to draw out of the player while experienceing it.
Cons:
1. Obvious lack of time on developing it. Yes, I know this isn't a consumer issue. Anyone who has dealt with Unity, even a little, will be able to see what you did. I can describe how you developed your game in just possible 2 paragraphs.
2. This ties in to Pro #2. Lack of music variation though the music sets the tone.
3. Bad level placement desicions. The water able to walk on? Along with electrical poles and such in the water? Is this hell or something?
4. The dev tested little to none.
5. Lack of game playablitly. I was able to complete this game within just 15 minutes. Sorry son, you need more to be asking for that price.
So do I like this game, and would I recommend it? Yes, I would. Though this game does have more flaws than pros, I still appreciate what the dev was shooting for. Who would've thought that amazing loop playing music and simple line of texts to read would give you sense of lonliness anyway. I just hope the next game this guy works on will have him invest a little bit more into the game (cash wise) for us consumers to get more out of it.

One final plus point that no-one has mentioned yet though - the music is great!

If the developers put half as much effort into making this game fun to play as they did making it look bad♥♥♥♥♥ it might be worth picking up. Despite the clunky cover system, monotonous gameplay, overdone lighting effects, and boring AI, there were a few moments of joy. The time between those moments however, which is most of the game, was a chore.
The squad mechanics were interesting in that you still have control over when to start shooting while the AI squad members take their own paths. Unfortunately it leaves little room for true tactical decisions. The invisibility gig ruins the heart thumping stealth moments you'd experience in something like a Splinter Cell game. Now, instead of timing movements and frantically hiding, you simply walk right through with only slightly more than "not a care in the world," only occasionally breaking concealment if you move too fast or literally walk right in front of someone.
The synced shot is neat... for the first few times anyways... Seeing as the invisibility only makes stealth stupidly easy yet no more interesting, the game falls flat on the sync-shot being about the only semi-unique feature. This is highlighted by consistently finding enemies in groups of four, much like finding enemies standing side by side once the Assassin's Creed games introduced double hidden blades. The actual levels this all plays out in are not totally linear, but the gameplay sure is. Sync shot, camo on, move up, rinse, and repeat.
The gadgets are all same stuff; different game. Drones and sensors that give you god-vision and can blow up. Neat, but nothing that makes or breaks the game. Not really much to say there.
The cover system seems more concerned with making sure you see your character's bad♥♥♥♥♥animations than actually allowing you to have control over trivial things like aiming or moving. It's not the worst I've ever seen but it's certainly not the best.
In the end, I was willing to accept the continuing departure from the roots of the series, but I simply did not enjoy GR:FS at all. If you like flashy action games with chintzy features that trick you into feeling like your are playing as tactical bad♥♥♥♥♥complemented by cool (but impractical) animations, hollywood-esque dialog, and surreal lighting, pick it up on sale. Otherwise, I unfortunately cannot recommend it.
TL;DR: All flash; no fun.

I bought this game 2 years ago when it was first released, and was extremely happy with the fun combat aspect of the game as well as the level of customization housing offers, but the endgame was lackluster, rng dependant, and way too grindy for my liking. Wildstar has come a long way since then, and I have a few minor complaints I'll get into, but the jist of it is: This game is fun, challenging, and rewarding.
The game features combat where you have to actively be moving and avoiding enemy attacks while dishing out your own telegraphed moves with a wide array of unique skills that can be further tuned to your liking. Every class can DPS whilst also fulfilling the side roles of Tank or Healer, which is wonderful as it allows you to experiment and play the game to your liking.
The crafting system is where my first complaint comes in, it's original in the sense where you have to discover the recipes through adding components and trying to land in designated areas, but the problem is that this system relies on rng, so it can be frustrating to lose crafting materials trying to discover recipes that should be found reliably, but again, this is very minor as losses aren't major.
Dungeons are the part I love, chaotic frenzy as you're trying to interrupt the bosses channeling abilities whilst simultaneously dodging fire and staying within the healer's range, it's a wonderful mix of chaos and challenge. The better your crew performs the higher chance you'll get at the gold medals which will give you better rewards, and these are worth collecting as they'll be one of the fundamental ways you get raiding gear. My suggestion, as with any mmo, is finding a group of friends or a guild to play with, as communication is important and having a tank / healer you can trust is vital to your success.
All-in-All, there's a lot of content that I can't go into detail about every piece, I just suggest giving the game a try and finding out for yourself, the f2p system is extremely forgiving with no gameplay content behind paywalls. I ended up re-signing up with my friends because we love the game so much.

This is an MMORPG that has almost everything right to make it a great game, it does many things right but what it does wrong is probably what is going to end up killing it.
I think this might be the first MMO that has taken the WoW Concept and actually tried to improve on it. The combat is by far the most interesting part of it, as they managed to incorporate movement into it in a way that WoW never could. It flows incredibly well, the abilities are different and easy to remember, to the point where after 6 months of not touching the game I was able to come back and remember exactly what everything did and my optimal rotation. It's surprising, I don't think that ever happened with any other MMO I've played.
Apart from that the combat is extremely well implemented even in PvE situations, where you will actually feel like you're playing a game instead of clicking on buttons at the right time. You will be in constant movement to get out of your enemies areas of effect, constantly having to monitor a bunch of keys for all your abilities while still moving around, it's fun. It's really fun and feels like a proper game.
The world looks great, despite some fps dips due to unoptimization, the game is quite good looking. I do wonder why bother setting the game on an alien planet and then making a lot of area look like they came from generic fantasy or the real world.
Progression is also very smooth. Yes, of course it's still extremely grindy, as any MMO is, but I don't think there was a single moment where I felt like I wasn't progressing in some way. I was never stuck for hours on the same level, I was always exploring through these large areas as I was finishing higher and higher level missions, much unlike WoW, where you're stuck in the same place for 5 to 10 levels at once. Thanks to the combat, you're also able to progress at your own pace. If you're very good you can easily take on areas that are 4/5 levels higher than you and still have a good time. Everything just clicks very nicely together... Except for one thing.
The content. I don't know how someone can put this much effort in a game, fill it with so many different quests, and stories, and completely new lore, and make the whole game so damn annoying.
For some reason Carbine Studios decided that it would be a good idea to adopt the "Oh so quirky" Borderlands style of exposition. Sounds fun right? No, no it is not. Soon you'll be finding yourself doing a quest that is not only repetitive but is full of interactions with characters that do not give a single ♥♥♥♥ about what is happening in the world. Everybody is constantly making jokes, everybody's a one-liner spouting♥♥♥♥♥♥
It's annoying, it takes you out of the game by filling it with memes, references to pop-culture and really makes you want to stop from knowing more about the world these people spent so much time building. I spent pretty much my whole playthrough without reading anything that happened in the quests since I had no way of knowing what was actually important to know and what was yet another annoying character giving me a pointless quest.
It's too bad. A lot of time was clearly spent writing dialogues, lore and story, but none of it matters since the exposition is absolutely abhorrent.
I think that's one of the main reasons as to why the game isn't doing that well. It's just not very interesting, neither visually or lore-wise. You can unlock lore entries, but all of these are shoved away in walls of text in a menu, was there really no way to put these explanations and expositions into the game in an interesting way?
I suggest you check it out nonetheless however, as it might not be around for very long. It is by far the best Free to Play MMO out there, but it has no chance to rival things like WoW or ESO, no matter how bad those become.
Wildstar has very deep flaws that can't be fixed, but they can be improved upon with expansions and updates, so hopefully that will happen. They might pull a Destiny, who knows.

I do love this game, and want to give it a  thumbs up simply from the time spent with a group of friends wailing on each other.
However, the devs have made some design decisions that have put a hamper on things for me especially, and feel like the game is going in a direction that I dont feel will keep my interest in the game.
When we initially started playing, all magic, items, and swords were available from the start, and it was a blast experimenting with them at first, and then switching on the fly during a match as we got more experienced, just to keep each other on our toes.
With recent changes, it's moved to a level up unlock system. It's not awful, but it's not good, and just makes it feel like most of the gameplay we had already been playing was now time-gated in a way.
Looking at the current test branch, there is now a system where upgrades are now an in-match unlock, which I do not find fun. Some people might, but this frustrates me far more than feels like it gives me something to work towards, and always seems to fall into that trap of strong getting stronger, and weak falling farther and farther behind.
When this game was just deathmatch, with everything available and on the table to use, it was the most fun. The way I see things going, I feel like it's going to just turn into yet another prestiege-unlock fest or worse, and this is something that really counts against the game in my eyes.
Hopefully, things will turn out for the better, and I do somewhat understand the reasons for the dev taking so long to update, but for now, I'm going to have to give this game a thumbs down, unless I see some promise that the problems I with the game are unfounded, or improved.
In short; I love the combat, I really do (magic barrier a bit too strong against everything though), but I dont like where I see things going.

This game is a cluster f*** of pros and cons. With horrendously hit or miss match making, and an ever metastasizing cancer of cheatering this game experience can be either elating or miserable. Certain stages do NOT lend themselves to certain match types and I recommend that all players maintain a vigilent watch over their tab team composition because I frequenly notice dropping out of players mid match who are rarely if ever replaced and this game is NOT balanced to begin with, let alone once one team outnumbers another in player count. I've had it get so bad that I was literally the only person left on my team, against 4 opposing players. I had no choice but to leave the match.
Whatever calculations Loadout performs to match up players, I can say with certainty that they are insufficient at present. It has been only once in a blue moon that I have encountered a truly close match. Most times one team wins handily without even a modicum of resistance. Keep in mind that it likely (if not then it should) factors in player level, weapon level, time played, matches played, blutes aquired, if the player is in a group (and if so how many players) and overall performance statistics that it clearly keeps track of.
I routinely encounter opposing players that I am virtually unable to kill, who kill me with seemingly minimal effort, and once the match ends I am informed that their mvp is using level 9 gear, obviously a player who has been around since alpha or beta. I have encountered players with bots following them constantly switching between boost and health weapons, along with their shield that make me wonder why I even keep queueing up.
But then I recognize that I do keep joining queue. Because this is a fun game that has some good potential if they could only iron out the match making, force team balance, and get a grip on cheating. Eventually I'd like to see some balancing with the weapon parts as well.
So overall I recommend the game, but I do so tentatively.

This game is gross with a capital EWW.  I like it.  It's one nasty breath of fresh air. The game rewards your weapon style with potential upgrades to make your weapon even better over time. And the outfits are tempting and a great way to stand out even more.  I don't think that this game is even remotely pay to win.  You can buy cosmetics, and extra loadout slots, or weapon slots (things that are just nice, but not necessary).
HOWEVER there seems to be a trend already forming among more "veteran" players.  Energy Shields are mega popular and quite frustrating (almost requiring you to use Tesla payloads to eat through shields faster), and  Beam Snipers are the weapon of choice for many "Skilled, swear they got to be haxing players"(and in the hands of said players everyone calls hacks because the shear number of head shots from jumping hip shooting dudes is extremely scary). A survival horror game which is ACTUALLY SCARY!? We haven't had one of those in a while. The game is one of the few survival horror games where surviving is actually difficult, as food and ammo is scarce, and your character is pretty useless at aiming at anything more than 2 meters away. Even your flashlight runs on batteries which you need to scavange for. You will spend a lot of the time making sure that your character is well rested and fed properly, as well as scavenging for ammo and later in the game flairs. The sheer tension created by the game is becoming rare in horror games in general nowadays, and it's nice to see a ruturn to psychological horror, instead of just jump scares and easily killable enemies. The main way this game does this isn't actually the surrealism of the story or the environment, or even the demonic, faceless monsters that you'll be facing, but the sound. Static starts playing whenever you're seen by an enemy, prompting you to run away or shoot it, and the little ambient sounds of the environment serve to make sure that you are fearing your next step. There are a lot of clever little things done with the music and sound which make the game a far better experience. The open eneded story is very enjoyable to play through, and many little things that you do in the game change the way it plays out. The only part I felt was out of place was a chase sequence in the middle which was mostly just memorizing paths, and the end boss, which was fairly dull and unimaginative, but other than that the enemies were terrifying and the story interesting and surreal. It's quite short, but you probably won't be able to do everything in your first playthrough, and maybe not even your second, so you won't be compeltly done with it for a while. All in all, it's an amazing game, and I would definitely reccomend it to anyone who likes survival horror games, or just games in general. I'm pretty sure it's also the first survival horror game in which you can adopt a cat. Get it.

A woeful tale of despair and loss.  I  liked Dear Esther and I was hoping this would be the same.  But the game is a quarter of the size with not much content at all in the way of exploration - the major part of which is a maze of underground corridoorsl.   I'm happy with the minimal interaction, and weak puzzles but only if it's a good mystery with plenty of interesting places to explore.  I don't think this game qualifies on either of those points. I'm hovering between recommending it and not recommending it.
If you want a good island adventure I'd recommend Miasmata.  If you want something that delivers an emotional impact that continues to make you think for a few weeks afterwards I'd recommend Dear Esther.  If you want to be entertained with something a bit different for 45 minutes or so, I'd recommend The Moon Sliver.

The Moon Sliver is minimalist horror done right: short, atmospheric, and with lovely, slow-burn writing.
As a game that relies almost entirely on the story, The Moon Sliver starts rather weakly with story snippets scattered every which way and no clear sense of what goes where. Find enough of them, however, and you begin to form a picture - an unclear one - of what went down, leading up to a hugely impressive ending that still leaves certain elements of the story mysterious enough to keep you wondering for a few hours more.
If you like "walking simulators" in the mold of Dear Esther or Gone Home, this is right up your alley. Also, for those who are scaredy cats like me, this game does not have jump scares, even though certain parts of it appear to be an excellent setup for one.

An extremely cautious recommendation.
TPS got a decent amount of flak upon release, and with good reason. While it tells a good story, the ways in which this story is artificially elongated to boost gametime is beyond frustrating. It is very clear that TPS was originally a big DLC for BL2. With this in mind, $60 for this title is an absolute joke.
However, for a little less/on sale, this is a pretty safe buy if you're a fan of the series. It's more of the same in good and bad ways, and the Oz/low gravity mechanic does add a fun twist to combat. The Vault Hunters are among the best/funnest in the series, and they feel like properly fleshed out characters this time thanks to their many lines of dialogue.
If you haven't played a Borderlands title before, don't start here. 1 or 2 are better and cheaper. If you're a fan of the series, there's pretty much no risk here if the price is right, particularly if you want more of the same game with a different environment/questline.

As the Game was on Sale during Ubisoft Publisher Week, me and 2 friends decided to get it.
First off we were a bit anxious because of all the bad reviews. But hey, since we only wanted it to play coop and it was just 3.74€, let's give it a try.
At First we had some issues creating a coop party (connection failed blah blah).
Since there seem to be a lot of people having these issues there was a ton of threads on the forums, but with no working solution in them.
We tracked the problem down and disabled the hamachi network client - and it worked completely well.
I hope that this might help some people here hating the ♥♥♥♥ out of this (pretty solid) game.
A few words on the gameplay:
Yes - it has nothing to do with the good old Ghost Recon games. It is pretty easy, but has some good intentions towards tactics and coordinated teamplay. The story is not bad, similiar to a COD or BF, so there's nothing new to surprise you.
I couldn't recognize any bugs or performance issues. Surely it's no graphical master peace but not as bad as some people say here. The Levels are linear (like COD/BF) but very atmospheric. Textures and damage models are nice to look at and the overall gameplay feels very smooth. I see a lot of people saying that it's a "bad console port". Yeah, in the menu it really feels like a console, but the gameplay itself is good and the 3rd person view suits the game very well. Also the controls are absolutly normal and in no way confusing(W, A, S, D to move, Q for orders, E for use, F for special equipment and 1-6 for weapons+attachements, right mouse for aiming and middle mouse for aiming down sights)
and the covering system is well thought.
As i bought the game simply for the coop i can't say anything to the multiplayer.
But as far as I experienced the game i cannot agree with all the haters around here.
The Coop works and that pretty good. None of us had any performance issues, crashes or bugs.
And the gameplay, controls, graphics and story are solid. No "WTF WOW" game, but overall a good, fun game to play with friends for a few hours. Also has some replayability since there are some challenges which are not that easy to achieve.
Features like the Gunsmith are pretty amazing. The synced shot on mulitple targets adds some tactical component and the stealth/covering system are also very well designed.
0.5 hours in... Crash, crash, error, fatal crash, CRASH. You may have fooled me this time Ubisoft, but I won't be buying from you again any time soon.
