A fantastic little puzzle game. I would describe this as a more sophisticated version of Minesweeper. You get clues to where the things you're looking for are by being told how many are nearby, and deducing the necessary configuration. Except the grid is hexagonal instead of square, the map isn't perfectly connected, and the clues can contain different information than just how many things are adjacent. But most importantly, the levels are designed instead of random, which means that you won't end up with a 50/50 guess like so often happens in Minesweeper. A very satisfying experience.

It's very satisfying to sit down and power out the puzzles, with the only really nagging issue being that flagging an open spot vs. a mine (or blue hex in this game) is swapped from minesweeper, so you have to be conscious of which button you're pressing for most of the game. First I'd like to point out that ,while I may have clocked only a handful of hours in Dom4/5 on Steam, that's because the game has no Steamworks DRM (a pro in its own right) and I prefer not to use the Steam client. In actuality, I have played the series since the original, for thousands of hours, and I can't foresee that changing with the fifth iteration.
And there's a good reason for that: unlike most other series, Dominions has been evolutionary rather than revolutionary, and instead of each iteration launching with negative amount of content and mechanics compared to its predecessor, in Dominions the 16 some nations of the original have turned to almost a hundred, on top of added mechanics, modding options and improved user experience. This admittedly does make it "Dominions 4.5" in a sense, but the benefits of this approach are not to disputed and since Dom 5 reworks some of the core systems of the game, the accusations seems very suspect to me. It's also worth pointing out that while some nations remain a bit same-y as they develop over the three playable ages (each with 20-30 nations), there's a great deal of variety between the factions, especially the new ones: there's still a lot of room in the design space to make unique and flavorful nations. And when I say "unique", I mean the degree of difference (in its extremes) analogous to one nation having slow Zerglings as recruitable units, while another fields +3/+3 Ultralisks. And when I say "flavorful", Dominions is a legitimate contender for having the best fluff and worldbuilding in strategy gaming, and as far as I'm concerned, video games in general.
But I digress, let's take a step back and look at what the game is about. You play as a pretender god (a powerful spirit, minion on the previous god, an ancient monster or just a human mage powerful enough to have mastered death) trying to fill the vacancy left behind by mysterious disappearance of the Almighty Pantokrator and aiding you in your quest for Godhood is a nation of loyal followers. Most of the nations are based on real-world mythology or historical nations with fantasy twist and include Tuatha Dé Danann, Zoroastrian birdmen, undead Roman Empire, Spanish Inquisition and Biblical Rephaite giants, and fluff tends to feature detailed mythological references or juxtapositions to real-world history. Dominions is also a very thematic game: An example I like to use is Heart Companions of Arcoscephale (a unit inspired by Sacred Band of Thebes) being canonically gay as they are immune to seduction, but while you can find deviations if you look hard enough, generally speaking mechanics down to combat resolution make thematic sense and when combined with the top-notch fluff (and ability to treat myth and history as expanded universe of sorts), the emergent storytelling potential in Dominions is matched only by the likes of Dwarf Fortress and NetHack.
Mechanically, it wouldn't be utterly wrong to call Dominions 4X, but it's certainly not a typical one and Dominions has more in common with board wargames and their computerized versions so "fantasy wargame" might be a more apt description. The map is province-based, turns are simultaneous and combat takes place during turn resolution based on deployment and scripted orders you can set up in advance with replay of the battle viewable the next turn. This style of combat isn't unprecedented (also seen in games like Frozen Synapse) but especially when you consider the scale (potentially hundreds or even thousands of troops all handled as individuals), it's fairly unique, and besides being a nice change of pace from the more typical omniscient control, it has several key advantages: Predicting enemy tactics and devising a counter in advance becomes paramount and seeing a good plan pay off in a decisive victory is extremely satisfying while anticipating those results is a huge thrill. It more closely captures the decision-making process of a historical commander even if they didn't have magical nukes or battlefield-wide mind control spells at their disposal (or gods fighting on their side). And perhaps most importantly, it enables simultaneous turns, making Dominions extremely well-suited to multiplayer. There is little to no development of provinces and no civilian research: instead, magical research effectively acts as the tech tree that allows you to broaden your strategic and tactical repertoire.
In terms of polish and similar details, I think Dominions by its fifth iteration has reached a good spot, although it obviously is a low production value game. Graphics are perfectly serviceable with clear and easily readable spritework (with a surprising amount of detail on a lot of units if you bother to look) - personally I actually like how the game looks in general despite its undeniably low-tech aesthetic. The soundtrack is solid, although it could use more tracks. Modding doesn't let you alter the core mechanics of the game, but in terms of modding the content, it's very robust and straightforward (plain text files you can edit with the editor of your choice). The UI isn't the prettiest one out there and doesn't adhere to modern ideals but at this point the efficiency is pretty close to local optimum once you figure out the workflow (pro tip: '?' shows all available shortcuts in any given game screen) and I feel it compares just fine against most modern strategy games.
Now that the general description is over, what can I say? Should I focus on actual endgame strategies like indirectly wishing more wishes, breaking dead Titans free from Tartarus and equipping them magical artifacts so as to enable them to wipe out unprepared armies single-handedly, polluting the source of magic with sacrifice of hundreds of virgin girls such that any mage daring to cast a non-blood spell can be detected and tracked by eldritch Horrors, seducing enemy commanders with dryads and then proceeding to rout their leaderless army, or simply buffing your elite troops, making each of them a one-man army? What about discussing the lore in more detail, like how Ermor (Rome) learns death magic from C'tis (Egyptian Lizardmen), inadvertently causing an undead apocalypse and forcing Marignon (Spanish Inquisition) to make a deal with the devil to save the world? Quantity of content (3k+ units, 90 some factions etc)? The multiplayer experience?
Ultimately, it doesn't matter because there's a simpler answer: Dominions has it all. It's undeniably one of the kings of fantasy wargaming, considered one of the greatest strategy/tactics games of all time by many, and at risk of sounding pretentious, I feel it even has value as an "art house game" (ie. you could ignore the exceptional wargame that serves as a vehicle for worldbuilding and simply explore the world the authors have conjured). As of writing this, I have barely touched games other than Dominions 4 for the last half a year, because in my mind they just don't compare, and Dominions 5 seems like a direct upgrade.

The dominions series. I've been a fan since Dominions 3, but, as far as games go, there was a few things that could have been improved.
I'm more than happy to say... It's been DONE.
Major changes from previous version are the combat (not sure it was useful, but it's certainly not detrimental to the game - it helps with cheese "I'm the one that casted the fastest" that was there before though, bonus points here), the recruitment mechanics, and the new bless mechanics.
The recruitment mechanics are awesome. Previously it was good for players to recruit "standard" commanders because it prevented you from recruiting mages. Now, standard commanders can be recruited along with mages. Provinces also have the ability to recruit multiple base commanders.  his is a huge shift in the game as you'll now be able to use the native commanders !
About the new bless effects... Not only there is the possibilty of choosing what effects you want, they also might occur differently depending on province scales ! And there are cross scale blesses too !
Also, smaller point, but... the main menu's been reworked.
One of the deepest and longest running series has just gone better. Fully recommend.
PS: quoted from another review...
"I suggest to activate the multi-turn movement option, as it is great to be able to plan armies movement over several turn, rather than turn by turn."
Ok, it may seems dumb as every other game has had since for ages, but... Dominions hadn't. And now it does. Devs of this game have always been committed but new nations and units had taken most of the attention rather than UI and QoL improvement. I'm happy to see that they focus more on QoL and UI. It was needed.
Another (much needed) QoL that's finally there: national units can now be seen on the nation selection screen INCLUDING the one with terrain recruitment (like the one that can only be recruited in forest for Pangaea for example).
There are probably others.
great all around

This is one of the best games that I've ever played with my friends.
If you have a group of friends that can (somewhat) manage to work together, or even if you dont,
messing around in this game is fun either way!
I have played this game a ton, and here are some of the things I found that make this game so appealing:
+ The levels are randomized every time you play to keep it interesting.
+ Lots of customization with traits, races, pets, hats and stat rolls.
+ EXP is shared! That's right! So if you have that one friend who storms through the level and kills everything while you
are peacefully catching fairies, you get all the EXP that they do too!
+ 3 different "Skill Trees" so to speak, based around Magic, Dexterity, and Strength. So you can be an archer, mage,
warrior, or even try to create a mix between them with the game's varied weapon choice.
+ Many different bosses that will kill you over and over with their plethora of unique, (yet annoying,) skills.
+ Replayability! I want to say that I've beat this game at least 10 times, while I've played it around 50 times. Even if you
beat the final boss, It's never over. There are so many hats and races to unlock that you can invest hours into running
the dungeon over and over with your friends!
+ Level scaling. Don't have any friends? That's ok because they make the game harder anyway! The bigger the number
of players, the stronger the enemies are! But that also means 4 times the resources to compensate.
+ An amazing soundtrack that is both ambient and exciting!
+ While this game has a pixel-style vibe to it, it's still beautiful! The glowing effects, the details in the landscape, the
blood of your enemies on the floor...
+ The game is updated frequently. Tired of running through the same levels over and over? Don't worry! The game
developers release patches and updates very frequently to add new biomes, weapons, races, or even just bug fixes.
Are you sold yet? Yes? Well then before you buy it at least let me tell you about a few problems...
- This game is a work in progress so there are bound to be a few small bugs here and there but they get fixed pretty
quick.
- The mechanic to sell items is still a little unbalanced. (ex. a single stick could be worth 3 gold, and then a diamond
sword could also be worth 2-3 gold.)
- This game IS a rogue-like so if you die, you have to start from the very beggining again. (I personally find this as a
plus, but most of my friends think otherwise.)
- You have to be able to port foward or at least use hamachi if you want friends to join your game. (Again I don't think
this will be much of a problem for most people but i decided to list it anyway.)
- Becase of the random stat roller, it can take a long time to roll good stats with equally good traits, or if you are
looking for a specific build, (Mine is Potion Brewer + Swift).
- Although the developers have been very good about fixing connection issues, some people may still lag or disconnect
from the game, though most of the time that's just because of their internet.
Obviously there are a few more bugs that I haven't mentioned, but they will probably get fixed over time and I didn't want this to just be a bug list.
And that's it! Overall the cons really aren't that bad or game breaking, and I would definitely give this game a try! It's worth the money, and if your friends can afford it, then even better! Now if you'll excuse me, I'm gonna go try to beat the new boss, Axelark III... for the 7th time...

Have you ever been bored in a 4x game?
Like when not enough things are happening in your country/empire and you just skip turns?
Or like when a friend you are cooperating with has something going on (like a war) and you don't, so you are stuck waiting long turns while doing nothing?
Well stellaris will have those examples beat by a mile.
Why? Because unlike in those cases boredom in stellaris doesn't end.
Welcome to the world of infinite boredom – welcome to stellaris.
Regardless of whether the above sounds overly dramatic or not, I know no better description for this game.
It's boredom is infinite and it's infinitely boring.
It's not that nothing is going on in stellaris, something is always going on, but it's always something boring.
Now, I should probably hurry up and “disclaim” something. See, I'm not the kind of person that is easily entertained by one's own imagination. And if you ARE, then probably your experience with stellaris is going to be vastly different from my own. Me, I'm more “grounded” than that, I pay more attention to what's REALLY happening, and, unfortunately, nothing is REALLY happening in stellaris that is worthy of notice.
Let me elaborate.
Stellaris spins a pretty entertaining tale, but it's an “imaginary” one.
You have various species with their own traits and ethics, you can tamper with their traits, play around with ethics, try several approaches to organizing “your” society, delve into synthetic “life”, catch a glimpse into psionics and sprinkle it with some exploration of the unseen.
But there's nothing to really play with in there.
So yeah, you unlocked psionics, big deal, think it's going to make your game any different from the game of that guy over there who didn't? Only in your imagination.
Stellaris is incredibly weak when it comes down to mechanical side of things.
It may tell you epic tales of “krogan uplifting”, but the real gameplay couldn't care less if you uplifted any warrior-like species to fight on the ground for you or not.
You may run into “epic” machine rebellion but more likely than not it'll just end up being a small bump on the road of your galactic snowball.
When it comes down to making the results of those tall tales count stellaris falls flat. None of those supposedly fun features has sufficient impact on the gameplay, and the gameplay itself is not one too look froward to either.
PI went out of their way to get
management out of your way. Unfortunately, and quite predictably (seeing how the two are next to impossible to precisely separate in 4x games), they also took the rest of the management away with it.
If you try your best to manage your empire's economy yourself your game will look like this – you settle/acquire a planet, you make a few easy choices about it's economical makeup, deal with a few nuances here and there, order a building for each slot on it and give it away to a sector and make sure that the sector is not allowed to do anything stupid such as overriding your building choices or building defense stations where you don't want them. Then rinse, and repeat.
If you don't you just stuff everything into sectors and let the sector AI “do the thing”. It's not going to be optimal, but hey, this is stellaris, PI got you covered, you don't need to bother with all the details, or in other words – nobody CARES if your economy is optimal. Long as you maintain the right rates your speed of development isn't going to suffer.
Economy in stellaris is pretty basic. The defining part of your income is defined by your buildings. There's an opportunity to specialize and optimize here and there, but ultimately you just have to build your buildings and you'll be fine.
The above sentence probably doesn't bring across the whole simplicity of the system as well as it should since it's hard to take it as literally as it was meant to be taken, so let me bore you with details for a bit longer.
You see, a typical 4x game will have you balance the economy of each and every settlement individually as well as your empire as a whole. You have to maintain a decent food surplus for food growth, decent production for development speed, and then get some research or money or something else global out of it once it develops. On top of that each settlement is usually unique in it's own way because it has unique circumstances that define it's growth potential and economical quirks. “Oh my, where is that city going to get it's food? but look at all the gold it can bring!” That kind of stuff.
NONE of the above happens in stellaris. Your quirks are, more often than not, barely noticeable - once in a blue moon you may find a planet with +50% mineral income or +40% society research, but don't count on it. Most of the time you just build your damn buildings and let their native impact bring over 70% of your income. And make no mistake, the other “up to 30%” of your income that comes from various bonuses isn't much of a challenge to grab either. On top of that there's practically NO need to balance the individual planet's economy. There's no “production” in stellaris as a resource AT ALL, and the impact of food balancing is rather tame. You get 10% growth speed for every point of food beyond the basic growth speed that you get from having any surplus food at all.
Your balancing is so primitive and typical that it's yawn-inducing – get enough food to support your population, don't bother building more than that. Then grab some bonus minerals that are the most lucrative, ignore the less lucrative ones, then go build up energy until you have a decent enough income of that, and then send the rest towards science – the only resource in this game that doesn't have a cap on how much of it you'd want. That's IT, that's the “depth” of economy in stellaris, and as long as you don't mess up your mineral/energy balancing the rest of snowballing is in the bag. You could try adding a “look at me mommy, my species are thrifty capitalists” element to the mix, but like I said, none of that is going to matter – snowballing in stellaris is a very streamlined process and like in any other 4x game out there, if you've done your snowballing right and your keyboard-walking cat didn't declare a wrong war at the wrong time nothing else matters.
Yes, you'll have to pick the right tech at the right time, yes you'll have to get the right ship designs, the right “political choices” (aka, “who do we munch on, with whom and when”) but those things are supplementary in 4x games, they are important moves and decisions, sure, but they are never difficult moves and decisions and as such aren't particularly fun ones.
There's nothing fun to do in this game other than dreaming of imaginary sheep. If you “get off” on the idea of leading thrifty capitalists or militant xenophobes or peaceful spiritualist to victory and don't actually care if their capitalism/xenophobia/spiritualism actually had anything to with the actual victory then sure, buy it, you'll probably enjoy it.
But if you want to play an actual game where your decisions have an actual impact on it's direction and outcome then move along, nothing to hope for here.

It is all about your "loadout" (right, guys... Girls... Akhem...). In general, the game revolves around you building and customizing  deep♥♥♥♥♥♥crazy weapons and then using them in battle against other players in an 4vs4 arena map with a lot of classical modes with great twists.
Alow me not to waist any of your time and get straight to the pros and cons...
I believe this game has one of the fairest business models a free-to-play game can have at this point. In general, with real cash you can only buy convenience and customization, you cannot buy weapon parts or damage enhancing power-ups that other players would not be able to acquire by only playing the game. In short, this is not a play-to-win game in any sense.
There is an acceptable amount of classical 4vs4 arena modes with great twists. For instance, we have capture the flag. In this game the flag is a hammer with which you can beat up other players. By the way, the more players you kill, the more valuable the hammer becomes – therefore, when you cash the weapon in, you will get more points.
There is a healthy player base and the game is one of the most played games on "Steam". Which means, that if someone disconnects from the game, a new player will join the fight almost immediately.
There is a huge amount of both weapon customization – you can create a healing rocket launcher with x-ray scanner or a bouncing-tesla-projectile sniper shotgun - and character customization – you can make a char that taunts a player by twerking in black lingerie and a tutu.
A unique gory sense of black humor and cartoonish art style that makes both the visuals, character models and maps look gorgeous. For instance, the maps have great details and are very colorful, the death animations are very funny...
I am worried that because of the pros, the general gameplay polish and the fair business model, the game has a lot of success and popularity, but will it be able to add more content when the weaponcraftinhg will become some what boring for someone who has played the game for weeks and is starting to want a bit more.
A lot of people say this game is like TF2. Therefore, those who did not like TF2 just ignore this game in general, but I believe that this game has its own art style, business model and sense of humor indifferent to TF2 (by the way, I did not like TF2, sorry). In short, the fact that some people compare this game to TF2 is doing injustice to it and people should stop doing that.

Peggle is a fun casual game. It's very straightforward. Aim for the orange pegs. Hit the green ones to get various power ups that change every few levels. The power ups are all very different and keep things interesting. Some are not as useful as others like the lobster claw flippers. Each power up makes you think differently about how to approach a level.
As straightforward as the gameplay is, Peggle isn't simple. You only have 10 moves to clear all the orange pegs and it's difficult to predict just where your ball may bounce at times. Most of the time the results are what you aim for, but sometimes the judging an angle slightly wrong can turn into a wasted ball. Other times, you might just get a layout that works against you. While the design is always the same, the placement of orange pegs varies. But that's the challenge of Peggle.
There are 55 levels in the game, so plenty to play through. You can always replay levels of your choice later outside of story mode to try your hand at clearing the entire playing field of all blocks.
I wouldn't really consider Peggle a largely re-playable game. I played through story mode twice on a non-Steam version of the game, and playing through again on Steam didn't really hold my interest. But I would definitely consider this a great game for at least one or two playthroughs that is worth it's price point.
The only negative aspect of this game is the resolution, which is low and doesn't stretch to fit widescreen monitors.

The total war franchise has always been known for its realistic and accurate historical backgrounds.
Medieval 2 is no exception and is possibly the best game of the series,with the exception of the newly released Warhammer. Although the graphics are not mind-blowing(expected as this is an old game), the experience is truly great.
The AI works well enough so that even early on,you can't just throw everything at the walls and see what sticks.
In my opinion what makes it better than Attila or Rome is the fact that not only did those have severe bugs and crashes,the system requirements were pretty unrealistic and very few people actually were happy with it or enjoyed them.
Last,but definitely not least, the modding community is alive and vibrant.
I CANNOT stress this enough, the mods make this game such a joy to play,whether it is the Third Age Total War Lord of The Rings modification which is fabulous or the stainless steel mod which improves the overall play.
Neither the Rome or Attila games have any mods that come near these.
If you can get Warhammer and run it on your PC well,great but otherwise,this is probably the second best game in the series.

Have you ever been bored in a 4x game?
Like when not enough things are happening in your country/empire and you just skip turns?
Or like when a friend you are cooperating with has something going on (like a war) and you don't, so you are stuck waiting long turns while doing nothing?
Well stellaris will have those examples beat by a mile.
Why? Because unlike in those cases boredom in stellaris doesn't end.
Welcome to the world of infinite boredom – welcome to stellaris.
Regardless of whether the above sounds overly dramatic or not, I know no better description for this game.
It's boredom is infinite and it's infinitely boring.
It's not that nothing is going on in stellaris, something is always going on, but it's always something boring.
Now, I should probably hurry up and “disclaim” something. See, I'm not the kind of person that is easily entertained by one's own imagination. And if you ARE, then probably your experience with stellaris is going to be vastly different from my own. Me, I'm more “grounded” than that, I pay more attention to what's REALLY happening, and, unfortunately, nothing is REALLY happening in stellaris that is worthy of notice.
Let me elaborate.
Stellaris spins a pretty entertaining tale, but it's an “imaginary” one.
You have various species with their own traits and ethics, you can tamper with their traits, play around with ethics, try several approaches to organizing “your” society, delve into synthetic “life”, catch a glimpse into psionics and sprinkle it with some exploration of the unseen.
But there's nothing to really play with in there.
So yeah, you unlocked psionics, big deal, think it's going to make your game any different from the game of that guy over there who didn't? Only in your imagination.
Stellaris is incredibly weak when it comes down to mechanical side of things.
It may tell you epic tales of “krogan uplifting”, but the real gameplay couldn't care less if you uplifted any warrior-like species to fight on the ground for you or not.
You may run into “epic” machine rebellion but more likely than not it'll just end up being a small bump on the road of your galactic snowball.
When it comes down to making the results of those tall tales count stellaris falls flat. None of those supposedly fun features has sufficient impact on the gameplay, and the gameplay itself is not one too look froward to either.
PI went out of their way to get
management out of your way. Unfortunately, and quite predictably (seeing how the two are next to impossible to precisely separate in 4x games), they also took the rest of the management away with it.
If you try your best to manage your empire's economy yourself your game will look like this – you settle/acquire a planet, you make a few easy choices about it's economical makeup, deal with a few nuances here and there, order a building for each slot on it and give it away to a sector and make sure that the sector is not allowed to do anything stupid such as overriding your building choices or building defense stations where you don't want them. Then rinse, and repeat.
If you don't you just stuff everything into sectors and let the sector AI “do the thing”. It's not going to be optimal, but hey, this is stellaris, PI got you covered, you don't need to bother with all the details, or in other words – nobody CARES if your economy is optimal. Long as you maintain the right rates your speed of development isn't going to suffer.
Economy in stellaris is pretty basic. The defining part of your income is defined by your buildings. There's an opportunity to specialize and optimize here and there, but ultimately you just have to build your buildings and you'll be fine.
The above sentence probably doesn't bring across the whole simplicity of the system as well as it should since it's hard to take it as literally as it was meant to be taken, so let me bore you with details for a bit longer.
You see, a typical 4x game will have you balance the economy of each and every settlement individually as well as your empire as a whole. You have to maintain a decent food surplus for food growth, decent production for development speed, and then get some research or money or something else global out of it once it develops. On top of that each settlement is usually unique in it's own way because it has unique circumstances that define it's growth potential and economical quirks. “Oh my, where is that city going to get it's food? but look at all the gold it can bring!” That kind of stuff.
NONE of the above happens in stellaris. Your quirks are, more often than not, barely noticeable - once in a blue moon you may find a planet with +50% mineral income or +40% society research, but don't count on it. Most of the time you just build your damn buildings and let their native impact bring over 70% of your income. And make no mistake, the other “up to 30%” of your income that comes from various bonuses isn't much of a challenge to grab either. On top of that there's practically NO need to balance the individual planet's economy. There's no “production” in stellaris as a resource AT ALL, and the impact of food balancing is rather tame. You get 10% growth speed for every point of food beyond the basic growth speed that you get from having any surplus food at all.
Your balancing is so primitive and typical that it's yawn-inducing – get enough food to support your population, don't bother building more than that. Then grab some bonus minerals that are the most lucrative, ignore the less lucrative ones, then go build up energy until you have a decent enough income of that, and then send the rest towards science – the only resource in this game that doesn't have a cap on how much of it you'd want. That's IT, that's the “depth” of economy in stellaris, and as long as you don't mess up your mineral/energy balancing the rest of snowballing is in the bag. You could try adding a “look at me mommy, my species are thrifty capitalists” element to the mix, but like I said, none of that is going to matter – snowballing in stellaris is a very streamlined process and like in any other 4x game out there, if you've done your snowballing right and your keyboard-walking cat didn't declare a wrong war at the wrong time nothing else matters.
Yes, you'll have to pick the right tech at the right time, yes you'll have to get the right ship designs, the right “political choices” (aka, “who do we munch on, with whom and when”) but those things are supplementary in 4x games, they are important moves and decisions, sure, but they are never difficult moves and decisions and as such aren't particularly fun ones.
There's nothing fun to do in this game other than dreaming of imaginary sheep. If you “get off” on the idea of leading thrifty capitalists or militant xenophobes or peaceful spiritualist to victory and don't actually care if their capitalism/xenophobia/spiritualism actually had anything to with the actual victory then sure, buy it, you'll probably enjoy it.
But if you want to play an actual game where your decisions have an actual impact on it's direction and outcome then move along, nothing to hope for here.

I'm a big fan of Paradox games and this is no different. The model of lots of DLC has added a lot to Crusader Kings 2 in my experience, although some may claim the features should have been in the game originally. In this regard it feels like Stellaris is the same, there are features in the game that are so shallow they are verging on uselessness or are very useful but have such huge time constraints as to make them unworkable beyond a small set of circumstances. Terraforming and Gene modding being the prime examples. The latter has uses but if you want to gene mod your entire species on a large scale you can forget it. Terraforming is expensive, takes ages and converts just 1 planet. It is essentially useless.
The fleet combat could also do with work, carriers don't do much because the strike craft they launch don't fly fast enough to get heavily involved before both fleets and blasting the living bejeezus out of each other. Federations could also be great but are again too shallow. Then there are sectors, factions, redundant technologies, excessive micromanagement and poor automanagement where it is used. All of this feels like it will be fleshed out with DLC, which does grate a bit.
Last negative, performance drops drastically late game and a fair few times the game will lock up for a bit. FPS regularly drop down to 30 and I have a pretty good system.
Positives, it is a very fun and addictive game, you can easily spend hours on it and realise you haven't done much more than colonised 2 planets. It may seem strange giving this a postitive review when I've mostly listed negative but it fundamentally is fun but just feels like it has the potential to be much much more.

Dominions 5 is a fantastic game. For anyone interested in strategy games, especially ones that rely more on thinking than clicks-per-minute, the Dominions series is a must. It's great for intense multiplayer games that span weeks, fantasy and history nerds, and the kinds of players who want to obliterate their enemies with powerful magic. Don't let the graphics fool you - if you're looking for excellent, deep strategy, this is your game. Yes, it's a long learning process, but it's easy to take baby steps and start playing the AI after a quick tutorial. You'll get good later, when you learn about more of the systems. There are plenty of great tutorials on Steam and online that can help you get started, and plenty for more advanced players too. The community actively writes strategy guides and makes whole new nations from mods. It's amazing. Buy it if you're looking for a strategy game where you have to use your head.
That's the pitch for new players. For those returning to the Dominions series, it's a tougher sell. The graphics of the maps are improved, they convey more information, and the randomly-generated ones have new features like rivers and bridges. There's some nice new music. The new bless system is an improvement, both for balance and for creativity. I can't tell yet how much the real-time battle system will affect high-level competitive play, but it doesn't seem to make a big difference in typical situations versus the AI. There have been some small improvements to lowering micromanagement, like the new research system and the option to plot moves that will take multiple turns (I enabled it in Preferences). Other than that (and 3 new nations) not much has changed. $36, or $40, depending on when you read this, is a lot to ask for people who own the very-similar Dominions 4. If I were them, and only played casually and in singleplayer, I'd probably hold off on buying 5 until it went on a meaningful sale, maybe this summer.

So first off, if you are even remotely into cars, you should check Automation out. I absolutely love this game, and have since I bought it when it had just come to Steam. That being said, I'm going to start by saying that this game is obviously not complete. However, the devs frequently post updates, and the game has recently moved over to a new engine. However, "more complete" version is the legacy version, running on the Kee Engine. I am going to start by going over some things that are wrong with the legacy version, even though they will hopefully be added in fixed form in the UE4 version with subsequent updates.
I play the "lite campaign" mode in the legacy version almost exclusively. Basically, this mode lets you run a car company, designing vehicles and selling them to the public. I find the challenge of balancing my budget with building desirable cars to be more fun than the sandbox, which is a pure designer module. Now, despite the lite campaign being super fun (to the point where I don't realize I've spent six hours sitting at my computer playing the game), there are some issues. I figure most of these are from limitations to the Kee Engine, or something along those lines, and were I a speculating man, I'd say that was a contributing factor to moving things over to UE4. Despite the move taking place, and despite the fact that these issues are probably already being worked on, I feel the need to talk about them.
So the main thing I dislike about the lite campaign is its instability. I frequently have trouble getting a game past 1980 without a game-ending error. This isn't a huge deal for me, since I would imaine this issue wouldn't be a problem when they release a lite campaign mode for UE4. My next gripe is also a pretty minor one: for all my hours in the campaign, I haven't discovered a way to use the same engine family in multiple models of car. You can share engines between trims, but not entirely different models, regardless of whether the engine would fit in the first place. I'm also not a big fan of the fact that there's no tabs for things like marketing, but it makes sense considering this is the lite version. There also doesn't appear to be a way of hiring more engineers throughout the campaign: the ones you select at the beginning are the ones you're stuck with. Now with this and the engine sharing thing, it's entirely possible I've just overlooked something, and if that's the case, feel free to kick me into a six mile deep borehole as punishment for my wrongness. Another thing I'm not a fan of, and this extends to the UE4 version, is that engine bays in certain vehicles seem too small. I should be able to fit something larger than a 900cc I4 in a notRanger! Also, I wish they would add more styles of engines to the game so I can make really weird stuff: diesels, rotarys, radials (yes, like airplane radials, I FANTASIZE ABOUT PUTTING AN AIRPLANE ENGINE IN A CHEVY CAVALIER), boxers, etc. Oh, and I personally prefer the Kee Engine's graphics and visual style, but I might just be a bit of a luddite.
My complaints are really pretty petty, and I'm a little bit surprised they took up so much space up there, but the pettiness of my complaints just shows how few notable flaws this game actually has. I have to reach to find things I dislike. As far as the things this game does strongly: virtually everything. You can make real-life engine designs in the game, or throw the map into a ravine and design engines based on the UNCHARTED MACHINATIONS OF YOUR MIND. The same is generally true for cars. I often find my vehicles looking like a strange amaglamation of Ford, Pontiac, and sometimes BMW. Whether you want to make crazy supercars or low-quality econoboxes, this game lets you do either with ease. The controls are easy to learn, and the game's interface (for the Kee version anyway) is incredibly informative. Also, when designing engines, you can get a fascinating look at the inner-workings of your creation. I honestly didn't know much about engines when I started playing this game, but I find myself knowing more than most of my friends and coworkers these days.
Make no mistake, this is a great game, and the folks making it are some of the better devs to make use of Early Access. If you're into cars enough that this game is even on your radar, pick it up ASAP. You won't be disappointed.

While I haven't spent much time with the game yet, I have to say I'm a huge fan of the changes so far from the previous iteration.
Dominions 5 features enough new content to justify paying for the new game, and also boasts some excellent UI and graphics improvements that really make the game more appealing to the average gamer. Although it certainly retains a fairly harsh pixel art look you might be accostomed to from the early 2000s, the UI as well as many other visual elements including some units and things like the icons for the various magical paths have been overhauled and look much better now.
The UI itself is much smoother looking, and although I'm not really a fan of the beta project look of the main menu UI, the UI in every other area is much improved from Dom 4.
The changes to movement, combat, and how bless effects work are what I'm really excited about though. The new bless system is far more flexible and complex than before, and I think will create many more interesting choices in standard gameplay, as well as better options for modding.
The addition of new movement options really increases the number of nations that can actually move one tile at a time, something that felt like it was true of almost all non-flying nations in Dom 4 due to the prevalence of alternate terrain.
I'll add to this as I test out more stuff, but as a huge fan of Dom 4 coming into the next game, I'm really happy with the changes.

Let's make one thing clear before somebody gets the idea of looking at my friends list - yes, I do have the author of the game in there. I am not actually affiliated with him in any reasonable way, aside from exchanging a few words now and again. Nonetheless, my opinion might be biased, that's why I'll try to explain it in detail. Oh, and I have finished the game when it wasn't on Steam yet.
So, first of all, a word of warning: The Moon Sliver is a game strongly focused on telling you a story, with very light puzzle elements. It stands somewhere between Gone Home in focus on freedom of movement and exploration and Dear Esther in telling a mysterious story which is quite open to interpretation. If this is something you are not into - not a game for you. If, however, previously named titles got your attention - read on. Or just buy the bloody thing, it's as expensive as two bottles of beer and my recommendation thingy glows somewhere around these words anyway.
Right, you're still reading. First of all, I stand by the comparisons I have made above, so I'll use them as a baseline. At first, you're likely to notice two things - quite apparently lower production values and fantastic music. To elaborate: In terms of graphical design and fidelity, the game is not nearly as flashy as games like Dear Esther or Gone Home might be.
Graphics are quite spartan, yet very functional. I feel that the simplicity of the graphical presentation is often enough used to set a feeling of loneliness and desperation, which it does quite well. At any rate, if pretty is what you're looking for, I'm sad to say that's not part of the package, and repetitive assets don't help much.
Music, on the other hand, is quite wonderful. It sets the tone very nicely and is used to underline the desired mood of individual locations.
When it comes to most important bit of the game, the storyline, I find that the less you know when you start it, the better. Suffice to say it's captivating and definitely kept me playing all the way until the end of the game, which is not a particularily long journey, nonetheless long enough for me to lose interest in most games. Writing is very good, and aside from the way it handles reading notes (no, there's no voice acting, just a lot of quality writing), I was very happy with it.
The story is told both trough enviromental cues you can see in various locations and notes and books as already mentioned. You will also run across a few simple puzzles and the entire game is based around exploration of a small, yet very open island - you will not see the linearity of Dear Esther here, you can go just about anywhere, at any time you want, altho some locations require information obtained at other ones.
Right, I have opened the subject earlier, but I feel I should elaborate on it a little more - the game is short. Even by Gone Home standards short. You'll beat it in under hour and a half, and you don't really have much of a choice in the matter as it doesn't support save states. The game is designed to be beaten in one sitting tho, and it's hardly too long, so that should not be an issue.
All in all, The Moon Sliver was an experience worth remembering, and that's more than I can say for most games that I have played recently. For the asking price, you're hardly even taking a risk, so if I got you even slightly interested, just go for it.

Gonna keep this review short and simple.
Music 10/10
First off,  the soundtracks are amazing. Like seriously amazing. Every areas in this game have distinguish theme music. And  the songs are cut into parts as you progresses the map. Once you reach a certain area, the music and tone changes to suit the game. Truly amazing soundtrack throughout the whole game.
Plot 9/10
As many may know, the game comes with 5 canon ending. Finishing the game once is literally just finishing the prolouge. At first the game throws us with questions, mystery and conflicts. Only by achieving all the ending one may understand what this game really means. Is simple, yet deep. As you may know from the title, you play as an android in this game, with sole aim to protect humans that have fled to the moon due to machines and aliens invasion. Ironically this game makes me thinks that the androids in this game are more humane than most human irl. Character development might be weird. But this is because the game is separated into 5 endings. You have to complete the whole game in order to truly understand the characters. Just when you thought you know the characters well enough after finishing Ending A, Ending C throw in some new characters development, and perspective you will havent see before. Mind you, though I say the game are separated into 5 endings, it doesnt means replaying the game 5 times. I have to commend the developers that the fact this game budget is low, yet they manage to recycle the game map and reuse it to tell another story. you wont be like, "hey this map area is awesome" then a few minutes later you wont be coming back to this place. No. This game reuse the maps, and each area in this game have big impact towards the game development. Heck, Nier Automata map size is so small than it might be smaller gta vice city's map. But really the amazing plot is what makes up the map size by giving more impactful meaning to the game map.
Gameplay 10/10
Plantinum Games. Nuf said. The combat is so fluid. And the enemies you encounter might not be as diversed as games like Dark Souls, but really what the game lacks in diversity they make it up by adding more difficulty combat situatuion. For example you started by combating some small enemies, which is quite easy to kill them. Then later on you encounter flying enemies. You have to dodge and at the same time shoots down the enemies. Then as the game progresses, they mix in many types of enemies to you to deal with it. This makes combat never boring. It might be the same old enemies you met before, but the situations are never the same. Oh and the weapons. God thats awesome. As 2B you be able to use two weapons, one for light attack one for heavy attack. The game have 4 classes (5 if you count bare hands as a class) Spear, one handed sword, two handed sword and gauntlet. by changing the weapons, 2B's attack changes. You could try out many crazy combos by changing your weapons during combat. For me personally I prefer using two one handed swords, and when theres a crowd of enemies, i changes to 2handed sword and spears to clear the crowd of enemies. And the side quests, never once in my life as gamer I try so hard to finish the side quests, in other games, side quests are mostly quests to grind ur characters or get more materials to improve your characters, While this game is the same, the main reason of me doing all the side quests are because the side quests give you a whole new perspective of the game. Every side quest are filled with meaningful impactful plot. While it is not compusolry to finish all quests, the quests itself is the main reason why I love this game so much.
Characters 9/10
2B♥♥♥♥♥joke asides, the game characters are really "humane". Though this time Automata have smaller cast than the original Nier, I have no complains as this smaller cast manage to make it up with more focused developments. Dont wanna spoil the game, playing this game without spoilers is the best way to enjoy the character developments. The charaacter design might be a bit oversexualized, but hey is a Yoko Taro's game. What would you expect? XD
Port 9/10
While many will disagree that nier is a good port, for me, i havent encounter any crashes at all. my junk laptop, which is far below from the required system, manages to play the game in medium setting 30-50fps.
Final rating 9.9/10
This game will stay in my heart forever. There's no other games that manage to captivate my heart so much. Hopefully after the success of Automata, Square enix gonna remake Nier in HD.

The BEST total war followed by Rome 1, Hands down. I put hundreds of hours into this game and Shogun 1, Shogun 2, Rome 1, and Medieval 1, mostly on disk versions before Steam. These games contains my some of my fondest childhood video gaming memories. Medieval 2 in particular was always special to me. The multiple unit textures, the setting, visual armor upgrades, new world conquest, mods it all was great!
PROS
+Great soundtrack, it really lends to the battles
+End of Dark Ages to early Renaissance time period
+Great battle system
+Awesome/funny in game movies
+Beautiful 3D tactical map
+Lots of building depth
+Roughly 20 factions
+Invasions
+Crusades/Jihads
+New world exploration
+Many units and unique units. New unit types unlock as years progress and some become outdated.
+Multiple textures for units, gone are the days of units filled with clones
+VIsible unit and settlement upgrades (on battlefield, armor/castle/wall upgrades)
+Realistically paced battles that allow you to plan your battles with tactics, so even if you are outnumbered say 1000-3000, you can still win if you take up a good defense (a hill) and perform flanking maneuvers all while pouring arrow hell down on the enemy. Battles don't last 10 minutes like in Shogun, so you have to make sure you have time for a battle!
+Available mods. Too many to name... I usually play Stainless Steel or Custom Campaign. Also, don't like every turn taking up 2 years? Change one line of code in the games notepad code to get 2 turns per year for 400+ turns!!
+Tons of cities to take
+Royal Lineage
+Diverse battle maps (generate from where you are on 3D tactical map)
+Kingdoms Expansion (Essential for some mods)
NEUTRAL
=The diplomacy isn't the greatest thing, heck, the newer Total Wars are probably worse, but it gets the job done for a game that is 10 years old.
=Trade, which can net you tons of extra income if used, is like a reworked version of the assassin mechanic
=Rebels could have had more depth, or even became new countries that would expand
CONS
-AI can be lacking. You can tweak the ai with mods though. Otherwise pump the battle AI to Very hard and put campaign AI to Hard, this will give you a good challenge without mods.
-The AI can sometimes spam massive amounts of units within a short amount of time, even if they have one city. Probably to compensate for AI being dumb at times.
-Repetitive seige maps
-A couple of silly units (Sherwood archers....). Some mods get rid of them and make the game more realistic.
-No faction reemergences, like they had in Medieval 1, so when a faction is gone, its gone. This makes late game a slugging match between a few factions, instead of multiple factions duking it out still (Like in real life, Knights of Honor or Crusader Kings)
-Bridge battles are kind of one sided, towards you. The AI has a tendency to rush into small places sometimes, getting slaughtered in the process.
Overall Medieval 2 Total War is one of the best in the series and you'll have loads of fun charging cavalry into exposed infantry, seeing knights hack each other to pieces and unloading into Aztecs with gunpowder all while being enamored by the glorious soundtrack! This is just to name a few moments out of the hundreds that this game will give you. If you call your self an Strategy gamer and haven't played this game, you've missed out on a classic!

(First of all, in the time that this was written, the game had just received an update after nearly a year, this is because one of the developers had a baby and they had to pause in the development. So if you read any more negative reviews that were made before or around the time this review was made, if they mention anything about the developers not updating, this is why.)
Delver is a simple roguelike dungeon crawler that is, I believe, heavily influenced by games like DOOM and Zelda.
The objective of the game is to enter a procedurally generated dungeon (Different every time) that consists of several floors with different themes, get the treasure, and return to the surface safely.
I don't want to spoil to much, because Delver, I think, is supposed to give you a feeling of wonder, suspense, and the unknown. And, despite being very simple, I feel it somehow does this very well, even after playing the game multiple times. Which I think is why I love it so much. The game is somewhat difficult, maybe even unfair at times, but hey, why would the enemy make it fair in the first place?
And also, that is part of the mystery, sometimes, dungeons are full of loot and as you make your way down, you will eventually become nearly invincible, other times, you really have to just make do what you have, and sometimes the traps and the general layout of the dungeon is a real pain in the butt. so, basically, the games difficulty is different EVERY TIME. Which, personally, I think is brilliant. But of course, I highly doubt anyone will be having any competitions with this for $10,000 anytime soon. Which is OK.
I cannot express the feeling of winning this, especially for the first time. It makes my day even more than cookies do.
Which is saying a lot. I challenge you to beat Delver, if you dare. But remember, it was hidden away for a reason.

Well done in comparison to most early access titles, Delver manages to keep a simplistic approach to gameplay yet keeps you coming back for more runs. The game allows little room for building your character as you progress, and you are left at the game's mercy when it comes to gear. As you progress deeper into the games dungeon, your play style will rely almost solely on what weapons and armor you find and your luck with the random level generator.
Still, the game is a real-time roguelike experience, and much like classic roguelikes, you will often find yourself backpedaling into doorways while trying to kite varied and numerous enemies. It's easy to catch yourself reserving all of your ranged attacks (wands rely on finite charges and bows rely on a rare stock of arrows) for dire circumstances, while searching constantly for a better melee weapon. Armor can be hit or miss, and is often a trade-off between movement speed and protection (both of which are very effective).
From death to death, your gold will carry over. The only opportunity to buy items and spells is at the beginning of each run. While the dungeon is currently very short (only seven floors), the environments are nicely varied and the randomly generated rooms keeps it feeling fresh with each attempt. It's worth the price.

In a sea of same-ish games, Wildstar stands out as a unique, witty and fun individual of a game. There's a sense of style and atmosphere that carries through every aspect of the game, and even in 'scary' parts of the game, it is uniquely fun. I specifically mean the game has a sense of humor and a definitive sense of self. You can get as much or as little out of the game as you want, with game content that you can tailor to how you prefer to play. I personally love the rich lore, and the absolutely mind-blowing freedom of the player housing system they have created. But even the awesome housing isn't just there for looks: it can also help you gain rested experience faster, or give you access to useful quality of life features such as portals to zones you frequent, crafting stations, and so on.
While no community is perfect, the community of players I have encountered in WIldstar are above and away some of the most helpful and friendly people I have met, especially in an MMO setting. There's the occasional troll or jerk, not trying to claim there isn't, but there are far more people who are willing to answer your questions and help you get to where you need to go or help you figure things out when you're stuck. There is even literally an /advice chat channel for this purpose, but even if you ask in the local zone chat more often than not you will receive quick assistance.

Last but not least, the developers are actually in the game and they DO listen. I have never seen such quick fixes to changes that the community ultimately disliked or encountered glitches with. I have also never before had the opportunity to run dungeons of PVP battlegrounds with game developers, but now I can say that I have many times.

I highly encourage you to give the game a try. The worst you lose is 30 minutes of download time, and absolutely no money. I have willingly setup a recurring subscription to this game and have no intention of stopping my subscription because I absolutely love what Wildstar has to offer, and sincerely hope to see it continue to do well.

If you like Dominions 4, you should buy Dominions 5. If you don't like Dominions 4, you should not buy Dominions 5. If you never played Dominions 4 at all, you should think long and hard before buying this game.
Not that it's a bad game. Far from it, it's a fantastic game once you get into it. But it's one of those games that's simply not meant for everyone. If you need high-quality graphics in your games, forget about it. If you need a cinematic experience, forget about it. If you need a good story in your games, forget about it. If you need a game that you can just pick up and play, forget about it. If you need a game that'll slowly teach you how to play as you move along, forget about it. If you need a game that requires no effort, forget about it. If you need a game that rewards your effort in any way other than the thrill of victory, forget about it.
If you're ready for a game that requires you to take your time, learn, think, and plan. If you're ready for a game with literally hundreds of races, units, spells and items and it doesn't even have the decency to tell you which ones are good and which ones are bad. If you're ready for a game that at times will leave you disgusted and frustrated, or suck up hundreds of hours of your life, or even both at the same time. If you're ready for a game which promises nothing but hollow offline matches against a barely-capable AI and maybe the glory of a few online victories if you even get that good... Then sit down, and prepare to enter the magical realm of Dominions 5.

I am this kind af player that waits for years after the release of a game before buying it, during some sale, but not this one : Dominions 5 is the first game I bought Day One.
I was introduced to the series with the 3rd game, and played it for hundreds of hours. Then again for the 4th. And now it is time for the 5th.
The changes between each are subtle, but make a huge difference when you switch back to the old one.
In Dominions 5, you play as the god of a nation, ranging from primitive, loincloth-wearing men-bats armed with clubs to ice giants, pious knights or even toad-fishes lurking the depths. You have to manage the military, magic and religious aspects of you empire, and have to get rid of evildoers (aka anyone that does not worship you)
This game will not take you by hand : you will have to put an effort to learn the game by yourself, although tutorial video are now available on the game's website. But most subtilities will be learned with time playing, and you will have to develop your own strategies to beat independants, IAs, and finaly other humans. You will learn not to rely on your troops but rather on your mages, take into account the ever-present randomness and overcome it, and adapt to any situation given your more or less limited options.
Last but not least : contrary to a lot of strategy games, you cannot control your troops during battles, and must carefully plan their positions and orders prior to combat, whereas many unexpected events will disrupt your well-oiled strategy. Hence my remark on randomness.

What a jewel! This game is deeper than deep - it is vast. In my humble opinion it is the best fantasy strategy game I know and one of the best strategy games in general.
Why?
You have near endless stragic possibilities, a deep nation setup based on the countless myths of our planet (celtic, german, indian, mayan, greek roman, middle eastern, northern, chinese, japanese and many more) and the battles need your tactical brilliance.
It is a world to dive into. Join the growing community and learn about myths, strategic brilliance and tactical finesse. You'll have a steep learning curve but you will enjoy a deep experience like no other.
So what is new in dominions 5 compared to previous titles of the series? Apart from a great new soundtrack (really beautiful), better graphics, an improved random map generator, further content (like new units and nations, random events, etc.), improved user interface, a new combat system was implemented (now real time and thus more realistic battles) and many inner mechanics were overhauled, streamlined and in my view perfected.
One example of these changes is the complete overhaul of the bless system. The mighty being you play in this game in your strive to godhood blesses his sacred followers (the priests and holy units (mages/commanders/warriors) of your nations. How these blesses function and what they do was streamlined. But also the mechnics were improved. For example that the most powerful blesses only work on your faithful sacred minions when you, the god pretender, is alive (when you die in game you can be called back by your priests what costs time) is new and makes perfect sense as well as keeping your pretender alive even more important than in Dominions 4 and before.
Another (minor) example is the unit log that you now have. The game keeps track of the actions every unit in the game did in the unit tab. So if you have one of your heroes or mighty summoned beings or even a "lowly" slave unit that you feel close to your heart (as it by chance chopped off the head of the mighty scorpion king that tried to pillage your jucy high income province :)) you can browse through his history and see what he did throughout the game in your glorious conquest.
The two guys behind of illwinter that are the creators of the Dominions series (backed by a growing and decdicated community) have shown in the past that they continuosly improve their products (Dominions and Conquest of Elysium series mainly) for many years. Its predecessor Dominions 4 has up to now 31 updates, fixing bugs, polishing the game (ai etc), delivering new nations, units, spells and so forth. This is more than good support to say the least. Thus, do not hear to people telling you that just a few things changed and that Dominions 5 is just a Dom 4 plus that costs a bunch of money. That's not true. It is worth every PENNY!
See you around as Zeus, a fourth armed Indian Goddess of destruction, a giant squid in the sea or in whatever embodiemened you chose to claim for ascension. ;-)
And now excuse me - I,  Tauron, Master of the Rock, the Hidden One, Nourisher of the fields (the game gives you names depending on how you design your pretender being) must return to my holy and rigthous cause to banish all other Pretenders to become - you know what.

The Dominions series is the best example I can imagine of designers creating a compelling world in their heads and then completely translating that world to the digital realm, to the point where the digital realm starts to take on an existence of its own.  The Dominions series has been steadlily improving in terms of game concepts and game interface since the very first game, and now with Dominions 5 it is more polished than ever.  But the polish doesn't obscure any of the wonderful facets of the game at all.  Highly recommended.

Finally I will review this game.
Where do I start? This, like so many Ubisoft titles, is heartbreaking to think about because the devs wasted potential. A game that would have been excellent had the devs spent more time fixing its issues instead of throwing the game out the door to get their money. I guess they wanted to because the game was in development for a while so it's quite understandable.
Future Soldier is a title that stands out in the Ghost Recon series because of its shift from being a tactical shooter to a stealth-action title. Tactics are stripped away in favour of clearing out areas of enemies. Well, mostly. Some areas can be "ghosted" meaning you don't HAVE to take anyone out but most of the time you'll find yourself taking out enemies with the "sync shot" a new mechanic that when you tag 4 people, shoot someone in the head and the rest of the 3 ghosts will do as well. It's a nice mechanic that works well and makes you feel like a special ops soldier.
There is a lot of action in this game though Ubisoft overused the "we're at the end of a level and we need a shootout!" thingy. They are spectacular though, with tons of explosions and the loud noises of your teammates shouting over gun fire.
Now the problems. Ever since Splinter Cell Conviction, all the cover systems in Ubisoft games are crap. Future Soldier has an unresponsive cover system so moving out of cover is quite obnoxious when the extremely DUMB enemies are flanking you and this results in a ton of frustrating and unneccessary deaths. Prepare to reload checkpoints a lot and this is made worse  as the challenges are stupid and make no sense. There's a challenge where you have to snap 40 necks. What??!!! Future Soldier doesn't have the mechanics for this challenge; it's not a Splinter Cell game. The Ghosts move clunkily and super slow and the enemy placement is meant for you to shoot them, not melee. Another example is in the same level where the "40 neck snap challenge" is, there's one that requires you to kill all the enemies stealthily at a certain point in a level. The problem is, the enemy placement is so stupid taking them all out without getting detected requires luck!
A stupid, unneccessary score system is implemented but has no purpose nor does it give you incentive to get 100/100. It just feels tacked on and unfinished. There aren't any level leaderboards!
Weapons can be customized extensively but you have to unlock attachments by completing challenges.
Now onto the multiplayer. This is where the tactics are. There's no TDM but a few modes. One that involves capturing points on the map. There's also a mode where you don't respawn! Team play and not dying frequently are required so if you suck, sorry for you but you'll most likely cause your team to lose. There aren't "perks" but the gadgets make up for this. An example would be a turret that fires at enemies automatically or a sensor grenade that highlights enemies. Unfortunately, the multiplayer has died so finding a match is hard so if you buy it now, you won't be able to get much practice.
There's also Ghost Recon's take on "Horde" mode where you fight waves on enemies; 50 of them. You can play with or without other people. Tedium starts to settle in at about 10 waves though.
But to sum this review up, Ghost Recon Future Soldier is a great change to the series, a neccessary one to keep up with a newer generation of gamers. The new features and improved shooting mechanics should provide a foundation for next titles to come. But because of its problems, it's not worth full price at $19.99 so better buy this when it's on sale. It's a dissapointment though and there are times I am shaking my head at how Ubisoft couldn't fix many of its flaws.
6/10.

The game is boring.
It's fun at first. It's an amusing premise, and the first few levels offer no shortage of fun "traps" to blow people up, poison them, electrocute, etc, places to hide, escape routes - basically you get a bunch of different options and ways to approach the level.
But that's only the first few levels.
The game quickly reaches the point where you can kill a few people with some traps at the start, but for the (literal) over 40 other people you end up standing next to the one re-useable trap on the level waiting for people to stand next to it or fall asleep near it.
To make matters worse, often after going through this monotonous grind, slowly using the same trap on 40/50 people, you invariably get spotted and arrested for some totally random-seeming ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t reason, forcing you to start all over again from the start of the level.
And there really isn't any other strategy at all.
You can't reliably lure people to specific areas.
You can't use disguises except as a consumable one-use item that you only get sometimes (rng).
You don't have any sort of inventory of different items.
You have to kill 50+ people per level but usually there's only one place to hide one body or none at all
There's almost never places where you can hide or "blend in"
There's a lot of rng - but it doesn't make the levels more interesting or replayable, just frustrating: to give you an idea, there are some items that are really useful - you can kill a lot of people at once with a smoke bomb, for example. There are two ways of getting items - a briefcase, which is rng if it spawns on some levels, and a dealer, who is rng to spawn on all levels. Each one only gives one random item, and you can end up with something completely useless.
The AI is simultanously unforgiving yet brain dead.
People do not react at all to you setting or using the traps. You can literally stand in front of everyone on the party boat pushing people into the water with no consequence. There's so much stuff that you can do in front of people that they just don't react to at all, that it's really hard to actually care or be immersed because they just don't act like people at all.
And yet, largely because of the points above about how you basically can't do anything, it's pretty easy to get spotted in the general vicinity of a corpse, and have the cops called on you. You're supposed to run away from the cop until he gets tired, but his run speed is faster than you (the protagonist would lose a footrace to a CoD:MW protagonist) and many later levels are too open or too small to actually do that. The cop does not go to the place you were last seen, instead he beelines to you no matter what you do. Unlike something like Hitman or Splinter Cell or even MGS you cannot kill your way out of a sticky situation if you're skilled enough.
Basically as a sandbox stealth game, it's garbage.
Stick with that new hitman^tm that IO interactive died for, all the eps are out at this point.
(Don't get me wrong, I'm not saying a stealth game needs to be sandbox - it would've been cool if the levels in this game had been more like a puzzle you need to solve. But this game tries to be a sandbox stealth game without actually giving you various ways to approach the challenge.)
However, massive props to the people who made the cutscenes, they look great. The story is interesting and delivered in an entertaining and amusing way, but unfortunately I can't bring myself to slog through the gameplay to see how it ends.

The thing about Paradox games, they are like decent alcohol. You can drink it fresh and get burnt, or let it age and enjoy the flavors. If CK2 and EUIV are anything to go by, by 2018, Stellaris will be the premier 4x Space Game.
I recommend it now, but I suggest looking through the workshop, you'll find many decent things.

Still telling gaps, war is boring at times, the 1.6 inital patch was a ♥♥♥♥ing diaster, and the 1.7.2 patch was a mess, althought they fixed that quickly. I have high hopes still, but a year in, you have to accept that paradox moves slowly when fixing the game.
At least the mods make up for it.

This game is an indie game with a very unique approach. Your protaganist is a normal guy who apparently wants to sleep so he sets out to murder every one and their grandmother  on every party in the whole city and beyond. At least thats's you characters description but the story it self revolves around a psycho thriller tale about a serial killer and a cop who is desperatly trying to stop him until the  plot twist at the end of the game. It's all tongue and check filled with black humour. The gameplay is very laid back and you should have a lot of patience at certain time's to achieve your goal. You use traps to lur in innocent victims to their final doom or you use your knife to murder them directly but beware of bystanders who will immediatly call the cops if they see a corpse. If you stand right next to someone's lifeless body the police force will hunt you down but sometimes someone else gets framed for the murder so that guy pays for your action which leads to pretty funny moments. There are also random encounters which are  hilarious, a zombie herd could invade the party or you could call a chainsaw wielding maniac to do some dirty work for you, before he gets arrested. The the art style in this game is great if you are into old school pixelgraphics and over the top pixel blood violence. The soundtrack reminded me of hotline Miami's score and to me that is just awsome and absolutly suitable for the occasion.
On the downside are some minor bugs and the AI has it`s ups and downs. In my 7 hours of playtime I only had one gamebreaking glitch that lead to a situation where the cops could not be called by anyone and at the end of the leven I got a freeze frame. Got worse problems with AAA titles, I am looking at you Fallout 3.
Overall: I had a good time with party hard, if you ever plotted to kill your noisy neighbours due to their tendency to party hard every night, this is the game for you ;D
