I waited a long time. I had no faith in the game and waited until I could buy it for less than $10.
The game, as far as mechanics and play, is the exact same as 2 with air management and butt slamming added. None of the characters are fleshed out in more than a few snippets of history and consequentially you don't care about them at all. Every side character is also sporadically added and act as if they care about you even though you talk to many of them for only a mission or two. Literally every person in this game (that isn't from a previous title) is a throw away and feels like a throw away.
The enemies are nothing to write home about and the plot is very short, very sparse on details and still manages some plot holes. The worst part is Jack's "Transformation". They gave practically no reason or build up or even progression to Jack's personality. He went from nice guy to homicidal maniac in practically one mission. I had a random guess on his origin story and as quickly as I put that together, it was way better than what we got.
The writing is horrible in this title. The jokes are not funny, the characters are not engaging or entertaining, the plot manages to be badly constructed despite having very little substance and the overall run of the game is more tedious than either previous title.
Everything I said was bad but the game wasn't a travesty, just very bad. I'd say it is a 4/10. If you really want more Borderlands while you wait for a true sequel and you've worn out the last two games then I'd say go ahead and run through this one in 10-ish hours if you can get it on a big sale. Don't pay more than $15 for this title.
tl;dr 4/10 only buy it if you REALLy want something Borderlands, you've played the others, and this is on sale for under $15.

Okay, I've re-written this review about three times now? This is the fourth. I just can't decide on exactly what it is that makes this game so much more inferior. Now, before I start, this is probably gonna be long. Also, I went into this game with a very positive attitude, because, hey, Borderlands 2! AGAIN? That sounds awesome to me. Plus, you get to play with Jack. He's an ally.
Okay, but this is already where the game starts to fail. It seems to me 2k Australia kind of wanted to show Jack's eventual 'turn to the dark side' or whatever. He goes from a pretty normal guy (they subtitle him as 'in over his head' which I found interesting) I guess to slowly over the course of - okay, no. There are two specific instances which I remember, the only two which are really important.
Prepare your♥♥♥♥♥for spoilers - but it's Borderlands, so, who cares.
Jack flushes a bunch of scientists who you literally just spent like 20 minutes helping out for loot and other reasons out of an airlock. One of these self-same scientists mentions off hand one of them may or may not be a traitor. This is never elaborated on after the scientists are all killed off. And this is a point where the narrative... ♥♥♥♥s up. If one of them was, or was not betraying Jack for money or just because he's apparently evil, whatever, it's never explained after. But Jack murders them all on a whime, and we're apparently meant to kind of side with Lilith and Roland on this (who are visibly disturbed by the event)?
Spoilers end here, I guess.
Anyway, the second kind of event, is where Jack is tricked (hey, I can be non-specific here) into obliterating the station's big laser which has been chewing up the planet for ages now. None of this is a spoiler. The laser comes on almost as soon as you're on Elpis. Anyway. Jack goes a bit crazy after this happens, emphasising how 'the weapon was lost' and this is important, because he cares only about the loss of the weapon. The weapon being a big scary doom laser.
This is pretty much where Jack becomes evil, because he starts swearing vengeance on certain persons with whom the player will be quite familiar, and presumably attached.
Anyway, I'm explaining all this, because, eh, I guess for a 'villain' who really isn't all that bad, his 'origin story' isn't very full on. Jack doesn't lose anything, except for a big laser weapon. Jack just wants to burn every bandit camp to the ground, and kill the people who wronged him. Is that so evil? I dunno.
Onto the actual game. So you've got like 6 classes to pick, because you bought the season pass like a smart cookie. I played Nisha. Nisha is a lot of fun, because her ult autoaims critical spots for you, and - theoretically of course - if you had a bind to spam LMB as fast as can be with a Jakobs pistol - of which you get two, one in each hand with a certain skill - you could do a lot of damage very quickly. Very very quickly. As in, taking bosses down in seconds quickly. So this is all good here.
Cars suck♥♥♥♥♥ I hate them. It's MISERABLE driving around Elpis, and after playing Borderlands 2 I see why. I think 2k Australia either didn't have enough time to smooth the terrain in drivable areas enough, or simply didn't think to do it, because oftentimes you'll be driving, and then go into an uncontrollable spin out or something because you hit a bump in the road. It's ♥♥♥♥ing terrible, but thankfully you get the strictly superior hovercraft not too much later. And you NEED the hovercraft to get to certain areas you literally cannot go otherwise, so in every way... it's just an upgrade. Once you have it, you'll NEVER go back. And I hate that.
You can't even drive in every area. After a certain point, it's like they forgot to put in car stations, some of the areas are HUGE, despite you not being able to drive there. It sucks. Also, another thing, they stopped putting vending machines everywhere, suddenly they are so damn rare it's just inconvenient, the same with fast travel stations. Why's it so ♥♥♥♥ing hard to simply have fast travel everywhere? If you're not going to have cars, have fast travel. It's an incredible chore to walk around in this game.
Furthermore, jesus christ, bandit camps are now a serious pain. You'll walk away or respawn or something, and the second you walk back, they've respawned. Dudes would respawn a few at a time in previous games, maybe, usually you'd have to reload the area or whatever though to get everything to properly reset. As it should be. Doesn't feel that way in TPS, most of the time I spent in this game was refighting the same enemies I literally just killed because I have to backtrack, or fight through them, again, because of a crappy death or something...
And wow do the last areas suck, they basically take the shape of a massive underground dungeon that just goes on, and on, and on, forever. FOREVER. I hate it so goddamn much, because I appreciate the grandiose nature of such places, but it sucks having to walk past all of that♥♥♥♥♥♥ Especially since the whole time, I was being led on. I thought I'd like, walk in here, bam, boss. But no, the game has that sense of suspense the whole way through here. You know the one. The whole, 'this is really the end of the game' kind of feel. Also, what's with the pacing? You fight a big boss, and then maybe half an hour later, the final boss. Why aren't the bosses spread out better?
Okay, so let's talk about the characters I guess. They suck. All the new, original ones brought in by 2k Australia? I hate pretty much all of them. I like Nisha, she's cool I guess. But like, Springs? Screw her, she's so goddamn ♥♥♥♥ing annoying. Her voice just ♥♥♥♥ing kills me every time I hear her, just wish she'd shut up. I can't really think of anyone else I really cared about, and that's never a good thing. Nobody else was memorable enough for me to care about, hatred or otherwise. All the returning ones however, are still great. But why's everyone suddenly homosexual all of a sudden? What the ♥♥♥♥? Maybe Australia shouldn't be allowed to ruin games anymore. And yes, I AM Australian. I think the Americans know games better than us.
Let me elaborate a bit. Springs is definitely a lesbian. That seems pretty clear. It's very clearly shouted at us on at least one count. Sir Hammerlock mentions a boyfriend? Wtf? I guess I can't really think of many other examples, but when you think about exactly how many characters there actually are in this game, like, maybe half a dozen or something if that? It's more noticeable when you see these kinds of, uh, things, in a game like this. Honestly, most of the relationships ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that gets thrown in here and there during TPS just pisses me off and I don't even WANT to hear it. This is a game about GUNS AND LOOTING. I don't CARE that Springs just got the 'echo number' or whatever of the pretty lady we just rescued. Jesus christ. It's not even 'good for you girl' it's just 'I SHOULD NOT BE HEARING YOU GO ON ABOUT THIS'.
Right, let's see, what else. Oh yeah. Oz kits. I prefer relics. Simple as that. I hate the gravity in this game, it's unbelievably annoying. Takes a while to get used to, as well. And it's inconsistent, too. Cars jump like they're on Pandora, but you jump like you're on the ♥♥♥♥ing moon? LITERALLY. BECAUSE YOU ARE ON THE MOON. WHY DO CARS STILL HAVE THEIR GRAVITY FROM PANDORA? I guess they could never have made it work otherwise, because the cars need that weight to, you know, ACTUALLY ♥♥♥♥ING WORK. And I'm not going to get into the whole, 'cars need air' thing, because, cars very obviously keep you supplied with air. I think they can supply themselves with it. But that's not even the thing. The game needs gravity on the cars to actually have them work at all. Simple as that. Therefore, I guess they probably couldn't have fixed this anyway. OR THEY COULD JUST NEVER HAVE HAD CARS IN THE FIRST PLACE MAYBE?
Also, character limit. I had more to say, too. Shame.

A good but overpriced standalone Borderlands 2 expansion pack.
PROS:
+ Cryo element
+ Laser weaponry
+ Solid soundtrack
+ Low-gravity combat
+ Much better-written Jack
+ Same effective, addictive gameplay
+ An actually compelling story for once
+ Playable characters more involved in the story
+ Colonel Zarpedon, arguably the best villain so far
+ Fun new characters, returning characters used well
CONS:
- Overpriced
- Hit-and-miss humour
- Some remaining bugs
- Where are Blake and Angel?
- No apparent visual improvements
- Less content than its predecessor
- New enemies not as fun or memorable as in BL2
- No unique narration for Nisha, Wilhelm and Claptrap

The venerable series returns with upgrades in several areas. First, bless effects are available when setting up your pretender god. The random map generator has been improved, and the graphics for the map and interface are much clearer, upgraded for higher-resolution displays. Recruitment points are now required for obtaining units (in addition to money and resources). The non-interactive combat is now “real-time”, where simultaneous actions (like moving and shooting) can occur at the same time. The fantastic core gameplay remains: choose one of the many nations, design your pretender god, expand by attacking surrounding provinces containing magic sites, defend new territories with a garrison to keep unrest low, build forts to collect nearby resources, spread dominion with temples and preaching, construct labs to research new spells, cast local and global rituals, recruit new units and hire mercenaries, set up army formations and battle orders, equip leaders with magical items, watch automated battles, and try to survive against the very capable AI. Much like its predecessor, Dominions 5 is more like an incremental upgrade, but overall it is a fantastic, feature-filled strategy game.

It's like Dom4, but waaaay more polished and lovely.  Best strategy game of all time? Possibly.
And don't forget, there's an epic modding community from Dom4 just waiting to sink their teeth into Dom5...the game can only get dramatically better...
And Ilwinter was updating Dom4 for years after release, and I trust that it will be no different for Dom5.
Just hurry up and buy it.  And don't let the steep learning curve dissuade you.

During these processes you're moving on rails and can only shoot in a small area, you can't turn or control movement. TL:DR - Its a good third person shooter, and the first half of the campaign is really enjoyable. Towards the end it gets a little stupid.
Long version - Graphics and Audio are good, the majority of the gameplay is fun.
The annoying parts include:
1) an unbalanced AI - ie: if my team is engaging the enemy and I am just assigning targets (ie: not shooting) the enemy will still concentrate fire on me.
2) wierd effects - ie: in one level when it is raining, any cover you hide behind suddenly starts "smoking". (even if you are not shooting, and nobody is shooting at you)
3) Third-person shooter syndrome - little things like: if you run past something that could be "cover" then your guy automatically stops running and takes cover. If you are behind cover and find an enemy behind you, then swinging your camera around through cover becomes disorientating.
4) Forced interactive cinematics - ie: certain cinematics force your character to walk through areas without cover, and you only have control over where you are shooting. If one enemy ends up behind you, you don't have control over your movements to turn around and shoot the enemy.
For the fluidity of movements and the graphic presentation, it is among the best. I do not wish to complain of anything else. How well it was presented was all that matters to me. Enjoy the game :)

I have to start off by saying I love the visual style and all of the rave soundtrack. This music in this game is right up my alley and awesome to listen to as you murder people after people.
Now the bad part: The gameplay is not enjoyable. The main character is a turtle who has the running capacity of the call of duty guy. He has no abilities and has to rely on gadgets and traps. Depending on the randomization of the traps however, the level could be extremely easy or tedious and monotonous as you kill one person and drag their body alll the way to the trash. Since the way of killing in a stealthy way is so tedious, getting caught could send you back half a hour. Sometimes there aren't even enough traps in the level to lower the person count to just finish them off in one go. Sometimes you'll get the greatest killing tool of all time: a smoke bomb that covers your person if you stand still.

Short review: If you like dungeon exploring and the challenge of perma-death, in a game that manages to balance that challenge with enough play to keep you coming back, you shoudl check Delver out.
Long review:
The graphics are "Minecraft-like" for lack of a better way to put it. They're 3d 16 bit, nothing fancy, but they work. It definitely adds to the retro feel.
The gameplay is the same first person dungeon exploration that harkens back to Ultima Underworld. It's balanced and challenging. There is a learning curve but you will find yourself delving deeper on each try and more importantly, wanting to try again after each death.
This is one of the few perma-death games that get it right. It isn't frustrating but also is not easy.  Don't get me wrong, one moment of stupid can cause a restart but the build to your character is balanced with the difficulty in such a way as to make you avoid mistakes and almost always understand exactly why you died when/where you did. This balance is what makes me want to keep coming back and keeps me trying to delve deeper into the dungeon and hone my skills.
I've tied a lot of these rogue-like games with perma-death recently and this one definitely stands out a a diamond in the rough.

I seem to be playing a lot of Roguelikes recently, and this game is pretty darn good for Early Access.
Your mission is to explore the dungeon and find the orb at the bottommost floor, fighting through groups of people, bugs (ick), bats and skeletons. Get the orb and do your best to escape alive, because everything comes back at you threefold once you pick up the darn thing. The first-person perspective, coupled with a few small corridors and narrow walkways, really give you a mild sense of fear and excitement--you never know what's going to jump out from behind the wall (hopefully not a magic-user).
The game is pretty short. For some players, you could run through the whole thing and escape alive in only about 3 attempts. But don't let that deter you, as it is a lot of fun regardless. That being said, I would strongly suggest picking this game up when it's on sale, as there is a lot to be desired. Still, it IS Early Access...
Also, sometimes I feel like I'm being cheated. I went down there with around 80 arrows, never found a bow, found the orb instead, tried to escape, made it back up to the first floor and FINALLY found a single bow to use the arrows with. Great...

I bought this game (non-steam version) years ago and have been playing it on and off until now (a total of at least weeks if not months of playing time). Finally I have to add that it requires a particular preference for technical simulation/sandbox games and many might not enjoy that as much as I do, but if you like getting deep into technical things, particularly cars, then I can only recommend this title.

I never was a fan of survival horror games. The Resident Evils (pre 4) and Silent Hills were never my thing. However, for whatever reason, I loaded this up and was surprised at how much I enjoyed it. It's pretty simple and accessible for the genre. You've still got to eat and sleep, but thankfully, an unlimited inventory and fast travel points back to your bed make this much less annoying.
It's got that "retro" pixelated look that 98% of indie games have, but here you can actually SEE the blocks that make up the character and items. Despite this, it's still got a strong horror atmosphere and it was unsettling exploring some of the areas. Like a lot of indie games, it's got a decent soundtrack with a few songs I could probably listen to outside of the game.
The most interesting aspect is the "mental health" system. It seems that almost every action you take affects it somehow and therefore, what ending you get.  I went in without knowing that all my actions were being recorded and got a less than desireable ending. However, a second playthrough wouldn't take nearly as long as the first and will add a new challenge in keeping the character in good mental health.
If you got it in the humble indie bundle, try it out. If not, grab it at 75% off next time.

After playing and completing the game, I can officially say that Lone Survivor is nothing short of a masterpiece and I don’t use that term lightly especially when it comes to a survival horror/adventure game. The game can be easily summed up as a Silent Hill 2 2D side scrolling game. So does that mean is it scary? I wouldn’t go down that line but more like psychology creepy. Because you don’t know what is real or not and yet you have to deal with weird looking monster by either shooting them, distracting them or hide out of plain sight just to pass by them.
The game creator Jasper Byrne has really put a lot of effort by taking the 16 bit graphics and turning it into something special. The added mosaic textures and grainy effects makes this game visually stunning. Not to mention that he has created an original soundtrack specifically for this game that will sink into your ear holes and brain waves as soon as you run the game. Its games like this make me appreciate Indie games a lot more than big publisher companies that make AAA games like Capcom or Konami who have completely lost their roots to what made their own original survival horror  games a legend.
If you're a true survivor horror adventure fan, give this game a go. You will not be disappointed.

Hexcells is a relaxing and esthetically pleasing reincarnation of Minesweeper, so anyone familiar with the latter should be able to easily pickup the former (and should have a good idea of what they are getting into). Puzzles are very easy and addicting, soundtrack is pleasant and not intrusive, and minimalist user interface looks nice and clean, but the game is not without faults. User interface does not do a good job of explaining what all the various icons mean. There is an achievement for finishing all levels without mistakes, but there is no indicator next to each level and you seem to always get a full score regardless (if the achievement actually checks mistakes, good luck trying to figure out which levels need to be replayed). The same problems plague the provided instructions, which are not clear and fail to explain key concepts (such as whitespace between cells). The puzzles are extremely easy and don't really get any harder throughout the course of the game. In fact, there is no sense of progression in general as all of the mechanics are introduced all at once in Part 3 (out of 6), so it just feels like you are solving the same puzzles over and over. It would have made much more sense to introduce one new mechanic in each chapter, and to make the puzzles randomly generated to add replayability and remove guessing and memorization as viable strategies. The soundtrack consists of a single track that gets repetitive after a while too. Luckily, the game is very short so it never gets boring, and is very enjoyable despite feeling unfinished. It's just a shame that the developer didn't take the time to polish this gem.

Overview
Magicite is a rogue like platformer that has a mix of survival and exploration elements mixed in. The games developers SmashGames have create a game that is not only fun to play but challenging if not downright merciless. The game was originally on steams early access but has since left but is still updated with the funds that were raised on Kickstarter.
Story
Magicite doesn’t really have a story. But townsfolk that can be found between the levels can be spoken to and can give you a bit of info about the world.
Gameplay
Magicite seem to draw idea and concepts of other game, the platforming from games like Spelunky and the survival system from Minecraft as well as some RPG elements. The first thing that the player is required is to create is their character. At first the level of choice the player has is very limited with only two different hairstyle and the ability to roll a dice to determine what stats and the two random traits they will receive. After a few good play through, other options will be unlocked such as new races, hats and companions that can give some extra buffs and make the game easier. Different races have a different set of starting gear. Hats have special effect and companions will provide passive effects.
After the player create their character they are dropped into a forest biome with the starting item of their race. Every level is randomly generated when a level is completed the player will be given a choice of three other biomes which are also randomly generated. Player can visit towns in between levels were item can be bought or sold as well as craft new ones. When the player level up that gain more stat points and with be able to skills from skill trees melee, magic and ranged. Player can have three skill and they are given to them randomly.
Player must collected resources to craft new tool to help in the higher level as well to help manage hunger. Crafting is easy to make an item you must combine two other items. They are not many recipes so they are easy to learn and you just need better material to make better items.
Magicite is an unforgiving game health pools are few and far between and potion are rare. Playing with friend can make it easier because downed player can be revived by another player. However the reviver is left vulnerable for about three second.
The controls for Magicite are for keyboard and mouse only, the keyboard for moving and the mouse for interacting and aiming. The control are very responsive which is so important in a platformer with this level of difficulty.
Visuals
Magicite has a very retro feel with it simple 16-bit graphics and bright and vibrant colours, with the games background being as dark as it is make the colours stand out even more. The game can scale to high resolution without any problem.
Audio
The Audio like the visuals has a very retro 16-bit feel. However the is no menu music which is a little strange but once in the game the music is great.
Overall
I love the game from it brutal difficulty to its retro art style and soundtrack the game has so much replay ability, and with the controls being as responsive as they are SmashGames have created something that mixes survival, RPG, roguelike and platforming into something truly great. Anybody that likes a challenge, platformers or just like to play game with some friends or by your self should definitely give this game a go.

The series that fell by the way-side because it had to compete with Call of Duty.
Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon: Future Soldier is the latest in the Ghost Recon saga and it breathes fresh air into a long-running franchise.
Take control of a squad of special-op's in this tactical third-person shooter and infiltrate the most dangerous locales around the globe to take out national and global threats.
Commanding feels like the real deal - You tell your squad who and when to shoot, allowing for a vast selection of ways to approach your challenges.
Every gun is customizeable - Earning parts by completing challenges, you can customize your loadout before every mission. Play your way.
The gameplay is phenomenal and has replay value, but the port itself is a little lackluster.
It is definitely playable, but as with most of Ubisoft's PC ports, it has graphical glitches.
Easy, Normal, Hard, Elite and Hardcore difficulties available from the start.
Still recommended for fans of Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon franchise, as well as tactical military shooters.

Stellaris. A furturistic Spce exploration game that places the player in control of one of many species of life forms in the Milky Way Galaxy just at the outst of inter-stellar flight. YOU decide what type of race your species will be; benevolent or brutal; diplomatic or destructive. YOU choose scientific research to suit your species needs and support your goals. Colonization is paramount. Conquest, well, that depends on YOU. Resource management is vital. Food, minerals, energy and strategic elements support and, in some instances, enhance your ability to defend or conquer, colonize and co-exist.
The game itself is an ongoing work in progress. Developers are working to expand players' abilites to improve a planet and expand liveable area. Utopia, the next DLC due in April - for a fee as well - hints at setting a high bar for advanced technology and giving the player the opportunity to go big, or go home.
As with any game there are limitations because, well, it's a game after all, right? But don't let that deter you. Visit the Steam Workshop to find a Mod to satisfy your fantasies. (Space Exploration fantasies that is.) Bear in mind as well that many of these too are a WIP. Updates come infrequently but they are quite welcome. I use the Star Trek Horizons conversion mod. I very much like it. Oh, you like Star Wars? They've got that too. But, don't take my word for it. Go and see for yourself.

Delver is a fun, first person rogue-like dungeon crawler and it's pretty fun. Even though I beat it after 3 times, I still want to play again. I beat it fast, but it's still in early access, so many things can be changed. Now to the overall score;
GAMEPLAY is really fun and satisfying. While I played I developed a tactic for each enemy, taking them out really fast. for example when a worm is about to jump-attack, I wait just the right moment to strike and take it down. 9/10
VISUALS is actually pretty good despite the fact it is pixel graphics. However, graphics shouldn't decide if game is good or not, but it's still nice to look at. The inventory system is really easy use and understandable 8.5/10
LEVELING. The leveling system cool. I like games when you level up your character and tweak your stats. Even though the most important stat in my opinion is HP, that's how I won the game. But you can only level up one stat by choosing 3 random stats everytime, so it's not always you can level up HP. 8.5/10
DIFFICULTY. This game isn't really that hard, but it's not that easy either. For example, the magic wands is really good/ kinda op. I didn't need to level up magic at all, and they were still pretty good. It's in early access, so it can be changed. 8/10
So all in all I give this game a 8.6/10. It's not perfect, but it can be improved! If you like rogue-likes buy it. If you like dungeon crawlers, buy it. It's even on sale when I write this review. BUY IT NOW! :D

I have owned this game on mobile for ome time now, and I just recently bought the game on Steam. Let me say, this game does not disappoint. I got the game on sale, but the price of 7.99$ USD is totally reasonable. Here is why:

-Lots of Hidden Lore (Notes are scattered about the Dungeon, hinting about the games Lore)
-Lots of Monsters (Fight Mobs ranging from Spiders to One-Eyed Flying Things)

Dominions 5: Warriors of the Faith is the sequel to Dominions 4: Thrones of Ascension.
Both are unique games that once you put you're foot in them you get stuck in an endless quagmire of mechanics, strategy and diplomacy (when you play multiplayer, the AI is dumb as bricks, just can't handle the complexity of the game).
Dominions 5 brings multiple new and interesting systems to the table, notably an entirely new customizable Blessing system where you can decide what powers the holy warriors of your Pretender God are granted when a priest of the true faith blesses them with your God's powers as well as a revamped fort building and commander recruitment system.
I heartily recommend the game for anyone who wants to think hard and long about how many wizards to send and what you want them to cast while summoning demons from the nether realms or contacting the Angels and Harbingers of the One True God.

Instant purchase, because Illwinter Game Design is a company you can trust.
And additionally you also get the latest version of one of the best games in the genre.

*Bill Duke voice*
You know what I like best?
The price.
*Drives out through the window of Illwinter's office and escapes down the highway*
Well what can I say? Every new instalment in the Dominions series is an expansion on the last and so there's really no reason to stick with any of the prequels. Because of this, everything that I said in my lengthy Dominions 4 review still stands. Dominions 5 is a polished and expanded version of Dominions 4.
I was initially skeptical that the game would be worth the £30/$40 for me, as someone who owned Dominions 4. Having now played the game, I can safely say that my skepticism has been washed away and that I'm very glad that I bought the game the instant that it was released (and there was never any doubt that I would).
Dominions 5 continues the series tradition of being on an extreme end of the graphics versus gameplay scale. Namely the end that cares little about the visuals and everything about depth of gameplay. This is what makes the Dominions series so special and why myself and most other fans love it. And I say that as a relatively new recruit, having only discovered the series with Dominions 4. However, Dominions 5 has received a high degree of polish in the visual department and looks markedly better than its predecessor.
There are new nations, new events, and everything else that you'd expect from a Dominions sequel, including new features that only someone who knows the Dominions series can truly appreciate. For example, your characters will now make their own way to a destination without you having to micromanage them through every province. I'm not joking when I say that such a feature alone would make Dominions 5 tempting to me, and I didn't see anyone even mention it in the run-up to release. Dominions 5 seems to emphasise playing on random maps more than its prequel did, and they look utterly gorgeous compared to how they did in Dominions 4. What I personally love is how you can prevent random maps from wrapping around in every direction now. Of course if you've never played a Dominions game before that won't mean anything to you. But trust me, it's a good thing. The new music is gorgeous too.
To be honest, I just wanted to give the game the good review it deserves—I didn't really plan to say much. It's Dominions again and it's better than before. The trailer for the game claims that it's the deepest strategy game of all time, and that's no idle boast. I've been gaming for nearly thirty years now and I've never played anything that comes close to Dominions in terms of tactical depth and strategic potential.
If you're a fan of turn-based strategy at all, then the Dominions series is essential. You won't be able to understand its depths without reading the manual or asking for help on the forums, and even then you'll be pretty clueless for your first few games, but believe me, Dominions is a series that amply rewards perseverance. I myself am still learning, and I'm loving every minute of it.
Now excuse me, I must lead the nation of Atlantis across the bottom of the ocean so that I can spread the good word of our god, Kronos, across the lands of men from the safety of our underwater temples.
Oh, and I was just joking with the opening. Illwinter Game Design consists of two guys (Johan Karlsson and Kristoffer Osterman) who're responsible for not only the Dominions games, but also the Conquest of Elysium series. They probably make their games while sitting in their underpants in their living rooms. I know I would. I'd be surprised if they had an office, nevermind one with a window big enough to drive out of.

I've made it past the 1200 hours mark and I think Im qualified enough to leave a decent review.
Paladins is a great game with a small and growing community. This game is not perfect, don't expect it to be especially because it's still in "BETA". People Like to compare it to the big O, sure there are some similarities but this game is a completely different experience. It has more MOBA elements to it; loadouts, mounts and the credit system are what makes this game versatile and more complex. It has a great selection of "Champions" and i'm sure you'll find someone that'll match your playstyle.
I will List down the pros on cons that makes me hate/love this game.
- the community is smaller compared to its big brothers but this community is tight-knit and less toxic. You can see how the community support each other especially on twitch. The Paladins Twitch account periodically hosts smaller streamers but they host a lot of the bigger streamers a lot of times, they need to switch it up soon.
- currently, they are releasing updates once every 2 weeks. That is very impressive to me. They listen to the players and they make sure updates are pushed on time.
- If that's not enough reason for you to give this one a try , i don't what would convince you. I mean you have nothing to lose! I honestly think this is the reason why this game is getting so much hate from the other community. It hurts their ego that people are actually enjoying a free-to-play game.
- Paladins itself is a small file and can run on a potato! this makes it very stream-friendly and also wallet-friendly ;)
- you get free in-game stuff everytime you login and when you refer friends. You also get a chance to get free skins, weapons and crystals if you watch the Official Paladins Streams on Twitch. You dont have to spend a dime you can unlock a lot stuff. More stuff at their website.
- As much as I love this game, HiRez Servers are probably the worst game servers i've personally encountered. The amount of down time in this game because of server issues is disgusting. Don't even get me started on the drop hacks. By the way SEA servers are still messed up, first game you get 90ping, next  game you get 400ping. It's been months and still not fixed
-
Well as of OB60 they added more achievements in the game. Kudos to the devs
- matchmaking as of the moment is... crap. I have reached level 200+ and I sometimes get paired with/matched against people below level 20 and it's frustrating. People who are still new and clueless about the game. I'm sure they're working on improving this.
- Yes the updates are timely but hirez has a habit of "fixing characters" that are not broken. This patch he's nerfed, next update she's buffed. It can be a little discouraging sometimes.
- If you hate grind then this game may not be for you. It's not an easy grind especially if you dont have the Founder's Pack. You have to do a little grinding to unlock all cards and champions. This could be a little overwhelming for new players but playing with friends can help it make easier. You get extra XP and gold when u play with friends
- Easy Anti-cheat. where do i begin?... this software is a little controversial so im gonna leave it at that. Im sure other reviews have talked about this in depth
For a free-to-play beta game, Paladins has a lot of content and still has tons of potential. They are slowly adding lore and integrating nice story to some of the characters. New awesome skins and weapons that you can mix and match. If you really want to make the most out of this game, I say play with an open mind and stop comparing everything to other games, only then you will see its own beauty.

I think this is the sort of game that grows on you with time.
Initially I found this game very challenging to the point that I was very close to giving up. But, if you're persistent with this game you'll get better, to the point at which completing the game 9 times over (for the achievements) is do-able.
It's worth mentioning though that the first completion gives you a false sense of victory. If you dare to play it again you'll realise that it goes to a whole new level of difficulty (2 more levels to be precise). Everything will start damaging you double and the game has suddenly gone hardcore. But as I say, if you're persistent you will get good at this game and you'll find it enjoyable - especially if you're the achievement-hunting type.
So, to summarise I'd recommend this game as a self-purchase or a gift for more experienced gamers with at least a few years under their belt. It's definitely not for the faint-hearted though, or those less experienced (i.e. casual or intermediate gamers) simply because this is a difficult game, and they might be a bit quick to give up the game forever.

I've always thought Medieval II was rather bad, but after trying out newer, better Total Wars, I've discovered that Medieval II must be the worst game in the entire series. Don't get me wrong, this game would have been great if it weren't for the many oversights and bugs in it. The campaign map, meh, could be better with the AI and stuff. But what really gets to me is the ridiculously poorly made battle map. For starters, it takes ages for artillery units to prepare to fire. Imagine it, the enemy infantry is coming, and you have ballistas or later in the game, cannons, ready to fire when they get within range. The enemy is in range, but you notice that your artillery batteries aren't firing, you zoom in and it's because one guy is taking a seizure trying to get into the right position to load the artillery, when the guy should already be in position, and the artillery loaded anyway.
And who the hell designed the UI? I've had this game for 2 years on Steam, and many years on CD before that, and it was only recently I learnt what I could really do on the campaign map. Due the the poor combat AI, battles are extremely unrealistic, whether it's two soldiers fighting eachother, or four armies. This is mainly because it takes hours for soldiers to do a 90 degrees turn due to the poor animations. What happened to the diplomacy? Why use "diplomats" on the campaign map? You should be able to contact any nation at any time. As far as I know, kings don't simply run out of diplomats. It certainly doesn't take years for them to reach another country either.
Every problem I've listed here is about 10% of all problems in this game. Don't waste your money here. Total War is brilliant, just not this one. Creative Assembly, if you're reading this, please create a Medieval III so we can enjoy Total War in that time period without all of the bugs and problems. Thank you.

Most weapons are actually imbedded in the code, but have no suitable loot source (or that loot source is bugged, like the Lady Fist) Understandibly, these unobtainable weapons are very powerful even without a proper build to back them up, but in BL2 with Shamfleeting, Pimperahabing, and Beehawking, there really isn't much of a reason to leave this game so...unfinished. The replayability is trash, the story just drones on and never EVER has the character's just saying a line and having you on your way. A great example of this is when Jack is telling you about the vending machines in the beggining. It would be great, if not for the fact that he takes forever to complete the objective that you could do in under 10 seconds! You don't even have to be near the machines, he'll just explain them anyway. A great option would've been to disable tutorials and tutorial-like dialouge, but no. You have to listen to these god damn explinations over, and over until finally you just go and download a lvl50 (or 70) save and have fun with that. Except that the endgame isn't even fun! The "mobbing" areas are either have way too much cover or way too open. And the worst part? They had a chance to redeem the game. The Claptastic Voyage was hyped and hyped and nothing came of it. Another story with awful slow speed and extremely cringe-worthy jokes. The glitch weapons were way too unreliable and weren't really much better than purples. Hell, if it hadn't been for BL2, I probably wouldn't have even touched this game. The co-op wasn't even that decent. The only "support" was Athena and if she went down you're whole team was screwed. Please 2K, I hope you take this is a regretable mistake and build off of it. We don't want another TPS for BL3.

Some feats of human endeavor have simply hit a plateau and will advance no further: the presidential autobiography, the drunken bar fight, the hot dog-eating contest, the movie biopic, the musical-legend-in-his/her-golden-years duet album. In these areas, revision is unthinkable; sameness becomes a structuring principle rather than a liability. Every once in a while, however, this wisdom is turned on its head, and an idea, maybe one that seems a little crazy at first, catches fire, revitalizes old forms, and we have what's called a “game changer.”
For the racing genre, Glacier 3: The Meltdown is not that game-changing game: It's like an artifact from early-'90s arcades, the kind you might still see at shopping malls and in movie theater lobbies. Tempting though it may be to chalk the game's throwback texture and jerky movements to nostalgia, Glacier 3 feels, finally, cheap and fly-by-night (and weirdly unfinished), the kind of thing that might blow your mind if you caught a glimpse of it while standing in 1989, but 20-plus years on it's a bit like Lola at the end of the Barry Manilow song, wearing faded feathers and a Havisham-grade evening gown while attempting to obliterate any thought that might separate the present from its glorious past.
The only thing that dates it to within five years of its release date is a pronounced design influence on the vehicles by the 2008 Paul W.S. Anderson demolition-derby-dystopia actioner Death Race.
The only thing that dates it to within five years of its release date is a pronounced design influence on the vehicles by the 2008 Paul W.S. Anderson demolition-derby-dystopia actioner Death Race. Team 6, Glacier's designers, might have been better off had they spent less time cribbing that film's death-proofed gunship/crotch-rockets and more time taking a page from Anderson's textbook on matters such as hybridizing the anything-it-takes-to-win mentality with the guiltless pleasure to be had from blasting or mashing or skewering a rival racer into the next life. For all the minutes getting setup, picking the right car, figuring how to do basic things such as drive and shoot, there's next to no gratification to be had from winning or, if it's the big draw for you, smokin' other drivers.

Highly recommended - what an awesome surprise this game turned out to be. Bottom line is that it is a ton of fun to play, and it has a lot of fresh or interesting takes that make it stand out from other MMOs.
Combat
The action combat in particular is a total blast. Feels totally natural and is easy to learn, yet takes skill to master.
Graphics
I was a bit wary from the screenshots, but once you get in the game, the graphics are not that "loud". Instead the graphics are very pleasing, and have a distinct style that works perfectly for the game.
The Game Has Character
This game oozes with character and personality. The setting, the NPC personalities, the zany monsters, all create something that is fun to play and experience.
Your Path
The game allows you to choose a path of your interest, such as exploring or combat, and then gives you extra activities and quests to do related to this path. And the path levels separately from your character's level.
Housing
The housing is very nicely done. Tons of things to add to the inside or outside of your plot.
Lots Of Stuff To Do
There is a bunch of stuff to do such as quests, encounters, adventures, dungeons, world bosses, PVP, and more.
No Barriers F2P
They pretty much give you the whole game free, with no barriers. This is the way F2P is suppose to be. But I like the game so much that I WANT to give them some money.

First of all let me say, this is a great game. As far as tactical squad-based shooters are concerned, this is very well done. The tactical planning seamlessly integrates into the game play, you get a number of really cool gadgets to help you plan your assault, but at no time does it feel that planning ahead hinders or dulls the game play. Very well done!
The instructions are clear, the objectives varied, and you get a great arsenal of weapons. The AI, especially your team members never gets in the way and sometimes it really does feel like you’re are part of a real time. The combat immersion is above the usual standard. As far as stealth/tactical/military shooters are concerned, this one is at the top of my favorite list for sure.
As far as performance is concerned, on any even semi-modern computer you will get decent frame rates at 1080p. If you're struggling, turn off DX11 and run on DX9. I've not noticed that much of a visual impact to be honest.
So, in short: If you like Tom Clancy based games, if you like tactical (FPS) shooters, if you have a little bit of a black sense of humor, get this. It's fun!

An awesome little puzzle game, that takes the premise of Minesweeper but adds some additional logic rules (including some Picross rules, though not to the degree of SquareCells) and takes out the randomness. All puzzles are 100% logic solvable, with no guessing required - so at the risk of sounding condescending, if you're reading a negative review by someone who says guessing is required, they just couldn't logic the puzzle out. I was able to logic solve them all, and when I did make an error, I was able to figure out what error in logic I had made, or what I had failed to notice, that caused my mistake. The game lets you make a few mistakes without failing you on the level, but as a perfectionist I restarted from scratch each time, and was able to clear them all. I found both the difficulty and the learning curve to be fair.
The only downsides I see are:
1. Since the puzzles are fixed, not a lot of replay value...BUT, for the cost, it's still a solid value for the time to do even one playthrough - especially if you get it on sale, like I did.
2. The mouse buttons are opposite to Minesweeper, so if you're used to it (and that is kind of the target market here), it's hard to readjust. I messed up more puzzles by confusing the mouse buttons than by making a logic error.
3. There's no "maybe" flag like there is in Minesweeper, so you have to do all your "what if" analysis in your head or on paper.
Fully recommend.

As a guy who likes his money, I gave this game a try quite a while ago as a way to cope with my brother getting Overwatch. I enjoyed it a tad at the time, but felt that Overwatch had an upper hand in terms of community causing me to leave for a few months. I eventually bought Overwatch and went on a binge session going on for weeks. One day I saw my friend that I haven't talked to in a few years load up Paladins, thus encouraging me to get the game again so I could have something in common again. I was pleasantly surprised with the game, making its own identity and becoming less and less like what everyone made fun of them for, which was an Overwatch clone with a card system. Enough of my story-time, Anyway . . . I feel as that Paladins has made differences between the two games which seems to fulfill the need for more variety. In Paladins, there are many more "Champions" to choose from who each have strengths and weaknesses to your liking. If you like the basics of a champion but would like to change their play style, that is where the card system comes in. Legendary Cards make the biggest difference but you only have to pick from 3. Then, if you found you are not doing so well against your enemies, you cam do In Game upgrades for that game (including defense against blast damage, single damage, faster ultimate charging, faster movement speed, get more healing from teammates (sadly no one ever uses that one), life steal, cause reduced healing after hitting them, or do more damage against shields) to counter their compositions. Now this game also has a little less quality servers leading to painfully large hitboxes making snipers seem a tad overpowered going against bad teamwork. Now that I talked about gameplay mechanics, onto the community. The community is strange, since people made the game feel like a "poor man's Overwatch" now this attracts many young ones to play (really young) leading to horrible teamwork making competitive a tad difficult.
Overall, I enjoy this game quite a lot . . . the only thing that I feel helps Overwatch with their popularity would be their story and lore they have put so much work into which Paladins has next-to-none helping it out. If you don't believe me and most of the others in these reviews, I recommend at least giving it a chance, after all . . . It is Free to Play

It's a recommendation, but a hesitant one.
You play as the Party Hard killer, a man who is just trying to getsomesleep but can't because of all the people throwing parties through the night. So you set out on a cross country road trip to put an end to all the partying once and for all. It's a neat premise for a game and lends itself to some funny moments as you're offing people at parties.
Each level of like a much slower version of Hotline Miami,with more emphasis on strategy and not being seen. There are traps all around the environment you can use, and you can also make use of the phones scattered throughout the areas to call different people to different effects. One of them might call fumigators who poison the party goers with pesticides. Another calls a psycho with a chainsaw to take care of the partyers. There's lots of room for experimentation here.
There are, however, some very rough edges. For one, your player character moves far too slowly, and this leads to the game's other problems. There's a combo system that rewards you for killing many people in a short amount of time, but doing sooften involves exposing yourself as the killer. This calls a cop who will chase you and may ormay not give up the chase if you manage to maneuver your way around the environment or makeuse of an escape hatch. The thing is it seems random whether or not the cop gives up chasing you, and he always moves faster than you, too. It defeats the purpose of the combo system to me. Another thing is that the random elements of the levels can feel unfair. AI walks around without any clear patterns, and sometimes it seems like the cops identify you without any clear reason as to why. Then there are the traps, which can be usedexactly onceand often leave many people alive even if you carefully plan your attack out. Then it becomes a matter of luring people away andpicking them off one by one, which can take a good while.
I'd still say check it out, but just be warned it's very tough and could use some refinement. Here's hoping the sequel improves on its mechanics for a fairer experience.

Glacier 3: The Meltdown is a third person, combat racing game whose developers may have had big dreams for the game, but resulted in an overwhelmingly poor production. Released in 2010 on Steam, when games such as F1 2010, Blur, and heck even Need for Speed: World were their competitors (among others), this is not even a possible contestant among those other titles. Let us dive straight into it shall we?
I normally leave this section for last, but I think it's a pretty significant part of this review so here it is.
Images were pretty low resolution, car models were quite bad, even if this wasn't supposed to be a racing simulator like other titles. Animations were just barely acceptable and each level had at least a few different roads to drive on which didn't make a race completely linear. But honestly, after seeing the loading screen 3 times, I couldn't deal with it any more. It was visually cancer.
It is worth noting that this game has an options menu, but only has
settings in the ENTIRE menu. FX Volume and Music Volume (or something like that). This is absolutely unnaceptable considering resolution, controls, graphic quality settings, you name it! I plugged in my xbox one controller, and it would not detect it, nor did it give me the option to even change the controls. Even if a workaround exists, the fact that it lacks the basic courtesy to give me the choice in-game, feels pretty lazy to be honest.
Oh boy...you see, I'm sort of a racing game fan, a huge one. I love games that give me a certain thrill, a sense of speed, a decent bit of competition at the very least. I especially love simulators, ones that give me a huge sense of immersion so I can enjoy the game even more. This game...has none of that. It has the absolute worst handling of vehicles I've ever had the misfortune of playing, I mean can you imagine a car sliding across the ground going at 1 or 2 MPH? These cars will break every law of physics you can imagine. The view is fixed to 3rd person. No decent controller support means you'll probably be using a keyboard (an absolute no no for racing fans) and no multiplayer? What exactly would motivate someone to playing this then?
Let's see......well......hmmmm.....
Car sounds are quite bad, painfully so, and the rock music in the background half the time just grates on my nerves.
So let's see,
Whatever you do, don't spend full price, half price or even quarter price on this. You're much better off playing some flash racing game or F2P racing game than this. There's just nothing worth coming back to.
1/10 - Please, save your money.

Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon: Future Soldier is a third-person game from Ubisoft. It is the next installment in the Ghost Recon series.
Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon: Future Soldier gameplay is far more different than the previous Ghost Recon game, because Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon: Future Soldier use third-person rather than first-person like before, but that doesn't make the game bad, in fact I think this game is great, quite epic and fun to play. My favorite feature is the Sync Shot, where all the Ghost Squad tag and then shoot at the same time on different enemies. You can also customize your weapon with many thinks like scope, camouflage pattern, stock or magazines. There is also Guerrilla Mode, it's a game mode where you get to secure an area, then hold the area against wave of enemies. Guerrilla Mode can be played with friends too.
Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon: Future Soldier graphics is good enough, the detail on the Ghost Squad are impressive, but the rest of the pictures is somewhat like Call of Duty: Modern Warfare, well at least Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon: Future Soldier has better graphics. The performance of the game is good, no lags and the game runs smooth. If you see many people complain the game doesn't work, it's not the game, it's Uplay. The game works just fine after you get through the Uplay part.
Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon: Future Soldier is good tactical shooter game, with great features, too bad the multiplayer is empty now. I recommend this.

I wish I could recommend this. I really, really do.
This is a fantastic game. Extremely enjoyable gameplay, great graphical fidelity and good performance. Enjoyable missions and good level design, with different ways of approaching objectives and satisfying "sync shots", where your entire team shoot 4 people simultaneously. A truly brilliant gun customization menu, where you can customize everything from the optics to the gas system.
However, this entire experience is utterly ruined by two things; firstly, the mandatory use of UPlay. I'm not going to go on a rant about how much I hate UPlay (although I certainly could; and with good reason), because I'm sure that everyone else on Steam has had my exact thoughts every time they think of the word UPlay. You would think, however, that this would surely not ruin my whole experience of GR:FS? You would be correct. There is one problem which I simply cannot get past, and which ultimately ruins the whole game for me: Mouse Acceleration. I'm sure everyone here knows how awful this is, so I won't go on about it. However, if you are thinking of buying this game, beware; the mouse acceleration is there, it is
noticeable, and it cannot be disabled by any means. After hours of searching, I cannot find any way of disabling mouse acceleration in this game, not even through modification of the .INI files. What this ultimately means is that you cannot aim in this game without great difficulty. Not only does this make the game harder, it also makes it more annoying to play. It disgusts me that Ubisoft think that they can get away with no option to disable console features for a PC game, as well as the fact that they force UPlay upon us. In summary, don't buy this game unless you can handle very heavy mouse acceleration or intend to use a gamepad, and are happy with UPlay. For me, I cannot play this game, and will never buy another Ubisoft product.

Let me start by saying that I enjoy 4x and strategy games in general but often lack the patience to actually take the time to learn all of their mechanics therefore in the end loving the idea of the game more than actually playing it.  Often I'll get into a game such as this and either get frustrated with it in some way or feel overwhelmed by the sheer amount of content to wade through in order to know if the first ship that I created was done so properly.  Stellaris for me has been the exception to that.  My friend asked me to play this game with him and I told him sure but don't expect me to stick with it and as of this writing we are now planning weekly games sometimes lasting six hours per session.
So I'll start by saying that I love the mechanics of this game in almost every way.  This is a 4x game that runs in real time but you don't feel like you are micro managing every unit like a traditional RTS, it's a very good hybrid approach.  To elaborate on that point, when you send a fleet of ships into combat, you aren't controlling several squads of ships in real time, you tell which fleets you want to fight to engage and then they all just jump in and fight it out unless you command them to retreat.   This simplfies the combat mechanic more than some typically enjoy but in general makes this game less about players ability to control lots of units and more about the strategy needed before combat begins.  Combat in Stellaris is important as is the design and power of your ships but it's not the key focus.
Stellaris is a strategy game that's focus is truly strategy.  One cannot simply work towards researching the most powerul hardware and expect to win because you can't just declare war and steam roll through an empire.  War is a carefully planned process that requires demands to be set and met win or lose.  If I declare war on another nation then I have to openly state that I want planets, to vasalize them, demand liberation of a nation or other similar options.  After the war is declared and demands set the war begins and each side has a score value that must be met.  That score can be achieved in a number of different ways but once it reaches 100% then the victor earns their demands and the declaring party cannot declare war on that nation again for 10 game years and a lot can happen in that time.  The losing party could build up relations with other empires to prevent the next war for example.
Another aspect that I really enjoy are the mechanics in the game that reduce a lot of the micro management tedium.  One example of this is the Outliner that appears on the right hand side of the UI.  If not for this one UI element, I'm not sure I would enjoy the game nearly as much because it helps to expidite so many functions of the game.  It essentially provides a breakdown of the key units and areas you are actively managing and makes it very easy to quickly access them and see what they are doing.  If I have three science ships on three different tasks, I can easily see their progress and can quickly navigate to their current location.  I can at a glance see each of my fleets, planets, sectors, opposing factions, etc.  The entire panel can also be customized to your needs or even hidden if you don't like it.
The creation of sectors is also of great importantance and goes a long way to eliminate the tedium of micro managing planets.  Once you get more than five planets (in vanilla), you must start to create system sectors or you suffer penalties.  Once the systems are in sectors, you set the options for the sector and it has it's own resources and manages the planets building queues, production and populations on it's own.  This is major because once you get to 7-8 planets it can become a real chore keeping up with everything they need.  Sectors can set their production focus, can have their own rulers, their contributions can be defined and more.  For me, this is what makes the game playable.
Multiplayer is also amazing in this game.  A game can consist of up to 32 players and can run at normal or faster speeds.  Players can join in pacts and federations as well as create trade agreements and contribute to others conflicts.  Or of course can just play free for all and wreck each other.  Be aware that there are still some bugs with multiplayer that require the host to reload the game from time to time but games can be saved to any of the players and someone else can host if need be.
Other small details....
The achievements can only be earned in single player iron man mode so that's something to be aware of too if that's something you enjoy.
This isn't a game that is normally played in one to two hours.  If a game is that short then things went horribly wrong..or right depending on which player you are.  This game will often last for days or possibly weeks depending on the game setup.  That fact alone might tell you if you do or don't want to play it, so bear that in mind as well.  .
You can create your own custom races as with other games of this type but the creation system is very intuitive and adds a lot to the game for me.
Players also need to manage their ships.  You can customize your ship's componets in great detail or leave it up to the AI to automatically manage them for you.  Overall, you have better builds if you manage them yourself but it isn't required to play the game.
Players also are not assured a win by researching a specific tree.  Research is randomized and you are given three choices initially to choose from each time you start to research a new project.  This is one of the great equalizers in the game because it forces the player to carefully balance their empire focus.  For some reading this, that may sound like a negative but it actually adds a great mechanic to the game.
So, in short, if traditional strategy or RTS games aren't your thing, give Stellaris a look.  Watch some YouTube videos, live streams, Let's Plays or something similar for a while and see the mechanics in action.  Watching for 5-10 minutes might not give you enough of a feel for it, so give it some time.  I wish they had a demo of this game out so anyone that's curious about it could actually try it out and see how great it is.  There is no shortage of 4x and strategy games on the market, but Stellaris stands out and creates a fresh new experience.

It's not entirely unlike Dungeon Crawl: Stone Soup, in the style and story (1. Reach bottom of dungeon; 2. Grab shiny orb of arbitrary unexplained power; 3. GTFO while being pursued by respawning enemies). However, Delver is a much shorter and more straightforward game, and is a real-time roguelike rather than a turn-based one. But despite, or perhaps because of, its short length (7 floors, easily completable in an hour or two) it is incredibly fun. It has the right amount of RNG; enough to keep things fresh with new layouts and items, but not so much that you can ever really get wrecked by random factors beyond your control. Every run feels winnable; every death feels like it could have been avoided if you had just played better. Plus it has a level editor now, and is still under active development, so there's lots of potential for more things in the future.

For an example, tooltips didn't work for me but did with my friend when we both did fresh installs of the game without modifying anything. Also simple things that you would just assume would be coded into anything made post year 2000 were not implemented, such as text boxes that only sidescroll everything you type into the first line instead of dropping to the next line when you hit the end of the first one (seriously not a big deal, but the annoying things add up when there are a plethora of annoyances with the interface.)
Another one - the inability to equip items from your bag by moving it from your bag to your character slot, despite being able to un-equip the item with the exact reverse movement. Seeing how good Ghost Recon Advanced Warfighter was this is just weird. This seems to be a minor trend of some game developers trying to ruin their own IP, the classic example being what Crytek did with Crysis after Warhead. But where Crysis 2 and Crysis 3 provide some interest once you accept that they are really completely different games than Crysis 1, Future Soldier is just embarrassing. I must admit I only played the first scene, but stopped there out of principle. No military team, certainly not a fictional one in the Ghost Recon series would open up in a market full of civilians. I don't know, maybe the Future Soldier team are the terrorists this time ? This is just a major no no here, not just because its plain wrong, but it throws out all the fun military accuracy and "standing up for whats good" that make the other games in this series interesting. There's no hold fire order, so I can't even step in and tell my team to wait until the civilians have gone away. The rest of the game feels off as well. The "HUD gone bananas" future theme just does not feel believable and is clearly not based on any actual research. Where in the first Crysis the Nano-suit sounds like something believable, even into Crysis 2 (yes I even read composite material chemical names on one PDA that I recognised from some science paper I read years ago about advanced omposite materials), the "future" theme here just feels pasted on. Huge level name and "Huddy bits" hover over the level as part of the 3D environment, probably meant to represent some "super HUD" display. But all connection with you as a soldier it lost along with all immersion. Crytek always include this kind of thing strictly from the PoV of the player so as not to break immersion. So, this game is not recommended by me. For future themes try Frontlines Fuel of War (underrated in my opinion), or if you like this kind of thing with sqaud mates following you around but with no squad commands then Medal of Honor 2010, or Warfighter is much better. Lastly my message to Ubisoft and other games developers ... when do I get soldiers back who actually follow orders ?

Party Hard is the game that let's you capitalize on all those years of hate. A mix of Hotline Miami, Commandos and Hitman but with multiple targets, your objective is to kill all party goers without being caught by the police. Simple enough, no? WRONG!!! Each party is a puzzle with moving parts (the party goers) that you have to carefully put together. You have a knife, traps, ambient hazards, explosions and much more to deal with at the party, but you must be careful with the police... They are faster then you and the more they are call to the party, more time they spend searching for you.
An excellent game with a dark vein in is humor that will give lot's of hours of enjoyable strategy and thinking.

I beat the game in about 2 hours. It was somewhat interesting, but rather shallow and not very difficult. The player goes down a few floors of a dungeon and then picks up an orb that's guarded by a rather unintimidating boss (I had no idea I had killed him). After you grab the orb, you make your way back to the entrance, which you can basically just rush using a hammer. Bow and arrows are extremely buggy, bouncing all over the place and phasing in and out of reality. While it's an interesting set of ideas, it's extremely slim on content and I feel like I saw the majority of it in two hours, as layouts didn't really seem to change much between my three attempts at getting the orb. I don't think I've ever beat a rougelike in three tries before. I think my opinion on the game would change if they vastly expanded on it, but it looks like it's been in this sort of shape for a while according to the forums.

It can be frustrating the fist few tries until you manage to get a setup that drops some decent gear on you and gets you moving, but it's a heck of a fun little RPG once you reach that point and really start making progress through a dungeon.
The Minecraft-like graphics also help give it a feel that's somewhere at a happy compromise between retro and modern.
My only grip is that is DOES have some balancing issues that cause it to occasionally generate a dungeon that kills you right off the bat due to lack of equiptment (the starting dagger is horrid because it's range is so short) and to many tough enemies clogged into one early area.
I got it in the Rouge-Like Humble Bundle, but I see it's only $8 on here so I'd say it's definatly worth it if you're into that sort of thing because being a fully realized 2.5D, first person dungeon crawler seems to be a bit of a rarity in this genre that tends to favor retro-style top-down or side-scrolling RPGs.

Stellaris is the best 4X grand strategy game that I have played.
And I've played a lot.
I suggest this game to anybody who likes realistic and incredible empire builders.
What will follow is basically a far-reaching tutorial for how to play the game if you're too snobby to take advantage of the tutorial robot your loving engineers will make for you.
The days go by in seconds on normal speed. I always have to jack it up to the highest speed because anything slower feels too boring, but I pause time flow constantly. Take advantage of the time flow settings. If you don't, you will find your homeworld under direct assualt once you make your first diplomatic transmission. If you aren't a micromanager then you're screwed. In the first years there is no 'explore until there is nothing left' option for science ships that will be surveying distant solar systems. There also isn't an 'improve and build everything until there is nothing left' option either meaning that the auto-construct option that you put all your civ 5 builders on is now your job. Construction ships are very important, but you only normally need 1-4 in your whole empire history, assuming you throw them to the wolves once a decade. Military is kinda necessary because if you don't have a strong navy then everbody else thinks you're pathetic, even if you have ten times the wealth they do. Without a navy everybody wants to go to war with you because they think they'll win and war is just really annoying, and devastating if you aren't good at it. Without a good army, it's hard to win wars. When you are running an offensive war and have essentially stripped several planets of spaceports, navy ships, and system outposts, then you have probably realized that the planets can easily reboot and clean up the damage left by you. This becomes a big issue if you can't leave a smaller force behind to babysit the planet. One of the things that isn't really made known is that the army is meant to invade planets that have been beaten to the ground and bombed by your navy ships (just select the option by right-clicking on the planet with your fleet selected). If you send your transport ships from embarked army units with your vanguard fleet and invade the planet right off the bat, your invasion force will be instantly defeated because of 'planetary fortifications', or just the general number on how tough it is to invade a planet. When an invasion is successful the planet will become occupied and partly under your control. Occupation gives a big warscore and neutralizes enemy systems until another army comes and liberates them. Occupation is different from annexation. You cannot annex a planet into your empire just by occupying it. Any occupations made during a war will end with the war. And that brings annother weird concept, war. War in Stellaris (sounds like a book) is really convoluded compared to war in other games. Firstly you have to establish war demands, basically you will stop fighting once you have open borders, free trade, ended slavery, etcetera. These war demands cost something called warscore, basically ending slavery is worth 20% of a war, or something. You can only have a warscore less than or equal to 100. You cannot annex every planet in an empire, end slavery, open borders, humiliate them, and make them a vassal all in the same war. You also cannot change your demands after the beginning of the war. Until you establish war demands you cannot gain warscore. Stellaris war makes war as a means to an end rather than fighting with a fun surprise at the end. Foreign policy is very complicated but very interesting. Your relative power to another empire is different from their opinion and their idea of you. If they are pathetic in comparison and have a -50 opinion of you, they may be 'receptive' to your policies. If they have a 200 opinion of you and are overwhelming in comparison, then they may have a 'protective' attitude. Unless they're a fallen empire. They hate everyboody and everything.
So, this is by far not everything in the game, but I think that if you read this you should understand how to interact with foreign empires and get started with your empire a bit better.

I was expecting more of a grand strategy but this is a bit too much 4X for me. It can be fun but the early game often feels like a chore. Also this is a nitpick but I don't really like any of the ship models which makes building navies and combat feel boring. Armies also feel underdeveloped and need more work. But this is a paradox game so expect a boatload of DLC down the pipe and a much more polished experience years from now. I'd say if you really like 4Xs and find space exploration to be exciting then this game will have alot to offer but if you prefer a rich diplomacy system or statisfying, deep and fun combat then this'll leave alot to be desired. I'll vote "yes" just because Steam makes me pick one but my true feelings about this game are of ambivalence.

Honestly, not a day goes by where I get bored of this. Every game/campaign is unique with the randomisation of empires, species, and rather well-made AI. It's even more fun when you create your own race and empire from scratch, as well as having the option to actually play with/against empires you've previously created, and see how the AI would fare with them.
I have yet to actually try the multiplayer feature, as Singleplayer is just so much fun already. However, I am sure Multiplayer is even more interesting, since the other empires aren't as predictable or easily persuaded. I will update this part of the review after playing on Multiplayer for some time.
Overall, I give this a strong 9.8/10. My only gripes are the somewhat limited options in empire creation, being colour schemes for ships and certain species, as well as the somewhat static skyboxes of the galaxy and star systems (although rotating the camera pleasantly shows that each skybox is very gorgeous and virtually seamless). However, that's some real nitpicking there, considering I just love this game so much, and truly recommend it for any Space RTS fans (or even general RTS fans) out there.
"Space exploration is a force of nature unto itself that no other force in society can rival."
~Neil deGrasse Tyson

Hexcells is a terrific, relaxing puzzle game. It takes place on a hex-based grid, and the point of each level is to figure out which cells to mark and which to not, similar to the premise of Minesweeper, but in the best possible way. There are several different mechanics introduced throughout the game, and each is introduced well and used in interesting ways in the following levels. There are 30 total levels, and some are short, mainly for the purpose of introducing a concept, but some, particularly the later levels, can take quite a while. I don't remember how long it took me the first time, but I've played through a few times to get to my current playtime.
It is nice that there is a unique solution to each level, and guessing is never required. You can always progress purely through logic, it just may take a bit to see how. There's no time constraint involved at all, so there's no reason not to take your time and work carefully through the levels. I found that almost all the mistakes I made were when I went too fast and hit the wrong button. The soundtrack is ambient and very relaxing, and the game does a good job of making the sound effects for actions in the game go with the music too.
The achievements come from progressing through the game, and from perfecting every level. The game's definition of 'perfecting' a level is nice and generous, and you can make a single mistake and it still counts, which comes in handy in some of the larger levels where at least one mistake is fairly inevitable. The achievements aren't too hard to get, though you may need to retry a level of two to minimize your mistakes.
Overall this is a wonderful, relaxing, puzzle game, and while it is somewhat on the short side, if you like it you should definitely get the other two, Hexcells Plus, and Hexcells Infinite. They're all wonderful, and Infinite even comes with a level generator.
Very relaxing puzzle game. If you like Minesweeper, you'll love this game. I highly recommend it. Especially for the price.
