I can totally see why people dislike this game.
But personally, I can't exactly tell you whether it's "good" or not. In fact, it's very confusing at that point.
I used to be a massive fan of the game when I was younger and played it upon it's release, but at the same time I paid a lot less attention to detail, and I had to quit it after a certain point because I couldn't get past the pre-last mission alone due to how difficult it was and I had no friends that would own this game.
So, now that I came back and completed it with my friend
, even though I had my fun, I struggle to make a conviction. Therefore, I'll just leave the following detail and you'll judge it from there:
The storyline of the game is nonexistent. It's like a cluster of random movie plots that were unfinished but somehow connected in a very odd manner. You'll play as the same characters all the time, yet it'll feel like they enter completely different worlds each time.
The combat system is one thing that it doesn't entirely fail at. It may feel a little bit choppy and weird here and there, but you'll certainly get used to it after a couple of missions or multiplayer sessions. However, you'll sometimes struggle to get past certain points if you're not careful enough and don't notice that an enemy randomly appeared to be behind you. It's not the best one, but it works well enough and it's guaranteed that you'll have fun with it. Certainly, it's nowhere as bad as Front Mission Evolved.
There's not much to say about the customization. However, it offers you thorough weapon adjustment, letting you change right about every single part of the gun. It's unique, but feels like it influences the weapon a lot less than it did in Ghost Recon: Phantoms.
As for the loadouts, you get to choose 2 grenade types from about 6 in total, as long as a primary(can be heavy, but can also be an SMG/shotgun/compact rifle) and secondary(can be a pistol or, again, SMG, shotgun, compact rifle) weapon.
Visually, the game is rather decent, or perhaps outstanding, for 2012. However, there's a lot better eye candy games out there if you're here for that.
That department has been handled quite well by the devs, surprisingly. One thing they didn't fail at all.
Even though there's only 12 missions in the entire game, each one of them feels completely unique and offers various types of action.
As an addition to that, each mission gives you "challenges" that you may complete to unlock certain customization options. They also add extra spice to the difficulty of the game. However, some of them may be questionable, considering you only get armor-piercing rounds almost at the end of the game and fixed stock in the final mission. Why? I honestly don't know, and that frustrates me, because I really wanted that fixed stock since the very start.

This game is absolute madness. The setting is unoriginal and generic, the characters cartoonish and ugly, and the gameplay over-the-top and messed up beyond belief. Combine that all together, and you get a love you either can't stand, or love beyond belief. And I went with the latter.
Loadout is fun. That's all it really is, fun. There's no stress you might get from other FPS/TPS games like CoD or Borderlands, mostly because of the fact you can't take this game seriously. The creators did everything they can to deliver a game that'll make you lose or die with a smile on your face, without feeling the frustration from similar games. Of course, this doesn't apply to everyone, but you get the general point here.
The weapon customization is awesome. Instead of choosing stock guns from different categories, you can design it in any way you want, from snipers to mini-guns to healing rocket launchers and whatnot. Even though some combinations might be considered "OP", it's all about the way you use it, or the way you dodge it. I have to agree the balance tends to tilt a teeny bit from time to time, but you can find that in a lot of similar games. The main point is, you can be as creative as you want with them,
The game modes currently available are Blitz (Control Points), Jackhammer (Capture the Flag), Death Snatch (Kill Confirmed), Extraction and Annihilation. The first three are what they are: Blitz is a simple "capture the control point" mode, where you need to stand on a point long enough to capture it, and 6 captures will decide the game. Jackhammer is basically Capture the Flag with a hammer instead of the flag that allows you to smack your enemies in one shot. Death Snatch is that CoD game mode with Blutonium (ore) instead of dog tags, and the most fun if you just like killing people. Extraction involves collecting the beforementioned ore enough times to win, and Annihilation is pretty much a combination of the first 3 mentioned game modes, also known as the "Competitive" mode.
Of course, the game isn't perfect. The outfits are awfully expensive (but look epic), the server still bugs out from time to time, and the party system might still throw your friends into the enemy team, even if there's enough space in the lobby. But then again, the game's still fresh, so they're expected issues.
In overall, this is currently one of the best F2P shooters out there. It's easy to pick up and play, a lot of fun to play with friends, and just insane in overall. If you're more of a serious gamer, it's best to stay away from this (although giving it a try won't hurt). If you're a casual(ish) gamer, give it a shot. And if you're a flying grapefruit like me, you'll absolutely love this game. Even if it's just to see yourself walking around with a giant hole in your body, or with just a brain and eyes, Loadout is fun for every game who likes to have a laugh every now and then while shooting off someone's head or arm. It's mindless fun with rather mindless characters.

Brilliant. Some fairly interesting gameplay, especially for a 2D game. Simple, yet good stealth/combat mechanics. It's more about learning to use your brain, and fast. Some good story as well. More than nothing though, this game has atmosphere.  It's dark, your flashlight won't shine two feet ahead of you, your ammunition is limited, you need food(and the means to make it. You can't exactly munch a can of beans, can you?). The building is confusing, it's long corridors seem all alike and you never know which step will put you face to face with... something. The main character is the perfect expression of this game: he gets tired; he feels claustrophobic; he freaks out when things happen beyond his comprehension. Is he really alone? Is he even sane? As you give in to the story and setting, this game keeps you on edge without any cheap scares. It's psychological trauma at its best. Worth every penny.

Let me start by saying that I enjoy 4x and strategy games in general but often lack the patience to actually take the time to learn all of their mechanics therefore in the end loving the idea of the game more than actually playing it.  Often I'll get into a game such as this and either get frustrated with it in some way or feel overwhelmed by the sheer amount of content to wade through in order to know if the first ship that I created was done so properly.  Stellaris for me has been the exception to that.  My friend asked me to play this game with him and I told him sure but don't expect me to stick with it and as of this writing we are now planning weekly games sometimes lasting six hours per session.
So I'll start by saying that I love the mechanics of this game in almost every way.  This is a 4x game that runs in real time but you don't feel like you are micro managing every unit like a traditional RTS, it's a very good hybrid approach.  To elaborate on that point, when you send a fleet of ships into combat, you aren't controlling several squads of ships in real time, you tell which fleets you want to fight to engage and then they all just jump in and fight it out unless you command them to retreat.   This simplfies the combat mechanic more than some typically enjoy but in general makes this game less about players ability to control lots of units and more about the strategy needed before combat begins.  Combat in Stellaris is important as is the design and power of your ships but it's not the key focus.
Stellaris is a strategy game that's focus is truly strategy.  One cannot simply work towards researching the most powerul hardware and expect to win because you can't just declare war and steam roll through an empire.  War is a carefully planned process that requires demands to be set and met win or lose.  If I declare war on another nation then I have to openly state that I want planets, to vasalize them, demand liberation of a nation or other similar options.  After the war is declared and demands set the war begins and each side has a score value that must be met.  That score can be achieved in a number of different ways but once it reaches 100% then the victor earns their demands and the declaring party cannot declare war on that nation again for 10 game years and a lot can happen in that time.  The losing party could build up relations with other empires to prevent the next war for example.
Another aspect that I really enjoy are the mechanics in the game that reduce a lot of the micro management tedium.  One example of this is the Outliner that appears on the right hand side of the UI.  If not for this one UI element, I'm not sure I would enjoy the game nearly as much because it helps to expidite so many functions of the game.  It essentially provides a breakdown of the key units and areas you are actively managing and makes it very easy to quickly access them and see what they are doing.  If I have three science ships on three different tasks, I can easily see their progress and can quickly navigate to their current location.  I can at a glance see each of my fleets, planets, sectors, opposing factions, etc.  The entire panel can also be customized to your needs or even hidden if you don't like it.
The creation of sectors is also of great importantance and goes a long way to eliminate the tedium of micro managing planets.  Once you get more than five planets (in vanilla), you must start to create system sectors or you suffer penalties.  Once the systems are in sectors, you set the options for the sector and it has it's own resources and manages the planets building queues, production and populations on it's own.  This is major because once you get to 7-8 planets it can become a real chore keeping up with everything they need.  Sectors can set their production focus, can have their own rulers, their contributions can be defined and more.  For me, this is what makes the game playable.
Multiplayer is also amazing in this game.  A game can consist of up to 32 players and can run at normal or faster speeds.  Players can join in pacts and federations as well as create trade agreements and contribute to others conflicts.  Or of course can just play free for all and wreck each other.  Be aware that there are still some bugs with multiplayer that require the host to reload the game from time to time but games can be saved to any of the players and someone else can host if need be.
Other small details....
The achievements can only be earned in single player iron man mode so that's something to be aware of too if that's something you enjoy.
This isn't a game that is normally played in one to two hours.  If a game is that short then things went horribly wrong..or right depending on which player you are.  This game will often last for days or possibly weeks depending on the game setup.  That fact alone might tell you if you do or don't want to play it, so bear that in mind as well.  .
You can create your own custom races as with other games of this type but the creation system is very intuitive and adds a lot to the game for me.
Players also need to manage their ships.  You can customize your ship's componets in great detail or leave it up to the AI to automatically manage them for you.  Overall, you have better builds if you manage them yourself but it isn't required to play the game.
Players also are not assured a win by researching a specific tree.  Research is randomized and you are given three choices initially to choose from each time you start to research a new project.  This is one of the great equalizers in the game because it forces the player to carefully balance their empire focus.  For some reading this, that may sound like a negative but it actually adds a great mechanic to the game.
So, in short, if traditional strategy or RTS games aren't your thing, give Stellaris a look.  Watch some YouTube videos, live streams, Let's Plays or something similar for a while and see the mechanics in action.  Watching for 5-10 minutes might not give you enough of a feel for it, so give it some time.  I wish they had a demo of this game out so anyone that's curious about it could actually try it out and see how great it is.  There is no shortage of 4x and strategy games on the market, but Stellaris stands out and creates a fresh new experience.

The Binding of Isaac is a roguelike game in which you play as a child traversing through randomly generated levels with the goal of stopping your mom from killing you. There is a large number of items that also randomly generate each playthrough that you can use to aid in your adventure. As you play the game, you unlock secrets and additional items to use in future playthroughs.
With the Wrath of Lamb DLC, there are additional items, a new item type, floors (as opposed to levels), and bosses. The DLC also introduces challenges that limit (or otherwise challenge) you, which upon completion unlock new items for the main game. If you are considering buying The Binding of Isaac, I highly recommend also purchasing the Wrath of Lamb DLC.
This game is heavy on both skill and luck. You will die a lot when you start playing the game. It will take many, many attempts to defeat the first final boss for the first time. As you complete playthroughs and unlock secrets, you will gain skill and new items that may help you in future playthroughs.
The biggest issue with this game is that the framerate drops when a lot of tears (projectiles) or flashing enemies (flies), probably due to using the Flash engine. This is highly noticeable while playing the game, especially upon completing two certain bosses. It took me at least 10 in-game hours to get used to the wild framerate. Another issue is that the game may almost crash when it tries generating certain floors, which can be resolved by waiting for the program to respond even if the option to close the problem comes up.
If you are interested in the game and would probably play this game a lot (tens and tens of hours), I would recommend purchasing The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth, which is a remake of the original game and DLC. A lot of new items, challenges, characters, enemies, and bosses are introduced. The art style is better (imo), the mechanics are better due to the change in game engine, and the game runs much more smoothly. The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth costs $14.99 normally. It is up to you on which you purchase if you want to.

The Binding of Isaac's strong point isn't its straightforward controls, its childish-yet-still-horrifying aesthetic, or even the way the soundtrack works alongside the small bits of background context to create a strangely immersive environment for a game that generally only lasts a half hour. No, its strong point is in presenting the same familiar things over and over while still, somehow, making each run unique. Everything is randomized. Each new door represents a nearly complete unknown. Each new power-up morphs Isaac into something new and different. Every divergent combination changes the way the game needs to be approached. That's what makes this  game so addictive; no run is exactly the same. Add to this the new possibilities that come along with each achievement won and The Binding of Isaac's legendary difficulty seems more manageable. That unbeatable floor or boss feels less daunting on the next run. Until, of course, the next unbeatable floor or boss. That will take another run entirely.

TLDR: An absolutely fantastic dungeon crawl that is casual and smooth, and feels more like a finished small team indie game than something in early access.
Gameplay takes less than a minute or two to get into and is helped by the butter smooth controls and simple control scheme. Attacking, either with magic, a melee weapon or a bow (when you find one) is simple but satisfying with the casual nature of the game.
Loot is plentiful and  takes after the genre of roguelikes because items must be used to figure out their effects. The simple hotbar system popular these days lets you see what your useful items are but provides challenge at later levels because potions and scrolls don't stack, leaving you with the choice to equip the scroll of resist magic you might need or the extra healing potion so you don't die.
Easy to get into, and hard to pull yourself away from, Delver is a diamond in the rough and offers fun in spades for casual dungeon crusaders.

After hearing great things by word of mouth and from a few reviews, I decided to purchase this game.
After playing through the game multiple times, (which is the only way to get a somewhat coherent story), I personally wouldn't reccomend this game.
The graphics are good. Pretty cliche hot-topic wearing female androids with oversized swords in school girl outifits. The action is okay, but it's pretty much arcade button mashing. While your attacks come off as cool, there wasn't much challenge or skill level in what you were actually doing.
Leveling up is fairly pointless, as you start and finish with pretty much the exact same move-set. You never learn new abilities, with the exception of a lame hacking mini-game, or making your Pod shoot somewhat different attacks. By level 15, I had the money to unlock all "chip" slots, where tthe bulk of your power ups and customization come from. Sure, you may later find a "Weapon Attack +5" as opposed to "Weapon Attack +1" chip, but  that's about as exciting as upgrading your character is ever going to get. You can get different weapons, but they all play so nearly identical, you could simply ignore this altogether and stay with your beginning weapons.
The characters themselves, while well animated, are devoid of personality for the most part. Proabably the most often said thing by 2B is "Understood." 9S was a little more lively, but again, he simply plays to generic anime tropes, and there was really no character development, nor any real reason to care about the characters.
A few of the battles were visually impressive, however, much like a lot of the game, the whole thing is very "on rails". You fight the boss in a generally obvious manner, then a cutscene insues, during which you miraculously find his weak spot and destroy it, etc.
Invisible walls permeate the world, and while it appears you would be able to explore the desolate abandoned city, etc,  you're pretty much limited throughout the game on where you can go. There's a few explorable parts out of the way, but they're few and far between.
Drops, aside from the few scant weapons you might find, are pretty terrible. Once I picked up my 75th plant seed or copper ore, I pretty much realized that they weren't worth the time to pick up. All they are is upgrade materials which you'll very, very rarely use. There simply wasn't a reason to even look in chests, as pretty much the only power-up's you'll need are healing items, which can be bought. Others are also fairly generic: Weapon attack up for 15 seconds, Ranged attack up for 15 seconds, ad nauseum.
The one shining beacon I did like is how the game would seamlessly turn from 3d, to suddenly being a sidescroller, shooter, or 3d shooter. While these elements didn't happen often, I will say they were pretty neat when they did ocasionally occur.
The story is about as absurd as one would think. Long ago, aliens attacked and sent machines to overtake earth. The humans lost, and vacated to a base on the moon. Now, they send school girl outfit wearing Androids to fight the war for them. I did like the low-tech approach to the machines, which was an interesting take on it. But the story is very sophmoric, grasping at the point of humanity, and the difference between Human consciousness and machine. I managed to get hooked on this game fairly quickly. Though under development and containing the usual Alpha-eque problems, the game offers an admirably realistic series of design elements. The game isn't for everyone--it's a game of numbers, spreadsheets, and it requires quite a lot of thought.
I'm not at liberty to name my employer IRL, but I can say I'm a test & QA engineer for an automaker in the United States and I've got to say that this game is very educational. There are a number of practical limitations that a sim must make for the sake of playability but nothing in the game is misrepresented. Design elements are heavily intertwined--cam selection, compression ratio, ignition timing and fuel mixture to name a few.
On the campaign side, the supply / demand aspect is very well done. The best feature, in my opinion, of the supply and demand is that your own designs start to compete with one another, and that requires some very nuanced tweaking by the player to maximize profit in a very well-simulated, cyclic economy. The cyclic economy means that your marketing people can be wrong with their sales forecasts, which some will find off-putting, but purists will love--you have to deal with error. It is a game for tweakers. the forum is great--lots of contests and active developers.
Disclaimers:
This game is not for everyone--this is not "minecraft meets GTA." The focus is on design and saleability.
It is early access, so it is quite buggy. Save often.
I am an automotive engineer IRL, but this is *not* a paid endorsement, and I'm not affiliated with any of the development team for Automation.

...is stealth puzzle game. Woken up in the middle of the night by the loud music of a neighboring BBQ, you snap and go on a murderous streak, killing everyone from party to party.
You walk around, stabbing people and killing them in various creative ways, trying not to be seen or caught next to a body. Each level has various traps you can make use of, such as poisoning punch bowls, setting rooms on fire, exploding ovens, and more. There's some level randomization that may change available traps, rooms or even party goers.
Each level feels very different, with its own theme, music and unique traps, and offer varied difficulty, including 4 much harder and tricky ones in the
. Additional challenges include bouncers, dogs, cops and FBI agents, which you must escape from using traps or escape routes, overuse of which can have them condemned, limiting your options as the crowd thins.
While stabbing is the most common way you'll kill people, there's plenty of variety to be had. In most levels, you'll be able to get your hands on a special item, be it beer poison, swords, bombs and more to add to the level's own traps. You can even use the phone to cause a random event to happen, such as pest control dropping by to fumigate rooms, zombies eating out the crowd, or an even crazier killer to come after you.
There's plenty of replayability offered in this game. Beyond light level randomization, you have a bunch of unlockable heroes with different play styles: Katie can knock people out and drag them to a discreet place to kill them, the Ninja can use smoke grenades but mustn't be seen by anyone, and more. Steam Workshop integration allows you to try new challenging levels and locations indefinitely.
While the pixelated aesthetics won't please everyone, most of the soundtrack is an epic retro party 8-bit style that, while repetitive after a while in the same level, will get stuck in your head.
Difficulty levels aren't consistent with the game's progress. You may have a very hard level you'll fail at over and over again, followed by a rather generic stab and hide level you'll complete in no time. Levels just don't have enough traps to them, just a few, and most of which only work once. Seeing there's only one item per level, the later half of the levels will often leave you with nothing but your stabbing knife.
You'll have to go through a lot of trial and error in some levels, and the slight level randomization makes it harder to master any of them. You'll sometime get killed for no good reason, such as when you're dancing to disperse a crowd, or being branded as a murderer because someone happened to have died near you from poison you had given them at an earlier time in a totally different location (although it's funny to see other people get accused of the murder for the same reason).
This was a lot of goofy fun! It was challenging at times, and will have me come back to try things differently. If you're looking for a psycho-movie experience, turn your gaze to
or
instead. But if you want a puzzle game with a very original twist, you have got to give
a try!

Party Hard is a stealth-based puzzle game? I guess that's the best way to describe it.
Each map has the simple objective of "kill everyone without getting caught" - and so the puzzle aspect comes from how you can set up traps on the level to kill people without having the death linked to your action, or leaving bodies near people who are sleeping so the person who finds the body calls the cops on the sleeping person, blaming them for the crime.
It is deceptively difficult for the goofy premise, and some levels can become very long and drawn out if there are a handful of people left all close together so you need to wait for them to split up unwittingly which can take a very long time, or take a risk and get them to split up while making your presence known with a silly dance.
The final level is very buggy, unfortunately, but other than that the game is quite fun.
Local co-op certainly adds to the carnage, as poor communication will lead to your friends being arrested for murders that you committed because they get spotted near a body you forgot to hide.
And of course, if you do finish the game and get sick of the levels having unlocked all the characters, there is Steam Workshop support with people making new levels, admittedly of varying quality, but at least you'll never run out of content.
The multiple characters are interesting - all have advantages and/or disadvantages, and being able to combine them in the local co-op by having a cop playing with the regular man allows the man to set traps that the cop can't while the cop can flag people for arrest for when the trap is set off and the body is found.
The Dark Castle DLC I couldn't really get into, and there are some bugs (worst one being where the number of kills required to finish the level is more than the number of people at the party - which is usually fixed on a restart but can be frustrating if you learn that AFTER clearing the entire house), but overall it is a solid experience that benefits from having people over, but is still wholy complete on its own.

One of the best RTS/Turn Based strategy games I have ever played, Medieval II: Total War is a gem within a greatly honored series. Medieval II follows the early portion of the Medieval period (~1080) all the way through the late Medieval period and the discovery of the new world (~1530), this RTS/Turn Based hybrid is a slow paced strategy geared towards domination through war and conquest.
The game features a diplomacy system and incorporates a grand strategy map with RTS battles. The hybrid allows for players to enjoy one or the other or both systems in their path to ruling Medieval Europe.
The initial stages of the game are slow going, and patience is a requirement unless one doesn't care about the grand campaign. Other than the grand campaign, one can partake in custom and quick RTS battles or historical RTS battles inspired by actual events. One can play a number of factions including France, England, the Holy Roman Empire, the Moors, the Byzantine Empire, the Danish, and many more, all complete with strengths and weaknesses. The only con is that only about five or six of the factions are playable from the beginning until one completes either the short or long campaign (the difference between those is the amount of regions one must own and the factions one must destroy. For example: England's short campaign requires 15 provinces and the destruction of France, while the Long Campaign requires 50 provinces, including Jerusalem, as well as the destruction of France and Scotland).
Overall, a well made game to pour a large number of hours into as you await your destruction by the Mongols :)

Stellaris is the best 4X grand strategy game that I have played.
And I've played a lot.
I suggest this game to anybody who likes realistic and incredible empire builders.
What will follow is basically a far-reaching tutorial for how to play the game if you're too snobby to take advantage of the tutorial robot your loving engineers will make for you.
The days go by in seconds on normal speed. I always have to jack it up to the highest speed because anything slower feels too boring, but I pause time flow constantly. Take advantage of the time flow settings. If you don't, you will find your homeworld under direct assualt once you make your first diplomatic transmission. If you aren't a micromanager then you're screwed. In the first years there is no 'explore until there is nothing left' option for science ships that will be surveying distant solar systems. There also isn't an 'improve and build everything until there is nothing left' option either meaning that the auto-construct option that you put all your civ 5 builders on is now your job. Construction ships are very important, but you only normally need 1-4 in your whole empire history, assuming you throw them to the wolves once a decade. Military is kinda necessary because if you don't have a strong navy then everbody else thinks you're pathetic, even if you have ten times the wealth they do. Without a navy everybody wants to go to war with you because they think they'll win and war is just really annoying, and devastating if you aren't good at it. Without a good army, it's hard to win wars. When you are running an offensive war and have essentially stripped several planets of spaceports, navy ships, and system outposts, then you have probably realized that the planets can easily reboot and clean up the damage left by you. This becomes a big issue if you can't leave a smaller force behind to babysit the planet. One of the things that isn't really made known is that the army is meant to invade planets that have been beaten to the ground and bombed by your navy ships (just select the option by right-clicking on the planet with your fleet selected). If you send your transport ships from embarked army units with your vanguard fleet and invade the planet right off the bat, your invasion force will be instantly defeated because of 'planetary fortifications', or just the general number on how tough it is to invade a planet. When an invasion is successful the planet will become occupied and partly under your control. Occupation gives a big warscore and neutralizes enemy systems until another army comes and liberates them. Occupation is different from annexation. You cannot annex a planet into your empire just by occupying it. Any occupations made during a war will end with the war. And that brings annother weird concept, war. War in Stellaris (sounds like a book) is really convoluded compared to war in other games. Firstly you have to establish war demands, basically you will stop fighting once you have open borders, free trade, ended slavery, etcetera. These war demands cost something called warscore, basically ending slavery is worth 20% of a war, or something. You can only have a warscore less than or equal to 100. You cannot annex every planet in an empire, end slavery, open borders, humiliate them, and make them a vassal all in the same war. You also cannot change your demands after the beginning of the war. Until you establish war demands you cannot gain warscore. Stellaris war makes war as a means to an end rather than fighting with a fun surprise at the end. Foreign policy is very complicated but very interesting. Your relative power to another empire is different from their opinion and their idea of you. If they are pathetic in comparison and have a -50 opinion of you, they may be 'receptive' to your policies. If they have a 200 opinion of you and are overwhelming in comparison, then they may have a 'protective' attitude. Unless they're a fallen empire. They hate everyboody and everything.
So, this is by far not everything in the game, but I think that if you read this you should understand how to interact with foreign empires and get started with your empire a bit better.

The Binding of Isaac's strong point isn't its straightforward controls, its childish-yet-still-horrifying aesthetic, or even the way the soundtrack works alongside the small bits of background context to create a strangely immersive environment for a game that generally only lasts a half hour. No, its strong point is in presenting the same familiar things over and over while still, somehow, making each run unique. Everything is randomized. Each new door represents a nearly complete unknown. Each new power-up morphs Isaac into something new and different. Every divergent combination changes the way the game needs to be approached. That's what makes this  game so addictive; no run is exactly the same. Add to this the new possibilities that come along with each achievement won and The Binding of Isaac's legendary difficulty seems more manageable. That unbeatable floor or boss feels less daunting on the next run. Until, of course, the next unbeatable floor or boss. That will take another run entirely.

I really want to like this game but I can't. I bought this game back when it wasn't on steam and the engine designer was all they had made.

I feel they have taken a step backwards in implementing the performance index number and now there are just boxes with percentage numbers to show what state the engine is in. There are just too many numbers in this game. I really liked the old view where you had all the parts of the engine and when they were working correctly they were green and when they weren't, they were red or orange. I think that a lot of the numbers are just for the tycoon aspect of the game and altough calculations still need to be done maybe just don't show them to the user or possibly come up with words to describe the attributes. For example smoothness is a value out of hundred which affects the car's comfort and probably others but could just be described as poor, okay, good, very good. In all honesty it's just starting to feel like an excel spreadsheet where you have to balance the numbers, not something that feels like real life. Another complaint I have is all the graphs showing up over each of the screens, it's overwhelming and turns the screen into a mess. Overall the engine designer is great and you won't experience anything like it anywhere else but I wish they would maybe stop playing around with it as it once felt finished. I'm not even a fan of the new UI for the engine designer, it's just a mess.
The car designer is terrible. Sure it's a great idea and you won't find anything else like it but it is a long way from living up to what the engine designer is. To me the car doesn't feel real. The engine feels real and alive but this doesn't. I think the UE4 is a step in the right direction and at the moment it is still buggy but there is a lot of work to be done. Like where is the interior? Why can't i see my car lowered? Can I turn the lights on? Can I open the doors? It's not real. Again there are a lot of numbers in this mode which just seem useless. I mean ofcourse a truck/ute is going to have a high number of utility and be practical, whereas a 2 door sports coupe isn't. I mean these calculations need to be made but why do we see them on the screen? I already know the type of car I want to make why do you have to tell me what it is? Unless it's a real life measurment it doesn't make sense to show it.
I was really excited when I found out they were making a tycoon aspect to this game. I enjoy tycoon games and to be able to design your own car and sell it? Even better. Let's be honest. Do you really even enjoy the tycoon side of this game? No. You don't. It is the worst and if they continue with the current format it's just going to be terrible. I'm not sure that the tycoon aspect should even be included in this game. The car market screen is just plain bad, I thought with the new UI it would be different but it's still the same! What is the point of spending 2 years on this port just to make it worse??? Note that the tycoon isn't in UE4 but the market screen is and it is still terrible. My main complaint about the tycoon part is that you spend all this time designing a piece of art and in the end all the car turns out to be is a number on an excel spreadsheet.  Like are the developers going to turn this into the level of detail the engine designer as a really detailed business simulator or is it just going to be simply that you sold x amount of cars and made this profit... I feel the tycoon part of the game isn't thought out very well. The game needs to be structured so it is the main part of the game. At the moment it's just one big workflow that you work through and the tycoon is just a bit at the end. It needs to be structured better. You start off by building a car. You should be starting off by building a company/small business. Make it feel entrepreneurial. It doesn't make you feel like you're running a company which I feel would give you the biggest sense of achomplishment. At the moment I don't think the tycoon mode adds any value to this experience. Afterall this is Automation - "The car company tycoon game"... A more appropriate title should read : Automation - "The car designer game".
I get that this game isn't finished but they aren't making progress as of the first release of UE4. The engine designer has gone backwards, the car designer has got slightly better and has a long way to go but the tycoon side feels like an after thought. At this stage, the game is a car designer first and a tycoon game second and I feel the focus lies in the tycoon part of the game. This whole game sounds like a great concept in theory but it doesn't really deliver. It doesn't deliver because I don't feel like the game modes work together and I don't find it fun as a whole. I don't regret buying this game, it has potential and has provided me hours of fun with the engine designer it's just that I was promised so much more.. If you don't own the game I would still encourage you to buy it if you like cars but if you're expecting a 'tycoon' game, don't bother.

provides you with multiple shapes, lights, trim pieces to play with.
Then there's the Tycoon element. Ironically, the main goal of this game but also the

of game engine. One thing i particularly appreciate from the developers of this game is
their constant news updates, wether or not they release something. That goes a long
way in keeping a community supporting the game and nurturing the feeling of 'being
part of developement' which is the main reason any game can get away with charging
you for what is essentially a beta.
Would buy again, on sale. Full price maybe once the new engine update is done and
most elements are functional again.

I have been purchasing and playing every NBA 2k game since 2005. This is the third one I own for PC (15,16,17). First of all this game has improved in the physics department in terms of you cannot simply pass through people and must actually manuever around them and rebounding/passing is more about your tmiing and position as opposed to spamming the button. However this game is by far the most flawed and incomplete NBA 2k game to date. The load times are still bad as ever (game is installed to my SSD), the shot stick has changed for the worse in terms of having to aim it in a particular "sweet" spot angle to get a close to perfect release. The slightest misdirection can result in an airball even for those that have HoF shooting badges. The online community is sadly divided into regions, which normally would not be bad but with the lack of people that buy this game for pc to play mypark it can make finding people to play with/against impossible at times. The rewards system does not work as I have unlocked myplayer reward cards that failed to redeem in myteam, people still get online with hacked stat characters that are 98 or more overall without having attained superstar mypark rep. The game has a nasty bug for those that run on 144hz or more with v-synch off that seems to affect text msgs in terms of it will scroll down super slow to a point it is not playable and cutscenes will move at a fast speed often resulting in them concluding before you can even hear all the dialogue. The game has a lot of pointless events and things to do that waste time and take away from the experience of just wanting to play basketball. Loading screens for everything. If you just enjoy the single player/offline experiences I would suggest this game for PC. However, if your looking for depth and serious about online play I would rec getting it on console as they seem to get patched and supported way faster than pc. Consoles have already received their first 7+ gb patch to resolve some issues while pc is left in the dust once again.
PROS
-Good physics
-fun game
-good shooting (with botton not stick)
-lots to do
Cons
-buggy
-people hack and get away with it
-lack of dev support for pc version
-horrible load times
-glitches for monitors higher than 60hz
-myplayer - myteam card redeem issues
-VC money hungry to almost force you to buy VC with real $
If you like basketball you really have no choice as this is the only real basketball game to play. Enjoy it but do not have your expectations set to high and try not to fall for their VC cash grab. Earn it slowly but surely and use your actual $ for something productive.

So I put about 40 hours into NBA2K10 and around 20 into NBA2K11, I enjoyed both those games quite a bit. That was in the campaing alone as in either of those games the online was complete trash and if it did happen to work, it would be sluggish. I'm happy to say that just about all online issues have been ironed out for the PC. I've spent 15 hours into the game and I've only completed the first college match, the rest has been all MyPark.
As of now I'm sitting at Pro 1 and I'm slowly going up in rank, the experience has been very smooth so far. You can even deck out your character in gear from the store. It's not hard to earn gold if you play well and win, if you play poorly and win you won't get much of anything. The only downside to MyPark so far is the lack of players and I feel like that's because a lot of people are either doing quickplay matches, or the PC community is just very small due to all the previous games being done so poorly.
If you do get the game and want to try it out, I highly suggest going to sunset beach, that way you can at least get into some matches during peak times (when everyone is out of work/school). If you choose the other two, there is a low chance you'll see anyone playing frequently. Usually later in the day all the courts are full which is nice because it's easy to queue up for the next game.
I just wanted to shine some light on the multiplayer aspect of this as it's all I ever wanted in a NBA2K game for PC. It works, I enjoy it a lot, that's all that really matters to me. Nit picking the mechanics really isn't my thing as the game feels smooth as is, if you play smart you get rewarded well, if you're hitting bricks the whole game and hogging the ball, you won't be ranking up any time soon.

Unfortunately for this game, due to how it's made. A great deal of intial manual setup needs to be made. Read on for information on how to get proper smooth performance so you can enjoy this great title!
This game suffers from some weird performance issues related to how incredibly CPU intensive it is. Even though the game looks great, it doesn't rely much on your GPU hardware and unfortunately only utilises 2 processor cores properly. You'll find from using apps like CPU-Z and GPU-Z that only really uses about 40% of the GPU and yet 80% or more of the CPU.
This is an issue with most NCSOFT games, such as Guild Wars 2 and Blade and Soul.
___________________________________________________
To fix performance issues in Wildstar on 99% of machines (even very good ones). Follow these steps:
In-game options -> Video -> Set
to LOW.
In-game options -> Video -> Set
(the first slider) to about 300, or as low as possible.
In-game options -> Video -> Set
to LOW, or OFF.
Also
In-game options -> Addons -> Disable [CombatLog]
In-game options -> Addons -> Disable [Who]
and if possible, please get a different UI like "PotatoUI".
___________________________________________________
Just about every other option you can actually leave at max with a decent PC. If you have an i5 or i7 and a decent GPU like a GTX 980 or 1070,
. Changing just these 3 settings should give you a massive performance boost of about 30fps or more in all situations. In fact, you could even leave most settings at max so long as your GPU has a good amount of dedicated RAM as only few GPU stream processors are utilised in this game.
I was hovering around 35fps in small village areas with other players. This put my frames to a constant 55-60 no matter where I am and with a GSYNC monitor I don't notice any lag what-so-ever. For me this is the difference between recommending the game and not recommending it (and obviously not playing it).
Wildstar has gotten a lot of optimisation updates over the last few years however a lot of them have come too late. It's my hope that more people will give this game another shot because it truly is fantastic and contrary to years of experience, it can be played very smoothly now.
Give it a try and play around with the settings because we no longer have to sacrifice nice details for performance any more (at least not as much).

SIDE NOTE/ Word bank for the new or casual gamer: Power Creep is when a Game usually forces you to use a higher leveled piece of gear to do more Damage or take more damage from higher leveled baddies, even if the gear you had before had better stats. Stellaris is the best 4X grand strategy game that I have played.
And I've played a lot.
I suggest this game to anybody who likes realistic and incredible empire builders.
What will follow is basically a far-reaching tutorial for how to play the game if you're too snobby to take advantage of the tutorial robot your loving engineers will make for you.
The days go by in seconds on normal speed. I always have to jack it up to the highest speed because anything slower feels too boring, but I pause time flow constantly. Take advantage of the time flow settings. If you don't, you will find your homeworld under direct assualt once you make your first diplomatic transmission. If you aren't a micromanager then you're screwed. In the first years there is no 'explore until there is nothing left' option for science ships that will be surveying distant solar systems. There also isn't an 'improve and build everything until there is nothing left' option either meaning that the auto-construct option that you put all your civ 5 builders on is now your job. Construction ships are very important, but you only normally need 1-4 in your whole empire history, assuming you throw them to the wolves once a decade. Military is kinda necessary because if you don't have a strong navy then everbody else thinks you're pathetic, even if you have ten times the wealth they do. Without a navy everybody wants to go to war with you because they think they'll win and war is just really annoying, and devastating if you aren't good at it. Without a good army, it's hard to win wars. When you are running an offensive war and have essentially stripped several planets of spaceports, navy ships, and system outposts, then you have probably realized that the planets can easily reboot and clean up the damage left by you. This becomes a big issue if you can't leave a smaller force behind to babysit the planet. One of the things that isn't really made known is that the army is meant to invade planets that have been beaten to the ground and bombed by your navy ships (just select the option by right-clicking on the planet with your fleet selected). If you send your transport ships from embarked army units with your vanguard fleet and invade the planet right off the bat, your invasion force will be instantly defeated because of 'planetary fortifications', or just the general number on how tough it is to invade a planet. When an invasion is successful the planet will become occupied and partly under your control. Occupation gives a big warscore and neutralizes enemy systems until another army comes and liberates them. Occupation is different from annexation. You cannot annex a planet into your empire just by occupying it. Any occupations made during a war will end with the war. And that brings annother weird concept, war. War in Stellaris (sounds like a book) is really convoluded compared to war in other games. Firstly you have to establish war demands, basically you will stop fighting once you have open borders, free trade, ended slavery, etcetera. These war demands cost something called warscore, basically ending slavery is worth 20% of a war, or something. You can only have a warscore less than or equal to 100. You cannot annex every planet in an empire, end slavery, open borders, humiliate them, and make them a vassal all in the same war. You also cannot change your demands after the beginning of the war. Until you establish war demands you cannot gain warscore. Stellaris war makes war as a means to an end rather than fighting with a fun surprise at the end. Foreign policy is very complicated but very interesting. Your relative power to another empire is different from their opinion and their idea of you. If they are pathetic in comparison and have a -50 opinion of you, they may be 'receptive' to your policies. If they have a 200 opinion of you and are overwhelming in comparison, then they may have a 'protective' attitude. Unless they're a fallen empire. They hate everyboody and everything.
So, this is by far not everything in the game, but I think that if you read this you should understand how to interact with foreign empires and get started with your empire a bit better.

Honestly, not a day goes by where I get bored of this. Every game/campaign is unique with the randomisation of empires, species, and rather well-made AI. It's even more fun when you create your own race and empire from scratch, as well as having the option to actually play with/against empires you've previously created, and see how the AI would fare with them.
I have yet to actually try the multiplayer feature, as Singleplayer is just so much fun already. However, I am sure Multiplayer is even more interesting, since the other empires aren't as predictable or easily persuaded. I will update this part of the review after playing on Multiplayer for some time.
Overall, I give this a strong 9.8/10. My only gripes are the somewhat limited options in empire creation, being colour schemes for ships and certain species, as well as the somewhat static skyboxes of the galaxy and star systems (although rotating the camera pleasantly shows that each skybox is very gorgeous and virtually seamless). However, that's some real nitpicking there, considering I just love this game so much, and truly recommend it for any Space RTS fans (or even general RTS fans) out there.

In my own opinion (please don't hate me internets) this is one of the best roguelike games out there.
The art style is charming, the music is catchy, and the environments keep the dungeon from getting to stale and repetitive.  I've been playing this game since it was in the alpha stages before it was even on Steam, and every time an update is released, it introduces new and exciting features to the game.
One of the strongest features though is the balance between difficulty, length, and permadeath.  The game isn't tremendously long, but it is quite challenging.  This is fantastic because when you win it feels like an accomplishment, but if you die it isn't a crippling blow as you were probably only 3-6 floors down.  Another 20 or 30 minutes and you could potentially get there again.
This game is a hidden gem of the indie developer scene and I sincerely hope it receives the recognition it deserves.

Unfortunately there is a problem here in that for all the control you have over where to fling your marble there's very little skill involved and that lowers the experience to something like a cheap carnival game with better visuals and no toy prize at the end.  The marble bouncing is just too haphazard which makes some of the more advanced stages feel hopeless.
No matter.  The game is bright, cheerful, and easily played in small doses making it a perfect snack break of entertainment.

When I bought the game I expected something in the likes of one of my all-time favorites Perfect Dark for Nintendo 64 which was published the same year as Deus Ex. I got exactly that. It's a game that looks old. You can see the polygons on people's faces and lip sync was out of question back then. Yay, nostalgia! First of all I think allowing the player to take different routes, customize their character with skills and upgrades(augmentations), and upgrade their weaponry is a big plus. You can literally finish the game without killing a single npc. And the story develops really well. However, I would have taken a different route in programming the ranged weaponry and weapon skills. Sneaking up to someone and shooting them right in the head should ALWAYS kill them but in this game it only does so 100% of the time when you got your weapon skill high enough. I would have done that by increasing the spray for automatic weapons and crosshair movement to simulate breathing and heartbeat while aiming for non-automatic guns as they do in modern shooters. Also, I find the ending cutscenes are pretty poor. The game offers 3 endings. Initially I wanted to play them all but after finishing the first I decided not to take the hassle but just watch the other 2 on youtube instead. Only in the last 15 minutes of the game or so you decide which ending you want so you don't miss anything in the game should you decide not to play all endings. Other than that I think this is a great game.

Hexcells is a short puzzler somewhat similar to the traditional minesweeper. Essencially, you have to follow the hints within the board to find out if each one of the hidden cells is blue or grey; as you turn up the cells, they might give you more hints to help you proceed.
The gameplay is fairly simple: you must use the mouse's right button if you think that the hidden cell is grey and left button if you think it is blue. At the end of each level, you earn blue cells as a reward: the less mistakes you make, more cells you earn.
This is a relaxing game with a beautiful design and calm soundtrack; the difficulty increases progressively, but you will probably have to try some levels a few times before you complete them without making mistakes. The final levels might keep you busy for a while, but keep in mind that it is a game you can finish in less than two hours.
Extremly fun and addictive puzzle game.  I also recommend the sequels.

If you fancy some numeric/spatial puzzles, Hexcells is a great, mouse-only game. The soundtrack and sound design are immensely soothing, as complementiary musical notes are played everytime you correctly click a hex. If you are like me, and like the feeling of 'cleaning up' a game board, then this game is for you. It also rewards you with a strong audible and visual cues of progression.
Only downside is that it is a bit short, but then again, it is very cheap.
In short, it's like a relaxing mix of Sudoku and Minesweeper, that is challenging, but not very punishing.
incredibly addicting.  A definite need for logic puzzle lovers. :)

A straight forward puzzle game. Simply reveal all the hexagons in a given level (turning them to black or blue). There are various clues that are provided to let the players know which cells are which. The game ramps up in difficulty with larger puzzles and more clues.
I found the puzzles sufficiently challenging (particularly when trying to solve with no mistakes). The music is nice. There are only 30 maps with limited replay (the game can be completed in 2-3 hours) and there isn't much in the way of options (music is on or off, you can flip mouse keys, change the resolution). There wasn't a save feature but I found I was able to complete most puzzles in 15 minutes or less.
It's a good game for a few bucks that you can judge if you want to move on to the more challenging Hexcells + and infinite. While I do have a favorable opinion about this game, you wouldn't miss out on skipping it and going to Hexcells Plus.

Glacier 3 is, supposedly, a game that mixes racing with car combat: I say supposedly because the actual game is horrible whether you're driving ot trying to shoot an opponent.
The aforementioned issues paired with bad graphics and unfair AI makes this game a wreck.
-gotta admit, the devs were brave to put their names in the credits of this thing
-the music is somewhat decent
-graphics look as if they came straight out of an early PS2 game
-weak sounds for cars and weapons
-laughable options menu, only music and fx volume, no graphics/ resolution options, no keybinds
-no tutorial whatsoever,you'll have to blindly tap buttons until you find the right ones
-horrible driving mechanics, the car turns way too much on the spot and slides all over
-aiming weapons is very hard, since there's no target lock and they shoot far and high from you, you'll basically miss most shots even when opponents are near due to the height difference between cars and targeting reticle
-unfair AI gobbles most boosts and sprints to the finish line while you trail behind
-no story whatsoever, even in Story mode
-races are very short (about 1 minute long)
Considering the horrible production values, that make the game look way older than it actually is, Glacier 3 also fails in providing at least an enjoyable experience when played: the unbearable driving and shooting mechanics makes for a frustrating and pointless experience as you trail behind AI controlled cars with little hope of winning at least a race.
Story mode is a joke since there's no story, it's just 4 races one after the other and a final leaderboard where you're supposed to finish first to unlock more features: even without the aforementioned issues making said races very hard to win they'd be bad regardless, since each race is just a very short lap from point A to B in boring environments.
Sorry but I have no idea what positive reviews see in this game, especially when there's better offers in the genre (Gas Guzzlers Extreme for example): Glacier 3 is a mess and simply isn't worth the asking price, nor should be purchased even if on sale.

Loadout - Now this is how to Free-2-Play. In this brainchild of Team Fortress 2 with hints of Borderlands, two teams of four players each are pitted against each other in several different gamemodes.
The name of the game here is customisation, while you can only choose from three different playermodels, each one can be customised with a plethora of clothing-items and accessories to make him or her stand out. More noticably though are the options for customising your weapons. Apart from the very basic assault rifle you get given at the start, you can unlock dozens of new gun parts through playing the game and researching them down a tech tree. Pretty much any kind of weapons you can think of can somehow be recreated through weapon-crafting. The main inspiration here can be Team Fortress 2, as handheld rocket launchers or a healing beam-weapon can easily be made, but the options exceed this by far. Want to make a mortar that shoots flaming clusterbombs? Go ahead. A sniper rifle shooting electric beams? No problem, once you have the parts for it.
Very big props go out to the developers for not messing up their Free-2-Play model here, all of the things you need for weapon-crafting can not be purchased through microtransactions, they must be earned by actually playing the game. This game's premium currency is solely used for the cosmetic aspects. The only downside here is that, while you can earn clothing-items occasionally, they are very rare, so your character will end up looking fairly bland and generic until much later, unless you spend real money on it.
Now, with all the options for different weapons there are of course quite a few combinations that do not make sense or are just not viable on the battlefield. You can come up with some extremely situational boomsticks and still find yourself outmatched by a boring beam-sniper. It is completely up to you, however, so you can find the combination that best suits your personal playstyle.
The game is still not finished, so some features are not yet implemented. This means that for those who love variety, not much is offered after playing a few rounds and testing out some of the guns. The game seems to lose its novelty-value fairly quickly right now. But hey, it's completely free to play, full of humour and the microtransactions, as of now, will not allow anyone to get unfair advantages over those who won't pay. Definitely worth at least a look.

This is the 4X space empire builder I've been waiting for since GalCiv II. It's abundently clear a great amount of time, effort, love and care were invested in Stellaris, and it was time and effort well spent. The core concept (colonise planets, build space stations, build ships and build a galactic empire) is superbly well done, with just the right amount of "just a bit longer..."-inducing management required without getting bogged down in it.
Random story chains spawn and develop, with each set of ethics you choose influencing what is the recommended (but not compulsory) route to go down, meaning you won't have the same game twice.
True, the game does tend to slow down a bit in the middle era when everyone has expanded as much as possible, but the initial colonise/develop phase is very fulfilling and can swallow up long, long joyful hours, and the end-game crisis phase to help speed up the resolution is a great way to end things.
The game is also being regularly updated to try and make as many different playstyles as possible viable (eg - so you can play as Space Gandhi if you want to), and it's clear this already great game is only likely to improve as time goes on.

Lone Survivor is a brave experiment: attempting to bring a visceral horror experience with a distinctive 2D pixelated graphic is not a common thing, especially because the game must provide the player with a lot of atmosphere to make the imagination replacing what such simple graphic cannot show. To achieve this goal, J. Byrne decided to add some rpg elements to a classic side scrolling adventure game, like the necessity to properly rest and eat/drink while exploring the spectral and dangerous city. Ammunitions and supplies are scarse, enemies are tough and numerous, but exploring rewards the player with useful items. Several characters can be met during the travel, they have sidequests for the player and they also help to put together the pieces of the puzzle of a very interesting story behind "You", the main character of the game. Unfortunately the game suffers of a certain repeatability which may cause some yawns in the second half of the adventure, and a confusing and rushed ending

Full disclosure, this review is based on the single player campaign only.   I have been a big fan Ubisoft's Tom Clancy games, from the original PC Rainbow Six and Ghost Recon games though the XBox 360/PS3 generation.  I wanted to like this game, I really did, but as a single player experience, I can't give Future Soldier my recommendation.  First off, this is a pretty meh port of the console version.  Graphically at times the exteriors look pretty decent, but interiors tend to look low-res and muddy.  Also, don't expect a lot of graphic options to tweak.
All that aside, my major issues revolve around AI and gameplay problems.  The friendly AI is not the sharpest and tends to get shot a lot, even in small firefights.  The enemy AI, as is typical with many "squad-based" shooters, has a tendency to focus in on the you, regardless of the relative danger presented by your AI controlled squad mates, as if to acknowledge, "those dudes aren't very sharp."  The implementation of the mark & execute system, borrowed it seems, from the latter Splinter Cell games, is nicely done and provides a welcome tactical element.  However, most firefights descend into chaos, which DOES happen in real life, yet unlike real soldiers, you very much need to babysit your AI counterparts in the heat of battle.  And therein lies my biggest issue with this game, it sits somewhere between a tactical squad-based shooter and a third person action shooter, while not being a shining example of either.
I suspect there is fair amount of fun to be had as a four player co-op experience, and the overall design seems like that is what the devs were aiming for; I would grudgingly give it a thumbs up for a like minded group-just don't expect to be blown away.

Legendary game for those who just want to sleep while your neighbours are having a party

Do you have THAT kind of neighbor? You know, the kind who has a noisy party every stinking weekend? And you've talked to that guy before, but he never seems to invite you over while he has seemingingly EVERY OTHER PERSON ON THE PLANET over? And you call the cops every time, but they can't do a thing about the noise? I can't blame you for taking matters into your own hands; and it appears Pinokl Games can't either!
You are some shmo who decided living in a college neighborhood was a smashing idea; somehow not suspecting this would entail weekly shindigs.  How one couldn't expect this forever escapes me.  Anyway, one night you decide the wisest and most level headed thing to do is to sneak over and kill the party, as well as every other person there.  I guess shooters and fighting games can't be the only ones that get to have all the violent fun.  Although, I do have a question; If you did want to get back to sleep why wouldn't you just bring a gun or a chainsaw to get the job done quick? And how can you expect to escape suspicion when you live literally next door to the crime scene?  Although, I guess anyone within earshot of all the hooplah would also be included in the list of suspects.
If not for the ungodly hour of the party, though, I'd personally be willing to forgive the noise, since it involves one of the catchiest soundtracks I can think of. Seriously, what party would be complete without great music?  I absolutely LOVE the music in this game! There were a bunch of times where I found myself dancing along with every other character on the screen until I remembered what was going on in the game and had to take a paranoid look over my own shoulder... Though this actions shows significantly more of a sense of self-preservation than any other person there.  Seriously, 20 people could be lieing dead on the floor and the other party goers would still refuse to let the party die along with their friends! Sure, they might call the Fuzz to come and pick the bodies up and arrest someone, but the party goes on!
Thankfully your neighbor has a wide variety of friends, including people of every race and gender; cause then no one can charge us with any hate crimes when we do inevitably get caught.  However, I will say this, it sucks that we have to play as a white guy, since he's only able to run five feet before having to lie down and take nap, which especially sucks when you have to run from the cops!  Somehow this character is even less fit than me!  Though, I guess if you did get to play as a black guy, you'd probably get the cops called on you the moment you stepped in the door, NOT RACIST!  But this does bring up another question: When bodies do start piling up, why does no one think to point at the guy who arrived without an invitation?  People won't point you out to the occifers as long as you can avoid the bodies for a few seconds; which gets can be pretty easy when you murder people with traps, Hitman style, unless someone you poisoned by spiking the punch manages to follows you around.
But even when you're found out, you can still manage to escape.  If you can manage to outrun the Heat for a few seconds, the Bacon may decide to sod the whole business and pop off screen for a donut or two.  But the jerks never bring any back to share.  Who knows, maybe my next murder spree will result from being hangry.  THE BLOOD'S ON YOUR HANDS NOW!!!

I consider myself to be quite savvy in terms of experiencing many forms of storytelling and narratives across multiple mediums, be it movies, books, anime, and of course; video games. Among all of them, only a handful few managed to really touch me emotionally – I’m talking about those who leave you with a sense of emptiness after you finished it, a deep feeling of despair for the many days to come, thinking that it will be a while before something could dazzle you in equal proportion as the one that you just had.
If anything, one of my complaints for this game would be just that; that I won’t be able to experience other games the same way again for quite a while after finishing Nier:Automata. Now I said “one of” because moving on from the excellent story, highly absorbing atmosphere, and the on-point music that accompanies every aspects of the game, I do have some personal issues with N:A.
The combat and gameplay mechanics is one of the many things that I love in this game, however as you level along you’ll start to get overpowered, especially when you start farming exp to get to lv90+ if you want to fight the secret boss of this game. The lv of the enemies are mostly capped to around 60+, the intended lv for the players to finish the game apparently, save for the flying enemies in any of the shmups bullet hell section, which seems to be always sync’d to your level. This ironically means that the game has a system in place to sync enemies’ lv to yours but chose not to do it for the field and in-scenario enemies. Even on the highest difficulty none of the enemies would survive more than 2-3 hits after you reach lv 80+. The combat system allows you to do a lot of creative fancy combos, but that’s not going to happen if all your targets die so fast.
There’s a feature after you finish the game where you can place enemies freely in a room while also setting their lv, but such a ghetto method feels a lot like a hassle than anything. The arena DLC is coming soon on May 2nd – I could only hope that it can bring something similar to Devil May Cry’s bloody palace, with enemies that are equal to your level. I just can’t help but feel that the combat system is wasted if they don’t do so, plus it will give a lot of replayability to the game.
All the ramblings after my appreciation of N:A is just my own opinion as someone who enjoys challenge in an action game, as well as my personal taste in PlatinumGames’ designs in their action games. I would recommend N:A as 10/10 for other people, though I’d personally give it a 9/10 for the time being until my dream DLC comes.
Afterwords: The game thanked me for playing after I finished the final ending yet the gratitude is mine for being given the privilege of experiencing this outstanding game. Thank you Yoko Taro for creating all the complex yet relatable characters that I learned to hate and love. Thank you Keiichi Okabe for creating his sets of absolutely captivating music that absorbs me into the world of Nier, and thank you to all the folks at PlatinumGames for creating a beautiful, beautiful world that I could roam and feel at home with. Thank you very much.

After almost 50 hours with NBA 2K17 I can say it is a superior basketball game to it's predecessor - 2K16. You won't see the improvements on video footage since graphics are pretty much the same (except sweat and players body types) but as with the gameplay improvements - they are there.
First of all, when you play your first game you realise how much more fluid the controls over players feel. Slower players are finally not totally useless as even they can contribute to the score not only by attempting 3 point shots but also SUCCEFULLY driving to the basket. Yes, attacking the basket off the dribble actually makes sense this year and yet it's not really easier. New thing with this game is that you have to time your every shot - including layups, floaters, post hooks and shots under the basket. It's difficult to get a hang of at first but later you can appreciate this addition as every "green release" goes in - yeah, NO MATTER WHAT. Shot meter this year is different too and it seems that timing the shot perfectly is a lot harder. As I mentioned before - controls are fluid, there is almost no imput lag (in offline games) and you can go from one crossover move to the other without your player bumping into the defender and being stuck in the animation afterwards. Crossing people and getting by them is a lot of fun and isolation plays make sense.
What do I hate? Getting stuck on the moving screen and ending up 10 feet from the opposite team's player which happens constantly and some funky elements of MyCareer mode within its plot. It's far better than last year (10-minutes cutscenes are gone, HELL YEAH) with pretty interesting role of Michael B. Jordan playing Justice Young - an NBA prospect coming to the league undrafted which becomes your teammate and your best friend as well. The chemistry between your MyPlayer and Justice is pretty believable and not-so-in-your-face as with Vic in NBA 2K16. Playing a game with him on the floor is a lot of fun, too.
There is a subject of face-scan for MyPlayer as well. I'm absolutely happy that it has finally arived on PC version but there aren't any more positives that come to my mind. It's a horrible process, horrible companion app for Android/iOS, just horrible overall. If you are not keen on that function coming into the game - don't even try it, because you will find yourself wasting HOURS on trying to get any decent scan that doesn't make your nose appear on your chin. You'll probably check it anyway so I won't bother spending any more time on it - it seems that creators were thinking the same. yuck.
So overall, if you are a fan of both NBA and NBA 2k games there is no reason not to buy this year rendition of this franchise. There are a lot of neccesary improvements from previous game which makes me almost sure that I'll beat my time from NBA 2k16 at 508 hours in-game. Think no longer - get it!

This is unquestionably the most fun I've had with a multiplayer video game since the early days of TF2. The game does "fun" ridiculously well, everything from the character designs and animations, down to the gunplay, it's just good ol' fashioned fun. The game screams "if you take me seriously at all it's your own fault". The weapon crafting system is simple yet fun and satisfying. Once you've researched the parts you need, you can make pretty much anything you can think of - I've currently got some sort of electrified blunderbuss on the go, and it's hilarious (and surprisingly lethal!).
The business model is also extremely fair. All they ask you to pay for are cosmetic customisation options, XP boosts and in-game currency boosts (you can't buy currency directly). So it's perfectly possible to play for free and be competitive - it'll just take longer and you won't look as stylish.
The game modes are fun, too. Team Deathmatch is not a thing that happens! The game modes are:
- Blitz: a fun capture-the-point style game that involves raising underwear up a flagpole (as you do...). Only one point is active at a time, and it works on a tug-of-war style system (being on the point slides the bar in your favour, an enemy on the point slides it in their favour, more players on the point = faster capping). So it's usually pretty intense and see-saw, if a little spammy. Once a point is capped, another is activated at random somewhere else a few seconds later. First to x caps wins the match.
- Extraction: Blutonium (the ore from which the game's currency is made) is scattered all over the map and one designated player on each team has to collect it and take it to a specific location (the collector can't use weapons while holding the ore, so will need protecting). You get points for killing the enemy collector, and when your collector dies a new player is selected at random. Pretty fun game mode.
- Death Snatch: Essentially Kill Confirmed. Kill an enemy, get points for collecting his dropped blutonium. Collect your own team's blutonium to deny the enemy points. x number of snatches wins the round. This is the most likely to devolve into TDM arenas where people only snatch the blutonium by accident. :p Still fun though, because it's Loadout.
- Jackhammer: Capture the flag, with a hammer in place of a flag. Whoever has the hammer uses it instead of a weapon, it has five 'shots' and one-shots anyone in the small AoE. Each kill increases it's value when capped (but resets if it's returned). This suddenly makes CTF very interesting, as running and hiding with the 'flag' is pretty pointless, since a hammer with zero kills isn't worth a lot (but still worth something!) when returned.
Overall, I love this damn game, and can't wait to see what other awesome stuff gets added in future.

An endearingly crafted story about the situation everyone dreams of but no one is ready for.  It's you, and you alone, against the hoard of monsters that have either killed everyone or left their spirits crushed and broken.  This is the apocalypse, and few games capture the desperation and everyday struggles of living as a dying race so thought-provokingly.
The gameplay is all about planning, exploration, and resourcefulness.  The story itself is provocative and timeless, as we go into the mind of a man forced to reconcile the past so he can survive the present.  Twists and turns abound in this indie title, so get ready for a brainbender.  The graphics evoke a simpler time, and it's a shame this game was never officially on the SNES.
If you are looking for a psychological journey with a dark premise, desperate situations, and retro graphics, then this is the place.  Lone survivor delivers exactly what it promises and then some.
