Definitely earns its underrated tag, though it's held back by some questionable design choices. Firstly, the gameplay mechanics are pretty much all terrific. All the gadgets serve useful purposes and the squad commands (like sync shot) are very well done. Your AI squadmates can also handle themselves for the most part and contribute at a decent level to any combat. Infact in many areas, especially when stealthed, you can leave most of the killing to them whilst you scout. Level design is varied and whilst the storyline and character are fairly generic, it's all delivered in a fairly engaging manner.
Cons? Missions periodically use dated autofail conditions where you can't alert a single guard, must complete a task in a fixed period of time or cannot let a target get further than a certain distance away. The later two conditions in particular have a negative impact on gameplay as they force you into a run n' gun Call of Duty-style rush which the game doesn't pull off well at all. The use of these extremely rigid conditions also kills immersion. They could have achieved similar goals in ratcheting up tension without this autofail nonsense.
Anyway, still recommended despite these annoyances - impressed me a lot more than the Advanced Warfighter games,

Story, a tentative check. While undoubtedly gripping and immersive, I was moved in certain parts rather than the whole story itself. For secrecy's sake, where I shed my tears will not be disclosed.
Gameplay, another tentative check. I was never a fan of arcade-ish game style, so it's obvious that I did not come for the gameplay. Not like I hate it though. 2B looks both powerful and stylish when fighting, even with my clumsy control.
Overall, this game is worth every cent of your money and then some.

Short story:  Buy it on sale if you can.  Not worth the full price, but still good.  I got it on summer sale for $20.99 for the game and season pass together.
Disclaimer...if you are one of those folks who passionatly HATE parkour games...you might want to wait till you get a good sale.  You play mostly in low gravity and use jumps, boosts and stuff to get to some needed areas for missions.  It's not terrible, but I know folks who can't stand that Mega Man jump around stuff.
The game is a bit short.  I feel that there isn't enough "meat" on it.  There are way fewer side missions than in previous games.  (Good or bad?...there were too many in the first one, if you did them all you were overleveled for the next area.)  I played as clap trap and found the game play challenging.  The story is so so, you get a back history about how Jack became what he is in BL2.
The guns are as always fun, they lost the stupid slag guns and made cryo guns.  They also added laser guns, which are fun.  They brought back the chest and keys so you can unlock good (only purple this time) gear with shift codes.  They took off artifacts and gave you and O2 kit that gives bonuses...and lets you breath.  They also removed eridium as a form of payment and replaced it with much more pleantiful Moonstones.  You also use moonstones to open some rare chests.
The gameplay is mostly in low gravity on the Moon and the big Hyperion space station seen in previous games.  This adds a different feel to the game play.  You can jump around and use your O2 to hover, as well as slam down from the air and damage foes below.  If you are not playing clap trap, you  have to keep an eye on your oxygen, after it is gone you slowly loose health.  Most enemies drop O2 cans though to keep you going.
The characters (4 with the base game and 2 extra with the season pass) are fun in my opinion.  I have tried half of them, with clap trap going the farthest so far.  They still each get 3 skill trees and a unique action skill.  Yes they did "recycle" characters from previous games, but they were not playable before.  Overall I like the choices.  Lady Hammerlock seems to be fun as well, she can freeze enemies and starts off with a purple ranked sniper rifle and a lot of cash.
Graphics are the usual hand drawn textures.  Alot of it is recycled/reskinned from previous versions.  You will find yourself opening the same yellow boxes from BL2 all the time.  Music....well I didn't think it was as good as in previous versions, but it didn't bother me.  Voice acting is ok.  Most of the new voice actors are Aussies (fine by me my BF is an Aussie and I love his accent lol).  Many of the original cast also make a cameo of some sort.
There are some DLCs that come with the season pass.  One of which is a mission inside of clap trap...I haven't played this yet, but it sounds like some fun.  The Clap Trap revolution is still my favorite expansion for any Borderlands game.  The DLC's start at lvl 30 as they previously have.  So best to do them after your first run through the story.
Overall a solid game.  I think they turned off the community with the high price tag at launch.  I do not feel it is worth the same as BL 1 or 2 when they came out.  It's sort of a...hold you over till we make BL3 game that 2K Australia made.  I think it should have been priced as such.  $40-50 tops for the base game with the season pass included would be fair.
So if you are a fan of the Borderlands series it's worthwhile to play through this, you will have fun and laughs, just don't overpay for it.

I purchased Stellaris at launch, loaded it up, played for a couple hours, then quit.
Six months later, I came back to the game, played about ten hours, quit again. I didn't dislike the game, but I didn't feel like I 'got it' either.
When I returned the third time, after the 1.4 update, I sank into a great galactic sandbox in which I could build any kind of space empire. I could be friendly or antagonistic, religious or rational, embracing or erradicating. I'd found the learning curve steep and the features wanting, but once the game had been improved and updated from its launch state, I was hooked.
Of course, not all of these systems function equally well. The diplomacy screen is still spare. There aren't options for spying, espionage or sabotage. Ground warfare is abstracted, but quickly dispensed with. The weapon technologies are unbalanced, with missiles and fightercraft hard countered by point defense systems, leaving fewer viable fleet loadouts. Warfare itself turns into single massive doomstack battles that determine the course of a war.
However, the game also includes rich stories uncovered by exploring science ships, leading into all sorts of variations. Some are one-offs, but others can chain into several different permutations with a range of outcomes that can have a significant effect on your empire.
The graphics are lovely and the operatic soundtrack must have been great, because I played for more than a hundred hours before I shut it off. The advisor and all his verbal reminders gets old fast, however.
Each time I've started a game of Stellaris, whether in making my own race, choosing from the pre-fab ones or letting the game spin out a totally random species, I've landed in a different galactic storyline. Sure, the events repeat and the basics of exploration, diplomacy, comabt and expansion remain the same, but the geography and the arrangement of the AI empires, as well as their attitudes, makes for a very different experience.
I've had an empire that started in a tight cluster of stars, containing multiple inhabitable worlds. Just reaching beyond those neighoring systems, however, I found three other clustered races. Each reached out in the same way I was, all of us of similar ethic and government type. Almost instantly I had the basis for a federation that would take me through to the victory screen.
But I've also begun a game on the fringe of the galaxy, with nothing habitable in range of my home planet. Exploring the few stars my starting ships could reach revealed a massive Fallen Empire, an ancient species that expanded vastly, threating to conquer the galaxy until they caught a case of the mehs. These particular stagnant ascendents were xenophobes, so that all my nearest habitable planets were close enough to their border to provoke the Fallen Empire. I was plunged into war after war that I survived by suffering a humiliating surrender and occasionally purging colonies whose influence has grown too close to the xenophobes. In the end, growing in the shadow of this titan, did I build up my own strength and find far off allies to come to my aid. After more than a century in game time, I was able to invade and conquer this ancient enemy who had been a terror to generations of my people. I can't tell you how satisfying it was, after more than a dozen hours of game play and all sorts of terrible compromises, just survive, to occupy their home system.
Stellaris supplied just enough context, elements and dynamics to trigger my imagination to fill in that story, to give me a unique sandbox experience.
The developers, Paradox Interactive, have a history of creating and then improving massive grand strategy games. Stellaris is no exception. New content, fixes for issues and whole new systems are constantly in the works. It's tempting to suggest to potential buyers to wait for the next patch because of all the new stuff, but since the flow of fun seems almost endless, why not just jump in and tell the story of your own galactic empire?

Stellaris is initially quite engaging, but doesn't go anywhere with the initial momentum.
The main problem is the game is just entirely too slow. Now you may say to yourself "Aren't most Paradox games slow?" and you would be right. But not quite this level. Mid-game you'll probably be on fastest speed while alt-tabbed or maybe reading a book. It takes entirely too long to research any technologies (thank you based tech costs scaling up with your population and planet count). Very little of note happens for long stretches of time. Except the AI spamming you with inconsequential offers for the 5000th time.
The other major issue is that combat devolves into massive fleet vs massive fleet. Does your massive fleet have slightly less strength than the enemy fleet? Then prepare to lose all your ships while only doing 5-10% of the enemies fleet's damage in return. It's extremely anticlimatic to play the game for a long time, only to have the entire your entire fleet crushed and have little recourse. Other Paradox games also encourage blobbing to a degree, but at least they have attrition. There's no attrition in space. The other annoying thing is your ships suck up enormous amounts of power if they're not orbit of a world your control. So you have to do your absolute best to build a fleet capable of beating your enemy but don't use too much energy, or your entire society collapses due to ineffeciency.  "Please sir, may I have another energy credit so I can wage war without getting annhilated by the xenos who fanatically hate me."
I can't believe I wasted 18 hours of my time on this.

Deus Ex's design is excellent, but not in the ways most people think it is. It masters choice and consequences on the gameplay level rather than the story level. Your choices aren't going to dramatically affect the direction of the story. Most of the time you are just going to be rewarded with hidden dialog and item rewards, and most of the consequences are front loaded in the portion where you have a job with job expectations put on you. Now, the plot is well handled, so those extra lines will usually feel pretty rewarding, but they aren't actually what you should be here for.
Deus Ex's inventory, energy and augmentation, health, and skill systems are built so that you can't ever get through a situation without facing the some kind of consequences or be optimized for every situation in the game. Basically everything in the game is consumable and non-regenerating.
These systems, placed in a game where most objectives are located in buildings you can walk around (at your own risk) and enter through multiple paths, results in one of the most well designed, surprising, and flat out incredible games ever made.
Practically every door can be opened at least two ways (be it keys, lockpicks, electronics, hacking, explosions, laser sword, bullets), and you have to carefully think through the consequences of whatever method you choose.
Deus Ex is a game about choice thanks to its carefully balanced gameplay that constantly gives you interesting choices and consequences.

Delver is a great game. It takes the roguelike platform and brings it into a charmingly minimalistic yet exciting experience. You may notice the visual similarity to Minecraft. Several people have in fact seen me playing the game and asked if it was Minecraft. Although they look similar, they are completely different. Delver is all about dungeon crawling, getting new gear, and exploring the various randomly generated levels (another Minecraft parallel). The game maintains a perfect balance between frustration and fulfillment. The combat is suspenseful and keeps you on the edge of your seat, and is generally more intense than other roguelikes. The story is fleshed out by miscellaneous notes which you will find in the dungeons, and the various NPCs you may encounter. The storyline is just full enough to keep you interested and immersed; very artfully done. I should also mention the incredible atmosphere, which is held together by the asthetically pleasing visuals and the fantastic soundtrack, which I would definitely purchase if it were an option (take note developers!). Oh, yes, and the development has consistently improved throughout the early access period, which is always a plus. Overall, Delver is a fun and charming little game, which satisfies completely.

So I've never written any reviews ever in Steam, nor in any games. But, for once, just this once, I did a review, simply because this game is well-worth receiving its praise, and I wanted to review it once its region-restriction is gone.
Let me just say that getting this game wasn't exactly an easy decision. It was a toss-up between this or Mass Effect: Andromeda. At first, my heart was fixed onto ME:A. But, after seeing the review days after release, I was swayed. So, I thought hard, and in the end, I did the simplest thing: Toss a coin. NieR wins, and so I bought it
Do I regret it?
Simply put, NieR:Automata was one of the best games that I played. Okay, let me rephrase that. NieR:Automata is one of the few games that manage to stirred myself. The game manages to put you in a rollercoaster ride of emotion, up and down, while looking cool in the process, and its a damn good feat on its own.
I'll make this into two parts of the things I like and the things I...kind of don't like it. Do take note that from the hours I played is a normal playthrough of Route A to E, speeding up the playthrough in Route C.
- A simple, yet well-executed story.
NieR:Automata tells a story of 2B and 9S
, androids created by humans with the purpose of retaking Earth that has been taken over by machines. A simple story, in my opinion: Fighting machines that have taken over things, yet from the start, you'll notice how they speak words like humans do. Until here, it's a still quite simple set-up, and one that has been done previously. But, in spite of this, NieR still manages to twist and surprises its audience well. There wasn't any moment where the plot twists didn't surprise me, and it's endings ( Again, A to E ) make my jaw dropped jaringly. Ending E, in particular, is a damn well-constructed ending, but we'll get to that later ( Yes, I put it in a different point. It's that good )
- A combat system that's easy to learn, but hard to master.
Let's put the obvious things out of the way first: It's also made by Platinum Games, and I'll say, they don't dissapoint with the combat one bit. You name it: Bayonetta, Metal Gear Revengeance, Vanquish, those games are games with an amazing gameplay. So, does that mean NieR: Automata is the same? Short answer? Yes. Long answer? Yes, but the combat will have its "feel" later. Early on, the gameplay is simple: It follows Bayonetta's combat system. You got light attack, heavy attack, and dodge as your main source of defence, with perfect dodging exist as a source of damage. The unique aspect here is your "Pod", drones that can shoot and shoot with an even bigger boom. Early on, you only got two types of weapon and one Pod "Charged shot". A bit dry, but once you got spears, gauntlets, Charge shot that will shoot grenades, create a black hole, slows down enemy, and more? It's a satisfying game. The best part? Every route adds a new form of gameplay that'll drastically change your ebb and flow, and that adds a good fluidity of the gameplay
- A very, very, VERY good soundtrack
If there's one thing that will always be a good or positive point in the game no matter what, it's the soundtrack. There is not one bit, I repeat, NOT A SINGLE MOMENT where I DO NOT like the music in NieR. Every new song that was played, I always stop and listen to it for a good while, even when I'm about to be beaten to a pulp by a bunch of angry robots. From a calming vocal, to an song full on war, the soundtrack got everything. Heck, if they ever released the official soundtrack as a DLC, I'll buy it in a heartbeat, prices be damned.
- A moral lesson that's actually on-point
There are few games that made an impact to me, even fewer that I actually put a thought about it. There are two games that manages to put out a good lesson for me: First is Spec Ops: The Line. Guess what's the other one? This.
I feel that this needs to be put in a separate point than the story aspect, because NieR manages to put out a portrayal of something in a way that makes them think twice about what we usually know, especially in the game. Do these machines try to be human? For what purpose? What's the difference between us and them? How are we today related to them? These are the points that the games give, and it gives its answer that will give us, "Huh?"
- A damn-well satisfying ending
I'll not spoil much. Ending E, the true ending, is exactly how people say it: It's touching, it gives the biggest lesson to you, and it will make you spill your tears....at least, a bit for me anyway, which is quite rare, in fact.
- Port Optimization
This is probably the only biggest gripe so far for me. Okay, my PC isn't actually top-notch (i5 4690 3.50 GHz, GTX 770 4GB,16 GB RAM ), but it should at least gave me 50 fps or rather a solid performance. This isn't actually a major gripe, and please, don't discuss technical things by much.
So, Conclusion.
NieR:Automata is one of the few games which I am actually grateful for buying it. It manages to gave me a solid 30+ hour of entertaining gameplay, with an amazing story and ending, coupled with a goddamn awesome soundtrack. You'll rarely found a game like this nowadays. Buy this game, it is WORTH it.

Review updated, 14th of September. Original review as follows, update below.
A fun game rendered unplayable by technical issues.
Nier: Automata offers fun gameplay and an intriguing story, what little of it I was able to access. The first ~5 hours were fun to play, but then the "white screen of death" struck: The game will briefly freeze, then the screen will go black, then white. At this point the game still seems to be running based on the sounds I can hear, but the screen will remain white. The only solution is to shut the game down.
A little searching has revealed that this is a not-uncommon problem with the game, and has been since launch. The developers have not provided a fix for this bug, and the community has not be able to find a reliable workaround either.
This bug is quite unpredictable. Some have played through almost the entire game before encountering it, others get it every five minutes. The ones who are most affected by it can't progress in the game at all, as it can take a player anywhere from 15-30 minutes to reach the first opportunity to save in the game. If the wsod occurs before that they have to start over from the beginning.
But even for me this bug is crippling, as the game deliberately makes use of checkpoint starvation at times and, as it so stringently reminds us, does not have an autosave function. If it decides to wsod on me, all progress since the last manual save is lost.
At this point I decided to pursue a refund, but as the bug did not rear its ugly head until I was well outside Steam's 2-hour "no questions asked" refund window I was denied one. Apparently "game rendered unplayable by technical issues" is not a valid reason for a refund. Caveat emptor - let the buyer beware. I would have a 60 euro paperweight, but a digital purchase is not even good for that.
I am very disappointed with Platinum Games' post-launch support. In addition to this un-addressed game-stopping bug, the game also suffers from a few other graphical issues and performance issues, issues that community modders were able to swiftly address. And yet Platinum Games, a professional developer selling a 60 euro game, is either unwilling or unable to deal with these problems, leaving it to their paying customers to repair their faulty product. Again, caveat emptor.
So in conclusion, I can't recommend this game, and that's a shame. I can't recommend it because it is gambling, and you shouldn't need to gamble 60 euros in hopes of getting a good game and be left with nothing if you lose.
If you do buy it, hope that the wsod bug manifests immediately, or not at all. If you don't get it, you will have a fun game. If you get it immediately you can get a refund and be on your way with nothing lost except a little time.
But if, like me, you get it after the refund window closes, you're screwed.
Update, 14th September 2017. Shortly after midnight.
This review was originally posted on the 27th of April, and I want to provide an update. In the months since then, both AMD and nVidia have released driver updates intended to alleviate the white screen crashes, while the developers have remained silent. For some, these updates have fixed the problem, but for others the crashes remain, including me. The other technical issues remain as well.
To some, the driver updates constitute an admission of guilt on AMD/nVidia's part, but I feel the need to point out that if these issues are due to driver bugs, other developers know how to work around and avoid these bugs and make games that don't crash the display drivers. I expected the same expertise from Platinum and Square Enix, and they haven't displayed it.
So why the update now? At time of writing my time played says 47.3 hours. Although the crashes still happen, they happen less now, both due to driver updates and a host of other measures taken. I decided to see if it was possible to struggle my way through the game, and despite roughly two dozen crashes, I made it.
And what a journey it was. At times uplifting, at times emotionally devastating, and ultimately cathartic. I fought, and I persevered, and while I wouldn't call the technical issues a plus by any means, they only made the struggle that much more desperate. At times I felt like I was limping along, desperately praying that the game would finally allow me a save point so I wouldn't lose half an hour of progress that I would then have to replay with the same sword of Damocles still hanging over my head.
But I made it, and it was good. It was a good game, wrapped in a bad piece of software. And it's a shame. It's a damned shame that a game this good should be this technically deficient, this mired in issues.
I bid a bittersweet farewell to Nier: Automata. A game that I enjoyed despite all its attempts to prevent me from doing so. A game that I would recommend to all my friends in an instant, were it not for the sorry state it is in. A game that I sincerely hope will some day receive the treatment it deserves. Maybe someone will one day fix it. Maybe. Because as the game would tell you, there's always hope.

"What does it mean to be human?"
For a game with such an obviously low budget, you'd wonder how it gets all the acclaim. It does have a myriad of issues as a videogame; the combat may get boring, the visuals look dated at times, and the open-world is a mere illusion. However, the true focus of director Yoko Taro was not to create the perfect videogame. It was to paint a deep, emotionally gripping tale of two androids in a sad, torn-down world of lies.
"ThANk you for ...foR the FLOWErs. Desert FLOWErs are BEAUTIF, arEN't thEY... Th-Th-thank You..."
NieR: Automata may lack in a few areas (much like its predecessor), however, the technical aspects of any game, no matter how flawless, will eventually be beaten. These shortcomings do not take one bit away from what the game strives to be--from what it conveys. Where most if not all triple-A titles fear to take risks and defy industry standards, NieR: Automata goes all out with its eccentric personality unafraid to be as it is.
- Thought provoking narrative masterfully executed with innovative storytelling
- Developed, multi-dimensional characters you care about
- One of if not the best score ever composed for a videogame
- Poignant atmosphere with philosophical themes
- Well animated, stylish, and satisfying combat (duh, platinum games)
- Mysterious and captivating world that hides subtle, lore-rich, details
- Beautiful art direction despite technically lacking graphics
- The most clever and original game design I have seen in years

You don't look for straight lines or perfect circles in a work of art. What makes this game truly special is its ability to mesmerize. It made me feel and think, a feat that no amount of pixel perfect textures, open-worldness, or *even fun* could ever achieve. This is what separates a mere videogame from something incomparable... a masterpiece that will stay with me for as long as I live.
As unreasonable as it sounds, the emotions I've felt reaching the final [E]nding says just that.

You’re meant to plan out the murder of several dozen people, in an open space, where any mistake can ruin the entire effort at any point. Any good designer would give the player just enough time, and info to properly react to a change in scenario like this. If anyone honestly finds this masochistic-♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t approach to difficulty enjoyable, I have to question their sanity. It’s hard in the cheapest and laziest way. Short story:  Buy it on sale if you can.  Not worth the full price, but still good.  I got it on summer sale for $20.99 for the game and season pass together.
Disclaimer...if you are one of those folks who passionatly HATE parkour games...you might want to wait till you get a good sale.  You play mostly in low gravity and use jumps, boosts and stuff to get to some needed areas for missions.  It's not terrible, but I know folks who can't stand that Mega Man jump around stuff.
The game is a bit short.  I feel that there isn't enough "meat" on it.  There are way fewer side missions than in previous games.  (Good or bad?...there were too many in the first one, if you did them all you were overleveled for the next area.)  I played as clap trap and found the game play challenging.  The story is so so, you get a back history about how Jack became what he is in BL2.
The guns are as always fun, they lost the stupid slag guns and made cryo guns.  They also added laser guns, which are fun.  They brought back the chest and keys so you can unlock good (only purple this time) gear with shift codes.  They took off artifacts and gave you and O2 kit that gives bonuses...and lets you breath.  They also removed eridium as a form of payment and replaced it with much more pleantiful Moonstones.  You also use moonstones to open some rare chests.
The gameplay is mostly in low gravity on the Moon and the big Hyperion space station seen in previous games.  This adds a different feel to the game play.  You can jump around and use your O2 to hover, as well as slam down from the air and damage foes below.  If you are not playing clap trap, you  have to keep an eye on your oxygen, after it is gone you slowly loose health.  Most enemies drop O2 cans though to keep you going.
The characters (4 with the base game and 2 extra with the season pass) are fun in my opinion.  I have tried half of them, with clap trap going the farthest so far.  They still each get 3 skill trees and a unique action skill.  Yes they did "recycle" characters from previous games, but they were not playable before.  Overall I like the choices.  Lady Hammerlock seems to be fun as well, she can freeze enemies and starts off with a purple ranked sniper rifle and a lot of cash.
Graphics are the usual hand drawn textures.  Alot of it is recycled/reskinned from previous versions.  You will find yourself opening the same yellow boxes from BL2 all the time.  Music....well I didn't think it was as good as in previous versions, but it didn't bother me.  Voice acting is ok.  Most of the new voice actors are Aussies (fine by me my BF is an Aussie and I love his accent lol).  Many of the original cast also make a cameo of some sort.
There are some DLCs that come with the season pass.  One of which is a mission inside of clap trap...I haven't played this yet, but it sounds like some fun.  The Clap Trap revolution is still my favorite expansion for any Borderlands game.  The DLC's start at lvl 30 as they previously have.  So best to do them after your first run through the story.
Overall a solid game.  I think they turned off the community with the high price tag at launch.  I do not feel it is worth the same as BL 1 or 2 when they came out.  It's sort of a...hold you over till we make BL3 game that 2K Australia made.  I think it should have been priced as such.  $40-50 tops for the base game with the season pass included would be fair.
So if you are a fan of the Borderlands series it's worthwhile to play through this, you will have fun and laughs, just don't overpay for it.

It's putting a more modern actiony touch on the Ghost Recon series while still keeping the tactical elements that make this such an interesting and worthwhile experience. It is a bit more linear and unlike earlier titles (minus the console offshoots of the Advanced Warfighter games) you do get the possibility of just blasting your way through bad guys, allthough expect it to not be an easy task! All accompanied by a very fancy presentation, I liked the GoPro-style camera that directly follows your guns motions and the interface that blends into the gameworld, a concept already well established in the latest Splinter Cell-Games, also from Ubisoft.
It's a pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥ PC Port nonetheless, apart from the already mentioned connection troubles it follows the sad trend of Ubisoft PC games not having proper support for standard resolutions. If youre running a 16:10 monitor, expect to play this game with big fat letterboxes.
If you're willing to look past these flaws, you'll find a fun tactical third person shooter that is willing to break free from mainstream military shooter tropes.

I have a bit of a love/hate relationship with Stellaris.
The things I love are, as follows,
-The creation of my own unique races, from appearance to culture, even naming trends. Having the chance to actually create the name, appearance, and history of a new race for the game was a lot of fun and made me feel invested in their progress, and it's something I wish a lot of other RTS games (at least sci-fi ones) would have.
-The scale of the galaxy, and exploration of it. I've played previous space RTS' like Homeworld and Sins of a Solar Empire, but the former is in a closed arena for straight up fights and the latter is just this even larger sandbox with very little depth. Exploring each system, learning even minute details about the planets and stars made the galaxy in Stellaris feel alive in a way both those previous games never did. Seeing my empire's borders mapped out gave me a sense of scale of the influence I had in that universe.
-Events in the game, wether they were scripted or not, kept me interested and didn't make the game feel stagnant, at least in the early section.
-Kinda going hand in hand with the creation of my own race, but getting to design and build ships was a nice little treat that again, I'd love to see in more RTS games. It's fun to use the pre-made models, more-so when I get to use custom units.
-Meeting and talking to other races was certainly an enjoyable part of the game, if frustrating in certain areas.
Now onto what I just kinda hated....
-The lack of easy mode, for starters and before anyone tries calling me a filthy casual or newb or what-have you, let me explain that whenever I try a new RTS, especially one like Stellaris with whole new rules and ways to play, I like to play it easy the first few times, treating it like one drawn out tutorial. May not make sense, but that's part of how I play a new game and get a feel for it.
-I didn't win, not once. Yes, makes me a sore loser but there it is: I would always find myself somehow offending an alien empire who just so happened to be my technological/military superior. In one such match a superior race of religious fungi declared war on me and sent a fleet ten times the strength of mine, with four battlecruisers to boot, stomping through my borders and wiping the floor with me.
-Kinda wish there was a real tech and research tree, or at least a better one that didn't feel like I was getting options pulled from a hat. Especially when, if I chose one, it'd take maybe another one or two projects before it'd show up.
-Finally, for one of the most important resources (to me at least) in the game, the influence resource really needs a tweaking in terms of flow. You need it for building outposts, colonies, elections, hiring leaders like scientists and military officials. And the only ways you get it--that I know of at any rate--are from your developed capital, colonies (which you have to spend influence to make) but only when they've been upgraded to it, missions in the game, and declaring another race your rival.
Now does all that mean I don't recommend it? Hell no. I wholeheartedly recommend this game for every die hard 4XRTS fan out there. Stellaris is a great game with so much in it. Now I just wish it was a little easier to play and get used to,

I purchased Stellaris at launch, loaded it up, played for a couple hours, then quit.
Six months later, I came back to the game, played about ten hours, quit again. I didn't dislike the game, but I didn't feel like I 'got it' either.
When I returned the third time, after the 1.4 update, I sank into a great galactic sandbox in which I could build any kind of space empire. I could be friendly or antagonistic, religious or rational, embracing or erradicating. I'd found the learning curve steep and the features wanting, but once the game had been improved and updated from its launch state, I was hooked.
Of course, not all of these systems function equally well. The diplomacy screen is still spare. There aren't options for spying, espionage or sabotage. Ground warfare is abstracted, but quickly dispensed with. The weapon technologies are unbalanced, with missiles and fightercraft hard countered by point defense systems, leaving fewer viable fleet loadouts. Warfare itself turns into single massive doomstack battles that determine the course of a war.
However, the game also includes rich stories uncovered by exploring science ships, leading into all sorts of variations. Some are one-offs, but others can chain into several different permutations with a range of outcomes that can have a significant effect on your empire.
The graphics are lovely and the operatic soundtrack must have been great, because I played for more than a hundred hours before I shut it off. The advisor and all his verbal reminders gets old fast, however.
Each time I've started a game of Stellaris, whether in making my own race, choosing from the pre-fab ones or letting the game spin out a totally random species, I've landed in a different galactic storyline. Sure, the events repeat and the basics of exploration, diplomacy, comabt and expansion remain the same, but the geography and the arrangement of the AI empires, as well as their attitudes, makes for a very different experience.
I've had an empire that started in a tight cluster of stars, containing multiple inhabitable worlds. Just reaching beyond those neighoring systems, however, I found three other clustered races. Each reached out in the same way I was, all of us of similar ethic and government type. Almost instantly I had the basis for a federation that would take me through to the victory screen.
But I've also begun a game on the fringe of the galaxy, with nothing habitable in range of my home planet. Exploring the few stars my starting ships could reach revealed a massive Fallen Empire, an ancient species that expanded vastly, threating to conquer the galaxy until they caught a case of the mehs. These particular stagnant ascendents were xenophobes, so that all my nearest habitable planets were close enough to their border to provoke the Fallen Empire. I was plunged into war after war that I survived by suffering a humiliating surrender and occasionally purging colonies whose influence has grown too close to the xenophobes. In the end, growing in the shadow of this titan, did I build up my own strength and find far off allies to come to my aid. After more than a century in game time, I was able to invade and conquer this ancient enemy who had been a terror to generations of my people. I can't tell you how satisfying it was, after more than a dozen hours of game play and all sorts of terrible compromises, just survive, to occupy their home system.
Stellaris supplied just enough context, elements and dynamics to trigger my imagination to fill in that story, to give me a unique sandbox experience.
The developers, Paradox Interactive, have a history of creating and then improving massive grand strategy games. Stellaris is no exception. New content, fixes for issues and whole new systems are constantly in the works. It's tempting to suggest to potential buyers to wait for the next patch because of all the new stuff, but since the flow of fun seems almost endless, why not just jump in and tell the story of your own galactic empire?
Great game, and it's only getting better!

I haven't been scared by a game so effectively for a while.
Let's see, I'm gonna talk about the levels, the monsters, the gameplay, and character growth.
LEVELS:
The levels are premade rooms randomly sewn together as is common practice. The design of the rooms is very good, though the game needs more variety, still. The only outside area is the starting point, unfortunately. Going underground, there are the dungeons. Then there are cavey caves. Then there are sewers. Then there is lava...you'll have to play for more details. There are bottomless pits, pulleys and levers, keys and locked doors, doors that you have to bash down, secret doors, and trap-plate traps (teleporter traps are kinda annoying).
MONSTERS:
The monsters seem to fall into a few categories, which are perfect for the gameplay setup. There are fast dodging monsters (bats, flying skulls), typical meaty melee fighters (thugs/bandits/giant spiders), jumping melee fighters (they jump at you when you get close, hard to time attacks), and magical ranged fighters. Perhaps there should be some physical ranged monsters or magical melee ones? There probably will be later. The monster difficulty balances well with player development and the combat shines.
GAMEPLAY:
Getting onto gameplay, most everyone else has already mentioned it, the combat is very decent and straightforward; melee weapons are more dangerous to use because you might be hit (and starting out HP is very scarce). Thankfully they don't break over time like other games. Ranged weapons are bows and arrows and wands that have limited ammo. Though missed arrows can be picked up, wands never recharge. As it is a roguelike, don't expect ammunition to be too plentiful, especially for the late game. Potions are random but scrolls are not. Potion effects take about 2-3 uses to learn what they are (which I think is dumb because the player can remember them...and after playing a few times having to re-remember just gets annoying [Note to the maker: can we have it be just one potion use == in-game player learns it?]).
PLAYER DEVELOPMENT:
For character development, as far as I can tell, in the late game, increasing your attack or magic seems worthless. If you are good at predicting monster movements, even if your attack is low, you can take as many hits as you want without getting hit. Near the end of the game, no matter how good you are, once you start getting swarmed by mage-skeletons and flying skulls, you're gonna get hit a lot, so my advice is put most of your points into speed, health, and defense. If you ever get swarmed well...RUN!
MY MAIN THOUGHTS:
1) Magic is a stat that seems mostly useless, I can't imagine relying on wands near the end game when there are a lot of monsters but probably not nearly enough dropped wands, nor inventory space to hold them. Same with arrows. This is a minor balance concern that can be directly adjusted, but what I'd really rather see is a more traditional MP and learned spell system, also wands that recharge for those who are not magically-inclined.
2) I 100% wish the game wasn't just a roguelike and was more developed as an RPG. The music, graphics, and engine are so awesome, I don't want my game to end just because...I won. I want more. I would pay a full $60 to play just a Diablo clone with this engine, graphics, musical, and dungeon layout feel.
3) So, I was looking at the development log and there's an awesome overhaul coming to the editor. Until it comes, the current map editor is essentially unusable and the assets needed to mod the game aren't readily available so it's not really even close to being as moddable as I'd hoped. My main reason for buying this game is cause I heard it was uber-moddable. I hope as it develops the assets are more open. Modding is what opens small games like this to the masses and makes them become legendary.
4) I am in love with this game. It is very charming.
Pros:
- Fast, easy to learn, first-person roguelike
- Good music and graphics schemes
- Fluid gameplay, sensible difficulty
Cons:
- Needs more content
- Without modding, little replay value

What you can expect to come in Glacier 3 is best forewarned when you boot the game. When you are greeted by a shrill, obnoxious siren that caps off the title music, you have to wonder if the rest of the game and all that it entails will be so unpleasant. The answer, sadly, is an unequivocal "yes".
Glacier 3 is a series of races undertaken around - you guessed it - glaciers. It has a "story mode", although there is no story. It is merely a sequence of races. Each race contains you and three other AI controlled drivers, as there is no multiplayer. On the map you may find powerups, two that charge your turbo and three that provide ammo for your weapons, with which you may take other competitors out of the race.
In the one hour I spent in this game, I completed all six campaigns or four tracks each. Really, it is my opinion that there were only three campaigns and twelve maps, as each map and campaign has a counterpart reversal, with nothing more than the direction of the track changed and the start and endpoints swapped.
The map design isn't entirely bad. There is some variety, and the environments are as varied as you could ask for in a game called "glacier". There are ice sheets, cliffs, mountains and caves. However, while some heart was clearly put into their design, the game also feels very rushed and incomplete. This may be most obvious in your first race, when you drive into a massive jump and realize that you can change direction in mid-air, the worst sin committable in a "realistic" driving game. Perhaps you can forgive it as you race along the minute-long track, but you suddenly find yourself crashing into a wall of rocks placed at the middle of an overhang. You think you've crashed - and you technically have - but it's okay, as that rock wall is also the end-point of the race. There is no finish line, there is no obvious landmark, just a pile of rocks in which you and your three competitors burn until the game decides that it is time to show the results of the race.
The physics are wonky all around, even beyond the ability to change direction mid-air. You will find yourself moving in a direction other than that in which your wheels are pointing. You will hit objects or other cars, only to be vaulted back 30 feet, do a ragdoll flip or clip through a barrier. You will fire your weapons on flat ground, only for them to literally blow up in your face. While you hopelessly bounce along the track, you may despair, as you can only unlock new content by winning a campaign. However, the AI is just as helpless as you are, and with a few turbo powerups you will find yourself abusing the game mechanics, deliberately turboing off a cliff about a sharp turn, resetting, and turboing again in your newfound direction.
Bad music, barebones graphics, lack of customizability and content, lack of multiplayer support and so on are all forgivable. However, everything about this game is mediocre, and I do really mean everything, including aspects that you wouldn't even think about in most other racing games because Glacier 3 does wrong what most games do not. That this game was published on the Wii is astonishing, although that perhaps explains what is possibly the least comprehensive menu - consisting of two audio sliders - ever accomplished in a video game. To summarize, the game plays poorly, does not look nearly as good as the store page's screenshots suggest and is outdone even by racing games produced in the 90s.

After playing this game for almost 100 hours I can say that I would recomend it to any petrolhead out there. As the game is only in early access it is missing a few things like v10's and superchargers (both of which will be added later). The game is very easy to learn when you first start playing and it can be very fun when designing some pretty redicoulis cars!

Note: my experience with Automation is not current as I haven't been able to play it in about three months because of migrating my main gaming machine to Linux.
Good way to explore vehicle engine parameters, such as stroke and bore and their effects on power and efficiency.  Several useful scenarios and tutorials to learn about what does what.  Developers are active and responsive and have added a ton of features and are working on porting to a new 3D engine.  The Campaign mode is apparently now active and looks pretty good, although the sandbox and scenarios were plenty to keep me busy and happy.
Game would crash periodically, usually after updating.  Not sure if that is still valid for newer builds, and crashes weren't a gamebreaker.  It happens, especially when using a program that is still in active development.  No Linux version (yet), but hopefully that will come.
The engine parameterization simulator is interesting and accurate from an engineering point of view.  As the game is not a complete product development is in a constant state of flux.  If you are a car guy like I am, you will love fiddling with all the different bits that go in to a motor while trying to get the best efficiency and power out of it.  Great fun!

TLDR mode:
I really want to like this game. But I have to give it a "not recommended". It doesn't mean it's a bad game by any means. It just has a lot of detection rules that feel half the time random. And halfway through the game you have crowded completely outdoor areas which makes stealthing a poor man's guessing game on who to kill and when.
Long description mode:
This game you play a faux stealth "kill EVERYONE" game. That's it. That's the point of the game. Kill everyone.
Along the way you have some fun death animations and unique ways of killing people in sneaky and not-so-sneaky methods. This is good fun.
However at the halfway mark the game takes a serious turn (read below) and I have to say this is the part that turned me off.
Seriously. The first several levels are fun. I didn't mind dying several times to learn how to play, even! Even having the level near complete and losing, it's still fun. The core gameplay is a bit flawed and weird, but with these early areas it works well.
There's random events and some random scripts that pop up as you go through. Drug busts, giant bears, pizza deliveries, etc. And there's a Twitch integration for letting the audience pick the random events that pop up. These are good features.
However... here's the thing:
The main problem I came across was that the eyesight detection rules feel random.
You have a listen button, that hilights who can see you if you kill the person you're next to. So "USE LISTEN TO SEE WHO NOTICES YOU" is a must. Sight ranges are completely ridiculous and you can't trust them. Someone can be looking right at you, but they don't notice you at all. And sometimes they're NOT looking at you, and you triple checked the sight ranges using "LISTEN", and then you are seen when you kill the person you're targeting. And even if you kill someone, you have to get out of range of the body OR with the body before someone else sees you. And you have such a small run stamina bar it's unnerving.
Heck, you could just push someone into a fire, you're RIGHT THERE and everyone sees you but nobody detects you and they run away from the man on fire. No detection.
You could poison someone's drink and they slowly die over time. If you're near the body when it drops, possible detection.
You still can kill the person who saw you if you can off them before they reach a phone. That would be great, but walking speed they can outrun you without even trying. You will almost never succeed in running to catch up to anyone who is heading to a phone unless they're RIGHT next to you when they detect you. You can intercept them if you kill strategically though which CAN work, but hit detection is also a bit hard to aim. Did I mention you have to stop moving to stab with a knife as well?
You CAN kill the police with a well timed trap. I've done it quite a few times to escape.
I got through the first half of the game using basic stealthing tricks. These leves are indoors. You can kill people in a room without being line of sighted, or use traps, then dispose of bodies, lure more people, repeat. Just pick off people till the crowd dwindles. This works. These levels are good fun because you have a multitude of options to kill people.
However... the halfway point the game goes to some outdoor areas. These are NOT fun. One doesn't even have a body disposal. You have to trust in RNG of the detection system to win. Kill the furthest person from the group, run away from the body, let the cops bag the corpse, then return to kill more. It's... tedious. You can't stealth an outside mission with random detection rules unless you know how to fully exploit the system. And this just is where the game is not fun I find. Maybe there is a method to just strike down everyone in a frenzy. Maybe there's some other exploit I'm not abusing. Either way, this doesn't make for a fun game.
I don't want hand holding, I just want to be able to tell WHEN I can get away with in game murder without it being randomly detected. And the listen button is not reliable enough to trust.
Also I have to say that there is a level where you are forced to play a second character who can "kick" and "stab". You'd think that they'd put "Kick" and "Stab" on two different buttons. Nope. Same button. Kicking you don't get detected. Stabbing you are detected. You kick someone, they hit the ground knocked out cold. Then you hit the button again to stab. This does NOT work as intended as there are times when you're intercepting a phone call person and you won't kick, you'll stab. Or you're wanting to stab someone and you'll kick the other person. WHY? I have no friggin clue. Even someone who is already drunk sleeping, you kick them to make them roll over THEN stab them. This is poor design. There are plenty of keyboard buttons that could've been assigned. The "having to be sleeping before being stabbed" is a good character flaw, just take out the stabbing while awake is fine.
Other things that would've been nice to have in the game that would make sense:
"While carrying a sleeping person, your stab hits them instead of having to set the person down then you kill them"
"When walking by a bouncer to the Las Vegas Club, he should not run after and kill you unless you try to go inside."
"You should be able to melee stab a cop that is coming after you since the cops are only armed with clubs"
"Proper NPC rules for who wants to kill you and who just wants to knock you out."
"Being able to frame someone else for a murder"
"Being able to see under objects that are in the sky over you... I'M MAINLY TALKING ABOUT THE GIANT UFO THAT SHOWS UP AND BLOCKS A QUARTER OF THE SCREEN"
In short, if you like hard games, you might have fun with this, however if you dislike RNG and trying to learn complex detection rules, then skip it.

Stellaris is initially quite engaging, but doesn't go anywhere with the initial momentum.
The main problem is the game is just entirely too slow. Now you may say to yourself "Aren't most Paradox games slow?" and you would be right. But not quite this level. Mid-game you'll probably be on fastest speed while alt-tabbed or maybe reading a book. It takes entirely too long to research any technologies (thank you based tech costs scaling up with your population and planet count). Very little of note happens for long stretches of time. Except the AI spamming you with inconsequential offers for the 5000th time.
The other major issue is that combat devolves into massive fleet vs massive fleet. Does your massive fleet have slightly less strength than the enemy fleet? Then prepare to lose all your ships while only doing 5-10% of the enemies fleet's damage in return. It's extremely anticlimatic to play the game for a long time, only to have the entire your entire fleet crushed and have little recourse. Other Paradox games also encourage blobbing to a degree, but at least they have attrition. There's no attrition in space. The other annoying thing is your ships suck up enormous amounts of power if they're not orbit of a world your control. So you have to do your absolute best to build a fleet capable of beating your enemy but don't use too much energy, or your entire society collapses due to ineffeciency.  "Please sir, may I have another energy credit so I can wage war without getting annhilated by the xenos who fanatically hate me."
I can't believe I wasted 18 hours of my time on this.

Move on to GRFS, at first it didnt seem so bad. Upon starting up the campaign we sort of realized that it wasnt like R6V2 at all in that you are now playing Generic Soldier Number 3 and customizing anything in the campaign was out of the question. We played for about an hour or so(Steam bugged out and didnt track the time correctly it seems, shocking) and decided to try out the Guerilla Mode, surely this would let us use a MP loadout, change weapons, customize a soldier. I know it might seem like a minor thing to complain about but I LOVED the customization that R6V2 had and it was a game from 2008. To the point where theres apparently no more female soldiers in the military in the future?
And as far as the multiplayer goes, assuming you can find a match after sitting in a search for 10-15minutes and avoid getting into a lobby filled with 3-4 people scattered among sides and squads. You'll most likely get destroyed by hackers and people that have been playing this since the game came out.
My friend and I are enjoying the Coop Campaign as much as we can, but after coming from something with a lot more interesting systems in it. This is a fair bit dissapointing.

Talking about Kingdoms Rise is difficult because it's a title dear to me and I wish more people played it, but it's been in early access for years and with the accompanying quirks. This is an amazingly fun game that can really be summed up as third person Chivalry with magic. But it's much more than any of those things.
Normal melee uses a charge/release system. When you release, you swing in the exact 360 degree direction that you moved the camera while charging. You also block in the same manner, holding a direction, up to a couple seconds at a time. There is no magic block button in this game. You have a dodge roll, but there are no invincibility frames. You have a backstep, useful for counterattacking, as well as a disarming strike that render's the opponent's weapon unusable for a couple seconds by hitting your roll button during an attack charge.
There's an assortment of weapon choices in the game from the tank sword, which reduces incoming damage by 30%, to the Sneak Sword that basically functions like a TF2 spy knife to the Mobility Sword that increases your movement speed and enables you to double jump. There's a sword and shield option if blocking in a given direction proves too much for you and the Warhammer has a large amount of knockback useful for sending players flying off ledges.
You're allowed to carry a bonus item into battle as well, and these vary in form and function. You could enter battle with a longbow strapped to your back, a bear trap to place on the ground, or an amulet you can consume for a health boost. Maybe you want to use throwing knives instead of the bow, or an axe that explodes like a grenade and can stick into a player if you hit them with it.
You can take two spells into combat (or the same spell twice), though if you're good at using the menu you can swap these out on the fly, assuming you're willing to wait their full cooldown duration before use. Spells include a long-range teleport, turning invisible, force pull and push, multiple slows, a buff that grants temporary immunity to non-melee hits, some nukes like fireballs and lightning bolts, the ability to turn intangible for a couple seconds, a healing spell, and more.
Spells (and their cooldowns) are where all the game's strategy comes from. Do you want to rely on your sword to kill opponents? Take spells like teleport and pull to get up-close and personal. Afraid to get in close? Try using Fireball, Lightning Bolt or Ice Shot to deal with enemies at a 'safe' distance. Having touble against that kind of player and want to juke out their cooldowns? Go for Phase Shift, Teleport or Magic Immune to dodge their damage while you approach. Are you losing in the melee? Consider using Force Push and Invisibility to sneak up on any player standing too close to a pit for a kill and a good laugh. The most recent spell, Ice Spike, summons a large crystal which pops up players on top of it and once summoned, can be used as cover or to platform on top of.
The only real problem with this game is that no one plays it. Nine times out of ten, the servers are all going to be empty. There is a survival mode and a practice map with bots that can show off the game and give you the opportunity to test your loadout, but it's not the true Kingdoms Rise experience. I would buy this only if you have a friend to play with or if you want to be one of those guys and add random people like me onto your steam list hoping for some matchmaking.
I write this fresh out of an hour and a half streaming session in which I played Kingdoms Rise for none of the world to see, because people watch the game as much as they play it. If you want to see the game in action, the different maps and spells available, and you don't mind a bit of vulgarity because the friend I'm playing with and I are disgusting when put in the same room, I suggest you at least take a peek. If you'd rather watch footage that's safe for work, just turn the sound off. It's probably for the best anyways, though the gradually increasing music volume as the timer reaches zero is a nice touch by the dev.
tl;dr: Buy this game, then buy it again. Then buy a four-pack. Buy one for all your steam friends. If you can get one of them to play with you, regardless of who they are, you're gonna have a good time. If you buy enough copies, maybe the dev will be able to afford a marketing budget finally and we might get opponents on a more regular basis.

When it comes to games that epitomize the genre hybrid of Role Playing Games and First Person Shooers, this is one of the founding games for it. There's a lot to say for this game, both negative and positive. Still for the historic position that the game holds, it's worth playing no matter what. This is especially true if you like dystopian cyber-punk science fiction stories. Which is a style that this game just oozes from every facet.
On the down side there are quite things, that especially from today's perspective, are just awful. The graphics of this game have aged really poorly is a definite place to start. The game it self can be very difficult to get running, without some know how on running older games, this can be a problem. Although not one that's insurmountable. Although the worst aspect might be the gameplay, which has aged even worse than the graphics. While revolutionary, between engine limitations and some questionable gameplay choices, the game can be frustrating to play. Especially with some dead-end and useless upgrade paths offered. All of which can make this game daunting to someone who has never played.
Balancing out the negatives are some really spectacular positives. The most noteworthy shining positive of this game is the spectacular narrative it offers. The story is deep, compelling, dark, and offers a lot of player choice for its time. The gameplay, while somewhat limited, was revolutionary for its time. There's a good ammount of ability to play in a way that suits your prefrences. Weather you like to go for a stealthy approach, kick the doors down and go in guns blazing, or talk your way though situations. When the game presents an obstacle, there are almost always multiple ways to solve the puzzle. While the visuals are very dated, they also add a level of nostalgic charm to the dark dystopia cyber-punk world and story the game offers. Then there's also an upside to the limitations of the engine and gameplay: You can often exploit the game and the world, to solve a puzzle in ways the developers never intended.
All things considered, the dated nature of the game might make it a turn off to many. Still it's a revolutionary game that inspires a lot of the gameplay mechanics we take for granted today. It's definitely worth a look for that alone. The fantastic story and lasting legacy that exist to this day are what make this game totaly worth a recommendation. So while the game might not have aged the best, it's worth looking past the issues and forgiving the game for its age. There's still plenty of fun to be had in Deus Ex to this day.

I love this game. As a puzzle junkie who really gets into logic puzzles, this has been one of the best I've ever come across. It combines some elements of nonograms with minesweeper and given the twist of putting it all into a hexagonal grid to add an extra axis to contend with. Also, the soothing ambient music that accompanies the gameplay is a perfect match that I thoroughly enjoy every time I find myself playing.
Hexcells, Hexcells Plus and Hexcells Infinite should be considered a single game, and should be played through in that order. This entry to the series started it all and is essential to play through first in order to really learn the rules of this series properly before moving on to the more challenging puzzles that come with the other games. There is a natural progression of gradually increasing difficulty as you work through the puzzles. More rules get introduced over time as well. Each adding a new level of complexity and challenge to the puzzles that follow. But one of the greatest strengths of this game series is that you never have to guess, as the puzzles can always be solved with proper application of logic and deductive reasoning.

This is one of those games with the benefit of simplicity - with familiar controls and clear, uncomplicated mechanics, it's very easy to get into with a learning curve you can get to grips with good and quickly. But it's also one of those games that's easy to learn, hard to master - as you'd expect from a permadeath roguelike, it presents a decent challenge that favours a tenacious and moderately tactical playstyle, but never feels overly unfair. Keep your equipment up to scratch and your wits about you, and you should do fine.

Total War is a great series that you should really get into, Medieval 2 Total War is the game that will get you into the Total War series I have recommended this game to countless people and most if not all of them have thanked me for it while some games like Attila are pricey they still deliver the experience of being in a battle.
Medieval 2 Total War is one of the best strategy games I have ever played, it's simple to understand interface and mechanics are very effective when it comes to cramming them into one small easy to access UI.
You can have fun by playing the expansive campaign to conquer Europe and the middle-east or play a historical battle that actually happened hundreds of years ago or create your own battle with your choice of map armies and roster. You can even spice your game up a bit by installing mods (you will probably need the Kingdoms DLC to do so) onto your computer, like Third Age or The Elder Scrolls Total War, to say that this game was released in 2006 Creative Assembly have done a great job making this game.
Gameplay is simple: build an army, attack a castle, expand your kingdom, WIN, but where this game really shines is in the battles themselves have up to a maximum of 24,000 soldiers on the battlefield and witness the true bloody history of Medieval battles.
The downside of this game are the graphics although they are playable the fact that the game was released in 2006 tells us that the graphics aren't going to be as good as other Total War games, you'll know what I mean if you compare the graphics to Total War: Attila.

As much time as I've put into this NBA 2K game, the hundreds of hours I've put into prior NBA 2K games, and also including the countless time I will put into this game from now on, I still can not, and will not recommend NBA 2K17 - or any NBA 2K game for that matter.
I really do enjoy NBA 2K17: The MyCareer mode is great this year, the story is fleshed out enough to keep you interested, but not blown out proportionally that it becomes a laughing stock - especially compared to Spike Lee's awful attempt at an NBA story last year. (Not to mention Michael B. Jordan does a great job as Justice Young, the on court sidekick to your MyPlayer.) My only problem with MyCareer is that you can no longer simulate single matches without starting the match first and then pressing "Sim to End" from the pause menu. You always have to play a match to be able to do anything else in MyCareer.
The mechanical side of the gameplay has really been improved, defense in particular; you can really put a good amount of effort in on D, and you will almost always have positive results, assuming you know what you're doing. Defense has always been a fault in NBA 2K games, you would often feel like you couldn't do much more than you did and still get beaten to the basket by the opponent.
ISO moves have also been slightly improved, feeling less slippery, but also somewhat harder to use; you really have to practice the input timing, the distancing from the defensive player, and also have good enough court vision that you don't clumsily spin into another off ball player.
I must say that sometimes it feels like the AI defense feels a little too good at spotting your movements; if you are expecting to drive the basket all the time, smashing the ball into the net, it is likely not going to happen, unless if  you are an NBA 2K master. The game really asks you to keep moving the ball around, because the AI defense will stick to you like white on rice.
Moving onto what completely shuts down any positive outlook I have for this game.
The single player experience is fantastic, in fact sit me down on a couch with a few friends for some offline multiplayer and we'd have a blast, but as soon as you bring the internet into the mix everything starts to go wrong.
After years of NBA 2K releases you would think they would for once aim to make the online play work flawlessly, but that is once again not the case. it feels like all online modes are riddled with latency issues atleast 50% of the time, and sometimes the game likes to freeze up, telling you "WAITING FOR OPPONENT" but the game somehow still continues behind the frozen state.
The My Park matchmaking is awful, actually there is no matchmaking - you would expect there to be some kind of balancing system in place to find a game, but instead you have to race other players for a place on one of the 9 courts, and hope a "squad" doesn't waddle in and steal up the match you've been queueing for, for the last 10 minutes.
Pro-Am isn't the worst, but it does still have the latency issues, and not to mention that it often feels like in online matches your MyPlayer's stats are decreased considerably, as shots you take in Pro-Am, that would always be guaranteed baskets in offline play, often completely miss, no matter how open your MyPlayer is.
The micro-transaction system has been hugely boosted this time around, 2K really want you to spend more money this year. And yes, I did - I know I'm only helping the terrible micro transaction system, but the grind it would take to get to a level where you can compete on a similar level to the other micro-transaction boosted players, and to even play at a level that is enjoyable would take such a long time that I caved in. I just wish you could carry your player over from the prior year, or just shorten the grind to level your stats. Either way after paying out for micro-transactions, you have to grind for a long time anyway to continue levelling your MyPlayer after a certain point, and that takes a long time in it's own right.
So in conclusion/TL;DR:
+ Improved MyCareer, better overall story
+ Improved Gameplay Mechanics
+ Good offline play
- latency issues online
- Lag issues online
- Unimproved matchmaking
- MyPlayer feeling "Debuffed" online
- Micro-Transaction pushed THROUGH THE ROOF
I will continue to pray for the next NBA 2K game to be the one we deserve.

A dry husk of repetition.
PREFACE
The first Borderlands came out years ago. It was new in tone and gameplay and it was a lot of fun, despite some problems. By today's standards, I think we should know better by now and should have improved. A lot of the problems in the first Borderlands plague its sequels. Play your first Borderlands game. Play a second one for more of the same. Don't play a third. Take the amount of hours you've played in Borderlands 1 and 2. That's how long you've already been playing this game.
+++PROS+++
If you happen to like Borderlands, then this is more of the same. It's at least that.
The new frost element is much funner to use than slag.
---CONS---
STORY
It doesn't feel very good to play characters who are so unlikably cruel. A lot of people have a taste for sadism, but usually as revenge or justice against wrongdoers; our characters seem unnecessarily uncaring. It also doesn't help that we're helping someone who we know is a jerk, and playing as some characters who we know will die deservedly in the next game. Our characters' motivations seem weak as well. We're there because... we were hired?
On a small level, the story drags on and on, with predictable excuse after excuse to lengthen your adventure.
On a larger level, we know what's going to happen, and don't even like the side we're fighting for. When you do a movie about nazi protagonists, you watch their side of the struggle, as they truly believe they are fighting for the good of their country, and you portray a new perspective that most people don't consider. This was not done here.
The story is always delivered through expository audio dialogue, boring as the only way to get story. Then again, what else was supposed to be done? The story isn't very complicated or emotionally stressing, so there isn't much material for cutscenes with subtle and strong emotional animations, or set pieces showing the lives and personalities of people.
The Borderlands series has also taken this bizarre twist in tone, with serious dramatic and political matters at hand while fabricating tragic deaths. This dramaticism clashes harshly with the game's silly dialogue.
The dramaticism also feels unearned when crudely force fed through audio dialogue. The game keeps verbally telling me the way things are, not showing me; is this character kind hearted? Why don't they affect my gameplay? It could be argued that I'm being greedy, demanding masterpieces when I suppose audio dialogue could be enough, but I push for story and gameplay melding so that I'm paying attention and I care; I was just absent mindedly following waypoints and killing.
The characters are not as memorable as they were in previous games. It seems the strategy was to just make a character with a new accent and a one sentence description. They don't even stick around for very long. I remember the cast of Borderlands 2, because they stuck with me the whole time, the whole city against this evil man.
The humor is also getting worse. It seem that as long as you have people saying ridiculous things with no punchline, exaggeration, or surprise, it'll be funny. It's the kind of things you hear when you're playing multiplayer and someone decides to be a radio dj comedian, saying anything desperately hoping to be funny and popular.
The recycled assets of Borderlands continue to build an unforgiving wasteland well, but other than that, the sense of the world isn't built very deeply; it's all just a 2d poster backdrop to your adventure. The citizens walk idly and never say much; they're not alive. The buildings themselves are not very memorable either, repeated cut and pasted spaces.
GAMEPLAY
Repetition, over and over. Shoot, walk, use, shoot, walk use. Pick up guns, sell. The elemental and RPG elements? They hardly matter. Just shoot critical points, pick the thing with the highest numbers, oh, keep a corrosive weapon for robots. It was fun the first game, getting better and better treasure.
The open spaces. The maps are sprawling with empty space to lengthen your boring game time.
The objectives are often placed in deceptively far off places, like on a super high cliff right next to you. It looks close on the map, bu you actually have to travel all the way around.
You can get lost a lot, especially with all the vertical space that is not well represented on the map.
The AI is still the same as always. Idle until aggravated, perfect aim at all distances, moving erratically with no turning animations to read movement. They're deceptively hard to shoot, dull, and annoying; flying enemies are worse.
The low gravity and oxygen does not really add anything new to the game. In fact, it's just annoying to have to manage them.
The design and balance seems sloppy. You can be a little more loose in design in PVE than in PVP, but this is just too sloppy. It feels as if players are just thrown into a mess of complications, without testing, without consideration for gameplay and strategy, and it's expected to be okay because, "well, if they keep trying, they'll make it." I've had skirmishes of enemies spawning all around me, sporadic cover, jump pads that didn't help, and enemies with rocket launchers while I still only had two weapon slots.
Even the special abilities are less interesting. In Borderlands two, I could wait patiently for my cooldown, then pull out my skill that allowed me to engages waves of enemies. Now, I have to use my skill much more often to kill 1 or 2 people at best. I played as Nisha. Her skill is to, for a brief period, automatically aim at enemies and gain increased gun stats. A lot of her skill tree depends on her being able to get kills during this period; it's so brief and can hardly kill. The skill itself also functioned quite uselessly. As long as enemies were moving, none of my showdown bullets would hit. I would also lock onto enemies behind cover. I would aim at far away enemies rather than the ones right in front of me that I wanted to kill. If the enemy was posed in the right way, their head would be cocked to the side and all my bullets would miss.

This game... Wow. I love it. I love it to bits. But instead of ranting how much I love it, I will tell you WHY I love it.
---Stealth Mechanics---
This is absolutely MASSIVE part of the game that you need to get a handle on. You're cloaking system makes you harder to see, but you cannot move fast in it. You are hard-ish to see when out in the open, but you look like a blurry blob walking around like that. When leaning up against something, you are nearly impossible to see. But don't let that cloaking system fool you, it is not perfect, not by a longshot. Enemies can notice you if they try hard enough, and when they do, stealth is out of the question, and you are dead in the water.
---Combat---
The more important type of combat, which I like to call CQC, but its just referred to as take-downs, is rather nice and easy to get a hold of. You sneak up on someone, press a button, and you snap their neck. Pretty simple. The open combat when you are discovered is quite complex. You can order you're teammates to focus fire on up to 4 enemies. You can throw grenades (or dodge them). You can make a well placed headshot with you're fully customized gear. You can do all kinds of stuff. Don't go with shotguns though, they are terrible in this game.
---Sync Shots---
Pretty simple, mark up to 4 enemies, and shoot them simulteneously so the enemy stays unaware to you're presence if they are close together. It cannot be used in all scenarios though. Sometimes there are more than four, and you're best bet is to sneak by in any situation anyway.
---Story---
The story is downright BREATHTAKING, except for the ending, I never really understood that.
My rating for this game is a 10/10.
