The best F2P MMO out there. Keep in mind this is based off my current experience of 1-49. Not max level content.
Pros:
-Non intrusive micro-transactions
-Amazing reactive based combat
-Best housing I have ever seen
-Great community (Thus far)
-Great custimzation of just about EVERYTHING. Either through In-game currency or Micro
-Fast paced dungeons (BONUS: Plenty of side content outside the typical 3 dps/1 healer/1 tank stuff)
-Path system is amazing
-Challenges
-Humor and theme (This is personal)
-The level up guy. (Trust me)
-Active and fair economy
Cons:
-Weird UI issues which can cause quest issues.
-Long que times (Depending on certain factors)
-Quests can be grindy
-PvP can be and is a mess at times. (1v1 is great though)
-Tutorials are hit and miss
-Abilites cap out at level 24. (Meaning the rest is skill/ability points) This is a persoanl gripe.
Just expect a wildly different combat system. Something more the along the lines of Guild Wars 2 but way more directional based.(No ability is auto aimed for you) Like I mentioned in the last con, abilites cap out at 24. Which makes the last 26 levels purely focusing on your build. That is fine as the game wants you to master your class mechanics before you hit 50. However, the lack of new abilites takes away from the overall excitement of finding that next cool new ability while leveling.
In all Wildstar is a game that is far underrated. It's fun, over the top, and easy to play.
Is it perfect? No, Is it fun? Hell yes. Does it re-invent the wheel? No. Does it do things unique and in its own style. Yes.
Ultimately you have nothing to lose. The micro-transactions are there but is COMPLETELY optional. No game feature is held back. Only enhanced by the store.

Minesweeper on a hex grid, with additional mechanics and hand-crafted puzzles that never require guessing. If that sounds good, you will like this game.
This release (Hexcells) has much easier puzzles than its sequels in the same series (Hexcells Plus and Hexcells Infinite), so if you're experienced with logic puzzles, you may prefer to start with one of those later releases.

HexCells is a delightfully entertaining little twist on MineSweeper.     Rather than trying to beat the clock,you just have to find the mines.  If you so choose, you can see if you can do it without setting any off.  If you manage a perfect score on every level, there's an achievement for it, but the game is geared up towards pleasant play, so you tend to get enough lives per level that if you do mis-click a few times, it's not the end of the world.
The twist is that it's like Minesweeper crossed with those Logic puzzle games you used to do as a kid, or maybe a bit like the logic you'd use with Sudoku... You have to work out which cell to click by looking at some numbers that tell you the configuration of the hidden mines.
Those numbers can be
* A certain number of mines on a column or diagonal
* A certain number of mines adjacent to a hex cell
And these can be modified such that the clue tells you whether
* they are adjacent to each other.
* They are not adjacent to each other.
Once you look at the various numbers, it's relatively easy to figure out the logic, and before you know it, you're sticking down blue hexes (the flags in minesweeper), and right-clicking to unveil number tiles.
The total game takes about two hours to finish.  I'm a perfectionist, so I did another speed-run through the game to re-do all the levels I tripped up on.  Unfortunately the game doesn't seem to tell you which those were, so I just re-played the whole game, and managed to finish it again in about 45 minutes.
there are definitely some strategies you can use.  It takes a little thought, but once you work them out, you can just look at the tiles and KNOW that a certain two will have a mine, while the other two might not.  That's fine, you mark the knowns, and come back to the unknowns later.    Doing that first 'pass', means that the other evidence just flows right through, and the level's over in a blink.
Some of the levels are set up beautifully, and the way the various adjustments to the hex hints combine together means your mind is always working, and piecing little bits of puzzle together.  Very rarely are you completely stumped.
The only weirdness is that one level just introduces hexes which hang out by themselves with nothing around them.  These are always mines, apparently.  I guess you have to use elimination to get to the end and see those two hanging out, and have two 'flags' left to plant, I suppose.  It was kinda odd.
One level which is a real doozie with numbers all over the place and most of the screen filled with hexes took me almost 30 minutes to clear on the first pass. On the second, once I'd figured out the routine, I cleared it in under 5.
I REALLY enjoyed this game. The creator has nicely meshed Minesweeper and logic puzzles into a short but sweet little game.

Really, this game is a top-notch free-to-play.  I'd rank it right up there with the likes of Team Fortress 2.
The weapons crafting system is where the game really shines.  You earn XP through playing games, and spend the XP buying new parts to build weapons with.  I think there are currently something like 6,000,000,000,000 (yes, Six Billion) possible weapon designs available.
The artwork is great for what it is, and the effects are just brilliant.  From bouncing, flaming, or electrical bolts flying everywhere to actually seeing the bullet holes and damage in your character, they really paid attention to detail.
The game modes are great renditions of the classic capture-the-flag and team deathmatch modes that you find in most team shooters.  I found the Ranked Annihilation mode to be awesomely fun - you earn points and choose which buffs to buy your character when you can afford them, between 3 possible choices.  This mode imparticular gives it a moba-ish feel that I really enjoy.
You're missing out if you do not give this game a try, that's the bottom line.  It's free, but I'd easily be willing to pay 20-25$ if they wanted to charge that for it.  It's certainly that good.  I'll probably be buying the 20$ Steam Starter pack for it soon, too.  Those steampunk goggles look too cool!
TL;DR:  Great game.  10/10 for a Free-to-Play.

Now onto the long list of negatives which ruin this car game and would deter anyone from wanting to buy or even play it.

A dry husk of repetition.
PREFACE
The first Borderlands came out years ago. It was new in tone and gameplay and it was a lot of fun, despite some problems. By today's standards, I think we should know better by now and should have improved. A lot of the problems in the first Borderlands plague its sequels. Play your first Borderlands game. Play a second one for more of the same. Don't play a third. Take the amount of hours you've played in Borderlands 1 and 2. That's how long you've already been playing this game.
+++PROS+++
If you happen to like Borderlands, then this is more of the same. It's at least that.
The new frost element is much funner to use than slag.
---CONS---
STORY
It doesn't feel very good to play characters who are so unlikably cruel. A lot of people have a taste for sadism, but usually as revenge or justice against wrongdoers; our characters seem unnecessarily uncaring. It also doesn't help that we're helping someone who we know is a jerk, and playing as some characters who we know will die deservedly in the next game. Our characters' motivations seem weak as well. We're there because... we were hired?
On a small level, the story drags on and on, with predictable excuse after excuse to lengthen your adventure.
On a larger level, we know what's going to happen, and don't even like the side we're fighting for. When you do a movie about nazi protagonists, you watch their side of the struggle, as they truly believe they are fighting for the good of their country, and you portray a new perspective that most people don't consider. This was not done here.
The story is always delivered through expository audio dialogue, boring as the only way to get story. Then again, what else was supposed to be done? The story isn't very complicated or emotionally stressing, so there isn't much material for cutscenes with subtle and strong emotional animations, or set pieces showing the lives and personalities of people.
The Borderlands series has also taken this bizarre twist in tone, with serious dramatic and political matters at hand while fabricating tragic deaths. This dramaticism clashes harshly with the game's silly dialogue.
The dramaticism also feels unearned when crudely force fed through audio dialogue. The game keeps verbally telling me the way things are, not showing me; is this character kind hearted? Why don't they affect my gameplay? It could be argued that I'm being greedy, demanding masterpieces when I suppose audio dialogue could be enough, but I push for story and gameplay melding so that I'm paying attention and I care; I was just absent mindedly following waypoints and killing.
The characters are not as memorable as they were in previous games. It seems the strategy was to just make a character with a new accent and a one sentence description. They don't even stick around for very long. I remember the cast of Borderlands 2, because they stuck with me the whole time, the whole city against this evil man.
The humor is also getting worse. It seem that as long as you have people saying ridiculous things with no punchline, exaggeration, or surprise, it'll be funny. It's the kind of things you hear when you're playing multiplayer and someone decides to be a radio dj comedian, saying anything desperately hoping to be funny and popular.
The recycled assets of Borderlands continue to build an unforgiving wasteland well, but other than that, the sense of the world isn't built very deeply; it's all just a 2d poster backdrop to your adventure. The citizens walk idly and never say much; they're not alive. The buildings themselves are not very memorable either, repeated cut and pasted spaces.
GAMEPLAY
Repetition, over and over. Shoot, walk, use, shoot, walk use. Pick up guns, sell. The elemental and RPG elements? They hardly matter. Just shoot critical points, pick the thing with the highest numbers, oh, keep a corrosive weapon for robots. It was fun the first game, getting better and better treasure.
The open spaces. The maps are sprawling with empty space to lengthen your boring game time.
The objectives are often placed in deceptively far off places, like on a super high cliff right next to you. It looks close on the map, bu you actually have to travel all the way around.
You can get lost a lot, especially with all the vertical space that is not well represented on the map.
The AI is still the same as always. Idle until aggravated, perfect aim at all distances, moving erratically with no turning animations to read movement. They're deceptively hard to shoot, dull, and annoying; flying enemies are worse.
The low gravity and oxygen does not really add anything new to the game. In fact, it's just annoying to have to manage them.
The design and balance seems sloppy. You can be a little more loose in design in PVE than in PVP, but this is just too sloppy. It feels as if players are just thrown into a mess of complications, without testing, without consideration for gameplay and strategy, and it's expected to be okay because, "well, if they keep trying, they'll make it." I've had skirmishes of enemies spawning all around me, sporadic cover, jump pads that didn't help, and enemies with rocket launchers while I still only had two weapon slots.
Even the special abilities are less interesting. In Borderlands two, I could wait patiently for my cooldown, then pull out my skill that allowed me to engages waves of enemies. Now, I have to use my skill much more often to kill 1 or 2 people at best. I played as Nisha. Her skill is to, for a brief period, automatically aim at enemies and gain increased gun stats. A lot of her skill tree depends on her being able to get kills during this period; it's so brief and can hardly kill. The skill itself also functioned quite uselessly. As long as enemies were moving, none of my showdown bullets would hit. I would also lock onto enemies behind cover. I would aim at far away enemies rather than the ones right in front of me that I wanted to kill. If the enemy was posed in the right way, their head would be cocked to the side and all my bullets would miss.

WildStar's concept is a mega-hit and could be so much better!! It includes just the best from all known MMO(rpg)'s. I need to tell tho:
No wonder about WildStar's counter-balance aka there is only one server available and no players seem to be online...
Myself as a hardcore PvE-Quester who doesn't leave one single Quest and Mission alone as for the amazing NCSoft titles like Aion NA, Blade & Soul, Lineage2 and various other MMO(rpg's) just as EVE Online, Rift, Firefall, Global Agenda, WAKFU <3 and more, WildStar is in that case the worst. Especially for newcomers. I really don't get the current Steam-Hype about WildStar.
This game is a mess and absolutely confusing about questing, especially in path-finding/following quests as well as these high amount of receiving quests at once. You walk here and run there and randomly get a bunch of quests. Also bugged quests, showing you spots but objectives ain't there...
Walking here and again running there, random appearing and annoying challenges for every feet you move which you auto-ignore, since dozens of other quests are already running in meantime. How to ful-fill 3 running challenges at once and to complete just any of your current on-going missions in general? You will never be able to complete everything to 100%!! Hidden or more likely "unseen" Quests are so available which I totally dislike. A total mess and please don't confuse here "mess" with "being complex".
Personally for me I had tried to like WildStar for a few times, but without a success (yet). It is free and all, but heck... Too much of much. WildStar is absolutely unclear and confusing in this questing matter. I even like Firefall more than this.
Fighting for ranged classes is kinda annoying. If you compare WildStar's gameplay as in controlling and moving with Global Agenda or Firefall, I wish this has nothing to do with these game's playstyle at all, but looks similar to them. Graphics are too darkish in WildStar, makes me kinda dizzy, especially with all these unclear waypoints to find.
A 1on1 PvP fight takes like a minute with all your inflated HP and stuff. About 10vs10 in PvP, if you all fight at once it gonna take ages to even kill one level 14 enemy. That is.... way too easy and long-wided.
Good things are the cute characters and the beautifully made landscapes, terrains, colors and ambient in later regions.
Well, I am going back to Aion NA after this try. At least Aion is/keeps linear in questing and also gets its next major v5.0 Update in a few weeks, still #1. Aion NA is not such a confusing mess as WildStar (currently) is, especially while path-finding and even finishing multiple quests. Is there any Storyline for WildStar present? I guess not or at least I didn't get it after the tutorial, since I have had been overflowed and bombarded with quests. This needs to be changed, really.
As a seriously MMO-RPG player and hardcore quester, I cannot recommend this game for questers. You better have to accept one single quest and finish it, then to gain the next single one. You like it? Then try it and become a bored greyed old. Stay on low-level for months.
In Aion NA as well as for other NCSoft titles I can easily handle and finish 40 quests in a parallel manner which is fun, while doing 5+ parallel quests in WildStar makes you raqe quit, re-join to try to continue questing after a 30-mins Counter-Strike: Source run, and rage quit again. Excuse me.
For WildStar I would suggest to half-down quests within a square-meter and more importantly to "enhance" path-finding in general as well as for the map!!

If you've played games like Ratchet & Clank, and popular MMORPGs like World Of Warcraft, you definitely need to try out this game. It used to be paid to play but now it's completely free to play. The things I like about this game is the skills, AMP Builder, and the three types of setups you can choose from:
- Basically you can customize your skills, and upgrade them according to tier levels.
- As you increase the tier level of a skill, they gain new modifiers that can allow the skill you upgraded to become more     powerful and useful throughout end - game content.
- The only way you can upgrade your skills is by using Ability Tier Points.
- Just to let you know, 1 Ability Tier Point is required to upgrade a skill for one tier.
- Assault Rating is basically one of the stats of increasing the damage of Assault and Utility skills.
- It's primarily called Assault Rating in items or gear you equip in - order to increase your Assault Power.
- Primarily, characters intend to go for Assault Rating if they choose to be a DPS char and do a lot of damage.
-I would pretty much recommend getting Assault Rating for gear if you choose to be a Warrior, Engineer, Stalker, or Esper since they intend to become good DPS dealers but also provide good Tanking if you become a Warrior, or Engineer.
- So going support rating is becoming the support for a team.
- It would be best to be a Medic, or a Spellslinger since they intend to have a variety of healing, and support skills that can help aid a team.
- Plus, support gives benefits to buffs, and healing making it more useful throughout end - game content.
- Going with utility is pretty much becoming the tank in the game.
- Also, it's going with the most defense and HP to provide tanking while in raids, dungeons, and expeditions.
- Tanking may be hard or easy depending on the way you play it if you go with utility rating.
- The disadvantage is doing weak damage but the advantage is withstanding more damage.

Review updated, 14th of September. Original review as follows, update below.
A fun game rendered unplayable by technical issues.
Nier: Automata offers fun gameplay and an intriguing story, what little of it I was able to access. The first ~5 hours were fun to play, but then the "white screen of death" struck: The game will briefly freeze, then the screen will go black, then white. At this point the game still seems to be running based on the sounds I can hear, but the screen will remain white. The only solution is to shut the game down.
A little searching has revealed that this is a not-uncommon problem with the game, and has been since launch. The developers have not provided a fix for this bug, and the community has not be able to find a reliable workaround either.
This bug is quite unpredictable. Some have played through almost the entire game before encountering it, others get it every five minutes. The ones who are most affected by it can't progress in the game at all, as it can take a player anywhere from 15-30 minutes to reach the first opportunity to save in the game. If the wsod occurs before that they have to start over from the beginning.
But even for me this bug is crippling, as the game deliberately makes use of checkpoint starvation at times and, as it so stringently reminds us, does not have an autosave function. If it decides to wsod on me, all progress since the last manual save is lost.
At this point I decided to pursue a refund, but as the bug did not rear its ugly head until I was well outside Steam's 2-hour "no questions asked" refund window I was denied one. Apparently "game rendered unplayable by technical issues" is not a valid reason for a refund. Caveat emptor - let the buyer beware. I would have a 60 euro paperweight, but a digital purchase is not even good for that.
I am very disappointed with Platinum Games' post-launch support. In addition to this un-addressed game-stopping bug, the game also suffers from a few other graphical issues and performance issues, issues that community modders were able to swiftly address. And yet Platinum Games, a professional developer selling a 60 euro game, is either unwilling or unable to deal with these problems, leaving it to their paying customers to repair their faulty product. Again, caveat emptor.
So in conclusion, I can't recommend this game, and that's a shame. I can't recommend it because it is gambling, and you shouldn't need to gamble 60 euros in hopes of getting a good game and be left with nothing if you lose.
If you do buy it, hope that the wsod bug manifests immediately, or not at all. If you don't get it, you will have a fun game. If you get it immediately you can get a refund and be on your way with nothing lost except a little time.
But if, like me, you get it after the refund window closes, you're screwed.
Update, 14th September 2017. Shortly after midnight.
This review was originally posted on the 27th of April, and I want to provide an update. In the months since then, both AMD and nVidia have released driver updates intended to alleviate the white screen crashes, while the developers have remained silent. For some, these updates have fixed the problem, but for others the crashes remain, including me. The other technical issues remain as well.
To some, the driver updates constitute an admission of guilt on AMD/nVidia's part, but I feel the need to point out that if these issues are due to driver bugs, other developers know how to work around and avoid these bugs and make games that don't crash the display drivers. I expected the same expertise from Platinum and Square Enix, and they haven't displayed it.
So why the update now? At time of writing my time played says 47.3 hours. Although the crashes still happen, they happen less now, both due to driver updates and a host of other measures taken. I decided to see if it was possible to struggle my way through the game, and despite roughly two dozen crashes, I made it.
And what a journey it was. At times uplifting, at times emotionally devastating, and ultimately cathartic. I fought, and I persevered, and while I wouldn't call the technical issues a plus by any means, they only made the struggle that much more desperate. At times I felt like I was limping along, desperately praying that the game would finally allow me a save point so I wouldn't lose half an hour of progress that I would then have to replay with the same sword of Damocles still hanging over my head.
But I made it, and it was good. It was a good game, wrapped in a bad piece of software. And it's a shame. It's a damned shame that a game this good should be this technically deficient, this mired in issues.
I bid a bittersweet farewell to Nier: Automata. A game that I enjoyed despite all its attempts to prevent me from doing so. A game that I would recommend to all my friends in an instant, were it not for the sorry state it is in. A game that I sincerely hope will some day receive the treatment it deserves. Maybe someone will one day fix it. Maybe. Because as the game would tell you, there's always hope.

"What does it mean to be human?"
For a game with such an obviously low budget, you'd wonder how it gets all the acclaim. It does have a myriad of issues as a videogame; the combat may get boring, the visuals look dated at times, and the open-world is a mere illusion. However, the true focus of director Yoko Taro was not to create the perfect videogame. It was to paint a deep, emotionally gripping tale of two androids in a sad, torn-down world of lies.
"ThANk you for ...foR the FLOWErs. Desert FLOWErs are BEAUTIF, arEN't thEY... Th-Th-thank You..."
NieR: Automata may lack in a few areas (much like its predecessor), however, the technical aspects of any game, no matter how flawless, will eventually be beaten. These shortcomings do not take one bit away from what the game strives to be--from what it conveys. Where most if not all triple-A titles fear to take risks and defy industry standards, NieR: Automata goes all out with its eccentric personality unafraid to be as it is.
- Thought provoking narrative masterfully executed with innovative storytelling
- Developed, multi-dimensional characters you care about
- One of if not the best score ever composed for a videogame
- Poignant atmosphere with philosophical themes
- Well animated, stylish, and satisfying combat (duh, platinum games)
- Mysterious and captivating world that hides subtle, lore-rich, details
- Beautiful art direction despite technically lacking graphics
- The most clever and original game design I have seen in years

You don't look for straight lines or perfect circles in a work of art. What makes this game truly special is its ability to mesmerize. It made me feel and think, a feat that no amount of pixel perfect textures, open-worldness, or *even fun* could ever achieve. This is what separates a mere videogame from something incomparable... a masterpiece that will stay with me for as long as I live.
As unreasonable as it sounds, the emotions I've felt reaching the final [E]nding says just that.

Loadout is a fun, fast paced and massively irreverent multiplayer 3rd person shooter.  New twists on standard game modes, a bright, gory and nudity ridden (in an amusing and disturbing way) graphic style and ridiculously customizable weapons take what should be a very derivative game and make it feel fun and fresh.
The flag is now a giant hammer you can smash the other team with to get extra points when you cap.  Team death match now requires you to pick up a glowing blue vial (dropped from enemy corpses) to score and a mode called extraction assigns people, on rotation to grab blue crystals of the ground and throw them in hoppers to build up points, all while the whole other team can clearly see location of the collector and will do everything in their power to pin him/her to the wall.

The graphics are unique, cartoony, and over the top.  Not only are the death animations hilarious (think just your lower half running around after taking a rocket hit) but your character will actually reflect damage done while you are still alive.  If someone burns you (one of several ammo options) your character will be burned black.  If someone perforated you with slugs you will have holes more or less where they hit you, have bone exposed in your leg or be squirting an imposable amount of blood out of an arm.  Now to touch on the nudity… let’s just say they blur the dangly bits, a little, somehow making it all the more disturbing.  This is the only game I have ever seen where someone could honest to god teabag your mangled corpse... (Assuming they paid real money for the taunt and the… let’s call it… the commando skin)
The weapon modification system is impressive.  It allows you to build and or customize, basically on the fly (you do have to wait to be in the lobby between games) your weapon type and its attributes.  I don’t have the patience to list all of the options but for the four main weapon types (rifles, launchers, beam and pulse) you can commonly modify the trigger group, stock, optics, barrel, type of ammunition and magazine, as well as a set of proprietary options for each.
Loadout is free to play and while I have heard a lot of grumbling about it being pay to win.  I have not personally found this to be the case.  I possess no great skill at these types of games and have not felt the need to invest anything to stay competitive enough to still enjoy the experience.   Most of the items you can buy are cosmetic and while this usually holds no appeal to me.  The idea that I can purchase options to outfit my massively muscled character with a beer straw hard hat, world war 2 gas mask, heap-o-gold neck bling, way to short tied up pink t-shirt, leopard thong and knee pads makes it almost too funny to resist.  Particularly after I purchase the gangnam style taunt so I can cap points in king of the hill (called blitz in Loadout) with so much swagger no one will be able to bring themselves to shoot at me.
On a final note.   Any game that starts a match with both teams mixed up in tiny huddle, everyone’s guns pretty much pressed into each other’s guts, insuring that when the countdown hits zero you will get to experience what may be the most chaotic 2 seconds in video game history,  gets my vote!
It cost you nothing to give it a try.  If you do my name is AOEisForNoobs (often found wielding a rocket launcher) look me up.

I have been playing multiplayer online RPGs for close to 20 years, this game may not be the best I have ever played but it is a lot of fun.
If you already know the basics of how to play this style of game, you will be able to overcome the difficulties with things like a poor tutorial that does not effectively teach you how to use your newly unlocked skills.  For example, when you unlock the "costume" ability all it says is that you have unlocked it, it does not tell you how to access it or how to use the UI once you do access it.   This problem, regrettably, is all to common.  Once you unlock a new feature it can be tricky at times to figure out how to use it.
The "Path System" is a lot of fun, however I have found a few bugs where I was unable to finish path quests.  After googling the quest I found that it was a bug and it was best to just ignore the quest because it was not likely to be able to complete it.  This is not a big problem for progression but I like to complete achievements and receive the bonus loot from doing all the path quests in a zone.
What I find most enjoyable about games would be crafting,  and regrettable, at this time, the crafting in WildStar is broken.  One such instance would be how in tailoring you need cloth thread, and a variety of other things depending on what you are making.  I have the cloth, and I have the "variety of other things"  and I have a rather nice pile of them, however after not being able to find thread in game I googled the thread.  And guess what,  even the official WildStar wiki does not have the thread listed as existing, and all the recipes on the wiki are outdated.  Does the thread exist?  Is it a bug?  or is it just not explained anywhere in game or on the internet as to how you find the thread?
One last area that I think could, and probably is being worked on, is the store.  I have seen the style of store where the more you spend the higher your "purchase rank" is and if you spend enough you get a new rank and some special items.  I love this system because if the special rank only items are good it makes me want to spend money, and if the item were available for cash I would simply buy the one item.  However if it's free with rank I have to spend more money to get the fun item. It is a great system,  only problem is that the store does not have a lot of things to buy.  Don't get me wrong, there is enough in the store that if you had money to spend you could easily spend $100.  The problem is that to get the top rank you need to spend around $1000, and there is not enough in the store to spend that much, even if I had the money and the desire to get the top rank.
Putting those problems aside, the game play is solid, the art is amazing, and the classes that I have played have been a lot of fun, even if they are a bit silly (a medic using defibrillators as a weapon :P  )
This game has been, and probably will continue to be, a lot of fun to play.  I think that with time as the bugs are squashed and the Aurins fur is fluffed out a bit, this game will be an amazing game.

This is game I should like, instead it has become an excersize in frustration.
Want an example ?
Google Stellaris fleet sizes, or fleet caps. See the answers experts give to questions about fleet sizes. Usually it goes along the lines of I have 24k in my fleet, they never actually answer the posters question and those that try too leave out vital information. So most players, dont actually know how this game works, they just manage to some how stumble on a formula that works.
You see the answer to that question pretty much reveals the games flaws.
Fleet caps are a combination of space station upgrades, large populations and research. Where as research goes faster when you only have a small population. So the larger your population gets, the slower you research is and the larger your fleet becomes. From then on you fall behind and end up losing to an empire with only 3 planets to its name.
So you have to gather research resources to boost your research as your empire expands, this means expanding slowly, letting your population on planets grow before settling new ones and using your influence to build frontier out posts in resource rich areas.
These require energy and energy is the one thing that is in short supply.
So you have to balance expansion, with research with the need to build mines and research out posts in order to keep your empire growing and competative.
That is why nobody ever answers that question properly.
Sounds like I just did right, well kind of.
You see, whilst your happy with your 2000 strength fleet, that 3 planet AI turns up with a 16,000 strength fleet that it really should not have because you now know how that fleet cap is worked out now and you can see from the diplomacy screen that his tech level is not any higher than yours, so his fleet should at best be comparable to yours.
So you know beyond any doubt that the AI cheats like crazy and whilst your limited by these rules, it is not.
Next we come to diplomacy, an AI that loves you to bits makes you its rival, which gives you an instant -100 rep with that AI. All the bonuses recieved before that gave it a +93 rep, meaning it loved you to bit, yet sees you as its enemy. It attacks you, you beat it. You conquer all its planets, destroy all its mines and out posts and end up drawn in a war because its ally beat your ally. Even though you pretty much wiped him out.
After the war, a truce is declared and your ally invites this AI in to your Federation, before the flames of war have even gone out, this AI is now your best friend and the truce setting is still clearly visible on the AI that is now your ally. Meaning that uneasy post war peace is still uneasy as it joins your federation and becomes your bestie.
These 2 examples reveal what is wrong with this game, it is less of game you play and more of a system you learn and then exploit. It makes very little sense because the game mechanics are not there to make game play, they are to stop one AI from steam rolling the entire galaxy.
You see, if they just let an AI grow and linked research to empire size as most games do, then the biggest AI would always win. So instead they make the smallest AI research things faster, so they catch up, grow in size, suddenly their research slows down and they become an out dated large empire too.
Mean while the tiny Mr Nobody empire with only 3 planets has quietly researched everything and is now a super power that nobody can beat.
That is whats wrong with this game, the mechanics make no sense so you end up playing the system, not the game.
In infact, I am absolutely certain the lead designer spends his nights licking magic mushrooms in some damp English field someplace.
If you like spending 70 hours saying WTF, I strongly recommend this game, but if you dont, go and by Galactic Civ 3 instead. At least that makes sense.
And remember the reason people tend not to answer questions properly about this game is because they dont actually know how it works either.  Just ask them for a full answer and you see what I mean.
Just to ram that point home, look at the Global Achievements for this game, only 19% of those who buy it manage to settle a planet. In game thats pretty much about settling planets, that means 81% of those who buy it dont even get started in this game.
Nah.

I got Stellaris last week and instantly became addicted, the depth and immersion sucking me in like a black hole. Much of the game was excellent, but I'm here to share my experiences with some problems, and offer suggestions for improvement.
#1 "Fallen" Empires
I started out with this setting turned on, assuming it meant I'd have (extinct) ancient civilizations to explore, for story and research opportunities. As my people reached for the stars, they discovered these "Fallen" Empires were actually galactic superpowers. Without warning, hostile fleets (50k-100K in power) invaded while my empire was in its infancy, eradicating every last trace of my race.
#2 War Goals (and altering them)
I like the war goal system as a concept, but in practice it has numerous problems. Some war goals I never considered because they were too costly, such as vassals--it's cheaper and simpler to take total control of their planets. I see no logic in that.
Also, why are we unable to change war goals? In the flow of time and in the ever-changing state of the galaxy, certain events can radically change you perspective and goals. (Why can't we change our mind about liberation and force our enemies to cede instead?) If you're invasion is fairing better than anticipated, with every planet invaded or blockaded, I should be able to force my demands for their entire empire. With the system as it is now, taking an empire piece by piece over the span of decades (because of the forced truce system--a related issue) can be frustrating and, again, I see no logic in that. The system is too limiting--I don't want the game to tell me I'm asking for too much, that is something for ME to decide.
#3 Space Warfare, Fleet Management, Idle Ships, and Disobeying Direct Orders
Managing a galactic empire isn't always about sunshine and lollipops and rainbows. Sometimes, you have to get your hands dirty. The war itself can be stressful, but not nearly as stressful as managing your fleets. In war, one small mistake can result catastrophic loss of life, or give way to defeat. There are so many problems with fleet management I'm not sure where to begin.We need more information on the map. Give us icons for space ports and armies (not just occupying armies) and the races in each system. I need to know which system is inhabited by which race, so when I'm trying to raise an army I don't have to click every planet in the entire galaxy to find which ones are inhabited by a certain race--a simple icon or just a word would alleviate this issue. I don't want to have to zoom in a search every time.
Military stations also have too large of a dead-zone radius. I understand the "balancing" effect of this dead-zone, so that you can't stack too many fortresses together...but why? Isn't the balancing effect that they cost resources to maintain? It's space, by the way, (it isn't flat) with plenty of room to build whatever I want wherever I want. Nothing is stopping me from building 10 fortresses around a world except the game telling me to "be fair."
Well I have news for you--life isn't fair. Wars are fought by seizing advantages and exploiting weaknesses, stacking the odds in your favor or crippling the enemy so they don't stand a chance. Instead, my admirals are more concerned with fairness. "This world is too fortified, its defenses too tight. The enemy won't be able to break through easily, so we need to spread these stations out and give them a fighting chance." What?
#4 Armies, Attachments, (and varieties)
I have another strategic issue. Armies have an "attachment" feature, but to apply an attachment you need to go through an externally tedious process. You need the build the army, select each army individually (while still planet-side) and then manually click to add an attachment. When you're raising multiple armies across and entire galaxy, this feature is far too tedious to bother with, so despite the advantages I simply ignored it--I'm not wasting my time clicking individual every army.
The fix is simple. When building an army, just incorporate the attachment feature at the army creation stage, not after. Just click "build with attachment" or add another army type to the build option list.
Give armies the option to upgrade too. I'd like to see more done with them, like selecting weapon/armor types, or other features that can be added. Army policies and tactics would also be a great feature (set armies to liberate slave populations or auto purge). I want my troops to feel more real than little green circles. There are not enough options for planetary surface defenses.
Also, if the planet is full and still raising any army the "excess" troops automatically go into orbit.
Planets have a maximum troop limit? I understand this from a balancing point of view, but really, what's stopping me from building or landing a massive force on a planet? Why can't the balance simply be resource consumption, like food! If I want to devote a planet for the sole purpose of troop training and residence, I should be able.
#5 Rebel Scum
Rebel factions are impossible to eliminate. In 60 hours, I never quelled one rebellion despite my best efforts. I would adopt social welfare programs, information quarantine, propaganda broadcast, employ re-education campaigns, and even genetically modify species to become conformists, suppressed them and integrated them in the factions tab--I even had the strategic resource to pacify them--I did EVERYTHING I could.
There was no peaceful solution.
#6 Diplomacy (or not)
I didn't deal much with diplomacy and trade not because I had no interest, but it was a rather barren feature. Sure, you could interact with species diplomatically, and there were some options, but I was shocked that forming an alliance or "federation" was a technology that had to be researched.
Trade had so few options. I attempted a few resource and star chart exchanges, sometimes a research agreement (which I still don't understand how it works). There wasn't much there. Diplomacy needs many more options, especially since its a defining feature of the game.We should be able to exchange researched technology through diplomacy. Again, it happens all the time in reality. This way, we have other options rather than watching the clock as the paint dries. This would encourage diplomacy and making friends. Instead of only political options like war and peace, and very limited trade, a whole new aspect of the game would open up. I would actually have incentive to stay on an empire's good side if they have tech I want and we could become better economic partners. Trading resources is bland. You could also trade slaves.In the diplomacy window, it would be nice to make demands without going to war. Why not encourage a peaceful alternative? Instead of "war goals" why not "peace goals" as well? With systems recently acquired or conquered, instead of purging or integrating the population, I wish there was an option to deport them to the empire they belong to. The more options, the better.
#7 Parting Shots
Adding (or removing) systems to a sector can be buggy. Sometimes I accidentally click the wrong system and take it out of the sector, costing influence. This mistake happened to me far too many times and I hate losing resource over a system being buggy (sometimes I had to click a few times.) If you click on a system, and it would be removed from a system, give us a warning first that says "are you sure you?"Another issue was that automatically surveying systems was a technology, not a default order. Why? Auto "assist research" should be an option too. Adding the same feature of auto-building to construction ships would eliminate some frustration. Planets need an auto-upgrade structure option--I hate forgetting about surface tiles and having to check for upgrades years after the upgrade was researched.Some things in Stellaris made me rethink the phase "slow as molasses" (I have newfound respect for how fast molasses moves.)

Those familiar with the Ghost Recon franchise will quickly notice quite a few changes from the old formula when compared to Advanced Warfighter. Future Soldier improves the overall acessibility and trims some of the fat of the previous installments. This moves it out of the Hardcore Tactical bracket while still retaining its emphasis on tactical coordination, teamwork and stealth.
The most ovious change is the switch from the 1st person perspective to a 3rd person perspective. This allows for a much better view over the combat area and helps with planning and coordination. Another change is that the player regenerates health now. While being a debatable decision among its changes, it does however add a little more tolerace to minor mistakes and the HP pool of the player is still very low and regenerates slowly (especially on higher difficulties), discuraging open combat.
What I really like is the new weapons system. New weapons and parts can be unlocked by either progressing through the story missions or by completing very specifc tasks during the missions. Each weapon handles differently and has certain advantages and disadvantages compared to other weapons within the same group. Most modules are compatible with all weapons, however some weapons lack cerain customization options (for example a fixed stock) and some modules are not compatible with certain groups (you cannot mount a bipod on a submachine gun). There is a lot of variety to be explored and every player will find themself accustumed to different playstyles and loadout, which adds tactical variaty and adaptability to group dynamics.
When playing with less than 4 human players, the companion AI is great and awkward at the same time. It's great because it is able to think for itself and relocate when nessecary. However, you will notice that the enemies are completely unable to see them during stealth phase and they are seemingly invicible during combat phase, which throws you out of the flow quite a bit. Speaking of flow, there is one addition to the game which I feel was both unnessecary and inappropriate to the game: The mandatory rail-shooter-esque segments the game likes to refer to as "Diamond Formation". This is the only time the game tries to sell itself as an action game and falls flat on its face when the player dies multiple times because he didn't memorize the enemy patterns fast enough or missed a crucial shot with the worst pistol controls ever.
The tools the game offers you are pretty cool as well. there is a sensor that can track enemy movement for a set amount of time, you can scout the area with a UAV or detect enemies through walls with metal vision (or XRay according to the HUD). There are a few more but you do lose some tools for others at certain points in the game. It would have been cool if players could change those tools to add more variety in coop but the given tools make sense for the environment so its not much of a big deal.
Overall, the game offers a lot of new things which will interest people familiar with the earlier installments and will probably feel right at home one the highes difficulty. Those who are new to the franchise or had some trouble with the earlier games will be able to find a difficulty that suits them best but will still get challenges throughout the story. Diamond Formaion can go sit in a corner and think about its life choices though.

Lone Survivor is an odd puppy. It's a pixelated sidescrolling survival-horror that takes inspiration from many great places - most notably Silent Hill. You begin the game trapped on the second floor of an apartment building and must set to work finding a way out (for a start), while making sure to collect supplies, avoid (or kill) a good many monsters, look for other survivors, ocassionally obsess over cats, eat regularly, get a good night's sleep here and there, and most of all: stay sane. Which is easier said than done. It doesn't seem like you can ever truly screw up the game for good. Running out of bullets or dying is usually treated with a fever dream and some mercy supplies, but it puts a massive strain on your sanity. There are several endings, but the basic gist is that high sanity equals the good ending, low sanity equals a bad ending. Of course, what all effects your sanity - and how - is a much more complicated story indeed, and one you shall have to discover on your own.

A rather small game with a simple concept - you're a guy who just wants to get some damned sleep, but there are all these people partying hard. The solution? Murder them all of course.
There's actually not a lot of depth to it - you kill people without getting detected and arrested, until they're all dead. You can use various environmental traps or rely on a quick stab. There are usually a couple of containers per level you can hide bodies in. Different levels have slightly different challenges, but that's all it essentially boils down to.
However, the game makes the most of this basic concept. Its consistently surreal and tongue-in-cheek tone makes the subject matter morbidly funny rather than truly disturbing. And the over-the-top gritty story told in cutscenes interspersed between levels is a legitimately good parody of the kind of cheesy hard-boiled detective story you might find in a low-budget direct-to-TV movie.
Levels usually last 15-20 minutes. Because of the repetitive nature of its gameplay, I found it difficult to play this in hours-long stretches - this game is better-enjoyed in small chunks. Play a level, put it down, play another level in a couple of days. Somewhat ironically, this game is a pretty good 'party game' - it is easy to pick up and quite entertaining to watch. It also helps that controller support is basically flawless.
Worth picking up, especially on sale like I did.

I've been playing WildStar since launch and, boy howdy, it's been a ride.  This game's gone through a lot of ups and downs and, honestly, I hope it continues to go up.  With WildStar being free-to-play, you'll very likely get some good bang for your potentially nonexistant buck.
So, those sound good and all, right?  But of course, there's bad that comes with the good.
Of course I'm biased.  As a previous WoW refugee looking for something new, I
thought I'd find a game that'd replace it.  But here I am, a consistent raider of the current tier.  To me, WildStar is my home.  The friends I've met here I'm happy to call my friends, and I'm happy to have played this game through all it's been through.  If WildStar was shut down, as some would believe it will be, and I was asked if I regretted my time here, I would say
.  I'm not a kid anymore, so I can't stay up like most did in WoW's heyday, playing for hours on end.  But it comes close to capturing that magic.  I would say that it did successfully capture that magical feeling of something entirely new.
Give it a try.  All you have to lose is a few gigabytes of disk space that can be freed up if you don't like it.  And what you have to gain?  Memories that you'll be able to look back on nostalgiacally.  For a sci-fi MMO, WildStar certainly feels magical to me.

The way its handled now, isnt right. If you sub, and unsub, sometimes the files are just left in your system. So you get piles of old files, unused that the game, still looks at. Finally you have to delete two directorys worth of files, unsub and hope things disappear properly (it takes two, sometimes three tries) then you get to resub to all the mods, that you currently want.
There needs to be more file checking done. When you unsub from a workshop mod, steam should delete, everything immediately. There also needs to be a better way to sub and usub to multiple files. Im at 109 mods atm, yea, its a lot of clicking if you need to make changes.
Thats the only real issue though. The game runs like a champ, doesnt crash so far, and late game fights are crazy tough..and darn fun if you enjoy the space empire aka 4X series.
Update: The developer is changing the game somewhat, and a few out there are rather unhappy. Folks, its their game, they will change it as they see fit. It will still be an enjoyable game, modders will adapt, so will players. At the end of the day folks, its just a game. Chill out man.

This is the sort of game that gets you exited, whethrer you've got the time (and are good at "difficult" games), or maybe 10 minutes (when you first try the game). I haven't gotten the chance to play the remake yet, so don't expect me to make any sort of comparisons.
The Binding of Isaac, is a masterpiece. It knows when to pay homage to other game giants (too many to count), and knows when to not become yet another gimmicky steam game. The controls are superb, and the game can run on even the oldest computers (well, far as I know, I could play it on my XP). What's really nice, is that it comes at a cheap price, but it's worth far more than the price that's given. The game is sort of like a bullet hell, in the fact that you may sometimes have to make very precise movements to avoid taking damage, and that sometimes, the room may be full of enemies. What's really appealing, is the difficulty. As you progress through each floor, obviously the enemies are far more difficult, but past that, the game increases in difficulty as it expands upon each completion, until you've beaten it about 16 times. By then, when you get to the very last floor, let's just say every place will be as hard as a boss stage. Don't fret, you get many cool items from treasure rooms, boss rooms, devil rooms, and the "spiky entrance rooms," and let's not forget the... SECRET ROOMS :D. Also, if you get bored of one character from your many plaaythroughs, just know that you've most likely unlocked a new character (if not many new ones), from your playthroughs. Each character has their own unique traits, so the game will never get boring.... I could keep going, but I'm sure I'm not the only one who has written this sort of review.

First impressions:
Glacier 3: The Meltdown is your typical "destructive" racing game. It's nothing too special, but it did a fantastic job keeping me entertained during my first play session.
Nothing much can be said about what makes Glacier 3 special from other, similar games. Like I said, it is pretty typical. The game features eight vehicles to choose from and a variety of tracks that can be driven on. There are several power-ups spread throughout each of the tracks, each granting you some kind of advantage. I stuck with missiles the entire time. They act like the red shells in Mario Kart, homing in on enemies (most of the time).
The game's physics, however, were very amusing. The vehicles each made very sharp turns, very easily, at high speeds. I also bounced off a rock at one point, like a basketball, landing back on the track. That was quite fun. The AI beat me everytime, aside from one track, where I went all-out with missiles, so the game can be a bit challenging at times, but nothing that a good missile or two can't solve.
There's not much else to say about Glacier 3. If I were to attempt to justify its price, I would pin that on how ridiculous the racing is (physics, weapons, etc.). It is fun, but has some technical issues that I wish had been addressed, such as the resolution, which is locked at some low resolution.

There is no Manual, no option to see Controls (Key Bindings) in the game's menu. Ugly graphics, absurd physics. I like such kind of games very much. For example, I like very much the game "Gas Guzzlers Extreme", though the "GGE" has its own defects, but I really enjoy "Gas Guzzlers Extreme".
It's a pity that there are too little such games. And I wish more games of such type but of HIGH QUALITY. "Glacier 3: The Meltdown" is the worst game of such sort.

I want to recommend the game for the $13 price tag - it's not a bad price for what you're getting, but it's not the amount of content that is the problem here.
The reason behind not recommending this game? Like almost all games, it gets repetitive; but unlike great games that share this trait, Party Hard's repetition becomes stale and downright boring. It was a chore to get through the last 1/3 of the game, and I couldn't even will myself to play the DLC.
But first, there are a couple of things that I did like about it. The biggest positive to me was the game's soundtrack. It follows with the retro graphics by having retro wave 80s synth. The tunes are pretty catchy and didn't distract from the gameplay. Also, I appreciate the retro graphics, especially the cutscene quality that you can sample in the preview pictures above.
The gameplay concept itself is fine, but I think it's the way its handled that makes playing through this a chore. Firstly, I found few traps to be worth more than a few kills at a time, which meant I had to stalk people until they end up alone or with people not looking their direction. When you have 30+ guys on screen you have to do this with, it gets a little nauseating level after level. I became very dependent on smoke grenades, which blind everyone in the vicinity and allow you to knife people as quickly as you can before the smoke disappears. Not only was this helpful to cut down your target amount, but if you left anyone nearby alive, they would all begin acusing each other once the smoke clears, and more people would be removed from the level by the police. However, this game has a number of RNG elements to it, and the items you're given are included in this. An example of a useless item - for me - was the bomb. While it killed a lot of people, it would attract the SWAT team who would come in and begin knocking out everyone in the area. If they see you, they knock you out and the game is over. Now, why I consider this useless is virtually every time I used it, the SWAT would remain on the map, knocking people out, forever. It was then impossible to kill anyone else, as these guys run faster than you and can catch up to you real quick. I think this was a glitch pertaining to the amount of people alive on the map, but it happened nearly every time I tried using the bomb. Only once did they run in, knock everyone out and then leave (I assume after arresting someone who was blamed for the bomb).
This leads into my other issue with the game that made this very tedious: glitches. There were numerous glitches that ended a level prematurely for me. Off the top of my head, I can think of two I'll share: one, I had 3 people left in a house, and a cop was summoned to zip up a dead body. After he zipped it up, he began to make his way back to his police car. He suddenly turned and ran right to me, knocking me out and ending the map. There were NO dead bodies around me. I had NEVER had anyone call the police on me or inform them that I was a murderer. This cop just seemed to know that, out of 4 suspects left, I was the guilty party. It made no sense to the in-game logic of the police - who are not all-knowing. Secondly; I have had people call me out as being a murderer when there is no reason for them to. I will have no bodies linked to me, none laying at my feet, no weird behavior noticed - they have just suddenly run from me saying "murderer!" and informed the police on the site. To me, again, this seems to go against the NPC logic and only further delayed my progression through the game. It kind of reminds me of the old Atari Pinball game, which, on a whim, will begin sinking your pinball straight down the middle no matter what you do. NPCs calling me out as a killer have also occured after I've changed costume, which is essentially a "quick fix" that drops any recognition of you. Even if there is a stipulation that no one can see you change, this was still not an issue when it happened to me - no one saw the change: I was in an upper corner behind a house with no doors, windows or passages.
If it goes down in price or is nicely discounted, it's probably worth the pickup. You'll get a fair amount of hours of gameplay for it, comparative to some AAA action game titles (thanks in part to the active Steamworks community); but the tedious repetition kills it for me. If you think you're okay with it, just do me a favor: don't blow your money on the DLC until you've completed the core game.

I'm going to write an honest review for this game since A LOT of people seem to be very biased.
This is not a perfect game. No 2K basketball game will ever be a perfect game. Does that mean this game is bad? No. Should you hold off on the game for now? Probably.
Let's start with the positives:
- A lot of people seem to gloss over the fact that 2K rehauled a lot of mechanics for this game. Shot meters feel more legitimate, this game is MUCH much more realistic (fouls, shot tendencies, etc...) This game is better and more fluid to control, and the gameplay reflects each players' ratings (defense, shots, etc...) much more accurately.
- Online play seems to be better and more fluid. I've yet to encounter any latency issues online with quick play and the such.
- MyCareer is MUCH better than last years. There is no cheesy story and the cutscenes feel much more integrated into the game. Orange Juice and dynamic duos are a great idea in general. The UI for MyCareer (and the game in general) is so much cleaner and more functional.
- The game is visually beautiful, not much else to say on the matter.
Now, the cons:
- Help defense is broken. It's quite ridiculous that 2K hasn't fixes this lingering issue in such a long time but it's still there. This is a BIG issue in MyCareer and not quite as bad in other modes since you can manually control players.
- Stat allocation is broken. This is a huge issue in MyCareer and has deterred me from playing the mode any more until 2K fixes this issue. Introducing the idea of stats that can only be raised in practice is actually quite a neat idea. However, these boosts are not permanent, even though 2K has stated they are. This is detrimental and demoralizing and discourages players from playing the game more. Limit caps are ridiculously strict as well. 2K NEEDS to fix these issues ASAP.
- Numerous glitches.
- 2K introduced broken mechanics along with the good mechanics. Ankle breakers are now pathetically easy to pull off (using Stephen Curry behind the back moves is a surefire way to have your defender fall). Moving screens are now a thing.
I would hold off on buying this game until 2K patches it. There are just too many issues with the game that prevent it from being a playable game. I like this game. I really do. That's why I'm hoping 2K listens to the community and starts working on the issues at hand immediately.

This is game I should like, instead it has become an excersize in frustration.
Want an example ?
Google Stellaris fleet sizes, or fleet caps. See the answers experts give to questions about fleet sizes. Usually it goes along the lines of I have 24k in my fleet, they never actually answer the posters question and those that try too leave out vital information. So most players, dont actually know how this game works, they just manage to some how stumble on a formula that works.
You see the answer to that question pretty much reveals the games flaws.
Fleet caps are a combination of space station upgrades, large populations and research. Where as research goes faster when you only have a small population. So the larger your population gets, the slower you research is and the larger your fleet becomes. From then on you fall behind and end up losing to an empire with only 3 planets to its name.
So you have to gather research resources to boost your research as your empire expands, this means expanding slowly, letting your population on planets grow before settling new ones and using your influence to build frontier out posts in resource rich areas.
These require energy and energy is the one thing that is in short supply.
So you have to balance expansion, with research with the need to build mines and research out posts in order to keep your empire growing and competative.
That is why nobody ever answers that question properly.
Sounds like I just did right, well kind of.
You see, whilst your happy with your 2000 strength fleet, that 3 planet AI turns up with a 16,000 strength fleet that it really should not have because you now know how that fleet cap is worked out now and you can see from the diplomacy screen that his tech level is not any higher than yours, so his fleet should at best be comparable to yours.
So you know beyond any doubt that the AI cheats like crazy and whilst your limited by these rules, it is not.
Next we come to diplomacy, an AI that loves you to bits makes you its rival, which gives you an instant -100 rep with that AI. All the bonuses recieved before that gave it a +93 rep, meaning it loved you to bit, yet sees you as its enemy. It attacks you, you beat it. You conquer all its planets, destroy all its mines and out posts and end up drawn in a war because its ally beat your ally. Even though you pretty much wiped him out.
After the war, a truce is declared and your ally invites this AI in to your Federation, before the flames of war have even gone out, this AI is now your best friend and the truce setting is still clearly visible on the AI that is now your ally. Meaning that uneasy post war peace is still uneasy as it joins your federation and becomes your bestie.
These 2 examples reveal what is wrong with this game, it is less of game you play and more of a system you learn and then exploit. It makes very little sense because the game mechanics are not there to make game play, they are to stop one AI from steam rolling the entire galaxy.
You see, if they just let an AI grow and linked research to empire size as most games do, then the biggest AI would always win. So instead they make the smallest AI research things faster, so they catch up, grow in size, suddenly their research slows down and they become an out dated large empire too.
Mean while the tiny Mr Nobody empire with only 3 planets has quietly researched everything and is now a super power that nobody can beat.
That is whats wrong with this game, the mechanics make no sense so you end up playing the system, not the game.
In infact, I am absolutely certain the lead designer spends his nights licking magic mushrooms in some damp English field someplace.
If you like spending 70 hours saying WTF, I strongly recommend this game, but if you dont, go and by Galactic Civ 3 instead. At least that makes sense.
And remember the reason people tend not to answer questions properly about this game is because they dont actually know how it works either.  Just ask them for a full answer and you see what I mean.
Just to ram that point home, look at the Global Achievements for this game, only 19% of those who buy it manage to settle a planet. In game thats pretty much about settling planets, that means 81% of those who buy it dont even get started in this game.

'Adventure Capitalist' takes a nice little spin on the clicker/idle style of gameplay and somehow creates a recipe that leaves this game addictive as hell!
The aim of the game is simple...make money. Things start off pretty quick in the early stages of the game, with money coming in so fast you begin to shadow Pablo Escobar however it soon slows down to a point where it can take you a number of hours/days to progress at a slow rate. It reminds me a lot of feeding a fish? you know? just pop in every now and then to make sure it's alright , give it a little bit of food and then come back tomorrow.
So why is it so damn addictive ? Its the visual nods that you get. Whether it's the huge pile of cash in the top left just climbing and climbing, or the cool 50's artwork, or the downright hilarious manager references to modern day characters . It keeps you coming back!
'Adventure Capitalist' is a simple, beautiful and charismatic game that keeps in house in order for you and is constantly giving you something to aim for, and the theme tune is catchy as herpes ....

This game. I can't praise it enough. My first two hours in this game was basically spamming "OMIGOSH" to all my friends because I had never seen something as amazing as this.
Beautiful gunplay, really advanced customization menu for guns (though you should just listen to your benevolent overlord who recommends everything for you before the mission), there's so much you can do in combat, from super-stealth to Sync shots, to infiltration (slow-mo retro style shooting included), prioritization of targets during normal combat, marking out targets with airborne devices such as drones, etc.
You also have X-Ray vision and sensor grenades (which are pointless once you have X-Ray vision). Your team is equipped with extremely futuristic weapons, gear and outfits (you actually wear a Chameleon camo that changes your color according to the surrounding, making you nearly undetectable). The cover system while firing is extremely impressive.
The main missions are co-ordinated and always point you in the right direction, so you don't have to worry about wandering off into the deep forests of nothingness.
Conclusively, amazing game, totally worth it, definitely something I'd play repeatedly, however, there is a small issue. This game does not run from Steam independently. Lauching it actually lauches uPlay (the Ubisoft content delivery client) which requires you to register/sign in and then use the CD-Key provided by Steam to activate the game. However, this is only initial and you can launch the game normally after that.

In all seriousness, Automation is a great 'build-a-car' "sandbox" as it is right now. If you are at all interested in car design you should give this game a look. While you will not get the same designability if you were to design the car in CAD or some other program, for a game (and it is a GAME, not a toolset) the options are numerous and your creativity is the real limitation. Seriously watch the vids (though they are of earlier builds and dont show everything available) and look the discourse forums for this game and see what people have built.
You cannot drive the cars you build, that is not a planned feature and as far as I know right now not even a thought of devs. Its not this game's purpose, at all. If you want to drive cars I'd recommend Asseto Corsa. If you want to design and build cars then look no further. This game is one of kind and in a class of its own. There is only one game that I know of that even tries to do something similar and this game, IMHO, out classes that game at every level.
The currently implemented Lite campaign is fine, but if you play a game to beat it then this might not be for you, right now. The game will have a full campaign with too many factors to go into, but there is currently no real end-game. If you can't sustain interest in something out of pure curiosity and creativity then this might not be the game you want.
The game really shines is its sandbox mode. The base game has a good selection of starter parts and bodies that can allow you to get a good feel of piecing together you're own car. You can deform and the adjust various part of the carbodys in order to attain a shape that appeals to you the most. You then apply everything from headlights, taillights, and door handles with options hood-variations, vent and grille variations as well as exhaust types. Don't see what you like, there is a great catalog of modded pieces that add a huge amount of extra variety. New car bods, headlights, taillights, exhausts, hoods, handles, grilles and much more. The devs will sometimes add these parts to the games, but don't worry they havent allowed modders to take over piece development and are actively making more pieces of their own.
The engine builder is a little confusing for people who know very little about cars, but its easy to catch on to whats happening. I3, I4, I6, V6, V8, V12 and more engines coming later. Pushrods, DAOHC, OHC, DOHC, MOHV with 3,4 and 5 valve options as well as VVT and VVL all available. Don't know what any of that is thats fine the game has helpful tooltips that explains most things which are all over the place in the game, just hover over the header and it'll explain whats going on. The tutorial section is also helpful here. Seriously the engine designer is vast and impressive.
Then there are customization options for tranmission types, tire and rim sizes, brake types, aero adjustment, susupension adjustment. Soon enough you'll also be able to customize factory/production options such as how many are produced and how good that production is and more. B/c remember it is a tycoon game and once youre done designing you can see how your car would sell in the 3 fictional game regions being compared against other cars built by the devs and some community members.
I could go on for a while about the great things this game does now, but I'd be here all day. The devs are always talking to the community about what is going on and what is coming. They have big updates every couple of months that often add several new large features. They are a very devoted small team who deserve a lot of praise. Seriously i've more than got my money's worth from the Alpha/Beta alone. If you've even the slightest interest please watch the vids on here and youtube then look up the forums because this game is honestly a great purchase. It has a great dev team, a great community and hours upon hours of creation possibilities as it is right now. The jump to UE4 can only make this game better.

I have a small laptop to play games on. It's about the size of an average spiral ring notebook, was bought two years ago, has a couple of dinks and chips in the shell from some unfortunate drops. Thus, when I look into MMO RPG games, I don't expect much. My computer can't handle it. (Neither can my wallet.) I got bored, though, and went into RPG>Free To Play, found this, spent an hour and a half downloading it (because of my horrible wifi), opened it up and was pleasently surprised.
For once, 'free to play' actually means 'free.' So far I haven't found any section of the game that forces you to spend money -- I mean, for godsakes, all the DLC for WildStar is free! It doesn't crash when my wifi cuts out, the graphics are easily customizable and the gameplay is smooth and entertaining. The many races make me curious to see what kinds of fighting styles are available, and customization for your character, though somewhat limited, is fun and charming.
My only critique in that realm is that when picking races, the female counterparts of the male designs are significantly less original and charming, and tend to all have the quintissential RPG genderbend look. What I mean is that they make the female designs significantly more human and less alien, and give them a standard-issue hourglass form, with the exception of a single race, which is a literal rabbit. I'm not even joking. You can play as a rabbit.
That being said, I found while customizing the race and gender I picked that the many options make each character look surprisingly individual. I do wish there were more hairstyle options, but I found that the options for customizing body type more than made up for this defecit. Like, seriously! I can make my character a little chubby! It was a welcome surprise.
On the topic of happy surprises: I'm a mage geek. Magic and spells are so appealing to me and I find that that form of combat tends to be my favorite - that along with archers. The problem with being a mage geek and being a woman in the RPG genre is that, when you look at costume designs for women in RPGs, you tend to find "bikini armor." I should hope I need not explain the concept. So when I was looking at the different classes I was really hesitant to look into the mage-like options because I was worried I'd end up with that caliber of design. However, I switched to Esper (the most  mage-like class) after a little bit of debate and was surprised to find that the costume design for that class was nothing like I expected. It wasn't overly sexualized and the preview for the higher level armor was actually much more practical than most convential RPG costume designs. And the armor drops I found while playing were the same way. Huzzah for sensible armor design!
I have not played much of the game yet but currently I'm hooked. The gameplay is fun, the races (if at times hindered by gender-based design) were interesting, and the armor wasn't just there for eye candy. I look forward to playing more and seeing what WildStar has to offer. 9/10 to me.
TL;DR:
+ Fun combat
+ Charming graphics + character customization
+ Sensible armor designs
+ Graphics customizablity easy
+ Doesn't crash when wifi cuts out
- Female race designs less original than male counterparts

Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel is the third chapter of the Borderlands franchise and is settled between the event of the first and the second game; the game tells the story of the man who once was nothing but a programmer on the Helios, Hyperion's space base on Pandora, and his quest to save not only the moon Elpis, but the planet itself, from the madness of the Colonel Zarpedon, the chief commander of the Dhal Lost Legion. Through the game, we will see how Jack has become the Handsome, the sarcastic and over-the-top CEO of the Hyperion, and how he changed - the odissey of a man that once wanted to be an hero, and following the light of his ambition, got blinded by it.
The gameplay of TPS is, basically, the same of Borderlands 2; there are a few differnce, the major two being the new element (Ice, instead of the Slag) and the Oxygen, used to dash midair and to slam on the ground, something I liked a lot and I miss when I play Borderlands 2.
While the story itself is pretty short, and the quests are not even close to the enormous amount of the previous game, it retails the same, caustic and exaggerated style and humour. The story, while short, is actually very good and it explores in a very interesting and catchy manner the past of our beloved Hyperion president; and it does an incredible job on charaterizing the Vault Hunter, who are, excluding the Doppleganger and Hammerlock's sister Aurelia, all NPCs or bosses coming from both Borderlands and its sequel - they speak, they comment the situation, they agree or disagree, they hold back their comments, they feel like real characters, which was, for me, way better than the almost mute Vault Hunters from the second chapter. Also, you have the possibility to see Claptrap from the inside, exploring its thoughts, fears, insecurities and the so terrible and desperate research for affection and love: at the end of the DLC, which you should play after the main story, I felt very sorry for Calptrap, and I'm not even joking when I say that the Claptastic Voyage made me revaluate it.
TPS is often despised, because it is not Borderlands 2; honestly, I found it incredibly entertaining, especially characters-wise, and I got sucked in the plot and in the overall story even more than in the Borderlands 2, because I had a cast of Hunters which acutally reacted to the situations, and because I wanted to know more about my favourite character from the 2, Handsome Jack.
If you want more Borderlands, but without expecting big changes or a titanic amount of content like in Borderlands 2, if you want to dig in past of your enemy, if you want to see someone's ideals and personality fall apart, if you want to feel bad for the guy you kicked in the stomach, then play The Pre-Sequel and you won't be disappointed.

Kingdoms Rise is without a doubt a game with a lot of potential but one that still needs a bit of work.
