A couple weeks ago I had a couple £ in my Steam wallet and was not sure what to buy. A friend pointed me to a small puzzle game called
. I was sceptical, but after buying & downloading it, I am glad I took the plunge. Not dissimilar to the old Windows game Minesweeper, Hexcells is a little Indie game created by a man by the name of Matthew Brown. There are two other Hexcells games, Hexcells Plus and Hexcells Infinite.
It is not easy to explain Hexcells' concept in a review; you mainly learn as you go on. Through the later levels, you are taught extra rules and slowly the puzzles increase in difficulty. If you enjoy logical puzzles, you'll have a blast with Hexcells. No aspect of this game requires luck or guessing, every puzzle can be solved using your mind. Too easy for you? Keep going, the later puzzles are not only giant but also pretty darn hard. Of course, multiple people have created guides showing what to do in each if you want to cheat your way through, but that takes the fun out of it! In all, Hexcells is a calming puzzle experience that is perfect when you just want to chill out.
PROs -
CONs -
There are tons of Indie puzzle games on Steam. Some succeed. Some fail. Some are absolutely horrible. Some are actually great. And Hexcells absolutely nails it. I love nearly everything about Hexcells. Thank you, Matthew Brown for making such a chill puzzle game that really hits the spot when I'm bored.

I was looking for a few good twin-stick shooters with
, and among the many I've tried, this is one of my favorites. I've spent over 16 hours on it so far, and I played all the way to the end, fully upgrading my character, called a "Walker."
The
and animations are wonderful! The screen is very clear, and the characters have unique attributes and expressions which make them identifiable. If you pay attention, you'll even notice quite a bit of humor, particularly in how the workers on the conveyer belts move, the billboards, and the final boss battle.
The
is also good, and it's extremely helpful while playing, because certain sound effects alert you to what's coming. I played most of the game with the sound off, just so I didn't disturb my husband watching T.V., but if you leave the sound on, you'll have even quicker reaction times with the advance warning that the sound effects can provide.
Your character is the uncle, and you're in a mech called a walker. This walker can be upgraded multiple times, and gold bars are the currency by which this is accomplished. Bars are obtained through normal gameplay as you complete levels. You also gain experience points through gameplay, and these are used for cosmetic unlockables: skins, effects, and pets. These don't impact gameplay in any way and are purely cosmetic but can certainly gain you some bragging rights.
There are 5 full chapters, each with area levels that progressively introduce more enemies and increased projectile speed. The game sports fully functional, and very responsive, controller support, so this is definitely a game that can be fully enjoyed with a controller. I used an XBox 360 and didn't have any issues in that regard.
Gatling Gears can be played on easy, normal, and hard
, and it also includes campaign and survival
. Additionally, you can resume the game right where you left off if you die or exit the game. You have 3 lives, but never fear, this is
a permadeath situation, because once you've completed a level within a chapter, you can always pick right back up where you left off, and any upgrades or unlockables stay with your walker. You'll never go any further back than repeating the specific area where you died.
Hardcore gamers, never fear, because you can still strut your stuff and create an even harder challenge by utilizing the hard difficulty setting or simply not using grenades and rockets. If that's not enough for you, then you can actually use gold bars to
upgrades, creating a whole new difficulty level for those who are gluttons for punishment. If you're into
, the niece can also be played for some tagteam
.

While I like the upgrade system for your weapons, I don't understand why the upgrades are purchased with the gold bars placed through each level instead of the parts or "gears" that you're already collecting from everything you destroy - it seems that would create more incentive to try and destroy everything (at least, as much as possible) in each level.  Regardless, I still think it's an incredibly fun game, though challenging enough to not be completely mindless.  I definitely recommend this to fans of twin-stick shooter action games.
Note: I've only played with keyboard/mouse so I can't speak to controller functionality.
UPDATE: The one big thing that annoys me about this game is how you can't go backwards.  As you advance through the (completely linear) pathway, the camera moves to follow you so, if you miss a gold bar and walk too far ahead, you're out of luck until you play through the level again.  However, I read somewhere that there are more gold bars in the game than it takes to fully upgrade your mech so it's not that big of a deal but it still delays your ability to upgrade if you miss some gold.
Something else that may be of interest to some prospective players is that there seems to be little if any replay value to the game.  The entire game is very straightforward and totally linear so the only reasons I can see to play through again would be 1) to collect any gold you may have missed or 2) to try a higher difficulty setting.  Of course, this depends on what type of player you are - it's feasible that you could love the rampaging shooter action so much that completing the game once just isn't enough.  If you think a single play-through is kind of a ripoff, you'll probably want to wait for a sale.

You earn Virtual Currency (VC) for everything you do in the game.
2k also sells VC for real money.
VC is the currency you use to purchase upgrades of all kinds, such as stats in MyCareer for your player.  You also use it to purchase MyTeam card packs, cosmetic items, and anything else you can acquire.
2k blatantly gives you very small amounts of VC while playing the game in order to make you buy VC with real money.  This is in a game you spend $60 for.
They do this in a few ways:
1) Your "MyCareer" player starts off with a 55 rating, which makes you the worst rated player in the game.  Upgrades cost VC and you do not start with VC to put into your player.  So at the most, if you don't buy VC and don't have it from some source, you'll have about a 57 or 58 rated player overall.  Still the worst player in the league.
2) Card packs are expensive (!!!) and the cards can only be used for X number of times before expiring.  You have to get a resource to refill your cards called contracts.  It's ridiculous.
I don't really pay attention to the other modes but those are the two main ones and both use VC.  The simple act of playing online basketball is hard because they split you into leagues based on skill.  That's fine by itself but makes the matchmaking so damn long if you're just starting out and the game has been out for at least a month.
Overall I hate the direction of this game.  NBA 2kTV is a waste of all time, energy and life, in spite of how attractive the host is.  The MyCareer story is awful and always will be.  The MyCareer should have an emergent narrative; if anyone at 2k is reading, that means the game reacts to what you do on the court as opposed to following a dumb script.
The other problems are numerous and I could write a fifty page manifesto on everything I hate about this game and franchise which I've bought games for since NBA 2k5, and have played since NBA 2k1 on Dreamcast.

I've finally played enough of this game to feel comfortable writing a review. To start off, I'm a huge Paradox fan. EU4 is in my top 2 games of all time, and I love Crusader Kings, Vicky II, Cities, and Hearts of Iron. I think EU4 is about as perfect as you can get in terms of Grand Strategy - for reference, I think Civ IV is about as close you can get to perfect in 4X territory. Stellaris comes close to being great in both categories, with a lot of interesting mechanics and events, but manages to fall short in both, making it a kind of jack-of-all-trades game, master of none.
To reiterate, in its current state (1.4.1 I believe), Stellaris is almost a great game. It has a lot of potential, which is not something most want to hear when they buy a finished game, but Paradox has shown that they are looking to support games for years down the line. This is hopeful, because I think it will be like EU4 - shaky at first, but amazing later. That being said, usually this also comes with a load of DLC, but as long as they don't pull a Common Sense or Art of War and basically require you to spend money to get the full value out of the free features, I think it's a decent business model. At least they don't have Season Passes.
Now for the Pros of Stellaris -
• The pre-game and early game are a lot of fun. They've added a ton of features for universe customization, a fair amount of features for species creation, and there are a lot of mixes of governments and ethics you can go with. As for when you get into the game, it feels like Civ when you start out - you're doing basically the same thing each time, but it still manages to feel new and refreshing as you continue on.
• The events are fantastic. I love reading them, and it feels like they've packed a lot in here. Even when I see repeat events, I still read the text, it feels like a compelling story. And best of all, I feel like they do a decent job of having events drive gameplay decisions, kind of like in CK2.
• I like a lot of the gameplay mechanics, mainly the ones that deal with the POPs. I find the POP management, building, migration, slavery, robots, occupation, ethics, edicts, and government mechanics all really fun to play around with.
• The late game crises are fantastic, a great touch to the game. They really make great stories, which is one of the best things about 4X games. Being able to recount a story later about how you fought off extradimensional invaders is one of the most appealing things about getting to the late game.
• Like most Grand Strategy games, it's fun to zone out to for a couple hours after work, or play on the weekend. One of my biggest problems with 4X games is that they sometimes feel too contained - I feel like I need to finish a game of them at once. The biggest appeal of Grand Strategy, to me, is that I can invest as much or as little time into and still feel like I got the same gameplay experience.
Now the Cons -
• Biggest con by far is that there are far too many mechanics in this game, none of which are particularily fleshed out. This works for Grand Strategy games, where you can automate a lot of stuff and just focus on a few more pressing gameplay concerns (like trade in EU4, or everything in Vic II). Stellaris has a lot of great IDEAS for mechanics, where I feel like they just need some patches to get right. But here's just a laundry list of mechanics that aren't at all fleshed out - factions, terraforming, government, enlightenment, vassalage, protectorates, fallen empires, federations, alliances, anything to do with technology, anything to do with sectors, anything to do with ships, anything to do with armies, and trait modification all need a lot of work.
• The other problem, past having WAYYYY too many game mechanics, is that none of them affect the game that much. If you want to, you can ignore things like ethics, factions, and pop development completely, which are (supposedly) things Paradox put a lot of time into in this game.
• Something that might not bother other people, but actually destroys the game for me, is the lack of any interesting in-game analysis ability. I'm talking about having minimal maps, no ledger, no good search ability, and no empire history. Add this stuff, Paradox! It makes your games so much more interesting when I can look at 20 different map modes and learn about the world.
• The UI sucks in this game. Absolutely atrocious. There are too many menus, they contain too little information on each menu, there isn't an easy way to initiate diplomacy, you have to click too many times to do things, it is not obvious where specific things are in the UI (even to someone who's played 60 or so hours), there isn't enough info displayed in the banners at the top of the screen, and there is FAR too much information displayed in the sidebar. All of these are relatively easy fixes for Paradox, especially since they have good UI in their other games - this is a real problem that it sucks in its current state.
• This isn't a new complaint for many 4X games, but the diplomacy needs work. There isn't much you can do with it and you can't automate it if you want the most out of it, which is the worst combination.
As I said before, Stellaris is almost great, but it falls short sooo hard that I can't recommend it in its current state. There are just too many things that aren't fleshed out or just aren't finished. Wait for a few more patches, maybe some DLC, and then a year or two down the line it will probably be great. But until then, I would say hold off.
Sorry Paradox. I still love you! Keep doing what you're doing.

Art: 9.5/10
The style of this art is amazing. The UI is minimalistic. The character models are well-detailed :). Animations are beautiful. There are several different environments in the game, which broadens the art styles.
Graphics could definitely be improved if it wasn't just a port from console.
Music: 11/10
Gameplay: 9/10
For the most part, gameplay was enjoyable. At this point, I am just nit-picking things that I thought could have been added or improved on.
Play as 2B and you primarily do hack-n-slash. Play as 9S and you get to slash a bit and hack stuff. For me, the hacking elements were rather boring. The hacking games are, for the most part, done in a square box which limits what can be done in the game. I would have liked to have more difficult dungeon-crawler type hacking games.
Aside from the quests in the game (which can only be completed once), there not much else to do as far as minigames go. As of right now, I am waiting for the DLC where you get to fight the CEO. I hope they add more DLC for minigames.
As for controls, I started out playing with keyboard and mouse, but the camera and some actions aren't really designed for raw input from a mouse and keyboard. The camera movement was too slow for my liking and the evade mechanic of having to tap a direction key (WASD) twice was annoying and made the action more difficult than it needed to be. I decided to borrow my friend's PS4 controller and most of my problems were solved (Still wish I could use a mouse for faster camera movement).
The game has a bunch of things to collect. I've got everything at 100%. Lots of fun farming and exploring.
Story: 10/10
Story is great. The main theme of the plot is pretty much nihilism in a nutshell. Values don't matter, yet here are some values you have to follow anyway. Pretty much all the characters deal with existentialism and nihilism. There are 26 different endings ranging from A-Z. A-E are the main story endings. F-Z are "joke" endings (leaving battlefield, kill wrong person, etc.). Ending Y is particularly interesting and is considered to be end-game content.
Overall:
62 hours in about 5 days. Buy the game. No regrets. 2Booty. ♥♥♥♥ 9S, but I understand. Pascal selling machine body parts. lol.

So I played and got all the achievements for the Hexcells series.
The order of which game should be played is Hexcells, Hexcells Plus and finally Hexcells Infinite.
FIRST OF ALL! This game and its ENTIRE series can be solved LOGICALLY! No guessing was NEVER required.
As people stated in other reviews, this game is a combination of minesweeper and picross (nonogram) which sounds about right.
The first of this series is quite simple and fun.
Numbers tell you a number of blue cell around it or on the line.
Left click to select a blue cell or right click to get a blank cell (for some reason, my brain took a while to understand what I wanted...)
Great game, recommended.
HOWEVER, if you expect the following games to follow the same format, it does not.
The new game is more challenging and longer.
If you expect the same pace, it is not but heck it is more fun!

1. Enjoyable puzzling - even though the core concept is very simple, enough mechanics are introduced to vary things up.
2. Pure logic puzzles - you can guess, but you never have to. There is always a way to figure out the puzzle 100% without mistakes. This is also true of the following games (Hexcells Plus and Hexcells Infinity, though they increase the difficulty significantly).
3. Very clean, functional and nice interface.
Overall I had a lot of fun with this game and its two sequels. While the core concept is similar to minesweeper, the added mechanics and the fact that you never have to guess to solve the puzzles makes it a far superior game to its inspiration. Recommended for anyone who likes pure logic games.

Hexcells is a logic puzzle that's similar to other number games like Minesweeper and Picross, as you use processes of elimination and deduction to fill in patterns of tiles. The distinction here is that since the tiles are hexagons, they're not restricted by square grids, and most puzzles look like abstract shapes or very loosely defined objects.  hexes have numbers on them from 0 to 6 indicating how many of the gold tiles around them can be clicked to turn blue, which counts toward stage completion.

An amazing minesweeper like game that brings so much more to the table. ONe of the best, if not the best puzzle game I've played.

Take Minesweeper, swap to a hex grid, add several other mechanics, you get the gameplay for Hexcells.
The audio is very relaxing, which is exactly what you'd want for this type of game. I particularly like the way you get melodies by clicking through several hexes in a row, I ended up clicking in rhythm many times. It fails occasionally, but not often enough to really break it.
The level list is a bit short tough (I idled a bit during the course of my 3.4 hours), and it ends just as the difficulty is starting to ramp up, so you'll have to get the sequels for a real challenge.

The game provides a couple (2-3?) hours of entertainment. While I think it was worth the meager sum I paid for it, it sadly lacks replay value. The puzzles are not difficult or exhausting enough to leave you unclear as to how they were solved once you've completed them; you simply look at the numbers, do some counting, perhaps think 2 or 3 steps ahead and voila: puzzle solved. No additional clarity is gained from doing it over, and you will most likely be able to do the puzzles perfectly on your first attempt. The fact that all information is either given or easily excavated from what is given is both the strength and weakness of this game. It means you never have to guess, and that you don't have to bring prior knowledge apart from basic counting know-how. That's the way I like my puzzles. Sadly, it also means that if you get what's going on, the game becomes an exercise in doing something pretty rote. I found it relaxing.

I was looking for a new MMO now that FF XIV is waiting for a new patch, and I decided to try Wildstar since it is free and finally came to Steam.
I actually didn't really expect much but I was pleasantly surprised. The game is very good so far and it has one of the best battle systems in an mmo, something that I was sure FF XIV was a king at.
The graphics remind a bit of other MMOs like WoW but they are polished and are pretty good for cartoony graphics. The expressions especially are very funny and nice.
The story is less serious and generally the game is heavy with humour, so if you are looking for an epic serious story maybe ethis it's not for you.
The final thing I want to mention is the housing system which is really good! I have spent hours (providing I have the funds xD) buying stuff and decorating my house.
The game is completely free to play, with an in game store although everything is more or less for  cosmetic purposes, although some boosts (for faster lvling) are available. Everything can be purchased with either real time money or in game currency that you accumulate by completing missions or killing enemies, similar to Marvel Heroes,  if you have played that.
Tl;dr if you need a new MMO that is free to play and really fun, with no annoying pay walls everywhere,   give Wildstar a try!

The game is exactly what it looks like, except for the end area. You descend 6 levels, have to pick up an orb, and re-climb them all to get out. When you pick up that orb, you have to deal with infinitely re-spawning enemies throughout the 6 levels, and all the care and patience you took in dealing with them before flies out the window. You leveled only health and made sure I had the best weapons, armor, and healing items you could have before taking the orb. It does not matter. You are swarmed with flying skulls that you cannot outrun and must fight. As you do so, Skeleton mages bombard you with magic from beyond the game's very tiny draw distance, and you die. In a game about resource managemeant and dungeon delving, rushing things leads to death, and the game forces you to do so.
I do not recommend this game, and doubt it will be fixed.
Concept reminds of a bit of Oubliette on PLATO, which my dad talked about playing when he was in college.

Despite appearances, much of Delver's charm actually manages to stem from the voxel-based imagery. The combat isn't anything to write home about, but certainly keeps things entertaining as  you journey through randomly generated dungeon mazes. As a fan of rogue-likes, it's nice to see a first person one with a focus on melee combat, rather than the usual go-to standards of side-scrolling platformer or Quake-style shoot-em-up. Believe it or not, the music is pretty great, too.
As long as the devs have the foresight to include a jump button and mouse-wheel scrolling in the finished product, this could be a lot of fun.

Being entirely randomly generated, from the size of each floor to the quality of each weapon, there is exellent replay value.   Each floor has a mix of challenging enemies and total pushovers, keeping the experience fun throughout the playthrough as the difficulty slowly raises. For its price and file size, the game is a fantastic little timewaster that is very easy to pick up but very hard to put down. If you're concerned about the Early Access status, I bought this game when it first popped up on Steam and felt it was a complete experience then. And yet somehow every update seems to make it better and better. No regrets.

This is one HECK of a game!
My hand/eye coordination is pretty lousy and I had reservations about trying a controller-based action game like this, but I am a basketball junkie and the vids I'd watched online looked absolutely fantastic.
In addition to my lousy hand/eye coordination, I was a horrible basketball player when I was a kid and never played on a team or tried to coach later on....  Those factors and the fact I hadn't tried any sort of sophistacated graphics-based basketball game in any series for a long time meant I was *waaaaaaayyyyyyyy* behind the 8-ball on learning this game and getting any good at it.
Long story short, I still suck, but not so badly that I didn't outgrow the "rookie" level in just a couple games.  Took awhile to get "too good" at the next level (its name escapes me), but I am now playing at "Pro".  There are three higher levels that I'll never get good enough to play.   Ever.
Because of those six play levels, I can't imagine anyone getting so good at the game that they can regularly beat the computer at the Hall-Of-Fame level.  Of course, just cuz I can't imagine it doesn't mean it's impossible...  But it'd be reallllly hard to do.
Anyway...  This game is flat-out *AWESOME*!  I've finally figured out how to successfully do stuff like dunk and get a good running game going with my now-I-can-dunk Warriors.  Nipped the Spurs in a tough battle just now...
The flow of the game is terrific, graphics sharp and smooth, at least with my snappy new gaming-level PC.  Yes, this game needs quite a bit of computing power to run well with graphics settings on High.  I would think most reasonably up-to-date "everyday"-rated PC's would do okay on this game with video settings knocked down a bit, but to really enjoy this game at its best you'd probably need something pretty close to my rig (Intel i3 chip running at 3.9 Ghz, 16 gig RAM, Nvidea 970 GTX video card with 4gig rom).
Thus far, I haen't done things like MyPlayer or MyLeague, and so far I have almost no interest in even trying them.  I've just played random games with me always controlling the Warriors.   LOTS of games!  Haven't tried any games against online opponents either, and don't really wanna try it.  So, on those sorts of features, I can't say anything.
To those who are complaining about things like missing legs or arms on players or other strange graphics glitches...  UPDATE YOUR VIDEO CARD'S DRIVERS!!
The few things I've gotten a little tired of would include things like the pregame and halftime shows (fun at first, but quite repetitive after not very long at all) and the really repetitive timeout huddles...  Oh, and the rather creepy-looking player and coach interviews where the lipsynch is rather off...  Fortunately, you can skip through these for the most part.
Overall, this game just plain kicks butt!

Kingdoms Collide couldn't have asked for a better sequel. Combat is somewhat like Chivalry, only everyone's on equal ground and there are 8 swing/parry directions, as long as a clever parry locking system to raise the skill cap extremely high. There's also a ton of character and loadout customization, like magic! You can have 2 spells ranging anywhere from nukes, teleport, crowd control, magic immunity, healing, etc. and use any combination you like, as well a special slot that is used for a bow, mines, traps, throwing axes, what have you.
There's a ton of game modes, ranging from huge FFA fights, organized duels, last-man-standing (Counter-Strike style), as well as a survival and practice mode.
The learning curve is sharp, but it's getting better. They're adding a lot of features into the game to make it easier to understand what's going on, but even then a good swordsman can take you out pretty quickly. I had to pull a player aside, pull out training swords and get smacked for a while as he taught me before I understood what was going on. The game is extremely satisfying, and has a bright future.
Even in it's early state, the devs have the genius and success of Kingdoms Collide behind them, and Kingdoms Rise is looking fantastic.

Hexcells is a polished modern variation on the old Microsoft Minesweeper game. Although it is much gentler, rather than game-ending bombs the player is identifying certain hexes. If a mistake is made then it is just recorded and the game continues. There is no timer or time limit, nor any way of scoring other than the number of mistakes made. The puzzles are hand-designed (no randomness) and provide a couple of hours of thought to perfect with mix of basic logic and memory (as the puzzles do not change if restarted). It is a nicely polished game with clean graphical style and nicely responsive music. It has no replayability, but it is cheap and well made. Definitely worth picking up in a sale or bundle, as I will be doing with its sequels.

A cool little roguelike to play with friends. You can play on your own just fine, but the revival system (other players can revive you in multiplayer) makes multiplayer much easier than singleplayer.
Note that I said "easier" not "easy", as this game can be unforgiving. Oh, you tried to attack that boar from the front? You didn't know that he could charge at you? Too bad, back to the start with you!
Basically, you go through a series of levels of various types, (Forest, Spider, Volcano, etc.) which contain much needed ores and sometimes even chests with loot. At the end of each you will be confronted 3 doors, which will dictate which biome you go to next, and each having their own look in accordance to the biome they will take you to. The game doesn't tell you which is which, so it's up to you to memorize them.
After you go through the door of your choice, however, you wont go straight to the next level, first you'll go to an NPC town where you can cook up the ores that you found and make them into weapons or armor. There are also items to buy there, but they are usually overpriced and/or useless. A bit of advice for free, if you're undergeared, don't kill the chickens that are there.
Now, so far it's all sounded good, right? Well mostly it is, but there is one glaring problem that will most likely affect many people. Remember how I said that multiplayer was how to best experiance the game? Well, you need Hamachi for that. For those who do not have hamachi, it might seem like a bit of a hassle to download it just for this game. I still recomend you do, mostly because you're bound to need it sometime in the future.

It's been 3 days and I've already racked up a solid 30 hours. So immersive especially on first play. The amount of crazy car builds and engine builds you can do in sandbox are ridiculous. And the engines are surprisingly realistic. I've created mock ups of both friends cars and my own and the dyno graphs are quite accurate to real life figures.
Your car creations in both sandbox and career mode are rated on comfort, drivability, smoothness, etc. and you can see relatively accurate 0-100 figures (based on power:weight, grip, wheelspin, gearing, etc.), top speeds (based on aerodynamics, gearing, etc.), fuel economy (aerodynamics, engine efficiency, weight, driving wheels, transmission, etc.) which are really interesting. They even look relatively accurate. Although some of the sportiness, offroad, etc. ratings are sometimes out, they still provide a good rating system and encourage you not to just chuck the biggest engine in the smallest car you can find.
Career mode is overwhelmingly complex and immersive, even if it still is in development. You get to determine the sizes of factories, the amount of shifts and quality control anad you get target markets for different areas. People will also buy based on reputation and the career mode can start any time between like the 30s or 40s to the current day, with engine technologies and consumer markets based around those time periods. It offers a new level of depth and involvment for when I eventually get bored of sandbox.
Yes the game has a few bugs. But the developers have worked really well on both ironing them out and delivering new content. You really see the commitment from the devs in this game. The bugs aren't game destroying either, they are minor hiccups that occasionally occur if you run the game for too long.
All in all, it is definitely worth my $30 for the amount of hours I am going to get out of it. For any car fan or engine nut, this game provides plenty of entertainment. 10/10 would reccomend.
Wondering if we will ever see any of the early type engine designs in this game. I was hoping they would add flat heads at the least at some point as they were a major part of automotive history.

Having so much fun with this game. Yes it has its bugs, but the devs are working to their maximum to iron them out. The Lite Campaign is quite nice, and I can't wait for new features to arrive. And it's always fun building insane (and stupid) cars in sandbox mode too.

If you're really into cars and are somewhat confident with what makes a car work (or even if you're not, try the tutorials), I would 100% recommend this game.
If you're anything like me, you've drawn your own cars before, and have imagined making your own and selling them. Automation basically lets you do this, allowing you to design every single part of your car, from the body, chassis and cosmetic design, to the engine configuration, cam profile and compression ratio.
Here are some of the pros and cons:
+ Infinite possibilties. Family cars, muscle cars, sports cars, luxury cars, hyper cars, pickups...
+ You have to ability to custom design your car to your liking.
+ The latest feature, the Lite Campaign, allows you to get a taste of what the final game will be like. Create your own company, precisely choose your starting conditions (starting cash, engineers, competitor markups, etc.) then play through from 1946 to 2020 building whatever cars you want, while researching new technologies and trying not to bankrupt yourself by building a full carbon fibre 3-door hatchback with a 50hp 12L V12.
+ An active, kind and helpful community.
+ Hundreds of mods to download from the Steam workshop to add to the design potential.
+ The developers are constantly updating users with what the next updates will include, when they will arrive and what will and will not make it into the final game, all via the official Automation page and the official Automation YouTube channel
- Poorly optimized currently, however, this is due to change with the port over to the Unreal 4 engine sometime around Christmas this year.
- The game is not yet finished, meaning the full extent of the final games content (Boxers, V16's, I2's, I5's, I8's, Diesels, etc.) is not yet implemented, however there is still tens of hours of fun (I've currently played over 200 hours and plan to play even more still).
- Difficult for people who don't have an atleast moderately detailed knowledge of how a car works (specifically the engine), however this can be learned relatively quickly.
Overall, Automation is a brilliant game and I highly recommend it.
In its current state, I would give it a 9/10, however be aware that this is likely to change (for the better) with the final release, coming sometime mid-late 2017.

I've finally played enough of this game to feel comfortable writing a review. To start off, I'm a huge Paradox fan. EU4 is in my top 2 games of all time, and I love Crusader Kings, Vicky II, Cities, and Hearts of Iron. I think EU4 is about as perfect as you can get in terms of Grand Strategy - for reference, I think Civ IV is about as close you can get to perfect in 4X territory. Stellaris comes close to being great in both categories, with a lot of interesting mechanics and events, but manages to fall short in both, making it a kind of jack-of-all-trades game, master of none.
To reiterate, in its current state (1.4.1 I believe), Stellaris is almost a great game. It has a lot of potential, which is not something most want to hear when they buy a finished game, but Paradox has shown that they are looking to support games for years down the line. This is hopeful, because I think it will be like EU4 - shaky at first, but amazing later. That being said, usually this also comes with a load of DLC, but as long as they don't pull a Common Sense or Art of War and basically require you to spend money to get the full value out of the free features, I think it's a decent business model. At least they don't have Season Passes.
Now for the Pros of Stellaris -
• The pre-game and early game are a lot of fun. They've added a ton of features for universe customization, a fair amount of features for species creation, and there are a lot of mixes of governments and ethics you can go with. As for when you get into the game, it feels like Civ when you start out - you're doing basically the same thing each time, but it still manages to feel new and refreshing as you continue on.
• The events are fantastic. I love reading them, and it feels like they've packed a lot in here. Even when I see repeat events, I still read the text, it feels like a compelling story. And best of all, I feel like they do a decent job of having events drive gameplay decisions, kind of like in CK2.
• I like a lot of the gameplay mechanics, mainly the ones that deal with the POPs. I find the POP management, building, migration, slavery, robots, occupation, ethics, edicts, and government mechanics all really fun to play around with.
• The late game crises are fantastic, a great touch to the game. They really make great stories, which is one of the best things about 4X games. Being able to recount a story later about how you fought off extradimensional invaders is one of the most appealing things about getting to the late game.
• Like most Grand Strategy games, it's fun to zone out to for a couple hours after work, or play on the weekend. One of my biggest problems with 4X games is that they sometimes feel too contained - I feel like I need to finish a game of them at once. The biggest appeal of Grand Strategy, to me, is that I can invest as much or as little time into and still feel like I got the same gameplay experience.
Now the Cons -
• Biggest con by far is that there are far too many mechanics in this game, none of which are particularily fleshed out. This works for Grand Strategy games, where you can automate a lot of stuff and just focus on a few more pressing gameplay concerns (like trade in EU4, or everything in Vic II). Stellaris has a lot of great IDEAS for mechanics, where I feel like they just need some patches to get right. But here's just a laundry list of mechanics that aren't at all fleshed out - factions, terraforming, government, enlightenment, vassalage, protectorates, fallen empires, federations, alliances, anything to do with technology, anything to do with sectors, anything to do with ships, anything to do with armies, and trait modification all need a lot of work.
• The other problem, past having WAYYYY too many game mechanics, is that none of them affect the game that much. If you want to, you can ignore things like ethics, factions, and pop development completely, which are (supposedly) things Paradox put a lot of time into in this game.
• Something that might not bother other people, but actually destroys the game for me, is the lack of any interesting in-game analysis ability. I'm talking about having minimal maps, no ledger, no good search ability, and no empire history. Add this stuff, Paradox! It makes your games so much more interesting when I can look at 20 different map modes and learn about the world.
• The UI sucks in this game. Absolutely atrocious. There are too many menus, they contain too little information on each menu, there isn't an easy way to initiate diplomacy, you have to click too many times to do things, it is not obvious where specific things are in the UI (even to someone who's played 60 or so hours), there isn't enough info displayed in the banners at the top of the screen, and there is FAR too much information displayed in the sidebar. All of these are relatively easy fixes for Paradox, especially since they have good UI in their other games - this is a real problem that it sucks in its current state.
• This isn't a new complaint for many 4X games, but the diplomacy needs work. There isn't much you can do with it and you can't automate it if you want the most out of it, which is the worst combination.
As I said before, Stellaris is almost great, but it falls short sooo hard that I can't recommend it in its current state. There are just too many things that aren't fleshed out or just aren't finished. Wait for a few more patches, maybe some DLC, and then a year or two down the line it will probably be great. But until then, I would say hold off.
Sorry Paradox. I still love you! Keep doing what you're doing.

Despite the very low resolution/pixelated graphics, Lone Survivor successfully comes off as a very creepy game through effective use of tone, lighting, music and pacing. The gameplay itself is very reminicent of old style adventure games, which if you think about it is what the survivor horrors of old used, just with the distinct possibility of combat and the ability to (mostly) defend yourself.

It's obvious this game was inspired by the Silent Hill franchise with it's great audio presentation and twisted plot.  The graphics style pulls off deliberately lacking visuals, which, in a horror game, is a good thing when visual details are shrouded in mystery, and not hi-rez and in your face.  Unfortunately, now we come to the gameplay ... all 4 hours of it.  Due to the 2D perspective, the map is difficult to follow and encounters with the 3 total monster types often leave you with no choice but to shoot them, as avoiding them is only possible in a few context sensitive areas.  Survival through food and rest feels off because there is no meter to tell how badly you need either, except for the main character complaining without warning.  Finally, the story becomes complete nonsense the further you progress, leaving tons of questions un-answered to where horror game veterans may sense a common ending cliche approaching.  A triumph in atmosphere, but lacking elsewhere.  Tread lightly!

I played through this whole thing in one sitting today (around 3 hours).  I always thought Minesweeper was a better game than it was given credit for, and Hexcells improves on Minesweeper in pretty much every way.  There is no guessing in Hexcells, everything is completely 100% solvable.  There are also some interesting new mechanics at play, like seeing the "mine" count for certain rows or columns, or getting information beyond just a number, like whether all the adjacent mines are touching each other or not.  I was VERY pleasantly surprised at how much I enjoyed this, and I'm looking forward to trying out the other Hexcells games soon.
Side note-- the function of the left and right click are swapped from how they are in Minesweeper.  If you have played a decent amount of Minesweeper, do yourself a huge favor and swap the Hexcells controls before you start playing.  I didn't, and it screwed with me more than I'd care to admit.

Serious review for serious people:
Do you like Rogue-likes? Then you'll like this game. Do you not like roguelikes or have never played one? You might still like this game, I dunno.
Pros
- The crafting system is awesome (shift+click two items), particularly because you aren't given any of the recipes - part of the fun lies in experimenting and figuring things out (or if you really want to you could use the wiki)
- Lots of recipes
- Different races provide for different playstyles - if your starting items don't include an axe, for example, you have to kill everything to get coins and then buy an axe in the marketplace at the end of each level so that you can get wood and sticks to make handles for more tools. (I think there's actually another way but I don't know what it is)
- Challenging (I think that's a pro anyway)
- Procedurally generated everything
- I can't make any guarantees, but I feel like you don't need to be a roguelike fan to enjoy if, but if you are then you'll definitely enjoy it
- Co-op up to four players
- Plenty of unlockables that aren't too easy to unlock
- Haven't encountered any bugs
Cons
- No LAN play, so you'll still have to set up port forwarding to play locally
Tip: Don't stay still for too long

Art: 9.5/10
The style of this art is amazing. The UI is minimalistic. The character models are well-detailed :). Animations are beautiful. There are several different environments in the game, which broadens the art styles.
Graphics could definitely be improved if it wasn't just a port from console.
Music: 11/10
Gameplay: 9/10
For the most part, gameplay was enjoyable. At this point, I am just nit-picking things that I thought could have been added or improved on.
Play as 2B and you primarily do hack-n-slash. Play as 9S and you get to slash a bit and hack stuff. For me, the hacking elements were rather boring. The hacking games are, for the most part, done in a square box which limits what can be done in the game. I would have liked to have more difficult dungeon-crawler type hacking games.
Aside from the quests in the game (which can only be completed once), there not much else to do as far as minigames go. As of right now, I am waiting for the DLC where you get to fight the CEO. I hope they add more DLC for minigames.
As for controls, I started out playing with keyboard and mouse, but the camera and some actions aren't really designed for raw input from a mouse and keyboard. The camera movement was too slow for my liking and the evade mechanic of having to tap a direction key (WASD) twice was annoying and made the action more difficult than it needed to be. I decided to borrow my friend's PS4 controller and most of my problems were solved (Still wish I could use a mouse for faster camera movement).
The game has a bunch of things to collect. I've got everything at 100%. Lots of fun farming and exploring.
Story: 10/10
Story is great. The main theme of the plot is pretty much nihilism in a nutshell. Values don't matter, yet here are some values you have to follow anyway. Pretty much all the characters deal with existentialism and nihilism. There are 26 different endings ranging from A-Z. A-E are the main story endings. F-Z are "joke" endings (leaving battlefield, kill wrong person, etc.). Ending Y is particularly interesting and is considered to be end-game content.
Overall:
62 hours in about 5 days. Buy the game. No regrets. 2Booty. ♥♥♥♥ 9S, but I understand. Pascal selling machine body parts. lol.

Automation was a lot of fun when I first discovered it in 2013 and played the free 4 cylinder demo. I then got the full version and had a decent amount of fun with the other engine types that were released. V8, Inline 6, V6, V12 and now I3 engines.
This is without question the best simulation for building and designing combustion engines and just getting some more performance or improvement out of your engine can be extreme fun. As it is it could cost 4.99$ for the engine builder set that it never got past in 5 years, or 50,000+$ if it were a professional simulator for the car industry, but for some reason they thought they could turn it into car tycoon game if they just worked on it long enough.
From there it only goes downhill. The other parts that have been released are a total dissapointment, with the low point being the "lite campaign". It's a full dead-loss. I held off from writing a review but it terminated my hopes that anything can be expected from this game in the future. The campaign feels more like a software for video editing than a game, you are basically just clicking from one modal window to the next, and if you quit before the entire process completed your progress is lost. If you're not painting little cars on a piece of paper and make appropriate factory noises with your mouth you're going to see/hear practically nothing in terms of presentation.
The second problem is that it hangs in E/A for much to long, year after year after year after year. The developers now decided to port the game to a new engine which basically means that the waiting starts over again. I have seen screenshots that looked like from a completely different game, so by the track record of this project, it could take many more years still.
The game at time also had a great amount of bugs, there are constantly values lost and the famous "LUA Errors" especially if you click the tabs out of order. The save system is awful, you never know when what gets overwritten and better manage your files manually from outside.
I can however still recommend this for the engine designer, if you skip the other parts.

The funny thing is, this game saves everything you do all the time because their amazing programmer could find no other way to keep the state of variables consistent from one of his window to the other. So he stores everything to disk immediately and loads it back whenever a windows opens, totally circumventing the purpose of RAM memory in computers.
Before they introduced this novelty I have seen this game crash often and badly, it was like badly written VBA only worse. I guess it took them halfway through this project to realize the difference between local and global variables. That's why they came up with DiskRAM™ technology, where everything you ever do goes into the savegame immediately, so the games code cannot mix up different copies of the same variable.
That's also why you have to use this odd "remember settings" button on the left as soon as you can, otherwise you will eventually totally ♥♥♥♥ up hours of work once you realize there is nothing to load from disk beside what you already see in the window. Oh and when you restored the values, click it immediately again because restoring also erases the stored values.
Even better is it to have a near perfect memory or a notebook in front of you where you write all important values, because you can already prepare yourself that sooner or later you will lose all your work anyhow. Without going into the fact that the car directory screen is totally unworkable if you have more than 1 page of cars/engines, and managing more than a few is a total pain in the ****. I always have Excel running beside the game and keep my settings there. I also make screenshots with Fraps all the time, which is much more productive than using the inbuilt save system and comes second from writing down everything.
On a scale out of 10 I give this design a -3 .. Let me not even go into how managing copies of designs works because I have not even been able make any kind of sense out of that and because it would simply be too infuriating to try and understand this insanity. Let me just say that when I make an important change I just go directly to creating a new car from scratch, because this saves me all the inevitable frustration down the road, resulting from absolute harebrained design choices.
Though I still like the engine designer very much, the rest of this game should be ceremoneously and irreversibly erased with a 10 meter industry magnet and programmed again, which is apparently what they are doing right now (the so called engine "switch" looks like a total restart to me. Probably the only efficient solution ... )

I've finally played enough of this game to feel comfortable writing a review. To start off, I'm a huge Paradox fan. EU4 is in my top 2 games of all time, and I love Crusader Kings, Vicky II, Cities, and Hearts of Iron. I think EU4 is about as perfect as you can get in terms of Grand Strategy - for reference, I think Civ IV is about as close you can get to perfect in 4X territory. Stellaris comes close to being great in both categories, with a lot of interesting mechanics and events, but manages to fall short in both, making it a kind of jack-of-all-trades game, master of none.
To reiterate, in its current state (1.4.1 I believe), Stellaris is almost a great game. It has a lot of potential, which is not something most want to hear when they buy a finished game, but Paradox has shown that they are looking to support games for years down the line. This is hopeful, because I think it will be like EU4 - shaky at first, but amazing later. That being said, usually this also comes with a load of DLC, but as long as they don't pull a Common Sense or Art of War and basically require you to spend money to get the full value out of the free features, I think it's a decent business model. At least they don't have Season Passes.
Now for the Pros of Stellaris -
• The pre-game and early game are a lot of fun. They've added a ton of features for universe customization, a fair amount of features for species creation, and there are a lot of mixes of governments and ethics you can go with. As for when you get into the game, it feels like Civ when you start out - you're doing basically the same thing each time, but it still manages to feel new and refreshing as you continue on.
• The events are fantastic. I love reading them, and it feels like they've packed a lot in here. Even when I see repeat events, I still read the text, it feels like a compelling story. And best of all, I feel like they do a decent job of having events drive gameplay decisions, kind of like in CK2.
• I like a lot of the gameplay mechanics, mainly the ones that deal with the POPs. I find the POP management, building, migration, slavery, robots, occupation, ethics, edicts, and government mechanics all really fun to play around with.
• The late game crises are fantastic, a great touch to the game. They really make great stories, which is one of the best things about 4X games. Being able to recount a story later about how you fought off extradimensional invaders is one of the most appealing things about getting to the late game.
• Like most Grand Strategy games, it's fun to zone out to for a couple hours after work, or play on the weekend. One of my biggest problems with 4X games is that they sometimes feel too contained - I feel like I need to finish a game of them at once. The biggest appeal of Grand Strategy, to me, is that I can invest as much or as little time into and still feel like I got the same gameplay experience.
Now the Cons -
• Biggest con by far is that there are far too many mechanics in this game, none of which are particularily fleshed out. This works for Grand Strategy games, where you can automate a lot of stuff and just focus on a few more pressing gameplay concerns (like trade in EU4, or everything in Vic II). Stellaris has a lot of great IDEAS for mechanics, where I feel like they just need some patches to get right. But here's just a laundry list of mechanics that aren't at all fleshed out - factions, terraforming, government, enlightenment, vassalage, protectorates, fallen empires, federations, alliances, anything to do with technology, anything to do with sectors, anything to do with ships, anything to do with armies, and trait modification all need a lot of work.
• The other problem, past having WAYYYY too many game mechanics, is that none of them affect the game that much. If you want to, you can ignore things like ethics, factions, and pop development completely, which are (supposedly) things Paradox put a lot of time into in this game.
• Something that might not bother other people, but actually destroys the game for me, is the lack of any interesting in-game analysis ability. I'm talking about having minimal maps, no ledger, no good search ability, and no empire history. Add this stuff, Paradox! It makes your games so much more interesting when I can look at 20 different map modes and learn about the world.
• The UI sucks in this game. Absolutely atrocious. There are too many menus, they contain too little information on each menu, there isn't an easy way to initiate diplomacy, you have to click too many times to do things, it is not obvious where specific things are in the UI (even to someone who's played 60 or so hours), there isn't enough info displayed in the banners at the top of the screen, and there is FAR too much information displayed in the sidebar. All of these are relatively easy fixes for Paradox, especially since they have good UI in their other games - this is a real problem that it sucks in its current state.
• This isn't a new complaint for many 4X games, but the diplomacy needs work. There isn't much you can do with it and you can't automate it if you want the most out of it, which is the worst combination.
As I said before, Stellaris is almost great, but it falls short sooo hard that I can't recommend it in its current state. There are just too many things that aren't fleshed out or just aren't finished. Wait for a few more patches, maybe some DLC, and then a year or two down the line it will probably be great. But until then, I would say hold off.
Sorry Paradox. I still love you! Keep doing what you're doing.

I'm a relative noob at this game, so keep in mind I'm only scratching the surface of the game's content. With that said, let's move on.
Wildstar is a rather simple MMO - at first - with bright colors and cheery furballs. But behind this cheery smile the game wears, this game is surprisingly dark - think Madoka Magica, but without so many little girls. The gameplay is good, and the game in its entirety makes me think of a cross between Tera and WoW.
So far, in the early stages of the game, I've found the community to be very friendly and helpful - I've had very few people being negative nancies or trolls, unlike most games, and thankfully the Elin worshippers haven't quite gotten a look at this game's equivalent, so we don't have quite the number of pedobears. Ask a question in Zone chat or in the 'Advice' channel, and you'll usually get a response within a minute or two, and a bit of extra information because people are talkative like that.
Combat in the game is simple at first, but the telegraphs tell you quite a bit early on about how the game's going to be in the endgame - monsters use slow wind-ups in the early game, much like in Tera, to get you used to dodging them, but you see quite early that they didn't just limit themselves to cones and AoE circles. I've seen telegraphs for rapid dashes, spirals, large AoE circles with holes in them - the game definitely keeps you on your toes. So far, I've yet to see any enemies that were just recolors as well - because of this, there's generally a bunch of different monster types with different movesets. Unfortunately, from what I've heard, monster spacing could use a bit of work, as sometimes enemies are too tightly packed, and other times it could be a few minutes before you see another ♥♥♥♥er to gut.
When picking your character at the beginning, there's one other thing you get to choose beyond 'horde/alliance,' 'race,' and 'class.' Before you finish your character, you get to choose a 'path' - a secondary level that, while it doesn't directly contribute to your character's stats, gives you a few boosters to make leveling through the game more fun. They also serve as pleasant diversions, from scouting out caves and mountaintops to arena-style deathmatches against endless waves of enemies. You also have challenges, which can be picked up and completed as you go through the game, and often are directtly associated with quests you're already doing - adding a timer to get a bonus reward.
Quests are usually pretty straightforward. Not a lot of errand quests, thankfully, but plenty of 'kill X amount of X enemy' quests. I've seen a few quests, though, that make you actually take your time to look for where you're going before you can start killing things - obscure caves and mountaintops, hoe! I think the best part about the game's quests, however, is that you don't ALWAYS have to go back to town to turn them in or even pick up the next one - by default, the game gives you a communicator that lets you turn quests in remotely. So far the only quests I haven't been allowed to turn in that way were ones that required me to get a specific item from enemies I killed or quests that had cinematics attached to them.
The game's character classes are significantly more diverse than in most games, though not in the sense that you have a lot of classes to pick from or that you make your own - each class is capable of both a DPS role AND a supportive role, whether that role is tank or healing. The healer can destroy, and the invisible assassins can jump into the horde and tank. Nobody is any more or less effective at healing or tanking than anyone else - and since everyone's skills are generally AoE damage, ANYONE can mob effectively, too. Even the most basic attack for each character I've seen has an AoE of some sort, though mostly I've seen the skills state their AoE skills are capped at hitting 5 targets - considering how many targets I've seen pop up in dungeons, that's probably a good thing since it'd be a bit laggy if everybody was hitting the entire horde of fifty.

So Borderlands The Pre-Sequel is not a bad game.
I like it, and I find myself acutally wanting to play it a lot more than BL2. Still there are some things that I really don't like about it.
First of all, I feel like the story is lacking backstory. While the story is interesting and finding out more about Jack's backstory is certainly fun, there was still not enough explained. Why exactly do those people attack the Helios? Who even are these people? It's never really explained to you and let's be real who actually wants to search for recordings to understand the story?
Second, it had a massive difficulty spike at the end at least for me it got really hard to kill the bosses as I was also insanely outleveled even though I only skipped two or three side quests.
But there were also things that I really liked about it.
For example, the characters are much better than the ones in BL 2, especially because now your character also talks back and they get a real character.
The new laser weapons are extremely cool, even though you need some time to get used to them
The cryo element is so much better and more effective than slag in my opinion.
I personally also liked the jumping mechanics, even though many people found them annoying and I can see why but I still thought it was pretty fun and an interesting concept.
In conclusion, it's not a bad game and I would recommend it but I feel like it could have been much better if they explained the backstory better and handled the balancing a bit better.

Right off the bat you are able to customize your knight in some impressive fantastical armor and clothing, but there are also choices for some more 'realistic' gear. Devs are adding new things all the time and are always showing off their progress on the Kingdoms Rise facebook page.
As of right now there isn't a tutorial in-game, but one can be seen in the guides section made by the devs. You don't need to look at the tutorial, but believe me when I say, at the very least look at the parry and parry lock section of the manual. It will save you a lot of grief in game and once you master those skills, gameplay becomes even more addicting. You can get away with spamming away attack with other new players, but once you meet someone who knows how to parry, you will most likely lose. Luckily, those experienced few in the community are always willing to help out new players and usually it isn't too hard to ask these guys for some help.
There are many different swords in the game, each with their special effects and stats. They aren't perfectly balanced, but your use in magic and skill with the sword is enough to offset any of the swords' abilities currently available. Magic in this game isn't over powered and is meant to be used to complement your swordsmanship as well as mold the playstyle you want. You can only equip 2 spells, however, you are able to have doubles of any spell as well as have a large selection to choose from. There are many types of spells from attack, to defense, to healing and mobility. Mix and match to create the playstyle you want.
You will have a hard time at first controlling the sword with your mouse due to the nature of the screen moving with you as you strike, but like I said, look up the tutorials and get some practise performing the moves. They do require some timing and precision, so if an easy mode game is what you're looking for, then you are in the wrong place. However, if you're looking for a competetive game where the skill cap is high and it is very much possible for a skilled player to take on an entire team, without the use of cheap tricks/exploits, this game is for you.
**AUGUST UPDATE**
AI has been added to the game and makes for quite the training partners as well as a challenging surviving mode that will have you crying for mama within the first 5 waves. Really fun if you just want to mess around by yourself, or can't currently find a game. Just remember not to use the disonnect button while you're in the survival server as it will crash the game

I remember playing this on the Xbox360, and the Visuals made me want to puke, I'm glad to report it isn't the same with the PC version, in fact the visuals are something to love if you have a fairly decent spec system, the DX11 tessellation on the characters at points is laughable, but i'm sure you can get over that, they look very fuzzy during the african missions.
This game, contrary to popular belief, does have a few elements from the first game, civilians being one of them, more to the point, civilians that actually die when you friggen shoot them. You are required to use the "swift silent and (quite literally) invisible" motto that the original Ghost Recon used, you stand around for too long, #1, you get bored and #2 someone will come over and shoot you up.
Some of the features I liked, visuals aside, was the new stealth tactics employed in the game, even with your super amazeballs cloak of badassery on, you can still get detected, and it's story is pretty gripping, certainly the first mission, if you've played the game from Ghost Recon 2 onwards, you'll know who Ramirez is, and if you've played GRAW, you'll know who Allen is, and the first mission involving them, while I can kind of see some things, I personally would have done differently, being primarily a milsim player and a military nut, it was a good prologue to start you off, sets the mood, what you're after... then something bigger comes along and pow piddy pow! you're stopping a full scale war from breaking out... and there's four of you.
It isn't the typical "america vs russia" crap either, in fact, if my memory serves me right, you're actually helping the majority of Russia at more than one point, against an international force of crooks and cronies.
some missions are more relaxed, some missions carry a lot of tension, and some missions will have you on the edge of your provebial seat.
and at some points, some missions will have you very infuriated, but in a good way.
one thing I did like, and this is just a tiny thing that makes ol' Klaus happy, is when you throw a grenade into one of the buildings in the second mission, it blows up and some dust comes off the roof, I thought that was pretty cool, but this is the person who thinks fountain pens are cool.
Gunsmith is an excellent feature, I like it a lot, it's pretty different, I mean you don't see customization options depicted like that every day, personally I think it's genius, I enjoy using it, and while this random dude called "Marcus Kelso" will advise you, you can take whatever weapon type you want. I would've liked this Marcus Kelso dude to be Marcus Brown, it would've made more sense in terms of context, but hey! who cares!?
For those wondering where all the ladies in the game have gone, my theory, basing it on what Alicia Diaz ended up doing, is that all the Lady Ghosts, have moved into a specialized area of the CIA Special Activities Division, or have taken on support/HQ roles in the group, rather than have a main front line role.
Personally, not having any more than one notable female character (twisting's pilot) in this game wasn't such a big deal, but with women being in all installments previous to this one (console versions for GRAW1+2) it's kind of out of character, for a better word. But like I said, you do appreciate not having many female Ghosts around, certainly ones that don't shut the hell up, not naming any names...
But please Ubisoft, if you are reading this, and you are making a next installment, being able to choose your squad, and some women would be great to have back in the game.
I did like the Melee kills, because #1, they make sense and #2 they don't half come in handy! they also look pretty cool, you don't just smack that guy with the butt of your gun, you smack that guy silly, break his arm and slam him into the ground, it looks pretty epic.
Some features of the game could've been left at the door, though. most notably health regen, in the games before GRFS, if you got shot, there's a pretty decent chance that you'll die, in this one, you can get shot in the head but you take cover so you'll be fine in a tick. there's this very odd sound that plays when you hit someone too, it's okay, but it gets annoying in an onslaught. Then there's the "you can't do anything else until you've done this that and the other" palava, also known as 'tutorials' which I'm pretty sure in previous PC versions of these games except Advanced Warfighter 1, there was a separate, optional, level for it, even still in advanced warfighter 1 you weren't limited on what you could do until you did that one thing it told you to do, if you knew how to do it, you did it, if you didn't, you learned something new from, being honest, a quite redundant feature in almost any shooter.
And then of course you have the "unnecessary cutscene extravaganza!" basically, if there's a door that needs opening, expect to have an uneccessary cutscene showing off tacticool movement and♥♥♥♥♥♥ y'know, all I did was open a door, it's not that significant! While it was pretty cool at first, it gets a little repetetive, and boring.
It also has the typical norm in most shooters now too, on the rails shooting gallery-esque modes, in this one, that is 'diamond formation' where you have to escort a person from A to B with you holding that guy's hand, with your magically appearing pistol and shooting any threat to you or your new friend, because it's obvious that you as a gamer are not mentally capable of getting them there alive in the normal play mode. Aaand of course helicopter gunning, because, y'know, there's not an assigned crew chief for that crap in 2020- something.
you'll probably allso notice at points, it still has xbox 360 button hints at places, the grenade change button is the most prominent, telling you it's the left bumper on the pad to change grenade type for those of you with a smattering of common sense, you'll realise that it isn't that button.
overall, for what it is, it's a decent game, if you're like me and you've played and enjoyed the entire series, then you'll probably be VERY slightly disappointed by it, but if you take the game as a standalone addition to the Tom Clancy franchise, it'll go down pretty well, I sort of do a bit of both, I know it's got the Ghost Recon name, but it's a new game in its own right.
I'd recommend this, certainly now that it's been patched and it works.

Judging by its cover, one wouldn't immediately assume Gatling Gears to be a bullet hell shooter. Features familiar to this genre include dodging insane amounts of enemies and projectiles mid-combat as the camera forcefully pans horizontally or vertically.
Gatling Gears mixes the formula up by letting the player drive a ground-based machine. This not only heightens the player's maneuverability, but it also allows him to control the pace of the camera - a nice addition that aids the less hardcore audience.
For combat, there are a total of four different weapons at the player's disposal, three of which are upgradeable by collecting gold scattered through the levels. Using them skillfully is pivotal to maintaining a high multiplier which will boost your ranks in the leaderboards and unlock aesthetics.
In terms of a bullet hell shooter, Gatling Gears is arguably the most beautiful. However, it is neither the most challenging nor the most memorable. It's also pretty repetitive.
Grade: C

While the narrative is rather vapid, it's hard to notice since the action is perfectly paced and the levels are solid. The only other thing that is lacking is the number of players ready for co-op - multiplayer is essentially limited to local games only, since there is no drop-in multiplayer mode. Had this game been released in the arcades, I would have probably spent a ton of money plugging quarters into a Gatling Gears arcade machine.

This game is pretty good... but it could have been better, and because of that its actually more of a disappointment in a way.
Goal is to explore the apartment complex you are in and progress towards an ending.  Horror setting is heavily inspired by Silent Hill, but honestly it went too far.   The item use / find sound being basically the same as those in the SH series is a reference.  Monsters making static distorion when they get near you is borrowing / inspiration.  Directly ripping sections from those games and using them both without storyline purpose and without original spin (locking room, object in mouth-like hole, etc) is just too blatant.
On top of that, every character you meed is of the 'mysterious' archetype, save one.  When everyone has confusing dialogue, nothing makes sense.  A lot of the dialogue for the main character is definately breaking believability too.  More on that below.
Also, enemies should not become invulnerable when stunned by a flare.  That is just dumb as bricks game design.
Because of the nonsensical dialogue, it made me feel like my player-driven actions that I took in the game meant nothing. I shot monsters that tried to kill me, ate when complaining of hunger, slept when tired, and acted like the survivalist the game portrayed my setting as necessitating. So then why does my ending involve my character exploring a mental ward, finding a clipboard with his and room number, then entering his room, suddenly deciding he's nihilistic (after 4 game hours of survivalist behavior), taking a pill he finds there, and then lying down on the bed and having a dream of his girlfriend saying 'Hey, you found me even though you're mental and everything's ♥♥♥♥ed up. That's cool right?' The character agrees, then the credits roll.
Excuse me what? Where was the survivalist drive? He even just swore revenge for a buddy he made being killed a second ago. If anything he'd react to this exactly like he did to being locked in a random room before (aforementioned direct ripoff) and exactly like a survivalist would -- "Crap I got locked in! I gotta find a way out!" There's a theory the character is insane... but then that arbitrarily obsoletes the whole story I just played through. He gave up? Not believable. Was there something I missed in the bunch of mysterious dialogue from every character I meet? Yeah, probably. Games with open storylines are best when they're actually well crafted -- A mailbox with a slot that you decide what letter to put in, not a jumped arrangement of nailed boards that you could... yeah I could jam the letter in that crooked triangle space at the top but it might fall out of all the holes in the sides and bottom.
There are two other endings, but given that the one I got is likely to be the default most-common one. The others are obtained for more pacifist behaviors and another for self-destructive ones (not eating, sleeping, killing everything etc). Thus if anything, this 'default' ending shouldn't be so nonsensical and break from the theme the game has presenting the whole time.

I've played this game on and off since its release, and I've always enjoyed it. If you're a fan of WoW or SWTOR, Wildstar is their ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child. Don't let the cartoony graphics fool you; some of the questlines/dialog gets pretty dark, but for the most part, it's all pretty fun and not totally monotonous. It's only gotten better since switching to F2P, and I wish more MMORPGs would use Wildstar's F2P model, 'cuz this is how it should be. You don't have to pay a cent if you don't want to, and you can still access ALL of the content, including endgame raiding. But let's get to the most important factor: HOUSING.
You get access to player housing pretty early on and materials for it are pretty easy to come by in-game. You can pretty much do anything you like with it, and you even get bigger bonuses for cramming more stuff into it. Don't like any of the prefab houses? BUILD YOUR OWN! Build it as high as you want! The entire plot could be a house. The player housing is, without a doubt, my favorite thing about this game.

Borderlands 2 did a great job of fast shooting with surprisingly deep character customization. It did have its share of pacing blemishes though - blemishes I was really hoping that a new standalone game like Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel would fix. It doesn’t, but it does provide an entertaining story and a handful of successful gameplay additions that spice up its already excellent core of shooting and looting. This is, essentially, more of the Borderlands I love with just enough new twists to pull me back in, and mostly make up for the things the series still doesn’t get right.
The real star of the show in The Pre-Sequel is Jack. In Borderlands 2 he was perhaps the most gleefully sadistic, and effective video game villain. Seeing his journey from hero to maniac is perhaps the biggest reason to make the 20-or-so-hour trek across Pandora’s moon, Elpis. There a real knack for storytelling here, drawing a more sympathetic portrait of Jack without ever making him into the clichéd misunderstood villain. He's every bit the hilarious, ego-centric asshat here that we remember him as, and his excellently written and delivered dialogue is responsible for the lion's share of the laughs.

It's greatest flaw is that it is an incomplete game; which is perfectly fine seeing as it is in early access. Make sure you take this into account when analyzing the game yourself. Another thing that might initially be a turn-off is the lack of an active player-base meaning those trying to play the game solo won't get to do much playing, which is a shame because the gameplay is quite enjoyable despite all its buggy unfinished-ness.
I have yet to play the game extensively, and I bought a four-pack for me and some friends so we've had someone to play with. What we have experienced is a genuinely fun melee-combat game, which is something we have been searching for for quite some time. The combat is visceral; every hit and parry feels great and the spells are a great way to add some flair to what would otherwise be just a sword-fighting game. There's plenty of variety of tactics that you can utilize to take down your opponents in creative ways by mixing sword-type with spell choice, and if you get tired of one build, just try another. Get a few people together and you'll have a lot of (admittedly unpolished) fun.
If I were to compare this game to any others that I have played I would have to place it somewhere between Mount and Blade and Star Wars Jedi Knight: Jedi Academy. It has swordplay reminiscent of M&B and the magic/force powers of Jedi Academy, but the swordplay is more active than M&B and without all the confusing randomness (that I felt) in the lightsaber battles of JA.
I hope you find this useful and would absolutely reccommend purchasing the game. Buying the game increases the player base and gives support to a game that has a lot of potential. Even though it is rough and incomplete, with support and patience I think this game could turn into something truly unique.
Anyway, that's my impression. Take it as you will and with discretion; thank you for your time.
