Oh man. OH MAN, this game. With the release of The Binding of Isaac's sequel, The Binding of Isaac; Rebirth having happened a couple months ago, I haven't played this in about as long of a time. However, it's still amazing. While the graphics are a bit strange, and Flash just sucks, if you've got patience and good hand-eye coordination, you'll be fine. In Isaac, as it's called, with the new one being Rebirth, you run through rooms, completely naked mind you, crying at enemies. I'm not sure how your tears fly forward and not just straight down Isaac's face, but physics. You can find different rooms, like a treasure/item room with a gold bordered doorframe and a keyhole, which will give you an item. You can get almost anything in there, from a bent spoon that makes your tears turn this way and that towards enemies, to a fetus in a jar with a snazzy tophat letting you call an airstrike, to a giant eye that makes you a cyclops with MASSIVE tears. There's also boss rooms, which hold some different monstrosity in it every floor. If you've every played the old Zelda games, this is that, but on a much bigger scale. First game, you've got three sets of floors, the Basement/Cellar, the Caves/Catacombs, and the Depths/Necropolis. In the Depths, you face and hopefully kill your mother. Next game, there's one more, the Womb/Utero. Turns out Mom isn't so dead, since her heart's still there. Later, you can go down one final trapdoor and fight Satan in Sheol, or rise up and fight Isaac in the Cathedral. He's... probably not you. If you beat him, too, you can run around a giant chest, where every chest you open has an item, like you find in the treasure rooms. Overall, Isaac is a huge game, and there's no way I can explain it all here. Go read a wiki, or watch Twitch, or even just Youtube.

We all know it: the rage that fills us when a party next door plays their music way too loud while you're trying to get some sleep. But what would happen if we put that rage into action? Well, this game certainely gives you an answer for that.
In the game you can play as several characters, but ultimately the story follows Darius, a guy who just wants to sleep. His rage for loud parties eventually turns him into a serial killer known as the "Party Hard Killer", who is hunted down by a cop who lost his daugther due to his first massacre. The story is told through the cop's perspective.
While the story is suprisingly indepth and has a well written ending, that's not really what's important for this type of game. As the Party Hard killer we have to kill all the guests of a party without dying or getting arrested. Your goal is it to kill everyone in secret and hide their bodies, though the game will not instantly fail you if someone catches you and calls the cops. On each map there are many traps you can use to flee or kill partygoers in total secret. You can also poison their beverage, but you don't want to find yourself right next to someone dying as it will be instantly blamed on you.
Overall, Party Hard is a great stealth strategy game with an amazing soundtrack that couldn't be more unique. The game has a medium difficulty, but it requires a great amount of patience to make it through all the levels.

Stellaris is a fantastic grand strategy, set in the vast expanse of space.  It is very detailed and takes some time to learn how to play, I restarted a few times just to be doomed to failure early on.
Once you gain a firm grasp of the game's concepts it becomes nearly impossible to stop playing. Starting with a small faction and setting out to create a vast empire, in whatever way you see fit.  In my case I took a small sect of humanity that had gotten lost among the stars, long forgotten by earth, and had them rise up through hardships to conquer the entire galaxy and purge all sentient life that was not human.  This is just one of many ways to play the game, you can choose from one of the many default factions or create your own faction and play your own story, complete with tons of traits and perks to really customize things your way.
The early game is where things really shine. Setting out into the unknown and colonizing new planets, researching new technologies, raising a fleet and armies, establishing contact with new species, going to war and taking other empires for your own, the list goes on and on.  Sadly the late game does not provide you with enough to really keep going, there are some late game crises which are a daunting task to deal with, but other than that it becomes quite slow. In my case it became a chore to wipe all life from the galaxy because I was so powerful and it just became a tedious task, I didn't really feel like I was accomplishing anything.
Despite things ramping down in the late game, Stellaris is still a worthwhile investment if you enjoy strategy games. It also has great mod support for when you get tired of the main game, I turned the whole game into the Star Wars universe from the Old Republic.
Definately worth playing.

I purchased the Galaxy edition last May, but did not spend much time with it until recently. I feel the simulation has great potential in so many ways. The interface (UI) is informative and unobtrusive. UI scaling is available, but the vanilla version is readable, and does not detract from the overall graphics. The graphics themselves are well done, and project a feeling of the immense size and complexity of the universe.  I cannot say that I fully understand the mechanics of the game as yet, as there are a wealth of decisions to be made.  I like the slower pace very much. The musical score is relaxing , appropriate, and varied. I would recommend the game to others who enjoy 4X simulations. Just be prepared to be patient, and not try to rush or speed things up. Also be prepared for a somewhat complex and steep learning curve. The reward is a thought provoking, challenging, and enriching gaming experience, with virtually endless replayability.
I also commend the developers for continually adding to the simulation, improving, tweaking, and balancing.
I do have two major suggestions for improvement:
1.Include a full, complete, fully narrated, step by step tutorial.  As it stands, you can elect to have continuous advice, which helps, but a full tutorial (game playthrough) with explanation would really help. This would help the simulation be more of an enriching challenge, rather than a source of overwhelming bewilderment, confusion, and frustration.
2,The second suggestion would be to have more difficulty levels, including a beginner level, such as "Very Easy", to help those who are just beginning and might be otherwise overwhelmed.  I would suggest two easier levels below "normal".
I can fully recommend the simulation, just be prepared to be somewhat overwhelmed at the onset of play, and don't try to rush through it.  It can be very relaxing and rewarding.

Sound and Music: 10. Also, this is moddable.

Gameplay: 9. I mean, it's a Paradox game. You're gonna tab out and do something else at some point...
Story: 10. I've not had the joy of doing the Horizon Signal Event yet, but there are a whole host of Anomalies with simple and Empire-shaking consequences. This contributes greatly to the replay value, especially given that your Empire will react to it based on their Ethics.
Length: 10. As slow or as quick as you need it to be, unless you need it to go superfast (like a month per second or something.)

Personal Enjoyment: 10.

If you took 2 of my favourite games "warrior king battles" and "civilization" moulded them together and then launched them into space this is what you get, a massive sink hole of time. This is a truely massive RTS with the length of a civilization game multiplied many times, this game is not for the misguided married people out there. There is plenty of replay value although 1 game on a large map ( not the biggest map the game has to offer ) will take you weeks to win at max speed. There are lots of events in the game, quite often triggered by the player but sometimes the AI that you may never witness ( which i like the fact no ones game will ever be the same ) that earn different rewards some only obtainable if you're the first and some are death. So when you get the choice always choose cake.
Most empire building games you learn the skill then produce the unit, while in this it's learn the skill to make part of a unit, at first you will only be able to make the smallest unit available, but what you make is all down to you. You decide what guns to use, maybe you dont like guns then why not torpedos or missiles or lazers, shields or no shields, thrusters or bigger thrusters, intelligent computer guidence systems or a casio calculator all limited to what you have learnt and all limited by power usage which can also be learned and improved. Unlike most games invention has no end, there is always an improvement to be learnt which means your going to have to work hard to catch up with the most advanced empires there is no plataux.
Like most of these games, the beginning can be the hardest but unlike all others as this gets towards the midway point it still retains a massive challenge. The AI is not daft, quite often by the time you have owned half the universe the other empires will usualy form a massive federation which presents a new challenge. I had a fleet with over 1.4 mil firepower and decided it was time to end the game due to the massive lag I was starting to get, declared war and headed to their largest fleet, with the lag rife and full on attack I had no idea what was going on, then after about 5 mins the bad things came lots of my ships were going red, this was a 2 weeks in the making of the fleet that was slowly being destroyed infront of me, a few minutes later and that was that, 2 weeks down the pan, no fleet and no hope although lag had settled down now.
Some general tips : making new civilizations ( native enlightment ) your protectorate, this will give you a .5 influence gain ( which is good ) but unlike what description says, they will never turn into vassels if you're playing the game right. You can learn as quick as your protectorates even with the 70 or 80 % bonus they get which means they will never get to the 40 % threshold needed for change, I made 5 protectorates right at start of game, week and a half later they are still cavemen in comparison to me. So only make protectorates if you dont want the system they are in, i.e no rare resources. So when it comes to new civs best option is to wait until they in the industry era then convert them unless you really need the influence gain. Planet size is massively important as to which planets to colonise 1st, as you add more planets to your empire this will directly impact your learning capability so more planets then more science is needed to compensate or you will just become a massive empire with cavemen weapons.
Always have the strongest fleet possible, just like most RTS the first battle you lose is a step to dissaster.

Reviewing this game as it is still only early access.
I LOVE This game, it is freaking awesome, the old school feeling, the sense of exploration, the sights! However, I know it is still only in early access but I think there needs to be a few things added, such as a slightly larger array of weapons, Toning down the OP-ness of Enemy Magic attacks (Seriously, it will kill you almost instantly with about three hits, when melee attacks to you would usually take only about 10 hits or more) A little bit more variety of elevators and/or secrets such as Buttons to uncover a secret passage, keys to open doors, Maybe add in chests for items, SUPER (That's right, different from the normal!) Secrets, a slightly more diverse Enemy Encounters, Like, more enemies, then again, there is a good selection of enemies already but eh. I don't think maybe adding in the ability to Jump in the game would be a good idea, leave that out, it's a dungeon crawler, no one can jump while crawling. (lol)
What this game is strongest in however is the difficulty, already mentioned how OP enemy magic attacks are, and that needs to be toned down ever so slightly. The sense of exploration is there and is great, the Music (Or ambient noises I guess) REALLY Immerse the player into the game, seriously, sometimes I even get shivers being creeped out, it gives you a sense of danger and fear, Afraid to turn a corner, there have been times I have been jump scared in this game because of the noises almost sounding like they bounce off the walls of the rooms. The inventory system is pretty good, you open the Inventory and the game does not pause, I like that, it gives the player a sense of panic, ESPECIALLY When you are trying to get out a potion of healing (You hope as the potions are randomized each time you play) which means you setting up your inventory bar is CRUCIAL in this game. A thing I would like to see but I kind of have gotten used to, is the ability to use the Mouse Wheel, as haing to use the 1-6 keys on my keyboard have more than once caused me to use a potion when I wanted to use my magic wand.
This game is FREAKING AWESOME, if you were ever in the times of floppy disks, and played those old dungeon crawlers, and love rouge-likes, and having to fear for your life because there is perma-death in the game, this game is your new best friend!

This charming little piece of dungeon crawling may have nothing truely unique to offer, but besides that, it's simple,solid and stylish. And it provides that eerie feeling I remember from exploring the caves in the Minecraft.
The combat is simple, yet engaging. There is a variety of melee,  ranged and magical weapons available and balancing quick, strong and ranged attacks is the key to survival.
The graphics of this game are really appealing. While pixelated, they perfectly fit together to create a consistent "minecrawl" experience. Special mention goes to the utterly hilarious, 80-90s anime styled facial expressions the human enemies make when hit. Music is also likable and moody.
What I didn’t really enjoy is the character leveling system.  While it is traditionally experience based, on every level the player is given 3 choices on what to upgrade. The problem is that there are more than three stats and thus sometimes there is no option to improve the desired characteristic and the  progress gets a bit random. Furthermore, there is no description regarding what a particular stat does. While most of them are self-explanatory,  a seasoned RPG gamer in me desires at least a basic defining of the difference between the Speed and Agility. Not much of a problem though – characters don’t usually live long enough to regret.
On the other hand, the game goes to the great lengths to make itself as user-friendly as the dungeon crawler can be. Traps are always clearly visible, and one cannot die of hunger, food restores the hit points instead.
The greatest problem with this game, at least for me, is the fact that it gets boring after a few runs. Nonetheless, it is perfect for the short evening sessions. Furthermore, when I decide to play a rogue it means something, since I’m usually too tired of starting over again and again in the real life to follow the same pattern in games. Still, Delver seems to be the right choice to spend a few nights with sword in your main and a glass of whisky in off hand. Yeah, I too used to play an ambidextrous character in the good, old DnD days.
Wersja polska
Delver jest uroczym, małym dungeon crawlerem. Nie wprowadza do gatunku nic nowego, ale za to jest prosty, solidny i stylowy. I powoduje to samo osobliwe uczucie co długi spacer po jaskiniach w Minecrafcie.
System walki jest prosty, ale wciągający. Gra daje do użytku spory wybór broni białej, dystansowej oraz zaklęć i znalezienie między nimi balansu jest kluczem do przetrwania.
Grafika, mimo pikseli na pół ekranu, robi świetne wrażenie. Kolory są jaskrawe i dobrane tak, że idealnie pasują do tego „minecrawla”. Gra dostaje ode mnie dodatkowe punkty za miny które robią niektórzy przeciwnicy kiedy oberwą – przypominające anime z lat 80-90, potrafią naprawdę rozbawić.  Muzyka też od razu wpada w ucho i świetnie buduje nastrój.
Gra podpada za to sysyemem levelowania postaci. Tradycyjnie, opiera się on na expach zdobywanych na wrogu, a przy każdym levelu dostajemy do wyboru 3 staty które możemy „podbić”. Problem polega na tym że cech opisujących postać jest więcej, więc czasem nie dostajemy opcji ulepszenie tego co akurat by się przydało i sprawia że rozwój postaci przebiega nieco losowo. Dodatkowo, cechy nie są w żaden sposób opisane. Niby nie problem domyślić się od czego jest atak a od czego wytrzymałość, ale zatwardziały RPGowiec we mnie domaga się jednak wytłumaczenia różnicy między szybkością a zręcznością. Inna sprawa że nie jest to jakiś straszny problem – bohater i tak na ogół nie żyje na tyle długo żeby żałować dokonanych wyborów.
Z drugiej strony Delver stara się jak może, by być przyjaznym graczowi. Pułapki zawsze są widoczne z daleka, a jedzenie odnawia HPki – nie można tu umrzeć z głodu.
Największy problem, przynajmniej dla mnie, to fakt że gra nudzi się dość szybko. Na krótkie sesje jest jednak idealna.  Co więcej, jeżeli polecam jakiegoś rogulca, musi coś w tym być, na ogół brakuje mi cierpliwości by zaczynać grę od początku po tym jak zginę. Podsumowując: Delver nadaje się idealnie do spędzenia kilku nocy z mieczem w jednej, a szklaneczką whisky w drugiej ręce. A co? Też grałem „oburęcznymi” postaciami w starych, dobrych, DnDkowych czasach.

A little more the same but some additions which i personally do not like. It's decent but not incredibly compelling. I cannot say I would recommend it and having bought every single nba2k game since 2k9 (when it came to pc), I find myself seriously considering whether or not to get the next one.
Do note that most of these comments are directed at mostly single-player MyCareer gameplay which is the feature I found/find most compelling and fun. It's not intended to apply to online multi-player play which I do not do enough of to form any informed opinion.
A big sour-note for some time from the series is how MyCareer has pretty much become you playing out a story written by someone else. While some of the stories have been interesting most of them are cliched and pigeon-hole you into some one's idea of what a baller should be. If there is going to be a story about my career, I would want MyCareer to be my story and one that I can choose for myself - not live out someone else's fantasy. In many ways. the older MyCareer without so much story-mode was so much more open and dynamic. With the last few iterations, it's always the same old story - high school phenom, such a nice person, yada yada yada. At least, the story a few iterations back (about not being drafted and having to work to find a team) was compelling (and also fit the starting stats they gave you). The recent ones including this one have literally all been such a drag. Which brings me to my first comment: -
1. You can't skip the cut-scenes! If I wanted to watch a movie, I'd watch a movie. I just want to play. Granted that some may enjoy these but I'm sure there are many like me who don't. Just give us the choice to skip through the cut-scenes at least after the first play through! Sometimes I like to re-roll a player, I like having different permutations/builds and players in different positions. Sitting through 3-5 minutes of cut-scenes every 6 minutes is terrible.
2. Not sure what they did to the movement/running mechanics but controlling a player feels like he's running on ice or has his feel stuck to the ground. The addition of momentum/inertia et al is well and good, but i figure that if a player is playing a college level (much less NBA-level), he should generally be able to run where he wants to.
3. A crap-load of illegal moving screens by the pc. Last instalment got too whistle-happy with the illegal screens, this one seems to forget it all together.
4. Not sure I like starting out MyPlayer pigeon-holed with the archtypes they think are appropriate. For once, I would be able to like to choose some starting skills/badges instead of being pigeon-holed. The whole best player in high school/lottery pick but starting out at 55 player rating is getting old. Either do away with the super baller rheotoric or do the stats some justice.
5. The practice routines start out ok, but become a serious grind after a while. The routines also need to be more varied and positional. It's ridiculous to expect a PF/C to go one-on-one with a star guard or take threes all the time. That said, after you've been playing for a while, it can get incredibly monotonous which while perhaps realistic is not the quite of simulation 2k was hoping for.
6. While the concept of having a buddy on court sounds great, I'm not too thrilled with the whole Justice Young thing. Firstly, this guy who supposedly couldn't even break into the 1st round draft because 'teams were put off by his size' comes out from the blocks having an 89-rating (my player got drafted by the Raptors, Kyle Lowry's a 88, this MBJ-clone is an 89 ... so much for immersion and credibility). Game-breaking much? Secondly, this developer-created guy is taking valuable minutes from legit real-life players. There's really only room for ONE imaginary player in MyCareer. Would have been more interesting if they made you earn the buddy with chemistry or something else with an existing player.

Borderlands 2 did a great job of fast shooting with surprisingly deep character customization. It did have its share of pacing blemishes though - blemishes I was really hoping that a new standalone game like Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel would fix. It doesn’t, but it does provide an entertaining story and a handful of successful gameplay additions that spice up its already excellent core of shooting and looting. This is, essentially, more of the Borderlands I love with just enough new twists to pull me back in, and mostly make up for the things the series still doesn’t get right.
The real star of the show in The Pre-Sequel is Jack. In Borderlands 2 he was perhaps the most gleefully sadistic, and effective video game villain. Seeing his journey from hero to maniac is perhaps the biggest reason to make the 20-or-so-hour trek across Pandora’s moon, Elpis. There a real knack for storytelling here, drawing a more sympathetic portrait of Jack without ever making him into the clichéd misunderstood villain. He's every bit the hilarious, ego-centric asshat here that we remember him as, and his excellently written and delivered dialogue is responsible for the lion's share of the laughs.

UPDATE - 10-10-2016
TL;DR- I do still enjoy the design and building aspects of the game, and the community has produced some great add-ons through the Steam Workshop, but I think the latest update adding the "Lite Campaign Mode" is actually a side step or, more accurately a downgrade.
****Updated Review****
I've been playing the Open Beta, which has just been pushed out to all Early Access customers. The "Lite Campaign Mode" is now available. This long awaited update is an improvement in some respects, but it's more confunding than anything.
First thing I noticed is that the game loads MUCH faster than it used to. We're talking probably 3-4x faster loading than before. So, the dev team has been hard at work at refining efficienices. The music still plays while it's loading, even though I have it set off in the menus. Can't have it all, right?
When the main menu loads, I noticed that Scenarios have been taken away, they now say In Developement. Well, now that Lite Campaign mode is here, I shouldn't need those any more... but it's a little odd to see functionality taken away. For those who don't have the game already, Scenarios was basically where you got a set of circumstances you had to design for and then you got scored based on how closely you matched or exceeded the circumstances. One I remember off the top of my head was to build a "Generator" for the Russian military in the engine designer. These scenarios were fixed (no random variety) and there was about a dozen of them, but there was replayability, as they were challenging enough that you had to work to get the platinum score.
I head right for the Campaign button. I click on the Lite Campaign mode, and am immediately presented with a screen full of selections and sliders. The three countries you can choose from are right there at the top, and each one has it's own set of likes and dislikes. Write these preferences down because this information will only be available in a giant number-filled grid which is not a pleasing nor easy to read format.
Next we have Company Tech. Seems self-explanatory, give yourself a head start in certain areas (or all areas), but apparently there's a limited number of points you can assign, which isn't explained anywhere, and when you adjust points up and down, and a points total at the top changes, but by adding the new point total by the old point total for some reason. You add one point in Drivetrain, there's one point added to the counter at the top. You add another point (totalling 2 in Drivetrain) and the counter at the top reads 3. Now you add a 3rd point, to drivetrain (I want to be really good at building drivetrains), and there's six points at the top. But, if I add 1 point to bottom end, it adds 1 point to the total at the top.. add a second, it adds 3 points to the top total... What? Why? How?
Doesn't matter, don't care, I want to PLAY! I give myself 2 points in each category. Next is Team, where you select team members, I guess. It's not really explained. So I select six random people... But, I don't have to? I can run the factory single handed? Should I hire the ceramics expert? Well, I'm starting in 1946, so maybe? Did people use more ceramics back then? I'm not entirely sure.
Next we have Cash & Competition, pretty self-explanatory, except the heading with "Competition" and then the $ sign. If you hover over the dollar sign, (which is the opposite of how most of the sliders in the game work, usually you hover over the slider, not the slider title) it says Competitor Car Markup Multipler. So, is that how much your competition marks up their cars? Is that how much higher you can markup the exact same car from your company versus your competition's? And this is represented as a straight number, 1.05 initially. Well, markup is usually a %.
Still reading? I'm sorry. We just got the lite campaign setup, this isn't even the gameplay, but it hints at what's ahead. Finally, I give up guessing what all this is supposed to do, and just start.
The next screen looks like the Sandbox screen. New Car, Revise Car, etc. Now I get to do my favorite part of this game, design a car and engine. Unfortunately, there is no additional help now that we're in campaign mode. There's no little inset window, or button you can click for a pop up to show how you're doing at hitting target categories. You just have to guess how to make the best Pony Budget, or Sport Budget, and can't tweak settings to see your changes affect it, without an unncessary amount of work.
So, I design a car and engine, get pretty close to the targets I want to hit, then I have to build the car, right? Well, here we have more confusion. You can select from Small, Medium, and Large factories; easy enough. Now, do I want a size 1, 2, or 3? I don't know, it doesn't really elaborate any more on what each of them do. There's also no price attached to any of the choices. And no prices for any of the factory upgrades you can purchase.
Factories are set up, I skip to when the car is ready to go into production (but I only get that dialog, if I step linearly through the game, that dialog never shows up if I go back and make a tweak to the car or its production). So, I run the production, and that's when I notice EVERY month is 30 days long... even February. I'm done.
Camshaft software has done a great job creating a beautiful car and engine designer, but I think they're a little lost on creating the tycoon aspects. Maybe you guys should team up with the lone guy who's creating GearCity. His car/engine designer is nowhere near as sophisticated, but he's got all the Tycoon aspects down really well.
*****Original Review Below******
I love being able to design a car from the ground up, but that is all this game currently is, and all it has been in the year since I purchased it. It's supposed to be a tycoon game, but there are NO aspects of this yet. Updates are EXTREMELY slow. There hasn't been one since April, that I've noticed.
Let me tell you what I HAVE noticed that's changed in the last year: V12's and V12 turbos. That's it. Nothing else from the devs. I paid $29.99 on July 11, 2015. That's a long time in Early Access, and a long time with so little content update. I'm still a fan of this game, but because of the long wait between updates and the lack of ANY tycoon elements, I can't recommend this. When/if this game ever nears completion I would be very happy to consider recommending it.
For the gearheads: This game reminds me of those great drag racing games of the late 90's (NHRA/NIRA Drag Racing) where you can build motors and such. But, it is extremely unfinished, and is conspicuously lacking certain features. For instance, there are NO flat engines (boxer type), no Inline 8's (the game starts in the 40's.. c'mon!); you just have a generic slider to adjust camshaft profiles, which doesn't really reflect the nuances of adjusting duration, timing, etc. Does 100% mean a lumpy cam? Does that mean it doesn't run well on the bottom end?

I must say after A LONG time playing this game, I've seen its good side and bad side.
Let's start with the good sides.
-The game has a solid game engine, the designs are impressive, and the realism of the statistics are superb. I even learned how to tune a turbo from Youtube. The community is amazing and supportive and aren't the kind of people that would brag about their knowledge and skills, they treat one another with respect. The game is pretty unique for its genre and you can't argue with that. When you start playing this game, I recommend experimenting as much as you can with the engine designer. The Car Body designer is pretty straight foward, the wider the wheel arches, the bigger the tire width. The mods can make a huge difference, you can get headlight mods and grille mods to make your car EVEN MORE unique then before. Its definitely a potential force to be reckoned with, after its Early Access phase.
Now the bad sides.
-The learning curve in this game is EXTREMELY steep, if you aren't willing to go through the pain of learning how to play and make engines, then good luck. The game is Early Acess which means the bugs are everywhere...and I mean EVERYWHERE. You can crash out of nowhere in this game and it gets pretty annoying pretty fast. Oh yea and the updates aren't as consistent as you would think. Sometimes it could be every week, some times it could stop out of nowhere without them telling others what they are working on; happens rarely though. And Finally, the designs are pretty limited at the moment. You can get mods but... They aren't updated as often and they are the main reason why they crash the game, when you install them. Unless you are creative, you will be spending a lot of time in this game. I've been playing this game for 5 hours a day in a month then I stopped after it got boring. It gets pretty boring after you try EVERYTHING in the game.
Overall, this game has HUGE potential and A LOT of work needed to complete it. This game is probably one of my favorite Car Simulator, in terms of engine and body designing, that I have every laid eyes on. Yea...This game has tons of flaws but hey! Its made by a 3 person team. That is very incredible to see how much dedication they have done to this game in more than 3 years+. The complexity may overwhelm you at first due to the learning curve but as you get used to it, you'll be having fun,
My score would be 7.9/10. Mostly due to the learning curve, the Beta, and the bugs associated with this game. But, this game gets interesting as soon as you get the hang of it and get more creative with your designs and how you create them.

This is a great f2p title. After my short time in the game here are my thoughts:
Pro:
-The cash shop certainly feels optional and the devs show restraint in advertising it.
-The graphics are not ground breaking, but certainly they are certainly appealing. They remind of update Ratchet and Clank.
-The combat is engaging. The slight twist on the skill tree and hotbar mechanics compliment the action well, and allow for a lot of experimentation in the early levels before having to commit to a build.
-The quests available are plentiful and varied enough to hold interest. They Path quests and world challenges make it very easy to take break from you story line quests.
-The Path feature is nice because it certainly does a good job of changing the experience for each character.
Cons:
-The UI sometimes feels uninspired or even unfinished. For example, the character and target portraits seem to be at a lower resolution than the game world itself. Unless I'm missing something in the options, it's a strange distinction.
-When following the main story line, I had the quest system break on me twice. When completing and turning in the current quest the next one was not available to me. I had to have a party member accept it and then share it with me. Then it was back on track.

FIRST IMPRESSIONS REVIEW. This is the only MMORPG that after I played for the first time I begged for more. I don't have much time because I'm leveling with friends, but just know that if I had no friends you'd see double digits. First of all, this game has CHARM. This normally isn't talked about when reviewing a game, but I think it's extremely important. The humor is great in this game, and the characters have a ton of, well... character! Games like World of Warcraft were so successful because they WERE unique and their own thing. You can't really say Wildstar is a copy of anything. Sure, it has elements similar to WoW (like literally every MMORPG ever) and Ratchet and Clank. But the combination of all the attributes is very unique. Second, the visuals are amazing. I personally LOVE the cartoony style they went with, and the fact that it looks very polished and clean makes it even better. It also runs very well (at least on my computer). Third, the combat is really fun and appeals even to people that don't play MMORPGs. The questing so far has been really fun, mainly because of the world. The narrative is pretty good too. I honestly have no legitimate complaints about this game AT ALL since the developers can't help the low popularity. I can't say much about the dungeons, raiding, and pvp yet because I haven't played much of the game. However, you can't criticize me about this until you criticize the countless numbers of negative reviews with even less hours than me. Overall - 10/10/ Underrated masterpiece.

Stellaris is your run-of-the-mill 4X grand strategy game (think Europa Universalis(but in space!)), It also has many of the in-game concepts I find so appealling and realistic about Paradox titles; both of these coming together to create a realatively GOOD game. You know what this game is about so I'll tell you how it differs from it's competitors. For starters, the real-time pause-for-command scheme works well in a grand strategy format (As opposed to your turn-based), and this title is the culmination of Paradox's years of releasing solid titles w/ similar ideas/controls/UI. It also applies many of its geo-political and cultural decisions to make the running of a space empire more interesteing as well as "real" which I feel many games of the genre lack. The ship designer is more like a customizer, fun but really lacking the depth and freedom of something like Galactic Civilizations. However, the detail and graphics for the game allow you to zoom in quite close and rotate the camera around the individual ships of your fleet, making for a true 3D experience, which during massive firefights can be quite amazing to watch playout. Your leaders/generals/admirals all have names/skills/ and an age, which means they all vary in use and inevitably die (Your race can largely depict the factors of this). Diplomacy (as referred earlier) is just as in-depth as you'd probably like w/ little micromanagement but enough to make you keep your eye on it (ie HOI, EU). Now for the bad part; successfully doing all those things so well, I feel the game really falls short in the combat area (IFFY COMBAT). Although there is a large variety of ships/classes/races/tech I feel like the battles were truly just a matter of numbers when I wasnt just geting my♥♥♥♥♥handed to me using mass drivers and FTL. That is a commonly found issue with Paradox titles I know, but maybe more so in this case?

Favourite part about this game is the freedom to create your own empire in your own image. For example, i made squid aliens and called it The Cthulu Empire which destroy and enslave entire star systems for there supreme emperor Cthulhu.

Absolutely try it out, if you haven't in the last 12 month!
It's a highly polished game with absolutely awesome combat and tons of content!

Ok,
, where do I start?
Well first the good parts. I am very fond of the art style and the story. The game has a lot of details: from how the characters interact, how the environment has many interactive elements. The cut scene explains the story while keeps the player entertained (I like the voiceover very much). The game also brims with dark humor.
The game has potentials. The theme of "disturbed neighbor at 3 am turned mass murderer" is very unique and interesting.
Then why do I not recommend it?
Because the gameplay is poor. As the killer you are not supposed to let anyone see you do the killing, and that's it. If somebody does, they call the police and identifies you as the killer and you get caught. Problem is that the people in the game have no moving patterns; some stay put and some alternating between walking somewhere and staying there for a minute. So even though you need to go stealth and have "strategy", you really don't. All you do is to wait for your next victim to wander to some corner and then kill him/her, ideally hide the body.
The gameplay for every round goes like this: interact with environment (set trap) and kill whoever you can, carry sleeping people to corners and kill them, wait for people to wander to corners and kill them, kill the rest of the people who don't move before the cops come.
Again, no strategy involved. Before I purchase the game I did not look close enough; before I played I guessed the game to be either a massacre game or an assasination game (I preferred the former for the theme). For the former, I figure
is pretty good. For the latter, I guess
? But either way, not this one.
It's not terrible, but it delivers little, and you get bored soon. Stress relief? There are plenty of violent games on Steam.

Stellaris is a fantastic grand strategy, set in the vast expanse of space.  It is very detailed and takes some time to learn how to play, I restarted a few times just to be doomed to failure early on.
Once you gain a firm grasp of the game's concepts it becomes nearly impossible to stop playing. Starting with a small faction and setting out to create a vast empire, in whatever way you see fit.  In my case I took a small sect of humanity that had gotten lost among the stars, long forgotten by earth, and had them rise up through hardships to conquer the entire galaxy and purge all sentient life that was not human.  This is just one of many ways to play the game, you can choose from one of the many default factions or create your own faction and play your own story, complete with tons of traits and perks to really customize things your way.
The early game is where things really shine. Setting out into the unknown and colonizing new planets, researching new technologies, raising a fleet and armies, establishing contact with new species, going to war and taking other empires for your own, the list goes on and on.  Sadly the late game does not provide you with enough to really keep going, there are some late game crises which are a daunting task to deal with, but other than that it becomes quite slow. In my case it became a chore to wipe all life from the galaxy because I was so powerful and it just became a tedious task, I didn't really feel like I was accomplishing anything.
Despite things ramping down in the late game, Stellaris is still a worthwhile investment if you enjoy strategy games. It also has great mod support for when you get tired of the main game, I turned the whole game into the Star Wars universe from the Old Republic.
Definately worth playing.

I purchased the Galaxy edition last May, but did not spend much time with it until recently. I feel the simulation has great potential in so many ways. The interface (UI) is informative and unobtrusive. UI scaling is available, but the vanilla version is readable, and does not detract from the overall graphics. The graphics themselves are well done, and project a feeling of the immense size and complexity of the universe.  I cannot say that I fully understand the mechanics of the game as yet, as there are a wealth of decisions to be made.  I like the slower pace very much. The musical score is relaxing , appropriate, and varied. I would recommend the game to others who enjoy 4X simulations. Just be prepared to be patient, and not try to rush or speed things up. Also be prepared for a somewhat complex and steep learning curve. The reward is a thought provoking, challenging, and enriching gaming experience, with virtually endless replayability.
I also commend the developers for continually adding to the simulation, improving, tweaking, and balancing.
I do have two major suggestions for improvement:
1.Include a full, complete, fully narrated, step by step tutorial.  As it stands, you can elect to have continuous advice, which helps, but a full tutorial (game playthrough) with explanation would really help. This would help the simulation be more of an enriching challenge, rather than a source of overwhelming bewilderment, confusion, and frustration.
2,The second suggestion would be to have more difficulty levels, including a beginner level, such as "Very Easy", to help those who are just beginning and might be otherwise overwhelmed.  I would suggest two easier levels below "normal".
I can fully recommend the simulation, just be prepared to be somewhat overwhelmed at the onset of play, and don't try to rush through it.  It can be very relaxing and rewarding.

--THIS IS A REVIEW OF THE GAME AS OF THE 19TH OF OCTOBER, 2014. THE GAME IS SUBJECT TO CHANGE IN THE FUTURE.--
Now, I shall get all of the potential negatives out of the way first. Yes, the game is light on content. With only a few enemy types and one dungeon, skilled players may find themselves quickly consuming all the game has to offer. That, and some occasional bugs that very rarely appear but can be annoying sometimes.
With that all said, this game is brilliant value for money. £5.59 for a game as addictive as this is a steal, and in my opinion the dev could get away with charging a little more. The pixel art aesthetic is pulled off expertly, as so many other indie dungeon crawlers are from a top down perspective or 2D, it's refreshing to play a FPDC (first person dungeon crawler). The potion system in the game gives a tense atmosphere when you are at low health, having you gamble with fate as you could consume a health potion, or get a poison debuff alongside many other potion effects. Combat is very simple, but this works in the games favour as it makes all combat encounters very quick, which is essential as it makes runs shorter going hand in hand with the permadeath mechanic.
All in all, for the stage it's at now and the price tag it has, this is a great game, and with more content on the way, I highly recommend you buy it now.

Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel is FPS RPG developed by 2K Australia and Gearbox Software, and released in 2014.  Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel is pretty much Borderlands 2 but on the moon/station seen over Pandora. If you're not sure if you'll like borderlands: The Pre-Sequel, go give Borderlands 2 a try.
Borderlands: The Pre-sequel takes place between the first Borderlands game and Borderlands 2. If you couldn't figure that out for yourself based on the colorful word-play.
To add a bit more clarification or to completely lose you: The story is actually taking place AFTER Borderlands 2, but in story format, as told by Athena
.
The controls feel pretty much the same as Borderlands 2, or generic FPS's, WASD to move, mouse to move the camera, keyboard rebinding is available, mouse wheel up or down to change weapons, or press 1,2,3,etc. I've always liked the controls in Borderlands games, simple straightforward, no keyboard piano playing.
But wait!
! Namely Gravity! If you're outside of a location that has artificial gravity
you will float higher on your jumps. While definitely entertaining, and adding a whole new level of stress when you miss a long jump.
There's a new mechanic that you can also press CTRL (or whichever key you bind) to slam down onto the ground, or on top of enemies. A new gear slot will represent an air container which is necessary for all humans to survive in the vacuum of space but furthermore doubles as being used for double jumping in space.
Enemies sometimes drop air canisters that will replenish some of your air, there are other locations where you can go to get oxygen filled up, buildings, and specific devices which create a force-field of air you can stand in.
There are several sources you can get a sensation of progression in Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel. The most obvious representation of progression is by story progression or level progression. After you finish the story you can repeat the story again to continue leveling until you reach the cap.
Or you can reroll another character, if you made the mistake of playing Claptrap on your first play through like I did. For those that don't know, even though claptrap is hilariously annoying vocally... he makes a terrible playable character, when you use your special ability you're basically rolling dice and the game tries to judge your situation for whichever vault hunter power to immitate.
Unfortunately the game decided my situation required me to blow myself up 9 times out of 10. Yes I'm a bit salty about that. I don't use self destruction abilities in any video game really. So yeah, good times. It was fun hearing his cackling while I bounced on top of people, and it was nice not breathing air. Butttttt... I was a liability.
Borderlands doesn't try to aim for "realism" in their game assets, instead they stylize their characters, models, and textures. This is very good in the long run, because it increases the longevity of the games appeal. You don't need to jump into the most recent game to enjoy the newest aesthetics, they start to average out over all their games.
Don't get me wrong, there is a sign of improvement from game to game, but the style they use stays very uniformed rough and "Borderlands-y".
Borderlands: The Pre-sequel is priced at $39.99, and the game with the season pass is priced at $69.99. If you're an achiever you will need to get the "Holodome Onslaught" and "Claptastic Voyage" DLC to earn 100%. At the time that I'm writing this review I've played 36 hours of Borderlands: The Presequel. That number will definitely change, there is still plenty to do, so you can definitely get your moneys worth out of game time.
All in all, I've enjoyed what I've experienced with Borderlands: The Presequel, It's been most fun playing it with friends. I've enjoyed "flying" around
and as I so eloquently imaged it
the NPC's.
In a way the game feels shorter then it's predeccessor
, so if you're looking for the best quality borderland games, this one doesn't have too much to offer outside of a couple new gimmicks and a few new playable characters. Story-wise, it's definitely worth it and very interesting! This game makes me want to own Jacks Hyperion Jacket.
In conclusion, I'm not sure what to tell people, It's borderlands 2 ...in space! If you like borderlands, if you enjoy FPS, if you like the humor in the game series, you'll love this game just like borderlands 2.

A fantastic survival horror game with a distinct emphasis on survival.  Draws strong influence from Silent Hill series (no secret that the game's creator, Jasper Byrne, is a fan).  It feels like a 16-bit version of Silent Hill with a dash of Eternal Darkness thrown in.  You are a survivor of an outbreak that has devastated your city.  You awake in your apartment alone, supplies nearly exhausted and find yourself forced to confront the horrors outside to both gather life-sustaining supplies and perhaps find a way to escape the decaying city.  Along the way you will encounter mysterious figures and come to question which, if any, of these encounters even happened.  Unlike many run n' gun action survival horror games. Combat is not something encouraged and you must also take care of your basic biological needs such as eating and sleeping lest your mental health deteriorate and cause you to descend into madness.  It's a bit short but it's execution and artistic style are superb.
Honestly one of the best horror games I've had the pleasure of playing through :)

I like this game, but it has a ton of glaring issues. It's not what it should be nor is it what it wants to be, yet.
This is a rogue-lite in its lightest form, providing hardly any differentiation between runs. The differences will be in the traits you obtain at levels 5/10/15, the items you get from chests (which are varied in usefulness, but are mostly similar and few) and of course mob drops/mob spawns. The layouts for each district follow a very strict pattern, involving massive sections next to each other as opposed to the standard 1x1 platform-style stage randomization. Each non-town district would blend into each other if it weren't for the differing biomes, which serve as alternate mob spawn pools for easier access to certain resources often at the cost of an increased difficulty.
Towns in this game currently serve very little purpose outside of a few obvious fantasy tropes. You have the Blacksmith, the Tailor and the Leatherworker, the latter two having static and unchanging names. You also have two shopkeepers which offer normally pointless and randomized items from the shop pool. Tools and weapons being sold are typically out of your price range when you'd need them, and entirely skippable once you have the gold for them. There are sometimes potions on sale, as well as herbs and hilts for treeless runs (I'll mention it later) but other than those the item pool for the shops aren't fantastic. Finally, there's the Hoarder that allows you to sell your items, which you'd think would be absolutely useful... But the sell price for each and every item you'll get ranges from 1-3 gold depending on said item. Weapons don't offer large sell prices, nor do armors. The Hoarder is a very cheap man.
The main issue with shops (again) is that they're normally pointless as far as tools and weapons go. With enough experience and proper door selection, you'll almost ALWAYS find the resources you need to make shops irrelevant. Heck, normally the only thing I'm missing at the end of each run are rings (which fight against a rather large and annoying chest drop pool) and rarely one piece of armor. I can go ahead and find a friend to wear a miner's cap to completely resolve the ore deficiency we may have.
Finally, Altars sometimes also spawn in towns, and are the only non-constant you'll find outside of giant chickens and normal chickens. (They're not worth talking about, food and potion drops if you're curious.) Altars are currently money sinks for the runs that offer their bounties long before the shops care to stock them, which is normally what happens as stated before. Altars cost 500 gold, which is a steep price for what they offer: A chance at a minimal stat buff, debuff or nothing at all. Rarely you'll earn a return to full health which is by far the best result most of the time, but the game is very stingy with both the spawn rate and good results of the Altars. By the time you have the money to trigger an Altar, you may not even find one... And sometimes they'll spawn when there's clearly no way you could have the money already without chopping every tree down. Normally, it's not worth the min-maxing.
... Min-maxing... Forgot about that. This game's mechanics are often lacking fluidity. Min-maxing is something that seems to be discouraged, due to the Scourge Invasion mechanic (a mechanic Spelunky players will find familiar, but irrelevant) and the rewards often not being worth the effort. Most of your min-maxing is for gold, from chopping tons of trees to continuing to break open each ironite ore deposit even when ironite is otherwise out of uses. Your reward for gold farming is, again, Altars and the occasional shop item before you have the chance to forge it.
Forging is relatively self-explanatory, but crafting can be a little tricky. Crafting is done via shift-clicking two items like an awkward Bejeweled puzzle. It's an easy mechanic, the issue is just the recipes at times. A lot of the early crafting recipes build off of each other, which provides cohesion and ease of access to tools and weapons. Some of the later items are either wiki bait, or "Oh, I didn't know that existed!" items. It can get awkward, but with enough thought it's not too bad. There's not too many crafting recipes to memorize, so once you have the main ones you're set.
Combat is simple. Grab a weapon, attack. If you want to use an item, hold it in your hands and right-click. Every item can be left-clicked with to hit enemies melee-style, and that's based off of your ATK stat. Staves and Bows can be right-clicked with to cast spells/shoot arrows, which are based on MAG and DEX respectively. Typically, people break down their runs to three classes. (it's often necessary with the lack of inventory space if you're somewhat new to the game still) With the speed of some mobs, and the fact that a lot of mobs in the game fly, melee is at a huge disadvantage. Ranged players will be able to aim their shots from afar, without aggroing enemies and easily taking out a majority of the mobs they'll see. The downside to Ranged play is that walls can often prevent shots, and by the time you get past the wall they'll have seen you. With the addition of the Fire Bow, you won't be having any issues with damage should you find it. Resources for arrows are normally quite plentiful as well.
Mages are strong. Too strong. Fireball shoots horizontally, moving forward seemingly infinitely and even passing through walls. While this is a powerful weapon, there is the downside of accidentally killing enemies and having their xp despawn if you're not careful... But honestly that's the only con to it, which is absurd. Bolt is pretty much the god staff, allowing you to shoot directly both above and below you. With jumps, timing and practice, this is normally the superior option. There's also a strange bug that makes each shot hit the target enemy once for each player in the run, which Fireball is unable to do. Frostshard is more of a melee supplement, offering additional damage that's halved from your current maximum mana. Mages are normally a distance away from their enemies, so it normally provides little to no benefit... If it costed one mana like the other two staves, it might be worth the effort of even using. Summon Zombie is also an option if you find it or use the Scourgeling race, but against flying enemies it's worthless.

Speaking of races, each race has it's own specialties. However, some are clearly superior to others. Typically you'll want to unlock the best races early on to put yourself at ease. Some races such as the Qualogg provide utility instead of immediate additional power.
Unlockables for character creation include the aforementioned races, the hats and also companions. Like races, there are a few certain hats and companions which are obvious choices once unlocked over the other ones, which is unfortunate. Each unlockable set has at least one thing that's insanely challenging, but most are either freebies or based on RNG which is really unfortunate.
The game is simple. Once you know what you're doing, it's as easy as going through the motions. You'll get all the items you need to beat the final boss, and you'll always win even if you're not a seasoned veteran. The skill cap is so low I feel like I'm in a hobbit hole.
If you want a game to play with friends when you're bored and you don't have better options, this is a nice game to pick up. (just be weary of multiplayer issues such as de-syncing) If you want a fully featured game with proper balancing and potential for failure even after learning it's mechanics and practice, you'll want to wait on your purchase of this game. I still recommend it, just don't expect wonders in it's current state... I'm sure with time the balance issues will be ironed out and the game will have more to accomplish and do.
Sean Young, if you're reading this I do hope you can find some ways to take care of these issues.

Overall, I've really enjoyed my journey alongside Jiayun and her friends through the select locations in Nanjing. To end this review, I think this particular quote sums up the whole experience rather well:

Shortly after I originally bought Shan Gui a strange occurence happened which left the developers with no control of their novel in any significant way, which left them in a fairly unpleasant situation where the only options were asking Valve to take it down or give up and no concern themselves with it any longer. It was most disappointing news since despite its short story it was a well made visual novel with an engaging soundtrack and nice art, and though I was looking forward to the next game after reachind the ending, it didn't seem likely that I'll be able to see a sequel. Thankfully, I was wrong.
Much like the previous game this one too introduces a small group of people who happen to meet on a quiet afternoon as they are led there by simple wishes, that would pass unnoticed even by those who are there, like any other moment before arriving there.
An unexpected meeting. A chance encounter.
Yet it is this seemingly everyday moment so seldom seen in modern age that brings them who would never have known one another under other circumstances to spend fleeting days in their company, that they do not see as significant yet. And as time passes on they become more and more precious, discovering much that was always nearby never being noticed, influencing not just their present, but so much more.
One of the first art pieces that greet the reader after starting the game is the main menu's familiar style reminiscent of watercolor paintings which Shan Gui's graphics featured as well, beautifully illustrating many of the sights found in the story as it slowly unfolds before us. Since it's meant more for the special events though, one will also see photographic looking backrounds on quite a few occasions that fit in pretty well, not unlike other doujin novels with similar looks. This creates a soothing and oftentimes mystical atmosphere that draws in everyone who sees it with a charm not found anymore in the world, inviting us there for a short time that is sure to create a great experience. Therefore be it the interior of a cafe or a night illuminated by faint lights, there is little doubt that even with the seemingly limited space where this title takes place, it is much more pleasant as one might expect from an indie game.
To my sadness and disappointment I found that the soundtrack in this game doesn't feel the reach the same level of feeling its predecessor had, the simple tunes of a piano playing not present where I was looking for them and the performance of a different kind acts as subtle invitation to begin the story. That is not to say that it isn't enjoyable or can't be listened to at all as it has many nice songs which would be to one's liking, but still different enough to be noticable which may influence the novel's atmosphere in a pleasant way or perhaps less so if one is inclined so. Still it is a very good album with tracks that lend themselves well to the game, therefore it's certainly worth listening to them since they're part of the whole experience, much like anything else.
It should also be noted that unlike the previous installment this one isn't a kinetic novel with only one storyline but has several points where the choices made will influence how it ends, providing not just a measure of replayability, but a lot more that can only be seen by engaging in several playthroughs. These simple yet great additions offer a great experience which are while not strictly required to discover in order to understand the events there, it is still strongly recommended to do so since they form an important part of the game. Sadly there's only so many of them due to limitations on its length, but they are still worth looking for when one gets the chance all the more since access is fairly simple unlike what it may suggest at a single glance.
While Bai Qu is certainly not the greatest visual novel ever created even when considering other similar indie titles, it is no doubt still a nice game different from most in many areas, gently offering for a short time a journey that will certainly leave a pleasant impression. And while its price may be a little offputting to some seeing that it's noticably more expensive as Shan Gui was, but it's still within the acceptable range when bought during a sale, so that shouldn't necesseraly be problem either. For a journey holds many wonderful moments that are only waiting for someone to discover them, and even a single step that may pass unnoticed at other times may become the beginning of a transient yet amazing chance, serving as an invitation that few will ever see in their life.

Amazing visual novel. I really don't have the words to express how much I thought of the story, the characters, and the VN as a whole, but I'll try to organize my thoughts as best I can. (ps I definitely played for much more time than it says, but I had Steam offline most of the time so I think that affected it. Oops.)
Setting: Excellent. There are a TON of different backgrounds and character portraits. Unlike a lot of VNs that you'd spend a lot more money on, the constant changing of scenery and expressions made sure that it never felt monotonous. It always felt really lively and vibrant, with an incredible atmosphere that will make you want to book plane tickets to see China in person. The characters didn't feel like they were hastily pasted over a background, but like part of the scenery, and there are dozens and dozens of beautiful CGs. Some are more eye-catching and artistic, others are more casual but still well-composed and nice to look at. You won't go a very long while before getting a new CG to stare at.
Characters: All of the characters were very well-rounded, expressive, and distinct from one another in personality. The main characters were all really strong emotionally, to boot. I really felt an attachment towards Jiayun, He Jia, Nurse Yang, and even the POV character Qiuwu. Even Qiuwu's parents were really funny, though we didn't get to see them drawn. My only criticism is that I wasn't really invested in He Jia's extended family/family acquaintances, though I liked them well enough. Qiucheng was pretty cool.
Voice Acting: Stellar. Like many VNs, not all characters have portraits (though the vast majority of them do), but for the ones who don't, you barely notice due to how professional and emotive the voice acting is. Again, Qiuwu's parents are awesome. Most VNs I skip through and don't bother listening to the entire sentence, but this one made me want to hear them out even though I don't understand Chinese AT ALL.
Music/Sound: Not bad. It definitely sets the mood, but you could get tired of it after a while. Still, I left it playing most of the time, which is more than I can say for most VNs. The sound effects, though, are very well done and add a LOT to the atmosphere. There was definitely a lot of effort put into them, and they really make it feel more life-like. Occasionally, you even get to hear characters play an instrument or sing.
Story: The overarching story is a very simple one, about a boy meeting a girl in the last few months of her life. This is not a spoiler; it's explained that she died as the set-up for the story which is told as an extended flashback. In this time, the pov character Qiuwu makes a major impact on the lives of Jiayun and those around her, as they do the same for him and he ends up with several new, unbreakable bonds and a close-knit nakama. Dealing with terminal illness is never easy, but this game is NOT a tragedy. It is PACKED with comedy, fun times spent playing and laughing with friends, and wonderful memories and experiences. Trying not to spoil too much but there's an arc where Qiuwu tries to teach a few other characters to ride a bike, and a class play featuring Jiayun and He Jia, and it's good. It's really good. Only in the last 2.5 chapters out of 10 is there even a hint of sadness, and the game never tries to milk the situation for tragedy or make the player cry. There's like a REALLY good chance you'll cry, but you will NOT feel manipulated into it.
English Translation: More than passable! I was really worried that it would be awkward and difficult to read, but it certainly gets the point across! It's not perfect and you can tell that the script wasn't originally in English, but I never felt like this was a huge hurdle to get over.
Cons: This is gonna be really short, but the con is that there aren't a lot of choices at all. I think there are like 5 of them, more or less? So it isn't a very interactive VN like I usually prefer. There are multiple endings which is definitely a big plus, but I've only gotten one so far.
Overall: 100/100 just read it already!

Many of you are probably aware of Shan Gui, an indie kinetic novel made in China that comes with some really adorable emoticons. While it was a cute story, it didn't come with no flaws: it was very short, its "educational" angle with Wikipedia links was silly, and the characters were drawn in an...
fashion. Nonetheless, I still enjoyed Shan Gui for what it was and was pleasantly surprised to hear that the sequel is finally coming. Now that I have it, what do I think?
The story is told from perspective of Wei Qiuwu, student from the Chinese city of Nanjing who befriends Li Jiayun, an ill girl. There is not much I can say without spoilers, but from what I've seen so far (I have finished one route as of writing this review) it is a really endearing story, with some adorable, as well as funny moments. Ties to Shan Gui are really loose, there is only one returning character (He Jia) and both VNs take place in Nanjing, and that's it. On one hand it might be disappointing that Han Hui did not return, but on the other it also means that you could skip Shan Gui and go straight to Bai Qu.
Bai Qu is also definitely pleasant to look at and listen to. The background illustrations are beautiful, and the music easily justifies buying the OST. As for other aspects of graphics and sound, I was okay with the characters' voices, although with them speaking in Chinese I could have missed some minor screw ups. It did at least have higher production values than Shan Gui, which had some recordings sounding like they were recorded in a closet with a cheap microphone, while in Bai Qu I only recall one scene with a minor character with low quality voice. There is also the matter of how the characters are drawn, which is an improvement over Shan Gui, but the artist still has a... distinctive style to them, which may deter some people.
One flaw as of now (August 3rd, 2017) that I don't really want to talk about, but I feel like I must mention, is the English translation. At first it looked quite good, but soon it turned out it has its share of typos and some other mistakes. Luckily it never becomes incomprehensible, but it absolutely needs more polish. There is at least a sticky in the forum that requests mistakes pointed out, so improvements are absolutely a possibility.
Bai Qu is probably a hit or miss kind of VN, but for me at least it was a hit. It will definitely be much better once the translator team cleans up the text, but it's still something that Chinese readers can be proud of.

Alright. First off, i just wanna say that at the time of writing this review, I haven't reached the full extent of this game's potential- I haven't even finished the first playthrough myself (iteration? i don't want to spoil anything I know). In my opinion, this game deserves Game Of The Year award, and i give huge amounts of kudos to Yoko Taro and his group. This is a third-person, open-world hack-and-slash rpg, implementing many elements from completely different genres, like bullet hells, and top down puzzle-solvers, as well as side scrollers, sometimes. There are also rather unique, but not entirely unheard of game mechanics, that CAN be explained through lore- for example, when you die certain items stay behind, in a "corpse, " which you can choose to collect from, or revive as a temporary ally.,This keeps the game interesting, for the most part (if sometimes maybe a bit annoying). The soundtrack has had a HUGE amount of work put into it, and it shows. The storytelling (again, in my opinion) is right up there with excellent games like SOMA, Undertale, and The Last Of Us (I could name a few more great ones). One thing it has that many things, not just games, fail to reach nowadays- the ability to convey a message, to make people cry, to (maybe) encourage people to take action, for whatevewr reason they feel they have to take action for. There is MASSIVE amounts of replayability value (hint, hint) in this game, and I think DLC for the game is going to drop sometime in the next few months. Now, it's not to say it doesn't have its flaws- sometimes, things may seem a bit boring or confusing, as is with some open-world, single player games? However, when the action really gets going, many parts of the game come together to get you pumped- up, and in that urgent mood- the game seems to save certain variations of songs for those particular situations. I think that should do for all I can think of. I should try to put a few more negatives, but at that point I'd be nitpicking about small issues. My point? GET THIS GAME. YOU (probably) WILL NOT REGRET.

Stellaris is your run-of-the-mill 4X grand strategy game (think Europa Universalis(but in space!)), It also has many of the in-game concepts I find so appealling and realistic about Paradox titles; both of these coming together to create a realatively GOOD game. You know what this game is about so I'll tell you how it differs from it's competitors. For starters, the real-time pause-for-command scheme works well in a grand strategy format (As opposed to your turn-based), and this title is the culmination of Paradox's years of releasing solid titles w/ similar ideas/controls/UI. It also applies many of its geo-political and cultural decisions to make the running of a space empire more interesteing as well as "real" which I feel many games of the genre lack. The ship designer is more like a customizer, fun but really lacking the depth and freedom of something like Galactic Civilizations. However, the detail and graphics for the game allow you to zoom in quite close and rotate the camera around the individual ships of your fleet, making for a true 3D experience, which during massive firefights can be quite amazing to watch playout. Your leaders/generals/admirals all have names/skills/ and an age, which means they all vary in use and inevitably die (Your race can largely depict the factors of this). Diplomacy (as referred earlier) is just as in-depth as you'd probably like w/ little micromanagement but enough to make you keep your eye on it (ie HOI, EU). Now for the bad part; successfully doing all those things so well, I feel the game really falls short in the combat area (IFFY COMBAT). Although there is a large variety of ships/classes/races/tech I feel like the battles were truly just a matter of numbers when I wasnt just geting my♥♥♥♥♥handed to me using mass drivers and FTL. That is a commonly found issue with Paradox titles I know, but maybe more so in this case?

Stellaris is a fantastic grand strategy, set in the vast expanse of space.  It is very detailed and takes some time to learn how to play, I restarted a few times just to be doomed to failure early on.
Once you gain a firm grasp of the game's concepts it becomes nearly impossible to stop playing. Starting with a small faction and setting out to create a vast empire, in whatever way you see fit.  In my case I took a small sect of humanity that had gotten lost among the stars, long forgotten by earth, and had them rise up through hardships to conquer the entire galaxy and purge all sentient life that was not human.  This is just one of many ways to play the game, you can choose from one of the many default factions or create your own faction and play your own story, complete with tons of traits and perks to really customize things your way.
The early game is where things really shine. Setting out into the unknown and colonizing new planets, researching new technologies, raising a fleet and armies, establishing contact with new species, going to war and taking other empires for your own, the list goes on and on.  Sadly the late game does not provide you with enough to really keep going, there are some late game crises which are a daunting task to deal with, but other than that it becomes quite slow. In my case it became a chore to wipe all life from the galaxy because I was so powerful and it just became a tedious task, I didn't really feel like I was accomplishing anything.
Despite things ramping down in the late game, Stellaris is still a worthwhile investment if you enjoy strategy games. It also has great mod support for when you get tired of the main game, I turned the whole game into the Star Wars universe from the Old Republic.
Definately worth playing.
