I once spent a fun summer playing happily away at this game, and whilst at the time I wasn't very good at it (I'm quite a fan of empire, as it  favours slower, more stragetic thinking that the vicious free for all that this one becomes) I eventually got the hang of it. To my delight it was ported on to mac a few weeks ago. However, now I find that either the mac version has serious issues, or the rose tinted spectales of nostlagia have hidden more than I realise.
As I stated before, the diplomacy system, simply put, does not work. Any of the incredibly contentious minded factions  that you have the slightest bit of border contact with will invariably declare war on you for not no reason (and forever refuse a ceasefire) and will perpetually attack you, often with armies so pathetic that it is outright offensive. Or indeed, massive armies of nothing but weak units, who the broken autresolve function will always let win. And I kid thee not, the autresolve system is ♥♥♥♥ed. It does not work. Reloading a save for one autreslove often will give the polar opposite effect, and even for the side that does manage to cheat the numbers, about 40% of the army will ALWAYS be scythed off, regardless of the size or strength. A small army will also sometimes be able to cheat, and will win regardless. But back to diplomacy. Allies will sit and do nothing, then will, without fail stab you in the back the moment you stop paying attention to them. You may think that this makes for a difficult and unpredictable game, but in truth it comes across as more annoying than anything else... trying playing as the Holy roman empire, and within the first thirty minutes you will be at war with Venice, Milan, France, Poland, Denmark, Sicily, Hungary and the Papal states. And that's only if you are lucky, and the Byzantines and the English don't join in the fun as well. As previous stated, none of these factions will ever agree to a ceasefire, excepting the rare instance of both near defeat and a massive cash payment from the player. As so much of the economics are based on trade, you will also have no trade because that involves neighbours who aren't trying to kill you, and who won't break a long alliance at the drop of a hat the moment your economy begins to outperform theirs (Or, more likely, for no reason whatsoever). Some regions are notably richer than others, although this placement seems arbitrary and in some places outright historically wrong, as quite a few factions (I highlight Hungary, The Byzantines and Egypt in particular) are outright unplayable as they are unable to create a functioning economy at all.  The economy also has the added bonus of being night impossible to manage, with nothing but a tax slider with a couple of settings, and the amount of public disorder rising as taxes and prospective income does. However,  buildings intended to increase public happiness doing almost nothing, and even normal taxes leadi to public disorder, forcing the player into massive expenditures for garrisons, which you will barely be able to afford, or to go through the game with everything stuck on low taxes, which results in massive population growth, which then results in squalor (Of which it seems nothing can be done about) and the same problem with public disorder again.  There is also the insanely idotic managment AI, which takes over your settlements when the family member that is running them dies, (and unless you are able to remember every single family member's name this is more of a problem than you would think, as it's likely to be hidden in the "Faction announcements" card along with two dozen other unimportant messages), which thinks that "management" is simple.... spawn as many useless units and buildings as aggresivley as possible until the player notices and deletes them all... I got a city entirely filled with ballistas and catapults, and nothing else. The ai will also immediatley flick the taxes to very high , which will probably result in you losing the settlement unless you already have a decent sized garrison, and if you do they will be pushed out to make room for the horde of ballistas.
However, these were an issues that Rome also shared (although less aggressive neighbours, but still a broken diplomacy system), and later games made massive strides in improving. There are also a few troubling gameplay elements that seem to be somewhat broken on the mac. A lot of the units have an annoying habit of completley ignoring your orders, or even doing the exact opposite. A strategically timed cavalry charge will often fail because your knights decide to gently trot off in the opposite direction, or attack the enemy one at a time, or a few will run forward, and the rest will gently walk behind them. Archers will universally take high casualties becasue they refuse to behave as if in skirmish mode when it it turned on, and obstinatley refuse to budge when it's not. Infantry units that are supposed to attack en masse will often awkwardly pause and let the first two ranks run forward, then sit and do nothing as their comrades die in front on them. They also seem to possess the ability to magically rugby tackle their way through enemy formations if ordered to. I've also encountered quite a few instances of them deciding that the treeline to their left looks so much more interesting than the battle, and wandering off to investigate it even as a enemy battalion is walking in perfect step behind them stabbing them in the back.  Artillery, as always in a total war game is also completley ♥♥♥♥ed, and I personally regard it as a completely useless investment, as in the very rare event that it actually manages to hit someone, it will almost certainly be your own men.  Soldiers with guns, who are suposed to be able to outrange the enemy archers, will also obstinatley refuse to fire until the archers come within range, and will then all die due to their slower rate of fire, although I suppose this is in the spirit of chivalry. They also love to run off in the opposite direction to the battle at any opportunity. General's units are also often criminally overpowered, cutting through anything else that comes near them with ease, which is particualrly annoying when one sees how weak the rest of the cavalry is. Despite the fact that this set in the days of knights in impenetrable suits of armour, cavlary will invariably take massive casualties for any action, regardless of how much their armour has been upgraded, and when coupled with the afformentioned reluctance to actually charge at the enemy, they can quickly become far more of a hinderance than a help. The armour ugrade buildings are also totally useless beyond the third or fourth tier, as despite the fact that all factions can build them, only one or two (And I really mean one or two) can actually get use out of them, meaning that armour upgrades for most sides are a time consuming and expensive waste.
There is also a glaring graphical issue. If the game is minimised for any reason, especially in battle mode, there is a high probablity that the in game graphics will break, leading to gigantic intersecting walls of nothingness tearing their way through the map, along with random tree textures popping up in a broken green sea all over the land that is visible. This can make answering a skype call, or changing what  music you are lsitening to  because of the limited soundtrack into a very challenging prospect.
There is also the late game, which features the Timurids, an unplayable faction who are broken, and near impossible to beat, and make the late game a nightmare.
However, despite all of these flaws, the core game is still it's reasonably solid original self... the port just needs some work, particualrily in the Ai department. If you love total war games, this is still one of the best (particualrily as it doesn't expect you to pay for each faction seperatley)

I've sunk a lot of hours into playing this game outside of steam, having actually broken the discs from overuse several times. The game is just good enough to buy a replacement!
As a turnbased strategy game based in medieval times from 1088 onward, you'll see your fledgling kingdom emerge from the dark ages, embark on (or defend against!) crusades, weather the ravages of the black death and finally settle into a bustling empire at about a 1500's level of technology, sailing to the new world. Depending on your proclivities, this could be to get some of that sweet aztec chocolate or to teach the natives all about christ or muhammad. Sadly, you can't possibly set sail without the proper late game ships so you'll see no vikings looting aztec gold outside of custom battles.
Holy wars in particular have their own feature, allowing catholics to petition the pope to claim non christian lands (if sufficiently worthy in his eyes) or if you're a muslim ruler, have an imam stir the ummah to march westward. In practice, this causes you and the AI factions of your religion (if they comply) to amass quick and cheap armies who move much faster on the campaign map to reach specific goals such as Jerusalem or hell, why not London? The Orthodox factions of the Byzantine empire and Russia lack this feature for understandable reasons and must simply endure the indignity of foreigners marching through their lands in a religious frenzy.
Religion isn't all about cheap conquests and disgruntled greeks, though. The pope can get very disgruntled on his own and a particulary bellicose, impious king can easily awaken his ire to call a crusade on your sorry royal backside. Muslim factions should consider this as the pope will always be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at you, all the time for being muslim. Even if you court the christian kingdoms with gold, pope AI is likely to randomly declare a massive war on his best muslim buddy!
Furthermore, failing to maintain your particular religion in your far flung provinces will cause heresy to rise. Once that gets particularly bad, heretics units pop up, acting as priests of a new religion you'll have to squash to avoid rebellion. If catholic, sufficiently heretical provinces will have the papal states send inquisitors. These hardasses aren't particularly concerned if the agent spreading faith in the province is a heretic or your very own frickin' cardinal. Don't let divergent ways take root. Beware the heretic, the Emperor protects.
At the start, you only have a few factions unlocked. England in its freshly conquered Norman suit with its classic longbowmen, the French with their legendary knights, the holy roman empire (amusingly beset by heresy), Spain or rather a version of Castile at the onset of the reconquista and the republic of Venice (don't worry, you still get crowned emperor at the end).
As you conquer other factions, you actually unlock them for future playthroughs with the exception of the timed event invasions of mongols and timurids so if you ache really badly to play Scots and don't want to mod the game, swallow your pride and march the English north for a quick, new faction. Pick your kingdom and get crackin' because destiny awaits!
Aside from the basic features, the developers put a lot of effort into the little things which adds a lot to the experience of your campaign. Sending a spy to peek on an enemy army or an assassin to deal with enemy nobles and even the pope(!) will trigger its own video sequence. In addition, as your nobles age and aquire various traits, it can and will, especially in the case of the English and French, cause their real time battle speeches to take on hints of their personalities. A noble leading an army tends to have entertainingly scathing remarks about the rival nations even if they aren't particularly awkward, alcoholic or frothing mad.
Furthermore, Jeff van Dyck contributes with some pretty breathtaking pieces of atmospheric music that'll set the mood for your battles. It's some pretty exceptional stuff that I've yet to see other total war games top almost 10 years later.
All's not sunshine, however and the game is plagued by the same basic empire management and faction flaws that hampered Rome: Total War. Specifically, squalor can and will cause unguarded cities to rebel and there's little to be done about it. On the plus side, a rebel city counts as heretical which allows you to call a crusade or jihad to claim it from the obviously ungodly rebels.
As for other issues, given how the autoresolving of battles works with unit statistics, AI fighting AI will tumble easily to high hitpoint cavalry. In Rome it was chariots, in Medieval 2 it's the elephants. Where this meant Egypt would usually consume all of the middle east in Rome: Total War unless you personally stopped them, this now applies to the late game Timurid hordes.
The problem with both mongol and timurid invasion is that these factions don't need to pay any upkeep for some of their units, allowing the situation to snowball fast and turning the late game into an endless slog. I've ended up fighting back a massive mongol empire that held all of russia and poland well into the 1700's using English longbowmen!
Additionally, the timescale of the base game runs on two years per turn while your royal family only ages one year. This is an oversight but is easily modded out by subtle edits to a file that even a modding halfwit like myself could figure out without breaking the game.
Overall, it's a nice, relatively polished game of compelling history and strategy. If this appeals, get it now.

I wouldn't call this a review (Because I haven't got to end game yet) more like a First impressions from someone who makes a living from playing and critiquing many different MMORPGs
- It feels like a well polished, quality game, the sound effects are great, and it runs really smoothly
- Wildstar is a free to play game on steam that isn't pay to win, there's a lot of cosmetic and convenience items on the cash shop but nothing that could really be considered pay to win
- I didn't notice it until today but the Wildstar soundtrack is really beautiful and well composed, I feel like music is a really important yet overlooked thing to get right in an MMO, luckily wildstar delivers in this aspect.
- Wildstar is full voice acted to a high standard, again this just adds to the overall polish and quality of the game as well as helping players keep up with the general narrative without having to read too much text
- The questing in wildstar is actually quite good, sure you've got a few kill and collect quests but wildstars collect quests are a bit more interactive, the main story quests are like scenarios that feel like solo dungeons and there's enough variety to keep things from feeling too repetitive, If you get bored of questing you can level up through Dungeons, Expeditions, PVP, public events, challenges or even wave defences out in the world, it feels like you have a lot of options in this game.
- Wildstar has a unique action combat system where most of your abilities are telegraphed, I love the combat in this game as you need to constantly be on the move, the animations feel smooth and it's fun to dodge enemy telegraphs
- Wildstar has arguably the best player housing in any MMORPG out there, you're basically given your own huge plot of land to build whatever the hell you want, you can choose from hundreds of decor items and resize those items to be giant if you want, the best thing is most of this is available with in game currency for a low price rather than it all being locked behind the cash shop
- PVE content in Wildstar feels challenging, there's a lot to dodge and failing to execute the mechanics will result in death, for me the difficulty in this game is nice, It's not too hard but not too easy, It's enough to keep you on your toes and not fall asleep at your keyboard
- Due to Wildstars Stylised graphics the games system requirements aren't too high and it should age pretty well
- The game doesn't take itself too seriously, it has a tonne of character and it feels like it's trying to be its own thing however if you have played other MMOs such as World of Warcraft the game will still feel quite familiar to you
- Wildstar is an open world game, whilst it may look like each zone is sectioned off there are paths that allow you to run between them without a loading screen, the zones them self are pretty huge so it definitely feels like an open world game
- The character creation in wildstar is pretty decent, It's not the best out there but you get plenty of sliders and options to make a distinctive look for your character also no gender locked races or classes
- The User interface in Wildstar feels like a bit of a cluster ♥♥♥♥ at times, it's a bit busy when you've got a lot of quests on the go, achievements are popping up and NPCs are trying to call you, It functions well and you can customise it but it's a bit much by default for me personally
- Something I found a bit annoying was how challenges seem to start randomly without any warning, most of these challenges are timed and it sometimes takes you a while to figure out what you actually need to do by which time you've already lost the chance for a gold, I think it'd be nice if you had a bit more notice before challenges start.
- From what I've heard there's a big faction imbalance between the Exiles and Dominion towards the Exiles side and players can't communicate or group up between factions meaning it's harder for dominion players to find groups
- Players with a bad internet connections might struggle with the end game content due to how the combat is very reactionary and apparently quite punishing
- (Personal) - I find it hard to be truly immersed when playing wildstar just because of how weird and wacky everything is, in terms of gameplay I think it's fantastic but I don't feel like I can relate to any of the races or characters
Wildstar is one of the best free to play MMOs out there and It's a game I'd highly recommend giving a try if you haven't done so already, unlike a lot of MMOs it feels like a lot of effort and love went into making it, It doesn't feel like a cash grab and I find the gameplay genuinely fun, I'd consider Wildstar to easily be in my top 5 MMOs and after revisiting it I wanna try to find the time to get to max level and experience end game,
I feel like the two fundamental reasons as to why Wildstar isn't more popular is that from an outsiders point of view it seems like a casual game that tries to appeal to kids with It's cartoony art style when in reality It's a very hardcore and punishing MMO at end game, I feel like there's a bit of a disconnect between the games theme and the type of gamer the end game's trying to appeal to, Wildstar also suffered a horrible launch that caused people to leave in their masses, back then the game had a subscription model so not many people were willing to give it another chance until it went free to play.
Regardless I'll be playing more Wildstar myself, It's a solid game and since it's free to play you've got nothing to lose in trying it.

I finished the main story of
a few weeks ago. I've only been playing it until now to finish the last few achievements, and yet not a day goes by when I haven't thought about it. It is clear that
had brilliant writers and directors behind it. This game will certainly pull at your heartstrings, surprise you with novel twists, and perhaps have the capability to cause you to question your own way of living.
takes place in a dystopian future, where the earth has been razed and taken over by seemingly mindless machines. Humanity has been pushed away to the moon, and it's up the android Resistance and elite android squadron YoRHa to take the planet back. It's a typical enough backdrop, but of course that's not all there is to it.
I'll be avoiding spoilers here, but the story presents itself not through exposition but slow and careful worldbuilding through a large cast of characters, android and machine alike. The differences between android and machine are made clear repeatedly throughout the story, and thankfully the two factions behave in character throughout. When inevitable change or shifts in view happen, this results in it actually being a weighted, understandable event.
characters are smart and internally consistent, making them entirely enjoyable.
The game's themes are intertwined primarily with absurdism, with a few blatent Camus references sprinkled throughout. An analogy towards the status of the human condition and value is frequently made with that of the android's, who are placed in a situation where they are forced (via programming) to love a seemingly absent but once certainly real god. In the world of video games this is actually rather unique, and
makes excellent use of its medium to play with this topic in a novel way, and comes to a satisfying conclusion by the end.
Moving past the story, graphically, the game is nothing to write home about. It ranges from looking like a late PS2 title to solid PS3 level, but doesn't really move past that besides the quality of the character models. Where it does shine is the camerawork - perspective shifts are common and there's a huge number of cinematic shots that just beg for a screenshot. Coupled with the voice acting, well, let's just say there is no way I'll be forgetting a few of the scenes. The game's story is only matched by its overall presentation and it's quite clear that love was put into every level. Again, I have to give special homage to the voice acting, and also to the soundtrack. After the first
I don't think it's surprising to anyone that that
also has an excellent OST that can even stand tall on its own.
Lastly, gameplay. Platinum did it. It's good, great even. It's fast-paced, predictable, and satisfying, though in actual execution a bit shallow. Fancy combos and juggles are possible, but the game is easy enough to where there's no need for difficult techs - you can't quite button mash through everything but at the same time the dodge system gives you a large enough leeway that there's no need to be careful either. The difficulty settings also aren't particularly well done. On normal, as said, the game is quite easy but on the hard difficulty challenge is made through an increase in enemy health pools and a decrease in yours. This is by far my least favorite system of adding difficulty to any game, and as a result I skipped over it in Automata even if it does make certain segments, like boss fights, more enjoyable. Having each random mook take 30 sword swings to kill ruins sense of pace.
Anyway,
is an excellent game with an incredibly memorable cast and story. It's well worth a playthrough, multiple especially.

I've played a lot of strategy/4X games, and in light of that: Stellaris is a huge disappointment.  It has a few interesting ideas brought into the genre, but implemented poorly.  Most of the core mechanics are derivative of other, better games and implemented more poorly.  Exploration is largely limited, and requiring science ships for exploration doesn't provide a meaningful change to the game (I just send a science ship instead of a scout).  It takes a while for it to survey, which is kind of neat, but in practice it just slows things down.  The story beats that can be discovered are a neat concept, but in execution it is just like a generic fetch quest from an MMO.  Ship design is technically in the game although there are very few meaningful choices to be made, combat is completely uninspired and might as well be fully automated.  The game has a highly legalistic feeling to it, and at no point did I feel like I was "playing" the game, instead I was carefully "driving" it on the road, between the lines.  Colony management is abysmal, combining the zone system from games like Galactic Civilization (but with mostly rote decisions rather than interesting ones like choosing a proximity bonus vs leveraging an exploitable bonus), but with the need for upkeep of another game.  Diplomacy is terrible.  The large number of races all blur together and have virtually zero personality.  Visually I think the game looks 10 years older than it is, it's got all sorts of hideous typographical and color choices interspersed with competent ones - as if the visual designers were only around for half the project.  On top of it all it has been very buggy at times.  It's received many patches to fix it, but still... what a mess.
I'm also confused by the choice to make it "real time", as in practice I alternated between full speed and full stop - basically rendering this a turn based game.  It doesn't have the flow of a game like Sins of a Solar Empire or Star Craft, which use the real time method effectively... it's just a mess.
I think someone who enjoys filing taxes they would enjoy this game, or possibly people who are really into role playing.  If you want to feel like you are the Emperor of a mighty space age civilization go play some other game.  If you want to feel like a high ranking logistical clerk in a mighty space age civilization then this might be your thing.  Either way... between the new Master of Orion, the old Master of Orion (1 or 2), Endless Space, Galactic Civilizations II, Distant Worlds or Sins of a Solar Empire, you should be able to find something better that matches up with you.

Gifted to me during the Xmas Steam Sale, I wasn't sure what to make of Magicite. I started the game and died literally a minute later. The game is quite harsh to the new and uninitiated, and can be difficult to learn when under such oppressive circumstances.
But give it a chance, and you won't regret it.
Best described as a Terraria and Rogue Legacy lovechild, MAGICITE has you traversing randomly-generated biomes, collecting resources and crafting tools/weapons while fighting off hostile creatures. Between levels (called 'districts') there are towns where you can trade, sell, and buy.
However, if you die, you lose everything and have to start over. The higher your score, though, the more chests you can open, giving you a chance to unlock more classes.
The game can be quite punishing, but ultimately feels satisfying when you make it further than the last attempt. It borders on downright addicting.
After a few runs you start to get better and travel further. Might want to try giving it a shot yourself.

It's like Overwatch, except it's actually fun!
I hate that I have to compare the two. Especially since Paladins isn't a clone of Overwatch... THEY'RE BOTH CLONES OF TF2. But the comparison is unavoidable, so I suppose that's the best way to review it.
Let's start at what I think is the biggest difference: game design philosophies and fundamentals. Overwatch is almost a very literal name. Most of the levels involve very large open areas and long sight-lines. Flank routes are limited, and are either only accessible by certain characters with special movement or only assist in getting closer rather than behind your enemy. The characters have weapons that have deficient accuracy and range (for the most part) forcing you to push across no man's land to get in close. Healers can do their job VERY effectively, and Reinhardt has a god-shield. The best way to kill the enemy is usually a cheap combo (like McCree's flashbang then fan-the-hammer) to burst down an enemy, or wait on an OP super or a well-timed dive with several teammates to nab a kill and break their line. The end result is a game that is one giant CHOKEPOINT where kills and deaths are frustrating. Games can be as short as 2 minutes, or as long as... 10? 15? I don't remember at this point. Combat, as a whole, feels like it drags out until there's an unexpected SPIKE. I don't know how many chances I've given Overwatch. I wanna be like the cool kids and be part of the crowd, but it really is just NOT FUN.
Paladins feels like it has gone out of its way to avoid almost all of the things I hate about OW. Right from first opening the character select screen, you can see how it tries to veer away from the turtley chokepoint nature of that game. Their classes are damage, flank, tank, and heal. Whereas OW is attack, defense, tank, and heal. See that? 2 offense and 2 defense versus 1 offense and 3 defense. Now, that's not an entirely fair comparison since some of the characters in those 3 defense categories are straight killers (Widowmaker, Roadhog). But to me it's just the start of painting a more complete picture.
Each level in Paladins has GREAT flank routes, forcing defenders to keep their heads on a swivel. They are also littered with way more odd pieces of cover here and there, allowing for more combat opportunities at different ranges. Weapons have more variance as to what ranges they are effective at, too, so matchups can happen more often. None of those giant no-man's-land style open areas like OW. EVERY character has a weapon that is effective and deadly (when used in their intended capacity) and healers have very diminished effectiveness compared to OW. What this does is makes Paladins more of a slugfest. Every match feels intense as everyone just beats the hell out of eachother. I don't think I've ever had a match that felt like a massive turtle, even when the team had like 3 tanks and two healers! Probably because tanks and healers are more rounded combatants in Paladins (which is why despite me saying that healers are less effective at healing they are still super important to team makeup). In OW, there are characters like Mercy and Reinhardt who are the best at what they do but are entirely single-minded in that purpose.
So that's the biggest difference: the overall game feel. But that's not even all the ways that this game is better. Here's a few more little things:
-Paladins is cheaper. It's free, for one, and the "all heroes unlocked forever" that OW comes with can be bought here for half the price, too.
-You can actually buy the things you want. OW just lets you buy the same lootbox that comes from leveling. No guarantees you'll get those limited time skins. But the chests that cost the premium currency in Paladins are all dupe-protected. So you WILL eventually get the skins you want. I think the most expensive one so far has been the Christmas chest. Basically it would cost about $15 to get every single thing out of that chest. The tradeoff here is that you can't get these skins just by playing the game. But I have friends who have spent $20 or more on chests in OW to try and get the skins they want only to be screwed by RNG. So... choose your poison.
-Loadout customization! One of the things I find dull about OW is that I can't make even minor changes to how a character is played. Paladins has a card system that gives at least a little bit of variety to each and every character.
-No Lucio required! In Paladins you spawn on a mount that gets you back into the fray quickly. You can't remount, either, so  this is simply something for helping with a push.
-More characters! There's a new character every month (currently, maybe this will slow down in the future) so there's always something new to check out. OW is what? Every 6 months? Takes forever.
The only point I can give OW is its art. Their style and animation is top-notch and Paladins will never be that shiny. But these are video games and not movies (despite what Blizzard's cinematics team seems to think) so GAMEPLAY FIRST. Ha! (for those who don't know, "Gameplay first" is one of Blizzard's mottos. IN YOUR FACE, JERKS)
The biggest issue I have with Paladins is how buggy some patches can be. I kinda look past it since I work in the industry and so I know that the release cadence they've set is INSANE for how much smaller their resources must be comparatively. But for a lot of people... you might not find that acceptable, heh. Not to say Paladins is a buggy mess like a Bethesda game, but it can be off-putting when something highly noticeable crops up.

One of the main reasons why Tom Clancy games are enjoyable is because their is a sense of overall command in the game.  You control your character and at the same time you direct your teammates to carryout certain orders; Ghost Recon: Future Soldier employs those same game play characteristics. Ubisolf utilized an action based/stealth approach to Future Solider, requiring one to stealth around a location, identify targets, sync those targets, and get out undetected.  On several of the missions, stealth is a requirement.  This aspect of the game is where people tend to have issues.  Future Solider is more of an action based game rather than a stealthy game; in a sense, it can go both ways (like Hitman Absolution, Dishonored, Assassins Creed, etc).  However, you are rewarded more by taking a stealthy approach; high scores, items unlocked quicker, etc.  In comparison to majority of other Tom Clancy games, OG Rainbow 6, Rainbow 6 III, Vegas 1 & 2, and the original Ghost Recon, teammate control seems to be at a minimum.  The only real control you have over your teammate is to set up sync shots and have them focus a target, you cannot send them to a location, you cannot have them set up a frag run, they cannot breach and clear, etc.  Overall, I liked Ghost Recon: Future Soldier, as an action based 3rd person shooter it was fun, as a stealth game it wasn't half bad, and remember...the game can be played both ways, as a stealthy inflitration game or as a Rambo game...it is your pick.
****Note: You have to download Ubisoft's platform Ubiplay to be able to play Ghost Recon: Future Soldier.  It only requires you to download it, install it, and login when you play.  It s kind of a pain, but its nothing too terrible****

Great game so far. This isn't as much a review as it is my thoughts on what the developers should change, as this game is still in development and has frequent updates (which is awesome. frequent updates are awesome.)
I love the art, although it's a little low res for me. Doom, the game this game's 2D-sprite-in-a-3D-world style is based off of, has higher resolution sprites and textures than this. I understand it's going the retro pixel art route, but it's honestly just kind of lazy to have characters this low resolution. Also, the blood is a little rediculous to me. Everything about this game screams "E for Everyone" then you go ahead and have these really stupid looking blood puddle decals that are left wherever you kill an enemy. I'm not saying this game isn't fit for kids, but it just looks odd and out of place. Either go a mature route and make the characters and art more realistic or take the blood out.
The combat is kind of wonky. You hold down Left Click to charge up your attack, and the longer you hold it down the more damage it does. So you can either stab an enemy a bunch of times or give them a couple big, strong slashes. I understand what they're trying to go for, they're trying to make the combat more intuitive, but it doesn't work, mainly because you slow down when you charge your attack. So If you're trying to charge your attack you end up walking painfully slow towards your opponent, and I can understand it's for balancing purposes, but it honestly is just annoying and slows down combat.
And probably the most annoying part about the game so far to me is hit detection. Since the characters are 2D sprites instead of 3D models, it can be really hard to tell if you're close enough to them to attack, and often times sword fights just turn into me slashing into the air not close enough to hit them, then moving closer to hit them and getting hit. It's especially annoying with enemies that don't actually attack you, they just touch you and you get hurt, because you're trying to get close enough to hit them but instead of hitting them you get too close and get hurt.
I don't really like the music much, but I'm sure a lot of other people like it so I won't tell you to change it or anything, so I just turn the music off. But when you do that, you pretty much hear the torch noise on infinite repeat. It's understandable, because the game takes place in a dungeon lit by torches, but it's so, so incredibly annoying. Either turn the torch noise down, add different ambient noises, or make better music. Any one of those options would be awesome. Besides that, though, the sound effects are awesome.
Although it has a couple minor problems, it's still a really fun game, and I recommend it. The magic in this game is really awesome, the feeling you get casting spells in this game is really unique, and the AI isn't bad. The level design is solid, but this game could definitely use some more rooms, I run into the same rooms fairly often. Bottom line is, it's a fun game that has potential to be a great rouge-like.

Party Hard is a pixel party game where you are a man who is just trying to get some sleep and believes that the only way to accomplish this is to kill everyone in every party everywhere. The gameplay involves you playing as this killer while trying to eliminate all partiers without getting noticed/arrested/killed. The ways in which you can accomplish this vary each level. Of course you can give someone a good ol' stabbing, but the environmental kills allow you to mix it up. The game itself (as the premise indicates) can be quite humorous both in the way party-people react and in how you can deviously destroy them.
The story mode primarily consists of going through different maps with each followed by a cutscene. It didn't take me too long to complete, but it was challenging at times. At just over 10 hours, I've gotten every achievement in the game (with some tedious grinding and you'll see what I mean should you try to do this as well) and had quite a bit of fun. While at times it can become bland, predictable, and repetitive, Party Hard offers just enough variation to keep things interesting. A sequel would be something I'd be looking forward to.
7.5/10 Recommended.

Splatter:Zombie Apocalypse is an unexpected little surprise at a really small price that is a steal,especially in a sale(personally got it for 0.49 euros/USD/whatever your currency is).
*****************Gameplay*********************
At that price,its actually sad or better,a bargain.It's not like the game is an amazing game that will fill you with hours and hours of content for years,no,it's this really good shot at a "top-down shooter" game,and a good one at that.There is a lot of effort put up here,voiced NPCs,voiced cutscenes and of course a voiced protagonist in the various stages of the game.Dynamic lighting effects,good graphics(for a top-down they are pretty good),nice effects like fires,bombs,bullets,flares etc etc.Comparing this to other games of the same genre,this one comes on top.
There are a bunch of different enemies throughout the game,spanning from zombies to worms,not huge variety but it works.Not a whole lot of weapons but they are decent and different from each other,from your small pistol to a laser rifle,yeah.
As for gameplay,stages take a while to complete,and are generally large,sometimes have more open areas than others.
And of course,since this is a top-down shooter,there are a quite a few boss fights waiting for you,which are really decent.
*************Thoughts and Final Verdict**************
The only problem is the content itself.There is not much of it,I finished the campaign in 4 hours and 17 minutes,which means that the campaign is roughfly 4-5 hours(Insert Angry Joe meme here),but anyway,if you are looking for replayability look elsewhere,there is the survival mode and some multiplayer modes but i doubt any people still play them.
But hey,at least they are there,and I appreciate that,there is also co-op available up to 4 players as well so that is very positive as well.And for those of you that like to collect stuff,there are collectables,like finding parts of a golden pistol hidden away on various stages of the campaign,and some "armor" parts that give you a small amount of shields in the battle next to your health.
So,to finish up this review.Do I recommend it?Yes,and please,get it in full price if you can,I mean it,its sad to pay only 0.49$ for something that clearly has so much effort put into it.Support the dev,don't be cheap,if you can of course.

Gifted to me during the Xmas Steam Sale, I wasn't sure what to make of Magicite. I started the game and died literally a minute later. The game is quite harsh to the new and uninitiated, and can be difficult to learn when under such oppressive circumstances.
But give it a chance, and you won't regret it.
Best described as a Terraria and Rogue Legacy lovechild, MAGICITE has you traversing randomly-generated biomes, collecting resources and crafting tools/weapons while fighting off hostile creatures. Between levels (called 'districts') there are towns where you can trade, sell, and buy.
However, if you die, you lose everything and have to start over. The higher your score, though, the more chests you can open, giving you a chance to unlock more classes.
The game can be quite punishing, but ultimately feels satisfying when you make it further than the last attempt. It borders on downright addicting.
After a few runs you start to get better and travel further. Might want to try giving it a shot yourself.

Quick Tip: Update drivers. Check Geforce Experience, then check the website, as sometimes the Experience app thing can be a bit wonky, especially since the app itself updated.
Hope this helps some of you out there.

Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel, in essence, is more Borderlands 2. Except gravity has decided to divorce you and when you think you are used to their being gone they come back for short amounts of time that can neither be described as a joyful reunion or an utterly gut-destroying staredown. Maybe somewhere in between.

If you have ever played a Borderlands game, you will find exactly everything you have come to know and love: the charismatic visual effects, the crazy characters, the non-sense story, the tons of weird weapons, and a lot of irony. In addition, you have zero gravity!
If you have never played a Borderlands game, it is a good place like any to start!
The game experience is more or less the same in all three of them... In the end, it is more of the same, but if the same is good, at least for a while it is fine! As usual, its worst enemy is repetition: the scenaries all look more or less the same, the enemies respawn as if there was no tomorrow, and no matter how creative and farfetched the background story can sound, in most missions you will just go from point A to point B and shoot everything on your way. Nonetheless, it still is fun - for a while. If you take it in small doses day by day, it's okay; leave it there for a while and you probably won't be coming back.

I like this game more than Borderlands 2. YES. Borderlands 2 has WAY WAY WAYYY more content but for what this game has it is amazing! The low gravity makes combat far more dynamic than in BL2. Now you have all three dimensions to maneuver in, making combat interesting,
Do I want to jump over my enemies and attack them from above?
Do I want to evade my enemies by jumping to vantage points and attacking them from there?
Or do you just want to run up and slam them away with the new slam mechanic?
Not only that the environments are more dynamic. Air is a resource that you must keep an eye on making some situations more intense then it would be in BL2. Also you can use the environment as a weapon. And I’m not talking about ye olde explosive barrels. You can shoot the enemies air supply and cause a suffocation DOT.
As for elemental gimmicks, fire will do big DOT damage if the enemy is in Air, and then we have Cyro, the best element in Borderlands history!
Know what was fun about slag? Nothing. I HATED always having to tug around a slag weapon in Borderlands 2.
To me, being forced to use a gun I don’t want to use, slagging the enemy, and then switching to a gun I actually want to play with is not fun. (True you could argue this is only required in Ultimate vault hunter mode, but that’s where the real game is at.)  Know what is fun?  Freezing your enemy, and them punching them in the face and watching them shatter into a million pieces. That’s Cyro. The freezing element that is one part crowd control, one part melee wet dream. I have over 210 hours on BL2 and so far NOTHING is as satisfying than freezing a badass and then robot punching them in the face with Wilhelm and watching them shatter.
As for the world… Pandora felt too much like Earth. You could replace all the alien animals with Earth animals and you could totally fool someone into thinking the game takes place on Earth. Elpis however… feels truly alien.
Also I found the character Wilhelm interesting. The more you level him up in his cyper commando tree the more robotic he becomes and his voice even changes. I have never seen that in any other BL character. (Physically changing as you level them)
Also laser weapons are etech weapons except they don’t suck and come in 4 different forms. (Assult rifle, ghostbustery beams, sniper, and shotguns)
So…
Pros
-3 dimensional fighting
- environments are fun to fight in and the O2 mechanic makes you more aware of your surroundings
- Running around a low gravity moon is fun
-Wilhelm (200 of my hours were just on him)
-Cyro being the best element ever.
-lasers!
Cons
-	Far less content than BL2
-	Not as hard as BL2
YES BL2 is the better game because of the content, BUT if you compare the games at their cores, Pre sequel is superior with my opinion.

TL;DR: 9/10, play it!
Pros:
+ Everything you love about borderlands and more! Lots of loot, very funny, a whole lot of action and a great story that actually explains a lot about whats going on in the Borderlands universe.
+ The playable characters actually have dialogue and interact with the storyline.
+ *Very* replayable, both in true vault hunter mode and as other characters.
+ Cyro weapons dont suck
+ Moonstones (TPS' version of Eridium) are plentiful and more common than Eridium in the first two games, but you can spend them in more places than just the black market.
+ Laser weapons are pretty decent. Well, except for laser shotguns (Sorry Mr. Torgue).
+ The ending basically confirmed that Borderlands 3 is going to happen and hinted at its storyline.
+ Low gravity and O2 kits (oxygen tanks for vacuums that also allow you to double jump, butt slam and have other small perks) are actually pretty useful and not just gimicky crap.
Cons
- Definetly a CPU intensive game, especially in heavy combat. I get worse FPS drops in this game than I do in BF4 with my AMD FX 4130 and GTX 760 in heavy combat, but it never drops below 35fps.
- Corrosive weapons are nearly useless, hardly any enemeies are armored.
- Fire weapons are useless in vacuums (which is like half the game).
- The grinder sucks, don't even bother with it unless you want the acheivements. You're much better off just selling the items and buying better ones.
- The story is shorter than the first two games and there seems to be less side missions.
All in all, its still a fantastic game and I would highly recommend it to anyone. Perhaps get it on sale, but I bought it full price and I have no ragrets.

This is unique in genre. It's an FPS roguelike. Others exist, like Paranautical Activity, but I would call that more of an FPS of Binding of Issac, while Delver is more of an FPS version of Nethack. I love Nethack, and have consequently played far too much of it. This solid FPS roguelike will actually fill that same itch in a fresh new way.
The graphics may be offputting, being that they belong more in the Doom era of gaming than they do today, but it is definitely excuted well. And I also do believe that it fits the style of roguelike very well, while allowing the devs to focus on other core gameplay features. And that's where this game really shines. It's built solidly. It may not do a whole ton of things. But the things that it does, it does fantastically.
I believe that if this game were to become as popular as the Dungeons of Dredmor, it could bring in a whole new legion of roguelike fans, as DoD did before it. If procedural generation and first person cameras are what you like, give this a try.

I don't really write reviews, but i feel inclined to say something about Automation.
I bought this game the day it came out in early access after having seen a TheSmokingTire video talking about it. Matt Farah's words were too captivating, so i went out and bought my first early access game not completely knowing what i settled myself into.
A year later, i really do not regret getting it, whatsoever.
This is by far one of the most promising games under development at the moment, as far as i see it.
The base game is relatively simple - You build and design cars and engines to produce and eventually sell as soon as the tycoon part of the game is added to the game.
The depth of these basic principles is brilliant. Essentially every component of the engine that makes a difference is adjustable and customizeable to some rather great extents. If you want a tiny 500cc 4 cylinder for a kei car, or a stupdily massive 12 liter V8 for a drag car, you're free to do it. This makes up quite alot of fun of the game - Being able to see what you can come up with and test the limits of what works. It's seriously alot of fun to mess about with.
There's also an incredibly informative guide troughout the car designing proccess, should you ever find yourself uninformed or curious about a certain car component.
The game itself is still a tad lackluster at the moment, only shipping off with a sandbox mode and some different scenario challenges. But, a proper tycoon mode is still under development, and at the moment it's not even fully a necessity, because the sandbox gives you very much to play with.
But i think what i want to highlight the most about Automation is the developers and development process. I don't think i've ever seen the developers of a game so involved with the community surrounding it. The developers are essentially constantly keeping an eye on the official forums and the Steam Community hub for the game, talking with the community, helping with problems and taking suggestions for future game addons. There's also occasional update videos on Youtube where a developer (A rather handsome german man ;) talks about new additions to the game, future updates and pretty much anything you might want to hear about.
It's this openness and community involvment surrounding the game that i really, really love, and i genuinely do think that Automation has what is the best developer-community relationship of any early access game i've seen.
The community aswell, is fantastic. It's welcoming and open, and you feel right at home whether you know alot about cars or not. This community (and the guides in-game) will make you learn more. There's also a healthy modding scene, adding different car bodies or fixtures allowing you to create whatever you want even more.
I'm aware this review seems biased, and it is, but i really cannot praise this game enough. It does have it's faults, but there's way too many positives to outweigh the negatives, and so far this game has just been a positive experience for me.
So i guess to sum it up; whether you like cars, want to learn about cars or just want to see an early access game that's actually being worked on; get this game.

And for those who have the japanese word Hachiroku carved in their skulls, check out the 1980's Japanese Coupe, inspired by the lengendary AE86. Or, for fans of the post apocalyptic wasteland and their big V8's there's the vanilla two-door 1970's coupe. One of the best action adventure titles I have played. Although slightly overrated.
Nier : Automata is an openworld action adventure that has hint similarities of the Legend of Zelda titles. With that said, This game has alot to explore, great combat mechanics, and an excellent soundtrack to boot.
The story has somthing to do with Androids fighting machine lifeforms, and mankind is close to extinction. At the start, It is heavily implied that the machines are with out a doubt evil and nasty. soon after you find out that there are machines that have grown personalities, and morals. and this gives the game a fantastic look at the qualities of what it is to be human. I did find it a little odd when I ended up saving a machine from death, and had my character talk to it like a lost child while escorting him to his mother, only to have them say 5 seconds later "machines are evil, they must die" (Heavy Paraphrasing there)
Gameplay is fantastic, there is tons to do in this game, and there is a great variety of gameplay mechanics ranging from the top down Ikaruga style shooter, to castlevania sidescrolling action, to full open world exploration. combat is very fast, where you have multiple types of weapons and abilities to tear and annhililate your foes, and a reactionary dodge function that if timed correctly allows you to counter attack your foes with an impressive move.
The Difficulty is painfuly obvious between normal and hard almost to the point of feeling extremely unbalanced. I picked hard to start off, and after 6 or so hours getting 1 shotted by every attack the first boss did. I decided to tone down the difficulty and the game became significantly easier to the point where I played through the game start to finish without ever dying once. With that said, C'mon. The first boss kills you in one hit with every attack? there is a difficulty that has it so everything one hits you. and even though the difficulty is hard, ITS THE FIRST BOSS! WTF!?
Overall, The Gameplay, Visuals, Audio, And content of this game is supurb. The main story I felt was lacking in some areas, but the side stories with the machines made up for it. The Difficulty i feel also needs some rebalancing between Normal and Hard.
overall 8.5/10

NieR: Automata is an incredible game and quite unlike anything I have played before and truly a work of art. I went in with very high expectations after everything I had seen and heard about it and they were far surpassed.
Pros:
+The story here is incredibly well done and incredibly unique in how its presented and just done overall. (Make sure to not stop after ending A because there is a lot more waiting for you afterwards!)
+Incredible soundtrack that might just be my favorite of all time tied with DOOM 2016.
+Platinum Games excellent combat just never gets old.
+Excellent and memorable characters.
+Very interesting Plug-In chips system that lets you customize what you do best and even remove parts of the HUD if you so desire.
+The game has this simple yet beautiful graphical style that I just fell in love with immediately.
+The side quests though not perfect do have some emotional weight to them that makes them worth doing (not Fallout 4 level side quests where you don't care about anything.)
+A solid port in which I was able to manage a solid 60fps for the most part on my 1070. Unfortunately doesn't go beyond 60fps but with a game like this for me thats not a big issue.
+As sad as it is to say in this day and age this is a COMPLETE that is not needing DLC to make it so.
Cons:
-The game could still have room for improvement in terms of optimization as its not perfect for everyone.
-Sidequests do have a TON of backtracking and some of them are a complete chore to do.
-The 30fps cutscenes make quite a jarring transition going between that and the 60fps gameplay.
Conclusion:
Overall if I had to score NieR: Automata it would probably be around a 9.5. For the $60 I spent I absolutely feel I got my moneys worth and would highly recommend this to anyone interested. This is a game I'm never going to forget and will certainly be playing again in the future. I certainly hope NieR: Automata's success will compell Yoko Taro and Platinum to work together again and create more games on this level of greatness.

It's like Overwatch, except it's actually fun!
I hate that I have to compare the two. Especially since Paladins isn't a clone of Overwatch... THEY'RE BOTH CLONES OF TF2. But the comparison is unavoidable, so I suppose that's the best way to review it.
Let's start at what I think is the biggest difference: game design philosophies and fundamentals. Overwatch is almost a very literal name. Most of the levels involve very large open areas and long sight-lines. Flank routes are limited, and are either only accessible by certain characters with special movement or only assist in getting closer rather than behind your enemy. The characters have weapons that have deficient accuracy and range (for the most part) forcing you to push across no man's land to get in close. Healers can do their job VERY effectively, and Reinhardt has a god-shield. The best way to kill the enemy is usually a cheap combo (like McCree's flashbang then fan-the-hammer) to burst down an enemy, or wait on an OP super or a well-timed dive with several teammates to nab a kill and break their line. The end result is a game that is one giant CHOKEPOINT where kills and deaths are frustrating. Games can be as short as 2 minutes, or as long as... 10? 15? I don't remember at this point. Combat, as a whole, feels like it drags out until there's an unexpected SPIKE. I don't know how many chances I've given Overwatch. I wanna be like the cool kids and be part of the crowd, but it really is just NOT FUN.
Paladins feels like it has gone out of its way to avoid almost all of the things I hate about OW. Right from first opening the character select screen, you can see how it tries to veer away from the turtley chokepoint nature of that game. Their classes are damage, flank, tank, and heal. Whereas OW is attack, defense, tank, and heal. See that? 2 offense and 2 defense versus 1 offense and 3 defense. Now, that's not an entirely fair comparison since some of the characters in those 3 defense categories are straight killers (Widowmaker, Roadhog). But to me it's just the start of painting a more complete picture.
Each level in Paladins has GREAT flank routes, forcing defenders to keep their heads on a swivel. They are also littered with way more odd pieces of cover here and there, allowing for more combat opportunities at different ranges. Weapons have more variance as to what ranges they are effective at, too, so matchups can happen more often. None of those giant no-man's-land style open areas like OW. EVERY character has a weapon that is effective and deadly (when used in their intended capacity) and healers have very diminished effectiveness compared to OW. What this does is makes Paladins more of a slugfest. Every match feels intense as everyone just beats the hell out of eachother. I don't think I've ever had a match that felt like a massive turtle, even when the team had like 3 tanks and two healers! Probably because tanks and healers are more rounded combatants in Paladins (which is why despite me saying that healers are less effective at healing they are still super important to team makeup). In OW, there are characters like Mercy and Reinhardt who are the best at what they do but are entirely single-minded in that purpose.
So that's the biggest difference: the overall game feel. But that's not even all the ways that this game is better. Here's a few more little things:
-Paladins is cheaper. It's free, for one, and the "all heroes unlocked forever" that OW comes with can be bought here for half the price, too.
-You can actually buy the things you want. OW just lets you buy the same lootbox that comes from leveling. No guarantees you'll get those limited time skins. But the chests that cost the premium currency in Paladins are all dupe-protected. So you WILL eventually get the skins you want. I think the most expensive one so far has been the Christmas chest. Basically it would cost about $15 to get every single thing out of that chest. The tradeoff here is that you can't get these skins just by playing the game. But I have friends who have spent $20 or more on chests in OW to try and get the skins they want only to be screwed by RNG. So... choose your poison.
-Loadout customization! One of the things I find dull about OW is that I can't make even minor changes to how a character is played. Paladins has a card system that gives at least a little bit of variety to each and every character.
-No Lucio required! In Paladins you spawn on a mount that gets you back into the fray quickly. You can't remount, either, so  this is simply something for helping with a push.
-More characters! There's a new character every month (currently, maybe this will slow down in the future) so there's always something new to check out. OW is what? Every 6 months? Takes forever.
The only point I can give OW is its art. Their style and animation is top-notch and Paladins will never be that shiny. But these are video games and not movies (despite what Blizzard's cinematics team seems to think) so GAMEPLAY FIRST. Ha! (for those who don't know, "Gameplay first" is one of Blizzard's mottos. IN YOUR FACE, JERKS)
The biggest issue I have with Paladins is how buggy some patches can be. I kinda look past it since I work in the industry and so I know that the release cadence they've set is INSANE for how much smaller their resources must be comparatively. But for a lot of people... you might not find that acceptable, heh. Not to say Paladins is a buggy mess like a Bethesda game, but it can be off-putting when something highly noticeable crops up.

This is a really old game! It's a F-Zero type racer (where your cars can blow up if you take too much damage, and you can heal by running over special tracks), with some Mario Kart items and Geometry Wars graphics. The soundtrack is very good if you're into electronica, and each racecar has different properties that can work with different playstyles or different racetracks.
For achievement hunters who happen to have this in their library already, it should provide about 10 hours of pleasant frustration. Otherwise, I don't really recommend it.
Firstly, this game has an outrageous number of technical problems. Sometimes when you try to run it, it doesn't initialize and you have to task-kill it before trying again. Sometimes it runs, but if something's hogging processor cycles, the framerate lag will snowball out of control until the game becomes completely unplayable. And the online multiplayer has long since been disabled, you can't host a server anymore. LAN play still works, however.
If you actually get the game to run, you might find that it's a very decent racer. There are some real magical moments of exhilaration when you're absolutely shredding the track and trying to maintain your first place lead. Unfortunately, the magic is killed by the game's terrible selection of items and the CPU players who will use them on you. See, when you get hit with an item, you lose the ability to steer your vehicle for about five seconds. It's just about as annoying as it might sound. If you're about to take a sharp turn and a CPU player comes up from behind and blasts you with a seeking missile... sorry! Now you're careening off the track and way in last place, and there was nothing you could really do to prevent it. Luck-based Mario Kart hell.
The items are not only unfun to get hit with, they're unfun to wield, and they require high precision if you want to do anything with them -- precision that the CPU players have, but not you. While I never caught a CPU blatantly cheating, they have an infuriatingly accurate aiming algorithm that leads their shot to exactly where you'll be when the shot will hit. It's very impressive and must use some kind of trigonometry calculation, but it will make you pull your hair out. They also have an uncanny ability to get a seeking missile or a tractor beam when they're in close second. Naturally, the shield item is the best item in the game, and it's usually the case that the player(s) who get the shield within the first five seconds of the race will be able to get a huge lead that they'll keep for the remainder of the race.
The weapon chaos wouldn't be so bad if the game didn't expect you to come in first place
if you want to get the final achievement. Luckily, you get infinite retries if you abuse the restarting feature, and you will absolutely need to abuse it if you want to survive the random chaos in the first ten seconds of every race.
Overall, it's a perfect demonstration of why an F-Zero racer shouldn't have Mario Kart items. It's one of those games that's a complete blast when you're winning, but utter bull when bad luck screws everything up. Give it another chance if you already own it, but otherwise avoid.

Great little top down racing game with bags of style and lots of fun to race around blowing up the opposition and trying to avoid all the mines and lasers flying around while staying on the track at the same time. The different racers allow players with different preferences or play styles to pick one that helps them out, the weapons all have their uses (although most are somewhat situational) and nothing is horribly unbalanced compared to the rest.
The tracks have a fairly good range of different dynamics and challenges - with some being a fairly straightforward and "clean" race where only people closely competing are likely to be able to attack each other, some have occasional crossover points where in some instances the leading players will cross in front of the chasing pack and often go down in a hail of gunfire for a much more open and messy race, and yet others will have masses of intersections and merges and be complete carnage for the entire race most of the time.
The racing side is well balanced for an arcade style game - going off the track slows you down noticeably, but even crashing into walls is usually not the end of the race for you, as sooner or later everyone hits a mine, or gets a missile up the exhaust.

This is the first time I'm buying and playing NBA2k17. In earlier titles of the series, I was seriously daunted by the controllable controls and gave up shortly after playing through a demo or two. This time, I actually persevered. So a thumb up to myself :). alright, to the game review. Generally, the game has a rather steep learning curve, with tutorial of 2ku not giving much in term of a coherent tutorial. However, after getting the hang of the controls and getting through a few shameful displays in the court, I can appreciate the charm of this game and the endless possibilities. I would seriously recommend this game. A number of points of cons though, so if you mind these, please dun buy:
1) Long cutscenes that can't be skipped in MC mode. After a few new profiles and careers, these cutscenes really become the number one headache. The only plus is I actually get to do some reading while waiting for the endless calls to mum.
2) The online currency. I can appreciate using online currency to buy animations, uniforms and sorts but to use the currency to upgrade stats of your character is really upsetting. This is especially so because you can actually buy these currency with real money. Not very (poor) user friendly. This also makes upgrading your character an awkward choice because attributes increase will not overlap to a new character so that's like money wasted when you start a new game.
3) Animation slow. I'm not referring to the slick animation in court. I'm referring to the slow and unskippable animation in between scenes. For example, when you return to your (i don't know how you call that) lobby with your bag. You have to literally see your character open the door, walk in slow motion to a particular spot. That's like what 10 seconds every time you complete a event. Totally unbearable.
Other from the above mentioned abhorable parts, the game is awesome. Really hope NBA2K17 would improve on these in future patches, at least and especially the unskippable cutscenes.

This game has been out for quite a while now but i just recently got around to playing it, being a fan of the advanced warfighter games i was looking forward to future soldier but i must say it still really impressed me. To begin with the visuals are excellent and the voice acting, gun sounds etc are top drawer as always. Most shooters these days push on the whole action element, i.e your in an over the top situation and you take on armies of soldiers in hollywood blockbuster style action sequences, Ghost Recon Future Soldier plays exactly the way it should, your an elite group of soldiers nicknamed ghosts because people don't know they really exist and the game wants you to play that way. Your presented with a situation which you can imagine spec oips soldiers being in, outnumbered (but not drastically) you have the option of stealth and team work, scout enemy patrol paths and potisions and take them out quietly as a team or you can still go in all guns blazing and spray everyone to pieces, i found myself doing that occasionally. But my favourite part of the game is the uav drone, so many times i found myself lasering enemy soldiers and just allowing my team mates to pick up the kills, it allows a whole new approach and gameplay option to the modern (if not slightly futuristic) shooter. If you like the all out guns plazing action of say Call of Duty or Battlefield then this may not be for you, but if you like to go for a game that allows you to use tactics, p[lan ahead, use different routes and strategies each time while fully utilising your squad then this game id for you. Sure it has its odd annoying grindy shooter bits, the ai can be dumb but surprisingly not often and the missions can seem similar to the ones before but having the option of going in Rambo mode, using a more splinter cell espionage approach or being support with the drone, it keeps the game fresh as you play through. All in all imo a diamond in the ruff of the saturated shooter market we have today. 9/10

The Good:
Deus Ex is an excellent FPS action RPG set in a dreary future world where morals are questioned and the lines between human and machine become blurred. Action, stealth, puzzle-solving and exploration are all well incorporated into the game, allowing you to play your own way as you navigate missions with different paths and outcomes, eliminating or avoiding enemies as you see fit. Multiple skills and upgrades encourage multiple playthroughs with different playstyles. Truly a gem in gaming history.
The Bad:
Without giving anything away, the plot starts to feel rushed by the end, and playstyles begin to be limited, with stealth becoming somewhat boring. Difficulty begins to ease off by the end as well; with certain skills and upgrades one could easily bypass most enemies without being seen with ease, even on the highest difficulty setting.
The Ugly:
Those textures are pretty bad, and the foreign voice acting is horrendous, but that doesn't change the fact that the game is amazing ;)

A window in to the old school ways of dungeon crawling and FPS gameplay that's just as approachable for new and old gamers alike!
Back when games didn't bog you down with forced tutorial segements where the game treats you like you have the IQ of a bee against a window, games presented you the tools and the world and said "you're on your own, good luck! You're gonna need it..." Through careful traversal of the world and observation of your enemies and the effects of your gear you became your own tutor. your victories and your failures were down to your strats, observations and reactions. This is what made games like Doom, Half Life and other 90's titles such classics and Delver brings back that style of gaming with grace and it's such a joy to see this approach to gaming still existant and appealing in this era of the industry!
Delver is a dungeon crawler, first person roguelike where permadeath results in the loss of your character upon death along with your items and level. That SOUNDS punishing but with out it, the appeal of this game is simply lost and it takes the experience of being in this amazing game to really appreciate that. You do however keep any gold you find which allows you purchase items you feel may help either balance the weaknesses in your gameplay style or further boost your strengths.
The game is split in to dungeon levels which go:
Dungeon 1
Dungeon 2
Caves 1
Caves 2
Sewers 1
Sewers 2
Ruins
The objective is to make your way in to the cursed ruins and obtain an orb to then double back and actually climb your way through those levels back to the surface, all while being pursued by the undead that roam the ruins looking for their orb!
Enemy types, difficulties and tactics vary through each level, constantly keeping you on your toes to see whether or not the enemy is fast, slow, hits hard or poisons or maybe they use projectile attacks. Eventually you'll come to recognise things like audio cues of monsters, the sounds of traps being detonated or particle effect remains on the floor, giving you clues as to what's gone on in the area.
The game's golden feature which makes this such an appealing experience is that everything is useful and thinking outside the box is critical to success. And the beauty of it is it's all down to you which makes the gameplay so rewarding with even the simplest of feats. for example. I noticed my run speed was still too slow for me to run over a trap and not get enough distance to get away from the blast radius it triggers but I remembered seeing enemies also trigger traps so I thought "what about items?" I took a broken wand with no charges left in it and threw it on the trap. Sure enough it detonated and I could move through it during the down time while the trap was resetting. Not only did that feel rewarding that my plan worked but I now knew that 'useless' items like empty wands still served a purpose, so I kept on to one or two as I explored.
Another example was when I was using a bow. I noticed sometimes when I missed, the arrow would bounce off a wall and I could pick it back up. When I came across the mage skeletons who are very projectile heavy and can easily be a problem, I wondered if I could bounce my arrows off the wall around a corner to fight them whilst being safe from their projectiles. I aimed at an angle and fired, sure enough the mage caught the arrow in his eye socket and he popped! Another rewarding feeling and a little more understanding of the game's mechanics!
Delver is a very small budget game and when you get the hang of it, it can easily be done in under an hour which results in the game resetting after a victory screen as if you died which is a shame because it feels like all the content can be experienced in a short manner of time and I want to spend so many hours in the world of Delver! The game is still early access as I write this so here's hoping the amazing guy behind this high potential title keeps dishing out further quality content!
(P.S. The projectile particle effects remind me so much of Heretic's visuals and that's just another 1000 bonus points to this title :P)

Borderlands: The Pre-Sequel, in essence, is more Borderlands 2. Except gravity has decided to divorce you and when you think you are used to their being gone they come back for short amounts of time that can neither be described as a joyful reunion or an utterly gut-destroying staredown. Maybe somewhere in between.

If you have ever played a Borderlands game, you will find exactly everything you have come to know and love: the charismatic visual effects, the crazy characters, the non-sense story, the tons of weird weapons, and a lot of irony. In addition, you have zero gravity!
If you have never played a Borderlands game, it is a good place like any to start!
The game experience is more or less the same in all three of them... In the end, it is more of the same, but if the same is good, at least for a while it is fine! As usual, its worst enemy is repetition: the scenaries all look more or less the same, the enemies respawn as if there was no tomorrow, and no matter how creative and farfetched the background story can sound, in most missions you will just go from point A to point B and shoot everything on your way. Nonetheless, it still is fun - for a while. If you take it in small doses day by day, it's okay; leave it there for a while and you probably won't be coming back.

I like this game more than Borderlands 2. YES. Borderlands 2 has WAY WAY WAYYY more content but for what this game has it is amazing! The low gravity makes combat far more dynamic than in BL2. Now you have all three dimensions to maneuver in, making combat interesting,
Do I want to jump over my enemies and attack them from above?
Do I want to evade my enemies by jumping to vantage points and attacking them from there?
Or do you just want to run up and slam them away with the new slam mechanic?
Not only that the environments are more dynamic. Air is a resource that you must keep an eye on making some situations more intense then it would be in BL2. Also you can use the environment as a weapon. And I’m not talking about ye olde explosive barrels. You can shoot the enemies air supply and cause a suffocation DOT.
As for elemental gimmicks, fire will do big DOT damage if the enemy is in Air, and then we have Cyro, the best element in Borderlands history!
Know what was fun about slag? Nothing. I HATED always having to tug around a slag weapon in Borderlands 2.
To me, being forced to use a gun I don’t want to use, slagging the enemy, and then switching to a gun I actually want to play with is not fun. (True you could argue this is only required in Ultimate vault hunter mode, but that’s where the real game is at.)  Know what is fun?  Freezing your enemy, and them punching them in the face and watching them shatter into a million pieces. That’s Cyro. The freezing element that is one part crowd control, one part melee wet dream. I have over 210 hours on BL2 and so far NOTHING is as satisfying than freezing a badass and then robot punching them in the face with Wilhelm and watching them shatter.
As for the world… Pandora felt too much like Earth. You could replace all the alien animals with Earth animals and you could totally fool someone into thinking the game takes place on Earth. Elpis however… feels truly alien.
Also I found the character Wilhelm interesting. The more you level him up in his cyper commando tree the more robotic he becomes and his voice even changes. I have never seen that in any other BL character. (Physically changing as you level them)
Also laser weapons are etech weapons except they don’t suck and come in 4 different forms. (Assult rifle, ghostbustery beams, sniper, and shotguns)
So…
Pros
-3 dimensional fighting
- environments are fun to fight in and the O2 mechanic makes you more aware of your surroundings
- Running around a low gravity moon is fun
-Wilhelm (200 of my hours were just on him)
-Cyro being the best element ever.
-lasers!
Cons
-	Far less content than BL2
-	Not as hard as BL2
YES BL2 is the better game because of the content, BUT if you compare the games at their cores, Pre sequel is superior with my opinion.
