TL;DR: 9/10, play it!
Pros:
+ Everything you love about borderlands and more! Lots of loot, very funny, a whole lot of action and a great story that actually explains a lot about whats going on in the Borderlands universe.
+ The playable characters actually have dialogue and interact with the storyline.
+ *Very* replayable, both in true vault hunter mode and as other characters.
+ Cyro weapons dont suck
+ Moonstones (TPS' version of Eridium) are plentiful and more common than Eridium in the first two games, but you can spend them in more places than just the black market.
+ Laser weapons are pretty decent. Well, except for laser shotguns (Sorry Mr. Torgue).
+ The ending basically confirmed that Borderlands 3 is going to happen and hinted at its storyline.
+ Low gravity and O2 kits (oxygen tanks for vacuums that also allow you to double jump, butt slam and have other small perks) are actually pretty useful and not just gimicky crap.
Cons
- Definetly a CPU intensive game, especially in heavy combat. I get worse FPS drops in this game than I do in BF4 with my AMD FX 4130 and GTX 760 in heavy combat, but it never drops below 35fps.
- Corrosive weapons are nearly useless, hardly any enemeies are armored.
- Fire weapons are useless in vacuums (which is like half the game).
- The grinder sucks, don't even bother with it unless you want the acheivements. You're much better off just selling the items and buying better ones.
- The story is shorter than the first two games and there seems to be less side missions.
All in all, its still a fantastic game and I would highly recommend it to anyone. Perhaps get it on sale, but I bought it full price and I have no ragrets.

Kingdoms Rise, in its early development presents players with the opportunity to beat the living S*** out of their friends or foes from around the world. Introducing a perfect blend between magic usage and melee combat, it could arguably be considered the magical equivelant of the Chivalry series. The weapon conbat is fluent and precise, with parrying and blocking working efficiently and allowing for some truly awesome duels.
Kingdoms Rise, though an awesome game has several flaws which hinder its sucess in the playability area. The foremost of which being a lack of players. Some games become simply outstanding when played on a full server, alas, Kingdoms Rise seldom presents the possibility for this. The game in its pre-release accomplished more by ways of player versus player melee combat than many other games have accomplished in their whole lifetime.
Whether you play Kingdoms Rise for its awesome character customization, to blow your friends to pieces with fireballs, to teleport behind enemies and impale them on a blade of flames, Kingdoms Rise is for you.
The only recommendation I offer to those playing it is to go in with an open mind. The game has its bugs, as one would expect from an early release game. Though any braincell-possessing human being can see the potential in this title. Regardless of what the game is like now, it leaves me and other players with a ready mind for the full release.
When this game fully releases, it will be a game to remember.

If Super Laser Racer were a pair of sneakers, mine would be worn-out, haggard shreds of leather, and I've enjoyed wearing them since they were bright, shiny, and sitting in a box with crumpled up packing paper.
SLC invites you to defeat all of it. It offers enough variety in tracks and levels of difficulty that it was fun to revisit until I'd completed everything.
The game is simple and straight-forward. The controls are relatively decent and you'll never have a tough time figuring out what your objective is (in case you're wondering: WIN THE RACE ;-).

The game has a few bugs and inconveniences:
-
With it plugged in I couldn't race. It gets stuck on the loading screen just before a race.
-
The gameplay will be extremely choppy. Fullscreen is basically required for smooth play.
-
If you run any other software at the same time that uses your CPU reasonably, this game'll be choppy. It seems a tad poorly coded for such a simple looking game.
That aside, for just under 1 euro (in a sale) you have an amusing little racing game. You have a choice out of various tracks, difficulty, and what type of race you want. You can do a normal race, elimination, survival, or time trial. Multiplayer's possible as well, though I haven't tried it yet. You can also decide which vehicle you want to race in, each have their own pros and cons.
The screenshots of this game pretty much says it all about what the game looks like. You get to be able to shoot at your opponents, after you've driven over those red square thingies. That is the weapon box. The other symbols have various effects like boost, or reducing your speed. You can customize tracks as well, including changing the colors.
I can recommend this game if you see it for cheap in a sale and you happen to like top-down racing games.. It's just that, a little racing game, worth a buck at most.

Contains what some may consider minor spoilers.
A decent enough sequel (oh excuse me, PREQUEL) to BL2, it removes some major annoyances of the aforementioned game whilst introducing new ones but it's mostly more of the same, so I'll use BL2 for comparison on several occasions throughout the review.
As for the graphics and sound effects - it's mostly the same as BL2. Many voice actors have an australian (or fake cockney) accent which is a nice enough change of scenery. Enemy chatter is not as entertaining as it was in BL2, sadly. Combat's not nearly as fun without people shouting "SEEEEEEEEMEEEEEEENNNN" while rushing towards you.
The story feels like it takes relatively little substance and elongates it forever. The idea of documenting Handsome Jack's rise to power (and descent into psychopathic megalomania) is good but their approach to it is a bit too heavy-handed and melodramatic in places. I do like some of the little foreshadowing references to the events of BL2.
There are several new gameplay mechanics which make the game feel fresh even though the core gameplay is still pretty much the same. The new things include:
○ Limited oxygen: many areas of the game don't have a breathable atmosphere so your O2 supply will drain at a slow rate there. Boosts and butt slams drain oxygen at a noticably increased rate so you need to ration it well because you'll start taking damage when you run out (unless you're a claptrap). This feature can be very annoying sometimes as it artificially adds a sense of urgency to everything - exploration is not that much fun when you've got a time limit. The good thing is that enemies need to breathe too and they'll start taking suffocation DoT when you break their oxygen masks, allowing you to save some ammo.
○ Low gravity & boost: allows you to reach places that'd be impossible to get to in BL2 so it takes a while to get used to the new possibilities. And you're going to have to – some missions require well timed jumps and boosts in order to reach the objective. If you really hate platforming, you might want to avoid this game.
○ Butt slam: a quick way to get to the ground from mid-air, plus it does good damage and can inflict DoT effects - invaluable for saving ammo, but costs oxygen.
○ Laser weapons: they pretty much replace E-tech, you can get various types which act shotgun-like, sniper-like, automatic or like the lightning gun from Quake 3. They're not bad but I found myself not using them much.
○ The Cryo element: replaces slag, feels more satisfying to use - you can immobilise enemies then deal increased damage to them. I really wish the player character wouldn't spout cheap ice puns when freezing an enemy though.
○ The grinder: insert 3 weapons, get a randomly generated, usually higher tier one. Basically another form of gambling, I got several legendaries from it.
There are also new playable classes (which I think may be better than in BL2) and new enemy types, some of which are a real pain in the bottom. Some BL2 enemies make an appearance, but they're not re-used nearly as heavily as BL1 enemies were in BL2.
Overall this is an ok game, it's worth playing but definitely not paying the full price for.

--- For the Glory of Mankind ---
The game was played with the in my eyes essential PC FAR patch.
After having played about 100h of this game. I think its time to elevate my thoughts into words.
NieR:A is unique: from its director the "Crazy" Genius Yoko Taro to its world, the gameplay variants and unprecedented musik in orchestral and vocal form.
There is no genre it can be confined too, as such its hard to even compare it to anything besides the original NieR and Drakengard Series.
Broken down its an Action, Sidescroller, Platformer, Twinstick Shooter, RPG thats sometimes a Visual Novel and the Bosses have Names and Characteristics of existential Philosophers) and it has the best Soundtrack of any game.
NieR:A is fresh: in a AAA Gaming Market were most games present itself as "Thanks for the 60€! have lackluster content and 20+ Paid DLC"! it's always suprising, simply because Yoko "Happy Ending" Taro dares going direction most games would not even touch
- The "Bad Guys" will not allways die or lose
- The "Good Guys" will not allways survive or succeed
- the Innocents will not be spared
and it breaks genre conventions at every possible moment handling replays of the game as Chapters of a grand Story.
Were you expect the same content but each time you get more until the great reveal of Chapter C.
With NieR you get one of the most complex storys hidden behind a depressing and at first glance silly Universe at least from a Videogame Standpoint that can only be told in a video game format.
Nier:A is an experience: This game loves to prove people wrong who think they know how the game will progress and that is so statisfying not knowing what can happen,Were the orginal lacked in the combat with NieR:A Platinum is on Board and the combat is so much better its fast, fluid and brutal. The ammount of tiny detailed animations in everything your Characters does speaks on a level of detail most game don't even bother with now a days.
The level of escalation from the 2nd play through to the 5th ending is one insanely special experience. NieR:A will make you feel emotions that are extremely hard to put down easily into words. After the original NieR (PS3 Gestalt Version) this is my game of the century. Essential!
"Join for the the best animated android butt, stay because nobody is allowed to leave Yoko Taro's wild ride once they get on board."
No other game besides the original NieR has asked me as the player of the game, not as the player of the game character to make the ultimate sacrifice at the end.

It's a hack and slash, but it is constantly moving between other genres and constantly remixing itself in both gameplay and storytelling. For the love of Mankind please play this game.

Interesting game for how short it is. There are about 4 or 5 maps to choose from, each one having different game modes already attached to the map. The game is also pretty comical in a sense that it's gorey and cartooney at the same time. For example, you can have a hole in your torso with a piece of ribcage sticking out, guts falling to the floor, and blood squirting from the extremeties, yet you are still able to limp along and fight against your aggressors. Now the interesting part is the weapon customization.

The only thing that uses microtransactions is that of outfits and stuff that makes your character different from the others. Overall, there are tons of different designs for the guns and overall, I believe that's what the devs were going for. It isn't like Team Fortress 2, even though, yes there is a medgun, but even the medgun can be interchangable with parts so it acts differently on the field, unlike that of TF2.

This is an amazing idea, and a beautiful execution.  It is a fun PvP game with a suprisingly deep combat system that is both easy to figure out (if you watch some tutorials) and has a very high skill cap. Then you have kind of a fast paced king of the hill mode, I say fast paced because the capture timer is zero; as soon as one team has the advantage near a capture point it is theirs.  This makes the king of the hill mode feel strategic and a little frantic on ocassion.  The commnunity is not non-existant, I've always been able to find a game, but the server lists do look a little empty.
Bottom line is that if you're wondering whether or not to buy this game, you should.  The biggest issue is the size of the community and that can only be fixed by more people picking it up; and it is shaping up to be an incredibly fun PvP game the likes of which hasn't been done before.

Party Hard has an awesome hook. You're mad at partying neighbors and decide to take revenge.  What follows is basically Michael Meyers on a nationwide one-man-play version of Falling Down. The idea is simple and corny, but fun.
Most of the gameplay is fun, but there are a couple things that can drive the fun level down fast. It's cool to use various and somewhat randomized traps against partiers, but the gulf in usefulness between some traps is simply too wide. This can result in some stages where you get really screwed by the trap placement RNG. There also aren't enough traps in most levels. You will probably run out of traps before you even get halfway through the crowd. Now, you mostly sneak about and pick off stragglers when they're alone. This is initially fun, but quickly becomes a tedious waiting game.  If you don't really enjoy the idea of patiently waiting for the majority of the levels, keeping in mind getting caught and arrested can happen from a single mistake, think twice before you pull the trigger on this. If you like the aesthetic and don't mind being very patient, the game is a lot of fun. If you're looking for a Hotline Miami-esque killfest at breakneck speed, Party Hard is most definitely not that.

Party Hard has a novel (though very much in the "dark humor" style) idea: you play a psychopath who is so annoyed by people partying and playing loud music at 3AM that he decides to go on a rampage and kill them all. So, on every level, you need to kill everybody while avoiding suspicion, or at least avoid the patrolling police.
Unfortunately, that concept isn't well executed. This game is no Hotline Miami, the movements are slow and imprecise, making it unlikely you would go for a fast and loose style (despite the "combo" bonus points that would indicate this is good ?). On the other hand, there are very few traps or ways to hide bodies, so playing stealthily isn't an option either.
Therefore, you're left with a mixed bag of traps that are usually very inefficient, a few secrets I won't talk about here, and your own knife that will do most of the work, usually in a far corner of the map (to be able to kill people one by one without one escaping from your very slow character). That leads to a gameplay that is repetitive (since most kills are just waiting for people to be alone, then knifing them), and very random (since the best way to kill people is what spawn randomly on the map, but can vary from being very useful, to being a big hindrance).
Moreover, the game fails to explain many of the concepts. Though there are "newspapers" you can read to learn some basics, even after finishing the game, there are still icons and game concepts that I do not understand properly. Like why sometimes suspicion gets diverted to someone else, or why sometimes people will freak out upon seeing you even though you're far from any crime scene.
The great music and interesting pixel art graphic style can't redeem the slow gameplay, the randomness factor being too high, and some unclear game mechanisms. Even if the game looks fun, I would recommend you to not buy it, there are better games out there.

It is with a heavy heart that I admit this game failed at being fun for me, despite being full of great ideas and in spite of me trying hard to like it.
Sure there are plenty customization options for your race, but in reality it's a cookie cutterfest with some options being so much better than others that choice becomes automatic.  Resource management and harvesting is well done, but the fleet capacity mechanics is counter-intuitive and not very well designed (what's the point of a fleet cap if you always have to double that for your fleet to be meaningful[!?!]).
The tech research, while appearing fresh at first thanks the multiple choice style, actually gets frustrating very soon as you realise you cannot plan your tech tree development at all.
When you finally start controlling a decent amounts of planets the mechanics of planetary sectors kick in, limiting the planets under your direct control to 5 (otherwise a global penalty gets slapped on your resource harvesting). I truly do not understand this mechanic and totally despise it.
In other various, I am not a big fan of space combat (a pure number game, bigger stack wins, smaller stack loses), the tutorial is poorly made (hard to even call it that).
Now on to the good side, the game looks really good and the music is great too. The scope of it feels very grand, galaxies are really huge and the system surveying together with the anomalies system really gives you a nice exploration thrill. Diplomacy seems to be well executed, although I have not played enough to really get a feel about it.
All in all while I can appreciate the attention to the details, pretty graphics and music, and the many customization options I personally can only recommend this game only if you are a grand strategy enthusiast.

I was the only nation strong enough to fight them and I had fun finally wiping them out.  Although i got no thanks from the nation that was being slaughtered.
Many of these grand strategy game I spend a lot of time "fast forwarding" to get money or wait for my army to build up etc.  There is enough depth to the game that I kept busy pretty much the whole time.  There is a lot of micro management but not to the point where it gets annoying and ruins the game for me.  I wasnt very happy with the secto system at first because i wanted to control the planets that i conquered but as I gained more and more planets I understodd the need for it,  The AI is completely horrible at managing the planets though, when i gained more core system i took one back over and it was barely developed at all, after nearly a 100 years.
I also wish that the AI was smarter to make combat and other aspects of the game more challenging.  They are pretty stupid most of the time and don't do much to fight back after you take out there main fleet.  I usually just send my entire fleet in (assuming it is larger than theirs) and slaughter theirs and start systematically taking planets from them till they surrender.  They will take fleets to the planets that I have taken and just orbititally bombard them, never making an attempt to take them back.  If they would take them back it would significantly hinder my ability to win the war.  Using worm holes with a large fleet takes a long time to get back and forth to system to defend them.  Most of the time i have totally overwhelmed them by the time their allies even show up and they surrender.  They will also very seldomly partner up with their allies to challenge an enemy fleet.  They will just come at you one at a time like lambs to the slaughter.  The same is true with your allies, they just meander around the whole time, engaging the enemy in with no discernable tactics, just whenever they happen to run into them.  Would be nice to have a diplomatic option to take control allied fleets to use them effectively, like defending conquered system or invading the enemies allies while you are attacking the main target.
Despite the AI, I have enjoyed playing this game very much and would recommend it to anyone who is a fan of these type games.  I am interested to see what happens as I continue.

Beneath Magicite's colorful rogue-lite veneer lies a surprisingly grindy platformer. Random stat gains and % effect items are exceedingly, almost excessively balanced - it's very rare to find yourself too low on any one stat, or for an item to fail to activate within the desired margin of error. This is not a flaw in and of itself, but coupled with the repetitive level generation, playing through Magicite quickly becomes a stale experience. The crafting system is quite shallow, and biomes contain virtually-identical enemies varying only in stats and artistic style. The races, abilities, hats, and companions all add some replayability, but since there are only three viable playstyle archetypes, these diminish in relevance, as advanced strategic combinations are not possible.
Magicite has the depth and simplicity of a mobile game, but with the time commitment of a much more robust game. A few hours of enjoyment may be had, but this is not a game that will tantalize you with additional progression for long.

I finished the main story of
a few weeks ago. I've only been playing it until now to finish the last few achievements, and yet not a day goes by when I haven't thought about it. It is clear that
had brilliant writers and directors behind it. This game will certainly pull at your heartstrings, surprise you with novel twists, and perhaps have the capability to cause you to question your own way of living.
takes place in a dystopian future, where the earth has been razed and taken over by seemingly mindless machines. Humanity has been pushed away to the moon, and it's up the android Resistance and elite android squadron YoRHa to take the planet back. It's a typical enough backdrop, but of course that's not all there is to it.
I'll be avoiding spoilers here, but the story presents itself not through exposition but slow and careful worldbuilding through a large cast of characters, android and machine alike. The differences between android and machine are made clear repeatedly throughout the story, and thankfully the two factions behave in character throughout. When inevitable change or shifts in view happen, this results in it actually being a weighted, understandable event.
characters are smart and internally consistent, making them entirely enjoyable.
The game's themes are intertwined primarily with absurdism, with a few blatent Camus references sprinkled throughout. An analogy towards the status of the human condition and value is frequently made with that of the android's, who are placed in a situation where they are forced (via programming) to love a seemingly absent but once certainly real god. In the world of video games this is actually rather unique, and
makes excellent use of its medium to play with this topic in a novel way, and comes to a satisfying conclusion by the end.
Moving past the story, graphically, the game is nothing to write home about. It ranges from looking like a late PS2 title to solid PS3 level, but doesn't really move past that besides the quality of the character models. Where it does shine is the camerawork - perspective shifts are common and there's a huge number of cinematic shots that just beg for a screenshot. Coupled with the voice acting, well, let's just say there is no way I'll be forgetting a few of the scenes. The game's story is only matched by its overall presentation and it's quite clear that love was put into every level. Again, I have to give special homage to the voice acting, and also to the soundtrack. After the first
I don't think it's surprising to anyone that that
also has an excellent OST that can even stand tall on its own.
Lastly, gameplay. Platinum did it. It's good, great even. It's fast-paced, predictable, and satisfying, though in actual execution a bit shallow. Fancy combos and juggles are possible, but the game is easy enough to where there's no need for difficult techs - you can't quite button mash through everything but at the same time the dodge system gives you a large enough leeway that there's no need to be careful either. The difficulty settings also aren't particularly well done. On normal, as said, the game is quite easy but on the hard difficulty challenge is made through an increase in enemy health pools and a decrease in yours. This is by far my least favorite system of adding difficulty to any game, and as a result I skipped over it in Automata even if it does make certain segments, like boss fights, more enjoyable. Having each random mook take 30 sword swings to kill ruins sense of pace.
Anyway,
is an excellent game with an incredibly memorable cast and story. It's well worth a playthrough, multiple especially.

Lone Survivor is a survival horror game that really makes you feel both the survival and the horror and thirdly the horror of survival.
Right off the bat LS has a demo out there, so you should give that a couple minutes to see if you can handle the retro graphics.
Not for you? Move on.
Pixel lover? Let's dig in.
LS takes quite a few cues from other survival games, like an auto updating mapping system and flashlight that needs new batteries constantly, but really the game remains largely unique. You play as a young man set in a town filled with zombies caused by disease. The game starts very quickly with little explanation and leaves the player to fill in what is going on, who you are, and how to really survive.
It becomes very clear very quickly that your character might not exactly be in his right mind, a large part of the story and vibe of the game is a psychological one, but this review is not going to expand on this because its best left for the game itself.
The biggest chunk of surviving the game is managing your food and sleep levels, which might not sound fun, but its so key to the game in multiple ways that its inescapable. The character will let you know maybe a little too often how you are feeling, tired or hungry.
You will need to find and cook, or combine food in different ways to keep yourself going. It takes some trial and error... is this bottle of milk still good? Whats more filling these crackers or a squid on a stick?
The more important question comes in while exploring and being harassed by critters that want to spit infected blood on you, or strangle the life from your body.
Should I push on, do I have enough food, am I well rested? Should I return now or risk it and explore a little more.
Thus the game follows a good pattern of exploration, and retreat, each day you'll either need to hoof it or use teleporting mirrors to return back to your apartment to rest and save before heading back into the mirror and continuing.
As you explore you'll find lots and lots of things a flashlight, a weapon, a cat, coffee, a ham, a source of water, fuel for your stove. Also you'll unlock several shortcuts and even pseudo vendors to allow you to get a helpful boost if you need more ammo or pills or rotten meat.
In several areas you'll need to use the flashlight to be able to interact with something in the darkness but the light will increase your visibility to the games creepy monsters, also the flashlight has limited energy and you have limited batteries.
Many monsters are near spots that allow you to sneak around them, but your character isn't a complete wimp and its not too hard to kill them off, if carefully watching your supplies and planning your attacks.
The controls work well, and are responsive but might take a bit of getting used to as you can only attack to one side at a time, and walk much slower while trying to do so, needing to lower your weapon before turning and re-raising it. Other than that the game is very minimalistic, a few hotkeys, movement keys, interact key, inventory key.
A real treat in LS is the sound that immerses you and gives you clues about your character's state of mind and health. Monster noises are creepy and while there is no real voice work, this is a retro-style game after all.
All in all Lone Survivor is a wonderful exercise in a lot of things, retro graphics, minimalistic controls, sound, creepiness, and of course survival mechanics. At 9.99 it's a steal for hours of enjoyment over many other games of lesser quality at many times the price... it might even keep you up at night.

Interesting game for how short it is. There are about 4 or 5 maps to choose from, each one having different game modes already attached to the map. The game is also pretty comical in a sense that it's gorey and cartooney at the same time. For example, you can have a hole in your torso with a piece of ribcage sticking out, guts falling to the floor, and blood squirting from the extremeties, yet you are still able to limp along and fight against your aggressors. Now the interesting part is the weapon customization.
For weapon, you have 4 base designs to choose from, then you have a multitude of parts to add from the stock of the gun, to the way the shell exits the guns (Cluster bomb, stickey mines, i.e.) There is a lot to choose from, but to get these parts, you have to unlock them with Butes which are gained throughout playing the game and matches. The only thing that uses microtransactions is that of outfits and stuff that makes your character different from the others. Overall, there are tons of different designs for the guns and overall, I believe that's what the devs were going for. It isn't like Team Fortress 2, even though, yes there is a medgun, but even the medgun can be interchangable with parts so it acts differently on the field, unlike that of TF2.
Overall, I would recommend the game as a try out. It is fun to play, and if you have friends, it is even better. I hope that devs do have extra continent coming along, for even some modes are still locked. If you have extra HDD or SDD space, just download this game and give it a try. It doesn't hurt to just try it for yourself. If you don't like it, you always delete it, simple as that. Have fun, and enjoy hope this small review helps.

Party Hard has a novel (though very much in the "dark humor" style) idea: you play a psychopath who is so annoyed by people partying and playing loud music at 3AM that he decides to go on a rampage and kill them all. So, on every level, you need to kill everybody while avoiding suspicion, or at least avoid the patrolling police.
Unfortunately, that concept isn't well executed. This game is no Hotline Miami, the movements are slow and imprecise, making it unlikely you would go for a fast and loose style (despite the "combo" bonus points that would indicate this is good ?). On the other hand, there are very few traps or ways to hide bodies, so playing stealthily isn't an option either.
Therefore, you're left with a mixed bag of traps that are usually very inefficient, a few secrets I won't talk about here, and your own knife that will do most of the work, usually in a far corner of the map (to be able to kill people one by one without one escaping from your very slow character). That leads to a gameplay that is repetitive (since most kills are just waiting for people to be alone, then knifing them), and very random (since the best way to kill people is what spawn randomly on the map, but can vary from being very useful, to being a big hindrance).
Moreover, the game fails to explain many of the concepts. Though there are "newspapers" you can read to learn some basics, even after finishing the game, there are still icons and game concepts that I do not understand properly. Like why sometimes suspicion gets diverted to someone else, or why sometimes people will freak out upon seeing you even though you're far from any crime scene.
The great music and interesting pixel art graphic style can't redeem the slow gameplay, the randomness factor being too high, and some unclear game mechanisms. Even if the game looks fun, I would recommend you to not buy it, there are better games out there.

I've played a lot of strategy/4X games, and in light of that: Stellaris is a huge disappointment.  It has a few interesting ideas brought into the genre, but implemented poorly.  Most of the core mechanics are derivative of other, better games and implemented more poorly.  Exploration is largely limited, and requiring science ships for exploration doesn't provide a meaningful change to the game (I just send a science ship instead of a scout).  It takes a while for it to survey, which is kind of neat, but in practice it just slows things down.  The story beats that can be discovered are a neat concept, but in execution it is just like a generic fetch quest from an MMO.  Ship design is technically in the game although there are very few meaningful choices to be made, combat is completely uninspired and might as well be fully automated.  The game has a highly legalistic feeling to it, and at no point did I feel like I was "playing" the game, instead I was carefully "driving" it on the road, between the lines.  Colony management is abysmal, combining the zone system from games like Galactic Civilization (but with mostly rote decisions rather than interesting ones like choosing a proximity bonus vs leveraging an exploitable bonus), but with the need for upkeep of another game.  Diplomacy is terrible.  The large number of races all blur together and have virtually zero personality.  Visually I think the game looks 10 years older than it is, it's got all sorts of hideous typographical and color choices interspersed with competent ones - as if the visual designers were only around for half the project.  On top of it all it has been very buggy at times.  It's received many patches to fix it, but still... what a mess.
I'm also confused by the choice to make it "real time", as in practice I alternated between full speed and full stop - basically rendering this a turn based game.  It doesn't have the flow of a game like Sins of a Solar Empire or Star Craft, which use the real time method effectively... it's just a mess.
I think someone who enjoys filing taxes they would enjoy this game, or possibly people who are really into role playing.  If you want to feel like you are the Emperor of a mighty space age civilization go play some other game.  If you want to feel like a high ranking logistical clerk in a mighty space age civilization then this might be your thing.  Either way... between the new Master of Orion, the old Master of Orion (1 or 2), Endless Space, Galactic Civilizations II, Distant Worlds or Sins of a Solar Empire, you should be able to find something better that matches up with you.

While I do enjoy this game there are multiple ways the AI constantly cheats in order to defeat the player. They can Mine planets without scanning them first, can pop out endless amounts of ships when they should'nt have the resources to, and WILL recieve the best outcomes no matter what.
I do Truley enjoy this game... But the devs are just adding features to cover mistakes and bugs up. If the DEVS REALLY wanted to improve the game they should start with the little things.
I hope to see things change in the future... But knowing how previous companies deal with similar issues, they most likely wont.
Current issues:
-AI dont need to scan planets to build stations on them.
-When ever they 'Discover' an anomaly they magic up the best result.
-Have seemingly endless resources despite buildings/stations to pump out fleets they should not have the capacity for.
-Cover up big bugs with promises of DLC. Which add more bugs.

PRO
-Combat system is quite fun (can take a bit of time to get used to)
-Raids are some of the best of any MMO I've played
-Dungeons are quite fun but do have a learning curve for new players
-Shiphands (expeditions) are good 1-5 man scaling content
-Game runs smoothly (engine is quite good)
-Not pay to win, most  cash shop items are cosmetic or are also obtainable by ingame currency
-Mostly friendly/helpful community
-preraid gearing is made quite easy for new people with the new daily zone Arcterra
-Housing there is loads you can do here, you can buy or find decor all over the place and place it how you want in your housing plot making things like jump puzzles or mazes or just making it look awesome, there are also functional "FABKITS" that offer something to its owner or visitors, the housing plot also offers rested experience boosts as you place decor that provides buffs to it.
-Dual/tripple/quad spec so you can have a DPS, Tank OR Healer, PvP build and 1 other build
PRO and CON
-Adventures are a good idea and can be fun but seem a little unrewarding
-PvP is fun but can be unbalanced especially prior to obtaining pvp gear
-LAS (limited action set) It's good to have to plan for the fight and not be required to have  30 buttons but it can be annoying at times to change between bosses/trash etc (there is mods to help with this)
-Leveling can suck especially the first levels as people don't get to see what the game is really like early on, it is not grindy and there are things to break up the constant questing like Shiphands (expeditions)/Group content and they sometimes hold double exp weekends
CON
-Terrible/useless customer support
-Runening system itself is alright but has many drawbacks, good quality runes come mostly from raiding or complete luck, it can be daunting to figure out the rune system when you are new to it and it has been changed multiple times and when it is they generally do not compensate you fairly for the cost of changing gear slots to suit the new sets, you generally do not get fair compensation for your previous BiS runes to the new BiS runes of equal level
-Raid Consumables specifically buff food materials come from raids and are limited/rare they are pretty close to impossible to farm outside of raids (cheaper crappier food is availalbe though)
-Crafting system half of the professions offer nothing late game at all, cooking (everyone can get) being one of the best late game professions is near impossible to level
-Population causes queue times to be terrible for PvP and PvE

It is with a heavy heart that I admit this game failed at being fun for me, despite being full of great ideas and in spite of me trying hard to like it.
Sure there are plenty customization options for your race, but in reality it's a cookie cutterfest with some options being so much better than others that choice becomes automatic.  Resource management and harvesting is well done, but the fleet capacity mechanics is counter-intuitive and not very well designed (what's the point of a fleet cap if you always have to double that for your fleet to be meaningful[!?!]).
The tech research, while appearing fresh at first thanks the multiple choice style, actually gets frustrating very soon as you realise you cannot plan your tech tree development at all.
When you finally start controlling a decent amounts of planets the mechanics of planetary sectors kick in, limiting the planets under your direct control to 5 (otherwise a global penalty gets slapped on your resource harvesting). I truly do not understand this mechanic and totally despise it.
In other various, I am not a big fan of space combat (a pure number game, bigger stack wins, smaller stack loses), the tutorial is poorly made (hard to even call it that).
Now on to the good side, the game looks really good and the music is great too. The scope of it feels very grand, galaxies are really huge and the system surveying together with the anomalies system really gives you a nice exploration thrill. Diplomacy seems to be well executed, although I have not played enough to really get a feel about it.
All in all while I can appreciate the attention to the details, pretty graphics and music, and the many customization options I personally can only recommend this game only if you are a grand strategy enthusiast.

I was a little hesitant about getting this game after reading several bad reviews but so far i am very impressed.
The tech tree is amazing to me, it just keeps going and going, some many not be impressed with it but i am use to the same tired old civ tech tree.  I havent finished my first game yet but i keep thinking im gonna run out of techs to research but so far it just keeps going.

I am usually not all that interested in the side quests and other such things in these kinds of games but paradox has but quite a bit of thought into the plot of the galaxy.  I had am interesting time fighting the ether drake, took me 3 times to finally kill it.  The invasion forces from outside the galaxy where a welcome challenge as well.  I was the only nation strong enough to fight them and I had fun finally wiping them out.  Although i got no thanks from the nation that was being slaughtered.
Many of these grand strategy game I spend a lot of time "fast forwarding" to get money or wait for my army to build up etc.  There is enough depth to the game that I kept busy pretty much the whole time.  There is a lot of micro management but not to the point where it gets annoying and ruins the game for me.  I wasnt very happy with the secto system at first because i wanted to control the planets that i conquered but as I gained more and more planets I understodd the need for it,  The AI is completely horrible at managing the planets though, when i gained more core system i took one back over and it was barely developed at all, after nearly a 100 years.
I also wish that the AI was smarter to make combat and other aspects of the game more challenging.  They are pretty stupid most of the time and don't do much to fight back after you take out there main fleet.  I usually just send my entire fleet in (assuming it is larger than theirs) and slaughter theirs and start systematically taking planets from them till they surrender.  They will take fleets to the planets that I have taken and just orbititally bombard them, never making an attempt to take them back.  If they would take them back it would significantly hinder my ability to win the war.  Using worm holes with a large fleet takes a long time to get back and forth to system to defend them.  Most of the time i have totally overwhelmed them by the time their allies even show up and they surrender.  They will also very seldomly partner up with their allies to challenge an enemy fleet.  They will just come at you one at a time like lambs to the slaughter.  The same is true with your allies, they just meander around the whole time, engaging the enemy in with no discernable tactics, just whenever they happen to run into them.  Would be nice to have a diplomatic option to take control allied fleets to use them effectively, like defending conquered system or invading the enemies allies while you are attacking the main target.
Despite the AI, I have enjoyed playing this game very much and would recommend it to anyone who is a fan of these type games.  I am interested to see what happens as I continue.

I just beat the game, and the battle with the Scourge was awesome. I had 11 big health potions, over a hundred iron arrows, a fire bow and a scourge blade. I shot all of my arrows at the scourge, but it wasn't enough to kill him. I had already used all of my potions, and things were not looking good for me at all. So I took my blade, swung it at the Scourge once, and it died. Victory! :)
The game itself is pretty cool, especially the graphics, but it seems a bit underdeveloped to me. For example: there are tons of different kinds of melee weapons, but only four ranged and magic ones. For ranged it doesn't really matter because it is extremely strong, but magic cannot be considered a real class here. Three out of the four magic staves that I believe are currently in the game are made with gems, which are made from flies, which are caught with nets. Those very same gems can be used on a sword called Zweihander to give the exact same properties as the staves have, but with the benefits of a sword. This makes these staves completely useless. The fourth staff is used to summon zombies, which is nice but definitely not enough to make it through the game. A game called MAGICite should contain a lot of magic items in my opinion.
Since I beat the game, let's talk about replayability. The races, hats and companions should encourage the player to keep playing until he or she has unlocked all of them. This is not the case, because many races and hats only have a 20% chance to unlock after the player does what has to be done to unlock it. Another example: the Trogon race has a 100% chance to unlock after the player beats the game in under an hour (which, by the way, is not much harder than beating the game normally. I think the developer told us on Kickstarter that play sessions lasted from about 15 minutes to 2 hours, but there is no way to play for 2 hours because if you stay in one district for too long, the scourge will kill you), the Noble class, however, only has a 20% chance to unlock after the player kills fifteen monsters in a single playthrough. I did unlock the Trogon class, but even though I have beaten hundreds of monsters in a lot of playthroughs I still didn't unlock the Noble class, which is supposed to be one of the first classes to unlock. If I achieve something, I want to get rewarded for it. Now I'd have to play the game again, which is not much of a problem, but I'd have to do a very similar run. There is just no fun in that.
Finally I'd like to say something about roguelikes. Roguelikes are turn-based games featuring permanent death, tile-based graphics and randomly generated dungeons. Therefore, games with permanent death aren't neccesarily roguelikes. Magicite isn't turn-based, so it's not a roguelike.
I don't recommend this game, because it just doesn't have enough content to be worth €10,- and the developer is an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. He promises to do a lot with his games, publishes them way too early and then counts his money while the players are stuck within walls or dying due to bugs.

I loved Borderlands 1 and 2, My criticism for the first game was that it was far too brown. Anyone who played it will understand what I mean. The second game improved on that, and everything else for that matter! It was fun, addictive, the story was great, the loot was epic! It was an incredible game!
So you can see why I was incredibly excited to play the pre-sequel and get more of the action right?
Well, I installed the game, checked out what the different characters were about and jumped into it!
From the off, playing alongside Handsome Jack was weird as hell! It was great, dont get me wrong, it was just a bit of an adjustment going from killing him to saving him!
I enjoyed the game a lot, right up until we left Jack and headed for the moon! Now, the first thing that got me was the fact that people who lived on the moon were Australian.....okay, I can roll with that, 2K Australia made the game, sure, why not.
Then there was the oxygen system, I could see that getting annoying but hey, it kind of made sense! Then I could use my O2 (It's O2.... not OZ.... that is just stupid) to manouver in the air, i could slam down and deal damage, all interesting ideas. Until the enemy humans can do the same, so you can never keep track of them, they constantly just pound you into the ground until you are begging for gravity to strengthen its hold! Honestly, it all feels a bit redundant and needless, Surely if you are a mighty vault hunter travelling through space you would have some kind of rebreather, something that would generate oxygen!
Whilst I mention the enemies, the generation of enemies in this game is screwy as hell, at level 3 and 4 I started running into badass variations of already annoying enemies! It's bad enough that these "moon skags" divide into smaller variants when killed, but then I suddenly have to deal with badass versions at level freaking 4!? I dealt with that, okay, sure, it's more challenging in the beginning than the first two, maybe thats a good thing! Then I meet Deadlift.... The first real boss of the game and I couldn't beat him. It's only after I looked up information on the internet that I discovered I had to complete the "optional" missions to get rewarded with a shock element gun to kill him. Right... an optional mission that the game renders almost unavoidable.
All of these problems could well have been ignored, I really could have gotten used to it if it wasn't for the godawful "humour" that 2K Australia have pumped into this game. In the previous iterations of the game the comments that enemies would make during a fight would often cause anything from a smirk to a full blown laugh. Playing this game I found myself scratching my head, shaking my head, scrunching up my nose, The only times I smiled or chuckled were when one of the characters from the previous games made a comment or a reference.
Honestly, I think I know why Gearbox Software weren't involved with this game, they took one look at the writing, the lack of humour, and the general lack of quality that this bullymong pile of a game shows off from 2K Australia and they decided to jump ship. Honestly, after sampling this atrocity I can't help but feel the same way.
TLDR:
The game is buggy. The humour is practically nonexistant and you will find yourself wishing that some of the games "key features" just didn't exist!

Hexcells is essentially an overall enhancement of Minesweeper. Where Minesweeper has mines, you have blue hexagons. Where Minesweeper has randomly generated puzzles that sometimes force you to guess, Hexcells has predesigned puzzles that always give you enough information to solve it without ever needing to guess. (Although sometimes it may feel otherwise.)
Why go for Hexcells over Minesweeper when there's a limited set of puzzles? Hexcells' puzzles are
well designed, starting simple and adding new mechanics as you move along. Beyond just telling you how many hexes nearby are blue, you get information on if they're all connected or not. Vertical or diagonal columns get similar treatment. Sometimes blue hexes have numbers in them, telling you how many blue hexes are in the surrounding area.
Eventually, you have to combine these hints in creative ways to determine where the blue hexes are—or where they aren't. When you're finally able to combine them all to work your way to completion, it provides a level of satisfaction that Minesweeper just can't compete with.
The only real downside to Hexcells is that it's pretty short—an acceptable downside, considering the price. Thankfully, Hexcells Plus (more puzzles) and Hexcells Infinite (more puzzles, a random puzzle generator,
player-created levels) are available, and getting the complete pack is incredibly affordable (and highly recommended), especially on sale.

I've heard from several (random) sources that this is believed to be a Team Fortress 2 clone. Let me assure you that this is not the case. Loadout is a fast paced, action packed and fun free to play shooter. It hardly requires any dedicated time to play, and its simplicity provides a truely enjoyable experience. The weapon modification is interesting and dynamic. I found myself really thinking about what kind of gun i'd like to use and why, and no weapon, upgrade, modification or attatchment is truely "the best". At the end of the day, the only thing that will make you come out on top is shooting your opponent to death, not some magical attatchment that one-shots the entire team. However, some of the game mechanics, like jumping for example, feel a  bit clunky and could use some smoothing out. Also, something i really would like to see is cosmetic customization to weapons. Having a baby poop green colored gun is nice and all, but i'd much rather choose the color myself. All in all, Loadout is a lot of fun and you don't have to be super dedicated and amazingly skilled to have a good time. Plus, it's free to play, so why not try it at least? Happy blasting.

This game is worth every penny and then some. I originally had this game through a friend's GOG account, but when i saw it on sale I was about half way through so I decided to buy it and transfer my save. I played this game for the first time 17 years after its release, but it felt much more recent, minus the graphics. The combat did seem tedious, slow and limited at first but upon gaining experience and upgrades it became very in-depth. This game was truly ahead of it's time, it provided meaningful choices, non-linear levels, superb level design, great voice acting, in-depth character customization, great writing/world creation, a soundtrack that aged well, and an expansive lore filled world. It basically has everything most modern games should but don't, making it a true must have/play for every sci-fi and rpg fan.
Story/Writing: 10/10 - Every choice felt meaningful, i.e. Stealth/confict, going the extra mile for the mission, data  gathering etc.  The writing was very well done, VERY rarely did a dialogue or remark seem out of character or half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ . The main character, Denton, has a great voice actor who nails every single scene and one-liner. But the npcs are also all very entertaining, from the first kid clearly voiced by an adult to every single npc in Honk Kong, Paris and more. The amount of dialogue is astonishing for a game this  old, after having started my second playthrough I tried to find more dialogue and I noticed that I missed half of the game's dialoge by not trying to talk to people after a conversation, it practically doubled.
Music/Sound:10/10  - From the memorable main theme to random conflicts in a sewer the soundtrack carried its own  weight. The soundtrack itself makes a lot of the moments throughout the game, being electronic it fits  the game perfectly. The stealth system benefits extremely from the superb sound system in this game, making listening for foot steps or machine systems essential. Gun sounds are little lacking but that isn't a huge deal when stealth is more difficult and more fun.
Combat/Stealth:9/10 - The only reason i give it a 9 is because it is dated and got annoying a few times. Don't expect Mass Effect level action, especially in the first hour, but the intensity picks up very quickly. Sadly the first half  hour to hour doesn't give a great picture of gameplay throughout and may convince some to stop  playing. Some weapons are super overpowered  making stealth  seem meaningless on lower  difficulties, but opting for stealth gameplay and weaponry is very rewarding. The stealth system in  this game cleary revolutionized the genre, absolutely perfecting the balance between sound and visibility(light), making it a staple for all stealth games.
Graphics/World:10/10 - Obviously it's 17 years old, but once you get past some of the character's faces the graphics are actually quite good and fit the game well. The areas are quite compact so there aren't many big  cityscapes or landscapes but the style of each area and npc is onpoint and really immersive. Some of the voice acting is rather poor, but for me that adds charm.
Gameplay: 10/10  - The controls were rather overwhelming and dificult at first, but after remapping to match a modern shooter, for example making flashlight "F", using mouse buttons, or moving   augs to other keys,  the game felt quite smooth. The character customization is rather in-depth for  it's time, offering a skill system and an augmentation system that allowed a choice of 2 augs in 11 slots along with levels themselves. The only downside to the skill system that I can think of is that you don't have an overall level just xp(skill points), which you have so check every once in awhile to determine if you can level something up.
Replayability: 10/10  - Having just started my second playthrough I noticed that I missed a ridiculous amount of dialogue and mission options. I think it could be played through 3 or more times with new things presenting themselves. Throughout the game I would sneak into a base and accidently exit it due to the ridiculous amount of entrances and gameplay options.

This is still early access, I understand.
However, there is too much left to chance, and no incentive to play through numerous times besides to kill time, or grind gold. Sure your accrue gold, but you retain nothing outside of the gold. If you spend the gold, then die, you receive nothing, and lose everything.
It's a cool idea, but I'm not a fan of the execution atm.

Stellaris is a game tries to offer a deep, methodical, and emergent scifi experience. What it actually delivers is hours upon hours of shifting your ships around to manually survey, guard, and build hundreds of planets while reading textbox events. The vast majority of the early game involves sending survey ships to new systems while your military sits at home staring at the starter alien fleets you won't be able to kill for 30 years.
That deep emergent plot? It takes the form of randomized events. Want to find a Precursor homeworld? Enjoy surveying 100 systems and rolling the dice on anomalies. Better hope that none of the systems you need are in another empire's territory! Your reward, if you finish, will be yet another textbox of pregen story and a bit more resources on a planet.
The early game is heavily luck based. With Fallen Empires, advanced start empires, and opposed empires, its easily possible to start wedged between three existential threats. Beyond that, since star position is randomized and habitatibility varies by species, you may end up with a capital that sits by itself and all of your starting expansions contested by a similar species. When it turns out you were screwed from turn one, enjoy restarting and setting up those 200 survey and exploration trips again!
In the midgame you get to enjoy the wonder that is Rock Paper Scissors in ship form. Do you know the AI ship patterns and build the hard counter? Grats, you can annhilate ships two or three times yoru size! Screw up and have missiles when you needed lasers? You're screwed. Enjoy resetting. If you're not at war, the midgame consists of crapping out colony ships and waiting on the next tech to finish in 30 more months.
Late game is a series of precanned events that all follow the pattern of dropping a bunch of massive fleets out of nowhere. Oh, look, a 100k fleet! Hope youve been building fleet power for the last 75 years! Oh, and you best have the right counter for those fleets, or there is no way to build enough ships.
Diplomacy is almost entirely based on two factors: If your species philosophy matches and if you have border friction. There is very little you can do to prevent war if an opposed philosophy butts up against you. Don't bother.
Even if all this doesn't sound droll, you can expect the 20 to 30 hour playtime for a proper game to drive you into a dusty grave. Much of that time is just waiting for more surveying, more ships to move, more construction to complete - even on Fastest, there are long stretches of nothing to do.
This game is an exercise in tedium with a randomized plot less structured than a tumblr blog.

I decided to let them join the future. But much to my frustration, they entered the galactic society with a desire to destroy and were repulsed by my people. So, I had to quickly land a ship on their planet, and enslave them.
These types of events occured regularly throughout my first (and so far only) play through. I will certainly play again, and again. And the experience will only improve through expansion and mods. tldr Great game with good mechanics, however can be tough at times.
Magicite is your not-so-typical Rogue-like side scroller. The game takes place underground and your goal is to escape by crafting using the resources available...and going deeper. Each level you go into is procedurally generated, meaning no two playthroughs are alike. There are plenty of different biomes to discover, each one with its own mobs, traps, and loot. However, the further you explore the tunnels of Magicite, the tougher enemies get and the more unforgiving the game becomes.
The thing that makes Magicite a not-so-typical game is mainly its customization. Starting the game you have one species unlocked, 2 varients for that species, no hats, and no pets. To unlock things you need to complete their asigned challenges, which can vary from getting to lvl 5 to completing the game without getting hit once. These hats, pets, and especially spieces can change the way you play the game immensely.
The skill system is interesting too. Your characters skills and abilities are "random". Your 4 skills are health, strength, dexterity, and magic. It may not seem like much, but magicite does it in a way where it doesn't have to be. Your health is important to all playing types, but the other three are what's really important. Dexterity increases your movement speed, the amount of dashes you have, and your damage with a bow. Strength indicates how much damage you do with the various amount of melee weapons available to you. And magic is responsible for the amount of mana you have and damage you do with staffs and other magic related weapons.
There are, however, some issues that need to be addressed. For one, some enemies have a very anoying attack strategy, called bouncing around like they don't know what they're doing. Also, some enemies seem very out of place. By that, I'm not saying that that they don't look right, I mean their stats are not right; specifically boars. They have an unreasonable amount of health to be anywhere in the starting biome, and they charge at you like a madman!
Final Verdict:
Pros.
-Good crafting system
-Beautiful level generation
-Procedurally generated
-Charming
-Good progression
-Separation between playing styles (as in mage isnt just warrior with a staff)
-Challenging, but not to the point of rage quit
-Extremely intricate customization options!
-Casual and Try-Hard friendly
Cons.
-A few things feel unbalanced
Overall.
9.4/10 Excellent!

NEW PLAYERS: Overall, one of the best basketball games in the market, but can be hard to pick up. If you do, you're in for a treat. (See below)
FEATURES:
- High quality visuals for a basketball game (or any game, really)
- Very immersive MyCAREER mode
- MyPARK: a game mode where your MyPLAYER can play pick up games with others online
- 2K PRO-AM: create and customize teams and play online
- MyTEAM: the ultimate basketball card game; build your team (of current and former players) and play against others online on the hardwood
- MyLEAGUE / MyGM: if you prefer controlling a team from the top-down (+ new features!)
- CREATE A PLAYER: in-depth player creation with several new categories
- SHOES: give your players some sexy sneaks. Available for MyPLAYER as well
[From here it's more in-depth.]
RETURNING PLAYERS: See below.
MyPROS:
- MyCAREER immersion is the best in NBA 2K history
- Handles feel great
- Face scanning available for PC players now
- Better AI + more control over them
- Kobe and Michael B. Jordan welcome you to MyCAREER, not Spike Lee
- MyNBA2K17 mobile app hooks you up with easy VC
- Much cleaner UI
- Amazing soundtrack (if you're into rap, especially)
- Lot more player customization (animations, attributes)
- No Spike Lee
- Faster MyTEAM unpacking animations
- Dynamic Duo / Orange Juice mechanic is a free stat boost
- Very natural dribbling in between plays
- Arms are actually tangible; you touch the ball, it's out of their / your hands
- Ball isn't on a string; higher mechanics now used for offense
- Harambe logos
- Better, race-neutral MyPLAYER voice compared to the past (never mattered to me though)
- Better player celebrations
- Pres is a decent nickname, but what isn't compared to Frequency Vibrations
- No freqin' and vibin'
MyTRIGGERS:
- Questionable player ratings (as of 9/20/16)
- Occasional FPS drops
- You start MyCAREER with a really low rating (as usual)
- Justice Young has better ratings than you
- MyPARK is just 3 ghost towns
- Sound is glitchy (e.g. player interview with PA going off)
- You can't make the player you want with the categorization of playstyles
- If you're a lower draft pick, you can't skip to yours in MyCAREER
- Your MyPLAYER has unforgiving attribute caps (e.g. low free throw and stamina ratings)
- The '+1 stat' you SHOULD be rewarded disappears
- No yeezys?
- Unskippable cutscenes
- Many players' faces are completely off
- Not the most hacker-proof game out there (as usual)
- You can still select 'Freq' as a nickname
- Lots of attributes for MyCAREER aren't recorded or saved
- Can be difficult to master the mechanics, especially for newer / returning players
- Spike Lee
MyTIPS:
- For face scanning, use an iPhone front camera while right in front of really bright white light
* Turn slowly, and per angle.
- Lower the difficulty to:
* Rookie if you're getting crushed or are fairly new
* Pro if you're fine at the level the game puts you at initially
* All-Star if you're ready to play at a respectable level
* Superstar if you need a challenge
* Hall of Fame if you want to find out how hard of a punch your monitor can handle
MyREVIEW:
- The latest installment to the NBA 2K series, NBA 2K17, is one of the better basketball games on the market ever--by default. It has a deep career mode, unlike any other game in its genre, but has once again failed to make it the best through acclaim. Its career mode--arguably the most anticipated part of the series now--tends to make critical errors annually. If you want to have the best career, then go buy 2K11. If you want to have the most IMMERSIVE career, then take this game.
- If you're new though, this game might be a headache. It's not the perfect game, it's just the "best basketball game" created, arguably by default. Lots of fun if you put in the work, but if you're way more casual than a lot of 2K players stick with the games that came out in the past.
- MyTEAM, MyLEAGUE/GM are back again and they've been upgraded. Had no issues with their content before (minus the actual gameplay on the COURT; that's another story), and even made adjustments to make the modes more enjoyable. (See MyPROS.)
- Several new mechanics have been introduced this year, including shot / pass aiming and the dynamic duo system. It certainly increases realism, but the game has too many other holes already for 2K to be working on something like that. (See MyTRIGGERS.) There are many issues that I'm sure you'll read about in the other reviews floating around, but the positives in tandem with them bring me to these opinions:
MyTHOUGHTS:
- FOR HARDCORE 2K FANS: Must buy
- FOR CASUAL 2K FANS: Great game; best 2K since next gen graphics
- FOR NON-2K PLAYERS: Get it on sale
- FOR ALL: No Spike Lee MUST BUY $$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$$

Borderlands 1 & 2 are two of my favorite games to this point, so I was pretty hyped up to get this one when it came out. Unfortunately, there's a lot more bad than good.
The characters you can play as are fun (I do not own the two DLC characters). They feel well done and are unique enough to really fit in well with the previous Borderlands PCs. Everything else though about this game just feels poorly done.
There aren't a whole lot of different environments. The game takes place on a moon of Pandora. The entire game is set in either a normal atmosphere or a zero gravity atmostphere. The latter uses a slowly draining oxygen feature and allows for higher jumping because of the gravity, but after a short while it feels like more of a hindrance than a neat new feature.
Weapons just don't feel quite as powerful in this game as they did in previous ones. It really seems like there isn't as much of a variety this time. There are also a LOT fewer farmable bosses than there were in the first two games. That was most of the fun for me in BL2, farming bosses for their legendary drops. There's a lot less of that in the Pre Sequel. There was none to begin with and a (somewhat recent) patch made a few of the sub-bosses farmable. Compared to BL2 though, it's nowhere near as much.
The music is not as great either. I eventually turned it off because in some zones it became irritating to listen to. YMMV.
The writing is ATROCIOUS. Beyond horrible. Most of the new NPCs introduced in this one are very unlikeable (Pickle, Janey Springs, etc...). What made Borderlands 2 so much better was the introduction of memorable characters like Handsome Jack and Tiny Tina, this game had ZERO memorable additions to the NPC roster.
There's a lot less humor in this one and what is there is filled with Aussie slang. No offense to any Aussie gamers out there but a lot of it made absolutely no sense to me. I am aware that 2K shoveled this one off to 2K Australia to make, still I found most of the humor in this one to be thoroughly unfunny.
Let's summarize:
1. Subpar soundtrack.
2. Extremely unlikeable NPCs introduced.
3. Nonsensical and completely unfunny attempts at humor.
4. Only a child-sized handful of farmable bosses.
5. Less unique loot in this one. A lot less.
This game is just not good.

Before I start this review, I want to say I have not completed this game. I got a decent ways in before feeling the need to give up. I enjoy the idea of this game, but the execution overall leads me to saying you probably shouldn't get it. The early levels manage rather well, but the further you get into the game, the more random it all feels. Now, randomness isn't necessarily bad, I adore rogue-lites and they rely on randomness, but there's a difference between this and something like binding of isaac or nuclear throne
BoI and NT it's almost always clear why you died, either a mistimed dodge or not being able to output enough damage for every time you're hit. The randomness is level generation, item drops, and the like
PH on the other hand feels random in the sense of "why did that happen". There have been numerous times where I've been caught by the police and I wasn't entirely sure why the police were called in the first place.
There are other things that bother me, such as bouncers are always hostile. If they see you they will always try to arrest you like the police would. I'm unclear why this happens, and it leads to a lot of frustration.
The moment that made it clear I should stop playing this game was the level where you play as the second story playable character. The level had so few interactables so spread out that my MO on the 10 or 15 or so  was to just cheese it by calling in zombies and trying to kill off the zombies before they can swarm me, since killing zombies counts as killing partygoers. When you feel the need to cheese the game in order to progress, the game is either too difficult or it's designed poorly.
There are good elements of this game, it's rather fun at times, but the slow process to getting to those fun parts is such a drag with reseting whenever something goes wrong.

Hyper Hippo’s financial management game (let’s call it that for now even though it’s not entirely helpful) came to our attention because it was an unknown quantity suddenly doing very well for itself in the Steam charts. It was free, it seemed to be a managementy thing, it seemed like it might be mocking the world of high finance, and so I reasoned it was a reasonable way to spend a little bit of my time in between other features.
I’ve been playing it for getting on for six hours now. I say playing, but what I mean is ‘watch numbers roll in and occasionally press a button when one lights up’. This is a game which solely concerns itself with the acquisition of money, which is then spent on buying things which mean more money. Speculate to accumulate and all that. An infinite snowball effect – buy a small industry, spend its profits on a larger industry, and then a larger one, and onwards and upwards until what began as a handful of dollars trickling in every second becomes billions.
All you have to do is click a button to buy/found/invest in/not sure but it doesn’t matter I guess a new company as and when you have the cash. So initially you’ve got just one lemonade stand, but its profits get spent on buying another one. Make it to 25 and the speed of its profits double. Same again and 50, 100 and 200 (and beyond, but I’m not there yet). Or you can wait a while longer and unlock a whole new industry – newspapers, pizza delivery, donut restaurants, all the way up to banks and oil companies. Each ‘new’ industry brings in vastly more sums of money, but at a slower rate, at least until you upgrade it. So you sit there waiting for these little money timers to reach their end, then you click again, repeat and repeat and repeat, spending everything you earn on making everything you own earn more.
With enough cash, you can hire managers to do the cash collection click for you. At that point, AdVenture Capitalist is supposed to become an idle game. It runs in the background, making lots and lots and lots of oh my God sickening amounts of money, and every so often you dip back in and unlock something more, in order that the next time you go back in you’re earning orders of magnitude more cash all over again. You can even exit the game and when you load it back up it’ll have calculated what you’ve earned since the last time it was open. It’s Fable III without the fighting, basically.
But I didn’t do that. I didn’t exit. I barely even alt-tabbed. I just sat there, watching, waiting, hungry for a button to turn orange so I could buy more of something. I was ravenous for more cash; cash which only had a function within this accursed game. Every line I write in this post, I flick out to see if I can buy anything else. And then I end up staring at these green rows, all refilling at varying speeds.
The lemonade stands on top left move like lightning, earning $762 a second, while the oil company at lower right will give me $89 billion every 10 hours. By tomorrow morning I can have upgraded the oil co enough that it’ll be making me something like $200 billion every five hours. By tomorrow night, I might see my first trillion. A few of them and I can triple profits across the board.
At some point, I’ll sell all my shares and start over, this time with a horde of angel investors impressed by my monstrous ability to make monstrous profits, their input meaning I’ll make money even faster, even bigger profits this time around. And it will go on and on and on and on and on and maybe that would be OK if only I could stop watching. If only I could tell myself I didn’t have to be there, watching, the second another button lit up, that it doesn’t matter if I don’t buy an upgrade as soon as I can afford it, that the world will not stop turning because I’m not at maximum revenue efficiency every second of every minute of every hour of every day.
It’s just numbers getting bigger. It’s the cynical serpent curled aroundthe heart of every social game, every action RPG, every MMO, every gambling machine, but at least it makes no pretence that it’s about anything more than that. There’s this thin veneer of Monopoylisms with a touch of sardonic Fallout nonchalance and lazy references to famous figures, but it’s just set-dressing and it knows it. This is an experiment in how venal we can be.
I know that, even by the standards of videogames, nothing I do in it has any meaning, that I could never begin to justify the time I spent with this. In my only defence, at least I’ve resisted the entirely optional in-app purchases which would make everything happen faster still. It feels like cheating, but I know that even so all I’m doing with this game is cheating myself of time and life.
Yet in an hour I can upgrade my Bank to 25, which will double the speed it cashes out, and that’ll mean something like $60 billion every half an hour. It would be wasteful for that bank to spend even a minute performing beneath this amazing potential.
A lifetime ago, I was making $2 every few seconds from lemonade sales. What a nobody I was.

This is the best and worse game I've ever played. It is SO good when you're actually able to play; it truly brings back the old-school gamer in me to experience a modern NES style 'once you're dead, you're dead' playthrough, and each time it's different in some way. However, when I'm no longer able to f'ing play the game, that's where I draw the line. Games that pull you in and make you want to continue playing are far too few these days. This game does it with remarkable ease. Unfortunately, it is fraught with such a bug, that I will most likely never play this game, or any of its line again. There is a bug in this game that restricts your input device from allowing input.... think about that. The game responds to input, but you're not able to give it what you're meaning to. I'm not talking about an enemy reversing your controlls, I mean, you try to walk or shoot in a direction, and the game simply ignores that request. Again, hatred built from accusing my past controllers or input devices of not 'working right', but in this case, it is documented and agreed upon across the board as a bug with the game itself.
I can't think of anything worse than to dangle such a wonderful game in front of you, then simply pull it away. I would've rather paid more money for a working title, than to have this fail in such a significant way.

First time I take time out of my under-scheduled, overly lazy life to do a Steam review.
First time I find myself 99% sure that I have found my game of the year before April is over.
First time for so many first times.
Jokes aside now:
NieR:Automata is THAT game that has everything it needs to rock your world.
It can make you laugh, it can make you cry, it can make you rage, it can make you love.
I never played the original NieR, nor the Drake..something from which this series spinned out of.
But after playing 73h on record (and still going) I don't find myself even close to stoping.
Even if the quests are done, the weapons gathered and maxed out, whenever I find myself playing a different game I am always drawn back to the desolate world of NieR, the never ending war between machines and androids, the conflicted emotions portrayed by 9S, the turmoil that is 2B's existence. The tragedy of A2's past.
The storyline is gorgeous, from the multiple endings to the quests, the uncovering of secrets...
Sorry reader, I don't think, after all, that I can make a coherent review of Nier:Automata. It triggers to many emotions, too many thoughts, too much to process.
I think that, in the end, the only thing that I can really say is "Play it."
It doesn't matter if it's £40 or £30. It is easily worth double that, short as the main story line might be.
This game is a masterpiece. It may not be remembered for the ages like ES, Fallout, MA:E, DS will, but don't let that fool you.
NieR:Automata is worth every minute of your time.
The only complaint I can muster, is that I don't have a way to play it blindly again, and experience every turn of the emotional roller-coaster for the first time once again.
This game is a masterpiece. It's one of the most powerful gaming experiences I've ever had. You need to play it to understand. But please, trust me. Games like this are the reason I play videogames.
