After crash-landing on Pandora’s moon, Alpis, I found myself staggeringly unprepared for the lack of oxygen in the environment and marginally creative assortment of enemies that awaited me. It felt like my character, Wilhelm and I were in for a science fiction treat of epic proportions; but I’m upset to report that after spending so much time with the vault-hunters in previous Borderlands games, I just couldn’t take enough of an interest in Wilhelm to keep him alive through the assortment of drawn out, exceedingly boring missions.
The trouble with this game is that on one hand it hasn’t veered far away enough from its predecessor (Borderlands 2) in most respects, but the laziness behind this game doesn’t really end at that point. Each mission has been designed to extend gameplay which results in tedious amounts of walking, sudden death-traps and sparsely spaced spawn points that will have you grinding out hours of gameplay to complete a seemingly stupid mission.
This installment is a far cry from those that came before it, so much so that I’m not even excited about the launch of BL3 (though who knows, maybe they will redeem themselves). If you’re a BL fan then this game won’t meet your expectations; but if you are just being introduced to the series, I would certainly recommend purchasing BL1 or 2 instead. If you think I’m wrong, then you’re likely a die hard fan with a bias opinion, which is also fine… the Borderlands series should receive a lot of love… always.

Stellaris is a game tries to offer a deep, methodical, and emergent scifi experience. What it actually delivers is hours upon hours of shifting your ships around to manually survey, guard, and build hundreds of planets while reading textbox events. The vast majority of the early game involves sending survey ships to new systems while your military sits at home staring at the starter alien fleets you won't be able to kill for 30 years.
That deep emergent plot? It takes the form of randomized events. Want to find a Precursor homeworld? Enjoy surveying 100 systems and rolling the dice on anomalies. Better hope that none of the systems you need are in another empire's territory! Your reward, if you finish, will be yet another textbox of pregen story and a bit more resources on a planet.
The early game is heavily luck based. With Fallen Empires, advanced start empires, and opposed empires, its easily possible to start wedged between three existential threats. Beyond that, since star position is randomized and habitatibility varies by species, you may end up with a capital that sits by itself and all of your starting expansions contested by a similar species. When it turns out you were screwed from turn one, enjoy restarting and setting up those 200 survey and exploration trips again!
In the midgame you get to enjoy the wonder that is Rock Paper Scissors in ship form. Do you know the AI ship patterns and build the hard counter? Grats, you can annhilate ships two or three times yoru size! Screw up and have missiles when you needed lasers? You're screwed. Enjoy resetting. If you're not at war, the midgame consists of crapping out colony ships and waiting on the next tech to finish in 30 more months.
Late game is a series of precanned events that all follow the pattern of dropping a bunch of massive fleets out of nowhere. Oh, look, a 100k fleet! Hope youve been building fleet power for the last 75 years! Oh, and you best have the right counter for those fleets, or there is no way to build enough ships.
Diplomacy is almost entirely based on two factors: If your species philosophy matches and if you have border friction. There is very little you can do to prevent war if an opposed philosophy butts up against you. Don't bother.
Even if all this doesn't sound droll, you can expect the 20 to 30 hour playtime for a proper game to drive you into a dusty grave. Much of that time is just waiting for more surveying, more ships to move, more construction to complete - even on Fastest, there are long stretches of nothing to do.
This game is an exercise in tedium with a randomized plot less structured than a tumblr blog.
would strongly recomend if new to real time strategy games. this was my first rts and it was very easy to pick up and enjoy

I do love being surprised when it comes to gaming. I was a bit worn out from grinding through scare fests in the Amnesia series and Outlast and really need to play something the completely opposite. Well I installed Party Hard and did not look back. The gist of Party Hard is you play a mass murderer going across the good ol' USA killing large numbers of people at parties using your trusty knife to stab people or traps (poison the punch, rig stuff to blow up etc.).  Party Hard really reminds me of Hotline Miami in that it's a murder simulator, only WAY more slow paced. Your sole mission is to kill everything on the level and not get caught. How you do it is up to you. I thought Party Hard was a great game to pick up and play. The controls are simple and you know what you have to do on each level. Each level is procedurally generated so you don't know what traps you'll have or what drops to pick up. It totally changes your strategy from level to level. Is it perfect? No. ADD gamers are SOL as the random behaviors of the party people keep you guessing (although I liked that), there were numerous times the cops randomly arrested me and the worst thing of all. The dang sprint button. Our (anti?) hero has maybe the worst cardio ever. You'll be running from cops and the stamina bar will let you down every time. That said, I thought Party Hard was a blast.  The concept was intriguing, the execution (while flawed) was good enough but I kept playing and playing until I finished. Looking forward to Party Hard 2. 8/10 from me.

It is clear this is a loving tribute to old pixel violence games, with gameplay that is similar to Streets of Rogue. While people compare it to Hotline Miami, it doesn't engage in that series's rampant surrealism, so the only real similarity is in general appearance.The main character is what really makes this game, a mysterious killer that lashes out at people doing hedonsitic behavior, the energy and rage of him constrasting with the police detective who is following him and has had it up to here with him yet is also subconciously understanding him in ways normal people couldn't. There is a good reason for this, but that is a SPOILER. Even the one level where you play a female copycat killer is pretty cool, if rather hard. This game has more fantastic elements than traditional brawlers, but less than other recent horror-themed games, resulting in a slightly eerie effect that bridges mundane crime drama with supernatural slasher horror, and creates a hybrid that works.

Thanks to actually good fan content, its the most played game on my playlist.

Party hard is a throwback to the glory days of the Atari/commadore 64, and unlike most of the "faux-retro" hipster games flooding the market lately, this one manages to get it right. While clearly more visualy and mechanically complex than a true atari game, this game really captures the spitit of the era, while still being complex enough to satisfy the modern gamer.
You play as the antagonist in this game, (something a raging ♥♥♥♥♥ like me can definitley appreciate), a man who lives next door to the party who just wants to GET SOME ♥♥♥♥ING SLEEP. Your objective is deceptivley simple, kill everyone at the party. This can be accomplished in a variety of ways, but if you are sloppy and get seen commiting a crime, the guests will call the cops on you and suddenly the hunter becomes the hunted.
You have a variety of ways to kill people depending on your enviornment. It's up to you to figure out the best way to dispatch your targets, and the levels can be played multiple ways rewarding your creativity. If you fail and either die or get "busted" by the cops, you'll notice the level reloads with different NPCs in different positions and locations, so you'll have to come up with a whole new plan, which adds a new level of challange and replayability that is refreshing to see.
As the game progresses you'll be introduced to new mechanics and playable characters, each with their own strengths and weaknesses. This adds an ever greater level of depth and strategy to an already great game. The levels are well designed and each has it's own theme. The game has a tounge in cheek tone and a level of irrevrent humor that keeps thing fresh and entertaining.
I very much enjoy this game, and would reccomend it to anyone who likes classic atari/Commadore style games, but also wants a challanging yet irrevrent twist on the 2D top-down action genre. If you liked Hitman, Postal, and classic 32 bit graphics, you're going to like this game.

Now that I've finished the game, I feel compelled to write a review.
If you like top down shooters, this is a lot of fun. You get a good variety of enemies, weapons, and scenarios. Sometimes you get to operate a car, or rescue distressed civilians, or defend settlements. If you like to just destroy stuff, this is really fun.
The graphics are not "amazing" but they get the job done. Despite the dark ambience, you can mostly see things clearly -- except when you're clearly not supposed to. Though games like these tend to be dreary, I was pleasantly surprised by the variety of colour. The cutscene graphics, however, are cringeworthy. More on that later.
One thing I love about this game is that it runs on a variety of hardware. If you have any PC made within the past 5 years, whether Windows, Mac, or Linux, you'll be able to run this game fine. Trust me, in addition to my plethora of Windows hardware, I also own a Thinkpad T440p running Ubuntu as well as a MacBook Air (2015). The game works on all of them.
This game also has full controller support, but with games like these, you're far better going mouse and keyboard. Sure, you could wield double analog sticks, but the real fun is with pointing at the enemies and laying them to waste.
Not all is good, however. The in game art style is great but the cut scenes are "fedorable". For some reason, the designers thought a shadowy man holding a fedora over his head looks cool but all I could think of was Neckbeard RPG. There's also lots of spelling and grammar problems in the subtitles, and the voice acting is over the top. If you like "so bad it's good" B-movies, maybe you'll like this, but I don't think it goes well with the game.
Still, the cutscenes are skippable. The real meat of the game is the overhead shooting. And in that, Splatter succeeds very well.
Overall rating: 3.5/5

Choice.
Something that video games rarely give the player. And most of the time, when you are given choice it is usually, in reality, just an illusion of choice. Especially in terms of narrative, because it means tons of "extra work" for the developers. Very few games truly give you choice, and when they do it's either trivial or very few in number. And I mean choice for both in terms of how you shape the story and how you approach the gameplay. Deus Ex however, despite being a 17 year old game in the time that I'm writing this,(The game is probably older than most people reading this I would guess.) does both of those things in a kind of perfection that hasn't been achieved since, and may even never be truly achieved in the future.
Let me explain the gameplay part: Getting from point A to point B in Deus Ex is an endless realm of possibilities. Not just because of your choice in skill and augmentation upgrades, or items and weapon upgrades. Sure they do help but if you're skilled enough as a player you can pull off a lot of things even if you're not equipped for it. This means, at any given time, there are endless amounts of ways a level in Deus Ex can be beaten. All you have to do is accomplish the objective, one way or the other. In fact, there are many levels where you DON'T have to accomplish the objective at all either! Now that, is choice. You can beat the game even if you don't augment your body at all. You can beat the game without picking up or using a single item or weapon. You can beat the game by just massacring everyone. You can just run away from the boss fights. Running from god damn boss fights, how many video games do you know that allow that? I only know one: Deus Ex, and I have played tons and tons of video games. I still haven't seen another video game where you can say "f*ck you" to the objective menu and do whatever the hell you please with the game, and have it still be connected to a comprehensive, well written story!
The story. Don't worry, I won't spoil anything at all. Everything about it, the characters, the world, the dialogue are all expertly put together. I have not played another game where I am this excited when I'm about to have a conversation with someone. Every single bit of dialogue in this game is great. and before you mention them, yes, ESPECIALLY the JC Denton One-Liners. JC Denton is one of the most entertaining video game characters of all time. Anyways, in terms of the story one thing is for certain, there won't be another video game that handles conspiracies this ballsy and "in your face" kind of way ever again. There is no other game in history that handles the Illuminati and secret government this seriously, openly and realistically. Deus Ex is, and it seems it will definitely stay as, one of a kind in terms of this. The plot constantly drives you further and further, you feel like you HAVE to know more about the story, you have to know what happens. It's like the video game equivalent of a page-turner book, that's how good the story is. And as I said above, you are always given plenty of choices on how to shape the story, and they are REAL choices unlike most games, but I won't spoil them. Let's also not forget to mention: The soundtrack is simply amazing. There are very few video games like this where you can honestly say there is not a single "meh" track in it. Role Playing Games are about choice, shaping your own character and dropping into a world and being immersed by it. Living in that world and shaping it as you see fit. I guess i'll give my two cents.  Since EA refuses to create any PC games, for NBA live or Madden I appreciate 2K continuing to release a PC version.  Overall I have found the game enjoyable and would recomend the game to any NBA fan.  I especially like playing the MyCareer game mode and have spent most of my time playing it.    This is the third time I've purchased an NBA game from 2K the last one being NBA 2k12.  My PC has windows 10 and a 1080GTX card I've seen a few minor graphical gliches as well as one crash but nothing major that would cause me to regret purchasing the game.
If you are someone that hasn't purchased NBA 2k in a while like myself, you will most likely be disappointed when you discover the implementation of 'Virtual Currency' better know as VC.  VC is used to buy things in the game which at first doesnt sound to bad until you realize it's tied into upgrading your player's stats.  This is a common practice in free-2-play games that introduces pay walls to get people to pay for the game.  Bascially you're paying them 'not' to play the game to skip all the boring grinding game play.  Just like any other free-2-play game they've added a varitey of ways to get small amounts of VC for free in the game, but not enough unless you plan on playing for several hours. In Mycareer they introduced player practices that allow you to do a variety of things to help unlocking upgrades as well as give small increases in attributes.  This is the grind mode of the game that you will want to skip at some point once the newness wares off.  If you want to go back and create a new player to try out the different positions and skills sets offered in the game you'll be stuck with the same routines wanting to reach for your wallet to avoid playing this part of the game.  If this was a free-2-play game I wouldn't complain to much since this is how the development team gets paid for their work. However NBA 2k17 is not a free-2-play game why is VC tied to upgrading a players attributes for a game that I've already paid for?  Cosmetic content I can see, but player attributes?  Really?  It seems like a very shady buisness practice to suck more money out of players.  Even worse gives 2K incentive to add in boring grinding pay walls that no one wants to play.  VC is not cheap either if you want to start out fully upgraded expect to fork out another $50 dollars.

At the very least, it is worth an hour or two for a good, honest try. The game itself is great; the mechanics, the economy, the characters, and the Humor.
I'm not going to describe much of the gameplay, because it is a F2P game, and as such, you could hop in and try it. It's active combat, to bait the switch. Not so much of 'spam abilities in place until things die' and more of actually dodging, choosing abilities and attacks, and moving consistently.
The economy is fair. There is the aspect of Pay 2 Win, but at least in the way this game 'does' it, you still have to work to some degree to get anywhere. There is a free currency used to buy things from the in game store as well, which isn't a horrible idea, in my opinion, and the way it is handled, it is very fair.
The characters all have some form of depth to them. Some will give you few quests, and either stop talking, get killed, or run off, never to be seen again, while others with more consistent quests actually have an actual 'Why they Fight' prequel story to them... And then there are few that mean a crap ton to the story, but die before they can actually do anything...
The humor is, in my opinion, one of the better examples i've seen in a game of this degree. It does try a little too hard at times, and there are certainly serious parts (or at least parts that are meant to be taken seriously), but overall, my experienbce so far has been a kind of 'Borderlands Meets Ratchet & Clank/ Jak and Daxter' feel to it all... And, by no means is that to be taken as an insult.
I certainly recommend that you at least try it out. I, personally do not like many MMO's, such as TERA or Neverwinter; Warframe is a different story, but it is also NOT a traditional MMO... Wildstar has had my eye for some time, and when i heard it was going F2P, i knew i was going to at least try it, and now i will certainly say that i will be returning quite requently.

After crash-landing on Pandora’s moon, Alpis, I found myself staggeringly unprepared for the lack of oxygen in the environment and marginally creative assortment of enemies that awaited me. It felt like my character, Wilhelm and I were in for a science fiction treat of epic proportions; but I’m upset to report that after spending so much time with the vault-hunters in previous Borderlands games, I just couldn’t take enough of an interest in Wilhelm to keep him alive through the assortment of drawn out, exceedingly boring missions.
The trouble with this game is that on one hand it hasn’t veered far away enough from its predecessor (Borderlands 2) in most respects, but the laziness behind this game doesn’t really end at that point. Each mission has been designed to extend gameplay which results in tedious amounts of walking, sudden death-traps and sparsely spaced spawn points that will have you grinding out hours of gameplay to complete a seemingly stupid mission.
This installment is a far cry from those that came before it, so much so that I’m not even excited about the launch of BL3 (though who knows, maybe they will redeem themselves). If you’re a BL fan then this game won’t meet your expectations; but if you are just being introduced to the series, I would certainly recommend purchasing BL1 or 2 instead. If you think I’m wrong, then you’re likely a die hard fan with a bias opinion, which is also fine… the Borderlands series should receive a lot of love… always.

tl;dr This game loses it's appeal very fast and isn't worth the price.
Party Hard is a stealth game where you need to kill everyone in the level. You do this by stabbing people and setting up traps. Each party holds 35+ people for you to murder(the highest amount I've seen is 55). If you don't hide the bodies people call the cops, the cops bag the corpses, the partygoers get paranoid. The problem with the game comes from how painfully slow it gets. I understand that stealth games aren't fast pace, but this game is slow for horrible reasons.
Here's a list of what ruins the game
-Everyone walks like snails. The levels are too large for your horrible walk speed.
-Your sprint lasts for 0.5 seconds.
-It is almost impossble to stop someone from calling the cops.
-The traps placed are RNG. You get randomized traps that can make or break your run.
-You at most will get only five traps to work with
-Traps can either be worthless (killing only 1 person) or amazing(10+ people)
-There's no way to lure people. There is only a way to make people leave (Which is also RNG. People can knock you out, people can leave to random spots, or people can just ignore you.)
-Aboslutely horrible game design choices on FBI/Guards. If you're spotted by either, you die. You could be doing nothing, but you still die.
-The party music gets tiring very quickly because you'll spend so much time on a level. Maybe that's the point? This game is about the main character getting tired of the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ parties. Either way be prepared to mute the game.
The traps being randomized was probably done in an attempt to give you a reason to replay levels. At least that's what I want to say. The problem with randomized traps is you will just softreset until you get a trap that's actually useful. Even then you can't guarantee good results because again, there's no way to lure people in. This decision to set up levels on RNG just makes the game feel like a chore rather than something I want to play.
Also if you're drawn into this game because you hear people compare to Hotline Miami: please ignore this game. These games have nothing similar to eachother besides having a pixelated man kill people to music. Hotline Miami is a much faster paced game. Party Hard is a stealth game that makes me want to go to sleep minutes into playing it.
The Twitch stream features and Youtuber mode should've probably been a give-away on what kind of game this is.
I'd say that the price of this game should be $5 or lower to be worth it. $12 is nowhere close to what I would pay for this, and I got this game for free!

I generally don't like puzzle games. They are far too slow for my liking, but I completely understand the appeal and wish I could like them more. Hexcells may have changed this for me, for it is a perfectly crafted game from the presentation to the mechanics.
You learn the rules as you go, but in a nutshell, you're tasked with finding all the blue hexes with a few clues. It plays very similar to minesweeper, but there is an emphasis on more complex rules to follow involving whether hexes are attached in a string and how many hexes are in a column.
"an ambient logic puzzle game" is the perfect descriptor for Hexcells, blending dynamic sound design with truly challenging and engaging problem solving. The sound interactions are employed in a way that only heightens the enjoyablilty of the game. The music and how your actions affect the sound is timely and bold, yet also soothing and ignorable.
My only real gripe with the game would be how certain mechanics are explained in a weird order, with one mechanic not actually being explained. However, it is easy to understand regardless, and overall the game is well worth a purchase.

It's quite similar to both Picross and Minesweeper, in that it gives you a little bit of information to start with, which you then use to fill in or rule out cells in a hexagonal grid via the process of elimination. Compared to either of those games, however, Hexcells is a lot more relaxed. This partly because of its calm music and colour pallete, but also because the game doesn't feature a timer and doesn't punish you all that much for making a wrong move (it's mostly up to your discipline to stop yourself from guessing).
Small note: there are three hexcells games on steam, each are basically level packs. All three have good difficulty curves,  but both Hexcells Infinite and Hexcells Plus start a bit harder and get tough quicker. If you're getting just one this is probably best.
Very good minimal puzzle game. I would recommend to buy the 'Hexcells Complete Pack' to get all three games.

This is my third attempt to post a review of Stellaris.  The first two disappeared.  Hopefully this one will get posted.
I really wanted to like this game.  The early parts of the game seemed promising.  The exploration and early expansion phases were enjoyable.  Searching the stars to see what special events/objects were hiding there gave a sense of exploration and momentum to the game.
From there, however, things ground down to a stagnant experience.  The first problem was simply bugs.  I would discover artifacts from the "First League", once I find 6 of them, I can find the honeworld.  Well, problem was you would find about 4 to 5 and then nothing, even after exploring the entire universe, the last items would not show up.  A later patch tried to address that by respawning anomoly locations in your explored space to make the missing items available.  Tht was better but I found that the icon indicating the presence of an anomoly would not stay displayed reliably.  Even them once I found all 6 items and was directed to the homworld, there was nothing there.  Just .... nothing.
Asides from bugs like this (that still seem to be present as of 2 days ago) the game dynamics seem to inevitably lead to a stagnant game.  The diplomacy system is to weak as it allows the creation of defensive packs and alliances to guard against attacks, but nothing to allow one to incite others to declare war together.  Federations are simply a dead weight on ones neck as more often than not, the fellow members will reject proposals for war.  And there is no way to strike a deal with someone to break an alliance.  The end result is that the ensuing tangle of pacts make war next to impossible.  Given that the only victory conditions for the game are conquest-based, that makes for an annoying game experience.
Even the war mechanisms are flawed.  One can only force an enemy to accept defeat by accumulating "war score".  The problem is that "war score" is based on how many enemy units on destrys and enemy planets are occupired.  if the enemy is too small, one can completely destroy every unit they have and occupy every planet they have and yet still not be able to force them to accept defeat because it did not generate sufficient "war score" and with no more planets to occupy or units to destroy, one cannot get any more war score.
In short, I think the problem is that the game cannot decide what type of game it wants to be.  It has many of the trappings in the early game of being a 4X game, but it always seems to bog down into something else by the mid to late game.

TLTR: Easily the best and deepest 4X sci-fi ever, with a lot of potential of becoming a good deal better.
Stellaris v1.4.1 is not on par with Crusader Kings or Europe Universalis yet, but it has enough deep elements to already rule its pride. There is meaningful racial customization, governmental customization and gameplay mechanics, superb technology-research mechanics, a very interesting universe to play around in and in general enough gameplay mechanics to make the fun last longer than any of its peers.
You don't retain full control of your empire. Once it grows to a certain size you must delegate power to AI-governors, just like in other Paradox titles. This is uncomfortable for some players not used to these kind of mechanics, but it's actually good in several ways. First it keeps up the pace of the game, preventing it stagnating into micromanagement-hell. Second it provides depth to the government and faction-mechanics. Third, it provides variety in the empire-management throughout the game. You may not believe it at a glance, but it's actually really good game-design.
The game doesen't let you control combat. Like all other Paradox games it focuses on the bigger picture. Combat is conducted by the AI in real-time while you play. It works well when you know the rules for how battles play out. But like everything else in the game, you really need to know what's going on to do anything well. You manipulate the battles by how you design your ships, so you need to teach yourself how to do good ship-design to feel in control of battles. Those who don't tend to dislike this part of Stellaris. Combat currently doesen't look good visually, and has room for functionallity-improvement. Luckily, mods fix some of that already.
Diplomacy is good compared to non-Paradox 4X-games. It can get alot better tho, and does have one big glairing fault. It just doesen't give you the tools to peacefully work towards game-victory. That means designing a pacifist and diplomatic race is more of an increased difficulty choise rather than a true playstyle choice. However, beyond a total pacifist gameplay diplomacy works well enough and provide lots of options.
Faster-than-light travel is interesting, like Sword of the Stars in that there are different types of FTL with different perks and drawbacks. They can be a little frustrating because FTL is so much faster than in-system sublight speeds that pursuing and catching a fleet that doesen't want to engage you is very hard and often feels impossible. You do get preparation tools that help you do this tho, there are ways to force the enemy to seek an engagement even when they can't win, and they can be tricked into engageing with a weaker fleet while your main fleet chatches up.
There are semi-random events both small, big and massive, that break up the routine. There are lot of alien enteties throughout the galaxy that doesen't care about who or what "rules", they just live their lives. There are normal alien life that haven't reached the space-age yet, and you can choose how to interact with them. You can help them develop for instance.
There is genetic manipulation. There is dangerous researchable technology that can end up dooming the galaxy. There are ancient stagnant empires and races who fancy themselves the true rulers of the galaxy, silently observing the squabbling child-races from their lofty technological peaks. There is marvelous almost game-changeing relics from extinct civilizations. And there are space-pirates and space-locusts.
Stellaris will likely see somewhere in between 20 to 80 DLCs throughout its lifespan, accompanied by many more free patches. The game will likely look quite different 2 years from now. That means Stellaris will continue to get better and better over time, but it also means paying for that development if you want to purchase and play this game before it's finally abandoned. It's part of the deal with this game, so only get it if you're ok with that.
The modding community is awesome, and they already enhance the game a great deal! Some of the mods are so good that the devs choose to integrate their concepts in the basic game.
In all, Stellaris is the best sci-fi 4X by a wide margin. Easy. And I say that having spent 150 hours on a save that ultimately "failed" because the game doesen't support the totally pacifist gameplay I was aiming for.

This game is absolute madness. The setting is unoriginal and generic, the characters cartoonish and ugly, and the gameplay over-the-top and messed up beyond belief. Combine that all together, and you get a love you either can't stand, or love beyond belief. And I went with the latter.
Loadout is fun. That's all it really is, fun. There's no stress you might get from other FPS/TPS games like CoD or Borderlands, mostly because of the fact you can't take this game seriously. The creators did everything they can to deliver a game that'll make you lose or die with a smile on your face, without feeling the frustration from similar games. Of course, this doesn't apply to everyone, but you get the general point here.
The weapon customization is awesome. Instead of choosing stock guns from different categories, you can design it in any way you want, from snipers to mini-guns to healing rocket launchers and whatnot. Even though some combinations might be considered "OP", it's all about the way you use it, or the way you dodge it. I have to agree the balance tends to tilt a teeny bit from time to time, but you can find that in a lot of similar games. The main point is, you can be as creative as you want with them,
The game modes currently available are Blitz (Control Points), Jackhammer (Capture the Flag), Death Snatch (Kill Confirmed), Extraction and Annihilation. The first three are what they are: Blitz is a simple "capture the control point" mode, where you need to stand on a point long enough to capture it, and 6 captures will decide the game. Jackhammer is basically Capture the Flag with a hammer instead of the flag that allows you to smack your enemies in one shot. Death Snatch is that CoD game mode with Blutonium (ore) instead of dog tags, and the most fun if you just like killing people. Extraction involves collecting the beforementioned ore enough times to win, and Annihilation is pretty much a combination of the first 3 mentioned game modes, also known as the "Competitive" mode.
Of course, the game isn't perfect. The outfits are awfully expensive (but look epic), the server still bugs out from time to time, and the party system might still throw your friends into the enemy team, even if there's enough space in the lobby. But then again, the game's still fresh, so they're expected issues.
In overall, this is currently one of the best F2P shooters out there. It's easy to pick up and play, a lot of fun to play with friends, and just insane in overall. If you're more of a serious gamer, it's best to stay away from this (although giving it a try won't hurt). If you're a casual(ish) gamer, give it a shot. And if you're a flying grapefruit like me, you'll absolutely love this game. Even if it's just to see yourself walking around with a giant hole in your body, or with just a brain and eyes, Loadout is fun for every game who likes to have a laugh every now and then while shooting off someone's head or arm. It's mindless fun with rather mindless characters.

What I appreciate most about the game is the inclusion of a casual difficulty level that makes it an accessible game for short play sessions.  The graphics are serviceable and appropriately gory.  The inclusion of trading cards and steam achievements, combined with the low price make this game a good buy for fans of casual games.  My only complaint about the title is the controller support could be improved.  While the controller does work, there are no on screen prompts and menu selection can be a bit wonky with the controller sticks.  Lastly, the steam overlay is supported making it easy to take and share screenshots on the steam playform.  For it's genre I would give the game a 4 out of 5.

I've played Empire, Napolean, and Shogun 2 (played Rome 2 for a couple hours but the graphics were♥♥♥♥♥♥on my computer and I couldn't play it).
Here are the pros and cons:
Pros:
-Each faction has a greater variety for its playing style. (spain relies on cav, venice relies on militia...etc. whereas shogun 2, empire and napolean, the faction differences are basically moot and don't change too much).
-two types of towns that require strategic use of each in order to win. Castles produce good units, Cities produce income. Without cities you're broke but without castles you'll be overrun be stronger units
-Population growth system (one of the few things that I'm upset wasn't included in shogun 2)
-You MUST use the layout of the map strategically during a siege if you want to win
-MERCENARIES (I love this and I wish napoleon, empire, and shogun did it)
-ranged units on walls are balanced so they aren't op
-population growth adds an interesting twist. Populations in cities will always become a problem at some point and will threaten with throwing you out (aka squalor)
Cons:
-Most agents are worthless. The only agent you need are priests/imams to convert people to your religion. You only need one diplomat at the beginning to establish contact at the beginning of the game, after that they are uselss. Assissin's are kinda useless. Merchants are useless initially (because they always get bought out by the enemy).
-balancing problems. Missile cavalry are stupidly op (especially early on). Crossbows are better than archers even though peasants of both costs the same.
-It's super difficult to get morale boosting traits for generals
-like every total war game, once you get to a certain point, no matter which difficulty, the game stops being a challenge and you just steam roll everyone else
-bad AI (generals always charge in front during sieges and get killed)

Yoko Taro is the one true troll fed up with conventional thinking. The man is a basket case in the best way. His madness combined with Platinum Games is pretty amazing.
This is the 5th game in the universe (Drakengard & Nier) but you can easily play this without prior knowledge of these titles, though there is a lot of references and plot points that tie these together that you will see throughout the game so if you are a long time fan you will be happy.
The game has a lot of different styles wrapped up into a seamless, tight and fluid bow, from bullet hell sequences, 2D platforming, to 3rd person combat and then again to a retro hacking minigame. You might think that this is a very strange combination but I feel the devs have created an instance where they compliment eachother nicely.
The story is a quite simple on the surface, but as you play the philosophical and emotional choices and revelations that are ever presented to you as you meet different people and the stories they tell are uncountable and they just keep coming, gradually becoming more amazing and shocking as well as touching you the player on different aspects of your life that you have been through. It is a touching and very sobering experience to the very end, and it will stay with you for a long time.
It is also very funny and wacky. The conversations between 2B and 9S with eachother and others will leave you in stitches and sometimes unsettle you due to what they are experiencing as you play. While 2B seems the more adult and professional of the two, 9S has a more 'human' personality that is always trying to keep the mood light, though they are 2 sides of the same coin. Their stories will leave you laughing, crying, happy, sad, angry, reflective and more words I can't think of to describe it. The music is masterful, with each area having their own music, and depending on the situation it can be calming and relaxing then turn into something far more foreboding and urgent. Absolutely beautiful masterpiece. I want to own the OST. I don't own any yet but I want this to be my first.
The game has 24 different endings. Granted albiet 5 of them are joke endings, depending on what you do, but of the 5 proper ends they are extremly heartfelt and leave you sitting back trying to hold back tears. You actually feel for these characters. And Pascal. Damn. ♥♥♥♥ing brutal. The sidequests flesh out more of the world and the characters in it; from lesbian android lovers, to revenge for fallen comrades, to Emil. Emil is best character! There is also nice 2B butt.
End A and B are in a sense a prelude. This will take you about 10-20hrs. Then once you beat these two the story continues, and continue it does for another good 10-20hrs. Out of the gates it hits hard like a truck on a toddler. It doesn't stop. There are no break on the feel train.
You will need to do wheelies to forget your feelies. LOTS OF WHEELIES.
10/10 don't forget your tissues.

I'm only writing this because of the flood of negative reviews I noticed at the bottom for most helpful.
The idea of this game is kill everyone at a party without dieing or getting caught by the police. You can use traps, stab them, or frame them (if other people notice a dead body next to them before they do). Traps come in many forms and dead bodies can be picked up, moved, and/or hidden. Additional characters with varying abilities can be unlocked (and are much more fun than the default guy imo).
I personally find this game very fun, since I enjoy methodically taking out the pixel people. The developer made levels felt the most satistfying to me, but there are plenty more community made ones.
First gripe, the system they have in place for community levels irritates the hell out of me. Incomplete controller support on the menu interface (despite having it everywhere else) and as far as I can tell you are stuck with the default guy (who I never want to play as after unlocking the other guys).
Second gripe, many of the traps in the game feel ineffective. Particularly the poisoned food, since it only takes out a few people. You will always end up taking out most people in a level using your weapon, so I think they could have designed traps to be more effective. Like I said though, I do find methodically taking them out fun.
There's funny easter eggs here and there (allways try using phones) that can dramatically change levels, but you can skip the "story" bits they have on loading screens (which are laughably voiced, im guessing by the developers). My sister was watching when I tried this game out, and it convinced her to buy it as well. There is something fun here, so I encourage giving it a try.

Stellaris starts off strong. I can guarantee the first thirty minutes to an hour of a new player’s experience will be in the species creation screen. Your mind will fill with the possibilities of a cuddly, fast breeding race of dog people, who also happen fanatic militarists firing off volleys of nuclear missiles at everything they see, or a bunch of spiritual hippie xenophile humanoids who want nothing but Galactic Peace. There is an endless amount of ways to customize your race to what you like, and you can even add traits which can give bonuses to your people, albeit balanced out with negative traits if necessary. At this point I was fully invested in the game, and was very excited to explore and settle the vast, empty expanse of space.
As the game begins, the galaxy is wide, empty and dark, and the mind races with the possibilities of what could be out there, and what might be lurking in the ether. The soundtrack is beautiful, and something I still listen to daily, day dreaming of humanity’s destiny among the stars. You send out your science ship into the void,  and survey systems for habitable worlds, resources, anomalies, and aliens. Some aliens may be hostile, some might be intelligent, and some might even be primitive, varying from stone age to early space age. This early game section is honestly the very best part of Stellaris. Research technologies, terraform new worlds, discover anomalies, design ships, exploit the galaxy’s resources, and meet your neighbors. The very first couple of empires you meet are exciting, they can be a race of collectivist spiders who HATE your guts and fire lasers on your ships if you stray into their territory, or entrepreneurial jellyfish who want nothing more than to make money and trade, the possibilities really are endless. The primitive races are great to play with, ranging from passively observing to going full on XCOM and enslaving them into your workforce. Good relations with other empires will also open up to possibility of open migration, leading to polyglot populations of settled planets, like humanoids living alongside giant geckos.
With the dormant ancient mining drones or hostile space borne aliens means that at one point you will have to fight, even if you are playing as peace loving hippies. There is a ship design  mechanic which may initially appear complex, but it’s a simple matter of maxing firepower and fulfilling energy requirements. It’s not hard after researching the right technologies to make the best ship, and this contributes to the ship’s “power” which is designated by the number. You would think that there is more to this system, such as different fleet doctrines, formations, etc. Unfortunately, there isn’t. If your fleet’s power number is 10, and the enemy’s power number is 8, guess what, you win. That’s the extent of complexity. Even when you are fighting gargantuan wars with hundreds of ships on both sides, is your number bigger? If so, you win. There is a tiny bit of strategy with missiles, mass driver guns, and lasers as well as point defense and fighters, but from what I’ve seen whoever brings the bigger number wins.
As you expand, the previously mysterious galaxy becomes filled with giant blobs of color. Borders become drawn, and if you’ve done a halfway decent job of expanding you will find that you are one of many large-ish empires sprinkled throughout the galaxy. Remember how unique and interesting that first other empire was when you met them? It gets real old when a new one gets revealed every few minutes. As unique and pretty as the species art is, and as varied as their randomly generated ethos/government type/ traits are, it all starts to…. blend together. You know how procedural generation can lead to blandness since everything feels the same? Stellaris has this problem with its empire generation. I honestly stopped trying to keep track of which species was which after the sixth or so, it was just a mess of xenophobic mushrooms, materialistic snapping turtles, pacifistic slugs, and what was once exciting becomes bland. This is also about the time when the game’s sector system comes into play. The sector system is mandatory but doesn’t add any meaningful gameplay. I understand why they added it, but forcing a player to basically start ignoring large swatches of territory isn’t fun. Now that my sector is automated, it can sit around and do nothing, despite me giving it an “energy focus.” The sector AI is a big issue for many players and has yet to be fixed completely.
At this point, there aren’t meaningful things left to do. Yes you are still constructing stuff on your colonized planets, yes you are still researching technologies that let you upgrade your spaceport/ colonize more planets/ build more powerful ships, but the game becomes mind numbingly dull and uninteresting. The once dark and mysterious galaxy is just another patch of space being held by Krillian Combine or something, and there is honestly nothing left to do. You can go to war with other empires in order to grab more territory, but since the space combat is just a matter of “who has the bigger number”, it just ends up feeling like busy work rather than being any kind of interesting tactical experience. Oh no, your military stack is 12k? Looks like I’ll bring 15k just in case. That’s it, no nuance or thinking involved at all. Don’t like war? You also have the option to unite everything with a Federation but the game’s diplomacy system is bare bones, not to mention how it often doesn't make sense. I was spending all this time sucking this empire’s♥♥♥♥♥♥to get them to join a federation with me, but despite having a +200 opinion, with more than two hundred years of peace and nearly that long with open borders, migration, technology sharing, they STILL didn’t want to make a federation with me. I eventually joined a federation with somebody else, but this doesn’t answer the question. What do you do now?
And honestly I feel as if Paradox doesn’t know either. You know how in Crusader Kings 2, events were always happening, and you always had to keep an eye out for opportunities to snatch territory away from your rivals? In that game, you had many options other than military conquest, but in Stellaris that’s all there is. Either make a giant fleet and attack people with boring combat, or join a federation and sit around, waiting to win. The early game starts of so good that by mid game I couldn’t believe that I didn’t know what to do anymore. The galaxy was no longer interesting and mysterious, but populated by a collection of randomly generated empires that all seem the same. I couldn’t think of a reason to continue playing because I didn’t see the point in dragging out the game’s uninteresting combat or its bland diplomatic options. I just stopped feeling the excitement of exploring the unknown cosmos and charting my species destiny. I just stopped feeling anything at all, other than boredom tinged with a hint of sadness.
Stellaris will probably go the way of other Paradox titles, adding in DLC until a big pile of ten or so expansion packs costing around $200 makes this game the deep, compelling experience that it can be. However, as of right now, I can’t recommend the game. Everyone is talking about how great the 1.5 patch and the Utopia expansion will be, but I’m going to wait and see if the game gets better. Your best bet at this point is to wait a couple of years until you can pick up the base game plus essential expansions for cheap, since until the point the Stellaris is “complete”, why pay more for an inferior product?
This game is big disappointment for me, but I am planning to revisit it in the future if and when Paradox releases enough content to make it a more fulfilling experience.

Ghost Recon: Future Soldier is the latest installment in the tactical shooter Ghost Recon series, a franchise which I hate...
Ghost Recon was released a bit after Rainbow Six, and to me...Rainbow Six won by a landslide (well, every R6 after Raven Shield sucked balls, but still, I don't count them, R6 to me is the original, Rogue Spear and Raven Shield). So when a new game was released I rolled my eyes to other, more interesting games like Spec Ops, Darkness 2, etc.
But then the game was so cheap in the summer sale I picked it up and... I'm shellshocked at the amounts of fun I've had with this game! In no other game I've felt so badass when clearing a whole room simultaneosly with my fellow A.I teammates...
Talking about the graphics, they are good, not Crysis 2 amazing or anything like that, but explosions look amazing, texture quality in some places is absolutely stunning, but most of the time it's just good...
Character models are great too except for face animations (lip syncing mostly) which suck!
The story is pretty forgettable...basically a "Ghosts" team died in an ambush and your team of Ghosts must get payback on them by dismantling this arms dealing group or whatever. Pretty basic Vendetta type of story, I never really gave a crap about it due to how forgettable it is...
What steals the show here is definately the gameplay, guns feel amazing, you can mark enemies so that your teammates kill them at the same time as you (the called "Syc-Shot" which is absolutely badass!) and the game evolves all around stealth (you belong to a team of "Ghosts" after all...)
You have other gadgets (this is a crossover between present and future (standard guns with standard attachments but some futuristic stuff, like the invisible camo "suit") and all play a very important role in the game.
The game also has the best cover system I've ever seen! It's fast, responsive and flows very naturally moving from cover to cover!
The game features a "gunsmith" mode which is amazing! Basically you grab the guns you want to use in the mission and customize them to the most little detail. I'm losing a word limit but here goes all the stuff you can customize on a standard primary weapon:
- Sights
- Stock
- Gas System
- Underbarrel
- Sidebarrel
- Barrel
- Camo
- Trigger
- Magazine
- Barrel Tip
Yeah...it's THAT deep of a customization! And guess what is the best part? Every. Single. Attachment! Alters stats on the gun (accuracy, range, damage, armor penetrations, etc.), so the customization is the deepest I've ever seen in a shooter, it's not superfluous at all!
Audio is quite amazing, every gun feels (and sounds) great, voice acting is good too! And also the weather effects (sand storms, snow storms, standard rain storms are in the game btw, levels are super varied too!).
Like I said above, the game is AMAZINGLY varied! You have around 15 missions, most of them different from eachother, there is a rooftop level, a favela level, snow level, desert-ish level, rain forest level, sunny forest level, night levels are there too, among others, very varied, like I said!
Another thing about the game is the characterization of the game, the "Ghosts" are like these top specialists in the game so they are a bit isolated in the base from the other soldiers/ marines... They have their own particular corner to hang out in. Characterization is the best I've seen in an shooter is years (Yeah...). Characters sometimes approach a certain situation with a joke and most of the time works, I literally laughed out loud at their funny moments. THIS. HAPPENED. IN. A. SHOOTER! So I guess this puts every MMS (Modern Military Shooter) around to the side right? Yeah if the game was a bit more polished...
You will encounter some bugs and glitches, some of them game-breaking! But it doesn't take away from the experience, they aren't all that common! But I expected more polish from a AAA title from Ubisoft...
It still puts most (if not all) MMS in the "shame-on-you" corner!
To end this worship session, 9.5/10! A must have, now at 15€, pick it now! Or wait for a sale...

Controlls like Terraria, and has crafting, but that's where the simularity ends.  Difficulty is high, but mostly because enemies move very quickly in very confined spaces while thwomp-like damage blocks fly up and down for no apparent reason.
The game incorporates 3 different class archtypes, warrior, ranger, and mage.  Don't bother with the ranger because crafing arrows require the use of valuable minerals that are better spent on armour and other weapons.  For example, 4 of iron are required to build a sword with 60+ durability, but the same amount of ore will only make 20 arrows.  This is clearly to balance things out since bows don't aggro enemies, but it would have been more fun to have them aggro enemies and allow you to craft more arrows.
The warrior class skills are straight forward and fun enough, while I can't say I got far enough to really get the full feel of the mage skills, though they had potential.
The reason I can't recommend this game is because it incorporates a mechanic where if you don't clear an area in 5 minutes, a group of enemies called "scourge" show up and one-shot you.   In a game that requires a substantial amount of menuing to craft, so it is extremely frustrating trying to make weapons on the fly, as time lost will limit your ability to collect resources and kill monsters for XP.
Powerful enemies show up very early in the game, forcing you to avoid them most of the time, which is fine, but by the second area, you start to run into enemies with hundreds of HP, that move very quickly and unpredictably.  Up until that point, the enemies you face had in the realm of 7-40 hp and have clear movement patterns.
If you are looking for a game that makes you feel frantic while you try to accumulate sufficient resources to only permanently die part of the way in to start over, this is the game for you.  People who really enjoy a hardcore challenge may take more pleasure in this game than I did, though I personally think most of the challange comes from the poor design decisions mentioned above.

I have really enjoyed this game so far and would definitely recommend it to my friends. I've only played single player thus far, so my review can only be associated with that.
The game itself is fairly simple. You start out being able to make a single type of character and unlock more as complete certain feats throughout additional playthroughs. You characters are semi-random as they have attributes that are generated when you start a game. If you don't like it, you can go back to the main menu and generate new random attributes.
You first play through a dungeon where there are monsters, trees, and minerals. You have to have an ax to chop down trees and a pick to mine minerals. Swords give you attack bonuses. The monsters are well designed. Each has an idiom that is the key to defeating it if you can time your attacks and movements correctly. After each dungeon, you enter a small town where you can smelt minerals and buy items you may not be able to craft.
Which brings us to crafting. Using your items you pick up in the dungeon, you can craft new swords, axes, pick, armor, etc. I'm not a huge fan of the "Figure out the crafting recipes on your own" (use the internet) crafting, but that is fine. It provides a good balance to the gameplay that each character starts with specific items which may not provide you with everything you need to get by, so you will need to either craft or purchase the rest. For example, the cyclopse rase starts with a sword and pick, but no ax, so you need to go through one dungeon picking up materials and coins so you can buy an ax the next time through which will allow you to begin your crafting adventures.
The monsters get progressively more difficult as you go. Some are very tricky indeed. Learning to use the skills you gain as your level up is important. Crafting better and better items, including armor, also becomes important if you want to make it out alive. Also, as always, attacking chickens in town is possible, but not recommended.

Party Hard is a very unique game where you play a serial murderer who tasks himself with killing everyone at various parties.  Using traps, tools, and your knife, you commit murders while trying to avoid being accused or killed.  You can walk amongst the guests unnoticed, but if anyone sees you near a body (or witnesses you stabbing someone) the cops will come to arrest you.  I've had a blast playing this game as it leads to many hilarious and outragous scenes that still crack me up to this day.  (See below for some stories of my favorites.)
PROS
+ Lots of varied levels, workshop content, and characters to unlock
+ Lots of traps, tools, and events to utilize to commit murders
+ Parties are somewhat randomized each time you play
+ Murders and traps can lead to hilarious outcomes (false accusations, accidental deaths, etc)
+ Allows you to satisfy your homicidal tendencies
CONS
- Often unclear why you were accused or arrested
- Frustrating if you lose after a long level
- Story, while somewhat interesting, is marred with cliches and subpar voice acting
FAVORITE OUTCOMES
- I murdered a victim near a stripper dancing at her pole (apparently, she didn't care.)  When a nearby drunk woke up from being passed out, he saw the body and accused the stripper of the crime.  The police arrived and arrested the stripper who continued dancing until finally being bashed and hauled away by the officer.
- A party guest noticed a dead body and ran to the phone to call the police.  After making the call she ran out to the street where she was then killed by the cop car rushing to the scene.
- Random quotes from party members still crack me up:
"All these dead bodies are ruining my party mood."
"I see another body here!"
"It tastes like a sh*t." (After drinking poison)

I really wish I bought this game when it was first released because it's that good. I hesitated buying it at launch because grand strategy games like Europa Universalis and Victoria have always turned me off due to the immense learning curve these types of games tend to have. However, Stellaris has a learning curve that is not nearly as steep and yet I suspect it still is complex enough to appeal to hardcore grand strategy players. On top of that, there is an excellent tutorial mechanism to guide you at every step of the way. It took me less than a day to learn all of the basics of the game. The game combines elements of the turn based genre such as diplomacy, tech trees, and citizen management with the time and combat mechanics of an RTS game. In addition there are many excellent fan-made mods for the game that greatly extend its replayability including a top notch Star Trek mod which I've played more than the vanilla game itself. I recommend this game to any fan of turn based strategy games like Civilization as well as RTS games like Age of Empires who has never played a grand strategy game before.

Bought the game at launch and had fun for a month or 2. After the declining playerbase when the 30-days trial was over, and the game became kinda dead, I left as well. Tried it again when it became Free2Play, but still the playerbase was way too low :( Now it's on Steam and somehow it's picked up enough players to make the world seem populated, and that's a good thing! And I also hope that it's not just a temprary thing, but that Wildstar will stay populated now.
About the game... It's as generic as any 2-faction MMO can get (I'm looking at you World of Warcraft). But the overall art and the (somewhat dark kind of) humor makes what Wildstar stand out in the crowd of all those generic WoW clones. Sadly, attimes I feel that the humor is a bit TOO forced though. Same for the narrator voice you hear when you level up and get help - way too popular (aimed at teens?) for my likings.
Quests are (as always) a lot of 'Kill 10 rats', but there's also a lot of extra stuff around the questing system. Your path for example requires you to explore the map to find the objectives. Having a science path myself, I get a lot of lore information from it.
Can't comment too much right now, because I've mothballed my old toon and have taken a fresh start. Things like gathering, crafting and PvP (which I loathe in fixed faction systems) I haven't done yet. And with it being so long ago I played Wildstar I can't even remember what it was like (and thus I started anew...)
In general, while not being a fan of fixed-faction themepark MMORPGs (which Wildstar certainly is), I think it's a good game and very much worth to try!

I've only been able to devote a couple hours to this game, but I find I can't continue playing it.  My general feeling toward WildStar can be best summed up as "Meh."  The general theme feels like a low-budget space-themed Disney movie to me, with excessive and irritating amounts of cheese (and not the good, delicious kind).
Combat, at least at low levels, is mediocre.  I appreciated the telegraph feature, but for some reason the low levels in this game felt particularly uninspiring and boring.  I have no motivation to continue playing.  Maybe the game picks up in pace and has more heart toward end-game, but if I can't even find myself able to get there, in all honesty, it doesn't really matter.
WildStar doesn't stand out from the numerous MMOs I've played, and is from my perspective, forgettable.  Aesthetically over-the-top in a downright garish way, bland classes, and a mundane storyline also put the proverbial nails in the coffin.
Admittedly, another thing that turned me off is the recent layoffs at Carbine, and the mumuring I've heard about a dwindling community.  Do I really want to invest a good amount of time in a game that appears to already be in the latter phase of its life cycle?  This may all be conjecture, but the grumblings are a bit too loud to ignore.
I'm not stating the above as facts - these are my opinions, and this type of game obviously appeals to some people.  But in my view, WildStar is worth passing up.

NOTE: Make sure you read my guide about how to find a match in multiplayer before calling this game "dead":
REVIEW:
A masterpiece from UBISOFT, don’t get fooled by the rating on other sites, this game on release date had many bugs and graphics were so crappy because of poor port so those ratings come from that time, but after 9 months UBI patching this game not only they improved multiplayer but also the graphics turned to be totally stunning. One bad thing about the graphics is that it does not have proper 1920x1080 resolution support. Without lowering the resolution to 1280x720, some players might experience massive frame rate drops, 1280x720 completely looks like 1080p in this game and i really have no idea why but it does, you can test it yourself.
About the game:
Features - Gun smith allows you to make your gun your self from paint to trigger, you can assemble it all yourself in both single player and multiplayer this option is available. graphics are really stunning but blood effects are really horrible. there are a lot of acrobat moves in this game which you can do both in multiplayer and single player. sync shot in single player allows you to mark and execute up to 4 enemy just like in splinter cell conviction. this option is also available in coop but not multiplayer.
Single Player & COOP - Just like other tom Clancy games like rainbow six or ghost recon old series the game is heavily depended on planning before executing, squad control and team plan is really important to pass the mission, unlike battlefield and CoD this game is not a run to shoot game and clearing waves of enemies etc. the gameplay is pretty much like splinter cell except with squad work, game has many ways to finish a mission and it doesn’t limit you from ending a mission, you can choose to be stealthy, or just avoiding all enemies, or just getting into direct fire and action. all single player missions can be done COOP and what makes it amazing in COOP is if you are not the host in coop you play the mission as another squad member so that means you see the gameplay from different view and your objectives will be different sometimes this means you have 4 views of each single player mission because each time you play as one of the 4 squad members you see the game from their perspective and their objectives. The story-line is okay, it's not excellent but it is fine, it is not that ALWAYS Russian devils vs ANGEL Americans. in fact like other UBI games it shows bad people are everywhere. most of the missions are in Russia and against Russian forces but you are also helping Russians to overthrow the president and get the control and give it back to the old president.
Multiplayer - This is where this game shines, that's true sometimes multiplayer has issues but if you disable all your virtual network adaptors such as Hamachi, and firewalls and some antivirus programs the game works just fine (read my guide about multiplayer tweaking). there are 3 classes in this game:
Rifleman -  Assault rifles and heavy machine guns, heavy machine guns have really nice suppression effect in this game and i would say it is the only game so far which heavy machine gun does a true suppression. armed with grenades and can resupply friendly teammates.
Engineer - Shotguns and Personal defense weapons such as carbines, can throw motion sensors and use UAV or UCAV assault drones and can plant sentry guns to defend objectives or spot enemy units. engineer has the key role in this game if one team plays with no engineers they have hard time winning the match.
Scout - Armed with submachine guns and sniper rifles, uses optimal camo to hide from enemy and can use flash bangs and claymore mines to trap the enemy. can also detect enemies through walls by IR lasers attached to the gun.
The most played multiplayer game mode is "Conflict", an objectives is randomly located on the map and both teams have to secure it, the first team which gets to it has to defend it from enemy team, the objectives are:
Securing sensor or resupply create - Both teams need to locate the sensor or resupply create and hack it and secure it for 2 minutes. if enemy teams kills the team covering the objective and get re-secure the sensor for themselves timer is not going to get reset, so that means if there is only 10 seconds left to completely secure the objective but an enemy starts to hack it in last 10 seconds then you lose the objective.
EMP Blast - One team is defender and other team is attacker the defending team should locate and cover the EMP from attackers, same about attacking team they should locate and manage to hack the EMP from defenders. if EMP is secured after 2 minutes it will lunch an EMP pulse which disables all the enemy HUD and intel for 1 minute.
HVT Tap into camos - One of the enemy or friendly members is randomly marked as HVT (usually the top score in team) the enemy team should locate the HVT and kill him before he reaches the intel swap point, if after 2 minutes HVT has not reached the point the enemy team has got the objective, if HVT manages to reach the intel swap point the friendly team gets intel over all enemy positions (wallhack).
in multiplayer you can stun enemies with stungun or stun-claymore mines or if you heavily injure them you can get to them and hack them by holding "E" if you manage to hack an stunned or injured enemy you get intel over their locations and stop their fireteam spawn. the goal in multiplayer is only and only teamwork, killing enemy is easy in this game but winning is hard.
I do recommend this game to anyone who is looking for hardcore tactical 3rd person shooter game, if you enjoyed GRAW series you will enjoy this more.

Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon: Future Soldier is a game. I'm pretty sure everyone knows that. But whether or not it's any good is difficult to say. Some good things about the game include the sync shot, where all team members target different enemies and shoot them at the same time, eliminating multiple opponents. The campaign is longer than Call of Duty campaigns, giving you more playtime in single player instead of basicly using the game just for multiplayer. The campaign is okay, so it is worth it instead of missing the mark like most shooters. The multiplayer modes are fun and addicting, bringing you back for more always. But, on the down side, online modes do not function very well, losing  connection to the server often, and stating that it is waiting for players when everyone is already ready to play. Back to the single player, the AI teammates are not that much of a help, besides the sync shot. Otherwise, they do not bring much to the mission. If you do end up in a firefight, despite the name Ghost Recon, they are not very satisfying, ultimately boring you. Overall, besides a few annoyances, Future Soldier is good.
Final Score: 5/10 -  Mediocre

This could have been a great game... indeed many contend that it is. I disagree however, because my criteria for a great game includes controls that are not broken.
Go on the internet and you will see legions of fanboys jumping through hoops to defend the obvious lazy programming and lack of anything even resembling QA testing that has resulted in controls so broken that even the simplest of maneuvers can reduce even normally patient gamers to shouting, fist-pounding emotional wrecks as they watch what should have been a gimme battle devolve into an embarrassing defeat simply due to the fact that it is next to impossible to get your troops to do as they are told.
Fanboys respond to this by saying "you just have to learn how to micro it properly", or "maybe if you learned to do it properly..." blah blah blah, ad nauseum. I call shenanigans. I'm not talking about advanced maneuvers. Not even the cavalry charges. I'm talking about "you three units, go over here and stand in a line". Ten minutes later, they are still milling around where they were before, apparently totally defeated by the entrance to a city street. And now you're out of position, and your strategy collapses as your longbowmen are outflanked by the cavalry your spearmen were supposed to be defending against. There is no excuse for this. And if it isn't getting stuck on each other and milling around, it's running *past* the spot where you told them to go, triggering a battle you're not ready for and resulting in units routing and strategies failing. No excuse.
Cavalry is similarly broken. You cannot have more than one unit of cavalry at a time, because one unit requires constant micromanagement just to charge properly. They have to be lined up *just so*, the enemy has to be clicked on *just so*, they have to be watched all the way to their target lest they encounter a tree or a slight rise and begin milling around in confusion, and they have to be told to retreat the instant they hit, or even the lowliest of peasants will begin to bowl them over like ninepins. If you can have more than one unit of cavalry in this game; never play it again because you can click fast enough to make money playing Starcraft professionally.

Given its price, this is a really smart, visually charming, pick-up-'n'-play crawler that manages to have entertaining combat, somewhat varied enemies and plenty of loot to work through. The dungeon levels are randomised, and each play has 7 levels, the last of which contains the Orb you're after. Grinding through each level to the end is great, and battling back up with the orb is even more challenging. There's a very small upgrade element, but by vast majority this is just one of those wee games you have that you jump into occasionally for a quick run around. No strings, no commitment, just a quick half hour of fun whenever you need it. Highly recommended.

Had nothing to play until Overwatch releases (24th of May), so I figured why not buy Borderlands Pre-sequel since I have them all with every DLC out there, since I really wanted to play Athena.
I heard quite a few negative things about this one and it was mostly compared to Borderlands 2, which most say is the superior game. So I figured, gonna try it myself and see what's exactly the issue here.
What I find interesting is that Borderlands 2 bored the hell out of me. I mean seriously, I would start a quest and at a very fast rate just get bored, so naturally I was scared that Pre-sequel might do the same thing... but nope. It was refreshingly fun, there's a lot to do with the thrusters (oxygen jetpack thingy) and the setting was just more appealing to me. There was however that classically boring Borderlands style questing where you go from A to B then back to A then back to B several times, but the thrusters atleast kept me going through it.
I do have to admit however that I did not buy the game at full price. It was on a 50%-75% discount with the Season Pass included. If I had to say whether this game was worth at a 50$ or whatever it was at release, I'd kind of start looking around. The game was short, but it's great. Took me 18 hours (with side-content and a few challenge searches) to beat the final boss. I just wish Gearbox did not always have to rely on countless DLCs and a Season Pass to make the game better. It is one of the reason why I prefer Pre-sequel more than Borderlands 2. Borderlands 2 is a mess with countless DLCs. GOTY does not include all the DLCs, Season Pass does not include all the DLCs. Truly a mess.
All in all, to me personally, this game is a great Borderlands addition at a discounted price. It does feel like an expansion and a sequel... the Oxygen and the Laser features were great, even the voice acting! I really like that my character is not a MUTE. I like the characters, the story and most of all, the setting. Gun play should have been a bit better developed (fire element being a bit useless here and there), but overall quite an enjoyable experience.
Pre-sequel pulled me back into Borderlands and I can now actually play Borderlands 2 without getting bored again.

This could be a great game, but so much drags it down.
For one, movement speed across the board is terrible. I feel like the game should probably be called Slug Hard. Everyone (not just your character) should move faster, and maybe make the sprint last longer than the average time it takes to blink.
Secondly, there's too much randomization going on. Why have a golf cart show up in one round, then have it vanish in the next? Why have crowd layouts/guard patrols randomized? It only serves to frustrate the player. If you want elements of randomization, the phones serve that purpose quite well.
Third, I was annoyed that on-screen key prompts didn't reflect the fact that I'd changed several key bindings. It's confusing at first, and just plain stupid once you've committed the keys to muscle memory.
It's disheartening to know that the developers are already hard at work on the sequel, as it makes them coming back and fixing the problems of this game highly unlikely. If they do, I might be inclined to change my review, but as it stands, I cannot recommend this game.

First off this is based on the Early Access experience I've had. So there are a few bugs that pop up and there is a lot of content still in the pipe line.

I'm pleasantly surprised at how the game plays and how enjoyable it is.
There is a really good tutorial system which is complete enough to get you up to speed. With the tutorials and the in game feedback you should up and running designing engines and cars.
This game is really in depth. the first car you design if you watch all the tutorials along the way will take well over an hour.
After you have designed 2 or 3 cars you can crank one out in a few minutes and then if you want spend over an hour tweaking it to exactly how you the the car to be.  I really enjoy shaving a few seconds off the cars lap time and seeing how much faster I can get it to go around the track.

The engine designer scenarios are a lot of fun. Make an engine within certain guidelines sounds easy. Some of the scenarios are really easy others are down right brutal as it states in the scenario.
Complete car designer scenarios are a bit trickier if not more rewarding at the end.
If you are into simulation games and like cars I would give it a go.
