So I'm going to write an extensive review for this, because I believe these devs deserve some more money than they're selling this game for. More than 0.49 cents USD anyway.
Gameplay:
Gameplay is typical run n' gun gameplay, top down. I don't normally play top down shooters but they did a pretty great job with this one. There are several guns to collect throughout the game as well as secrets hidden in every level, and they do a pretty good job of hiding them too. I've only played a little bit so far but from what I have played, it's pretty good. The weapon upgrades actually help you fight the larger hordes of zombies that are constantly coming at you. There is also pretty decent enemy variety, runners, large zombies, LARGER ZOMBIES, and at the end of my session tonight I ran into zombies shooting fireballs.
These aren't the typical Romero zombies or 28 Days Later zombies, they're from a chemical spill or something like that, so I'll give them a pass to use any kind of zombie they really want to at that point. Zombie origins are everything!
Shooting mechanics are great as well and with the wide variety of guns, it's pretty fun to be able to switch guns on the fly to gun down a LARGE zombie with a grenade launcher, dodging their shockwaves of them hitting the ground and switching to the pistol for the small fry. I am extremely thankful the pistol has infinite ammo and is upgradeable as well (At least on the easiest difficulty, I don't know about the other ones).  Also, there's no reloading mechanic, which is great for a game like this. Seriously if that mechanic was in this game it'd be 100% harder even on the difficulty I'm playing on.
Sound: Sound in the game is fantastic, as is the voice acting in my opinion. Though I pretty much like any voice acting unless it's REEEEEEEEEALLY bad, so. The explosions from explosive barrels sound great as well as car explosions actually being rattling when they happen. Also gun sounds are great.
Characters and Storyline: The storyline in the game is not rushed per se but it shoves you into the role of this dude chilling in his house, when he hears a guy yelling "STOP," etc and then a zombie busts through your front door and the SWAT guy shoots it. It goes from there pretty much just the character being on the run from the zombies (Not sure if the character has a name, if he does, I forgot it). There's some pretty interesting parts in the story so far, and from the weapon upgrades I'm getting, I'm pretty sure I'm barely into the game yet, but we'll see I suppose. The characters are very well voiced IMO and are worth listening to, they did a good job with voicing and the slight character development of the NPCs, of the limited time you're with them, and the character development of the main character, what there is anyway. He's pretty much already solidified as a "man's man" mentality but it keeps in character, which I can appreciate.
Well, generally I think that's it so I do recommend this game if you're looking for a fun time waster that's a zombie shooter. IMO, it is worth full price just from what I've played so far. The only gripe I have with the game is that in some of the levels the area is hard to navigate around, but that may be just my eyes tbh, all the levels are actually open and explorable for secrets and stuff, didn't run into any bugs so 9.5/10 game from me. Graphics aren't everything, kids.

Had nothing to play until Overwatch releases (24th of May), so I figured why not buy Borderlands Pre-sequel since I have them all with every DLC out there, since I really wanted to play Athena.
I heard quite a few negative things about this one and it was mostly compared to Borderlands 2, which most say is the superior game. So I figured, gonna try it myself and see what's exactly the issue here.
What I find interesting is that Borderlands 2 bored the hell out of me. I mean seriously, I would start a quest and at a very fast rate just get bored, so naturally I was scared that Pre-sequel might do the same thing... but nope. It was refreshingly fun, there's a lot to do with the thrusters (oxygen jetpack thingy) and the setting was just more appealing to me. There was however that classically boring Borderlands style questing where you go from A to B then back to A then back to B several times, but the thrusters atleast kept me going through it.
I do have to admit however that I did not buy the game at full price. It was on a 50%-75% discount with the Season Pass included. If I had to say whether this game was worth at a 50$ or whatever it was at release, I'd kind of start looking around. The game was short, but it's great. Took me 18 hours (with side-content and a few challenge searches) to beat the final boss. I just wish Gearbox did not always have to rely on countless DLCs and a Season Pass to make the game better. It is one of the reason why I prefer Pre-sequel more than Borderlands 2. Borderlands 2 is a mess with countless DLCs. GOTY does not include all the DLCs, Season Pass does not include all the DLCs. Truly a mess.
All in all, to me personally, this game is a great Borderlands addition at a discounted price. It does feel like an expansion and a sequel... the Oxygen and the Laser features were great, even the voice acting! I really like that my character is not a MUTE. I like the characters, the story and most of all, the setting. Gun play should have been a bit better developed (fire element being a bit useless here and there), but overall quite an enjoyable experience.
Pre-sequel pulled me back into Borderlands and I can now actually play Borderlands 2 without getting bored again.

A Fun Arena Shooter Plagued by Coding Flaws
+ large amout of weapon customization
+ large potential for multiple play styles
+ smoothly rendered animations
+ enemy health indicator increases potential for teamwork and competitive play
- exp system may deter newer players or players that have invested less time for weapon experimentation and map familiarity.
- poor netcode/lag compensation: for higher pinging players ie 80ms+ you must preaim their position to hit them. This is a major flaw when playing with mixed pings, you will hit high latency players and miss the low latency players depending on how you compensate your aim.
-poor regionality preferences: simply put, nobody in the US wants to play on a US server with someone in Brazil, Russia, China, ie somebody on another continent who will more than likely have high latency.
- poor hitbox registration: dodge roll spammers are a joke, i would really like to see a slow-mo hitbox demonstration mid-roll, or a roll cooldown or velocity penalty post-roll.
- specific weapon particle animation combinations completely block the view of crosshair and enemy players.
- gamemode jackhammer: while carrying jackhammer, sprinting, dodging, and jumping is enabled while velocity is increased. player velocity while carring jackhammer should be decreased and hammer kill radius should be tweaked to either implement a minimum output damage, or decrease the size of the radius.
Until these issues are fixed, nobody in the competitve community will take this game as a potentially serious esport arena shooter.

Do not be fooled by the trailer, the game moves almost half as slow as the trailer suggests.
You cannot run without putting away your sword at which point you have to draw it again in order to fight or defend yourself.

The sound in the game is overbearing as every character shouts out surly insults in a psuedo medieval male voice that gets old within the first match.
While it is refreshing that swords do realistic damage, causing people to die in 1 or 2 hits, it causes fights to boil down to people dying and respawning to run back to a central point and backstab the people already fighting repeatedly. This also gets old within the first match or two as there is no minimap or even a real way to hear people coming up behind you.
Graphically, the game feels a bit dated already, and due to the washed out color palette it can be difficult to even see other characters within parts of the battlefield.
While the game is still in early access status, there are still noticeable elements such as keybinding bugs and extremely awkward sword swinging controls which can hamper combat even further.
In short, the concept of the game is a very good one, but so far implementation leaves quite a bit to be desired. If you enjoy games such as Devil May Cry or Ninja Gaiden, you may be disappointed as the pace of combat is almost slower than in oblivion or skyrim.

I played through this using the Revision Mod available on Steam, but felt the need to write this using the original game. This game as a whole is absolutely fantastic in experience, atmosphere, gameplay and immersion. I am convinced anyone who debates that Deus Ex has aged badly did not get past Liberty Island and found that modern conventions in controls and gameplay have spoilt them from enjoying this game. Although I can agree visually the game has aged (released 17 years ago), everything besides that criticism is void.
The gameplay is intuitive, the stealth functions very well and while exploitable, can be fun in doing so. The weaponry is massively arrayed and almost everything is applicable in terms of viability. The set pieces and world overall are incredibly well designed, allowing you to ALWAYS find a way to the next objective without the typical "B-line to through a corridor" approach. Level design is one of Deus Ex's greatest assets, and definitely helps in terms of replayability, along with plenty of secrets and hidden items to find and furthering progression. Augmentations are a joy to use, from cloak devices to the use of a portable spy bot to disable robotics. The methods available to approaching each mission are incredible, and honestly make hundreds of modern games look primitive in contrast to its gameplay.
The story, without spoiling anything, is an amazing but simple intrinsic story about conspiracies, world domination and questioning the nature of man and machine. The themes that run through the original Deus Ex are one of the many huge reasons it has still got modern relevance. Mature storytelling, immersive world and also gives the player the REAL ability to decide how the fate of the world is molded.
Music score needs a big shout out, as the original soundtrack is easily one of my favourite parts to Deus Ex. Each song is appropriate to  the theme of the level, from the dire empty cyberpunk streets of New York, to the headquarters of the world peacekeepers UNATCO headquarters, each musical piece is an absolute blessing in a video game of this age. I also have to mention that the atmosphere of this game is cleverly done simply on the basis of it ALWAYS being night time, in mostly urban levels and industrial style levels.
There is a HUGE amount of this game that can be dissected and discussed, and still is today from people experiencing it for the first time. If you haven't played this game before, and are wanting a role-playing game like no other of its kind, definitely give a try; forgive its old school nature and get immersed into the world, I am sure plenty of people will agree with me they wish they could turn back the clock and replay this game for the first time.

I can safely say that this was one of the best gaming experiences of my life. Despite being a 17 year old game with aged graphics and clunky gunplay, I still found myself being completely immersed in the world and story of this game. Not a single game that I can recall comes close to matching the story of this game. The fictional dystopia and real-life conspiracy theories present here blend perfectly together and it really gets you thinking about the not-so-distant future of our world and how similar it may be to something like what is happening in this game.
Despite what I said about the clunkiness of the shooting, the gameplay is actually really fun once you get used to it. You have to take your time when shooting enemies, so stealth is encouraged for standard enemies. I recommend acquiring a GEP gun, as it just makes dealing with robots and MiB much easier, but sneaking past them and disabling security on certain robots is also a very good option. The movement in this game is actually pretty good, however.
I really recommend playing this game FIRST before playing the newer Deus Ex games. I feel like it will allow you to enjoy this game without being spoiled by the modern graphics/gameplay of the newer games, but if you would rather play the games in chronological order, then play Human Revolution first.
TL;DR: Buy this freaking game. The gameplay is fun, the story is amazing, and the soundtrack is some of the best in video games.

What do you expect in a Ghost Recon game?  A stealth shooter?  A shooter where you remain hidden most of the time and only engage open combat when things go wrong?  That is what I expected.
Things started off well enough.  You were sneaking around and you got some nice toys to play with.  However as the game progressed, it became more of an action shooter with a very small stealth component.  Did you carefully pick off your targets to clean out that seemingly impossible area?  Well sometimes the game says FU, combat starts anyway.
So your lightly armored squad survived that onslaught of men?  Ok, now we are going to throw vehicles in.  Still alive?  Next time you will also have clock, so you got to do it in 3 minutes or less.  To the developer who did that final level with the last general, I say thanks for the total BS level that has absolutely nothing to do with “Ghost Recon”.
Overall this game is more of an action shooter with a dwindling stealth component (one later level being an exception).  I think the game is about 8 to 10 hours long.  Steam just tracked it as being played when the UBI soft launcher was loaded, not when I was playing the game.  If you want a real stealth recon game, then I would suggest you pass on this title unless it is dirt cheap.  If you just want any old shooter FPS with a stealth component, then you be the judge for 8 to 10 hours.

This is one of those games that don't look as fun as the playthroughs of it. I was in love with the graphics, but the charm soon wears off, within only three hours for me personally. Regaurdless, don't be completely deterred from this game by my review. You can still get some enjoyment out of it (though I would never recommend it at full price). Don't have high expectations though. After watching several playthroughs of the game and seen what I thought was a ton of fun, I was disappointed with the actual product.
I've seen this being described as a "a rougebased 3d RPG game with permadeath" To put it more basic, it's a dungeon crawler at it's simplist. There's nothing complex about it. Explore the dungeon fighting enemies, leveling up, and picking up loot like weapons, food, potions, and armor. So anyone can jump into it right away. However it's not exactly easy either. In the beginning I struggled with not succumbing to foes as it's an art to get close enough to hit an enemy with your beginning weapon (a very short dagger) without getting attacked yourself every time. You have to be at just the right distance to hit them without getting hit back, and since you only start with a mere 8 HP, it can be tough for new players, but it's just something to get used to. The goal of the game is to descend down 7 floors, defeat a boss, collect an orb from him, and to work your way back up the 7 floors to leave without dying.
Some people have said the game is very easy, and that they were able to beat it in a mere hour or less. I've had a hard time with it, and I'll explain why. It's typical logic that you need to be a high level the farther you advance. Althoguh other players may disagree about this with me, I've found that I've needed to grind, or else I'm just not leveled up enough the deeper into the dungeon I get. The big problem with this is that it's almost impossible to grind in Delver. After you clear the floor the first time, enemies will continue to spawn a little (for a short time), but they'll spawn less and less until they stop all together. When I backtrack, I only run into a few to zero enemies, which means I have to go back and forth on a floor over and over again to try to level up. It's a very slow process.
I also have to cover the two glitches I noticed. The first thing I noticed was how very laggy such a graphically simple game was, and then I noticed more specifically, it was lagging in time with the music. I had to turn the music off because it really slowed down the game. Maybe it's just my laptop and won't happen to all computers, but I figured I would give the heads up to people. The sound effects worked just fine however, and I want to mention the nice touch it added to the gameplay. The enemies would say phrases like "I heard something" and "What was that?" that would make you aware of their presence. Now you could still be spooked by an enemy, because some enemies wouldn't make much noise, but it did cut back on the startling surprise. The second glitch only happens in the caves, which are the 3rd and 4th levels in the game. The cave walls are very uneven and blocky, over all very odd looking. It's not easily clear where you can fit through and where you can't. Quite a few times, I got a little too close to just the side of the wall when I was walking, and I immediately got stuck. I refused to start over, and so I would spend 10-15 minutes trying to get myself free. For anyone else who experiances this, first take off your helmet, and then repeatedly use a weapon (I found the dagger most helpful) to hit either above or below you while holding in the key to go backwards. It's very tedious and annoying, and there are no changes to show your progress, but all at once you'll be free. The very last time however, I got stuck for good and tried for probably a half hour to get out to no avail. There's nothing more frusterating then losing precious progress.
There are three other minor things worth mentioning. You collect gold, but you can't buy anything during that playthrough. Instead, the gold carries over when you die, and you can buy items the next round, before you enter the dungeon again. The way you leveled up bugged me. There are six different attributes, but when you level up, only three available ones show up, randomized each time. If you want to upgrade a certain skill, it often isn't there to choose. There are also different kinds of pressure plates in the game. Some hurt you, but one kind is a teleportation pad that will teleport you to a random place in the level. In all my time of playing, I have not once come across a single teleporter. I wondered if they had removed it in an update, but there are places in the level that you can not physically reach yourself.
You'll see in other reviews that this game doesn't have a lot of replayability. I didn't believe this at first, but it rings true. You'd think a game with randomly generated dungeons would have endless fun, but it actually gets old fast. I can't put my finger on as to why, but it does. Perhaps it's *too* simple, and needs something more to spice it up. It's still in it's beta state (at the time of writing this review) so I won't knock it off yet. It still has time to grow and evolve. I personally did not enjoy it a lot, but I feel like other players will get more, longer lasting fun out of it than I did because I'm very picky about dungeon crawlers. They are definately not my favorite genre, so that may have contributed to why I didn't enjoy this game more. For the record, this game isn't horrible or even bad. I just thought it was okay, and that's the only reason I'm not recommending it, but that's just my own opinion. It is surely possible to enjoy this game, so give it a try if you've had your eye on it.

Note: This review recaps my old review/experiences and then goes into more recent attempts at playing.
One year ago, I was longing to experience Dark Souls, but couldn't due to hardware limitations. I began a quest of looking for a suitable hold-me-over and found Kingdoms Rise. Kingdoms Rise reminded of the combat experience I longed for- up close and personal melee combat with some ranged and magic attacks mixed in.
After purchasing the game, I excitedly hopped in and was met with bugs and lack of features that killed the user experience (short recap: menus that didn't work, broken key bindings/controller support, no tutorials). As a new user, I was quickly turned off. As I tried playing, I became flustered with the lack of guidance and no tutorials to help me out.
I did eventually find the video tutorials that the developer posted, but found it hard to implement these lessons against players with 20+ hours compared to my newbie self. As I tried to persist, I was put off by the bad GUI and lack of a tutorial.
Players on community sites and Steam kept repeating that after about 10 hours of playing the kill cam, you would start to get better and that the bugs were not an issue. Ignoring the bugs issue, I was very put off by this. Call me weak or lazy, but I would rather not waste time (like my money) on a kill-cam simulator. In similar games, I was able to learn and start improving long before the 10 hour mark. Sadly, this was not the case with Kingdoms Rise.
As I now review other reviews on Steam, I can see that I wasn't the only one that burned out shortly after starting the game. Between bugs and difficulty learning the new system, players gave up.
------------------------------------------
Nearly one year later, and a recently built new computer, the Black Friday/early Winter sale reminded me of this game. So, I redownloaded it and gave it another try.
It is nice to finally see big bugs ironed out (menus function properly, controllers work, keybindings stick) and some areas of the game (practice range, menus, in game interface) improved.
Sadly, the developers took too long with these changes and lost nearly the entire playerbase.
On the server browser, I was presented with ~15 servers to choose from. Of all these servers and game modes, only one server had one person. Thinking it may be a bot/AFKer to draw people in, I decided to let the game find a match for me, hoping to find that one server that people were still playing on. I was given an empty server to fight NPCs on (alone) - which got old, fast.
Wondering if it was just my luck with the match system, I hopped on a popular site with karma points to see what discussions were going on. What I saw was not pleasant. The latest post was 6 months ago, and the next post after that was 10 months ago. Many of the comments on Steam and this site call this game "A quick cash grab by the developer".
It's sad to see a potentially great concept die out. Personally, I believe it is to blame for being released (even as an early access) too early and not enough speed from the developer.
------------------------------------------
Assumedly eager to make some money - which is very understandable - I feel like the developer rushed the publishing of this game. From my perspective, this effectively killed the game when the developer couldn't keep up. While it should be a topic of its own, I feel this is greatly to blame on Valve's allowance of Early Access games.
Between the dead player base and the improvements, I'm torn between recommending this game or giving it a thums down. But, because of the dead player base (the key aspect that makes this game playable), I'm going to keep my thumbs down.
As the game (hopefully) gets more exposure during the sales, I'll keep giving it more chances to see if the community sparks a bit and see just how much the game has ironed out. As I stated in my previous review, I'd love to give this game a thumbs up. It's a great concept. But right now, I simply can't.

Stellaris could be a great strategy game. I am a huge fan of sci-fi mystery movies about space exploration and revelations it hides, so this game looked like a great choice. This is where fun ends.
Why I do not recommend this game:
1. It was developed on an old 32-bit engine, so no matter how powerful your CPU is, somewhere in the mid-game you'll inevitably start experiencing terrible performance issues, and the further in the game you'll be the worse the issues will become. Somewhere in the late game the performance was so terrible, I could not continue the game at all. It became completely unresponsive. This is all because of the limitations of the old game engine, so I repeat, it does not matter how powerful your CPU is - be prepared to get frustrated after spending tens of hours on building, only to realize that you cannot finish the game properly.
2. This game looks uninspired. All the aliens look like they evolved on Earth. We have either insects, or plants, or freaking parrots in space suits trying to conquer the galaxy, and become superior. How come they all look like they are from Earth? Why can't there be let's say some "greys", or intelligent flying electric spheres. Instead, all the aliens look like they are a product of Darwin's dreams after a hard night of boozing. Ridiculous. Uninspired. Disappointing.
3. Politics. That's all this game is. You cannot roll through the entire galaxy with your OP forces (as anyone would do in the real world). Instead, you are allowed to conquer only 2-4 planets at a time, and then forced to wait 10 years before you can fight again. Why? This game is like your annoying mom that pulls the monitor plug every time you're winning. So annoying, and unneccessary. Just let me♥♥♥♥♥♥♥destroy everyone, and take over the galaxy! If there are 300 planets, and you can conquer only 2 every 10 years, imagine how long it will take to play just one single player mission. I can tell you how long because I tried. It took me around hundred hours to finish just one mission, and at the end of that I feel no satisfaction. I feel like I am finally done with an annoying chore, and thinking about this just makes me angry. MAKES ME ANGRY!
4. There are no differences in powers between aliens. Everything, and everyone is absolutely the same. How about that for the fun? The only difference is a picture of an alien. Everything else is the same. How can someone create a strategy game where there is absolutely no difference between powers? That's just another sign of a rushed, uninspired game that deserves to be in a hall of shame.
5. 95% of this game is reading text, interacting with politicans, and making political decisions towards other aliens. It's like some election game or something. I guess they wanted to make a game about politics, and elections, and promises they make, but they realized that no one would buy that crap, and at the last moment they just converted the whole thing into the space game. They just swapped the presidents with aliens, and♥♥♥♥♥♥that crap out onto the market.
If you are looking for some action you won't find it here. The only action here is jerking the more powerful presidents off until you become more powerful, and then it's a choppy bugged fight that looks just ugly, and lasts for minutes. After that, back to the politics. What a trash.
6. This game is boring. It's so boring it will make you rethink your life choices over, and over, until you feel absolutely ashamed of your life.
7. It's full of bugs, and glitches. It just looks like people who made the game are not professionals, but rather some guys who got together, and made an experimental game over night. Total trainwreck.
Even if politics, and management, and accounting is something that gives you a boner, I still not recommend this game because at the mid- end-game stages it becomes completely unplayable.
What a garbage.

Nier is a genuine masterpiece that defies conventional expectations and design norms. While not flawless, Nier is undeniably a work of art that is greater than the sum of its parts. With a wide variety of gameplay styles, a remarkably well-written story with incredibly deep characters, and a memorable sound track complete with a proprietary language, Nier is a definite contender for Game of the Year awards.
PlatinumGames, while not known for deep complexity in their combat systems, have still managed to form a brand for themselves in the past few years thanks to big successes such as Metal Gear Rising and Bayonetta 2. Their heavily-stylized "character action" game design fits perfectly into the anime-esque world of Nier: Automata: characters swing and throw teleporting greatswords twice their size with ease, slow down time to teleport-dodge enemy attacks, and run with an acceleration that feels like a 2-legged racing game. This also extends into the flight sequences, where you command a transforming airplane mecha with a moveset not dissimilar to your grounded counterparts. While the ground combat is even more simplistic than MGR (you can often just hold the "light attack" button [while dodging] to auto-combo normal enemies), there is such a huge variety of gameplay that you never get bored. Flight combat, hacking sequences, creative use of locked camera angles, and even mini-VNs all break up the hack 'n' slash to create what is probably the most creative mainstream "AAA" game in the past two console gens.
It's hard to talk about how good the writing in Nier is without spoilers. To put it simply, Nier is broken into two parts, each being played across two characters. One character, who surprisingly becomes the focal point of the story, has a gradual mental health degradation which even the game's support characters make it a point to notice. Most Japanese media seems to take characters who are "supposed" to be evil and has them instantly snap under pressure, typically caused by one traumatic event like a loved one dying. This game's character goes from a happy-go-lucky straight shooter and suffers multiple depressing events that I felt affected me more than him at times. His decline into insanity isn't a simple breaking point but a good dozen hours of misery that was so well written that it became the main driving force of the story. While replaying portions of the game again as a different character can become tedious, their story line splits provide a fresh look at each character and the main story itself.
So many great ideas and designs are incorporated into Nier: Automata that its hard to cover all of them in a simple written review. Nier frequently defies player expectations, creatively breaks the fourth wall, paints a rich sci-fi lore with excellent world-building, and leaves enough room to fill in the blanks with your imagination that I expect a fanbase similar to Undertale to crop up around it. Nier is the best game I've played since The Witcher 3 in July 2015. Hopefully it receives the attention it deserves because games like this are really once a gen masterpieces.

This game is not perfect. It has plenty of flaws. Visually, it is behind the times, especially the environments (character models are actually quite good). There are some repetitive gameplay elements and recycled environments as well. The RPG elements are really light and fairly meaningless.
Despite the flaws, this is one of the best games I have played this year. This is because the game's strongest elements are outstanding and are miles ahead of the competition. Main pros:
+Soundtrack - I cannot believe how ridiculously awesome the soundtrack is. It is its own work of art. It completely blew me away over and over again. It is in a made up language? It combines a dizzying array of instruments and electronics. Many tracks dynamically loop into different versions based on context. Wow.
+Story - There is nothing that amazing about the story from a purely plot perspective. However, it is a narrative masterpiece. It is remarkable that a story about robots in a completely ridiculous/insane/non-sensical plot can end up feeling so moving. This is an example of a story that would be hard to tell in a different medium. Compare this to most AAA games, where a story that would be purely average if in movie/TV/book form is dribbled out in little bits between gamey grindy elements. This should be a wake up call to developers that something bold and different not only can work but also can generate sales.
+Action gameplay - A simple but effective platinum style combat system plays well and consistently in an open world setting. It transitions remarkably well between different camera styles and even between 2d and 3d versions. Although not perfect, this is impressive from a design standpoint that I can go between different 2d and 3d viewpoints, intuitively understand the controls, and juggle the same set of mechanics. There are some major balance issues (some chips are hilariously OP). It looks much nicer in action than in screenshots.
+Eclectic - Many different gameplay types seamlessly integrated. Bold. Takes risks, mostly successful. You will absolutely be surprised multiple times if you play this game, even if you are a grizzled and cynical games veteran like me.
-Technical - It is a total mess. Get the fan-made patch and disable MSAA to make the game much more playable. I have a low to mid-range gaming PC and could get 50fps at 1080p after patching and tweaking.
Buy this to play something special.

NieR: Automata is like a rough gem: it's not perfect and yet its beauty comes from its imperfections, which make it unique and distinguishable from any other. "Unique" is the keyword here, because this game is guaranteed to be different from everything you've ever played before. The various gameplay mechanics it uses are not new per se, but they're put together in an innovative way, creating an absolutely original and remarkable experience. An experience that like I said, is not perfect and finds its weakest point in certain aspects of the plot. But let's go with order.
Gameplay-wise the game is fantastic, to the point that it could set a new standard for action RPGs. The original NieR already tried to combine different gameplay elements but ultimately failed due to an excessive repetitiveness and general lack in depth of combat; Automata instead brings its mix of platforming, shooting, action and RPG elements to the excellence and delivers an exciting rollercoaster ride where you never know what to expect next: a moment before you were shooting enemies with your airship in a top-down bullet hell, then you find yourself fighting on the ground with swords and a moment later you're running and jumping on side-scrolling platforms. All with the extreme fluidity and quality that Platinum Games got us used to. There's so much variety in gameplay that you just never get tired, and even the occasional fetching sidequests are fun (and quick!) to do. If I had to point out a defect in gameplay the only thing I could think of is the lack of difficulty once you get to the highest levels, but it's a pretty common thing for JRPGs and the difficulty can be adjusted in any moment anyway, so if you want a challenge you can always try the Very Hard mode where almost everything oneshots you. This way everyone can play the way he wants.
Unfortunately such greatness is undermined by a lot of technical flaws, that can make the game unplayable on some configurations. I myself had to make a rollback to a year-old drivers in order to have the game run on my RX 480 without systematically crashing during the first 10 minutes, and that alone didn't fix resolution and stuttering problems. Luckily for us, the good Kaldaien made
to solve most of the issues but a few minor problems with tearing and stuttering still persist and at present day, more than a month after the release, there's still no sign of an official patch. Which is obviously bad and should be taken into serious consideration before buying the game.
The story, which is the core element of a game like NieR, is good but predictable in some ways and honestly didn't live up to my expectations completely. While the first game lacked a convincing gameplay, it compensated with a captivating narration and great characters and that's what made it a cult title for many people. The fact that the overall plot of the universe that Drakengard started is needlessly convoluted and full of holes didn't prevent it from having a solid storyline of its own, and most importantly from having characters that the player could relate with. That's what Automata is missing the most, at least for me. I wasn't able to relate to the characters as deeply as I did with the ones from the first NieR, and that had a negative impact on my immersion into the story. But when I said that the beauty of this game comes from imperfections, I was referring to the narration, too. Because what this game is all about is not the story or the characters but rather the motivations at the basis of those character's actions and the questions that arise with them. More so, is about what makes humans human. Similarly to what Hideo Kojima did with MGS2 back in 2001, Yoko Taro chose to employ an established universe to convey a philosophical message about humanity to the players, a message that reaches its highest peak during ending E - which is, without spoilers, one of the single greatest moments I've ever experienced in video games. You may like this kind of "deeper-meaning-focused narration" or not, but its great value in terms of artistic maturity of the media is unquestionable. It's not for everyone's taste though, so think well about it before deciding to buy and play this title. Also, if you're completely new to the NieR and Drakengard franchise I suggest you to stop right there and play at least the first NieR before getting into Automata. If you don't, you may enjoy the game on the gameplay level, but you won't understand anything of the various references to the backstory, and everything will probably seem confused or senseless to you.
What I personally loved the most about the narration are the different perspectives that the player is invited to witness: even if you're replaying the same story (until a certain point) you're replaying it differently and that is a great way to both improve longevity in a non-tedious way and to elaborate the plot more deeply. I also loved the possibility to unlock the chapter selection after the third playthrough, which allows to retrieve any side quest or secondary ending left behind without having to restart everything from the beginning. All JRPGs should learn a lesson from NieR: Automata in this sense.
A little extra considerations about the music: it's beautiful, but I honestly think it is much less inspired than the original NieR's soundtrack. Many of Automata's tracks are re-arranged versions of the first game's ones and the new songs just don't reach the level of the old ones. I'm not saying they are bad, they just don't make me want to buy the OST like the previous one did.
So, in short my opinion about NieR: Automata can be summed up like this: it's a wonderful game to play, with a somewhat inconsistent story that is compensated by a deep introspective and artistic value. It might not be an absolute masterpiece, but to me it's beautiful enough to earn a place in my personal "must play" list. And I'm pretty sure I'll be replaying this game again someday, which is something that happens more and more rarely.

I have played this title around 40-50 times ever since I was a young teenager, when it was released. I probably know every secret place in the game, every code, could synchronize many conversation by my memory. I loved this game and part of me still does, even tho knowing this game too well made it less enjoyable for me over time. But if you've never played the original Deus Ex, please allow me to tell you one thing: It's a masterpiece. It is worth your purchase, it is worth your time.
Pros:
- One of the best storylines in gaming history, with many twists and turns, with many interesting side-stories and a lot of flavortexts to add up to that. The level of immersion that this game generates is huge and I'd say flawless. It will make you think and maybe even question yourself, if you get into it. I don't want to spoil anything by getting more specific, but it's a really great story. The story is the reason so many people love this game. But the rest really isn't bad.
- The game mechanics are well performed, even by looking at modern standards. Combat feels allright and realistic enough (with minor flaws) and you're not forced to actually engage into combat. To my knowledge it's entirely possible to play the game without killing any "normal" NPC (by sneaking and using secret passages) and as far as I remember there is only one "boss" NPC that has to be killed in order to progress. Maybe two. But the game is not centered around violence if you don't want it to.
I just learned a few weeks ago on youtube that it is actually possible to play this game without using any items. Challenging but possible.
- Level design is mostly clever and when you're cool with rather old, rather clumsy graphics, adds to the game's immersion. It's linear, but the linearity is done right. You usually have certain goals within the area of a level and you always have multiple ways to get the job done. What's the smartest way? The game doesn't tell you. You have to explore to figure it out. Or talk to people. This point also adds to the replayability of this title because you could always try another path and maybe get the job done more the way you like it.
- The music is actually pretty cool.
Cons:
- The AI, your enemies, are having a very small field of view and the slight tendency to act stupid and unnatural.
- All follow-up titles were garbage. Deus Ex 2 was a joke.  I could be argued into saying that Human Revolution was a solid game but maybe I came with too high expectations - I didn't enjoy it much. The Fall was a joke. Mankind Divided has fallen victim to DLC-ripoff strategies and I never actually gave it a chance. I really don't want to sound like a grumpy man from yesterday with a preoccupied opinion that can never be changed, but honestly, I have been disappointed badly by Deus Ex follow-ups. You can't blame the original on that but I thought I should mention it.
So yes. The original Deus Ex is upon the best the games I've ever played (the other two being "Gothic 2" and "Halflife 2") and I highly recommend this title. It's not something you should buy for casual quick entertainment but you should have a few hours each session to get into it. It is deep, it is dark, it is complex, there's hardly anything that compares to it on the market and it's cheap because it's very old. If you ask me, you should give it a shot.

Deus Ex is rightfully considered by many people to be one of, if not the best game of all time. Considering the fact that it is 17 years old, it already featured uniquely complex gameplay, deep RPG mechanics, back then good stealth systems, multiple ways to tackle each obstacle or objective and a completely branching storyline depending on the players actions, even very minor actions leading to unique dialogue from NPCs and differing mission debriefings. (As in walking into the women's restroom at headquarters and getting slapped with a formal complaint)
The game featured impeccable level and game design, one of the best dystopic cyberpunk atmospheres I have so far ever seen in a game and it also runs flawlessly, bug free, with better graphics and 4k support on new systems / Win10 by utilizing the GMDX (Give Me Deus Ex) mod with version 9.x
Gameplay wise Deux Ex hasn't aged a single day, the only two aspects where it shows its age are level and area scale as well as interactible object scarcity. After 17 years of varying (read as in ridiculous) amounts of collectibles added to games it suddenly became really easy to find close to all secrets within Deus Ex.
Truth be told, I just wanted to have a short look back into the game and find out whether it still was as great as I remembered. Needless to say, even so many years later, I got fully hooked and am currently on my third consecutive playthrough because the game is still that great. Not many games have ever managed to do that, except maybe Planescape: Torment, Baldur's Gate and Freespace 2. Well and Deus Ex is also one of those titles and probably always will be.
More than recommended, this is a true masterpiece which stands firm against the flow of time.

This is one of those games that make me regret the fact that Valve only allows a positive or a negative opinion, and not a neutral one.
This game is admittedly brilliant. An extremely addictive combination of Minesweeper and Picross, with pretty visuals and a nice ambient soundtrack that reacts to your moves. I loved every minute of playing this game. Why the negative review then? Because it's really effing short. There are 36 puzzles, but they are easy enough that you can finish the game (and I don't mean "finish" as in "reach the last puzzle". I mean "finish" as in "beat all puzzles perfectly and get 100% of the achievements") fast enough to refund it, and the replay value is nonexistent. It feels like a demo/tutorial for the later Hexcells games.
Overall, I'd recommend to only buy it if the Hexcells Complete Bundle is on sale. It'll teach you how to play the later games with a much gentler learning curve. On it's own, and at the full price, this game is simply not worth it.

Hexcells is a game about logic puzzels much in the vein of Minesweeper. Thankfully it gradually introduces more interesting game mechanics. But sadly it never goes beyond the tutorial stage and it isn't as upfront about teaching you the specifics of each mechanic as I'd like it to be. As a seasoned player of Minesweeper and logic puzzels in general it took me less than 2 hours to complete this game without ever making a single mistake. There is little replayability.
The design is clean and appealing (if a little bright), the sounds are neat and create an interesting atmosphere. I've never encountered a bug, error or crash.
If you pick this game up as part of the trilogy compilation it is a decent introducton to the series and you won't regret your purchase as the later parts offer much more gameplay and are well worth their money. I cannot recommend picking up the first part as a stand-alone and definitely not at full price.

Enjoyed this game a lot! Gives a minesweeper kind of feel, which adds in more puzzle enhancements as you progress through the levels. Starts off very basic so that you get a feel for the game, and then you look up and all you want to do is perfect all the levels. So the games goes, there are a few blocks with numbers on the board and you have to puzzle out whether the block is another number or a blue block. The block has 6 sides (obviously) and the number says how many blue block are touching it. As the game progresses, it adds {} around a number to say the blue blocks are sequential, or -- around a number to say they are split. It then goes father to say that there are so may in this line by putting the number on the outside of that row or column. The easy feature which helps a lot for bigger puzzles is that you can click on the outside number and it draws a line through that row or column to see which ones.
All in all lots of fun and challenging at the same time. Can wait to play the rest of the games to see what new puzzling features arise!

Honestly... games like this really make me yearn for a neutral recommendation option.
Is this a bad game? No, not really. It's not a cheap underhanded grab for trading card money or twee achievement spam. It's got heart and effort put into it. You can tell the developer cared for the world and the story they were crafting.
Is it a fun game? Once again, no... not really. As someone who enjoys walking simulators I know my standards are considered to be pretty low, but this game isn't really fun to actively interact with. It's mostly fetch quests -- pick flowers, chop wood, harvest mushrooms -- interspersed between exposition and lots and lots of mouse-controlled, somewhat fiddly, slow-paced walking, and while there are some minigames to break up the pattern... I only particularly enjoyed one of them.
But really, I think the main quibble with this game -- and I want to stress that it isn't a problem, just my own personal taste at work -- is that I went in expecting something cute and fun, and I was instead met with existential angst.
This is a game about depression and bad breakups. This is a game about how poor choices lead you to loneliness and regret. This is a really quite sad game wrapped in a ridiculously cute candy-coated shell and my god is it bleak. This isn't to say that a cute game can't have deep themes! Simply that I wish they had been better conveyed at the time, because I picked this up for something relaxing and I've been left feeling rather like a deflated balloon -- and the lackluster and rather abrupt ending is not helping matters. You will not leave this game with any sense of catharsis whatsoever.
For anyone that's been drawn in by the really quite wonderful graphics, they're a little intensive on the highest settings -- but honestly the gameplay is so simple that you won't even notice framerate skips in my opinion. Additionally, the game did hang once a little after I first opened it -- but it righted itself, so I don't think it's noteworthy enough to put off a potential buyer.
I would say this is appropriate for kids as it is completely G-rated (minus some potentially scary ghosts), but as far as the subject matter goes? At best they will get bored; at worst, they'll be sad, and the ending will probably leave them wondering if the game isn't complete. Don't be fooled by the cutesy and colorful graphics: this game is not targeted towards younger players. Older players might feel some relatable emotions from it, however -- longing, loss, regret, and a sense of not belonging with the people you love. It's really quite poignant, but the ending mars the overall emotional delivery in my opinion.
But is this a bad game for those reasons? I want to say no, honestly. The creator clearly put a lot of care and heart into it despite its shortcomings. It looks great, and it's not badly designed. The gameplay is simple enough that anyone can play it, and honestly, the fact that it isn't a cash grab stuffed with achievements or microtransactions -- it's a breath of fresh air in spite of its faults. I think it's simply not for me, at the end of the day.
That said, I would recommend purchasing this title on sale if you're interested in it, because it definitely does not have enough content to justify this kind of pricetag.
In all... I cautiously recommend this game for really only a few people -- those who want something casual and low-effort, something that looks good but lacks substance, and who doesn't mind bleak or depressing stories with subjectively unsatisfying endings. Because it really isn't a bad game... for the right person.
Thank you for reading.

“Kingdoms Rise” is a great melee game to pickup and go with. No leveling or unlocking, everything is immediately available, and lots of fun. I even picked up a 2nd copy for the occasional friend to play.
With in-depth & intuitive mechanics for the genre, blocking isn't frustrating or over powered like in "War of the Vikings". Instead the combat system makes a lot of sense, and not just because I read the manual – though it did help explain combos, counter-attacks & how to parry.
Character customization is also very impressive – whether you want to be a heavily plated knight, a nimble ninja, or something in between, you pick every piece of armor you wear (or choose not to wear). Combined with your choice of weapons & spells, players of all archetypes step onto the battlefield with a variety of builds – often resembling characters from different videogames (such as Link & Ninja Gaiden).
While "War of the Vikings" offers higher production quality, and a realistic experience in the genre - "Kingdoms Rise" offers more fun with its deep & balanced combat mechanics, character customization, and vivid colourful graphics.
I’m really looking forward to what this title offers in full release! Keep up the great work Flyleap Studios!

Deus Ex is a
. Rating: 1000/10
The setting is the not-so distant Dystopian future of 2052. Governments & corporations weild the power, while the masses fall into poverty, resort to violence or die.
Secret societies, factions & groups are preparing for the upcoming fight.
Government oppression, conspiracies, corporate warfare & terrorism (subjectively) are common-place, caring not who loses in the process.
You play as the UNATCO agent "JC Denton". Your job is to fight terrorism to help protect the world, at least, that's what you're made to believe. You soon get dragged into a global conspiracy between factions fighting to be on top, each believing they're the best faction to lead the world.
The graphics are old. The game was released in 2000 using the
. Despite this, the game still looks amazingly good in my opinion. Not everything is about graphics, the game definetly makes up for it. The way the game is designed, characters & each levels own design is truely amazing work by Ion Storm. The immersion of the world that you're in is on a whole new level, from New York to China or Paris, travelling this awesomely created world is entertaining & quite enough to do. There's many books to read and people to talk to.
The game is a Cyberpunk version of Dishonored.
(
One of the main developers of Deus Ex 1 & the Lead Developer of Deus Ex 2 eventually left Ion Storm & founded Arkane Studios, where he lead the development of Dishonored, a Steampunk version on Deus Ex, another game I highly reccomend).
The gameplay is old but still highly playable, it truely stood the test of time. It's super easy to understand and get the hang of. It's age means it's fairly simplified, yet the work they put into it made it so diverse. There's many ways to play Deus Ex. Kill everyone that stands in your way, render your enemies unconcious or simpyl sneak past them.
You pick some skills to start off with, with the ability to continuously upgrade them later throughout the game.
You're rewarded for your gameplay. Finding hidden areas of the map, performing certain tasks and missions earns you points you can use to advance your skills.
Alongside skills you also get Augmentations. Modifications to the human body to advance it beyond it's current, limited capabilities. Augmentations range from being able to lift heavy objects (this allows you to move blockages & place items to climb on to reach new places) to breathing underwater.
Each style of playing is up to the player, choosing your skills, augmentations & choices helps shape your game into whatever way you wish.
It's really a true RPG. Make the wrong choices, people die (or maybe you want that, who knows, that's why it's an amazing RPG). Throughout the story & people in the world, there's many dialogue choices and the choice of how you approach (or ignore) each task.
This game was awarded "Best PC Game" & is considered even to this day the best PC game of all time (of course this is subjective, but it's undeniably loved).
Deus Ex 2 (Invisible War) was not as successful, you will liekly hear a lot of hate about it. I must admit it's nowhere near as phenominal as Deus Ex 1, though it's still a really awesome game in it's own right. It was dumbed down as the game was to be developed for console too. I'd highly reccomend playing it, just know it's smaller & overall not as good, with worse controls. treat it as a spin-off and just focus on the story and factions, you should enjoy it.
The chronological order of the series is;
Desu Ex: The Fall
Deus Ex: Human Revolution
Deus Ex: Mankind Divided
Deus Ex (This one)
Deus Ex: Invisible War
If you read this far, thank you. I hope you try the game(s) out and enjoy :)

This is the only review I've ever written for a game on Steam. After playing Medieval 2, Rome, Empire, and Rome 2, I can safely say that Medieval is still my favorite in the series. Yes, the later iterations ARE prettier. This game was released in 2006 after all. However, in my opinion, you can't beat the game engine they used. The Warscape engine that is utilized by the newer games (empire onwards) has taken a loooooong time to reach the same level of melee combat satisfaction that I got from M2. Sure, there are no fancy one v one animations. BUT, those animations also wrecked havoc with how many battles played out. I don't think I ever saw two soldiers gang up on one soldier in any game other than M2 and Rome 1. Battles are played out more by training stats, upgrades, and tactics vs. a boat ton of special abilities and badas* animations. I know there are plenty of people who won't agree, but it's just my experience.
The biggest reason why I always come back to this game is the modding community. I had the game running on a virtual version of windows on my mac (years before the mac version was released) JUST so I could play Third Age Total War. Not to mention all the unit mods, engine and animation tweaks, etc. This is still probably the most mod friendy total war game out there. I spent dozens of hours over the last 8-9 years compiling units and tweaks to get my game just right, enduring hundreds of coding errors and game re-installs. Little by little (and somehow without taking over my life) Medieval 2 became a near-perfect game. And this is a guy with little to no mod creation or coding experience whatsoever.
All in all, it's a wonderful game that won't be surpassed until they potentialy do a new Total War in the Medieval setting. It's perfectly fine without mods, but if you're like me and discovered just how awesome the modding community is, it's the best Total War game to mod in my opinion.

Stellaris could be a great strategy game. I am a huge fan of sci-fi mystery movies about space exploration and revelations it hides, so this game looked like a great choice. This is where fun ends.
Why I do not recommend this game:
1. It was developed on an old 32-bit engine, so no matter how powerful your CPU is, somewhere in the mid-game you'll inevitably start experiencing terrible performance issues, and the further in the game you'll be the worse the issues will become. Somewhere in the late game the performance was so terrible, I could not continue the game at all. It became completely unresponsive. This is all because of the limitations of the old game engine, so I repeat, it does not matter how powerful your CPU is - be prepared to get frustrated after spending tens of hours on building, only to realize that you cannot finish the game properly.
2. This game looks uninspired. All the aliens look like they evolved on Earth. We have either insects, or plants, or freaking parrots in space suits trying to conquer the galaxy, and become superior. How come they all look like they are from Earth? Why can't there be let's say some "greys", or intelligent flying electric spheres. Instead, all the aliens look like they are a product of Darwin's dreams after a hard night of boozing. Ridiculous. Uninspired. Disappointing.
3. Politics. That's all this game is. You cannot roll through the entire galaxy with your OP forces (as anyone would do in the real world). Instead, you are allowed to conquer only 2-4 planets at a time, and then forced to wait 10 years before you can fight again. Why? This game is like your annoying mom that pulls the monitor plug every time you're winning. So annoying, and unneccessary. Just let me♥♥♥♥♥♥♥destroy everyone, and take over the galaxy! If there are 300 planets, and you can conquer only 2 every 10 years, imagine how long it will take to play just one single player mission. I can tell you how long because I tried. It took me around hundred hours to finish just one mission, and at the end of that I feel no satisfaction. I feel like I am finally done with an annoying chore, and thinking about this just makes me angry. MAKES ME ANGRY!
4. There are no differences in powers between aliens. Everything, and everyone is absolutely the same. How about that for the fun? The only difference is a picture of an alien. Everything else is the same. How can someone create a strategy game where there is absolutely no difference between powers? That's just another sign of a rushed, uninspired game that deserves to be in a hall of shame.
5. 95% of this game is reading text, interacting with politicans, and making political decisions towards other aliens. It's like some election game or something. I guess they wanted to make a game about politics, and elections, and promises they make, but they realized that no one would buy that crap, and at the last moment they just converted the whole thing into the space game. They just swapped the presidents with aliens, and♥♥♥♥♥♥that crap out onto the market.
If you are looking for some action you won't find it here. The only action here is jerking the more powerful presidents off until you become more powerful, and then it's a choppy bugged fight that looks just ugly, and lasts for minutes. After that, back to the politics. What a trash.
6. This game is boring. It's so boring it will make you rethink your life choices over, and over, until you feel absolutely ashamed of your life.
7. It's full of bugs, and glitches. It just looks like people who made the game are not professionals, but rather some guys who got together, and made an experimental game over night. Total trainwreck.
Even if politics, and management, and accounting is something that gives you a boner, I still not recommend this game because at the mid- end-game stages it becomes completely unplayable.
What a garbage.

+ Wonderful iteration of a classic top-down dungeon crawler
+ Fantastic and engaging soundtrack; really keeps you in the game and sets the mood
+ Boasts an art-style that strikes one as being both creepy and cute
+ Hilariously strange stage-to-stage intermissions
+ Wholly satisfying variety of enemies and boss creatures
+ Tons and tons of stat-altering item pickups
+ Controls are simple, intuitive and responsive
+ Contains an additional cast of unlockable characters, each with a differing playstyle
+ No matter where you are or what items you pick up, the gameplay is entirely skill-based; this, I think, is one of the game's biggest selling points
+ Gameplay is challenging in many ways, yet the lack of pandering to the player increases the sense of reward and accomplishment on completion
+ Between the unlockables and the randomly generated playthroughs, this game has quite a bit of replay value
+ Dungeon-map is easy to use and makes navigation easy; works well to help one backtrack to items that one might have passed over in other areas
+ Multiple endings

Automation is built around three elements; the engine designer, the car designer, and the tycoon. At the time of writing this review the mechanics of the engine and car designer features are more or less fully fleshed out, but tweaks and additional content are being added. The tycoon feature is partially present, but still being built.
Before its release on Steam and the implementation of the car designer, I spent at least a hundred hours with the game tinkering with the engine designer. For players with an interest in internal combustion engines, the engine designer on its own is going to take up a lot of your time. Fantasizing about a tiny 1.5 liter turbo I4 with 450 HP? Build it. A smooth, efficient 3.0 liter I6 for a mid-size sedan? Build it. They're all possible, and the level of detail is sufficient to allow for a lot of tinkering, but not so overwhelming that a degree in mechanical engineering is required to not feel overwhelmed.
The car designer is impressive, but less so. There are currently several dozen body types and even more variations (a small hatchback can turn into a small pickup truck by lopping off the rear roof, for example). It is possible to modify existing bodies in numerous ways, such as stretching the hood, modifying the slope of the windshield, extending the fenders, and so on. However, it's not possible to design a body from scratch in the game, which is forgivable. The issue is with fixture placement (headlights, taillights, etc). Currently, this can be buggy and tedious. Getting a specific headlight to fit in a specific place can be unnecessarily difficult because some of the bodies have very conservative placement limits to prevent clipping and warping.
For those with an interest in cars, the game is an easy purchase. It's easy to understand yet hard to master. The developer has shown themselves to be reliable at updating the game frequently, and actually improving it with each update rather than adding features for the sake of it. There's nothing else like it.

First, the pros.
I'm not the biggest fan of 4X, nor am I the best at them. I only heard of Stellaris a day or two before it came out and was a tad apprehensive of buying it, but then I watched the devs' stream and realized this was exactly what I had been looking for to fill my space RTS need. As of this review I have 360 hours on this game. The first 40 or so of that was a single playthrough without sleeping.(As a bonus, that one playthrough and every one since has been very unique.) That alone makes this a game worth its price, not to mention how good the DLC actually are. Paradox really did something great with this, hell they kicked off the stream of tons of space 4X/RTS games being brought to Steam.
Now that I've sucked the game's dingle, it's time to get in to the cons.
This is a Paradox game, so right now it is a bit lacking in terms of QOL changes and balancing. It also feels a little empty despite there being so much to do. Thankfully the updates listen to the community and fix whatever seemed most important to fix. The biggest issue for me is that in the late game there are metric butt tons of ships being handled by the AI which can lead to huge FPS drops for most players.
TL;DR
+Very much worth its price
+Almost every playthrough is unique
+Paradox game (Little biased here)
+Long lifetime in terms of replayability
+Gorgeous graphics for a space 4X/RTS
+Good DLC, though pricey at times
+Updates are very community focused
-Late game can get very laggy
-Feels empty at times despite the huge amount of stuff to do
-Right now it's a new Paradox game, so it still needs a few updates to be the best
Overall I give it 8.5/10, but with future updates it may go as high as 9.5/10.
UPDATE:
With the release of the DLCs I have to say Stellaris has steadily become one of the best, if not the best, space RTS games I have ever seen. I whole heartedly reccommend Stellaris to anybody who has any interest in the genre, since the only direction to go is up at this point. Now I have to give the game a solid 9/10 and it's only going higher and higher in my eyes. The devs are also extremely competent and listen to the community.

Hexcells is a fairly simple game, much of it employing a combination of mechanics from minesweeper and nonograms (Picross) on a non standard 2D grid. It is a logic game were rules of the levels are defined by numbered brackets (minesweeper style) that give information on whether nearby brackets are false or true. This is sometimes mixed in with column markers that do the same, but for a column (picross style). To deepen the gameplay a bit more, you are sometimes also presented with special rules beside the numbers which frankly, in my humble opinion, make minesweeper look like a joke. It feels like the kind of game you'd see in the crossword puzzle section in a digital newspaper of the future.
It's all good fun, really. Perfectly balanced, not hard nor easy. If any of these aforementioned games interest you, give this a try. For the low price point the developers are asking, you owe it to yourself to play this. Took me a good two and a half hours to get to 100%.

Wildstar is, in my opinion, a great MMO. One of my favorites, and I'm glad that it's made it to Steam.
Wildstar has a number of features that I think make it worth checking out. Player housing is amazing. Every player is given a floating plot of land that they can customize to create almost whatever they want. The housing system is pretty intuative, with two systems for placing items. The first, a simple drag and drop system, allows you to quickly create something that looks good with the items and building blocks that the game provides. The second, which allows for precise movement and rotation along the three axes, scaling, linking, etc., has more of a learning curve, but allows for the creation of almost anything. The interior of a giant spaceship? A walker based on the AT-AT from Star Wars? A cove with a pirate ship in it? A cathedral made from warped and corrupted flesh? The possibilites are nearly endless, and the housing community is very active and helpful.
Combat for me was one of the big draws to the game as well. The telegraph system is pretty intuative (although the finer points of it may require some reading up on, as well as some trial and error), and the pacing of combat makes it feel more like an action RPG than most other MMOS. The game encourages you not to stand still, to pay attention to what's going on around you, and to communicate and work with your teammates, or the fellow players you run into. Each class has a unique feel to it, and each has a wide range of abilities and builds that allow you to customize how you play to match your style.
The game's PvE offers a lot to do. Expeditions and Adventures are unique story-based instances that allow you, and a group of friends, to play through a short story (most take between fifteen minutes to an hour). Expeditions are generally shorter and straight forward, while Adventures have branching paths and options, which makes for excellent replayability. The game's Dungeons are fun a lot of fun, provide a balanced challenge, and interesting bosses and mechanics. Each dungeon has a unique aesthetic and challenges.
The game's Raids (there are currently three full-length raids and a boss-in-a-box) are a lot of fun. While the 20-man format does mean that starting up a raid group can be a long process, there are numerous multi-guild groups and pick up raids for players to join and experience the raids. Raid bosses are unique, interesting, and provide raiders with some real challenges to test their mettle.
The game's community is active, and generally very helpful and welcoming.
Now, if you've been following MMOs, or Wildstar, you've no doubt heard a number of negative stories and rumors surrounding the game's development, launch, updates, etc. Yes, the game went F2P about a year after launch. Yes, the Chinese release of the game was cancelled. Yes, there have been other issues, such as bugs, alterations to the timetable for content drops, to name a few. The game has not been without issue, but a number of news outlets and sites have, in my opinion, largely blown a number of issues out of proportion. No, Wildstar is not a perfect game. It does have issues, but I still love it.
If any of this sounds interesting, or if you'd just like to try out a new MMO, give Wildstar a shot. The F2P system that's in place is fair, and means that you can try it with no risk and without really losing anything.

Where do I start. Note, that this review is based on the current state of the game - 23. december, 2015.
This is a long, philosophy filled review, for a short and quick one, scroll down.
The idea for Automation seems just fine, as there's nothing similar to this game to current date. The game has been in development for quite a long time, and the pace for it goes snail-like. Don't mind my playtime, I didn't want to get over two hour mark, as I am still thinking, whether I really want to keep the game.
I  have followed this for quite some time, and by follower, I mean, passive. I had played demo version to get the overall feel, and of course, at some point a pirated version, which allowed full access, appeared. Let's not dive in to this, cause it's more about the experience this offers.
Development wise, there are huge plans for the future, but not actuall coverage or timelines beneath it, and let me explain why. Idea and gameplay, which Automation attempts to tackle, is for a very specific market of buyers - petrolheads and technical nerds. Don't get offended by this, as I am both of theese. Now, continuing on explaining, as I previously mentioned, the development is slow. Why? Because initially, it was developed by four people, and I assume, that this was/is their hobby right after their daily jobs. Quite recently there was an expansion in crew, and I hoped to see the new people accepted being programmers/scripters, not car modelers, as at some point and time, there's a plan to transfer the game to Unreal Engine.
A game which delves this deep in an engineering process involved to produce working engines for cars requires serious R&D, as it is seen in overall gameplay it offers. That what's the problem?
Engines consist of thousands of moving parts, and creating simulated versions where everything affects everthing is quite more difficult than producing precisely estimated engine from raw materials in real life. To be able to depict an engine and it's characteristics to at least a fraction of reality requres serious study, which becomes a problem, when so little people are involved in project like this, and, doing the simple math results in long development times.
I tried to recreate one of my IRL car engine, which is a 1.6 Liter 4 banger from B5, and surprisingly, with a little tinkering, I came close to the actuall power figures and peak-power delivery. And yes, I used roughly the same materials, with whatever parameters they are coded, but when trying something like this, it becomes noticable, that certain aspects are missing, which probbably is a good thing, cause who the hell would want to enter precise camshaft profiles and what not.
To add something, most modern cars are using ECU's. If something like that could be programmed in the game, and allowed people to tinker with ECU values, at least at basic level, would surely bring a huge difference, as pure, predefined metal parts would no longer be the only thing that makes power.
TL;DR
Good:
The game delivers what it promises and is supposed to;
Allows you to build an engine with simple yet hard to master tools;
Tutorials explaining what everything does, so you have no need to be an engineer;
Great educational material for people interested how stuff works;
Basic car designer, with click-and-drag functionality;
Very interesting at start, as ideas for engines and cars just plow your mind.
Bad:
Slow development;
Basic visual representation with 3D models, which is subjected to change after transfering to UE, i.e., become more beautiful and, hopefully, sophisticated;
Small team tackling huge project and idea;
Low replay value after you have tried massive, huge displacement POOWEEER roaring, small displacement usable moon-reving, and lastly, econobox engines.
-This would not coun't as a con, but it's not great either - the engine sounds. At the end of the day, all same confguration engines sound foggy. You can't make it sound like mean American Muscle, or crisp German high-reving V8. I hope this subjects to change.
Summary:
This product is rivaling it's genere between game and educational material. If this would take an educational route, and would be pushed further with techical details and every little asspect of engines, probbably, it would make it to school programs, I am sure.
I still recomend this game, although, it's possible to try a demo version, to get the overall feel what everything is about, and basically, that's it, at least for now, until core functionality of tycoon is implented.
Did they bite bigger than they could chew? In my opinion, probbably yes.

Don’t let the cute premise take you away, there is quite a bit going on in Rabbit Story. What starts as a hunt for carrots quickly becomes something more. You play Rabbit who lives with Kitty, his girlfriend. Something goes awry, Kitty is suddenly gone, and now you find yourself hanging out with Doggy. Wait, what?
To be honest, I was side-eyeing Rabbit like, you’re already moving on?? You don’t even know what happened to Kitty! But like all things, the story will become clear in the end.
The gameplay has you wandering the lovely landscapes of the forest, cemeteries, snowy mountains, and even The Persistence of Memory for a brief moment. There aren’t a lot of characters either, just animals that help you progress the story. Rabbit will also face enemies in combat, if you call it that, that plays like a little mini-game as well.
There are a lot little hidden areas to explore to find carrots. These are collectible. Collect them all and you will unlock a secret level. There are also 6 achievements and no trading cards.
There are a couple mini games and a throwback retro game that I quite liked. Along with the mini-games are some trivia, so get your thinking caps on. Not to mention the atmosphere became dark and confusing later on.
The game is also quite short with 11 chapters (12 if you count the hidden level) for the asking price. Without taking account of the puzzle towards the end, I finished the game in around an hour. That’s also with finding about 90% of the carrots as well.
The controls are simple as you need only your mouse to play. You can click anywhere and Rabbit will quickly move to the location or you can click, hold, and drag around the screen and he will move just the same.
This game is gorgeous. The low-poly, shaders, and particle effects are fantastic and add to the simplicity of it all. It also gives way to a feeling of dread a little later as the atmosphere plays heavily towards the climax. The music certainly takes you away and adds to the overall theme of the story. The point at which the story and environment turn is also when the music takes a darker tone as well. While not outright scary, the game does bring a sense of unease.
The game is cute and slightly surprising towards the end. Once the story comes full circle, you begin to realize that Rabbit is kind of a jerk and you figure out what really happened to Kitty.
The game makes you think about your relationships, your choices, the consequences, and the sudden dive into the 5 stages of grief as you cope. Under the guise of a cute and cuddly design lies the tale of a Rabbit who makes some pretty bad choices. You get a glimpse into the character's mind as you progress with the help of flashbacks and thought bubbles and you either feel for Rabbit or scold him for being so dumb.
It was quite enjoyable even for something so short. The story closes on the final chapter and after realizing everything, you kind of just go WTF, RABBIT!? But then you might look at it another way entirely, you might even sympathize with him.
It’s a strange twist to a fluffy looking, but suddenly cloudy tale. If you enjoy a casual chill experience with a wicked atmosphere, some collecting, and a slight mystery, Rabbit Story is definitely something to make you raise both eyebrows if the asking price doesn't turn you away first.
