Just played this for the first time about a week ago. A review detached from nostalgia:
I think it's pretty good in it's vanilla form, even after 17 years. Gunplay is a bit clunky but generally okay (headshots with the silenced sniper is the high-point). RPG mechanics are light, but helpful. I didn't bother with non-lethal routes to my objective, just being sneaky and killing groups as quiet and fast as I could sufficed. The game is full of little nooks and crannies to pick up, like wine and ciggs, but I personally found no use for them, as they took up valuable inventory space. Of which is managed pretty fairly.
What really shines in this game is the polish they put into the text you find. The newspapers, the emails, the books. All excellently written and don't over or under stay their welcome. Full of not only in-game lore, but even address conspiracies and real world problems that apply to this day (and possibly the future). This, with the excellent, non-linear level design are the highest highs in this game.
The lowest point in this game was near the end, and the end itself. Before what I guess I'll call "the last level", I was feeling a bit burnt on running around doing favors, even if I was enjoying the bits of text lying around. Maybe like the game was just one level too long. The last level itself? Amazing, easily my favorite part of this game, tying so much together. However, the end cutscene blueballed me hard. Way too short.
I wanted more, and I know that's how people must have felt 17 years ago. We never got more, and probably never will. At the time, this was probably a 10/10. Today, all things considered, I'd give it a 8/10.

Nier is a well made game in every respect. Not perfect but mechanically excellent, fun to play and thoroughly thought evoking.

I played it on a mid-range PC running Windows 10 and had a few minor problems but nothing major. I had one crash in over a 100 hours of play time and the framerate was a bit choppy in particularly hectic scenes. There is a mod available that cleans up its performance though, released by the same guy who fixed Dark Souls on PCV, along with many other titles. Try that if you do get any problems.
Overall, Nier Automata is a game that anyone with an interest in games as a medium should play. It goes beyond being an action game and uses its medium in a way that few games ever attempt. It's true ending, Ending E, is perhaps one of the most unique and beautiful moments in gaming history. Do not let the anime asthetics and lolita maid protagonist sway your initial impression. This game is very deep and deserves to be experienced.

Hexcells and its sequels are absolutely essential to anyone that loves logic puzzle games like Picross and Sudoku. Contrary to the belief of the occasional negative (bad) reviewer, there is ALWAYS a logical way to proceed, without any guesswork. It often requires that you change the way you think about solving the puzzles, as following the same rules will only take you so far. Particularly, when it gets to the point that you have to start systematically eliminating cells as possible answers one at a time, or weighing your options based on the number of blue cells remaining, I can see why certain players would simply give up and call it impossible. It's not; I promise. Keep at it, or try to find a spoiler free hint to give you an idea of how to think through it rather than just giving you the answers.

You will feel dumber for playing a game that requires just clicking on about 10 buttons, but not actually care. You will wonder whether you should leave the game running overnight or whether to close it. Game strategy keywords will suddenly appear in your browser search history. You will ignore hundreds of other Steam games you have bought in sales because this one will be quick to load. You will realise you can actually run Clicker Heroes as well at the same time to take advantage of the downtime between clicks. Game sales will come and go and you will amass even more games you don't install, since you just want to get all the achievements and finally uninstall it.
Of course your mileage may vary. So this game may be worth a look.

Deus Ex is without a doubt one of the best games ever made. It may have its flaws, but it more than makes up for it with it's terrific game design, unique and interesting story and great soundtrack.
First off, the story. Without giving away too much, it piqued my interest from the moment I started watching the intro. The game offers a compelling plot with interesting, morally gray characters but it goes beyond that. Deus Ex offers very good social and political commentary, so much so that it has only gotten more relevant and accurate as time goes on and as terrorism, mass surveillance, government corruption and corporatism, all of which are things which were just a dystopian nightmare 20 years ago, have now become part and parcel of living in the 21st century.
In terms of FPS gameplay and graphics, Deus Ex does show its age. And yes, the voice acting can be outright bad. Even so, it more than makes up for it with its level design. You have the option to navigate around the levels and accomplish your objectives in so many different ways, it blows pretty much every current game out of the water. Whether you want to be stealthy, use your silenced pistol and melee weapons and crawl through ducts or go guns-blazing with your assault rifle and flamethrower, you have many options to play the game. Oh and have I mentioned how amazing the soundtrack is? Because it is.
Overall, Deus Ex is just one of those games you just have to play. It may not be a great FPS by today's standards, but it is a timeless RPG. It is just absolutely phenomenal.

It's hard to see any faults in this game, but that's because my vision is augmented.
This game is the product of a time where Cyberpunk was at its peak, a cultural narrative blossoming that envisioned the future not as the shiny utopia we all expected, but a world ravaged by poverty, disease and war as technology widened the gap between the rich and the poor. While modern literature has lost what made Cyberpunk such an enthralling genre, there are still many great long standing examples of the niche littered around. Deus Ex is one of them; it's a pioneer in the immersive sim genre and arguably one of the greatest games of all time.
Looking through the obviously dated graphics and gameplay is a world that is immersive, realistic and engaging. The characters all feel like they could easily exist, the conversations you have feel real. Your character evolves depending on how you play, each level has many different ways to approach it depending on your playstyle. Sound familiar? That's because most modern games follow this formula, the most notable being Bethesda's titles like Fallout. Deus Ex is the grandfather of this type of gameplay, and I believe everyone should go back and experience the true roots of gaming.
As an enthusiast of Cyberpunk as a "genre" I think this is easily the best video game representing it period. I can draw so many comparisons between this game and William Gibson's work, which are basically equivalent to the bible for Cyberpunk fiction at this point. A lot of people forget what made Cyberpunk Cyberpunk, and instead default to the lazy neon signs and androids everywhere, while the real meat of the genre lies in the apocalypic and ruined worlds that are home to these technological marvels. Deus Ex hits the nail on the head, with its entire story revolving around the global elite manufacturing a virus to cull the population, and profiting from the cure.
For the price, there is honestly no better gaming experience available to you, if you like Fallout for its well developed fantastical setting, "however you like it" gameplay and interesting colourful characters then give this a shot.

While any features (story, combat, philosophy, etc.) of the game lauded by many players and critics are present, their presence is largely insubstantial. The game seems very underdeveloped which leaves it a mediocre experience. The art design is good, but it's not particularly creative. The graphics are fine, but they're low-resolution and glitchy. The story is interesting but predictable. The music is good. And the two most prominent characteristics of Nier are also lacking. The combat is fun, but it's samey and limited. And the philosophy is interesting, but it's not explored.
As a Platinum game, one would expect frenetic and flamboyant fighting. Unfortunately, there's only a lesser facsimile. The combat is much less frenzied than some of their other titles, like Metal Gear Rising, Transformers: Devastation, and the recently-ported-to-PC Bayonetta. It has the trappings of Platinum's fighting style, but the combat is hollow.
The other half of Nier's accolades is it's philosophy, and without a doubt it has philosophy. But it only has Philosophy 101. Nier introduces interesting philosophical considerations but does nothing with them. It does attempt, and often, but each demonstration is so limited that there's no time for proper scrutiny, so nothing of merit really develops.
Ultimately it's a competent game, but it falls short of being significant. It's not a bad game, but it will need a lower price, and players will need lower expectations.

Ok, so let me be perfectly blunt here. I have played little more than an hour of this game so far, but I can already sum up everything I have to say about Delver in one word: Potential.
Delver is a fresh, unique take on the rogue-like games that have been pouring in recently from many indie developers from all over the world. It takes on many thematic rogue-like elements: It's challenging, randomly generated, and as fun as a bag full of rabid chipmunks dumped into an elementary school.
I'm not saying this game is without its issues, but it's still in its early access phase, and must be taken with a grain of salt. Considering this fact, Delver is chocked full of endless potential. Its first-person perspective and highly pixelated environment and graphics allow this game far more room to breathe then one would expect at first glance. Even in its early phases, the amount of different consumable items and pieces of unique equipment are quite impressive, and the level-up system that resets after every miserable failure allows a very immersive RPG-like quality to the game. You're able to play differently every single run. Want to focus on high armor and melee combat? Go right ahead! Feel like going for a more mobile, long-range bow combatant? Be my guest! Or maybe you just want to pump all of your points into magic and blow the CRAP out of every enemy in sight with one of the many different elemental weapons in the game. Why wouldn't you?!
It is this amount of flexibility within a game that is comprised of so little options as of right now that makes me positive that there's no where to go but up from here for Delver. So many environments yet to be created; so many monsters yet rendered in that simplistic-yet-beautiful art style; many more items, potions, and pieces of armor yet to be looted off of bandit corpses or found in the dank corner of a cave! Heck, there is even a large part of the Delver community that claims this game has everything it needs to move on to an online co-op mode! Who knows?
All I can say is, that even after only an hour of gameplay, I can already close my eyes and imagine what can be done with a game this inventive, this creative, this simple, and this ambitious! If you haven't taken a peek at Delver yet, I suggest very highly, for the love of yourself AND your rabies-free elementary schoolers that you do. This game is nothing but raw potential and ingenuity, and I KNOW you don't want to miss out on it! That being said:

Finally a grand strategy game that won't require you to watch any "Let's play" YouTube videos in order to understand the basic game features.  It's a really deep game but without the overwhelming complexity that plagued Paradox's previous games like Victoria II and Hearts of Iron III. You can't find a single slider in this game which is a huge relief atleast to me. Stellaris got one of the best tutorials I have seen: there is no tutorial mission  or a 300 page manual. Instead you simple enable in game tutorial at the start of the game and It gives all the information you need. Still leaving you to figure out how to master the game.
Space combat is rather simple: when fleets engage you lose control and AI take command over your ships. You can relax and watch the entertaining fighting without worrying about the most efficient playing style. Land combat on planets work out the same way, except there is no eye candy available. You can just see army icons taking damage until other party is completely wiped out. While all this might not heard to be any entertaining, believe me it is. When all your careful planning, diplomacy and armament finally pays off, it's a feel like no other.
There are incredible amount of game mechanics in Stellaris, but they are far easier to learn than they are in other Paradox games. Mechanics also works perfectly, are well described and introduced with a good pace during the game. I for example came across with genetic modifications when I had played Stellaris for 65 hours total. Develop team has put great effort towards customization. You can choose and name your race, leaders, ship designs, fleets, planets, etc. This gives great opportunity for roleplaying and play as you please.
You only directly control 5 - 10 planets and rest is government by sector AI. This is a great feature that reduces late game  micro management that plagues pretty much every single strategy game in some level. Only problem I find with secors is that  you still control every single spaceport (compound where you product spaceships) and there is no one-click button to  sector spaceport. This is needless micro management and could be solved by simple adding every spaceport to the outliner list. Almost everything else in this game like exploration via science ships are done by easy one-click orders.
Stellaris got two bigger problems at the moment. First is a lack of midgame features. After you have explored the galaxy and colonized every planet, there might be nothing to do for a while, especially if you play with a pacifistic civilization (wars of aggression not allowed). This partially fixed with Leviathans dlc which adds midgame features. Still there is a chance that you won't encounter any of the Leviathan's guardians in your game. Second problem comes with a lack of victory conditions. Currently you can only win by war. Own 40%(60% with federation) off all colonizable planets or to conquer all other empires. I admit it's no easy task to find a victory condition besides current ones that would still keep the game challenging.
In my mind now is exactly the right time to get this game, because at its current state you will learn the game during your first game. Paradox just announced their first major expansion to Stellaris called "Utopia" which without a doubt makes the game harder to approach for new gamers, since it add many new features to the base game. Stellaris is all about the journey, not the destination.

When I first saw Kingdoms Rise on Steam Greenlight, I was excited for it. Who wouldn't be? The trailer and screenshots showcased a fast-paced multiplayer fantasy action game. So when I saw the game appear on sale as early access, I bought it straight away and got ready for some sword-fighting action. All I have gotten so far it disappointment and frustration. The controls are awkward and unresponsive, the classes all seem to be exactly the same, several of the specials are usless (for example, there is no way to aim the throwing axes/knives), and the game itself is laggy to the point of being unplayable. I'm aware that this game is still in early access, but it would be nice if I could actually have fun with it. It is supposed to be a game, after all.
I wanted to like Kingdoms Rise, I really did, but it is simply an unenjoyable experience. If you really are keen to try out this game, I would recommend waiting until it's out of early access or just avoid buying it altogether. After all, why spend fifteen USD for something this broken?

This one is still early in its development cycle at the time of this review, but it's showing a great deal of promise.
The game runs on the style of gameplay you see in games like Chivalry or Mount & Blade, where your attacks and blocks are directional, meaning you need to strategically place your shots and read your opponent's movements instead of flailing wildly on the opponent. The difference here is every character has access to 2 spells (of your choosing) plus a piece of equipment.
Gameplay is clearly early stage but definitely playable, in fact, it's pretty damned fun in the current iteration.
This is not a fast paced game however, if you're looking for a hack and slash game you may want to look elsewhere: Kingdoms Rise is more about planned, deliberate striking at the right moment and not about overwhelming someone with pokes. Every fight is usually ended with 1-3 well placed strikes depending which weapon you take into the fight.
The sound design so far is pretty nice, even for early stage. Every character is very chatter, shouting war cries and the expected grunting of swinging their swords, giving the game a bit of a brutal feel to it.
Overall, if you're into more tactical melee combat, I say give this one a shot! There's a lot to come with this one it looks, and is a great game to unwind with after a day at work :)
ps: It has colorblind mode, a major plus in my book.

This game took me completely by surprise. There are so many negative reviews about this game, but the important thing to realize is that most of these reviews are players who are really big into the multiplayer.
The multiplayer, from the two times I tried to connect, is essentially nonexistant so avoid this game if you're interested in a competitive experience.
Now the single player on the otherhand is absolutely incredible. This game looks great, plays great, sounds great, and is actually fun!
Graphics: The graphics look phenomenal. Lots of great textures, attention to detail on the character models, cool futurestic effects like enhanced thermal imaging, x-ray imaging, and cloaking. Lots of variety in missions ranging from rainy towns, snowy artic bases, to swamps. The only problem is you're going to need a hefty PC to run this monster. My framerate is pretty consistant on the highest graphics with the DX11 options turned off. I wouldn't try the DX11 settings unless you have a geforce 6 series or higher.
Gameplay: I played this game using an xbox360 wired controller and it works great. Full controller support including menus, button notifcations, and dualshock response. The game gives you several pretty linear missions with large spaces to explore and try different tactics. You can mark targets and pull off syncronized kills with your other squad mates, making the game a fast-paced tactical game unlike the previous Ghost Recons. The gadgets all seem useful in different situations. The game's customizability is some of the best I've seen since Battlefield 3. You can alter every single part of your gun right down to barrel length and compensator type. The enemies are challenging and gunfights feel realistic. Close quarter combat can feel a bit hectic when you try aiming very accurate guns at enemies right next to you.
This game also supports full 4 player campaign coop, meaning you can play all (or most I think) of the story missions with your friends. I highly recommend this game, ignore the reviews. They once again are misleading...

"There's a little bit of bad press circulating around this game as being a rip-off of Overwatch, but I am going to look past that, as it actually has little to no bearing on how good or bad the game is. I'm giving it a thumbs-up. It's smooth to play, and has a wide variety of roles to play, with customization on the levels of a typical RPG. Matches are quick, and fast paced, and it's free to play."
That was my initial review. After playing further, I've noticed a few disturbing trends. First of all, I think that HiRez studios is going a little overboard with the microtransactions. Every where you look, you are constantly bombarded with "New Skins!" "VIP Program!" "Loot Chests!", and unless you want to pay for the "Founders Package" you are limited to a few basic heroes and a few heroes on the "free rotation" until you can gather enough in game currency to unlock other heroes. Other than the free rotation and a "shooting gallery" there isn't any way to test-drive the new heroes, so you really don't have a good way to gauge how well are particular hero plays before you purchase it.
Secondly, the queue times are incredibly long, and if one person fails to "join match" it dumps everyone back to the lobby. If one person fails to choose their hero in time, it boots them, and dumps everyone back to the lobby. Back in the queue we go!
Thirdly, after finally playing the game, you are STUCK having to watch the "play of the game" without any way of skipping it, and re-queing. So, yeah, way to go, design team, way to keep players from *actually* playing the game. Spend less time on new skins and new heroes and fix the game first. A constant barrage of "buy this new skin!" gets old *really* quick.

This game is exactly the sort of game I've been wanting. It sits in my library of Best Three Games: Medieval II: Total War, Age of Empires II (not the HD edition, that's a buggy mess), and Freedom Planet. :P
(Grand Strategy, RTS, and.... platformer? What's this nutter up to! :P)
It's a fantastic blend of turn-based strategy and real-time strategy.
The whole Total War series is good, but Medieval II is extremely cheap. When on sale (and we all know how common those are!) you can get the game for $10 and the Kingdoms expansion for $5. Unlike later TW games, the Kingdoms expansion is a really really good DLC, adding FOUR WHOLE NEW CAMPIAGNS. Much better than one petty "culture pack." :P
If you don't know what Total War is, the screenshots & vidoes don't really do the game justice. Simply because there's SO MUCH to the game.
Basically:
On the campaign map, which in the main campaign goes from England to Russia to Egypt, you control things in a turn-based way. You make your moves, then another faction makes theirs, then another, etc. Because the game has about 20 factions for the Grand Campaign running it on a slow computer will be a bore. :P
However, when you are attacked you don't fight in a turn-based way. Rather, you fight the battle in realtime. Whether you win or lose, your results are transferred to the main map. If you can't be bothered fighting (e.g. 10:1 odds or naval battles - in Med 2 you can't manually fight naval battles but it doesn't matter since navies are a side point), there is an autoresolve.
There's spies, assassins, diplomats, merchants, wololos- er, priests which you can all use to further your objectives. Want to blitzkrieg? Open the gates with a spy. Can't be bothered killing a faction? Kill all their generals with assassins and rejoice in the Faction Destroyed notification. Send your Catholic Priests off to Egypt and laugh as either a) they cause Cairo to riot due to unrest or don't laugh because b) they all got assassinated.
Don't fancy medieval times? Don't like the Pope? No problem - you can either assassinate the Pope and wait until you get gunpowder units for those, or you can browse the vast section of mods.
Generally, mods are fairly easy to install and not too buggy.
Medieval II also is the host of the most functional Lord of the Rings mod: Third Age Total War. It also has two subsets to that: Divide and Conquer, which stuffs the map full of factions / settlements, and Massive Overhaul Submod, which again expands... well, everything.
And apparently there's "Hyrule Total War," a mod, which is apparently Zelda.
For some silly reason there's a Rome 1 mod for Med 2, despite the fact that Rome 1 is cheaper (get it on sale for $4 :P).
And there's also the four expansion campaigns which you can play to your desire.
Multiplayer is rather fun, though custom battles (in which you fight opponents out of the blue and the campaign map is utterly ignored) have the problem of no ranking - you can find yourself fighting battles with somebody who you can steamroll because his cavalry never charges, only walk, or find yourself fighting battles with somebody who can steamroll YOU. :P
There's also Play By Email games, which are for the campaign map. It's time-consuming (and difficult, partly 'cause timezones) to fight battles actually against the other human player - it is possible, just difficult - and hence most games just use autoresolve. Nevertheless, it's a fun feature which shouldn't be ignored.
The great thing about it is that no matter what skill level you are, you will be able to play & enjoy the game. Complete newb? Set difficulty to Easy and you'll never be fully conquered if you're vaguely competent. Veteran? Put the difficulty up and laugh as you steamroll the AI that took you 300 turns to do when you started.
Mind you, the difficulty settings are misleading. The same AI is used - all that happens is that as you go up the difficulty, they get combat bonuses, free money, and free public order. Normal tends to give the most balanced game (not because their Peasants are suddenly deadly, but because the AI leaves cities with even less garrison than usual).
Furthermore, the more you play the more you'll realise the game has a surprising level of detail that isn't immediately visible.
Generals (and Agents, but Generals are more noticeable) have a system that I heard described as "RPG-like;" fight the French 10 times with one general and voila, he gets the trait "Hates the French:+2 command when fighting the French." An assassin missed your general? He might get paranoid and thus decrease how likely he is to die from assassination. Keep on executing prisoners with one general? Enemies will rout & run away quicker. Leave a general in a city doing nothing? He might lose loyalty.
The economic system is simply masterful. Creating farms? Population growth goes up. Building roads? Trade income goes up, not just for your settlement but for the settlements it's trading with. Building a Market in a city in the middle of nowhere? Surprise surprise, your trade income went up by +6 (most units cost 300-800). Got gold nearby? Watch your mining profit soar.
Mind you, people who are new to the game can just build things that make them money and not bother about it. More experience players can see how much money it will make them and wonder if it's worth doing.
This game isn't for everybody. People who like to run around with guns blazing, die, respawn, have 10s of shooting, die, respawn, etc etc etc will not enjoy this game. But as for me, it's the best thing since Windows XP came out.
It is also the only game that I can play and feel tired - not physically tired, but mentally fatigued. You can play the game with little thought at all, but you'll progress slowly. The more attention you put in, the quicker your WORLD CONQUEST begins.
Still not convinced? Go get Rome Total War for $4 next Steam sale, see if you like the way it plays, and if you want to spend $12 (on sale) for five whole campaigns (plus a bucketload of complete mods, not some petty statistics change) go for it.
(Note: Later Total War games are extremely expensive in comparison, so go get Rome 1 & Med II)

These are the things I was really happy with (pros):

- The story, the story sucked me in like it was a black hole, a black hole that wanted to tell me an amazing story. It was very well made and I don't have complaints over it.
But there were some problems I had with the game (cons):
- At the time of writing this review there are bugs and glitches in the game that either break the game or ruin immersion, but this isn't something that can't be fixed in future patches.
- There is also a balancing issue in my opinion, the bosses felt really easy and some random enemies felt thougher than the bosses. And the game in general felt easy from time to time.
- The side quests, there were some side quests that were unique, gave an impact on you, but there were also some that were just the same thing with a different quest giver.
- Customization, if you were hoping to be able to change into diffirent outfits/change hair style then im sorry to be the bringer of bad news, but there simply wasn't any customization, you could get random accesories while playing and get some outfits after finishing the game, but it wasn't much. There is a chance that outfits and such will be available via DLC though.
Currently these are the pros and cons of the game that I could think of, some of them are minor other are major. But this IS a very good game, I really enjoyed it and it was money well spent. This is my first review so I hope it was useful :D

This game suffers from endless-runner syndrome. Let me explain. In most endless runners, let's take Subway Surfers as an example, the game is only really satisfying and fun when you've been playing for a couple minutes and already have maybe a hundred thousand points or so. It speeds up gradually, but as it does so, it becomes exponentially more satisfying and easy to die. When you finally do die, you feel disappointed that now you have to spend a few minutes before the game becomes fun again. Robot Unicorn Attack 2 solves this problem by letting you change the speed and acceleration that you run at, but these are both still free games on the app store. Now let's take a look at No Thing.
In Subway Surfers and RUA2, there are missions and upgrades, as well as in-game currency to give a sense of character progression. This does not exist in No Thing. I get that when you're going for this whole cyberpunk aesthetic, showing a character model breaks the fourth wall, as would upgrades and missions, but the game just isn't fun. To pass each level, it really isn't clear what you need to do, just play either until you die or until, magically, here's the next level. The music will get stuck in you head, and it's just a one-minute loop, so it becomes really jarring after a while.
As soon as you die, the weird robotic narrator talking to you in incomprehensible verses start over again. The same lines end up said over and over, and the gameplay isn't even interesting. It's just turning, that's it. Nothing else. You turn, and there's a bleep. There are floating cubes that don't do anything but change the color of the screen, and oh, have I mentioned the visuals?
Sometimes the screen get filled with "artsy" glitch-looking things that are like looking through a gummed-up contact lens. And everything is one color. It changes, but not much, and the colors aren't truly bright or varied enough to be interesting.
Let's remember, this is a paid game on Steam, not a free iOS game. And it's worse than a lot of free endless runners, even though it's basically a paid endless runner. There's no sense of progression, I'm on the third stage and I still don't even know who I am, who the narrator with the incredibly boring and repetitive voice is, or who the god damn Queen of Ice is. The visuals are a tiny bit interesting, but also jarring, the gameplay is completely uninteresting, literally just turning with a bleep sound effect, the plot is incoherent cyberpunk dystopian garbage, and the music is incredibly repetitive. This game is horrible.
P.S. I forgot to mention that very occasionally there are jumps. They are impossible to judge and control.
P.P.S. I know that someone must have worked very, very hard on getting the visuals, voiceover/plot and art just right, and maybe I'm just a simpleton who doesn't understand great art. But I do understand game design, and there's no effort put toward making actually satisfying gameplay in that regard. It boggles my mind how anybody could possibly enjoy playing this game for over an hour.

I have not reviewed any games since I got Steam but I really felt Stellaris diserves a review. It is by far the best space strategy / combat game ive played and I have played them all, or at least the ones worth anything.
- Excellent tech tree
- Awesome diplomacy
- Awesome war system
- Varied strategic and tactical options
- Beautiful design
- Great interface, extremely easy to use
- Intuitive management and everything is one click away.
I really like it that you cant simply steamroll opponents, and they cant do the same to you. Definately on my top 3-4 strategy games list up there with Age of Empires, Civilization and Medieval Total War 2

PROS:
-Really enjoyable storylines for whatever empire you've created to start with.  The more you mess around with mods for government types and ethics, the more fun you'll have.
-Mods.  Tons of very enjoyable mods,  at the click of a button in the workshop.  I currently have somewhere around 15 mods, and I couldn't play the game without them.
-Resource system is solid, and has only improved since my original review.
-Diplomacy system is simple and understandable.
-Games can end up lasting for days depending on the size (this could be a con, but I love it)
-Ship combat is satisfying and in the early to mid game its fairly manageable and fun
-Science ships, research, and anomalies are a great way to add flair to a fairly empty universe while also adding much needed depth to research.
-Ship designer is very well done and efficient.  Building ships can be done quickly without frustration
-The UI is a home run after it was updated, and I can only say good things about it.  One of the most easily picked up UI's in any strategy game I've played
CONS
-Planets, stars, and basically everything else is nowhere near realistic scale.  This is for the sake of gameplay, but completely ♥♥♥♥s immersion. The space station you make at the start looks so huge it would likely take more mass than is available on the entire planet.
-Space battles in the late game are a bit over the top.  You end up having hundreds of ships per battle and they take an insanely long amount of time.  It is not uncommon in late game for a single battle to last years.
-The notification system for ship combat is annoying.  It gives super loud updates every time a new target is engaged, even if a battle is already ongoing. In the late game, this could be a matter of 30 minutes or more of constantly targeting a new fleet within the same battle.  Not exactly the best feature.
-War is usually way more trouble than its worth, so unless you're building your culture on it, its probably something you should avoid.
-Once ships are in battle, you cant break off or control individual squadrons.  Its just x numbr of ships VS y number of ships with no tactics or anything.
SCORE & CONCLUSION
Stellaris is a very fun space strategy game that seems to get its roots in other great strategy games.  While it has some issues in the late game, there is a plethora of mods to choose from, and the game is being updated frequently.  Space fanatics and strategy game lovers will have plenty of good times awaiting them in Stellaris.
FINAL SCORE: 8/10
WHEN TO BUY: Get in on sale for <$20

Delver, mechanically, is a great, great game. I've had a ton of fun with it so far, and I'd recommend it to just about anyone. Right now it's pretty small, but I have high hopes for it when the full game is released.
The combat is very reminiscent of Minecraft, especially the swords and bows, though somewhat more complex. Elemental magic wands are an interesting option, though they're all basically the same. Enemies don't seem to have resistances or weaknesses, and there are no additional effects like the fire wand making enemies catch fire. Still, this is obviously an area the developers plan to expand on in the future, so I'm excited to see what they might add to the combat system.
The visuals are really great. There's a satisfying feeling in smashing an enemy backwards and watching him burst into a shower of red pixels, and the various enemies and environments all look fantastic. I was pleasantly surprised by the variety in the different dungeons you trek through. Cave levels are uneven and winding; a sewer I found myself in seemed extremely linear at first, but turned out to have tons of little alcoves and branching paths. Enemies all attack in similar ways (charging forward with melee weapons or shooting magic), but at this point in development it's nice to have some various enemy looks.
Honestly, this is a great game by itself. It just needs more... stuff. More content. The levels are pretty linear overall, and the end goal is fairly simple. Some other objectives could be fun... you could happen upon a corpse, with a clue that a great treasure lies hidden nearby. Find it, and you might be rewarded with some powerful armor, or a legendary magic wand. Special named weapons and armor would be so fun to collect, it would keep you coming back into the dungeons for more. I'd also love to see bigger levels, with multiple parts.
As of right now, this is a great base for a game. Once they add more content, supporting the already great gameplay with some additional items and places, this could become a favorite.

"There's a little bit of bad press circulating around this game as being a rip-off of Overwatch, but I am going to look past that, as it actually has little to no bearing on how good or bad the game is. I'm giving it a thumbs-up. It's smooth to play, and has a wide variety of roles to play, with customization on the levels of a typical RPG. Matches are quick, and fast paced, and it's free to play."
That was my initial review. After playing further, I've noticed a few disturbing trends. First of all, I think that HiRez studios is going a little overboard with the microtransactions. Every where you look, you are constantly bombarded with "New Skins!" "VIP Program!" "Loot Chests!", and unless you want to pay for the "Founders Package" you are limited to a few basic heroes and a few heroes on the "free rotation" until you can gather enough in game currency to unlock other heroes. Other than the free rotation and a "shooting gallery" there isn't any way to test-drive the new heroes, so you really don't have a good way to gauge how well are particular hero plays before you purchase it.
Secondly, the queue times are incredibly long, and if one person fails to "join match" it dumps everyone back to the lobby. If one person fails to choose their hero in time, it boots them, and dumps everyone back to the lobby. Back in the queue we go!
Thirdly, after finally playing the game, you are STUCK having to watch the "play of the game" without any way of skipping it, and re-queing. So, yeah, way to go, design team, way to keep players from *actually* playing the game. Spend less time on new skins and new heroes and fix the game first. A constant barrage of "buy this new skin!" gets old *really* quick.

Invited to a party only to murder everyone and start dancing in their blood in the middle of the dance floor.
Party hard is a rather fun and challenging game. You must kill everyone at the party....that's it very simple well sort of, you must watch out of the police, crazy party goers and must of all...if your a twitch streamer you have to watch out for your own audience...yeah that's right your audience can join your game by voting for the next random event that may either help you or doom you.
=========
The Good
=========
1. Gameplay - the idea of being this deadly killer that has been pushed over the edge by all the partying is rather fun. You have so many options to choice whether you want to use hidden devices such as cars, exploding barrels and etc is up to you. Or maybe you want to do it quick and up close with a blade or better yet do it quietly and hide their bodies as if nothing happened....or maybe have the police help you by arresting everyone instead. Again the choices are limitless.
2. Twitch - If your a twitch streamer  you can allow your audience to join you through a ingame voting system. This allows viewers to vote for your next random event whether it be having the swat team arrive to deal with you and everyone else, or a chainsaw killer that is only after you. This may help you or end you.
3. Steam workshop - This is an awesome idea to allow players build their own parties for others to play. I really enjoyed trying different levels made by someone else.
========
The 50/50
========
1. Music - the Music is enjoyable but seems to run into a loop which can be annoying after a while.
2. Death - You can die and you can die alot. The problem is when you die, you must restart the level which means it can be rather annoying espcially some levels having 100 or 200 people you have to deal with and having 1 stupid mistake kill you when your on the last 2 targets can be annoying. However it does allow challenge making you think and plan things out as best as you can.
=======
The Bad
=======
1. Glitches? or bad indictors - The biggest issue is determining how you die. Sometimes you can randomly die without knowing it, having you scratch your head for hours trying to figure out how you died or got arrested. This might be due to not having any indictors to tell you where everyone is such as when the FBI arrives they can be hard to see in the crowd or sometimes normal people are wearing costumes that match dangerous npcs such as someone wearing a doctor's outfit could confuse you with a real npc doctor which if attack can knock you out in one hit.
========
Overall
========
I do recommend this game but with a slight warning which is just be prepared for long missions and restarting alot. It may take some time to get use or have a proper plan but at the same time the levels are always difference in the aspect of where everyone spawns and what they do, not everyone will do the same thing as the previous time before you restarted making it fun but tough which is good.
It does feel great though clearing an entire level, it feels even better if you are a twitch streamer with viewers as they can join in on the fun and make your life a living hell. Either way I do recommend giving it a shot.

Hexcells is a sublimely simple puzzle game. Yes, it is short, especially once you get a hang of the game's core mechanics, but there's fun to be had in completeting all of the game's puzzles and 100%-ing it. Puzzle games are easy to come by these days. Unfortunately, for every Tetris or Panel de Pon out there, sometimes you can get a puzzle game that feels like it's cheating you by not giving you all the hints you need to solve the puzzle or worse, requires you to guess your way through puzzles leaving them to sheer luck.
Hexcells is not that game.
It starts simple, as most puzzle games do with a number on a hexagon that tells you how many hexagons are directly adjacent to that one. From there, the game builds on its rules, adding layers of complexity at a nearly perfect pace. The puzzles in this game and its two sequels are truly fun and challenging to solve in a way that only the best puzzle games are, leading to what really makes the game special :
Hexcells makes YOU feel smart.
You start to see patterns and infer more information than is just presented to you plainly on the screen. Your brain naturally takes over and starts to work within the rules provided in the game in a way that really makes you feel like you've accomplished something when you complete a puzzle with no mistakes. Every puzzle in this game can be solved through logic, no guesssing required.
Absolutely recommended as a great way to keep your mind in shape.

I thought this game would be better. I’ve played a couple Yoko Taro games in the past, Nier and Drakengard 3. They were low budget titles, with good intentions struggling to come through a sea of shoddy tech and compromised game design. With PlatinumGames on board, I hoped this would be the first Yoko Taro game I could recommend without first having to rattle off a long list of caveats about how absolutely everything in the game sucks. But that unfortunately isn’t the case. Nier Automata might run smoother, have more polished animation, and the sense of being a higher quality product. But in the end, it’s still riddled with huge flaws.
Biggest problem with the game is how almost all combat, including the bosses, feel like copy-pasted placeholders. I’ve seen many comments about how the game is a bit easy and simplistic. That’s an understatement. In the first 30 minutes, you see what most of the game will be like. There are a few variations on enemy types, but they’re underused, and uninteresting to fight. They look neat, and do a nice job communicating their story. But fighting one type of enemy didn't feel meaningfully different from another. The only thing that mattered was whether they used physical attacks, guns, or beam weapons.
On top of that, the visual style and camera make it hard to tell when an enemy is about to attack. Because of the reduced color palette, and low contrast, actions tend to blend together into an unintelligible mess. The game works around this by having an auto-heal system, and also gives you the ability to carry 300 healing items. This meant I was constantly blindsided by attacks, spamming healing items, and sometimes I died anyway from things I never saw coming. Instead of a blend of different camera perspectives, I would’ve preferred fixed camera angles for the entire game, because those were the only segments where I found myself able to tell what was happening. When the game makes a pretense of being like other PlatinumGames titles, it doesn’t compare well at all.
As for the story, it flows in an awkward manner. For example, after the prologue, it’s like the air goes out of the story. It’s unclear just what the overall direction of the story is supposed to be, beyond the immediate objective. The reason this is a problem is because there’s moments, often after a boss fight, where the story meanders, where you couldn’t answer if someone asked you what was going on, what characters wanted, or what was happening. Instead the story feels like it’s full of nonsensical sidetracks, punctuated by sudden emotional peaks that feel like they come out of nowhere. As a result of this choppiness, key emotional scenes feel unearned. The game is fairly long, so it’s not like there wasn't time to explore its cast and themes deeper. But there just isn’t much here. Characters are barely developed beyond their introduction, and I’m not sure what purpose some of the side stories served for the story as a whole. You could cut hours from this game without impacting the story or characters at all.
I didn’t want to dislike this story. But on several occasions I found myself staring stone faced at people screaming and crying, without feeling an inch of sympathy. Only a couple character relations felt well done, like the interactions with the communication officers. But because of plot developments they’re undermined and forgotten about. The relation between the protagonists 2B and 9S was a total dud. Same for their relations with the antagonists. On top of that, the story has what feels like blatant continuity issues, where people learn things out of order, and act like idiots because it seems like they’re too thick to understand what’s happening until they’re told about it for the fifth time. I could see the concept of what they were doing, but the execution doesn’t exist in the game properly. It’s thin, repetitive, and not efficient or respectful of the players’ time. Not good enough.
When I played Final Fantasy 13 I hit a spot of existential terror, where I was wondering what I was doing with my life. The game had been so unengaging, that when I was grinding away in a field, the game turned from leisure into borderline panic attack. Nier Automata is the first game since then to inspire similar feelings in me. It was during the route C finale that those kinds of dark thoughts started creeping into me, as the combat had become so rote that I was staring at the screen glassy eyed, looking at but not actually seeing the game. Is that what the titular “Automata” is supposed to be? The player robotically plugging away at the game, not engaged with it on any human level?
I can’t recommend this. I think it's a bad game, and the story is a fractured mess of unearned emotions that border on the manipulative. But I guess the music was good, so that's something.

I really enjoyed this title. I won't go into what the game is, as it's really quite straightforward and well-conveyed by the description. I didn't expect to enjoy myself as much as I did, because everything seems so low-budget. The voice acting isn't stellar, and seems to get worse as the game goes on. Some of the graphical assets look like something from the old Windows game "Chip's Challenge." However, the game is very stable. I only ran into one glitch in the entirety of my play-through - a worm boss got stuck on a structure in the lower right corner of the map during our fight. However, this just made the boss a little easier, it didn't require any sort of restart to the level or the game.

The game makes some very smart design decisions. First of all, the weapon system is solid. Each weapon feels notably different, and changes meaningfully with each upgrade purchase. The game does a pretty wonderful job of creating tension. The music during fights is not especially noteworthy but serves its purpose. The player takes very few hits (especially on the "Nasty" difficulty level), and when the player is at low health, the colors (graphically) in the game become washed out. This makes it difficult to discern the environment and the enemies. This serves as an added incentive to avoid taking hits, and makes being at low health more pulse-pounding.
There are a few rough difficulty spikes, and the game involved quite a bit of kiting. However, there are a few times the game spawns enemies behind you or puts you in a tight corridor with nowhere to run. Kiting doesn't work in these situations, and you'll need flares and firepower to stay upright. If you're a fan of tense, scary titles, and wouldn't be put off by a low-budget feel, I think you'll find a lot to like here.

So this game is no 2k10-13 (these were the best 2K games IMO). But I must say that compared to the last 3 years of the same game being recycled with updated rosters and graphics, and that horrid Joint with Spike, 2K didn't do a bad job on this one. The game mechanics for the most part feel very fluid and natural, and the enviornments are improved to feel more alive. MyCareer is a huge improvement to the last 2 years, although it lacks much of a story line, you actually feel like a pro with continuous visits and texts from teammates, your best friend Justice(Michael B. Jordan), coaches, and players around the league. In addition, you have to make certain decisions with you endorsements, and they feel pretty rewarding and something to work towards. WARNING: The difficulty of this game has been increased. It can be frustrating as you have to link dribble moves together to be effective. It is much harder to break ankles and get space for shots, and now you actually have to adapt to the game and read defensive schemes. But when you do make a great play and that time that you actually do blow by a defender it feels extremely gratifying. All-In-All I recommend this game to any fan of basketball as it truly is a step-up from recent years of 2K and offers a challenge as well as entertainment.

Things I really liked: enemies have set patterns, so you can do better at the game through personal experience and skill vs. just leveling up; melee weapons have a 'windup' time, so you need to properly time your attacks; all the character options are pretty fun.

Wildstar has had a bumpy ride in the world of MMOs, however it's one of the few that I always log back into every month or so just to see if the population has picked up enough to play regularly again. For some reason Wildstar has such charm and beauty in it's cartoony world, with a pinch of solid humor, which makes it a joy to explore. The questing is like any other mmo (read: boring), with a few fun minigames thrown in every few quests. My advice when levelling is to take your time levelling up and enjoy all the zones and storylines, there are so many hidden treasures hidden around that reward you for climbing, jumping and following your "oooh where's this go" instinct.
The PvE in wildstar is top notch, challenging enough to want to come back for more, but not so hard that you feel like tearing your hair out. The best mmo dungeon I have ever played is Ultimate Protogames, and I implore anyone who reaches max level to get enough gear just to experience that dungeon at least once! The dungeons are very group orientated and whilst they can be negated with gear, if you have gear appropriate to the instance, a dungeon could take a whole evening if it's your group's first time. On the flip side there have been countless bugs in PvE, which have kind of been fixed in "time", some still remain and can be an annoyance. I did not raid, but from the small parts I have seen, the raid instances look fantastic and the fights engaging.
On the other hand is the PvP which is mainly what I dedicated myself to in Wildstar, is pretty much dead. The class balancing is great (too little too late), the combat is great, what only lacks from making Wildstar have a decent arena or rbg scene is the lack of participation or awards, not to mention the plague of bugs and screw ups on carbine's front in the frist couple seasons from lack of dedicated pvp management. I do believe the pvp can still be fun and that the battlegrounds are very much worth playing! One tip: Always play objectives!
Housing is one of the best assets to wildstar, and if you really love building things this game has one of the most complex (but simple to build with) set of building blocks and collectibles to put in your home. A whole afternoon of joy can be had just from going to random plots and exploring. There have been many nights where I lost myself building a brothel on the housing plot of my main character, complete with strip poles and a "ominous leather couch".
Overall I would definitely reccomend this game to new players with an open mind as it is currently in a good place technically, it truly is a great mmo with a generous f2p system and a friendly, warm community. If you are looking for an mmo to waste some time on and have some casual fun without any expectation of big updates any time soon, wildstar is a really great catch.

This was a game where, after playing it for a few hours, it immediately became one of my favorites; moreover, I paid the full price for it ($30USD as of writing this) and don't regret that in the slightest either.
Let's start with one thing up-front: If you're looking for a game where you can drive your creations personally, well, that's not really what this game is about; on-screen rendered vehicle physics isn't a feature of the game. (It is a ton of fun to send your cars on the 'test track', though.)
This game absolutely shines for what it is meant to do - let you make a fantasy car company, complete with fine-tuning the engines for economy or performance or both. It focuses on the very satisfying kind of multi-dimensional optimization problems that come with tweaking each model for the best marketability in a segment.
My complaints about this game pretty much only center around the things that are either not finished or can be easily modded in. There are some decades where you run out of contemporary body styles, for example; and flat-four, flat-six, V12, and V10 engines would be great. That said, for what this game is, there really isn't anything major missing. Plus, I can't wait for the "tycoon" side of this game to start happening (although I tend to lose in money-management settings).
One other note: The graphics look amazing while still being able to run easily on my PC. The Lua side of things can be a little shaky in terms of stability, but compared to a particular car-building game from 2003 that I've sunk even more time into (it's not on Steam), it's immensely better.

**Updated Review** (Dec 4th 2015)
When I bought the game, I misunderstood the Tycoon elements as imminent. The Devs have really increased comm. around the long road ahead before that happens on the Store page, and responding to individual posts as well. As a result, I am changing my review to a "recommend".
On to the game itself, (coming from a person who is mostly into the Tycoon aspect): In my brief time with the game, I followed the provided objectives to fine tune a series of engines. Using an increasing number of menu sliders, you raise/lower those until you get the right combination.
I learnt some things along the way about engines (nice!), and then ran out of motivation-gas to keep playing... until the Tycoon aspect becomes playable.
Once I can Tycoon the heck out of the beasts I hope to create, I have a feeling the motivation to master mechanics of car tuning / creation itself will feel more rewarding too.

A game with mediocre characters barely worth remembering and humor as dry as the desert from the country it is based on, the story and gameplay are all that drives this game forward. Despite what many have said, the story in the Pre-Sequel is suprisingly enjoyable. Sure, it wasn't the best one they have done, but it was nevertheless engaging and enjoyable to follow. The sidequests were, on the other hand, unfortunatly barely worth doing and very few come to mind that were humourous, creative, and original. Thankfully, there are some special weapons that are rewarded from some quests that make them doing worth while. Shame that was my only motivation doing them.
The gameplay was, suprisingly, a thrill to play. Introducing lazers, a Zero Gravity Enviorment, and butt slams, this addition to the series was highly enjoyable. I found myself as a lazer-based class (Wilhelm) while buttslamming scavs from 50 meters in the air, and I enjoyed it quite a bit to say the least. Also, the option to use the Grinder, a machine that can combine items into something better, was a neat little addition to the game. A big downside, however, was the character skills. It felt rushed, unexciting, and focused more of co-op gameplay mechanics (E.g, Claptrap.) Not that I have a problem with co-op skills, it just felt punishing towards players who focus on Solo games rather than the Multiplayer, despite the fact that the franchise was largely known for it's drop in, drop out co-op. Borderlands 2 was fun for both Solo AND Multiplayer characters, and that is what I enjoyed most about it. Another downside was lack of respawnable bosses, which dimminishes the game's replay value with a single character. But I have spoken too long on the gameplay, so lets go right to the story.
The story, although stale at first, shines as being one of the more interesting stories in the Borderlands series. Regardless if you thought that Borderlands 2 was 10x better than the Pre-Sequel's, it was nonetheless enjoyable for me. It drove me to keep playing to see what will happen during the next mission. I wanted to see Jack go from Zero to Anti-hero. It was great, and the main protagonist dialogue was a treat as well, especially Claptrap's lines. As I stated in my first paragraph, the sidequests were forgettable and mediocre, which is disappointing for a Borderlands game. The humor gave me the occasional chuckle, and the rare "LMAO" moment, while the rest were either unfunny, "meh," or even cringe-worthy. That is a big turn off from a series built on it's humor and clever dialogue.
The DLC is probably the biggest turn off of the series, and here's why;
The studio had it's plug pulled after the negative responses from gamers and critics alike over the game. Which is a damn shame, since the Claptastic Voyage was a gem to play, rivaling that of Tiny Tina's Raid on Dragon's Keep from Borderlands 2. If they had kept going and had more time to extend the life of the game, maybe, just maybe, they would have redeemed the game. At least the studio, despite their game being hailed as the most disappointing installment, went out strong, and I commend them for that. Sure, the rest of the DLC is "meh" compared to Borderlands 2, but it is still worth checking out, along with the two Vault Hunter DLCs.
OVERALL:
If you wish to play a Borderlands game filled with mediocre humor, innovative gameplay, fun story but forgetable characters and sidequests, then this game will satisfy you until the next installment comes out. You may not spend as much time on this game as you did in Borderlands 2, but it will occupy you for a good 30-40 hours depending on your pacing ingame. I'd get this game on sale or at♥♥♥♥♥s website. Other than that, i'd wait until then.

This is one of those games that screams "why didn't I think of that?". At its core it may look like hexagonal minesweeper, but that is just the most visible aspect. You see, as a puzzle game, minesweeper has quite some randomness and, at times, guesswork. Hexcells manages to maintain and even improve the depth of that game while removing the randomness element. Every level is solvable, but at times, it introduces extra information about the columns or the adjacent blocks. But as you can guess, the trick to properly SOLVE the puzzle (meaning: reducing all guesses) is to combine the bits of data you have to come to clear knowledge on whether a block is a "bomb" (okay, "part of the pattern") or not.
I haven't played plus or infinite yet, but it's not hard to see why other reviewers treat these games and this one as a single game. It's because it is. And to be frank: the only reason the developer gets away with it is because even the single parts are easily worth the small asking price (3 bucks? You can just as well call these games stand-alone DLC). So even with this warning, this is a very easy thumbs up. :-)

Hexcells is really a fantastic game and value for logic puzzle fans.
The game is similar to Minesweeper with a few changes.  First, one mistake doesn't end the game, (and in fact a single mistake still gives "full" score.
Second the grid is made out of hexagons rather than squares.  Instead of the eight neighboring blocks, there's the 6 neighboring grid squares.
Third, there's a number of different solving techniques and clues.  Whether it be connected numbers, disconnected numbers, or just hints about rows.
Finally the game is based on perfectly solvable grids, rather than random (and potentially unsolvable) puzzles.   The game contains 36 levels, and they range in difficulty, but they're all quite well done.
There's two sequels that are more difficult, for someone who's looking for a real challenge, but as a introduction to the game, Hexcells does a fantastic job, and at a realistic price.
(I would recommend all three games)

A great little game to kill some time. I work as a teacher and this game was an excellent way to pass some time during the breaks.
+ The artwork is quite good, and it's consistent. Nothing stands out in a negative way.
+ The action sequences are quite good. They are neither overwhelming nor too over-the-top.
+ The game has quite regular checkpoints, so you don't have to play a whole area again when you die.
+ The voice-acting is quite good for an indie game. I especially liked the voice actor of our protagonist, Max.
+ Very nice, rock/metal-themed soundtrack.
+ The game has collectibles (secret locations, golden gun parts and body armor parts); nice for completionists.
+ All the weapons have many levels of upgrades, which sometimes changes how they work noticeably.
+/- Most games of this kind has a BFG-type weapon they hand out in the end. Splatter gives you all the weapons many levels before the last one, and none of them are truly devastating.
+-/ The story was interesting, but not a masterpiece. It was simple enough to follow, but not deep enough to really care.
- The variety of weapons is sufficient but you can finish the whole game with just shotgun. It's very effective, and you won't need another weapon if you fully upgrade it. I've almost never used the grenade launcher and the flame thrower.
All in all, I can recommend this game to anyone who is looking for a short game to play in quick bursts.

"A game that can get you hooked for months on end and still not win. 10/10 would donate life again."
That was my old review. Still good fun. However, such a game like this that has compelled my inner fetish of galactic conquest certainly deserves a much better analysis of why Stellaris has been in my personal list of "games to die for".
Stellaris? Isn't it a Civ BE mockup? No and don't ever compare that absurd game to Stellaris or even the astounding Civ series. The only similarity is the sci-fi genre and that's about it. Stellaris at its core is Real Time 4X Grand Strategy. Big draws for me? Real time. As a occasional Civ player and primarily Starcraft player, this seems like the perfect marriage of the two core mechanics of these two great games. Missing a few things of course but it evolves into its own thing entirely.
Stellaris is also as mentioned a 4X game which it sticks to very closely. The great dev patches have continually rooted the game back ever closer to a good balance of the 4X elements, notably in the "Banks" patch where "traditions" were introduced that define your galactic soaring or civilization purging race towards specific specializations like exploration or expansion (or conquest, which is my favourite for obvious reasons :P ). Now that we got the basics out of the way let's go into how the game starts, progresses, ends and of course the ever exciting upcoming content.
As a practical newbie coming into Stellaris, it certainly was a little daunting. Multiple sections of tabs to monitor anything from population to research to governmental style required quite a level of monitoring in order to ensure you don't just outright lose before entering the mid game. The "tutorial" per say isn't a traditional one. You are thrust straight into a full game where it seems like everything you click threatens to wipe out your starting planet but thankfully, your little robot helper just guides you along with appropriate explanations and even kindly pauses time for you so you can hear his annoying Dinklebot like voice on how to build structures or survey planets.
Once you get past the invertible failures of your first few games of Stellaris, you'll start heading deep into the early game and eventual mid game. In the early game, there are lots of things to do. Different styles and different races which you determine the traits of, from type of governance to individual bonuses that your race will have, will influence on how your early game progresses. Will you be diplomatic towards your immediate neighbours and avoid early conflict at the cost of some sections of the galaxy in order to expand peacefully? Or will you aim to subdue them with a mix of hard politics and a sprinkle of force that will cause other neighbouring civilizations to distrust you? The choice is always yours.
Then we enter the mid game where things really start to heat up. The pace of the game is a little slow to my liking in the mid game though things do move fast when you start to make moves on your opponents. At this point anything can happen depending on how you set up your early game. If you're like me when I first entered the mid game where I was the friendliest civilization in the galaxy, you'll encounter a couple of friends but start to get squeezed out of territory to expand to. Then its either you play politics to secure new areas from foes through alliances or if you're strong enough, just outright conquer them. Again, all actions have consequences and will make you think and plan ahead for your final endgame strategy. During the mid game (and sometimes if you're lucky in the late early game) you can encounter strange significant events that may change your predicament. From gleaming ancient powerful technology to horrors of the galaxy, depending on your luck (and certain DLCs) these events will affect your overall strategy. By how much? That is for you to find out.
So we now progress to my favourite and also at the same time, least favourite part of Stellaris, the endgame. When it comes to endgame time, it's basically how to meet the victory conditions of total conquest, domination or a federation victory. All of which require extensive amount of time and planning to execute before being able to achieve victory. As you steam along conducting diplomacy or waging war on a galactic scale, suddenly, strange events occur. Welcome to the endgame crisis. One of my favourite features of Stellaris. You see the endgame crisis is basically like a spanner in the works to your on going plan for galactic conquest. Depending on your luck and what technologies you have researched, the endgame crisis can be different. But all do the same thing, make the galaxy much more dangerous. I can go on about the different ways to take advantage of the end game crisis to weaken tough opponents or the different methods to defeat them, but that wouldn't be fun for you :). Instead, all I will say is that always turn it on and prepare to either cry or have lots of challenging fun. The end game crisis is a fantastic feature and as of writing, there's some rework coming to the crisis, so for all you veteran Stellaris players, get your fleets ready.
Now I did mention the endgame was also my least favourite part. Why? In super late endgame when you've solved the endgame crisis you tend to run into large enemy empires that are equal in power to you if not just slightly less powerful. Clearing them and eventually winning takes practically longer than the early and mid game combined. Not to mention much less exciting now that all the events, research and minor diplomatic squabbling is done. I've not heard of this issue in multiplayer as endgame tends to be exciting when the most powerful civilizations are controlled by your friends and everyone wants victory. That results in a mighty fun multi-way conflict. However since I am mainly playing against AIs this is my own issue with the super late endgame. The game just drags on and on with no end in sight as conflict can only be waged every 10 years or so and often you are not able to completely wipe out an endgame civilization in a single conflict.
Now that you've somehow survived the wall of text, do note that there are so much more features and depth to Stellaris that this review simply cannot encapsulate. These are the ones that stick out to me and my general feel towards the game and with that time for a quick summary.
SUMMARY
Good:
-Great depth
-Real time 4X Grand Strategy
-Interesting events, subplots and stories
-Complex and fulfilling game progression throughout all stages of play
-Great replayability
-Large, game changing patches, updates and DLCs constantly being put out
-Decent modding community
-Challenging and engaging AI for Solo/Co-op play
-Brand new dynamic when in PvP
-Very engaged community
-Fantastic soundtrack to fit game
-Built in and updated Wiki to help you along
Bad:
-FPS issues when large amount of artefacts on screen
-Long, drawn out super late end game
-Slightly steep learning curve
-Slightly buggy multiplayer (being looked into at time of review)
-Dull actual combat mechanics
-Poor player to player communication within game itself
Personal gripes/opinion:
-Time drain
Stellaris takes a lot of time especially on larger galaxies. Sometimes it is fun sometimes its a little too long and makes me not want to commit to a full game knowing that I'm not going to complete it anytime soon.
-DLC price
With the recent DLC priced at $19.99 SGD, its a little pricey for my taste. However, it does bring an interesting dynamic to the game. Worth it? To me? Its ok, I would be happier paying $10.99-$14.99 SGD.
Overall score: 9/10
Final conclusion:
With the direction Stellaris is heading and the active community plus dedicated devs, this game is ever heading towards being one of the best games I've have the pleasure to sink my time into. Looking forward to my next civilization to enslave :)

Very crashy. Devs have treated the game like it's still in early access since it was released, completely reworking one or more major systems with every single patch and not fixing any of the glaring issues that have been in the game from the beginning, such as sectors being garbage, trade not existing, diplomacy being less than halfassed... Very obnoxious ratio of downtime to actually doing anything interesting- I spend the majority of my playtime waiting. The randomized tech tree doesn't really improve the 4x formula. Stellaris takes a host of good sci-fi ideas-internal politics in a space empire, psionics, robots,  notable and important figures in your empire who have their own unique traits, fallen empires of aliens who have been around for thousands of years longer than you, terraforming, precursor species, abducting primitive aliens for research, customized starships...and then fails to implement any of it in a way that's fun. Just about the only place where Stellaris really shines is exploration, in which your science ships generate anomalies that can be investigated in order to create little storylets, kind of like episodes of star trek.  Diplomacy is pretty much nonfunctional-none of the computer empires are interested in any sort of treaty with me, including the ones that share my ethos. They happily mke grand alliances among themselves that prevent the player from any kind of military expansion, though, and unless you pay extra for the latest DLC there's nothing else to do. Even when you're at war there isn't much to do-combat is determined entirely by the size of the fleets involved, and because combat resolves so quickly even a moderately outnumbered fleet will be quickly and lopsidedly destroyed. Because of this, your entire fleet will exist in one giant doomstack at all times.
I might be able to put up with all of stellaris' flaws, however, if I could finish a game without it crashing. Unfortunately, I cannot.
