Hard to beat campy B-movie vampire flicks being brought to unlife in a video game.  This game has its tongue firmly lodged in its blood-stained cheek for the entirety of its 3-4 hour runtime.  I mean, they've called the main character Jeremy for goodness sake.  Also, if you're still taking the game seriously come the end the final line of dialogue in the entire game is "Oh...whatever...", which removes all doubt that the developers were not aiming for this to be their crowning magnum opus.  Now at times they did take this to the extreme and used it as an excuse to put absolutely zero effort into some things, like the dialogue and voice acting.  I get that it was supposed to be hammed up to 11, but sometimes the dialogue is overwrought and repetitive without adding any further fun factor.  But this is what it is, a senseless hack and slash through legions of vampires, werewolves, demons and evil agents of Rome.
The story is actually not half bad, with our main character, ahem, "Jeremy", being bonded to a vampiress to help battle a legion of vampires bent on stealing the "blood seal", the maguffin of the day, which will cause the moon to split and all natural order to break down.  Thus they begin their pursuit which takes them across the full spectrum of stereotypical settings - dark forest, haunted castle, a spoopy village, ruinous cliff-faces, and so on.
The levels are quite short and punchy and don't drag on too long, and by and large the save system is alright with checkpoints sensibly placed.  The platforming could be a bit trying at times with the less than stellar controls and fixed camera positioning, but nothing that will cause much hair pulling.
What the game did do wrong to its detriment was implement lots of pretty vestigial things.  For one thing, the trader.  Not once did I feel the need to buy anything as you are fed a constant supply of weaponry that you find in the field, each a little better than the last.  And speaking of loot, the inventory system is also made redundant as nearly everything you pick up you then equip as it is superior.  The only time a choice really comes in is in which weapon (both characters dual wield - either swords for Jeremy or crossbows for the vampiress) to replace.  And besides unlocking new skill at each level up and upgrading your armour/weaponry, you can also collect blood coins on your travels, and every 5 you get you can increase your attributes - health, strength or luck.  But these changes I felt added nothing to the power of my guys in any real way, at least compared to armour/weaponry upgrades, and I think was just an excuse to add collectibles.  Also the game is very much on the easy side, even on hard difficulty setting, once you get by the first level or so and start to increase your vampire skillset and get better weaponry and armour.  Also, after the first couple of levels I pretty much played entirely as the vampiress, as she was overpowered, and her ranged combat allowed me to devastate from afar.    Also, it was pretty easy to annihilate big groups without endangering myself by perching atop a ledge and blazing away.  And any health/money (which is pointless anyway as it can only be used at the defunct trader) doesn't disappear over time so there's no motivation to have you rush forward as it'll all still be there when you're done massacring the defenseless enemies.   I thought for one brief moment they were mixing things up by introducing enemies with shields which were immune to regular arrows, forcing me to put Jeremy up front to smash them with his heavy attack.  But no, a ranged fire arrow attack ( the vampiress's "heavy" attack) burnt those shields up like so much kindling.  And once I found a ring that halved the reload time on the fire arrow I was unstoppable.
Also, another missed beat was the bosses.  They were all pretty easy, just keep your distance and keep firing.  The first one during the tutorial was probably the most inventive as you had to hurl grenades at her blood altar to stop her healing.  And finally the last boss did try to add challenge by forcing you to jump every now and then to avoid his wave attack.  But they, like all the others before fell pretty quickly under a barrage of arrows and grenades.
But, don't let all these criticisms put you off.  It's a mindless, fun, and brief romp that I had fun with.  Definitely worth it on sale if you've aware going in that this is just goofy fun to unwind your brain with.

I'm a pretty big fan of vampires and action RPG stuff, so when I saw a bundle with a bunch of games in it I didn't care about, but it included Blood Knights, a game I had my eye on for some time, all priced less than Blood Knights by itself, I snatched it up without hesitation. I barely looked at the game, and unfortunately, didn't pay the reviews much mind, either, because I figured any adoration I had for a game revolving around vampires would outweigh any cons of the game. I've been playing games for far too long to allow this sort of naivete to compromise my choice in games I deliberately seek out playing, but I permitted it due to a moment of weakness based in my personal affection toward the vampiric.
Blood Knights actually looks pretty good, simply from a graphical standpoint as an action RPG. A family member stopped by while I was playing and was actually wowed by the graphics considering it was from a game he'd never seen or heard of. I didn't think they were
good, myself, but the're certainly tenable, especially from afar. I think the graphics are weaker when the camera is close to the character models, such as in dialogs. Their animations while speaking often seem lackadaisical when the voice acting would imply they should sound more lively as well.
On that note, the voice acting is alright at times, and poor at most. I think that most of the voice actors in this game
talent, but they either didn't give their best effort, or the developers didn't say "okay, that just wasn't what I was looking for. Could we trying it again, except this time try <insert different vocal inflection or attitude>?" The dialog is delivered in such a way that it's lacking any emotion, or it's rich with emotion but the visual feedback on the character's face shows an absence of such emotion. Music and sound effects were fine. I seem to recall the music being pleasant, but nothing was memorable to me.
I found Blood Knights' gameplay to be surprisingly competent. I expected something like Diablo, in so far as clicking and holding the mouse down on an enemy, and clicking elsewhere to relocate, but instead it's a bit isometric, with WASD controls, mouse buttons for attacks and a special attack, and a few other keybinds to use other moves. You can switch between Jeremy and Alysa every few seconds, doing melee with two swords as the former, and ranged attacks with two crossbows playing as the latter character. Alysa's maneuverability and ranged fighting seems to make her a bit of an unbalanced superior in combat to Jeremy, especially the more skill points you invest in her at level-ups. However, despite being a power gamer much of the time, I found myself frequently playing as Jeremy because his combat had more flourish and variety. In short, I enjoyed playing more as him than as Alysa.
The game also has an inventory system, and it seems to work alright, but I would've preferred a more blatant Diablo-esque user interface and controls for it. You get new items by walking up to specific treasure chests which appear in predetermined locations on each map. In regard to the maps, I didn't really enjoy them. They were fairly bland without much creative scenery, and unexpected events didn't come up. Moreover, most of the maps are narrow passageways. Although I liked Final Fantasy XIII, anyone who took issues with its methodology of almost exclusively putting "halls" everywhere could have some FFXIII PTSD from playing Blood Knights. That said, the game plays well enough and is just alright, but it's not something I would want to play
something else that's pretty good or great within either the same genre or another. When gameplay is just alright, story and lore is where the slack must be picked up. Does it deliver there?
The game's storyline follows intrepid human warrior-commander Jeremy... Yes, they named the lead character Jeremy, while other characters have medieval/fantasy-themed names. I don't know if this was some sort of self-insertion by a writer named Jeremy, or if the writer just had a moment of temporary insanity. He is magically bonded to a female vampire named Alysa ("uh-lie-suh"), so that they are both linked  to one another and if one dies, the other will also die. Alysa does not really emote or say anything of relevance until a little while into the game, which is incredibly bizarre and off-putting. I'm given no explanation as to how she got captured, why she doesn't just run away or kill everyone before the binding spell is cast, and she just becomes a so-so "reluctant companion" archetype.
Archetypes can be fun, either for hitting certain notes just right, or for being so badly executed that they're a source of amusement, but in Blood Knights, the mark is missed so badly with her and most supporting characters. Honestly, the only character I saw that I kinda liked was the Trader, who is a decent execution of the good-natured scoundrel/rogue sort of archetype. Alysa could have been a fantastic character, but she's uninteresting and the only good things I can say about her is that she serves as eye candy and is useful in combat. I was waiting for interesting dialog to come up with her, but anything that came up wasn't even fun on any simplistic, obvious level. Why not talk about her motivations, her views on humans, any morality issues or the lack thereof? Screw it, let's talk about the weather, even? Something! She is just a bore in dialog most of the time I was playing, and when she isn't boring, the void she leaves in her moments of silence are confounding to me.
I found the human characters' dialog to be poorly written - or more often than not - badly voice acted such that it undermined anything good there. The only dialog I liked that I came across was a female barkeep, and I thought she did a good job and I liked what was said, even though it was brief. Everything else just came off incredibly awkward and not in an entertaining way to me.
For all that the game
tell you, the times it does say something, it doesn't want to show you. What I'm referring to is show-don't-tell. A world in a game that's allegedly more detailed than something virtually "lore-less" like Pac-Man, needs to do a good job of explaining itself and its story, and not leave the audience "hanging" for too long without exhibiting an understanding for sating the audience's curiosity by throwing out morsels of lore and storyline intrigue. This is done to tell a story without lazily having a character or text give everything away in one exposition dialog or text crawl. If show-don't-tell isn't used properly, then simply "telling" the story should at least be done, even if it's sloppy. Instead, Blood Knights doesn't even do this adequately. If the plot picks up a while after leaving town, I won't know about it, because I absolutely could not stick with the game much further past that.
The game goes so far as to tell you that fire and holy water are the only sure ways to kill a vampire...yet your old escort mission buddy decides to kill Jeremy when he's turned into a vampire in the opening story scene, and opts to kick him off a cliff of indeterminant height. Yes. He kicks an immortal creature off a cliff...not even one rumored to be bottomless or to have jagged rocks at the bottom. He literally wants Jeremy dead, too; no remorse, so it's not like he's doing this to pretend he's trying to kill him. He really wants him dead, has him on his knees with his hands bound; same with Alysa, and boots them both off a cliff. Okay...
Blood Knights has decent visuals, alright gameplay, mostly alright sound (voice acting really, really needs work), and a severely lacking story/lore situation. Nothing about this game is appealing enough to me for me to stick around and want to finish it. =/

Ever play a game so bad it's good? This is one of those.
The story opens up and immediately I have no idea what the actual ♥♥♥♥ is going on. Like there's a story, but I feel like I missed half of it by time the intro is done. Like there was something that happened before that I really needed to know, but just wasn't told.
Not only is the story only kind of there, there's bad voice acting to go hand in hand. It's edited poorly and often times characters cut eachother off before there's a normal conversational silence. It's very discomforting. And emotion? I think maybe one of the characters has emotion. But it's hardly there if at all. It's like they got tired college students to read their script at 3 am, and payment would be breakfast at a diner.
If you can get past that-- then there's the combat system. Which honestly isn't too bad. My biggest complaint is it has a slight delay so it doesn't always pick up on stuff you hit. Like if you're in the middle of a combo it wont register that you pushed the special move button and you'll just be standing around awkwardly getting hit.
The worst part about the combat is the camera. The camera is on a fixed track and so if you move too far in a certain direction, the camera moves and puts you at a disadvantage. The camera always wants to face behind you, but if you're trying to strafe your enemy and the camera flips then you can really ♥♥♥♥ yourself. And as far as I can tell, you can't manually control the camera.
Which brings me to the next problem. The platforming is awful. There is one section where your character specifically states you need agility to get through this area. I don't know how many times I died trying to get across, and trying to collect the little tokens I needed along the way. But I was in tears. I was laughing so hard and how poor this platforming system is. One of the biggest problems is when the camera moves when you're trying to jump, your brain wants to correct the jump automatically, which can be your death. There were times I accidentally walked off the side of the platform by trying to move forward. It's bizarre and there's no clear way to know what's going to kill you and what you can jump into. I died. A lot. There's no real penalty for death except you go back to the last save point. But they are generous with their savepoints.
This game has choices too. You can side with humans or vampires. Or do a mix of both. I'm not sure how much it changes the story. I may do a lets play of siding with each side one day. But I'm not really sure if it affects any dialogue between you and the vampire girl you're stuck with.
The best part though, was earlier in the game you get to fight this boss lady named Blood Fox. She gets inside this creature called a behemoth and you fight her in that. Later on you get to control a behemoth of your own. I was so excited. I got to be this big thing that kicked♥♥♥♥♥ Well I get into it, and it's slow like you would expect, but then I had the unfortunate mind to turn around. And when I turned around what was I greeted with? The model of Blood Fox inside the behemoth. Not my vampire lady, but Blood Fox. So not only do I get to be big and clumsy, I get to be a character I may or may not have killed in the beginning of the game! YAY!
There's a lot of weird random dialogue in it too. Like when getting into the behemoth your vampiress says "It kills something inside you" and then she's just like "okay I'll go inside it." Like why put that in if she's just gonna be like "lol k"?
Over all I give this game a big thumbs up if you're the type of person to like bad games.
Oh and you know how protagonists usually have cool names? Like Commander Shepard, Isaac Clarke, Samas Aran, etc?
This guy's name is Jeremy.

Blood Knights is an average ARPG because it is equal parts good and bad.
The good - the game is pretty fun, you have two characters to switch between (or play in co-op), basic weapons and armor upgrades, skill upgrades as you gain levels, and a decent variety of enemies. The game isn't too difficult once you get used to the controls (which cannot be remapped, bad!), and some of the upgrades make your character pretty unstoppable (I played the archer most of the game). You can upgrade three basic attributes every time you collect 5 blood coins (I just put all of mine in health, don't know what luck does, and strength might be good if you play the fighter). You gain other abilities throughout the game such as sucking blood from random guys staked in the areas or enemies (someone mentioned you can only take blood from one enemy at a time, but other nearby enemies are slowed down as this happens). Later as you suck blood from enemies you can "force" throw them. You also get a blood shield toward the end of the game which gives you some protection for a limited time. The music is pretty good throughout the game.
The bad - the acting and cut scenes are atrocious. Not just the dialog but the actors as well. Just bad. Sometimes they drag on for forever. The story is very dumb as well. I also noticed the whole vampires in sunlight during the game, but just ignored it and tried to enjoy the game anyway. Someone mentioned a poor attempt at dialog trees - for the most part the choices are meaningless except in one or two instances. Someone else mentioned the platforming - very annoying, especially when they stand between you and a save point. The save system isn't too bad because you can actually save at the save points multiple times (for example, you can save, go fight some enemies, then backtrack and save again). The camera can also be an issue when fighting or platforming. The controls don't help either. As a console port, the devs decided to force you to use WASD and close by keys with no possiblity for remapping. One thing that irked me was showing an up arrow for using certain powers. I thought they meant the arrow up key; eventually I figured out they menat the Shift key. Note to devs, say <SHIFT> next time. Finally, there is a random mech-like part at the end of the game that ended up being more annoying than anything.
I am giving the game a recommendation because I think there is fun to had here, especially if you get it on sale. Just be prepared for some annoying parts and skip the dialog whenever possible; you are not missing anything.

SPOILERS, in case you even mind:
Story:
* In previous games, mankind nearly went extinct. (I didn't play them, but this is kind of the outcome.)
* Now in this game, a network tries to keep robots and androids in never ending conflict (also against each other), to try to evolve and understand and preserve humanity and the meaning of life.
* The morale of this is "Life doesn't have a meaning. Everyone has to give it his own meaning" (I already knew that..)
Graphics, Soundtrack, Gameplay and Result:
* A lot of the map elements have horrible map textures and models that will make you laugh.
* The android characters and animations are fine.
* The soundtrack is really a matter of taste (I didn't like it).
* The camera is messy and often you will fight it over the actual enemies or boss.
* Most open questions that you will have during the game, will be explained in the cheapest way possible later.
* The gameplay and fighting is often repetitive and the game drags you not only to visit the same ugly locations multiple times, but also through multiple playthroughs to get to the real ending.
* The flying / bullet hell scenes are boring after a while, because it will just spawn tons of enemies in front of you, while nothing really happens in the back.
* Most of the sidequests can be skipped as they don't play a greater role in the game.
* The ui and whole appearance of the game is greyish and sometimes it's hard to distinct between elements, also all items look the same on the ground.
* In some chapters, the game will just torture you and you will want to throw your controller/keyboard aside and unistall the game. (You are being defenseless and unable to jump and have to run through half of the map, while the game will require you to defend and jump ...)
*Altogether, if you are not really interested in existentialism and can see through the pseudo complex and confusing story, ultimately this game won't make you happy and there are better ones out for you.

NO THING is certainly a unique experience. The first time I saw the trailer, I couldn't even see what made it a game!
The game is an endless runner, where you do nothing but turn left and right, trying not to fall into whatever abyss lies off the platform. The tagline- "The year is 1994 and it is the future."- sets up the unconventional setting, which is made even more quirky by the disembodied narration and surreal imagery.
The music is brilliant, and helps motivate the player to go on in spite of extremely tough levels. Level 7 (
) and level 10 are the toughest, which both took me 300+ attempts to complete. Anybody who completes this game deserves enormous credit!
The game is far from perfect, though. A game that requires such precise actions deserves precise gameplay. Sadly, there were many times when I pressed left/right, only for the "simple office clerk" to keep going in a straight line. As this "phantom input" happened multiple times in the very same point in a level, I call this a bug rather than player error. Getting stuck in between two platforms, with no choice other than to kill the clerk, is another frequent issue in the last levels.
Some other bad choices by the designers:
Still, despite these issues, I do recommend NO THING. Its surreal setting, bizarre narrator and terrific music all makes it a unique game, and if you fancy a challenge to boot, this game will be rewarding for you.
6/10

NO THING is a runner game. It's addictive at first. The story ain't bad either. The game takes place in year 1994 which is also the future. The graphics is great. The effects are also kinda interesting. The colors, The surroundings, everything changes during the levels is actually great.
The soundtrack ain't bad. It gets faster depending on the speed of the level which is very good. The full voiceover and speech synthesis makes it even better.
The gameplay is super easy. Just the Left and Right arrows for movements which actually matters. It's a game based on you reflexes, concentration and timing. It's easy to play. Since you have only one life it makes the game more challenging. There ain't check points or anything like that. Once you fall you are die and have to restart the whole level.
There are ten levels each have a pretty unique style in something. The levels progressively gets harder from the first to the last level. Also the same as inside each level from the beginning to the end.
The Graphics flickers, glitches and the colors changes just to test your reflexes and concentration. The same thing happens to the images in the background and even to the platforms.
If you get motion sickness then this ain't a game for you tho.
The in game options ain't good you can just change the audio settings and nothing else. Either to change the key bindings or the graphics options you gotta do it before you get into the game.
You get four card drops of eight cards badge. There are twelve achievements.
Four dollars might be somehow high but it's an interesting game to play.

Loved this game from the very start, even with the rough times it had in the beginning.
Glad to see more people coming in as the only negative thing I could ever say about this game was the lack of population, and vast improvments have been implemented since launch.
Although a bit biased, as this is one of my very favorite MMORPGS, here is my personal pros and cons list;
PROS:
DOPE HOUSING - Easily the most enjoyabe and immense housing system I've ever experienced.
HOVERBOARDS - Bruh, you get to hover around and even have grand prix with events.
COMBAT - Super fluid, fun, and engaging. Each class is incredibly unique and you WILL need to depend on your party in PvP and PvE content.
RAIDS - Holy Moley, raids are a blast and very fun. Gotta be on your toes and wipes are pretty common. Super neat.
LORE - I find the stories of the towns, worlds, factions, and NPCs to be super immersive and interesting. Most MMORPGs I hardly ever read quests, NPC dialogs, journals, etc, but WildStar really has some great story telling.
GRAPHICS - Although not loved by all, I love the cartooney-sci fi elements of the artwork, characters, equipment, and environment. Pretty rad to look up in the sky and see planets and crap! The detail of zones always have me exploring around and junk!
INTERACTIVENESS - I absolutely love, love, love the fact that some quests you do completely alter things around you, from changing weather, spawining world/map bosses, buffing entire towns. Very niiiice.
F2P MODEL - Woah dude. Very pleasing model for an MMORPG this day and age. Money does offer benefits and quality of life improvements, but nothing that will impact gameplay as a F2Player; you have the exact amount of access to all content and items, even items in the cash shop as quest rewards, achievements, and just slaying junk in general will reward you with cash shop mulah. Does take some time to acquire vast amounts, but the fact that it's even implemented is pretty dang sweet.
CONS:
PVP - Dont get me wrong, PVP is a blast! But I feel as though not a whole lot of people are interested in it at low levels, or know they can even participate or something! Not really a huge negative, but PVP que times have ranged from 1 minute to 30+ minutes. More of a patience factor but PVP is just so fun it sucks waiting sometimes! Firmly believe that it is also a level bracket result too. Higher level have definately gotten me less wait times.
TRADESKILLS - Literally useless except for vanity items and titles. Which those aspects are actually pretty rewarding, but the crafting and gathering itself isn't. Few tradeskills, namely architect and technologist offer items you can't obtain via PvE or PvP. Runecrafting is also viable to an extent, but overall the tradeskills become less and less useful the closer to endgame you get. This is also personal prefence though; it is nice to craft things for alts, and I do enjoy process, just dont expect to make highend ultimate crud.
PATHS - Although you have the option to choose whichever, I feel some classes are pigeon holed into certain path choices. Back in the day you would be scolded for being a Stalker that wasnt a Scientist for the warp skill, so its maily an 'elitist' issue, but it would be cool if either all paths got their own versions of the same utility skill or offered something else entirely in terms of those skills. Explorer doesnt even offer any utility skills unlike the other 3 for raiding. Not detrimental though; definately not an issue if you just avoid the 1%ers or whatever, just would be cool if they were equal in a sense. Gameplay with them is still fantastic!
So yeah, overall thats all I have to say in the space alloted. I think this game deserves a second chance for sure and I highly reccomend it to anyone. The population was the main issue after a few hiccups at initial launch, but it has grown into a beautiful world of aliens, space zombies, and evil evovled chihuahuas, and I hope more people come to love it and enjoy it as I do.
Much love,
Crystal Beth XOXO

Stellaris is an enjoyable Early Access game that is no longer in Early Access. Yes, I said I recommend this game, but you will want to read on before you fully embrace that recommendation.
I originally picked up Stellaris because a number of my co-workers were talking about the game at work. They mentioned that it was a
. After playing the game for over 80 hours, I can say with certainty: All those things are true.
If I were to compare this game to other games, I'd say it's a cross between Crusader Kings 2 (They both use the same Clauswitz Engine, after all) and Endless Space (Similar galaxy maps and customization). The Random Events (much like those of CK2) make for interesting play with added replay value. You can customize your fleet as you gain technologies and upgrade your existing ships to the new specifications. Each planet you colonize can be micromanaged to have the right resource outputs that your empire needs. And other races will act and react based on the type of civilization you are.
The game has lots of interesting technologies, some of which leading to "dangerous techs" that can bring about a late-game crisis, like the technological singularity. Also there are old races that don't want anything to do with these young whipersnappers... until suddenly they do and they have much higher tech levels than everyone else.
Overall, there is a lot of interesting content in this game.
Another plus to this title is the accessiblity. Unlike Crusader Kings 2, I found Stellaris to have a much more usable tutorial. The game uses a series of in-game quests (with no reward) to help teach you the various features of the game and get your space exploration started. As an added bonus, once you no longer need the tutorials, you can recycle the tutorial-giver for a free 2 minerals (not enough to be unfair, but a nice wrapper to the action).
But the main negative points to this game (and the main reasons I will be putting it down for a while) are two points to why I called it an Early Access game.
Firstly, the game is very buggy. As I mentioned, there are many events and quests that take place in the game. One early quest chain you will get pertains to one of the numerous precursor civilizations of the galaxy. It will have you seek out various artifacts of that precursor civilization. In the two games I have played to completion (one on a small map to better learn the nuances of the game, and one on a normal map), I found myself starved for these artifacts. In my normal game I had found only 1/6 artifacts for 90% of the game. However, I received many times various events that hinted at discovering an artifact to study, but when I confirmed the event, no sub-quest would be added. In fact, sometimes the confirmation tooltip would say that "<blah> was discovered at ." (The location didn't get filled in, so the quest couldn't populate - ugh). Other bugs were often more superficial, such as races not getting a sprite, so my planets would look like they are empty, even though they were fully populated.
I really would like to see the quest bugs get fixed before I come back to this game.
The second issue that plagues this game is the poorly designed late game. The game has only 3 victory conditions, but really they are all the same condition: conquer the galaxy.
The first condition is to personally have colonies on 40% of habitable planets.
The second condition is to be part of a federation and have that federation have colonies on 60% of habitable planets.
The final condition is to be the only independent empire remaining.
So yeah, conquer the galaxy. Even when trying to get the second condition, I got the first.
So aside from there being only one goal, the game suffers because you will hit a point in the game where you cannot progress quickly anymore. The Clauswitz Engine forces you to make demands for your wars, and each demand has a corresponding cost. You can not have more than 100 points in a single war, which means if you want to conquere another empire, you may need to do so 4-5 planets at a time, with a truce period in between.  Eventually you can break through this period if your have a strong enough economy to support having such a powerful fleet that you can jump from war to war taking a bit from all of your enemies one after the other. But it gets a bit dull. At least in Civilization you have science and cultural and diplomatic victories to change things up and let you play differently. Not here. Also, as one more bug, you cannot see your federation's victory progress unless you are the current federation head (which lasts for 10 in game years before passing on to the next ally in the queue).
So in conclusion, I will say: Stellaris is NOT a bad game. I put 80 hours into it, after all. But it definitely has room to improve, and I genuinely believe that it will improve. The war system is interesting. The technologies are interesting. The various races are interesting. But there is definitely some bad execution in there keeping this from being a much better game.

TLDR is the bottom
"A game that can get you hooked for months on end and still not win. 10/10 would donate life again."
That was my old review. Still good fun. However, such a game like this that has compelled my inner fetish of galactic conquest certainly deserves a much better analysis of why Stellaris has been in my personal list of "games to die for".
Stellaris? Isn't it a Civ BE mockup? No and don't ever compare that absurd game to Stellaris or even the astounding Civ series. The only similarity is the sci-fi genre and that's about it. Stellaris at its core is Real Time 4X Grand Strategy. Big draws for me? Real time. As a occasional Civ player and primarily Starcraft player, this seems like the perfect marriage of the two core mechanics of these two great games. Missing a few things of course but it evolves into its own thing entirely.
Stellaris is also as mentioned a 4X game which it sticks to very closely. The great dev patches have continually rooted the game back ever closer to a good balance of the 4X elements, notably in the "Banks" patch where "traditions" were introduced that define your galactic soaring or civilization purging race towards specific specializations like exploration or expansion (or conquest, which is my favourite for obvious reasons :P ). Now that we got the basics out of the way let's go into how the game starts, progresses, ends and of course the ever exciting upcoming content.
As a practical newbie coming into Stellaris, it certainly was a little daunting. Multiple sections of tabs to monitor anything from population to research to governmental style required quite a level of monitoring in order to ensure you don't just outright lose before entering the mid game. The "tutorial" per say isn't a traditional one. You are thrust straight into a full game where it seems like everything you click threatens to wipe out your starting planet but thankfully, your little robot helper just guides you along with appropriate explanations and even kindly pauses time for you so you can hear his annoying Dinklebot like voice on how to build structures or survey planets.
Once you get past the invertible failures of your first few games of Stellaris, you'll start heading deep into the early game and eventual mid game. In the early game, there are lots of things to do. Different styles and different races which you determine the traits of, from type of governance to individual bonuses that your race will have, will influence on how your early game progresses. Will you be diplomatic towards your immediate neighbours and avoid early conflict at the cost of some sections of the galaxy in order to expand peacefully? Or will you aim to subdue them with a mix of hard politics and a sprinkle of force that will cause other neighbouring civilizations to distrust you? The choice is always yours.
Then we enter the mid game where things really start to heat up. The pace of the game is a little slow to my liking in the mid game though things do move fast when you start to make moves on your opponents. At this point anything can happen depending on how you set up your early game. If you're like me when I first entered the mid game where I was the friendliest civilization in the galaxy, you'll encounter a couple of friends but start to get squeezed out of territory to expand to. Then its either you play politics to secure new areas from foes through alliances or if you're strong enough, just outright conquer them. Again, all actions have consequences and will make you think and plan ahead for your final endgame strategy. During the mid game (and sometimes if you're lucky in the late early game) you can encounter strange significant events that may change your predicament. From gleaming ancient powerful technology to horrors of the galaxy, depending on your luck (and certain DLCs) these events will affect your overall strategy. By how much? That is for you to find out.
So we now progress to my favourite and also at the same time, least favourite part of Stellaris, the endgame. When it comes to endgame time, it's basically how to meet the victory conditions of total conquest, domination or a federation victory. All of which require extensive amount of time and planning to execute before being able to achieve victory. As you steam along conducting diplomacy or waging war on a galactic scale, suddenly, strange events occur. Welcome to the endgame crisis. One of my favourite features of Stellaris. You see the endgame crisis is basically like a spanner in the works to your on going plan for galactic conquest. Depending on your luck and what technologies you have researched, the endgame crisis can be different. But all do the same thing, make the galaxy much more dangerous. I can go on about the different ways to take advantage of the end game crisis to weaken tough opponents or the different methods to defeat them, but that wouldn't be fun for you :). Instead, all I will say is that always turn it on and prepare to either cry or have lots of challenging fun. The end game crisis is a fantastic feature and as of writing, there's some rework coming to the crisis, so for all you veteran Stellaris players, get your fleets ready.
Now I did mention the endgame was also my least favourite part. Why? In super late endgame when you've solved the endgame crisis you tend to run into large enemy empires that are equal in power to you if not just slightly less powerful. Clearing them and eventually winning takes practically longer than the early and mid game combined. Not to mention much less exciting now that all the events, research and minor diplomatic squabbling is done. I've not heard of this issue in multiplayer as endgame tends to be exciting when the most powerful civilizations are controlled by your friends and everyone wants victory. That results in a mighty fun multi-way conflict. However since I am mainly playing against AIs this is my own issue with the super late endgame. The game just drags on and on with no end in sight as conflict can only be waged every 10 years or so and often you are not able to completely wipe out an endgame civilization in a single conflict.
Now that you've somehow survived the wall of text, do note that there are so much more features and depth to Stellaris that this review simply cannot encapsulate. These are the ones that stick out to me and my general feel towards the game and with that time for a quick summary.
SUMMARY
Good:
-Great depth
-Real time 4X Grand Strategy
-Interesting events, subplots and stories
-Complex and fulfilling game progression throughout all stages of play
-Great replayability
-Large, game changing patches, updates and DLCs constantly being put out
-Decent modding community
-Challenging and engaging AI for Solo/Co-op play
-Brand new dynamic when in PvP
-Very engaged community

Developed by Deck13 Interactive (Released on Nov 2013)
Blood Knights is good example of hack-n-slash RPG with interesting settings, but somehow fail to deliver full potential RPG experience to the audience. Here's the breakdown

---------------------------------------------------------
Presentation:
• Interesting fictional storyline set in world at war between humans and vampires with solid background.
• Consistent story pacing, but decent and linear main storyline.
• Good variety of world and detailed environment, but filled with uninspired and repetitive designs to support gameplay.
• Some cliché and cheesy dialogues, few character development, lack of strong side characters which are forgotten.
• Lip sync issue and awkward eye contract for some characters in cutscene.
• Great soundtracks and ambient musics.

---------------------------------------------------------
Gameplay:
• Mindless and arcadey hack-n-slash combat, it’s fun and well entertained, but lack of depth and complexity. Most boss fight you can keep firing crossbow and it’s done.
• Fluid swap character mechanics (Melee / Range). Each character has different set of skills and playstyles.
• Character progression by defeating enemies. Skill-point upgrade system.
• You upgrade attributes and stats from collecting hidden seals and loots. The more you progress, the better gears you find in chest.
• Gear system is very engaging and well in-game presentation. The problem is best weapons from trader are the same where you can easily obtain from end-game. Eliminate the point of progression reward.
• The level design doesn’t emphasize the variety of gameplay in both combat and puzzle due to very linear and tight area. In term of RPG, it lacks of level exploration and side quest.
• Dialogue option has no real impact to main story beside change of some character attitudes and achievement.
• The game has fixed camera angle and rotation. It could be bit wonky in platforming section because the game doesn’t give you clear indicator where character facing to. Fortunately, checkpoint can be saved over as many as you want.

---------------------------------------------------------
Performance:
• Responsive keyboard controls
• Minor graphical and clipping issue on some levels
• Solid and stable performance, experience no single crash and frame-rate issue

---------------------------------------------------------
I personally love the story and mythology of vampire of Blood Knights. The game has potential to become great action RPG, but it lacks of polished features to support RPG elements. It’s very short experience (3-4 hours), but still fun game if you don’t take any mechanics seriously.

I like the game.
(Editing this after 131 puzzles: There's no satisfaction here just because there's no human-viable heuristic for solving these puzzles. I've resorted to using the guide to get one side of the equation and then finding the other side, which is actually reasonable to do)
I don't like having the game not save an hour of progress.
It's worth noting that I haven't lost progress again, but just knowing that it's possible for the game to decide you have to do a large chunk again... it's more than mildly annoying.
Three Digits is a game where there are 14 numbers from 1-999. All you have to do is find two groups of numbers with the same sum. It's fun for me because I like the math, but the scale is a little large: Two Digits was easy enough by getting differences and making the ones place match, while Three Digits feels a lot like a guessing game at time. 11 or 12 numbers would have been a little better.
The game doesn't save your audio setting. The background piano gets very grating very quickly and I've muted it every time I've started the game- and had to keep doing so! The UI is simple. Too simple- there's no back button, instead the game has to TELL YOU to use the Escape key to go back- on an otherwise entirely mouse controlled game! Oh and should you tab out for whatever reason, say to check IMs after finishing a level... you'll find the game does not advance while tabbed out. Meaning every single slow level completion/load animation can't be multitasked. This is a little nitpicky, but it's a completely needless addition and I'm already in an admittedly petty mood from this game.
Ultmately, there are way too many flaws with this game. Go play Two Digits instead- it doesn't avert all of these flaws, but it averts enough to be an enjoyable experience.

In my review of "Two Digits" I said you should go for Three Digits instead if you want a challenging math game. I want to amend that: if you want a challenging math game, get Hexcells or something similar. Don't get Three Digits.
It suffers from the same lack of game advancement as Two Digits, in that there is no innovation between level packs, and they become very same-y very quickly. With fourteen numbers rather than nine you'd think that would make it more difficult, and you'd be right. But it's less a puzzle game and more a really bad point-and-click adventure. I solved most of the puzzles I've completed through pure luck, randomly clicking until I make a connection and figure out what number I need to make.
The music isn't the worst thing in the world, but it isn't fantastic either, some plinky-plonky piano which is cheerful if irritating when you notice it repeating. You can turn it off with a tick-box in the options, but it's worth noting that the volume slider beneath that box doesn't work - the volume simply reverts back to full when you exit.
It's not absolutely awful - there is something to be said for the challenge of it when you're playing it - but the sheer number of false starts and leaps of logic it takes to actually finish these puzzles make it difficult in the wrong way. There's less math knowledge at work here and more random clicking.
I'm gonna finish it, because I'm nothing if not bloody-minded about gaming. But I don't think it's great as a game.

First and foremost, I will say that although I personally find this game's simple visual style and interface quite appealing (although it could use some sort of noclip mechanic to help with getting stuck in terrain), it occasionally makes me nauseous while playing for more than a few minutes.
As a fan of brutally difficult roguelike and platformer games, as well as difficult games in general (I love NetHack, Spelunky, The Binding of Isaac, the original arcade version of Ghosts n' Goblins, etc.), I bought this game due to the "roguelike" tag.
Every item is Delver is identified before you even pick it up, save for potions (identified after drinking the first of that color).  And there is only one negative potion effect out of six or so, a weak poison that is easily counteracted by eating any piece of food.
Delver has only 7 dungeon floors to its name, which are procedurally generated, true, save for the last, which is actually a fixed map.  Delver also lacks shopkeepers on floors, instead, there are only two NPCs, and they are on the surface above the dungeon.  So your character ends up carrying a bunch of gold with no way to spend it except by returning to the start or dying.
When dying in Delver, you lose everything except your gold.  This gives you a chance to buy an item when you start a new game to give you an edge, but the high prices ensure that you cannot buy a good item on every run.
The enemies in the first levels of Delver are relative pushovers (as well as possessing primitive AI that can only charge at the player in a straight line, think Minecraft Beta hostile mobs).  Most enemies in the game supposedly have no more than 4 HP, but player attacks seem to deal a lot less damage than they should according to weapon descriptions.  Charging attacks makes them hit every time, which makes fast charging weapons like daggers and shortswords much more effective than larger weapons like hammers or swords.

The enemies get more advanced as you proceed, starting with bandits and slimes and advancing to spiders and floating squid things, orcs and worms, and eventually skeletons and floating skulls.  Zombies and worms can cause the poison effect, which damages health.  Though the enemies are nice so far, there are issues with surround sound in this game.  Bandits commonly yell threats as they see you, but the sound seems to come out of the opposite speaker of their direction, e.g. I hear "You're dead!" out of my rear right speaker, when the bandit is actually approaching from my left.  Given how much I've come to rely on surround sound in this type of game, this can be frustrating.
**** the mages on the first two levels.  I have died to those guys way too many times.  Enemies cannot use bows, only magic and melee.  Melee enemies are easy to deal with, but magic can get annoying.  More annoying is the death screen, which often prevents you from knowing what exactly killed you.  This means you don't necessarily know what you did wrong to get you killed.
The level up system has six stats.  Each time you level up, the game randomly chooses three for you to pick from to increase.  Health, attack, defense, speed, agility (attack speed), and magic (increases wand charges and wand damage).  I find that health is always a priority.  I try to get my health to 16, then start putting points into speed and agility.  Attack, defense, and magic are usually made obsolete due to finding better equipment.  Note that to my knowledge, the other stats also increase by a small amount on level up, but the one you pick goes up by much more than the others.
Though this game is simple, it is not necessarily easy every run.  I can see this game getting much better once all the glitches with getting stuck in terrain are fixed.  I find that this game is actually quite fun if you are into dungeon crawling and exploration, and the surplus of loot is due to the ending.  At the end, you need to escape the dungeon with the treasure while being pursued by endless skeletons and skeleton mages, currently the hardest respawning enemies in the game, in addition to the extremely fast and mobile floating skulls.  The many supplies you find on your way down are basically preparation for this difficult rush section.  Upgrading speed comes in extreme handy for this action packed portion of the game.  The game has limited enemies and environments, but it is in beta and the soundtrack is solid as-is, and the enemies have enough diversity to vary with the current levels.
Most of the enemies with AI that only charges straight at you are gone after the first two levels.
Features I would like to see added:
Noclip or some other system to deal with getting stuck in terrain without having to delete your save
Better bandit AI
Spiders should deal poison instead of worms (It's gaming tradition!)
Many more floors
More level variety
More enemies
Enemies that use bows
More gold, shopkeepers and NPCs on floors
Armor with secondary effects
Something that fits in the glove slot, which is currently unused
More bosses and maybe even minibosses
More types of traps
More hidden doors and passages
Easter eggs
Local or online co-op could be really awesome if done right (of course, the difficulty level would have to drastically increase as well)

Nier Automata. So let's leave the hype out of the way.
I have NOT played the original Nier. I plan to in the future, but from what I've read it's not crucial for understanding this game's story.
This game looks beautiful, sounds beautiful and has incredible narrative. If I had to compare it with something, it's Dark Souls meets Final Fantasy. You decide your path (mostly). You can do things whenever you feel like it (unless you need to advance the main story first), but for every step there's tens of sidequests out there and lots of different areas to discover.
It really is worth the money, whether it be just for the music, the incredibly well-crafted scenes (the retaken city, the forest, the vast desert and the industrial district). There's so many things to choose from, you WILL find something to like about this game. And if nothing tickles your fancy, I'm sure at least the panty shots do.
To sum up: This game feels like it fused two of my favorite series (Dark Souls and Final Fantasy) together to create an interesting experience. It can be played on whatever difficulty you feel like (Baby mode, regular, hard [it's actually pretty hard] and hell). There's something in there for everyone.
9/10. Definitely recommended.
----
Now that we got introductions out of the way, let's go a bit more in-depth.
Here's the story of Nier: Automata in a few words:
Earth has been attacked by Aliens thousands of years ago and humanity had to flee to the moon. They dispatched Androids to fight in their stead and retake the surface for the humans to come back down.
There are multiple story paths to this game, so even if you complete it once, a whole new story is waiting for you to be discovered. As there are a few main characters, Nier: Automata has taken it upon itself to let the player take control from multiple angles and have multiple characters at their disposal. Some people might not like the "finish one path, then you'll get another" approach taken here, but me personally, I like to finish a story, before I start a new one.
Well then. That's it for now. I'm going to keep updating this review as I progress through the game.
Update:
So I've finished the first run of the game. There's still many things to do, many sidequests to complete. There are characters I do not fully know or understand yet and want to know better.
This game has taken my hand in a loving manner, saying "Come with me. I want to you show something."
It has been a journey. I loved the characters, the development, the gameplay. (Though I may have cheesed on a few parts (examples being destroying a huge machine from the ground when you're supposed to fight while flying, the fact that I healed more than the enemy did damage to me and the like)
I want you guys to look at this game not from a "oh, it's another one of these take-me-by-the-hand"-type of games. There is a lot of options out there. A lot of things to see.
This game makes you not watch as a bystander. It makes you walk with the protagonists, helping with their decisions. This might not let you move as freely as Dark Souls, but is every bit as lovely as the Final Fantasy X I've come to adore, even love.
I stand by my decision to give this game at least a 9 out of 10.
And to be honest, I can't wait to see what the next story is going to be like. Well.. gotta go. There's still so much more for me to explore, I have to keep playing.
See you guys around.

I will preface this review with the fact that I didn't get too far into this game and have not really seen all the content.  That said, once you've seen a number of WOW clones, you kind of have a handle as to how they will eventually play out.  When you do a clone of another game, I think you have to follow two simple rules to be successful - 1) do everything that game did as good or even better, 2) Add something to the game that was not in the one you are cloning.  For me, Wildstar succeeds (partially) at the second point but fails are the first one.
The map, quest and hud system is just really cluttered.  I have played a bunch of these games before and never have I been so lost as to find precisely what I am supposed to be doing, where on the map I am supposed to be going, and who the hell I  am supposed to be talking to when I get there.  The icons above NPC heads are not very clear or easy to see within the limited field of view.  The maps do have numbers associated with quests but then these numbers are not used in the quest list so there is no reference point for which one they bleong to.  The quest menu has just a ton of text it doesn't need and it always takes me like 30 seconds to find the actual quest tasks (which adds up to a lot of down time as the game trudges along).
The quest structure is nothing unique - go collect these and kill some of these.  Grind grind grind.  This really is going to be the death knell of this genre unless they figure something else out.  I was bored after the first few hours of play.
Character customization is rigid.  The character builder at the beginning is pretty cool but I feel like they bottleneck you into decisions too soon without knowing the consequences.  You have to pick a character class and a profession at the outset with no gameplay experience and then, as far as I could tell, you were stuck with it.  No backsies.  So, you then end up playing a character for hours and hours only to find out that one of the aspects you chose at the very beginning doesn't fit your play style and then you get to start all over again.  I also feel like the "this character class only uses this weapon type for all time" thing has to end.  It's stale.
Leveling is boring.  When you level in other games, you are presented with a number of choices to customize your character and mold it into a build you like.  With this game, everything just sorta happens automatically and you get no sense that it really affects your gameplay.  All your stats go up automatically, you get skills automatically, they even get added to your task bar in a specific sequence automatically (that is customizable though).  Levels come and go and you hardly notice anything happens.  There is no sense of accomplishing anything.
The combat is actually kind of interesting but may be annoying if you don't have an MMO mouse.  There is no auto targeting which is good.  You atctually have to dynamically move and aim at your target which makes for a more visceral experience than WOW, in my opinion.  However, what this means is that in something like PVP you need to be constantly using your directional keys to line up your target and the number keys often need to be held down to channel a spell.  Unless you have 10 fingers on your left hand, that can get frustrating pretty quick.  The only remedy to this I could think of is having one of those macro MMO mouse that have like 15 buttons on your thumb pad.
In the end, the only thing that would keep me playing a game like this is storyline and it just isn't interesting enough to keep me going.  I just have no investment in my character or the outcome of the story.  So, this just fades into a grind simulator.  I would tentatively recommend this for those tens of people who have never played an MMO because it's free.  Other than that, this was a pass for me.

NOTE: I played for some time after it went F2P before it hit Steam, so my hours played aren't accurate.
A vibrant game with a rather fair F2P model and the ability to change how you interact with the game (you can play it like a typical "click #'s till it dies" OR turn it into more action-MMO style where you use the mouse more).
One thing to note here is that this game takes a sharp left turn in terms of player interaction with the world compared to other MMOs. Where as in something like TERA or GW2, all players, regardless of class, can harvest the same materials and do the same non-storyline quests, in WildStar players have both a Class and a Job (seperate from crafting jobs). And that Job determins what non-story actions you can perform in the world. Want to discover new vistas? Go for Explorer. Want to discover new lifeforms? Go Scientist. Taken into account with the racial/faction starting areas and class based quests there's a lot of individuality here for those that look for it.
On the subject of classes, it should be noted that not ever race can be every class, Humans (either faction) being the only exception. Aurin can only be Espers, Stalkers or Spellslingers. Mordesh can't be Espers. And so on and so on. The problem with this is that there's no real explination as to why this is and it makes little sense in some cases, such as the Aurin since Stalker is a tank class and yet they can't be Warrior or Engineer, the other tank classes. If the point was to make players play more than one race, it failed, since it's easier to just play Human/Cassian since they can pick any class.
One other thing to note about classes; the game only lists the classes as being either Tank or Healer. Why? Because any class is able to go DPS if they choose to, even the Medic. My first character is an Esper that I set to DPS since I usualy run solo, but I can swap to healing/support if needed through the use of Skill/Amp Sets (more on that later). This means that no one class is really better than another and you can adapt them all to fit your unique style of play, so long as you take the time to get to know what each skill does and how to use it effectivly.
The game further divides the players by splitting them into one of two Factions, Exiles or Dominion, which, aside from Humans (Cassians for the Dominion), have their own unique races. Even their own furry bait races; Aurin for Exiles, Chua for Dominion. Each Faction has it's own backstory, it's own quest lines and it's own capitol city, as well as smaller cities in each zone. In some zones you'll ruin into the other faction, in others your won't.
Crafting is present and kind of deep (if a little annoying at times). You mine/harvest resources associated with your gathering profession (there are several), create items/gear tied to whichever crafting profession you picked (again, there are several) and you can cook (everyone can cook). This makes crafting a bit more unique to each character you create as you can pick the crafting/harvesting professions that let you make some of your own gear. The problem I notice it that you can't make more than one of something at a time even if you have the materials for it because all crafting uses this funky system that's individual to each branch. Some will like it, personally I find it mildy annoying, but to each their own.
This game also features player housing, which is a great feature to have. Each player is given a plot of land (in it's own instanced zone) that they can customize to their liking by adding decorative items and even mini plots to gain crafting materils like plants and ore. There are even plots that allow mini dungeons or special challenges that you, and visitors (yes, you can visit other peoples home plots) to try and complete. However, a lot of this is better kept till you reach end game, as it can be a massive money sink to buy the decor and plot items, known as FABkits (unless you went with the crafting job that allows you to make FABkits), as your earned gold will be better spent on things like gear. Once your at end game with decent gear though, you can go hog wild on your home, and you should as it's fun.
When it comes to skills, this game also takes a bit of a turn from something like WoW where you often end up needing several hotbars. You're given several Skill Sets with a limited number of slots that you can customize to your liking, and you can further power th4ese up with ability points that add to the selectred skills power as well as AMPs that give other power upds like +3% to your shields or bonuises to your PvP defenses (AMPs can also be used to unlock some skills, but most you unlock just by leveling).
Gear functions largely the same as in other MMOs. Each piece as level restrictions, things like attack ratings and other stat boosts. One notable advantage in WildStar is the Costume system. For a small fee (using in-game currency, naturally) you can unlock the visual apperance of any item and store it in your accounts holo-wardrobe. You can then set up to 4 (by default) costumes that consist of whatever visuals you like that will override the appearance of any new items you equip as you progress.
The game is also VERY friendly to modding, allowing you to even reload the UI *in-game* should a problem arise. The only thing to note here is that mods rely on the game's API version, and some, if the API is too far removed from the mods version, won't work as intended. Most can be force loaded without any problem, but some will cause issues, so be sure to check the API version before installing them (all mods can use Curse Client, so you'll be better off installing that to manage them, as it also tracks updates for installed mods as well).
One other thing to note, there is only one server. When I started there were two (then 4 due to initial F2P spike in players), one for PvE and one for PvP. The current server is tagged PvE, but open world PvP is still present, it's just something you toggle instead of server specific. Just right click on your character's picture and you can toggle PvP on/off as you please. But bear in mind that you won't encounter any world PvP for quite a while, as the first few areas are all speficic to your chosen Faction and you don't run into the other Faction until after you reach your Faction Capital, which takes a while. So even if you do want to partake in open PvP, the game gives you some time to get used to the controls and to build up your skills before it dumps you into PvP.
In all this is a fun game that's worth a look, be you a fan of games like WoW and RiFT or GW2 and TERA. The art style is lively, the world is well crafted, the characters are rarely dull and the game just playes well. Just be aware that this game does have a slightly low overall population, and given the age of the game, size of the game world and division by faction, you can often run through entire areas for hours and never see another player. But hub cities like the capitals will always be packed and with the age of the game, end game areas are as well as most veteran players have been there since before it went F2P off Steam.
One final remark and a tip for any new players. Be sure to enable two-factor authintication on your account ASAP. Doing so not only adds a layer of security to your account but it also gets you a free mount that you use on ever charcter you might create. This is helpfull early on as you won't be able to buy a mount (only rent them) until you reach your factions capital city, and the cheapest on is 10 gold. So getting a free one right from the start makes getting around much easier.

2) Added info on factions, classes and races, as well as some info on crafting. Also added info about games population.
3) Spelling errors.
4) Added info on housing as well as a tip to get new players a free in-game mount.

Quite honestly, I do love the game. Like probably many others, I bought the game out of impulse because I liked what I saw on the trailer. I understand that it's early access and, while I do keep that in mind, I gotta say I expected more. Now, I'm not saying I don't like the game, because I do, but I think there should have been a few more fixes before the early access.
Some issues I find with the game are things like the hitbox being wonky... at times, your weapon will go through an enemy and not lay a single scratch while you yourself are mowed down in 2 hits. another thing that bothered me, while on the subject of weapons, is the major inbalance there is. Overall, the tank sword will kill anyone in 2 hits.
Moving on to the spells, they do really allow for different 'classes'. There's the spellsword, throwing fireballs while slicing with the flame sword while the spell is on cooldown, yet keeping a fire blast tucked away as a last resort. There's the healing spell, which can be used to heal not only yourself, but friends as well. As for those who like to be sneaky,there's invicibility and teleport, which makes for a very stealthy class. the ice spell didn't really stand out because I never noticed anything, even when i hit someone directly with it.
As for secondary weapons, we have the mine, which explodes on contact. there's the bear trap, which keeps the enemy locked in place while dealing DOT (Damage Over Time). For projectiles, you have the bow, which is a bit hard to use but when mastered, is quite the killer. And then you have the throwing axe.
For character customization, there seems to be a few glitches where nothing changes color, and then there's also the fog in the customization screen that makes it a bit hard to customize. the selection isn't very broad but seeing as you can combine and customize various pieces of set (each glove and shoulderpad can be changed, for example), it does over a small sense of variety.
the gameplay, though a bit laggy and with its errors as is every online game, was quite enjoyable. Free for all matches offer quite the rush, since anything goes. See a group of enemies fighting? throw in a fireball! The blast is sure to get you a kill stolen or, like in my case, kill all the fighters and give you a nice boost in score. Team matches are exciting as well, especially when you all coordinate without even saying a word, as often happens in games as if the teammates were somehow connected.
Overall, I give the game an 8/10. Needs a lot of work but it's damn good for early access.

This game is a blessing
I've only played a short time and completed the first mission, and i can already say with great certainty this game and it's developers are something truly special.
First of all, don't let the top-down perspective try to take you out of the experience, as some people would argue the immersion of a game is better exemplified by an alternative perspective. This game is filled to the brim with atmosphere and charm. Every room of every level has clearly had hours of thought and gcare put into each one. Textures don't ever feel repetitive or overused, and the destructible environment lends itself beautifully to showing you exactly where you are and what's around you.
The combat is just plain lovable, very reminiscent of arcade shooters or even certain internet flash games (the kind you and your friends at school would play in the computer lab in 7th grade). It's responsive, quick, challenging but never unfair, and the lack of a reload mechanic keeps the flow of the game consistent and enjoyable.
There are plenty of secrets to uncover, with the added promise of an unlockable difficulty, and there are "golden gun" parts you can find on the levels of the campaign, wwhich I can't wait to get back to gathering. In a game like this, I can see myself relishing the challenge of an "insane" difficulty mode, and I greatly anticipate playing survival mode, especially if i can get some of my friends in on this.
The story is an interesting approach to the zombie genre. normally, a noire-type narrative in most games would be written as a parody, or a kind of satire. This story seems to take itself fairly seriously, with the main character being the typical black-and-white detective character, but in his case, he's not led to any of this by 'the job', this simply follows his experience being swept up into the apocalypse, reacting in his own way just like everyone else. During missions, there's even story-type decisions you can make that can affect how you play the rest of the level.
Finally, I have to touch on the developers and the game listing itself. Even right upon booting the game up, it's clear that Dreamworlds really, actually cares about it's customers. First, this game is priced the same as a bottle of root beer, and the game is arguably at leat 5 times sweeter. Knowing what I do now, I would easily have bought this for at least 5 bucks. Second, there is a direct contact feedback option ruight on the main menu of the game, encouraging you to tell them what you like about it, any suggestions, or even any criticisms. Not only that, but for nothing at all, a window popped up before the game booted offering to send me an email key to ANOTHER game, completely for free!
Honestly, before I found this game, the future of gaming seemed a bit bleak to me. It's so hard to find a developer willing to push themselves to not only make a quality product, but accept input,criticism, and treat it's customers fairly at the same time. This is the first game I've seen that truly showed how much pride a developer should take in making their game.
This is an honest to god 10/10, and i look forward to exploring the rest of what the dreamworlds team has to offer

Very crashy. Devs have treated the game like it's still in early access since it was released, completely reworking one or more major systems with every single patch and not fixing any of the glaring issues that have been in the game from the beginning, such as sectors being garbage, trade not existing, diplomacy being less than halfassed... Very obnoxious ratio of downtime to actually doing anything interesting- I spend the majority of my playtime waiting. The randomized tech tree doesn't really improve the 4x formula. Stellaris takes a host of good sci-fi ideas-internal politics in a space empire, psionics, robots,  notable and important figures in your empire who have their own unique traits, fallen empires of aliens who have been around for thousands of years longer than you, terraforming, precursor species, abducting primitive aliens for research, customized starships...and then fails to implement any of it in a way that's fun. Just about the only place where Stellaris really shines is exploration, in which your science ships generate anomalies that can be investigated in order to create little storylets, kind of like episodes of star trek.  Diplomacy is pretty much nonfunctional-none of the computer empires are interested in any sort of treaty with me, including the ones that share my ethos. They happily mke grand alliances among themselves that prevent the player from any kind of military expansion, though, and unless you pay extra for the latest DLC there's nothing else to do. Even when you're at war there isn't much to do-combat is determined entirely by the size of the fleets involved, and because combat resolves so quickly even a moderately outnumbered fleet will be quickly and lopsidedly destroyed. Because of this, your entire fleet will exist in one giant doomstack at all times.
I might be able to put up with all of stellaris' flaws, however, if I could finish a game without it crashing. Unfortunately, I cannot.

Accompanied by 80s cheesy yet catchy synth-pop tracks while playing the role of a “simplest office clerk” in a totalitarian setting. Indeed, this game is literally a visualization of Radiohead’s Fitter Happier. Since Fitter Happier is one of my all-time favorites, I fall in love easily with this game.
However - there is always this however - my honeymoon with it ends in less than one hour, ever since the moment all the fascinating voice-over, visual and soundtracks faded away in my senses, leaving nothing but the never-ending path in my tunnel vision; the moment a somehow expressive and sentimental experience took a sudden turn into a tediously hard quicktime reaction and muscle memory grind, where the difficulty does not come from well-designed challenges, but from irresponsibly clumsy mechanics.
I will explain the reason of choosing the rather uncommon word “irresponsibly” (in terms of video game review) in following sections. But first to clarify, I beat the game in 4 hours, which is far below the average completion time according to online statistics, to say the least, it proves that difficulty is not the major reason that prevented me from enjoying the game.
People tend to use the term “with rough edges” when reviewing indie titles. Like I mentioned in my other reviews, I do also prefer flawed but unique games rather than perfectly polished indistinguishable titles, for flaw and weakness is what really defines one’s personality. However, the roughness of NO THING has way exceeded my tolerance threshold for rough edges, it’s more like a sea urchin whose only smooth spot is hidden deeply underneath.
The level design starts reasonable, but gets increasingly random and messy as you progress. First we got this level 7, where you need to run through an extra-long sequence of extra-narrow platforms which are only half the width of normal ones with lighting speed (speed increases every time you take a turn), for 5 laps! More than half of my playtime was spent on this single level. After this cursed level is conquered, we got two of the easiest levels as level 8 and level 9, and the chaos eventually reaches its climax at level 10. It’s as if the developers finally ran out of all patience, and decided to just drop a bunch of platforms randomly into the space, then only made a little effort to get them connected somehow and call it a level. At the second half of level 10, none of the platforms are properly positioned and aligned (in any of the three axis!), which leads to unforeseeable gap or altitude offset everywhere. Since you don’t have the liberty to jump in this game, it means you’ll easily get stuck or launched sky-high at any time. BUT WHY???
It results from another disastrous design choice. The developers used Unity’s default physics engine based first person controller in full-scale without any optimization to handle such simple movement mechanism of this game. Player-wise, it means the “simplest office clerk” you control is actually a “capsule shaped rigidbody” which indeed has feet of a hemisphere as the name suggests, thus, thanks to the physics engine, any protrusion on the ground will easily launch you sky-high. Since there are barely any platforms that are seamlessly aligned like aforementioned, you’ll get high all the time, so dope. Now move on to the most ridiculous one, if you fall into one of the larger gaps between platforms, guess what will happen? Falling down? No! you’ll stuck there once the vertical part of your capsule body touches any vertical side of the platform, because of the existence of friction in the physics engine which the developers forgot (or never realized) to disable.
The point of listing all those defects in details, is to shed a light on the fact that none of these problems is that technically difficult for a responsible developer to fix. Therefore, all the confusion and misery caused thereby is per se a result of irresponsibility rather than inability. That, is an unforgivable sin of indie developer.
Now, let's step back and take a look at the bigger picture, NO THING is just another victim of the haunting dilemma that got tons other indie games as well:
The symptoms including but not limited to:
The list can still go on a few more, but the rest is not within the scope of this review, so I’ll just stop it here to conclude this review by answering the question you might be having the whole time: Why give it an upvote since all I do is keep talking about its negatives? The answer lies in the one-of-a-kind memorable experience NO THING provides, especially if you’re into cult classic sort of works, you might even find it enjoyable, but for how long? That’s totally depends on your patience and tolerance level. NO THING is irrefutably a bad game in all standards, however, the irreplaceable temperament it has, in my book, means much more than most good yet replaceable titles out there these days.

A fairly short FPS roguelike with a Minecraft feel to the graphics and the terrain, as well as the inventory, minus weapon/armor durability, your equipment is indestructible. Except for magic wands/scrolls, which have limited charges but can be very useful.
There are also several different colored potions which effects are randomized each playthrough, most of them are helpful, while one of them is poison, so be careful.
Then you got your EXP system and leveling up system where you can choose between several stats, I just usually get health every level when I can, you're gonna need it.
The general goal is to go down several floors of dungeons, always having the same tileset/theme but a different layout each playthrough, and get the treasure, and then traverse all the way back to camp from where you started as angry monsters chase you after stealing their treasure.
A decent enough roguelike, it was fun and lasted about 2 hours so far, going through the game twice. Could use more variety and maybe achievements in the future.
